Bhairava said: The Śrīyāmala, the great Tantra, which is independent, and the Viṣṇuyāmala have issued forth from the lotus-face of the supreme Śrī Parameśānī. (1.1)
The Śaktiyāmala has been declared for the purpose of praising Brahmā;
and the entire Brahmayāmala, which is an auxiliary limb (vedāṅga) of the Vedas, has also been told, O beloved. 1–2.
Now, O Goddess, by the power of my good fortune, speak the *Uttarakāṇḍa* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala* from your glorious lotus-face.
Whatever independent [teachings] have been bestowed upon the surface of the earth, proclaim the Mahātantra; do not find satisfaction in other tantras. (1-4)
Thereafter, that which is to be declared in all the Vedāntas and Vedas shall be told;
then, for your circle of devotees, spiritual perfection will surely come to pass.
O auspicious one! O Tripurasundarī, if you have compassion for me, tell me, O lotus-eyed one, the words of Mahābhairava.
Having heard this, Mahākālī spoke and addressed Bhairava.
Bhairavī said:
"O Śambhu, O destroyer of the pride of the great-souled ones, O you who are free from desire, O you who are both beyond and within the Kula!"
O you whose head and eyes are like the lunar disc, who partakes of the hālāhala poison;
O you of peerless and formidable form, blazing with a crest of red color! 1-8.
O Lord, master of the great sages, salutations, salutations to you all!
O Ānandabhairava, destroyer of the life-force of all, listen! 1-9.
First is the six-fold practice (sādhana) of Bālā and Bhairavī;
thereafter follows the most wonderful practice of Kumārī and Lalitā.
The sādhanā of Kurukullā and Vipracittā, the sādhanā of Śakti, and then the sādhanā of Yoginī, Khecarī, and Yakṣakanyā. || 1-11 ||
The practice of the Unmattabhairavī-vidyā, the Kālī-vidyā, and others;
the practice of the five mudrās, and the practice of the five arrows and so forth. (1–12)
And the practice of Pratyāṅgirā, which brings direct realization in the Kali age;
as well as the practices of Haritālī, Svarṇavidyā, Dhūmravidyā, and others.
Then follows the various means for attaining the celestial Gaṅgā and maidens;
after that, the means for attaining the creeper-like eyebrows, and immediately thereafter, the means for attaining the perfected ones (siddhas).
Then follows the practice for the Ulkā-vidyā and the practices for the Five Tārās and others;
thereafter, the practices for Aparājitā, Puruhūtā, and Cāmuṇḍā.
The sādhana of Kālikā, the sādhana of Kaula, the sādhana of Ghana; then the sādhana of Caccikā, and after that the sādhana of Ghargharā. || 1-16 ||

The *Vimalāsādhana*, the *Raudrītripurāsādhana*, then the *Sampatpradāsaptakūṭāsādhana* and the *Ceṭīsādhana*; the *Śaktikūṭa* and the *sādhana*s of the six *kūṭas* beginning with that, and the nine *kūṭas* and so forth. || 1–17 ||
Then follows the sādhana of Kanakābha, Kāñcanābha, and Vahnibhāsa;
then the sādhanas of Vajrakūṭa, Pañcakūṭa, and Asakala. || 1-18 ||
After that, the *sādhana* of Tāriṇī is taught, followed by the *sādhana* of Ṣoḍaśī;
then the most charming *sādhanas* of Chinnamastā, Ugrā, Pracaṇḍā, and the others. (1–19)
The sādhana of Ulkāmukhī and Raktamukhī, the heroic sādhana (vīrasādhana),
as well as the corpse-sādhana (śavasādhana) which fashions various kinds of faces.
Having performed the *sādhana* of the Goddess and then the *sādhana* of Ahi,
[he studied] the chapter on the science of constellations (*nakṣatra-vidyā*) as well as the chapter on Kālī.
The sādhana of the goddess Śmaśānakālikā, the sādhana of Bhūta, the sādhana of Ratikrīḍā, and likewise the sādhana of Sundarī. || 1-22 ||
The *Mahāmālāsādhana*, the *Mahāmāyā* and other *sādhanas*, the *Bhadrakālīsādhana*, and also the *Nīlasādhana*. (1–23)
The sādhanā of Bhuvaneśī and the sādhanā of Durgā,
as well as the most wonderful sādhanās of Vārāhī, Gāruḍī, and Cāndrī.
Next is the sādhana of Brahmāṇī, followed by the supreme sādhana of Haṃsī;
likewise, the sādhana of Māheśvarī and the sādhana of Kaumārī.
The practice of Vaiṣṇavī, the practice of Dhātrī which brings about the destruction of wealth, the excellent practice of Nārasiṃhī whose face is filled with offerings of five clouds. || 1-26 ||
The sādhana of Kālindī, Rukmiṇī, Vidyā, Rādhā, and others; the sādhana of Gopīśvarī, Padmanetrā, Padmamālā, and others. || 1-27 ||
Then follows the *sādhana* of the Garland of Heads (*muṇḍamālā*) and the *sādhana* of Bhṛṅgārī;
[and] the *sādhana* of the *vidyā* that attracts all, of Kapālinī, and so forth. (1–28)
The sādhana of Guhyakālī and the sādhana of Bagalāmukhī;
the sādhana of Mahābālā and the sādhanas of Kalāvatī and others. || 1-29 ||
The great sādhanas of Kulajā, Kalikā, Kakṣā, and Kukkuṭī;
the sādhanas of Ciñcādevī and the secret sādhanas of Śāṅkarī. || 1-30 ||
Then follows the sādhana of the Vidyā Kākinī, whose face is a full-blown lotus;
then the Kubjikā-sādhana, and the sādhanas of Nityā, Sarasvatī, and others. (1–31)
The sādhana of Bhūrlekhāśaśimukuṭā, Ugrakālī, and others;
the sādhana of Maṇidvīpeśvarī and Dhātrī; and the sādhana of the Yakṣas. (1.32)
The practice for bestowing the splendor of the *ketakī* and lotus, the practice of the *Abhedya* and others, the great vidyā of Vāgīśvarī, and the practice of Annapūrṇā and others. (1–33)
Likewise, there is the sādhana of Anvārī, who consists of the red Vajradaṇḍā;
and thereafter, the sādhanas of Ātaṅgī, beginning with Hastinī and Hastikarṇā. (1–34)
The sādhana of Parānandānandamayī is the means for attaining liberation;
the sādhana of Kāmeśvarī, Mahālajjā, and Jvālinī is the means for obtaining wealth.
Then follows the sādhana of Gaurī, Vetālī, Kaṅkālī, and Vāsavī;
and thereafter the sādhanas of Candrāsyā, Sūryakiraṇā, and Araṭantī.
Kiṅkinī, Pāvanīvidyā, and Avadhūteśvarī—by means of the practice of these perfected vidyās, he becomes Rudra himself. (1.37)
The means for the *alakā*, *kaliyugasthā*, *śakti*, and *ṭaṅkāra*;
likewise, the means for the *hariṇī*, *mohinī*, *kṣiprā*, *tṛṣyā*, and so forth. (1.38)
The practice for Aṭṭahāsa, Aghora, Nāda, Mahāmegha, and others;
the most wonderful practice for Vallarī, Kauraviṇī, and others. (1.39)
Next is the sādhana of the Raṅkiṇī, followed by the sādhanas of Nandakanyā and others,
as well as the sādhanas of Mandirā and Kātyāyanī.
The practice of Rajanī, the practice of Rājatīghonā, the practice of Tāla, the practice of Pādukā, the practice of Citta, and the practice of Ravi. || 1-41 ||
Likewise, there is the sādhana of Muninātheśvarī Śāntivallabhā,
as well as the sādhana of Madirā and the sādhana of Vīrabhadra.
Then follows the sādhana of Muṇḍālī, Kālinī, Daityadaṃśinī, and others;
as well as the great sādhanas of Praviṣṭavarṇā, Laghimā, Mīnā, and so forth. (1.43)
The Phetkārīsādhana, the marvelous Bhallātakīsādhana, and likewise the Uḍḍīyāneśvarīsādhana and the Pūrṇagirijāsādhana. (1–44)
The sādhana of Saukarī, Rājavaśinī, Dīrghajaṅghā, and others;
the wondrous sādhana of Drāviṇī, the goddess worshipped in Ayodhyā. (1.45)
The sādhana of Jvālāmukhī, the sādhanas of Kṛṣṇajihvā and others, the vidyā of the beloved of the Five-Faced One (Pañcavaktra), and the sādhanas of the Ananta-vidyā and others. || 1-46 ||
The sādhana of Śrīvidyā-Bhuvaneśānī, the sādhana of Kāya, the sādhanas of Raktamālā-Mahācaṇḍī, Mahājvālā, and others. || 1–47 ||
The practice of devotion worshipped by Kāma, which includes the inserted mantras;
and the practice of Lelihānā and others, attained through the wind residing in the breath. || 1.48 ||
Likewise, there is the sādhana of Bhairavīlasitāpṛthvīvāṭukī,
as well as the mantra-sādhana of Añjana, the sovereign of the Ākulī crown who is not to be approached.
The accomplishment of the mantras of Kulāvatī, Kulakṣiptā, Arati, Cīnā, and others;
and the accomplishment of the mantras of the youthful heroines beginning with Śivākroḍā. || 1.50 ||
The practice for the Mountain-Dweller suddenly increases one's success;
those who are worshiped through mantras, yantras, and independent rites are higher than the highest. (1.51)
In the Kali age, all these forms of Kālī, who are as tender as Hara, are such that by means of them mantras and the like are accomplished; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (1.52)
O Mahākāla Śivānanda, you who have reached the further shore of supreme bliss;
out of affection for your devotees, listen once more to this jewel of knowledge. 1.53
First is the daily practice of the mantras of the Vaiṣṇava deity;
thereafter follows that most wonderful and auspicious mantra-sādhana.

The accomplishment that was ordained spontaneously by him through which success is attained on the surface of the earth—this is the *sādhana* of Bālabhairava, the Lord of Yogins, which is the *sādhana* of Śiva. (1.55)
Listen with diligence to the *sādhana* of Mahākāla, as well as that of Rāmeśvara, and the *sādhana* of Aghoramūrti’s delight. 1–56.
The sādhana of Krodharāja, Bhūtarāja, Ekacakrā, and others; then the sādhana of Girīndra, and subsequently the sādhana of Kulanātha. (1.57)
And likewise, the means of accomplishment (sādhana) for Baṭukeśa and Śrīkaṇṭheśa,
as well as for Mṛtyuñjaya, Raudra, and Kālāntakahara.
Likewise for Unmattabhairava, for Pañcāsya,
for Śambhu the Lord of Kailāsa, and for the Trident-bearer himself.
O Śaṅkara, [I shall explain] the sādhana of Bhārgaveśa, of the entire Mahākāla,
of Surāntaka, and likewise of the perfect Deva.
The sādhana of Haridrāgaṇanātha, who wears a garland of Varada-īśvaras, has upraised hair, is smoke-colored, and possesses matted locks. (1.61)
Also [the practice] of Ānandabhairava, of Bāṇanātha,
of Karīndra, of Śubhāṅga, and of Hillolamardaka.
Also [is] the sādhana of Puṣpanātheśvara, the sādhana of Vṛṣanātha, the sādhana of the eightfold form (Aṣṭamūrti), the sādhana of Kālamūrti, and the sādhana of Candraśekhara. || 1.63 ||
Also the accomplishment of the mantra of Kramuka, which is terrible and propitiated by Kubera, as well as the accomplishment of the Tripurāntaka-mantra and of Kamalākṣa. 1.64.
Listen now as I explain in great detail and with joy the various meanings of such established mantras as these, which have been proclaimed specifically for that purpose. (1.65)
O Mahādeva, attentively consider that method by which all the deities, beginning with Indra, are accomplished upon the earth. (1.66)

And the means for accomplishing the secondary sciences (*upavidyā*), various mantras, diverse ritual acts (*karma*), religious duties (*dharma*), and the means for accomplishing the six rites (*ṣatkarma*). || 1.67 ||
The sādhana of Śrī Rāma, the sādhana of the Yakṣa, the sādhana of Yoga, the sādhana of all vidyās, and the sādhana of Rājajvālā and others. (1–68)
The method for attaining mantra-siddhi, the practice of Hanumān and others, the sādhana of the Viṣajvālā, and the sādhana of the subterranean realm (pātāla). || 1.69 ||
The method of the Bhūtalipi script, the respective means of accomplishment (sādhana), the practice of the ninefold nyāsa, and the eightfold types of supernatural powers (siddhi). || 1.70 ||
There are also postures, limbs, and many ritual means (sādhanas),
as well as the sādhanas of Kātyāyanī and the sādhanas of the maidservants.
The accomplishment of the black cat, and thereafter the accomplishment of the sword;
the accomplishment of the sandals and the power of swift-footedness, as well as the means for mastering one's own tongue and so forth.

The accomplishment of the pill of conditioned refinement (saṃskāra-guṭikā), the accomplishment of the sky-farer (khecarī-siddhi), the method for entering the earth, and the means for attaining the eternally exalted state and so forth. || 1.73 ||
O Lord of Gods, there are various kinds of medicinal herbs and other substances used for the fierce act of paralyzing, as well as for attracting even a sage. (1.74)

The accomplishment of yellow orpiment and other substances, the preparation of mercury and quicksilver, and the production of mercurial ashes and other compounds arising from various juices. || 1.75 ||
The most wonderful means for an old man to assume a youthful form,
the means for attaining the Vaijayantī [spear], and the life story of Vāsaka.
The conduct of Śiva, the conduct of a horse, and that of a crow;
the various types of maidens, as well as the warding off of thunderbolts.
The means for attaining prosperity, the means for attaining the sacred place, the means for attaining desire, the procedure for worshipping the guru, and the means for pleasing the guru. || 1-78 ||
The worship of one's own deity and one's own means of practice consist of the preparation of *vāruṇī*, *paiṣṭī*, *gauḍī*, *kaitakī*, and *mādhvī* liquors.
Going to one's own body in heaven is difficult for mortals even in the mortal world;
it is the nourishment of the body and the means for attaining the state of Kṛṣṇa. (1.80)
The attraction of the eyes, the vision of the black serpent, the method for agitating the battlefield, and the restraint of the five senses. (1.81)
Listen now to the practice of the yoga-science, the description of the course of food, and the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, for the sake of attaining success in that yoga. (1.82)
Whatever things they proclaim with the foremost of the Yāmalas,
whatever objects exist within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), Śiva is difficult to find everywhere.
Those who practice the Great Tantra—whether from the Bāla or the Mantra [Tantra], or the Yāmala which has arisen beautifully from the lotus-face of me—[attain success]. (1.84)
Extremely secret, a great secret, a secret of sound, and unconfused;
it is the auspicious abode of the oceans of various siddhis, consisting of yoga. (1.85)
Indeed, the essence of the entire web of scriptures is this beloved collection of various mantras,
which is ever-delightful and a source of happiness for the Lord of the City of Vārāṇasī.
That which has Sarasvatī as its presiding deity, situated on the peak among the Kālīs, is the Mahāmokṣa, the gateway to liberation, adorned with all the secret signs (saṃketas). || 1.87 ||

This Tantra, which is a wish-fulfilling tree for desires, consecrated by the purificatory rites of Śiva, the essence of ritual action, and adorned with a thousand hymns of praise, is not to be disclosed [to the uninitiated]. 1-88.
The hundred and eight names are an auspicious thousand-name hymn,
colored by the application of collyrium prepared from various substances and ritual means.
This is the description of the direct perception of Kālī, encapsulated by the Ṣoḍhā and other [mantras] of Kālī;
it produces great wonder and effects maintenance, destruction, and protection. (1.90)
And those who know Mahākālayāmala—which purifies the Kali age and consists of eighteen types for the sake of liberation through the sixfold bliss—[attain that goal]. (1.91)
From Brahma down to a blade of grass, there is no doubt that all is within his hand;
I shall describe that method, which is the auspiciousness of the Vedas and Agamas.

Since Rudra is the possessor of knowledge who has reached the further shore of the meaning of various tantras, the ritual performed at night is the means of accomplishment according to the Kula-tantra. (1.93)

"O Lord, because this [practice] consists of the nature of the five principles (pañcatattva) and is devoid of the Great Hero (mahāvīra), there is no transgression for me; it is well-guarded in this tantra. (1.94)
Then, O Śaṅkara, Lord of the Moon, the Yāmala has been declared:
the rudrākṣa is the most excellent means of accomplishment, bestowing the fruit of a hundred sacrifices. (1.95)
The extensive *Yāmala*, which bestows satisfaction of mind, has been proclaimed;
it contains the *sādhana* of the Bhairavas, beginning with Ruru, as well as that of the goddess Brāhmī. (1.96)

Since it is the means for acquiring golden vessels with tips like the *jāmbūnada* creeper, where the mind is the means of attainment, and which serves as the ornament for the splendor of Laṅkā. (1.97)
The armor of the deities, various meditations and great vows,
the prescriptions for internal sacrifice, and the fruits of the Kali age.
Those who read continuously this chapter, which consists of thirty sections and shines with the form of the light of effort— the reflection upon expiation— [attain the highest state].
One certainly attains whatever one desires on this earth through the practice of the Great Tantra by means of action, mind, or speech. (1.100)
Having understood this complete tantra, which sustains all things within the circle of the world, one performs [the rite] attended by the lotus-like hand of the Lord of Kamalās. || 1-101 ||
The practitioner attains accomplishment in just one month; of this there is no doubt.
This is the majesty of the various wheels, encompassed by various marks and mandalas.
The *Sarvajñasiddhiśataka*, the abode of the family of Khaṇḍakālī,
resembling the rising sun and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
Having first meditated upon and worshipped the supreme deity, the Swan, the Lord who consumes the Kālakūṭa poison, one should pay homage to Maheśvara,
who resembles the first flush of dawn and is adorned with ornaments of jewels.
I bow to the supreme haṃsa, the bestower of boons, who is intoxicated by the wine of Vāruṇī.
Bhairava said: If the *Yāmala-tantra*, which brings about all auspiciousness, is not studied,
then by what means could a practitioner become a possessor of *siddhi*?
And there are those people who are deficient in intellect and deficient in wisdom, unfortunate, deceitful, deluded, and encompassed by all manner of calamities. || 1-106 ||
Tell me, how do they attain perfection, and how has compassion arisen toward those fools who are lowly and devoid of mastery over the meaning of the scriptures? (1.107)
By what means does stainless knowledge arise, which is free from the duality of the living world? Out of affection, tell me that method for the increase of the merit of people. (1-108)
Bhairavī said:
He who, residing within his body, severs the thread of karma day by day—
he beholds my glorious lotus feet, O Lord of the World.

Because they possess intellects and activities differentiated by the impressions of universal absorption, and because they are intensely veiled by various objects of action, they do not know me. (1.110)
The terrifying messenger of Death seizes the body of those who practice the Great Yoga and possess the virtues of renunciation and relinquishment.
That unfortunate one who abandons me attains the womb of a beast;
he who directs his devotion toward me is rare and beloved by the world.
Everything is obtained through devotion; through devotion one gains the vision of the gods; through devotion one attains supreme knowledge; therefore, one should rely upon devotion. (1.113)
When one attains the state of the Goddess— the essence of all scriptures, hidden yet abiding within all the senses, and the root of all things— (1.114).
At that very moment, all perfections are attained, and then one becomes firm in meditation—
stainless, abstaining from food, with the mind fixed in its dwelling.

When he attains the state of being one whose limbs are purified by daily bathing and worship, who is skilled in ritual action, proficient in the great training, and has conquered his senses; || 1-116 ||
"You are a knower of the hidden meanings of all scriptures and are free from the bonds of worldly attachment;
tell me the internal state residing in their hands, just as one perceives the state within the body."
There is nothing higher than existence by which one may become possessed of grace;
from existence comes the attainment of grace, and from grace, one becomes one of great bliss. (1.118)
From happiness arises the power of merit; from merit comes the vision of the Immovable One (Acyuta).
When there is the vision of that which has been performed, it is the auspicious sight of the lotus of his face.
Having become a yogi, he beholds the subtle state, invisible even to other yogis,
which purifies the lotus feet of Mahāvidyā.
Having heard the words of the gurus who are supreme sages (paramahaṃsas)— words that purify the three worlds— the yogi, for the sake of attaining the goal of practice, shall attain yoga.
The parrot and the maina in the cage, and the winged birds of avian birth—the practitioner seizes them from heaven by means of my great and stainless name. 1-122.
O Lord of the Kula, for as long as the movement of knowledge continues, that man shall remain in the presence of practitioners and holy men. (1.123)
One who practices knowledge does not fall if they are intent upon awakening;
for birth is not for the sake of exposition, nor is the discourse on the meanings of various scriptures.
Without supreme knowledge, nothing whatsoever is accomplished on this earth;
O Bhairava, how then can there be mantra or the attainment of the Śrīkāya? (1.125)
The knowledge of Sāṃkhya and the knowledge of the rules of Vedic language are likewise equal;
for without Śakti, one is like a Śākta without the Goddess, or indeed like a wise man without [true] knowledge.
Just as the perfection of harmful conduct exists in the house of a poor man, so too does the power of discerning knowledge and right conduct exist in the house of a practitioner. 1-127.
If she, Śivakāminī, who is distinguished by ignorance, arises solely for the destruction of the state of union with her own power, [then that occurs]. (1-128)
At that time, one should not perform the seizing [of the disciple] nor the accomplishment of power;
for if the best of practitioners were to do so, there would be contact resulting from a lack of purification. (1.129)

Through defects such as improper consecration (asaṃskṛti) and so forth, the loss of accomplishment arises for the three types of entities—those characterized by power (śakti)—and for the practitioner. (1.130)
The three states of being have been declared for divine, heroic, and animal [practitioners].
In the state of the animal (paśu), there is the attainment of knowledge and the description of animal conduct.
In the heroic state (*vīrabhāva*), there is the accomplishment of action; one is directly Rudra, without a doubt.
In the divine state (*divyabhāva*) and the heroic state, there is a distinction despite their being of a single essence.
The Egg is the primordial, all-pervading characteristic of the divine state; the vision of the deity within that divine state is proclaimed as the [true] manifestation. (1.133)
The accomplishment of mantra in the state of a hero is characterized by the practice of non-duality;
having first attained the disposition of the bound soul (paśu), one should avoid ritual activity at night.
Bathing day after day, engaged in worship and daily rites, one succeeds through a state of purity by performing [the practice] as if it were a *puraścaraṇa*. (1.135)
Without the state of a *paśu*, what hero can certainly become a master?
The subduing of the senses is the true subduing, and it is the subduing of the mind. (1-136)
The ascetic, whose limbs are intent upon the training of yoga and who is devoted to yoga, practices throughout all moments during the nights until dawn. (1.137)
And at all times, one should practice that yoga which bestows all happiness—the eternal, youthful wish-fulfilling tree that destroys all sins. (1.138)

If the practitioner, remaining in the state of *paśubhāva*, should accomplish [this] with focused mind, he will attain the knowledge of the rules of the language of yoga, which is difficult to find among all states of being. (1.139)
Nevertheless, one who possesses firm devotion to the lotus feet of the gurus will certainly attain accomplishment quickly, even while in the state of a beast. (1.140)
He should be one who has completely abandoned desire; he should characterize himself by the mere state of being.
This is the heroic state, the great state—not the state of those with corrupt minds. (1.141)
The subtle state of slow movement becomes manifest through the form of Rudra; it is auspicious, the welfare of the three worlds, fallen from conventional conduct, and profoundly hidden. 1-142.

For the sake of accomplishing the five principles and so forth, [one should practice] the conduct of all the seats and families, which arises from great delusion and passion, and which is an ocean of bliss through forceful means.
Having become a knower [of reality], one who possesses only devotion toward the hero’s practice within the ocean of compassion,
and who abides in the state of a bound soul (paśu), should thereafter perform the conduct of a hero (vīrācāra).
Through the conduct of a hero one becomes Rudra; otherwise, one certainly does not.
Established in these two states of being, the mantra-practitioner should contemplate the divine state.
O Lord of the Family of all rites, one should always practice with a pure and divine state of being, well-composed in meditation, for the sake of pleasing the deity. (1.146)
Whatever is entirely accomplished from this auspicious source of phenomena (dharmodaya), one attains a state equal to the deity and becomes intent on the activities of the deity. (1.147)
Know that to be the state of divinity, proclaimed as possessing supreme divine fortune;
it is, without doubt, the root of power for all categories of existence. (1-148)
By what means does the best of practitioners attain devotion, having understood it through the instruction on his own duty regarding the body of the God? (1.149)
Knowledge is said to be threefold, arising from scripture and right conduct;
for that knowledge consists of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), and one perceives it through the path of knowledge. (1.150)
Having studied all the scriptures and the songs concerning one's own karma, the wise practitioner, remaining emaciated, should constantly rely upon discernment. (1.151)
Knowledge born of discernment reveals the wisdom of Śiva;
it is devoid of the two eyes and free from external phenomena.
Know that which is liberated from the worlds, which churns through time and non-time, the eternal knowledge, the supreme knowledge—that is the domain of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 1-153 ||
Human birth is fruitful and falls within the scope of all scriptures among the eighty-four lakhs of bodies belonging to embodied beings. (1.154)
Nowhere else than in the human state does the knowledge of reality exist;
a human birth is only occasionally obtained through the accumulation of merit. (1.155)
Human birth is difficult to obtain for one who has made liberation their staircase;
and among humans, they declare that the primary spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) are attainable. (1.156)
Therefore, the God who is the best of men is endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest;
without a body, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) cannot be attained by anyone. (1.157)
Therefore, having protected the body, you should constantly cultivate knowledge;
for those who know the Self as knowledge recognize the human being as a mass of knowledge and the Supreme as the essence of knowledge. 1-158.
The sages are of a silent disposition, and their domain is the tradition of the sages and so forth;
he is human, all-pervading, and eternally undisturbed in his station.
By performing the recitation of the *mitra* mantra and the yoga-recitation, which wards off evil, a human being attains supreme liberation; there is no doubt about this. (1.160)
Those who are my devotees shall read the tantras spoken by me;
having read them, they perform the ritual action, and having performed it, they shall attain my presence.
If a practitioner, without understanding the scriptures spoken by me, seeks enlightenment through other scriptures, he may achieve success only after ten million years. (1.162)
O Bhairava, just as the delusion of silver occurs with respect to mother-of-pearl, so too do people desire enjoyment and liberation based on other philosophical systems. (1.163)
Where there is enjoyment, there is liberation; where would these two not both be accomplished?
My servant, devoted to the lotus of my glorious sandals, attains both liberation and enjoyment.
The external observer perceives the light situated in space, and the observer who possesses knowledge of the cosmic egg perceives that which resides within the regional egg. || 1-165 ||
Just as at the time of the perception of a jar, light is the manifestor, so that without its connection with "jar-ness," the jar is not perceived. (1-166)
Even when distinguished from another, it does not undergo differentiation;
in the Puruṣa, there is no differentiation whatsoever without [the presence of] power (śakti). (1.167)
Just as an embodied being who is devoid of power, weak, and bereft of yoga does not perceive his own self, so too one who is devoid of knowledge does not perceive the two states. || 1-168 ||
Deluded by the ignorance regarding cyclic existence, they do not realize the intrinsic nature;
yet the world perceives that very state which is being conceptualized. (1-169)
Even for a lord, a messenger, or King Yama, there is bondage and they undergo death, having seen their own son and wealth. (1-170)
Having drunk the wine of delusion, the world does not know its own welfare;
prosperity is but a dream, and youth is like a flower.
Life is as flickering as lightning; who could maintain composure out of ignorance? A mortal lives for a hundred years, yet sleep steals half of it away.
The power of passion, which burns away reason and intellect, takes away half the life of a woman;
likewise, the wicked conduct of fools destroys their lifespan day by day.
All that is rendered fruitless by the sufferings of childhood, disease, and old age;
for what reason, then, should one have attachment to relations such as wife, son, father, and mother? (1.174)
For cyclic existence has suffering as its root; he who possesses it is suffering. He by whom its abandonment has been accomplished is happy—of this there is no doubt. (1.175)
What cannot be attained through action by one who has renounced both pleasure and pain?
For he who performs the ritual procedure merely out of fear of worldly convention— || 1.176 ||
I am the knower of Brahman for all those who recite [the mantra] without reverence, and for one who is attached to worldly pleasures yet claims, "I am a knower of Brahman. (1.177)
The wise man should always avoid such a person from afar, like an outcaste;
they are shameless and naked, appearing in the sight of houses and forests alike.
Do donkeys and other such animals also become practitioners of vows when they constantly dwell in the forest, subsisting on grass, leaves, and water? (1.179)
And do those deer, such as the *hariṇa* and others, become ascetics, enduring cold, wind, and heat, and regarding edible and inedible food as the same? (1.180)
Do pigs and other such animals practice vows? And do all birds in the sky, as well as spirits, ghosts, and the like, observe them? (1.181)
Do all those who move through the sky roam there at night, O Great Lords? And do they remain on the banks of the Gaṅgā and other rivers from birth until the end of death? || 1-182 ||
Do those who are headed by frogs and fish become observers of vows?
If wise men, whose limbs are established in this knowledge, go [to such a state], [then they too would]. (1-183)
Nevertheless, due to the fault of their past actions, they indeed remain in hell—those who have not abandoned crookedness, laziness, and association with the wicked. (1.184)
Those who are solely devoted to me attain my abode;
beings ascend upward with a subtle, transportive body.
Through a self-imposed curse upon his own body, a man may take on various forms;
through the defects of actions born of the body, a man falls into the state of an immobile being.
In this world, certain evil-minded men undergo a transformation of their physical form due to their own misconduct, as well as by the consequences of actions performed in previous lives. (1.187)
Those who are devoid of the feet of the Guru perish by my command;
for the Guru is the root of mantras, and the Guru is the supreme subduer of enemies.
By the mere grace of the Guru, success is attained; of this there is no doubt.
I am the Guru, I am the God, and I am the meaning of the mantra; of this there is no doubt.
Those who cause schisms go to hell, being devoid of the meaning of the various scriptures;
for all sciences, O Lord, initiation is the very root. (1.190)
For one whose independence is rooted in the Guru, the Guru is the self; of this there is no doubt.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. (1-191)
When an action is performed by oneself, then the accomplishment of its state occurs;
[one becomes] deficient in limbs, deceitful, diseased, a glutton, and fallen from moral conduct. (1-192)
Having established oneself in worship of me, one should constantly practice the secondary sciences (upavidyā),
as well as [the acquisition of] wealth, grain, sons, property, sovereignty, and the feeding of Brahmins.
One should apply oneself to what is auspicious; other thoughts bear fruitless results.
A mortal who is constantly devoted to faith, virtuous in character, is the best among men. (1.194)
The protector of the earth, whose conduct is pleasing, was intent on wandering from seat to seat;
for if the vision of Mahāvidyā is obtained at every seat. (1-195)
Then, all the siddhis, their mandalas unmanifest, arise spontaneously in his hand through the grace of Mahāmāyā. (1.196)
Whether he be a great hero, a great sage, established in a divine state,
or even situated in the state of a bound soul (paśu), he should cause the seat of mantra (mantrapīṭha) to be manifested.

O Bhairava, it has been declared that the three states of being, which are delightful, bestow the fruit of ritual action; and likewise, through the state of the Age (yuga), by means of the Divine Hero.
The great heroes perceive [the truth], whereas those of inferior birth are like beasts;
in the Kali age, they do not see it, their minds being overwhelmed by the scriptures.
Even in a thousand years, one never reaches the end of the treatises;
numerous sciences such as logic are millions of obstacles to a short life. (1.200)
Therefore, one should discern the essence from the milk, like a swan from water;
and in the Kali age, those whose minds are constantly fixed upon it [should rely] on the divine and the heroic [means].
Great devotees, who are silent by nature and always intent on spiritual practice, behold the supreme state of Mahāvidyā.
By means of the nature of divine heroes, they behold my lotus feet;
there are two dispositions among the Brahmins who desire the great and excellent fruit. (1.203)
Alternatively, two states of being have been proclaimed for the Avadhūtas;
by the power of these two states, a man becomes a great yogin.
Even a fool becomes a supreme master of speech through the grace of these two states,
O Mahādeva, for those who understand the means of accomplishing the purpose of my Tantra.
For those Rudras are indeed of two states regarding the phonemes; there is no doubt in this matter.
One who is full of devotion is the lord of the yoga of devotion, the means for knowing all states of being.
Like one who is perpetually insane or dull-witted, he has reached the further shore of the meaning of his own system;
as a tree bears flowers, so does the nose perceive fragrance.
They recite all the scriptures, yet those that awaken true realization are difficult to find; for one devoid of wisdom, study is like a blind man looking into a mirror.
For one possessed of wisdom, the treatise on Dharma serves as a means for liberation;
the determination of the meaning of the scripture is that "such is the reality. (1.209)
"I am the agent, I am the self, all-pervading and undisturbed"—even the Lord of Speech contemplates such a nature with his mind. (1.210)
When the one of great knowledge perceives for a thousand years the radiance of lightning, he sees a thousand moons as a single moon.
Whatever fruit a person obtains even in a hundred crores of years, that same fruit one enjoys by meditating for a single moment on the dust of the Lord’s feet. (1.212)
If one should wander everywhere increasing pure bliss,
[one reaches] Kāmarūpa, the great seat (mahāpīṭha), which is the radiant foundation of the triangle.
He who concludes with the word "bubble" (budbuda) [of water] shall become the lord of my servants, possessing infinite auspiciousness, and as beloved as Gaṇeśa and Guha.
The excellent practitioner should wander through the seats and sub-seats known as Kaṅkāla, Sāṭṭahāsa, and Vikaṭākṣa, if he desires my lotus feet. (1.215)
The great sacred seat of Jvālāmukhī is dear to me and beyond the reach of logic;
he who wanders there for my satisfaction certainly becomes a yogin. (1.216)

Those lords of practitioners who wander through the collection of the two states and so forth, and the sacred seats (pīṭha) of Jvālāmukhī and the others, are accomplished; of this there is no doubt. (1.217)
For those who desire the accomplishment of the three worlds, there is nothing higher than existence (bhāva).
Indeed, existence is the supreme knowledge, the unsurpassed knowledge of Brahman. (1.218)
What is the use of giving away ten million maidens, or of wandering through Vārāṇasī a hundred times, or even of going to Kurukṣetra, if the true disposition is not attained? (1.219)

What is the use of performing *śrāddha* at Gayā or wandering through various sacred seats (*pīṭhas*), or what is the use of various fire-sacrifices (*homa*) and ritual acts, if the true disposition (*bhāva*) is not attained? (1.220)
Through devotion, knowledge arises; from knowledge, one attains liberation.
By means of the mind, the Lord is said to be the Guru of the Goddess and of the Self. (1-221)
Meditation is said to be a fetter; liberation is the dissolution of the mind into the Self.
Merely through the grace of the Guru, there arises a great satisfaction of Śakti. (1.222)
By the mere satisfaction of his power, the practitioner attains liberation;
the entire world has its root in the Guru, and supreme austerity has its root in the Guru. (1.223)
By the mere grace of the Guru, one who is well-disciplined attains liberation; he should not transgress the Guru’s command, nor should he speak back to him. (1.224)
Day and night, one should carry out the command of the guru like a servant;
the wise person should not show negligence regarding tasks whether they have been explicitly stated or left unsaid. (1.225)
When the teacher walks, he should walk attentively; he must not transgress the teacher’s command.
He should not fail to listen to the teacher’s words, nor should he listen while turning his face away. (1.226)
Whether it be harmful or beneficial, even one who is highly intelligent, if by chance he violates the command of his guru, shall go to the Raurava hell. (1.227)
One goes to a terrible hell and may attain the state of a pig;
likewise, violating the teacher's command, censuring him, or acting in a manner displeasing to him [leads to this]. (1.228)
One should not associate with one who commits treachery against the guru, nor with one who covets the guru’s property, nor with those who commit adultery with the guru’s wife. (1.229)
That would be a sin for him, and one should not perform an expiation for it;
having treated the teacher with ill-will, one should remove him through censure as if he were an enemy. || 1-230 ||
In a lonely forest region, he shall become a Brahma-rākṣasa;
[he who steals] sandals, a seat, clothing, a bed, or ornaments. (1.231)
Having seen the Guru and paid homage, one should not employ them for one's own enjoyment;
and he upon whose tip of the tongue the mantra of the sandals (pādukā) always resides. (1-232)
A person may effortlessly attain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
they should always meditate upon the lotus feet of the illustrious Guru.
For the sake of devotion and liberation, there is no devotee superior to the Vīra;
therefore, a disciple residing in the same village should always go into his presence. (1.234)
A disciple situated in one place, having always gone into the presence of that [teacher],
should prostrate to the guru for one month while traveling across a distance of seven yojanas.
In whichever direction the lotus feet of the glorious Guru shine, in that direction one should pay homage with body, mind, and intellect. (1.236)

O Lord, having received from the mouth of the Guru all things—the seat that is a limb of knowledge, the mantra, the mudrā, the tantra, and so forth—everything becomes fruitful; otherwise, it will not be so.
Whether on a soft woolen blanket, or likewise situated upon a palace, or even on the back of a long wooden beam, one should abandon sitting alone with a heavy load. (1.238)
O Lord of Gods, one should never disclose the pādukā-mantra of the Śrī-guru, nor the root-mantra (mūla-mantra), nor one's own pādukā to any disciple whatsoever.

Whatever object is beneficial to oneself, one should never deceive regarding that substance; having received even a single syllable from the Guru, O observer of good vows, one must not betray it. (1.240)
Whatever food is prepared for the sake of the Guru according to one's means—even if it be small—is equal to a great offering; it bestows the first of all worlds and puts an end to poverty.
Even one who might give away all his possessions, if he is devoid of devotion to the Guru, reaches only the end of hell; for devotion alone is the cause [of liberation]. (1.242)
Through devotion to the guru one attains the state of Śakra, and through lack of devotion one becomes a pig;
there is nothing superior to devotion to the guru in all the scriptures on devotion.
O Lord, without the worship of the Guru, even ten million merits become futile.

Thus ends the first chapter in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the section on the mantras for attaining perfection in the practice of all vidyās, in the Mahātantroddīpana of the Uttara-tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
Therefore, I shall now fully proclaim [the teaching] through the science of all perspectives—O Omniscient One, Supreme Bliss, Seed of Compassion, Terrifier! (2.1)
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Śambhu, listen to the rules for the conduct of the Kula;
first, O Lord, hear the procedure regarding the violation of vows by bound souls (paśus).
In the event of a breach of the vow, a constant lapse, or failure in the daily rites of worship and so forth,
the practitioner of the mantra should recite it one thousand times for the pacification of the defect caused by the violation of the vow.

The daily ancestral rite (nityaśrāddha), as well as the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana), the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa), the beholding of deities, the beholding of sacred seats (pīṭha), and the beholding of holy fords (tīrtha). || 2–4 ||
By obeying the command of the guru and performing the daily worship of the deity, a mortal established in the state of *paśubhāva* will certainly attain great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*). (2-5)
The first state belongs to the animals, the heroic state to the hero, and the divine state to the divine beings; these are remembered as their three states. (2.6)
A practitioner who is firm-minded but devoid of the conduct of his own family will quickly become fruitless in his aims due to the power of that very family conduct. (2.7)
Bhairava said:
O lotus-faced one, by what means does a man who remains in the state of a bound soul (paśu) obtain a vision of the lotus-feet of the Blessed Lady? 2-8.
O beloved of the lineage, if I possess firm devotion and if there is affection for me, let that manner be described in great detail. (2.9)
Mahābhairavī said: Having risen at dawn during the time of sunrise,
the state of the sacrificial animals (paśus) is said to persist until eight watches (daṇḍas) of the night have passed.
In the morning, having prepared his bed and so forth, the practitioner, remaining on his bed like an animal [in devotion],
should meditate upon the Guru within the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of his head.
He who resembles the rising sun, a mass of splendor, the supreme guru,
an ocean of infinite and boundless majesty, and bears the moon upon his crest.
Greatly radiant, with a luminous body, two eyes, and two arms, the all-pervading Lord,
whose essence is the realization of the Self, is clothed in white garments by virtue of His splendor.

The cause that brings about the upward movement of the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*), the mouth of the worlds, the limb of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, the all-pervading Lord who bestows boons and fearlessness. (2.14)
Seated upon a full-blown lotus, the omniscient Lord of the universe,
flickering with inner radiance, adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
One should always worship the God of gods, who is richly adorned with jewel ornaments,
through the sequence of internal sacrifice (antaryāga) alone, honoring him with lotus flowers.
One should prostrate with exclusive devotion for the increase of longevity and health;
then, one should recite the mantra in the middle, preceded and followed by the *praṇava*.
Having joined the Vāgbhava syllable in the middle, one should then place the name of the Guru;
at the end of the word "Ānandanātha," one should extract the Guru's name ending in the dative case (ṅe).
Then one should utter the word "namaḥ" followed by the Praṇava, which bestows all accomplishments.
Having recited the mantra of the Great Guru, one shall become a master of all accomplishments.
Through the power of the Guru’s mantra, mastery of speech arises from the lotus of one's mouth;
[this is achieved] by reciting it daily one hundred and eight times, or a thousand, or likewise eight times.
Having performed the offering after reciting [the mantra], one should practice three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma).
Then, with the Vāgbhava [syllable], one should joyfully perform the rite of breath-control.
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state has been beheld—the state which is of the form of an unbroken circle and by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded. (2.22)
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance has been opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge. (2.23)
I bow down to the glorious Guru, the ocean of compassion, who is the cause for the vision of the deity and the bestower of all accomplishments. (2-24)
I bow to the divine Guru, who eternally displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who dwells upon a white lotus, and who is the destroyer of great terrors. (2-25)
His limbs are covered by great wisdom; he has the form of a man and is the bestower of boons.
He is the giver of the four aims of life and is endowed with both the gross and the subtle. (2.26)
The Lord who consists of eternal bliss, the perpetual joy, the stainless one, composed of pure being, the all-encompassing Kuleśvara at all times. (2.27)
In the great lotus at the aperture of Brahmā, within an undisturbed sphere of light,
there shines a radiant white wheel that is accessible through the meditation of yogis.
In the center of the pericarp, resembling a thousand-petaled lotus,
[he is] possessed of great splendor like ten million times ten million intensely white, radiant suns.

The stainless, supreme Haṃsa, higher than the highest, who resides in all sacred seats (pīṭhas), who eternally effects the revelation of the Vedas, and who bestows the fruits of desired actions. || 2-30 ||
The two feet are the eternal abode of the power of the mind and the seat of Māyā;
the face is like ten million moons, garlanded by clusters of autumnal moonlight.
Becoming one with him, I worship the Guru—who bestows more than is desired and is the lord of all perfections—upon the Haṃsa-maṇḍala. (2.32)
[He saw] himself as formless, yet as having form in the nature of Brahman—
the Supreme Lord, the bestower of the great mantra of Mahāvidyā.
I bow to the divine guru, the bestower of all accomplishments;
those who bow to him incessantly with body, mind, and speech. (2-34)
Indeed, they always reside within the lotus feet of the venerable Guru;
at dawn, the best of practitioners attains ten millionfold merit. (2.35)

Reciting this hymn at midday yields ten lakhs [of merits], while at evening it bestows the merit of ten million; one should recite the hymn or perform meditation in the morning with a well-concentrated mind.
Then one attains success; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 2-37 ||

I worship the Guru, the bestower of boons, who possesses the splendor of a multitude of beautiful rays; he whose head rests upon a white lotus with the luster of ten million young moons, whose lotus-hands grant the gestures of boon and fearlessness, and who embodies the form of all deities.
The two lotus-feet, which were revealed, possessed the luster of the tips of red lac.

Victorious is the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru, which dispel the fear of the world and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, wherein lies victory in yoga; I worship that supreme Guru who resides within the center of my lotus-eyes.
It destroys the fear of the ocean of existence and brings about the pacification of disease and the dissolution of the body. || 2-39 ||

I worship the Lord, the supreme and inferior Guru, who bestows all external enjoyments, seated upon a soft sixteen-petaled lotus that has been illuminated by the circle of lightning-like splendor from his two wide lotus-eyes.
It has dots like spots on a reddish-brown gem and like the spots on the pale moon. || 2.40 ||
In the twelfth petal, which is tremulous like a flickering body, one should meditate upon the Lord of Umā,
who possesses great splendor, whose right side is occupied by Vīga,
who is as radiant as a hundred suns, and whose face is like ten million spotless moons.
I worship the Supreme Lord, who is exceedingly venerable and radiant with splendor.

At dawn, one should constantly meditate upon that which is auspicious, beginning with the Guru; which is the essence of the golden cluster that burns away passion; which delights its attendants with various wonderful sounds; which possesses the beautiful triple-bend of the discus; which is as radiant as a hundred masses of dawn-red clouds; and which is attainable through yoga.
That which is meditated upon by yogis in the exceedingly beautiful lotus at the navel, resembling a ten-petaled jewel; || 2.42 ||
She who is my mother, whose own arms are the source of the Dānavas and others, who dwells in the city that is the limit of Nirvāṇa,
in the abode of self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) upon the six-petalled lotus at the root of Vaikuṇṭha—
she, the radiance of the Vedas, who effectively destroys the transformations of birth, is meditated upon by me.
She who pacifies the afflictions caused by Kandarpa, the mother of the womb, the beloved of Viṣṇu, and the consort of Śaṅkara.
She who is the Speech-Curl (bhāṣānanakuṇḍalī), who brings splendor through the beauty of the luster of the path of the Kula;
she who resides at the root of the four-petaled lotus in the region of the breath, endowed with the Kula;
she who is like a creeper on the wish-fulfilling tree for those desiring direct realization—may that beloved one speak forth.
The eternal Mother of the Guru is meditated upon as the remover of fear for yogins and the destroyer of poison. (2.44)
May the radiant, effulgent,
and subtle [Goddess] at the mouth of the Guru protect you— she who flows through the subtle path,
consists of nectar, and resides within the lotus from the root to the head, overflowing with the waves of bliss from the jar of nectar issuing from the upward-pointing lotus.
When on earth will my mother, ever ascended to the heights, be meditated upon in the mind as full? (2-45)
Whoever recites [this] daily, pervading [all things] through the yoga of maintaining stability, or through meditation, or through worship, is a god and not a human being. (2.46)
If a person of sound intellect recites this at both evening and morning, they shall obtain auspiciousness, wealth, grain, fame, long life, glory, and prosperity. (2.47)
He shall become the most excellent of practitioners, possessing a body like the wish-fulfilling tree;
by the grace of this hymn, he shall attain the status of the Lord of Speech.

Those who abide in the state of the sacrificial animal (paśu) are also undoubtedly perfected beings (siddha). At the outset, the practitioner (sādhaka) and the deity should always possess a mind intent upon right conduct.
Then the hero [attains] the state of a beast, and in the evening, he possesses the divine state;
the Guru, who has reached the further shore of Vedānta, is the master of these groups of states. (2.50)
He is peaceful, self-controlled, of noble birth, humble, and dressed in pure attire;
he is of pure conduct, well-established, clean, skillful, and highly intelligent. (2.51)
He is a forest-dweller devoted to meditation, proficient in mantras and tantras, capable of both restraint and grace, self-controlled, and a reciter of the meaning of mantras. || 2.52 ||
Free from disease, free from ego, great and devoid of transformation, he was a wise master of speech, illustrious, and always a performer of sacrificial rites. (2.53)

One who has performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) is accomplished, free from the distinction between the beneficial and the harmful, endowed with all auspicious marks, and honored by the multitude of great men. || 2.54 ||

One who has mastered the principles of breath control and other yogic practices, who possesses wisdom, observes silence, is free from passion, is ascetic, speaks the truth, and is always devoted to meditation— (2.55).
One who knows the specific meaning of the scriptures, is devoted to his own duty, maintains unmanifest signs and marks, and is a practitioner bestows auspiciousness. (2.56)
One who possesses fortune and steadfastness is called a "Lord" (nātha) or a "Guru.
A disciple, having become such [a person], should take refuge in a true Guru. (2.57)
And one should avoid those devoid of supreme bliss, those lacking beauty, those afflicted with leprosy, those of cruel deeds, the censurable, and a diseased guru. (2.58)

One who suffers from the eight types of leprosy, one whose leprosy is oozing, one afflicted with white leprosy, one who harms living beings, and likewise one who always seizes the wealth of others. (2.59)
One who sells gold, a thief, one devoid of intelligence, one who is very short, one with black teeth, one lacking family conduct, and one devoid of tranquility—[these are to be avoided]. (2.60)
One who is stained by blemish, afflicted by eye diseases, a frequenter of others' wives, unrefined, a speaker [of falsehood], one conquered by women, and one with an extra limb. (2.61)
One who is deceitful by nature, characterized by violence, excessively talkative, a glutton, miserly, and indeed a speaker of falsehood; (2.62)

One should not worship a teacher who is unpacified, devoid of essential qualities, abandoned by the fivefold conduct, and whose limbs are filled with webs of faults—unless he is the [supreme] Guru. (2.63)
But one who conceives the notion of a mere human being in the Guru, the notion of written letters in the mantras, or the notion of a stone in the images, shall go to hell. (2.64)
For parents, being the causes of one's birth, are to be honored with great effort;
but the teacher, who reveals what is dharma and what is adharma, is especially worthy of worship. (2.65)
The Guru is the father, the Guru is the mother, the Guru is the deity, and the Guru is the refuge.
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all [to save].
One should perform what is received from the guru through the actions of speech, mind, and body;
O God, by practicing what is harmful, one is born as a worm in excrement. (2.67)
From abandoning the mantra, death occurs; from abandoning the guru, poverty ensues.
By abandoning both the guru and the mantra, one goes to the Raurava hell. (2.68)
But he who, while the Guru is present, should worship another deity, goes to a terrible hell; that worship becomes fruitless. (2.69)
One should behave toward the sons of the guru as toward the guru himself, and toward his grandsons and so forth as toward him;
whether he is ignorant or learned, the guru alone is indeed a deity.
Even if he stands outside the path, the Guru who stands upon the path is indeed a deity;
between the biological progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the Guru who imparts the Veda is the more venerable. (2.71)
Therefore, one should always regard the Guru as superior even to one's father;
for I am dependent upon the Guru and the Deity in matters of scripture, mantra, and the Kula and Akula traditions.
O Lord, one who contemplates the feet of the venerable Guru does not fail to possess the qualification [for liberation].
The Guru is the mother, the father, the master, the kinsman, the friend, and Śiva himself. (2.73)
Having thus fixed his mind, he should constantly worship the Guru with his whole being as the one supreme Brahman, possessing the luster of a gross, white gem. (2.74)
One should take refuge in the Guru, who is the controller of all actions and is one's own self;
and the Guru is, without a doubt, the single essence of all states of being. (2.75)
The word of the Guru is beyond doubt; one whose nature is full of doubt perishes.
One who is free from doubt, having renounced everything at the feet of the Guru, shall attain the supreme state. (2.76)
One attains the state of a sky-walker (khecarī) in just one month; of this there is no doubt.
One should wait for one year for a disciple who has taken refuge in a true guru.

Having understood whether [the disciple] possesses qualities or is devoid of qualities, one should cause the mantra to be imparted; [one must also understand] all the characteristics of the disciple and the discernment between the auspicious and the inauspicious. (2.78)
Otherwise, through the fault of the officiant, it would burn away the fruit of accomplishment and worship—[the officiant who is] lustful, crooked, censured by the world, and devoid of truth. (2.79)
One who is undisciplined, incapable, devoid of wisdom, fond of enemies, always engaged in sinful deeds, empty of learning, and dull-witted; (2-80)
Its body consists of the multitude of defects of the Kali age; it is devoid of Vedic rituals, lacking the conduct of the stages of life (āśrama), and characterized by an impure inner organ. (2.81)
One who is always devoid of faith, lacking fortitude, prone to anger, deluded, of wicked conduct, deficient in virtue, and ever obsessed with the wives of others; (2.82)
The Guru should avoid that disciple who arises from a collection of false conceptions, who lacks devotion, whose mind is dualistic, and whose body is covered with various defects. (2.83)
O Hero, if it is not relinquished for the sake of giving wealth and other gifts,
that sinful person will become like a disciple in hell and shall obtain a state even worse than that.
In an instant, he would become unaccomplished due to the sins incurred by his disciples;
having suddenly fallen into hell, it would lead only to the destruction of the ritual purpose. (2.85)
Having deliberated with effort according to the prescribed rule, one should undertake the gathering of disciples;
otherwise, through the fault of the disciple, the teacher shall dwell in hell. (2.86)
A husband shall not initiate his wife; a father shall not initiate his daughter;
likewise, a son shall not initiate [his father], nor shall a brother initiate his brother. (2.87)
If the husband is one whose mantra is perfected, then he should initiate his wife;
for Bhairava [initiates her] as his Śakti, and she does not become a "daughter" (putrikā).
The deities of the mantras are to be known as the Guru in the form of the deity. (2.88)
One who desires his own welfare should not create division among them;
a disciple residing in the same village should prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day. (2.89)
Standing at a distance of one *krośa*, a disciple should bow to the Guru every day with devotion; from a distance of half a *yojana*, he should prostrate on the five sacred festival days (*parvan*).
Beginning from one yojana up to twelve yojanas,
a disciple situated in a distant land who has approached his presence with devotion— 2.91.
One should prostrate to the guru for the number of months stated in the *Tantrayojana*;
indeed, after one year, a brahmin becomes fit through his devotion to the guru. (2.92)
A Kṣatriya becomes fit to be a disciple in two years, a Vaiśya in three years, and a Śūdra in four years; thus has the fitness of a disciple been described. (2.93)
O Lord, if by the power of fortune one should obtain a perfected mantra,
one should certainly receive the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) from that lineage of the Three Powers (Triśakti).

One who practices the mantra with these [persons], except for one's father or maternal grandfather, in all cases involves transgression against the guru, whether through negligence or ignorance. (2.95)
Then, having performed an expiation, one should undergo initiation once again;
the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra should be performed one hundred thousand times as a vow for the Lord of the World.
Or else, O Mahādeva, the *praṇava* of Viṣṇu is traditionally taught as the object of focus for expiation;
if one is unable [to perform that], one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Recited ten thousand times, she destroys all impurities; Gāyatrī is the mother of all meters and a fire to the scales for heaps of sin. (2.98)
And my manifestation as Mūrtīprakāśā, free from the state of the bound soul (paśubhāva), is attained by Brahmā at night during the section on the arising of the fruit. (2.99)
O Lord, if by the power of fortune one finds a Guru whose mantra has been perfected,
then at that very moment one should initiate her solely for the sake of the eightfold sovereign powers.
The seedless mantra of the Father (Śiva) is not defective when used in the Śaiva or Śākta traditions;
it should be imparted to the eldest son by those of noble lineage who are learned in the Kula.
To one who is of noble lineage and self-controlled, the great mantra, the Lord of the Family, grants liberation at that very moment; this is the truth, the truth—there is no doubt. (2.102)
One's youngest brother, even an enemy, a uterine brother who has joined the side of an adversary,
a maternal grandfather, a father, and an ascetic living in the forest— || 2.103 ||
Having avoided those who belong to no stage of life (anāśramin), those with bad associations, and likewise those who have abandoned their own family,
he should perform the rite of initiation for those [worthy] disciples.
Otherwise, through opposition to that, one's desire and mental effort will be destroyed;
therefore, O Bhairava, one should accept even from a low-born family a mantra that has already been proven effective. (2.105)
O auspicious one who assumes form after form, concealing the contemplation of the true Guru—by receiving initiation therein, one attains victory over the eight sovereign powers. (2-106)
However, there is no fixed rule regarding the initiation of both teacher and disciple in dreams;
one who receives [the substance] from a woman in a dream is purified by the consecration alone. (2.107)
She is virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to her guru, and has conquered her senses;
she knows the true meaning and essence of all mantras, is of excellent character, and delights in worship.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, the reciter was lotus-eyed, adorned with jewel ornaments, and beautified by a complexion like that of the sky. || 2-109 ||
Peaceful, of noble lineage, born of a good family, moon-faced, and the source of all prosperity;
endowed with infinite virtues, she is the beloved who bestows the state of Rudra. (2.110)
She who is the embodiment of the Guru, the bestower of liberation, and the expounder of the knowledge of Śiva—
she indeed becomes fit to be a Guru, provided she is a widow and free from worldly attachments.
Initiation for a woman is declared auspicious, and her mantra is remembered as being eightfold in power.
A woman who has borne children or a widow may be accepted, provided she is independent and capable of fulfilling her obligations. (2.112)

If one who has mastered the mantra should receive [the teaching] from the mouth of a widow, the fruit therein is certainly exclusively excellent and eightfold that of [receiving it from] a mother. (2-113)
If a virtuous woman gives that mantra according to her own nature,
she obtains eightfold the merit, provided she is a chaste wife who has borne a son.
If a mother bestows her own mantra upon her own son, then he attains the eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi) on the path of devotion; of this there is no doubt. (2.115)
O Lord, at that very moment, if it is granted by my mother,
I shall first attain devotion and then liberation, assuming the form of Time.
He knows the meaning of ten million billion vidyās; of this there is no doubt.
Or, in a dream, his mother may give him a pure mantra. (2-117)
Having undergone initiation once again, he too shall attain the state of a Dānava,
provided that by the power of fortune his mother is indeed Dānavatī.
Then one attains accomplishment; at that time, one should contemplate the mantra.
Through the instruction of one's own mantra, one should not entertain thoughts of [another] guru.
Likewise, having become endowed with all siddhis through the great mantra of the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) of the illustrious Lalitā Kālī, one beholds her after one year. || 2-120 ||
In the practice of the Mahāvidyās and other rites of the goddess Kālīkalpalatā, those who understand the word of the Guru need not entertain doubts regarding the Guru. (2.121)
If the supreme practitioner, having deliberated upon the mantra, grasps it quickly, it will certainly become double the merit of infinite millions. (2.122)
The man who, having reflected upon the essence of the Cakra, takes up the mantra, shall have his residence in the city of Vaikuṇṭha for even hundreds of births. (2-123)
Having heard this from the Great Goddess, Mahādeva, his body bristling with horripilation and overflowing with bliss, spoke again to Sarasvatī.
To know the sixteen-spoked wheel, which bestows boons from the hand of the Wheel-Bearer, endowed with most wonderful fruits, and granting dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 2-125 ||
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Great Goddess, if your gaze of great compassion remains fixed upon me in this ocean of affection, please speak so that I may attain the true nature of the Kula.
By your grace, I am Bhairava; I am Time, the Lord of the Universe;
I am the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, fit for yoga, and clad in the directions as my garment.
Now, [I shall describe] the circle of the maṇḍala for the initiation and other rites of all vidyās; it is devoid of time and family (akālakula), and it is both Akāḍama and Kulākula. || 2-128 ||
The illustrious Bhairavī said:
"The Tārā-cakra, the Rāśi-cakra, and likewise the Kūrma-cakra;
the Śiva-cakra, the Viṣṇu-cakra, and the distinct Brahma-cakra. (2-129)
One should speak of the *devacakra*, the *ṛṇidhani*, and the *ulkācakra* after that; then the *vāmācakra*, the *catuścakra*, and thereafter the *sūkṣmacakra*.
Likewise, O Lord, the sixteenth wheel of speech has been described;
it is the mantra-transcending [wheel] which the best of men uphold. (2-131)
For them, there is certainly nothing in the world that is impossible to achieve;
what more need I say here? They shall obtain the vision of the deity. (2.132)
By the grace of the Wheel-King, he shall become one who goes everywhere;
yet that best of the twice-born does not know the movement of all the wheels. (2.133)
Whatever one knows should be investigated as that which brings pleasure to the deity:
the purification of the *tārā* for the Vaiṣṇavas and the purification of the *koṣṭha* for Śiva. (2.134)
The purification of the zodiacal signs for Traipura is remembered as *akaḍama* in Gopāla;
in Vāmana it is *akaḍama*, and in Gaṇeśa it is derived from the discus of Hara. (2.135)
The Koṣṭhacakra belongs to Varāha, and the Kulākula belongs to Mahālakṣmī;
likewise, [these are found] in the Nāmādicakra and in the Bhūtacakra of all.
The wise man should worship the Traipura mantra within the Tāra-cakra;
the Vaiṣṇava mantra is purified by the zodiac signs (rāśi), and the Śaiva mantra is known as Ākaḍama.
The auspicious wheel of Hara belongs to Kālikā and Tārā;
the wheel of the constellations belongs to Caṇḍikā and Gopāla within their respective squares.
One should rely upon all mantras in the wheel of Hari according to the predominance of the debt;
one should know that when the debt is predominant it is auspicious, but when the wealth is predominant there is no such rule.

Having purified the defects, the practitioner should take [the name] in the Middle Country, abandoning the names given by his father and mother, as well as those ending in *śarman* and similar suffixes denoting divinity. (2.140)
Then one should apply the Śrī-varṇa in the circles of the Vidyās in due order.
Listen now to all of that in sequence, which bestows both auspicious and inauspicious fruits. (2-141)
For those who recite and those who meditate, that which is pure is accomplished at that very moment;
it is certain that for the devotees, the mantra alone shall be fully realized. (2-142)
For those born of noble lineage who proceed toward the goal of the path of meditation, even the most perfectly pure great lore and great knowledge are accomplished. (2.143)
And as it was said by Maheśvara in the section on accomplished mantras:
"In that which bestows the eight siddhis, one shall attain the state of union. (2.144)
And the wheel with sixteen spokes is for the sake of the mantra-siddhi of all. || 2-145 ||
Having reflected upon all mantras, that which I have declared as beneficial—first, the system of Bālā and Bhairavī was considered by me as the most excellent. (2.146)
In the practice of Kumārī, Lalitādevī, Kurukullā, and others, the Śrīcakra is declared to be the bestower of fruit, granting the fruits of all cakras. (2.147)
In the practice of the Yoginīs and others, the Tārā-cakra yields great fruit;
likewise in the stainless practice of the Unmattabhairavī-vidyā and so forth. (2.148)
The wheel of the zodiac yields ten million fruits, bestowing various jewels and bringing auspiciousness;
it is used in the practice of Praty-aṅgirā and in the practice of the Ulkā-vidyā and others.
The Śivacakra is of great merit and bestows the fruit of all cakras;
it is [employed] in the Kālikā-carcikā-mantra and in the sādhana of Vimalā and the others.
In the rite of receiving the mantra from those who are Bhairavīs, bestowers of prosperity,
a human being obtains a hundred million-fold merit at Viṣṇu’s discus.
In the practice of Chinnamastā and the other Śrīvidyās, as well as in the sādhana of Kṛtyādevī;
and in the excellent sādhana of Nakṣatradevī, Kāmākhyā, Brahmāṇī, and the others. (2.152)
One shall obtain the great merit of the Brahma-wheel and the fruit of all vidyās; whatever merit is gained from ten million recitations, one obtains that same fruit from [this] retention. || 2-153 ||
In the practice of the great vidyā Vajrajvālā, in the recitation of the mantra, in the practice of Guhyakālī, and in the practice of the Kubjikā mantra. || 2-154 ||
The auspicious Devacakra is proclaimed to bestow the accomplishment of speech in the ritual practice of the mantras of Kāmeśvarī and Aṭṭahāsā.
In the practice of the mantra of the goddess Mandirādevī, who is the abode of Rākiṇī, one should contemplate the great wheel of debtors and creditors, which bestows all accomplishments. (2.156)
Likewise, in the practice of Śrīvidyā, Bhuvaneśānī, and Bhairavī, as well as in the practice of Pṛthvī, Kulāvatī, Vīṇā, and the two [mantras] of Vāmanī; 2-157.
The Ulkācakra is of great merit, bestowing the fruit of kingship and being auspicious;
the Bālācakra, within the mantras of Śivā and other goddesses, bestows happiness. (2-158)
In the recitation of the Phetkārī mantra and the mantra of Uḍḍīyāneśvarī,
the four wheels yield a hundredfold fruit, bestowing the fruit of the great mantras.

In the practice of Drāviṇī, Dīrghajaṅghā, and others, as well as in the sādhana of Jvālāmukhī and others, and in the sādhana of Nārasiṃhī, there is the subtle wheel (sūkṣmacakra) which arises from the fruit.
O Bhairava, the Hariṇī and Mohinī [mantras] are used in the ritual practice of Kātyāyanī,
as well as in the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Devī mantras.
Having carefully deliberated upon the Great Wheel, he who takes up the great mantra is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. (2.162)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature [of the Guru]," within the section on the Great Guru in the Practice of All Wheels (*sarvacakrānuṣṭhāna*), which is the Illumination of the Great Yantra in the Northern Tantra (*uttaratantre*) of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter.
Bhairavī said:
Now I shall explain the wheel that discerns between the opportune and the inopportune time.
The Great Hero, whether divine or possessing the nature of a sacrificial animal, is that upon which he depends.
Having thoroughly examined the Wheel-King (cakrarāja), one should not move a mantra that has been perfected;
for it belongs to a powerful, fierce, majestic, and high-minded [deity].
One should not purify the mantras beginning with Śaktikūṭa, nor those of Siddha and the others, nor those of Varāha, Arka, Nṛsiṃha, and likewise the Pañcākṣara. (3-3)

One need not examine the success or failure of a great mantra, of one belonging to the Time-cycle (Kāla), of one with the Moon as its crest (Candracūḍa), of one with a virtuous mind, or of a neuter mantra. || 3-4 ||
O Śaṅkara, mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are proclaimed as *mālāmantras*,
as are the mantras of the Sun, of Yoga, and of *Kṛtyā*.
One should not purify the Siddhas and others of the god whose seed-syllable is Śambhu, nor those of Cakreśvara, Candra, Varuṇa, or Mahāmanu. (3–6)
One should not examine the status of mantras such as those of Kālī and Tārā in terms of being "accomplished" (siddha) and so forth;
nevertheless, one should purify the mantra, for that [purification] is indeed supreme praise.
That action which results in supreme praise is remembered as being ordained by fate;
that action in which there is no praise at all, one should neither perform nor cause to be performed.
One should receive a mantra that yields ultimate results for the sake of protecting one's lineage;
likewise, one should not receive a mantra from a wealthy person, nor from one who is outside of one's own lineage.
Having grasped it, one goes to the state beyond death; through ten million recitations, one attains perfection.
It is "manana" because it is the supreme knowledge of the universe, and "trāṇa" because it provides protection from the bonds of saṃsāra. (3-10)
Since it brings about accomplishment, it is called a *mantra*.
A *mantra* beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) must never be given to a *śūdra* under any circumstances.
The mantra of oneself, the mantra of the guru, the mantra known as Anapa,
the mantra of the father, and likewise the auspicious mantra of the mother, which bestows the attainment of mantric power.
A Śūdra who performs such acts attains hell, and a Brāhmaṇa goes to a downward state, if they perform rites such as recitation and worship without having been initiated. || 3-13 ||
For those who lack initiation from the Goddess, there is no prosperity, just like seeds sown upon a stone;
for one devoid of the Goddess's initiation, there is neither spiritual accomplishment nor a favorable rebirth. (3.14)
Therefore, with every effort, one should be initiated by a guru;
the investigation of the essence of the *cakras* must necessarily be performed. (3-15)
Even one who is uninitiated shall go to the Raurava hell at the time of death;
therefore, initiation must always be performed with great effort by a Tantric master. (3-16)
On the day preceding the initiation (dīkṣā), one should carefully perform a thorough deliberation;
O you who are honored by the mountains, that procedure must be carried out with great effort. (3.17)
At the beginning and at the end, the wise one should transmit the mantra for accomplishment;
he should draw two lines from east to west and two lines in the middle.
Having rotated a circle with four lines at its corners to form a square mandala,
and having fashioned a great circumference, one should draw the [deity’s] color.
Then, one should write the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', excluding the neuter vowels;
thereafter, one letter each should be written for the signs starting from Aries and ending with Pisces.
O beloved of heroes, one should count them in successive order by moving counter-clockwise;
according to the method of the Tantra, one should count starting from the first letter of the name.

From Aries to Pisces, the scholar of the scriptures [should determine] the states of Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and so forth in sequence; furthermore, the Siddha and other states [are determined] again. (3.22)
The *siddha* [mantra] is established in the ninth, first, and fifth; the *sādhya* in the sixth, tenth, and pair (second);
the *susiddha* in the third, seventh, and eleventh; and the *ripu* (enemy) in the fourth, eighth, and twelfth.
O Lord, this supreme [mandala] beginning with Akaḍa has been described to you;
it is the great wheel in the form of a lotus, endowed with eight petals.
The two letters beginning with 'a' are in the first [row], and the second [letter] is in the second;
in the third [row] there is a pair of ears, and in the fourth, a pair of nostrils.
In the fifth [chapter] the eye is proclaimed; likewise, in the sixth, the upper and lower lips;
in the seventh, the pair of teeth; and in the eighth, the sixteen vowels.
The *kavarga* is on the eastern petal, the *cavarga* on the second, the *ṭavarga* on the third, and the *tavarga* on the fourth. (3.27)
The *pavarga* ending with *ya* is declared on the fifth petal;
having written *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* on the seventh, one should write *la*, *ha*, *kṣa*, and *ma* on the eighth position.
Having reflected upon happiness, sovereignty, wealth, knowledge, youth, and even life itself, as well as the state of being a son and one's own existence, he attains the Wheel. (3-29)
In that regard, one's own name-syllables and likewise the name-syllables of the deity are known to have two kinds of opposition: being in the same position or being in opposite positions. (3.30)
Having written "life" and "death" there on a leaf beginning with the letter 'a' and so forth, the practitioner of mantra should count them; he should always avoid death. (3.31)
Where there is death, there life is certainly not;
established by their mutual opposition, they are like a mantra and its root. (3-32)
In life, one should grasp life; everywhere, one should abandon death.
Indeed, I shall now explain here the distinction between the *kula* and *akula* for practitioners (*mantrins*). (3-33)
Air, fire, earth, water, and space correspond respectively to the fifty letters;
these consist of the five short vowels, the five long vowels, and those ending with the bindu (anusvāra), which arise from their combinations.
The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha*, are proclaimed in groups of five.
The first syllable of the practitioner is also the first syllable of the mantra. (3.35)
