If one knows that [the deity] has a single elemental divinity, it is beneficial for the entire family:
the deity of water is the friend of earth, and the deity of wind is likewise the friend of fire.
Fire is the enemy of all earthly things, and water is the enemy of fire.
The wind is declared to be the enemy of both Indra (electricity/lightning) and Varuṇa (water). 3-37.
An earthen gem is a friend to a watery one; a fiery one is said to be an enemy;
a celestial gem is a friend to all; one should never practice what is contrary to this.

One should indeed draw eight lines with their tips pointing eastward, and from the middle of the eleventh line, one should draw a line extending southward to its limit, passing through the southern and northern divisions.
The Kulākula has been described; now listen again to the Tārācakra.
One should draw four lines in the southern and northern directions. (3–40)
O one honored by heroes, ten lines with their tips pointing westward should be drawn;
then, one should again mark the lunar mansions (tārakās) in the sequence beginning with Aśvinī.
In the very sequence that will be described, one should draw the colored lines in their midst:
one pair, then a third, then the Vedas, and then each pair individually. (3–42)
One pair, likewise one pair, a couple, a couple, a yoke;
one pair, and a third, the moon-eyed one, manifold, and the moon. (3–43)
Two moons, two moons, and four Rāmas (sixteen) are in the auspicious house; these are the consonants, the semi-vowels, and the vowels themselves, both situated in Revatī and Aśvinī. (3–44)
The two *a*-sounds arise from the host of deities in Aśvinī;
the *i*-sound is Bharaṇī Satyā; and the entire group of vowels is Kṛttikā. (3.45)
The Rākṣasī Kṛttikā is on the ground, the destroyer of all obstacles;
she is the mantra of the nose and cheek, and she has the form of the Lord of Rohiṇī. || 3-46 ||
The constellation Mṛgaśirā is proclaimed as the deity in the middle of the lips;
and from the end of the lower lip to the Ārdrā [constellation], all human characteristics are located.
The pair of teeth is covered by Punarvasu; it is dear to humans.
Which deity is to be known as belonging to Puṣya? The bird is Āśleṣā, and she belongs to the Rākṣasas. (3-48)
Those ending in *gha* and *ṅa* under the asterism Maghā, as well as Pūrvaphālgunī, Chaj (ending in *cha* and *ja*) under Uttarā-phālgunī—these are proclaimed to be human. (3–49)
The host of gods has *jha* as its hand; the Rākṣasī is adorned with *ṭa* and *ṭha*;
the Delight of the Gods is *ḍa* and *svātī*; Viśākhā is the Rākṣasī of *ḍha* and *ṇa*. || 3-50 ||
Likewise, the goddess presiding over Anurādhā is Śobhitā;
Dhaniṣṭhā is to be known as the Rākṣasī, and Mūla as the Apanapharākṣasī.

Pūrvāṣāḍhā belongs to humans and is garlanded with the syllable *ba*; by means of Uttarāṣāḍhā, a mortal is associated with the syllable *ma*; Śravaṇa is likewise considered [to begin] with *ma*. (3.52)
Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, and likewise Pūrvabhādrapadā are proclaimed as the asterisms belonging to women. Those beginning with Aśvinī are said to belong to men. (3.53)
Likewise, Uttarābhādrapadā is Mānuṣī, born of Maṅgala; Aṃ, Aḥ, and Ḷha are Revatī, known as the daughters of the gods. (3–54)
Supreme affection exists among those of one's own kind, while it is moderate toward those of different kinds;
there is destruction between Rākṣasas and humans, and enmity between Dānavas and gods. (3.55)
One should calculate again and again: birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enemy, seeker, death, friend, and the supreme friend. (3-56)
One should avoid one’s own birth star (janmanakṣatra), the third, the fifth, and the seventh;
likewise, the sixth, eighth, and ninth are auspicious, as are the pairs and the twins.
If the best of the twice-born does not know his own natal asterism here,
he should [use] the one arising from the first syllable of his name as his own *tāraka*, provided it is not contradictory.

Having disciplined himself, the wise mantra-practitioner, reflecting upon the auspicious and inauspicious, should count [the breaths] in a clockwise direction starting from the first syllable of the practitioner's name. (3-59)
Thus has this been told, O Lord, my very self, O Sovereign of Men:
the Kula-Akula known as Ananta, the wheel of Tārās, which possesses the quality of Manas.
The Tārā-mantra has the luster of a lamp, and the nectar is contained within a jewel vessel;
by contemplating this, a human being attains great accomplishment. (3.61)
I shall now explain the zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*), the supreme characteristic of accomplishment.
Lines should be drawn in pairs in sequence, rising from east to west. (3.62)
In the middle of that, one should place two [lines], and then draw lines from the southeast (Agni) to the south;
likewise, one should draw them in the sequence of southeast (Agni), southwest (Nairṛti), northwest (Vāyu), and northeast (Īśa).

One should carefully inscribe all the letters beginning with 'śa' and ending with 'ha' into the houses starting from Aries and ending with Pisces, having diligently written those letters located in the house of Virgo.

The best of practitioners should calculate [the results] starting from the ascendant (lagna) and ending with the twelfth house (vyaya); he should employ mantras that are favorable to his own zodiac sign, deity, and square.

The purity of the zodiac signs (rāśis) should be understood; one should avoid the enemy sign, the sign of death, and the twelfth house (vyaya). The wise should calculate from one's own sign up to the sign of the mantra. || 3-66 ||

One should count from the letter of the practitioner up to the final letter of the heap [of letters] beginning with the one to be accomplished; the first, the fifth, and the ninth are proclaimed to be the "kinsmen" (bāndhava). (3-67)
Those situated in the second, sixth, and tenth houses are declared to be servants;
those in the third, eleventh, and ninth houses are declared to be nourishers. (3.68)
O Mahādeva, those [yantras] joined with twelve and four [syllables] are killers that bestow all defects;
however, in the Śakti and other [traditions], the *kulacūḍāmaṇi* is the pause (*yati*). (3.69)
One should avoid the sixth house, as well as the eighth and the twelfth;
[the remaining houses are] the ascendant, wealth, brothers, kinsmen, children, enemies, and wife. (3–70)
Death, dharma, karma, income, and expenditure are the twelve houses;
one should declare their auspicious and inauspicious results according to their respective names. (3-71)
In the Vaiṣṇava system, however, a relative is proclaimed for the great enemy.
I shall now describe the Kūrma-cakra, which consists of both auspicious and inauspicious results.
Listen with due respect to the Wheel that pierces the impenetrable, by knowing which the best of the wise understands all the scriptures. (3.73)
The great wheel is shaped like a tortoise and is surrounded by four legs:
the vowels are on the head, and the *ka*-group is on the right leg, while the *ca*-group is on the left leg.
The *ca*-group is proclaimed next, followed by the *ṭa*-group in the lower foot;
below that should be the *ta*-group, and the *pa*-group in the belly. (3.75)
The letter *ya* ending with *anta* (ya) is said to be in the heart; the letter *sa* ending with *anta* (ha) is in the middle of the back;
the seed-syllable of the enemy (*śatru-bīja*), the letter *kṣa*, is in the tail; and [the letter *la*] is in the middle of the penis. (3.76)
Having written it down, the practitioner of mantra should count the wheel that removes the impurities of the Kali age:
there is gain in the vowels, prosperity in the *ka*-group, and the granting of discernment in the *ca*-group.
In the *ṭa*-group [of consonants], one attains the rank of a king; in the *ta*-group, one becomes wealthy.
In the *udara* [group], there would be total destruction; in the *hṛdaya* [group], it bestows much suffering. (3-78)
On the back there is satisfaction for all; on the tail, death is certain. On the region of the phallus there is prosperity, but on the left foot there is suffering.
But when two conflicting [planets] are obtained, one should not perform the visualization of the wheel;
for with a single conflict there is the destruction of dharma, and with the fault of a pair, there is death. (3.80)
Where there is a divine syllable, if one's own [mantric] syllable is present there, yet it is contradictory, one should abandon that enemy and consider another mantra. (3.81)
O Maheśvara, if the garland of letters were situated in separate locations, there would be a state of happiness, and one would not even abandon that happiness. (3.82)
"If there is a defect in a divided house, one should abandon the auspicious mantra.
Thus, O Goddess (O God), I have told you that which bestows both seen and unseen fruits. (3-83)

He who purifies and practices the phonemes as the great lord of the mantra-garland—if he purifies the sovereign wheel, which bestows the auspicious accomplishment of mantras—[he attains success]. (3.84)
I shall proclaim the Śivacakra, O Mahākāla, Lord of the Kula;
by the power of the Śivacakra, one certainly attains accomplishment. (3.85)
In the center of the hexagon, the wise one should draw a square;
in its middle, he should draw another beautiful square of the same color.
Within the triangle situated at the head is the mantra of the abode of Śiva;
one should recite all mantras by moving in a clockwise direction.
One's own mantra is in the Viṣṇu-position within the second triangle,
and the mantra of the station of Brahmā is in the third triangle.
The arrangement of the Śakti-mantra and so forth is likewise below the triangle at the mouth;
the arrangement of the Nāyikā-mantra is likewise below the triangle at the mouth. || 3-89 ||
The mantra and configuration of the Nāyikā, which is auspicious yet difficult to attain, is on its left;
and above that, in the triangle, is the mantra of the configuration of the elements (bhūta).
Below Śiva is the location of the Yakṣa-mantra, which is exceedingly difficult to attain;
in the region at the junction of Viṣṇu and Brahmā lies the eternal station of Mahāvidyā.
O Great Lord, listen now to the place of the vowels and likewise the place of the consonants:
the two vowels *a* and *ā*, and the *ka*-group together with the nasal bindu, belong to Śiva. (3.92)
The eye and the *ca*-group are in Viṣṇu; the *ṭa*-group is heard in Brahmā;
the *ta*-group is in the Power of the Nose, which is the consciousness of the meaning of all mantras. (3.93)
The *pavarga* [consonants] and the pair [of *ka* and *kha*] are not prescribed for the heroine (*nāyikā*).
One should write up to the letter *ya*, ending with *va*, combined with the lower lip (*oṣṭhādharasamanvita*) in the element of earth (*bhūta*). (3.94)
In the Yakṣa mantra, the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) is proclaimed; in the Piśāca [mantra], it is the letter *śa*, joined with *ṣa* and adorned with a bindu, placed below the tooth.
The seed-syllable of the deity Śiva within the mantra is the letter *sa* together with the bindu;
it is proclaimed as the hundred-thousandth syllable situated at the beginning of the Mahāvidyā.
Thus it has been told to you, O Śambhu; now hear the description of the syllable-marks (varṇāṅka):
there are twenty-one in the case of Śiva, and thirty-two in the corner of Viṣṇu. (3.97)
For Brahmā, there is the sixteenth and so forth; in Śaktikūṭa, there are eight yugas; for Nāyikā, there are three fires and five arrows; and for Bhūta, there are seven and the digit nine.
For a Yakṣa, it is the moon (one); for a Piśāca, it is remembered as the eight Vasus (eight);
for all the gods, it is the arrow and the Vedas (five); and for Kṛtyā, it is the sixth every sixth day.
In the center, at the sixth [position], is the Fire-god (Hutāśana) in the auspicious abode of Mahāvidyā;
and for the practitioner and the object of practice, there is a single mark in the temple of the object of practice.
One should count the number of the practitioner (sādhaka) in the upper position and the number of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) below;
for Śiva, two arms are prescribed, and likewise for Viṣṇu, eight left [hands].
Ṛṣicandra is prescribed for Vidhi; likewise, Rāmāṣṭaka for Śakti; Vedabāṇa for Nāyikā; and Aṣṭanavama for Bhūta. (3-102)
In the case of a Yakṣa, the pair and the fourth [are used]; for a Piśāca, the Vajra-kāṣṭaka;
for a Śakti and for subjugation (vaśakṛti), these are to be known [as the respective measures]; and for a Kṛtyā, the Muni-ṣaṣṭhaka.

In whichever house those deities who yield great fruit reside—[Kaṇṭha]—the syllable situated in the body of the nameless letter is remembered as being doubled; having joined it with the number of the goal (sādhya), one should fill it with the sixth and fifth [notes]. (3.104)
One should diligently cause that house to be marked with the syllable of the deity and so forth, as appropriate;
one should make the letter situated as a single remainder, and not perform a separation [of the letters]. (3.105)
One should indeed recognize that as pure, and also through investigation from other sources;
likewise, the Vedāṅka and the Devavarṇaka are determined by the sixth digit.

O beloved, having first doubled the lunar digit (śaśāṅka) and added the digit of the deity-syllable (devatārṇaka), one should then divide that resulting digit by three (rāma). If the resulting digit for the sādhya is too large, it will certainly not be auspicious. (3-107)
If the mark of the practitioner is extensive, it arises in the house;
then, without doubt, he becomes a lord of all lineages, as heard from Rudra. (3-108)
One should double the number of the deity’s syllables and join them with the number of the practitioner’s syllables;
having written down the numerical total of the syllables, the best of practitioners should count them. (3.109)
Having filled it with six arrows (six), one should withdraw it by the number of tastes (six);
afterwards, it is mixed with the self and the limbs (one and six), provided that nothing remains. (3-110)
For one desiring their own name, one should also add twice that number;
thereafter, for the sake of liberation through happiness, one should divide by the number of fires (three).

One should adopt the more concise method, which brings ease to the practitioner; one should not adopt the extensive method involving the determination of the meaning of the vast scriptures for the sake of the subject to be accomplished. (3-112)
Through deliberation upon this wheel, one certainly attains sovereignty;
one should take the multiplier-digit with an equal angle and discard it here.
Indeed, this wheel must certainly be guarded by the gods and asuras;
I shall now describe the Viṣṇu-wheel, which is circular and well-concealed.
Having fashioned the pure wheel that bestows all perfections and grants the fruit [of one's desires], listen, O Lord Mahāviṣṇu, to the auspicious place [of worship]. (3-115)
Having drawn above that a nine-cornered figure consisting of the lap of Lakṣmī’s beloved, which possesses great luster, and above that, the auspicious eight planets; || 3-116 ||
One should draw a house in the shape of a quadrangle with eight voids at its joints;
having drawn that above it as well, O Lord of Wealth, this is the wheel.
In the east is Mahendrābharaṇa, with his hand shining in the upper region, marked by the moon and other signs of the sage Rāma, bestowing all prosperity. (3.118)
In the south is Vahnibharaṇa, with six and four [cells]; below that is Rāmacakra, and in seven and six [cells] is Rāmaka.
Below that, in Nirṛti’s heaven, is the abode of the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), which is exceedingly beautiful; it measures four thousand [yojanas] and is marked by the yugas.
Among the Rāmas, it is rich with void-arrows; in that very [Rāma], it is the abode of vital breath (āyu).
Rich with the strength of the hand-like arms, this wheel has the Lord as its essence. (3.121)
One should draw a nine-cornered figure in the center with five parts for its limbs;
in its middle, one should arrange the syllable within a triangle formed by five corners.
The wise one should draw the first letter and the seventh from Indra downwards;
in the southern sections and corners, he should write the syllable beginning with *ṛ* and the numerical mark.
The wise one should write the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭa* beneath that;
to its left, the letters beginning with *ṭha* and ending with *ma*, which are the cause of the characteristics of the phonemes.
Above that, one should then count the letters beginning with *ya* and the wheel (*cakra*).
Śakra is the lord of the eastern corner; Yama and Anala are the lords of the second [corner]. (3.125)
Nirṛti and Varuṇa are the lords of the third mansion;
Vāyu is the lord of the fourth, as is Kubera. (3.126)
The lord and master of the five houses, the sky-clad knower of all things,
resides within the five corners, established in the disposition of the five elements.
One attains perfection through Prāṇa; there is affliction by disease through Apāna;
all prosperity is found in Samāna; and one becomes destitute through Udāna. (3.128)
And in the Vyāna [vital breath], there is the attainment of lordship; this is the auspicious sign in this regard.
He who abandons a great mantra in his former abode [is characterized by this]. (3-129)
O Śaṅkara, that best of practitioners [proceeds] by way of Viṣṇu;
listen attentively to the distinction and grasp it with care. (3.130)
If there should be a seven-syllable, a three-syllable, and a ten-syllable [foot] in the first house, provided they are endowed with the initial syllable; || 3-131 ||
Then success is attained; everything is of this nature.
The great mantra consists of twenty syllables, with the sixth syllable being a Vedic letter. (3.132)
The wise man should count the syllables as fruitful, pervading from the beginning of the tradition;
likewise, in this my house, there is the auspicious seven-syllable mantra.
One should count the sixth syllable and also the thirtieth syllable, joined with the first syllable of both the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the practitioner (sādhaka). (3.134)
Even upon obtaining just one [of these], the accomplishment of the mantra remains unimpaired;
furthermore, one must certainly count the acquisition of the mantra’s syllables and so forth here in this world. (3.135)
In the southwest and in the direction of the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), the two-syllable and nine-syllable [mantras],
as well as the syllables of the deity of emptiness, O Lord, should be counted by the wise.
Likewise, in this case, one should count within the temple the auspicious syllable-mantra, the five-syllable mantra, and the fifty-syllable mantra. (3.137)
Likewise, one should count [the beads] in the temple of Kubera in the north-western corner,
using the twenty-two syllable mantra as well as the mantra whose sixth syllable is zero.
The five-syllable mantra of Tārikā and likewise the five-syllable [mantra] of Śiva are proclaimed to be fruitful when the seven excellent mantras are received. (3.139)
In the northeast corner of the pentagon, the wise one should count the nine-syllable mantra along with the eight-syllable mantra of the Vidyā, together with their respective fruits.
And this has been said: one should count [the breaths], but never practice what is contrary [to the rules].
Prāṇa is the friend of Samāna, and Samāna is the kinsman of Vyāna. (3.141)
One should accept [a gift] from one who remains in this state; otherwise, he would incur some fault.
O Dear One, affection exists only for a single person, and likewise, what is dear is found only in a single home. (3.142)
Having grasped it, a human being attains the state of Viṣṇu in an instant, provided that he always applies the mantra of the enemy without deliberating upon the discus. (3.143)
If one does not deliberate with effort upon what is dear and beneficial for all the wheels, one certainly cuts off one's own life-span and becomes mute. (3.144)
O Great God, this great mantra is quickly accomplished upon the earth.

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the section on the practice of all *cakras*, in the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*, in the determination of the *bhāvas*, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The venerable Bhairavī said:
"Now I shall describe another wheel; listen with reverence, O Bhairava."
Deprived of which, the great vidyās that bestow boons do not succeed.
Your wheel, manifested by Brahmā, is proclaimed as the Wheel of Brahman (brahmacakra);
through the knowledge of which Brahmā himself creates Bhava by his own power. (4.2)
One who removes untimely death shall go to the supreme state of Brahman;
[draw] a square within a square, and in its center, four squares each.
Having surrounded the central chamber, one should draw a desired, excellent temple;
O Mahādeva, within its eight corners, one should inscribe the sixteen vowels.
Having encircled the eight-cornered figure, the wise one should draw two circles; within the central square house, he should place the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*.
The most excellent practitioner should draw [the diagram] by means of a clockwise rotation;
having drawn the mark in his own house above that, the wise one should perform the calculation.

In the upper region of the four-housed [diagram], one should sequentially write the signs beginning with Aries and ending with Virgo for both the subject and the practitioner within the pair of houses. (4–7)
O Maheśvara, one should first write the signs beginning with Libra at the bottom; this sequence of zodiac signs and so forth is auspicious.
Then, O Maheśvara, one should write it on the right side of the house within the even-numbered houses.
One should write the stars beginning with Aśvinī from left to right;
one should draw them in the order of their syllables within the mandala of the Vedas' abode.
O Lord of the Gods, it should be written in sequence from top to bottom with the digits as its limbs;
then the mantra-practitioner should indeed count it, having joined them in due order.

Having understood that happiness, sovereignty, wealth, prosperity, conflict, the arrival of time, accomplishment, and success reside in the eighth house, one should likewise discern the auspicious and inauspicious therein.
One should count the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of the zodiac sign, avoiding the day of Manu;
thus one attains happiness in happiness and shall obtain sovereignty in a kingdom.

In Dhana one obtains wealth, and in Vṛddhi one shall obtain prosperity. Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, and Virgo are to be known as the presiding deities; now hear again of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). 4–13.
O Great Lord, listen now to those constellations that reside in the right and left portions of the upper pair of houses as well. 4-14.
Aśvinī, Mṛgaśirā, Āśleṣā, Hasta, Anurādhā, as well as Uttarāṣāḍhā, Ārdrā, or likewise Pūrvabhādrapadā. (4.15)
The stars held in the tips of the fingers of Dakṣa have become manifest as deities;
these zodiac signs, which are the lords of these [stars], take the form of planets. (4-16)
The lion is proclaimed as the deity of Cancer, and the virgins are the deities of Virgo;
these are also the zodiac signs that preside over these respective classes. (4-17)
The letter *ka* [is the seed] of *ḍha*, the letter *kha* of *ña*, and the letter *ṭa* of *pha*; the letter *da* of *pha*, and the letter *ya* of *sa*. (4-18)
O Lord, the lords of the syllable *na* should also be known in sequence:
listen, [they are] Rohiṇī, Puṣyā, and likewise Uttaraphālgunī. (4-19)
Viśākhā, as well as the star Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and likewise the star Śatabhiṣaj, are situated on the left side of the temple. (4.20)
These zodiac signs, appearing in the form of planets, are the presiding lords of these [signs]; Aries, Taurus, and Gemini are proclaimed as the sovereign rulers. (4-21)
Those residing in this house constantly protect these syllables:
the letter *ka*, the letter *na*, the letter *ṛ*, and the letter *u*. (4.22)
These are the presiding deities of the letters A, Pa, Ma, Va, and Ha; they bestow the fruit of supernatural powers and liberation. (4-23)
The zodiac signs are also the deities of the lower southern house:
Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius are the lords of the planets.
I have thus described the lords of these stars:
those who are the beloveds of Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, Maghā, Citrā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Śravaṇā.
Likewise, the zodiac signs are considered to have Uttarabhādrapadā as their beloveds.
Now, O Lord, dispeller of fear, hear concerning the color situated in the house. 4-26.
The letter *ya* [is the substitute] for *da*, *ṭa*, and *na*;
the letter *va* for *dha* and *va*; and the letter *ca* for *ya*. (4-27)
These are proclaimed to be the piles of the letter Kṣa and the letter Pa;
they constantly bestow wealth and livelihoods, and they dwell eternally in their own abodes.
The zodiac signs are the beloveds of the lower chamber of the left [side]; however, Capricorn is in the cell below, while Pisces is situated according to the results of the signs in the cells. (4-29)
These constellations are guarded by those bearing spears, nooses, and sword-blades:
Punarvasu, Kṛttikā, as well as Āśleṣā and Pūrvaphalgunī.
Svātī, Mūlā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Revatī are situated in the left house;
their presiding deities are these water-dwelling planetary gods.
Householders are the protectors of these castes; they are the nine clusters [of letters]:
the letter *dh*, the letter *j*, the letter *ṭ*, and those ending with the letter *t*. (4.32)
The letters na, bha, la, and ta-pa cause quarrels and other great evils, and bring about the perception of [impending] death. (4-33)

O Lord, one should avoid those astrological houses that bring ruin to the world; likewise, one should avoid a mantra that belongs to a single deity if it is separated [from its proper context], even if it be very beautiful.
A mantra situated in four places or in two places (yugasthāna) is prohibitive in every respect;
however, a mantra situated in a single house bestows great happiness.
When the zodiac sign or lunar mansion is forgotten, the best of practitioners should take the first letter of the name; in the case of a quarrel, it will result in a quarrel. (4.36)
O Lord of the Gods, if there is an enemy, there will be total destruction, and even a quarrel;
for the Lion protects the pair of eyes, the vowel, and likewise the Virgin. (4.37)

The pair of ears protects Libra; Scorpio protects the conjunction [of Libra]; Sagittarius protects the pair of thighs; Capricorn protects the shanks; and Aquarius and Pisces indeed protect the feet. (4.38)
The upper lip protects the letter *pa*, and likewise the lower lip is the sign Aries (*meṣa*).
The pair of teeth protects the sign Taurus (*vṛṣa*), while the sign Gemini (*mithuna*) is the remaining syllable.
Whatever signs (rāśis) belong to anyone, those are considered auspicious for him;
a single sign always bestows auspiciousness and fulfills one's heart's desire. (4-40)
Otherwise, it is said to cause suffering; yet the practitioner shall partake in success.
One must avoid discord and the sight of death when the signs are of different zodiacal houses. (4-41)
Listen, O Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain: the wheel consisting of the glorious thirty deities should be drawn with six lines, distinguished by east and west. (4.42)
One should draw ten lines from left to right;
in the five houses, one should place the number representing the inhalation (pūraka) and the number representing the extraction (hāraka) at the very bottom of all.
In the center of that, one should fashion the axle (akṣa) joined with the deities and planets;
in the central house, one should draw the filling mark (pūrakāṅka) joined with the seven sages (saptaṛṣi).
To the right of that is the twelfth, and likewise to its right is the sixth;
to its right is the eighteenth, and to its right, the sixteenth is recorded.
Then the number of *pūraka* breaths should be written, and the numbers for Indra and the others from the right;
in the house of Indra, the number one hundred bestows the fruit of the knowledge of the ritual (*vidhi*). (4-46)
O Lord, the wise one should draw seven zeros in the House of Dharma,
and eight zeros along with the gods in the Temple of Ananta.
Then, one should write the number marked by zero, four, and the first vowel (a) in the house of Kālī;
and in the abode of Dhūmāvatī, the lord of the night (the moon) in the positions of zero and five.
Indra and the others should be drawn on the right side, along with the digits and the presiding deities of the moon;
one should draw the deities everywhere, including those associated with zero, eight, and the moon.
Likewise, the two Aśvinīkumāras, [represented by] zero, fire (three), the pair (two), and the non-pair (one);
after that, the eastern house, endowed with a thousand suns (twelve).
The seat located in the temple of Tāriṇī consists of zero and four; likewise, that situated in the abode of Bagalāmukhī is joined with zero, eight, and the moon.
Then, below the Moon-house (Candragṛha), there is a beautiful Wind-house (Vāyugṛha);
this house, consisting of four openings (randhra), bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). || 4-52 ||
The house of Rāhu is a great evil, utterly void and dear to the sages;
thereafter, there is one Hasta, consisting of the pair of space and zero (00). || 4-53 ||
In the temple of Ṣoḍaśī, it is empty and endowed with eight moons;
in the temple of Mātaṅgī, it is empty and endowed with eleven moons.
Below the wind [element] is the abode of Varuṇa, beloved by seven moons;
it is situated in the middle of the house of the young woman and is endowed with eight voids.
The digit situated in the house of Mercury consists of zero, one, and four;
that which resides in the temple of Bhuvaneśī consists of eight zeros and one. (4.56)
Below Varuṇa is the house of Kubera, and there are six pairs; in the abode of Ānanta-Bhairava, ten [houses] are proclaimed. (4-57)
In the center of the earth-abode (dharaṇīgṛha), there is the conjunction of two voids and the moon; Bhairavī resides in the center of the abode, consisting of two voids and the moon.
Situated in the house of the zodiac sign, conjoined with the orbs of the sun, fire, and moon,
and marked by its own wheel beneath Kubera, it bestows all accomplishments.
The house of Īśvara consists of seven voids and is composed of the yugas;
situated within the house of Tiraskariṇī, it is endowed with a thousand marks.
After that is the Kiṅkiṇīmaṇḍala, endowed with eight moons;
after that is the Chinnamastāgṛha, which is a circle of eight empty moons.
Behind it is the abode of Vāgīśvarī, the seventh lunar orb, which bestows great fruit; furthermore, Dharma protects that place. (4.62)
Below the house of Īśvara is the house of Baṭuka;
then follows one's own house, beginning with the eighth from Śūnya, which bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
After that, the house of the ḍākinī, joined with the void (kha) and the sages (munis), destroys the practitioner’s happiness in an instant; of this there is no doubt. (4.64)
It is proclaimed that one's own mantra yields its fruit in one's own home;
thereafter, the abode of Bhīmādevī consists of seven zeros, seven skies, and a lunar orb. (4.65)
One should avoid entering the interior of a house that causes fear in every respect;
however, the most excellent of scholars should write the *lakṣavarṇa* mantra in the remaining two houses.
The wise practitioner should write the letters beginning with 'va' and ending with 'kṣa', bounded by the house of Indra; thereafter, the adept should count them there.
O Maheśvara, one should write the number of the *pūraka* above and the number of the *hāraka* below; the square-number where one's own name-syllable occurs is [the one to be noted]. (4.68)
Having brought [the image] there, the wise one should worship it with marks located on the upper parts of their respective houses;
O Lord Hari, then the remaining portion should be removed from the lower mark.
If the limb of the deity is broad, that limb is considered to bestow auspiciousness;
if it has small limbs, it is said to bestow auspiciousness and bring happiness to the practitioner.
In the single syllable there is great bliss; therein one should also count the speech.
O Lord, it is marked by the wise and leads to the void, and is likewise marked by the deity. (4.71)
Then one should not consider it auspicious, for it is destined for misfortune:
in the first [year] one acquires wealth, while in the second one becomes a favorite of the king. (4.72)
In the third [case], there will be success in recitation; in the fourth, death is certain.
In the fifth, there will be the fifth state (death); and in the sixth, there are intense sufferings.
The mark of five is adopted for the Śaivas and those belonging to the Śākta class;
and for the Vaiṣṇavas, the fifth mark serves as the indicator of their exclusion.
Whichever deities have a desire for violence dwelling in one's mind,
by merely taking up their mantra, one shall become endowed with the eight sovereign powers.
Those who steal the marks of the deity’s residence take away the very sign of that house;
having filled it with the upper mark, one should always remove it with the lower mark.
I shall explain the Great Wheel of Debtors and Creditors; listen to it according to its true nature.
By the mere sight of this grid, one knows [the karmic debts] pertaining to previous births.
Having known the God in His many limbs, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhi);
having grasped the Great Vidyā that is to be personally served, one shall attain liberation.
For those best of the twice-born who receive both the purification of the internal organ and the mantra, their sufferings perish; my command is most powerful. (4.79)
O Rudrabhairava, this great mantra, which purifies the internal organ and bestows fruit, must not be abandoned once it has been seen with affection from a true guru. (4.80)

In that regard, if one knows the subject to be investigated even without investigating the "storehouse" (koṣṭha), one possesses the merit of ten million investigations regarding the Great Vidyā and the Great Mantra. (4.81)
And when not analyzed, Kāmasundarī bestows the aforementioned fruit;
furthermore, the eleven cells have been filled by the God. (4.82)
The knower of reality should write the letters from *a* to *ha* within the squares;
first, in five squares, according to the sequence of short and long vowels. (4.83)
In that analysis, the practitioner should indeed write each pair twice;
the wise one should then write the remaining syllables one by one in their proper sequence. (4.84)
The wise one should write the numerical figures sequentially up to half of the two letters of the vowel *a*; however, within the first house, he should write the number six.
In the second [house] there is the sixth sign, and likewise in the third house;
in the fourth there is the sky-number (one), and likewise in the fifth there are three wheels.
In the sixth house, the fourth; in the seventh, the fourth;
in the eighth, the ninth; and likewise in the ninth, the tenth. (4.87)
Then, one should draw the three marks in the center of the remaining temple;
O Lord, these are certainly declared to be the letters of the sādhya in their proper sequence.
I shall explain the syllable of the practitioner, which defines all purposes:
the second [syllable] is in the first house, and the third is in the second.
In the third [group], the fifth is declared to be "gagana" among the five Vedas;
likewise, in the sixth there is a pair, and in the seventh, the lunar orb.
In the eighth [chapter] the Sky (gagana) is proclaimed; in the ninth, the fourth [element];
in the tenth, the Veda is proclaimed; and likewise, in the eleventh, the Moon (candra).

O Mahādeva, these letters situated in the center of the maṇḍala of letters are known as the *sādhaka* (the practitioner); [one should place] the *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished) letters, distinguished by vowels and consonants, [therein]. (4.92)
In this way, one should fill all the syllables of the mantra with the numbers beginning from eight;
having combined them, one should divide by the number eight, O beloved of Kṣaṇa. (4.93)
In that auspicious mantra, one should remove the syllable whose form has been discarded;
[one should likewise remove] the syllables of the name of the practitioner, distinguishing between vowels and consonants. (4.94)
Listen again and again clearly to those which are situated separately:
from the second letter up to the digit-moon (1), one should take them together with the eight letters beginning with *sam*. (4.95)
If a mantra should have an extra syllable, then the wise person should recite that mantra;
one may also recite it when the syllables are equal, but one should not recite it when it has an excess of syllables.
One should recognize death in the Śūnya; therefore, one should avoid the Śūnya.
Furthermore, a network of figures beginning with the second [digit] is traditionally held to bestow happiness in the Vaiṣṇava [system]. (4.97)
The array of digits beginning with two is remembered as bestowing happiness upon a Vaiṣṇava;
likewise, that very array of digits beginning with two has been fully described.
O Lord, likewise, a digit marked by Indra (1) is auspicious in the solar [family], and in the Śākta [family];
similarly, a digit equal in number to the directions (10) brings auspiciousness to the practitioner. (4-99)
Then listen with effort to that [method of] digits, which is remembered entirely as before;
the positions and the distinct digits are arranged in order from top to bottom.
One should fill in the digits of the goal and the digits of the practitioner according to the number of houses;
when [the total] is multiplied and then divided, that which remains clearly becomes the result. (4-101)
I shall now state its constituent parts as they reside in the eleventh house: Indra (14), stars (27), heaven (1), the sun (12), lunar days (15), the Vedas (4), and fire (3). (4-102)
The eight Vasus, the nine [planets] situated in the angles, and those multiplied by the letters of Sādhyā are: ten, one, seven, four, eight, three, seven, five. (4.103)

One should count the letters of the practitioner's name, starting from the first letter of the name up until the final letter of the mantra, using the number sixty-four (six Vedas and six fires) as the mark for counting. (4.104)
Having divided that number by three, the wise man should divide it by seven;
the remainder is declared to be a debt, while the quotient is called wealth. (4.105)
Alternatively, having performed it in another manner, one should resort to the mantra,
beginning from the first letter of the name up to the syllable of the practitioner.
A wise person should multiply that number by seven and divide it by the left [hand];
this is declared to be the method of calculation for vidyās other than Śrīvidyā. (4-107)
Alternatively, the practitioner should double all the letters of the name of the practitioner by means of the division into vowels and consonants. (4.108)
Then, having joined the subject [with the object] according to the distinction of vowels and consonants, one should reduce the number by eight; listen now to the form of this reduction.
By merely investigating this—the correct sequence of previous conduct regarding all things, whether auspicious or inauspicious—one attains the accomplishment that fulfills every purpose. (4-110)
For one indeed attains that deity who was propitiated in a previous birth.
Now I shall explain another matter; listen with careful attention. 4-111.

The *ulkācakra* is the essence of all things; it determines the defects and other qualities of mantras, is shaped like a fish with its head facing upward, and embodies the form of all mantras and so forth. (4.112)
O Lord, it extends from the shoulders to the tail-end,
consisting of the syllables from the first mantra-syllable up to the twelfth.
One should inscribe [the mantra] on the back for the purification of auspicious and inauspicious [karma], consisting of either thirteen syllables or up to twenty-one syllables. (4.114)
The mantra should be led by practitioners [through the body], situated on the back and within the belly;
likewise, it is declared to be auspicious and bestowing glory from the throat to the end of the tail.
One should not take up an auspicious mantra consisting of between twenty-two and thirty-four syllables if it is located at the tail, nor likewise if it is fixed at the mouth. (4.116)
One should also grasp that which is situated at the head; hear that syllable, O Lord:
beginning with the thirty-fifth, and ending with the twenty-second [of the second group of four]. (4.117)
That which resides in the head is declared auspicious; O Lord, hear now regarding the colors of the faces, beginning with the forty-third letter and ending with the fifty-first.
One should never grasp the inauspicious end that stands before one's face;
listen carefully, for that which stands behind is a useless and great exertion. (4-119)
The deity is constantly provoked by the pains of a weary body;
[this applies] from the fifty-second syllable up to the sixty-first. (4.120)
O beloved, hear now of these letters situated on the tail and those situated on the eyes, beginning with the sixty-second letter and ending with the sixty-fourth letter. (4.121)
The mark situated on the eye, and another situated on the tongue—all this is said to bestow auspiciousness; this is remembered as one or another [of these].
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men for the recitation of mantras belonging to the Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, and Śāktas, as well as for those devoted to other deities. (4.123)
Now, O Mahādeva, I shall describe the Cakrasāra, which is very difficult to obtain—
the Rāmacakra, the Great Vidyā, and indeed the abode of all.
One should take refuge in the mantra consisting of one's own name, which bestows all accomplishments;
at that very moment one attains success—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvara. (4-125)
Listen to that method, O Krodhabhairava, beloved one:
the wise man should draw nine marks from the left side to the right side. (4.126)
In the middle of that, one should gradually place seventeen numerical figures;
thus, one should inscribe the aforementioned vidyās in the sequence starting from the south.
One should write all the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' throughout the entire temple,
as well as all the deities beginning with Bāla and ending with Bhrāmara.
In this house of the nature of space, it constantly bestows fruit;
furthermore, by way of the reverse order, it resides in the temple of the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa'.
The wise one should write from "raktadantā" up to the end of the Śrīvidyā mantra;
then, he should write from the letter *kṣa* onwards in direct order up to the end of the letter *a*.
Furthermore, one should always write the remaining vidyās in the remaining houses, beginning with the mantra for the purification of the body, O dweller on the mountain. (4.131)
Then the practitioner should count those residing in twenty-five houses; O beloved of the Lord of Yogins, listen as I describe the numbers for the houses. (4.132)
From the Bālāgṛha up to the Śeṣa, regarding the measurement of the house according to the sage’s cubit—listen to all of that in due order and attend with careful attention. (4.133)
The wise one should count them in sequence by means of a clockwise rotation:
eight, seven, five, five, three, four, and three. (4.134)
The Vedas with the sages as the sixth, the seven arrows and the sages likewise;
the Vasus in the five Vedas, and the fires in the Vedas as well. (4.135)
Fire and the Vedas (three and four) are fully proclaimed; space follows immediately after that.
Within the house following space, fire is celebrated. (4-136)
Thereafter, listen to all the marks in all the houses starting from the right:
Vahni, Vahniveda-vahni, and Vedavahni. (4-137)
In the Vedas, [the numbers] are stated as seven, five, four, and three;
likewise, six, eight, and seven are mentioned in relation to fire and Agni; and similarly, the sage [is associated with] seven.
Among the sages, they are five, four, and three; likewise, the fires of the sages are three, one, and three; [the others are] three, four, five, and seven; eight, nine, four, and five. (4.139)

Five, seven, three, fire (three), fire (three), arrows (five), arrows (five), arrows (five), Vedas (four), moon (one), Vedas (four), moon (one), Vedas (four), and the fourth [Veda] (Sāmaveda). || 4-140 ||
Rāma, Śrī, Muni, and Ṣaṣṭha are the seven; Rāma and Veda are the eight; Veda, Sapta, Aṣṭa, Vasu, Nava, Aṣṭama, and Saptama [are the others]. (4.141)
Fire, fire, Vedas, and arrows; Vasu, Aṣṭa, Anala, and Vedaka; and seven and eight—these are proclaimed and celebrated as the numerical values for the houses.
Whatever knowledge always resides in the mind through meditative cultivation, relying upon that, the wise person should recite; then he will certainly attain success. (4.143)

The best of practitioners should fill in his own name and the names of the deities with sixteen numerical marks; he should then remove them by means of the numerical mark belonging to his own house. (4.144)
It is certain that for the deity, there remains a great abundance of merit;
even for one who accomplishes but a small portion, there will surely be happiness—of this there is no doubt. (4-145)
The practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the counting according to the stated sequence in the practice of the Mahāvidyā-nāyikā and other rites involving sacrificial elements.
The essence of the wheels (cakrasāra), which is concealed in all tantras, has been fully proclaimed;
through the investigation of these wheels, the practitioner attains accomplishment (siddhi). || 4-147 ||
I shall describe the four wheels; listen, O Lord of Pārvatī!
By means of the union of the left and the right, one should draw five lines.
The knower of mantras should draw five lines according to the east-west division; [he should do so] in four squares on the right side and in four squares on the left.
And below that, in a four-compartment grid located to its left,
one should draw four houses in sequence, starting from the center of the first four-chambered structure.
It is swift, cooling, recited, and furthermore perfected;
it consists of the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and thereafter the syllable *ḷ*. || 4-151 ||
O Lord, listen now to the phoneme situated above, which resides in the cool state:
the letter *a*, the letter *u*, and thereafter the letter *o* (along with *ḷ* and *ḹ*). (4.152)
O Great Lord, hear now the syllables situated below that in the house of recitation:
the letter *i*, the letter *ṛ*, and the letter *e* following after that. (4.153)
Listen to the syllable situated in the house of the Siddhas, which bestows all happiness;
I shall now declare those syllables situated in its four southern houses. (4-154)
Bliss, cognition, and the face, as well as purity—these are all the letters situated within the Kula, which bestow auspicious and inauspicious fruits. (4.155)
The letter *ka*, the letter *ṛ*, the letter *ṝ*, and the letter *ña*—this is called "Abiding in Delight" (*āhlādastha*), which bestows accomplishment through mere attainment. (4.156)
The letter *ga* situated in the palate, as well as *gha*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*;
the letter *ṅa* situated in the mouth, as well as *ca*, *cha*, and *ja*. || 4.157 ||
The letter *u* situated in purity, the letter *ja*, and also the nasalized *ṇa*;
below that is the fourfold abode, which is both worldly and characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*).
This mental, passionate state residing in the four houses, situated in the worldly realm, consists of the syllables *tha*, *da*, and *ma*. (4-159)
Listen, O friend, to the letter *dhakāra* situated in *sattva*, as well as *lakāra*, *yakāra*, the mental [letter], and also *pakāra* and *pham*. (4-160)
Listen, O Lord Five-Faced One, to the nature of the letter *bha* as "forest" (*vana*) and its state within the name consisting of four houses. (4.161)

The man who, situated in an upper chamber, seizes the syllables and mantras of one who is asleep, distracted, smeared with [substances], or under the influence of evil spells, is known as a practitioner of wicked incantations. (4.162)
Avoiding the mantra of one who is asleep, one that is discarded, smeared, or corrupted, one attains success in this world and shall obtain liberation in the next. (4.163)
If, by the power of misfortune, [the deity] is found in houses where one is asleep and so forth,
then one must indeed purify the mantra by means of [the rites of] sleep, paralysis, and pinning.
Having enveloped the inauspicious [impurity] with the net of expanded defects for the sake of purifying the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
and having performed the recitation while encased within the Bhūtalipi, one shall thereafter attain perfection.
But one should not avoid a house that is surrounded by a quadrangle of colored bricks; O Lord, Five-faced One, hear now about the color situated in the sleeping house. (4-166)
The letter *va* and the letter *ha*, as well as another situated within the house; the letter *śa* and the letter *la*, these two situated within the discarded house. (4.167)
The letter *dh* and the letter *kṣ*, these two situated in the smeared house (*liptageha*);
likewise, O Lord, the letter *ś* and space (*gagana*) situated in the wicked house (*duṣṭageha*). (4-168)
One should resort to that mantra which is endowed with one's own good fortune;
I shall now describe the subtle wheel (sūkṣmacakra), which bestows both beneficial and harmful fruits. (4-169)
O Śambhu, having taken up these aforementioned syllables, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).
Beginning from the left and the right, one should draw seven lines. (4.170)
Then, having divided those sections, the preceptor should draw four lines in the center of the bound mandira,
proceeding in order from the south.

The practitioner should write the syllables of the mantra according to the system of numerical signs (*aṅkācāra*). Listen attentively to those signs, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men. (4.172)
O Lord, one should first draw the mark of the arms (the conch and discus) in the first temple;
thereafter, the wise man should draw the mark of the Vedas (the four lines) in the house of Viṣṇu-mantra and the others.
After that, the eighth mark, and also the sixth below the arm;
that is the house of Śaṅkara as well, and after that, the tenth house.
After that, the twelfth mark and the very position of the heroine (nāyikā), then the pair of marks below the sixth, and after that likewise the eighth. || 4.175 ||
That house was displaced by Śambhu; likewise, the eighth [house] after that, as well as the fourteenth syllable in the house below the pair, were likewise [displaced].
To the south of that is the house of the Sun, endowed with fourteen syllables;
behind that is the sixteen-fold mark, and after that, one should write another mark.
To its south is the syllable of the Vedas, and behind it is the eighth syllable;
such is that Brahma-mansion. Now listen again to what is below the sixteenth.
Then the eighth syllable, followed by a pair, and then the eighteenth syllable;
one should take the first and the second [syllables], which is remembered as bestowing auspiciousness. (4.179)
The third position is declared in all mantras to be a great sin;
the second is the first source of suffering, while the third bestows all fortune. (4.180)
And likewise, O Lord, one should take the third for the sake of one's own accomplishment;
in the third [case], the first is auspicious, while the second brings suffering.
And the third is likewise declared to be the eight-syllable Bhaya-mantra;
the fourteen-syllable Bhadra-mantra is the second Sūrya-mantra.
The [mantra] situated in the third [position], at the sixteen-fold [node], bestows great auspiciousness;
the eightfold [mantra] at the sixteen-fold [node], in the fourth [position], is the slayer of enemies. (4.183)
The eight-syllable [mantra] situated in the middle of the third house bestows Brahma’s auspiciousness,
and it is likewise situated in the middle of every subsequent house.
And the eighth is Mahābhadra, which bestows mental fearlessness;
it is auspicious with eighteen marks, and likewise so in the remaining three houses.
Having understood whether the syllables of whichever mantra reside in the mind are auspicious or inauspicious, one should then practice that specific mantra-syllable. (4-186)

One who is devoted to Śakti alone should receive the mantra residing in Viṣṇu, the mantra residing in the Nāyikās, that which resides in Śiva, that which resides in the Sun, and that which resides in Brahmā. (4.187)

A Vaiṣṇava should take refuge in Viṣṇu for the sake of the meaning of Viṣṇu’s mantras; a Śaiva should take refuge in Śiva; and one who mutters the mantra of a Goddess should always practice the phonemes of that Goddess. (4.188)
One who seeks the meaning of the investigation into the Sūrya-mantra should take recourse to the Sūrya-mantra;
[it consists of] that which is situated in one, that which is situated in a pair, and likewise that which is situated in three.
Having understood the mantra, one should take it up; otherwise, it will become inauspicious.
This or another such mantra is sung among the divine heroes. (4-190)
Therefore, the wheel is said to bestow all accomplishments (siddhis) upon the bound soul (paśu) with certainty;
by the power of this wheel, the bound soul is considered equal to a hero (vīra).
Having become endowed with all accomplishments, he beholds her after one year.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahāmantroddīpana*, in the section on the practice of all *cakras*, in the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*, in the determination of the *bhāvas*, within the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter: the supreme among all supreme wheels, for the sake of the Great Wheel of Speech,
by the mere contemplation of which a man becomes one who can take any form at will.
Next, O Lord, listen in due order to the method for the heroes:
one should write the syllables within a square consisting of four compartments. (5-2)
In each of four quadrants, provided with four by four cells, the sixteenfold temple is proclaimed as the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires and aims. (5.3)
The wise one should draw a square grid consisting of four compartments; furthermore, he should draw another set of four there as well, in due order.
Then, having written [the letters] from *a* to *kṣa* in all the central chambers in a clockwise sequence, one should count them.
Likewise, the ninth pair consists of Candramas and Agni, who has the color of Rudra;
the tenth is Vedamarka, and the sixteenth is Vasu, who possesses ten flavors.
The fourteenth is the derivative (bhautika), and the fifteenth is the seventh; I have declared these syllables, situated in the fire and moon squares, by means of the symbolic numbers.
Immediately thereafter, one should count the numerical value of the syllables situated within this [maṇḍala], starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra. (5–8)
One [letter] for each of four squares, thus making a group of four squares; again, within those squares, starting from the beginning of the name according to its true form. (5–9)
The wise man should count them in order as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*.
The *siddha* [mantra] is accomplished in time; the *sādhya*, however, [is accomplished] through recitation and fire-offerings. (5-10)
The *susiddha* [mantra] destroys one's own lifespan because it is not grasped;
the *siddha* syllable is said to be a kinsman, while the *sādhya* is called a servant. (5-11)
The phonemes situated in the Siddha-chamber are kinsmen who grant all desires;
through recitation, great accomplishment shall arise, and through intensive service, one becomes a servant [of success]. (5.12)

The nourisher (poṣaka) who is desired nourishes; the destroyer (ghātaka) will certainly destroy. One who is accomplished (siddha) is accomplished according to what was stated; one who accomplishes through accomplishment (siddhasādhaka) is twice as effective. || 5-13 ||
A *siddha* [mantra] results from upward recitation; a *susiddha* [results] from downward recitation. A *siddhāri* destroys one's kinsmen.
A *sādhya* becomes a *siddha* when doubled; a *sādhya* [recited] against a *sādhya* is useless. (5-14)
A *susiddha* [mantra] kills the enemies of one's kinsmen through double the recitation;
a *sādhya* [mantra] kills them through a recitation twice as great as that for a *susiddha-siddha*. || 5-15 ||

A planet that is well-established (susiddha) destroys one's own lineage; an enemy that is well-established (susiddha) destroys enemies. An enemy that is established (siddha) kills sons, while an enemy that is to be accomplished (sādhya) kills daughters. (5.16)
If that mantra is well-perfected, it destroys the wife [of the enemy]; its enemy destroys those born of the same lineage.
If it should reside in the hand of the practitioner on earth, it destroys the enemies' desires. (5.17)
At the conclusion of that, for the sake of protection, one should indeed perform such rites as the *kriyā*;
O Great Hero, Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, hear now the method for that.
Having written the enemy's mantra on a banyan leaf, one should cast it into a stream;
thus he shall be liberated from the mantra by virtue of my command. (5-19)
Furthermore, the brahmin, filled with joy, should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over a measure of cow's milk equal to one *droṇa*.

Having drunk the milk and meditated upon it within the mind while reciting the mantra, one should cast it into the midst of water for the purpose of neutralizing the spells released by enemies. (5-21)
I shall further describe another method: having fasted for three nights or a single day according to this rite, one should perform worship on a Saturday or a Tuesday.
Having recited the mantra one thousand or even one hundred and eight times, one should then cast it away into the circle of the Ocean of Milk.
Alternatively, whether in the presence of that guru or in another place,
by reflecting upon the syllables of the mantra and grasping them, one shall attain liberation.
If the supreme practitioner obtains the great mantra in a dream, then he attains accomplishment; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Lord of the Kula. (5.25)
O Lord, one should diligently preserve that mantra of the Guru within the Kaulika tradition;
when [this is done], accomplishment will occur at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. (5.26)
O Lord of the gods, if one should cause an enemy to recite a mantra—having carefully considered another mantra of either Viṣṇu or Śiva—(then he shall be subdued). 5-27.
If one [desires to] subdue an enemy, then the mantra of power (śaktimantra) should be of this form:
accompanied by Oṃ, Vauṣaṭ, and Svāhā at the beginning, the end, and the middle.
Having performed [the ritual] and recited [the mantra], one attains great accomplishment as if established in a form at will;
of this there is no doubt—this is my command, O fair-complexioned lady. (5.29)
Listen, O Lord, to the fruit of the Cakra, which is auspicious through its contemplation and practice,
as well as the Prāsāda and the Mahāmantra from the lotus-mouth of the true Guru.
If it is obtained through good fortune, success is indeed attained without a doubt;
in its absence, there is the mantra of accomplishment (*siddhimantra*) which is oriented toward both visible and invisible fruits. (5.31)
It produces great wonder and increases the joy of the heart;
merely by attaining the presence of the true guru, whether in a dream or in reality, it bestows liberation. (5-32)
And having abandoned that mantra, they dwell for all time in the Raurava hell of terrible darkness, subject to the power of my command.
In that very place, the investigation of the *cakrasāra* and so forth is mere empty talk;
it is the enemy-mantra of great merit, the most supreme among all mantras. (5.34)
One becomes a refuge for the Great Vidyā through merits accumulated over ten million lifetimes, and even through the fruits of ten million merits produced by ten million lineages in a dream. (5.35)
The practitioner certainly attains the mantra for the sake of enjoyment and liberation;
therefore, the *cakra* is not to be deliberated upon—for to deliberate upon it would lead to death. (5.36)
But if the investigation of the wheels is performed with wonder even in a dream, then from the investigation of these wheel-syllables, the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi) are bestowed. (5-37)
Wind, liberation, wealth, the perfection of yoga, prosperity, auspicious riches, the purity of the body of dharma, and the destruction of untimely death. (5-38)
Beholding the lotus-feet of Gaurī bestows the fruit of one’s desires;
one attains worldly enjoyment, liberation, and the abode of Hara—of this there is no doubt. (5.39)
If the supreme practitioner performs all these considerations in due order, the results of the wheels and so forth, as well as the time, will be calculated accordingly. (5.40)
Then one attains the eternal fruit of all things; there is no doubt in this.
Through inquiry, one certainly obtains the great vow and discernment. (5.41)
One attains accomplishment suddenly by contemplating the King of Wheels;
all the gods praise water that has taken refuge in the mantra of the wheel. (5.42)
The accomplishment of speech will swiftly occur, and he shall possess the perfection of prāṇāyāma and the other [aṅgas];
the powerful practitioner should prostrate to all on the ground and move about. (5.43)
Thus, O Lord, I have described to you the sixteen-fold auspicious wheel;
by [worshipping] these wheels, O Leader of the World, one shall attain the state of union (sāyujya). || 5.44 ||
Therefore, one should everywhere perform the investigation [of reality], which is the auspicious beginning of all the cakras and so forth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the section on the Siddhitantra, within the practice of all cakras, in the Mahātantroddīpana of the Uttaratantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Bhairava said:
"O Śrīdevi, now speak of the state (bhāva) according to the sequence of the divine, the hero, and the animal."
He was eager to hear about the most marvelous state of the animals.
O Sovereign of the Universe, I desire to remain situated in the ocean of bliss; if by the power of my fortune it is possible, contemplate the essence of your command for my success.
Mahābhairavī said: O Lord of Beings, O Lord of Heroes, O Divine Lord, O Treasure of Compassion!
O You whose heart’s radiance is manifest, O Moon-crested One, listen to that. (6.3)
O Lord, listen in detail to Kālī, who has the form of a slender digit of beauty, who is united with the two-fold austerity, and who abides in the state of a *paśu* (bound soul). 6-4.
He who performs the worship of Durgā and the worship of Śiva is the best among men;
indeed, he who performs these is certainly remembered as the most excellent of beings.
If the practitioner performs only the worship of Śiva, he is a glorious "middling among the bound" (paśu); however, if he does so together with Śivā, he is "supreme. (6-6)
The exclusive Vaiṣṇava is indeed remembered as the supreme lord among bound souls (paśus), while those who always perform service to the elements and the deities are considered mediocre.
It is declared that those who stand in the midst of cattle dwell in hell; of this there is no doubt.
Service to you, service to me, and service to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others [are all equal].
O Great Lord, having performed [this] for all other beings, for the leaders, for the yakṣiṇīs, and for the bhūtinīs, service thereafter bestows auspiciousness.
Those who always perform service to Brahmakṛṣṇa and others, as well as those supreme among men who perform the twofold service to the venerable Tāraka-Brahman; || 6-10 ||
For them, the deities such as the Bhūtas and others, who grant all desires, are incurable;
therefore, a person devoted to the service of Viṣṇu should avoid the path of animal sacrifice.
And their respective explanations must be proclaimed in each of those chapters according to the appropriate procedure; listen in due order, O Lord, my beloved. (6-12)
Therefore, having risen early in the morning, the animal, who was now a most excellent scholar,
placed the auspicious lotus-feet of his gurus upon the lotus of his head.
If, after having dissolved [the visualization], one should indeed meditate upon a single auspicious foot,
having worshipped the Hero with offerings rather than with hymns of praise— 6.14.

The three worlds were pervaded by her splendor; she was the great festival residing within the mandala, blazing with a radiance like ten million flashes of lightning, yet as cool as ten million moons.
One should raise up the Great Goddess, who is of the nature of mind, intensely red, and encircling the self-manifested liṅga in the form of three and a half coils.
The Yoginī Khecarī, who consists of the movement of the two breaths— exhalation and inhalation— manifesting as twelve finger-breadths, whose form is wind, and who resides in the root-lotus.
She whose form encompasses the four castes from the letter *va* to *ṣa*,
who possesses the radiance of thousands of millions of millions of suns, and who deludes the entire world.
She who moves within the intervals between the limits of the great and subtle paths,
the deity of speech who protects the three worlds, and whose form is Śambhu.
To the Goddess who bestows great intelligence, who moves through the thousand-petaled lotus,
who consists of radiant light upon the path of the Great Subtle, and whose nature is death.

Having meditated again and again upon her who is the form of time, who possesses all forms, who is omnipresent, and who consists entirely of consciousness, as she is immersed in the ocean of nectar within one's own head; || 6.21 ||
Having caused the drinking of the nectar, one should bring it back again to its place;
at the time of bringing it back, however, [one should do so] within the center of the Suṣumnā.
Having caused her to be drenched with nectar, one should worship her again in her respective places;
at the time of her upward departure, however, one should contemplate her as consisting of great splendor.
But at the time of returning, [one should contemplate] Mahākulakuṇḍalinī, whose form consists of the bliss of nectar, bathed by streams of sudhā.
By meditating again and again, one shall become the Lord of all Siddhis;
having visualized the Great Goddess, blazing with rays of light, in that place.
Having joyfully worshipped that auspicious liberation consisting of nectar-bliss,
one should worship Māyā or the seed-syllable of Kāma by means of the seed-syllable uttered mentally.
Having recited it fifty times with the garland of syllables in the direct order along the true path,
and having recited it again in the reverse order, this hymn brings victory everywhere.
Having recited it, one attains accomplishment; listen to that hymn, O Bhairava. (6.28)

When on this earth will she—who rescues one from birth, who destroys youth, who possesses the seed-syllables of the Vedas and other scriptures, who moves through the words of the virtuous, and who bestows what is dear—be meditated upon constantly in the mind? O Earth, protect me; O Dispeller of calamities!
O Dhātrī, you yourself [are the mother] of those beginning with the wives of the primordial gods, yet [I am] a most wretched beast.
O Blessed Lady, you who consist of the syllables of the blood-hued nectar-moonlight, who are coiled in the form of a serpent,
and who rest upon the waking tortoise— look upon me!
I am stupefied by the defects of the foul stench arising from flesh, yet I am engaged in the duties prescribed by the Vedas and other scriptures.
Make your body exceedingly white by means of the rays of ten million fresh moon-disks.
One who seeks success and recognizes his own faults employs the artifice of traveling by land through the power of knowledge;
he follows a path crowded with serpents, having abandoned the city for the illusory wrong path of prosperity.
If he resorts to this at the time of dawn or even at midday—
He who constantly chants the lotus feet of Kulakuṇḍalinī shall become a perfected one (siddha). || 6-31 ||
In the exceedingly pure four-petalled lotus of wind and space, which yields the fruits of one's desires,
my own mother— now eternally embodied, known as Śāṅketitā,
and conceived as Vidyākuṇḍalinī— is meditated upon as the creative power of Māyā.
By those who have been born into the family of the Siddhas, through prostrations and true hymns of praise to Śambhu—
there resides the Yoginī, the deluder of Dhātṛ and Aśaṅkara, who emerges from the canvas of the shadow of the three worlds,
and who is the weapon that strikes down the great bliss of beginningless saṃsāra.

She who severs all knots, whose own arms are serpents, subtler than the subtlest, the delighter in the knowledge of Brahman, the abode of the Kula, she is meditated upon as the destroyer of obstacles. (6.33)

I bow to the venerable Kulakuṇḍalī, who, with her three folds and limbs, has spontaneously enveloped the sky; she who is the beloved, the restless mind of the Creator, the youthful maiden, and the partless one;
that Goddess who shines forth with the face of the Vedas, the source of all existence, and the purifier.
I perform the rite of honoring the Self-born Goddess upon the heads of those who are beloved.
She whose voice possesses the resonance of ten million mṛdaṅga drums and the sound of ten million lutes;
whose face is ever full with the splendor of the lotus at the root of the nectar-filled breasts of the Mistress of Life (the Goddess);
who dwells within the darkness of the faces of ten million horses born from the clouds of the month of Āṣāḍha.
May she, the Mother, protect me as I tread the subtle path; she is the benefactor of yogis.
Relying upon you, O Mother, men go swiftly to Vaikuṇṭha and Kailāsa—
to you, the sole sporter of bliss, whose face brings joy equal to a hundred moons,
the primal cause, O Śrī Kulakuṇḍalī, who holds the beloved hand, O Kālī, who illumines the Kula!
I bow down to that place, O lady of auspicious speech; lift me up, for I am but a beast.
This eightfold hymn, which yields great fruit and resides upon the path of the Kuṇḍalinī power—whosoever recites it having risen at dawn shall certainly become a yogi. (6.37)
Indeed, by reciting this for just a moment, one becomes a lord among poets in this world;
he who recites it, Śrī Kuṇḍala, becomes a great yogi absorbed in Brahman.
Thus, O Lord, I have recited to you this tender hymn of Kuṇḍalinī;
by the grace of this prayer, even among the gods, Bṛhaspati became the preceptor.
By the grace of her hymn of praise, all the gods became endowed with supernatural powers (siddhi);
and Brahmā, the lord of all the gods, became long-lived for two parārdhas.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the husband of Bhagavatī, is also standing near me;
know me to be the supreme Śakti, whose nature is both gross and subtle.
She who causes all things to shine, who dwells on the Vindhya mountains,
the daughter of Himālaya, the perfected one whose very nature is the perfected mantra.

She who abides in the Vedānta, Śakti-tantra, and Kula-tantra; she who penetrates the meaning of the Kula-tantras; she who resides within the Rudrayāmala; and she who brings about stability and preservation.
And she whose nature consists of the five mudrās, who is garlanded by the union with Śakti,
and who illuminates ten million strings of jewels like the light of the moon and sun.
She who bestows great intelligence upon all beings, who removes the afflictions of the Dānavas,
who effects the maintenance, creation, and dissolution [of the world], and who abides in an ocean of compassion.
She dwells in the abode of great delusion, resides within the body of Dāmodara,
is enriched with parasols, chowries, and jewels, and holds a great trident in her hand— she is the Supreme Goddess.
She who bestows knowledge, she who bestows growth, she who grants the collection of the jewel-garland of wisdom;
she whose radiance is the very embodiment of all splendor, possessing infinite millions of forms.
O Śambhu, O scholar who is the leader of yoga, always contemplate Lakṣmī, the bestower of wealth upon the poor, who is the delight of Nārāyaṇa.
Listen with due respect concerning the rebirth of the bound soul (paśu):
suddenly, the bound soul attains perfection, becoming equal to Nārāyaṇa. (6.49)
He goes to the city of Vaikuṇṭha with a four-armed body,
holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in his hands, and having Garuḍa as his vehicle.
By the grace of Mahāvidyā, he is the very nature of the Great Dharma;
he is the state of the bound soul (*paśubhāva*), yet also the Great State (*mahābhāva*) that bestows the perfection of all states of being.
Having first established the state of the bound soul (paśubhāva), one should afterwards perform the necessary rite:
the state of the hero (vīrabhāva) and the great state (mahābhāva), which is the most excellent among all states.
Thereafter, desiring the fruit [of liberation], he who is intent on the welfare of all beings attains supreme beauty, a divine state, and the great fruit that leads to liberation.
The man who desires knowledge, who desires wealth, and who desires jewels should perform the threefold divine disposition, the supreme means for accomplishing that disposition.

Through devotion, one obtains today musical instruments, wealth, jewels, and great fruit—[a fruit] equal to the merits arising from the gift of ten million cows and the gift of ten million Śālagrāmas. (6.55)
Whatever fruit is obtained by worshipping ten million liṅgas in Vārāṇasī, a mortal obtains that very fruit in an instant; of this there is no doubt. (6.56)
At the beginning, during the first ten *daṇḍas*, there is the state of the Paśu;
likewise, at midday, during the [next] ten *daṇḍas*, the state of the Vīra is proclaimed.
At the tenth *daṇḍa* of the evening, one should worship the deity who bestows auspiciousness while abiding in the divine state (*divyabhāva*),
or else, remaining in the animal state (*paśubhāva*), one should worship the desired deity and others.
If the practitioner performs worship until the end of his life, he shall attain great siddhi;
he shall become the preceptor of all and gain increasing sovereignty day by day.
If he possesses a heavy nature, then he may attain Madhumatī;
if he is discerning, he departs for a dwelling in the great forest.
Whether established in the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) or residing in his own city,
by means of the mere status of a Pīṭha-brāhmaṇa and through the Great Sixfold Hermitage (mahāṣoḍhāśrama), [he attains the goal].
The practitioner established in the state of *paśu* shall attain the perfected *vidyā*,
provided he [attains] the deity of the Great Kaula who resides in both the prior and subsequent states.
The mantra practitioner established on the family path certainly attains accomplishment;
if the vidyās are pleased, he shall then obtain the state of a hero.
Through the grace of the heroic state (vīrabhāva), one shall attain the divine state (divyabhāva). Those best of men who embrace both the divine state and the heroic state— || 6.64 ||
They are undoubtedly masters of the wish-fulfilling tree and creeper of desires;
they are established in the stages of life, devoted to meditation, and proficient in mantra and tantra.
Having become [one with] the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha), the wise ascetic should always dwell there;
what need is there for any other fruit, if he attains the state of being [the deity] and so forth? (6.66)
Merely by grasping this state of being, a man shall become a knower of me;
the power of his speech will be swiftly perfected, and his words will reach the hearts of others. (6.67)
Leaving Nārāyaṇa aside, Lakṣmī dwells in his palace;
my full vision, however, is fixed upon his body—of this there is no doubt. (6.68)
"One certainly attains success; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Mahābhairava said:
"O Great Goddess, you have indicated it; please speak out of compassion. (6.69)
Indeed, in all tantras and vidyās, there is only the symbolic convention of existence;
nevertheless, in the Śaktitantras, it especially bestows all accomplishments.
Having explained the procedure for the knowledge of existence (*bhāvavidyā*) and the means of accomplishing existence (*bhāvasādhana*), Ānandabhairava said:
"O God, existence is threefold, according to the sequence of the divine (*divya*), the hero (*vīra*), and the animal (*paśu*). (6–71)
In this regard, O Mahādeva, the guru of this [practitioner] is threefold, and likewise are the mantra-deities; this divine state bestows all accomplishments and the highest welfare.
The second is declared to be middling, while the third is censured by all;
[the latter results] from excessive recitation, burnt offerings, and extensive physical austerities.
O Goddess, without the state of being (bhāva), the tantras and mantras do not bestow their fruit;
what is the use of heroic practice (vīrasādhana) alone, or what is the use of the lineage of the knowledge of liberation? (6.74)
What is the use of worshipping the sacred seats (pīṭha), what is the use of feeding virgins and so forth, and likewise, what is the use of giving gifts to please one's own wife or others? (6.75)

What is the use of having conquered the senses, and what is the use of performing the duties of one's family tradition, if one’s disposition is not pure in its aim and does not remain devoted to the lineage? (6.76)
Through devotion one attains liberation; through devotion, the increase of one's lineage;
through devotion, the prosperity of one's clan; and through devotion, the purification of one's family. (6.77)
What is the use of such worship if the state of being [realization] does not arise?
By whom is the Vidyā worshipped, and by whom is the Mantra worshipped? (6.78)
O Lord of Gods, the absence of fruit arises from the non-existence of the [inherent] state;
my mind hesitates at the proclamation of this mantra. (6.79)
The gathering of all jewels would likely conquer the three worlds;
how could one act without first observing a secluded place? This I shall tell you.

The illustrious Ānandabhairava said: "O Great Goddess! By your grace, O Vidya Svapnaprabodhini, O Maheśvarī, the initiation for all the fivefold cosmic manifestations (pañcaprapañca) should be bestowed."
"O Lord, since I am the cause of the sleep of all beings,
tell me that which is the most excellent among the paths of being."
The illustrious Mahābhairavī said:
O Kaulika, listen with diligence to the first divine state,
the Vidyā worshipped by all the gods, which is filled with a mass of splendor.

Having visualized the entire world as consisting of light through the conceptualization of forms—either with those forms composed of that very light or, alternatively, devoid of attachment—one [should meditate]. (6.84)
Having made oneself identical with that, and likewise all states of being, one should meditate upon every woman and worship her with a restrained mind. (6.85)
