One who is endowed with an entire lineage, born of various castes, or even originating from various countries, and who is possessed of good qualities and free from indolence. (6.86)
From the second year onwards, until she reaches the eighth year of age,
one should recite [the mantra] and worship a maiden who is beautiful and enchanting.
Abiding in a divine state, one directly obtains the fruit of the tantras and mantras, simply through the worship of a maiden and by means of feeding her and other such acts. (6.88)
There is no doubt that seeds numbering one, two, three, and so forth, yield fruit;
having given them flowers, fruit, and likewise unguents and the like. (6.89)
Having offered oblations dear to him and the food offering, being permeated by that same disposition,
he joyfully [partook] of the garlands from his body, acting with the playful movements of a child.
One who is fond of birth, endowed with the curiosity for conversation and play,
having performed there that which is truly dear to him, shall become a master of accomplishments (siddhīśvara).
A maiden shall be the source of all prosperity; a maiden is the scorcher of all enemies.
[She is the embodiment of] the fire-oblation, the worship with mantras, the daily rites, and the noble practices of the Kaulika tradition.
O Lord, without the worship of a maiden, the supreme practitioner does not obtain that great dharma of various fruits; he obtains only half of each such fruit. (6.93)
A hero obtains a fruit a million times greater by worshipping a young maiden;
and a scholar of the lineage [obtains it] by offering a handful of flowers to a girl. (6.94)
If one offers that flower, one becomes a donor of ten million Meru mountains;
one would obtain in a mere instant the great merit born from that knowledge.
By him who has fed a maiden, the three worlds have been fed.
A one-year-old girl is Sandhyā, and a two-year-old is Sarasvatī. (6.96)
She who is three years old has three abodes; she who is four years old is Kālikā;
she who is five years old goes with the Sun; and she who is six years old is Rohiṇī.
With seven [syllables] she is Mālinī; with eight, she is Kubjikā in person;
with nine, Kālasandātrī; and with ten, Aparājitā.
In the eleventh [year] she is Rudrāṇī, and in the twelfth year she is Bhairavī;
in the thirteenth [year] she is Mahālakṣmī, the mistress of the sixty-two sacred seats (pīṭhas).
The *kṣetrajña* is considered the fifteenth, and Ambikā the sixteenth;
having worshipped them in this sequence until no more flowers remain. (6.100)
One should perform worship from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the full moon according to the various stages of increase,
especially on all the great festival days and during the Pavitraka rite.
O Lord of Gods, on the Mahānavamī day one should worship the Kumārīs;
therefore, those up to sixteen years of age are designated as Yuvatis.
In that regard, there may be the manifestation of existence; that existence is considered supreme.
It must be protected with effort, and once protected, one should cause those [teachings] to be revealed.
Having performed the great worship and other rites with garments, ornaments, and food, even one of meager fortune shall worship [the deity] and obtain the auspiciousness of victory. (6.104)
Furthermore, by explaining this to others, there is great fruit in the purpose;
he who worships according to the rite, abiding in the states of the divine, the hero, or the animal (paśu), [attains success]. || 6.105 ||
In the three states, there is great bliss; in the divine, there is virtuous action and its excellent fruit.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Elements," within the section on "Accomplished Mantras" in the *Kumāryupacaryāvilāsa*, from the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*. 6.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
Now I shall proclaim the worship of the Kumārī, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
For those who are free from the category of diseases, success is swiftly attained upon the earth.
O Mahādeva, Lord of the lords of heroes, tell me of that kind of place:
whether it be a site for worship, a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), or even a temple of the gods.
To the beautiful one, who increases supreme bliss and bestows victory;
to her whose nature is that of Kālarātri, the venerable Gaurī, adorned with red unguents.
A girl born of a temple, or a Rākṣasī, or an excellent woman;
a dancer’s daughter, a low-caste girl, or likewise the daughter of a Kāpālika—(7.4)
Likewise, they [approached] the daughter of a washerman, as well as the daughter of a barber, the daughter of a cowherd, and the daughter of a brahmin. (7.5)
Whether it be the daughter of a Śūdra, the daughter of a Vaiśya, the daughter of a Vaidya, or even the daughter of a Caṇḍāla, wherever she may reside in any stage of life (āśrama). || 7-6 ||
Having diligently brought the daughter of a circle of friends,
one who is devoted to meditation on the Self should honor her with supreme joys.
Listen in due order, O Lord of Devas, served by the hand of Varuṇa;
[he is] the embodiment of supreme bliss and the beauty of the cause of bliss.
Whoever performs my worship every day with pure devotion,
for him there shall certainly be the worship of young maidens and the offering of food to the Sun.
The radiant form of the moon and of fire is praised in all states of being;
from worshipping it, from speaking of it, and even from eating it, there is auspiciousness. (7.10)
May my own love, established as a deity protected by the gods, belong to the divine Bālabhairava and to Vaṭuka Kāminī. (7-11)
O Lord, my daughter has been honored with various divine rites of worship for my son, who is possessed of great splendor and is revered by all the worlds.
The maiden Kumārī is proclaimed to be the omniscient sovereign of the world;
having brought her here for the sake of the worship of all the worlds, the lords of the gods [assembled]. (7.13)
They worship the Great Goddess who dwells in the secret state, who is always worthy of offerings of food and longing, and who smiles with satisfaction at garlands. (7.14)
That goddess, the maiden who is the leader of the gods, does not cry out in vain;
she, whose very nature is Sarasvatī, is worshipped by all the leaders.
Worshipped by devotees of Śiva, devotees of Viṣṇu, and those who worship other deities,
she is honored by all people and is certainly worshipped by the wise.
Through worship one obtains worship; through worship one obtains prosperity;
through worship one acquires wealth; through worship one obtains the earth. (7.17)
Through worship, one obtains prosperity and the highly powerful Sarasvatī;
the great sciences become favorable, as do all the gods—of this there is no doubt. (7-18)
The Bālabhairavas, Brahmās, and Indras; the Brāhmaṇas who discourse on Brahman;
the Rudras and the hosts of gods; and the Vaiṣṇavas who possess the form of Viṣṇu.
The incarnations are two-armed Viṣṇus adorned with crowns;
likewise, there are other guardian deities of the quarters and the Teacher of the moving and unmoving. (7.20)
All the Dānavas, endowed with various sciences and full of guile—whosoever among them were established in liberation—were undoubtedly satisfied. (7.21)
If I am indeed the embodiment of contentment, what need is there to speak of others in the world?
By performing the worship of the maiden, one may bring the three worlds under one's control.
Great peace shall swiftly arise, bestowing the fruit of all merit;
through the excellent recitation of those respective mantras, one becomes endowed with merit in an instant. (7.23)
Having encased [the name] with the mantra and recited it, one becomes a master of accomplishments; O beautiful god, I shall tell you whatever methods there are for its utterance. (7-24)
One must certainly not allow a divided mind regarding each respective task.
Bhairava said:
Now, O you who are worshipped by Śaṅkara, speak of the differentiation of the seed-syllables (bīja).
If there is a mass of affection for me in you, who have entered for the sake of my family, then speak, O Bhairavī, supreme bliss, beloved of my life! (7.26)
Ānandabhairavī said:
Listen, O Lord, to my mantra for the worship of the Kumārī regarding the Kula doctrine;
it is a great mantra, a great mantra, a perfected mantra—of this there is no doubt. (7-27)
By the grace of this mantra, the wise one becomes liberated while living;
at the end, he attains the state of the Goddess. This is the truth, O Ānandabhairava. (7-28)
A mortal will certainly attain the perfection of worldly happiness and the grace of Madhumatī; have full confidence, O Śaṅkara. (7.29)
Through the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], there is agitation at the outset; through the Māyā-bīja, the eightfold qualities;
through the Śrībīja, the attainment of prosperity; and through the Māyā-bīja, the destruction of enemies.
By means of the seed-syllable Bhairava, the state of moving through the sky was attained by the gods and others;
for I am always a maiden, O Lord, and you are indeed a youth.
One should worship either one hundred and eight or even just one;
when worshipped they grant their favor, but when treated with contempt they consume [the offender] with fire.
The maiden is the yoginī herself; the maiden is the supreme deity.
So too are the asuras, the eight nāgas, and whatever malevolent grahas there may be.
O Bhairava, the spirits, vetālas, gandharvas, ḍākinīs, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and all other deities belonging to the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar.
All things beginning with the earth, the entire cosmic egg with its moving and non-moving beings,
as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— || 7.35 ||
They are satisfied, and all are satisfied, for whoever worships a maiden;
and one should worship a young girl who possesses a treasure, O Bhairava. (7.36)
Having worshipped with devotion by offering water for the feet, the arghya-offering, incense, and auspicious saffron and sandalwood paste, one should present these to the young maidens. (7.37)

One should perform three circumambulations— at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end— and afterwards, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given consisting of silver, gold, and pearls.
Having bestowed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) upon the maidens according to the rules and in due order, he himself should marry off the girl; thus he removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Furthermore, if one should arrange the giving away of a daughter during an auspicious time, the fruit thereof is enjoyment and liberation, as well as good fortune and all prosperity. (7.40)
The three-eyed Lord Hara dwells eternally in the world of Rudra;
[he is equal to] thousands of crores of holy fords and hundreds of horse-sacrifices.
He who marries off a daughter obtains that fruit immediately;
it is to be known as lasting for as many thousands of years as there are grains of sand in the ocean.
Having uplifted each family one by one, the wise man is glorified in the world of Rudra for the pleasure and satisfaction of those respective deities he worships. (7.43)
O Bhairava, having performed the gift of a maiden according to the specific year of her birth and with the corresponding intention, the practitioner attains liberation. (7.44)
Having meditated upon the state of being Śiva within the recipient of the gift,
and having visualized Śiva in his full form, beautiful in all his limbs, as the bestower of boons— (7.45)
The foremost of practitioners should choose Mahādeva Baṭukeśa, who is composed of splendor, lovely with fame, and possesses the form of Bālabhairava. (7.46)
Bhairavī in the form of a maiden, the most excellent beauty of the three worlds,
her limbs bowed with various ornaments, she who illumines the auspicious Vidyā.

Having meditated upon her who possesses a beautiful smile, whose heart is great bliss, who bestows auspiciousness, who is auspicious herself, and whose face resembles the full moon, [seated] upon a lotus of twelve petals.
Having brought [the offerings] together for the recipient, one should cause them to be given with their respective mantras.
Having heard this, the Great Hero, who is stainless and possesses the form of a child (or strength), [acted].
Again he desired to know the supreme Ānandabhairavī.
Ānandabhairava said:
[Tell me] the true meaning of the principle of the Kumārī-kula, the meaning of the mantra, and the sequence of its recitation.

The manner of sacrifice and so forth, as well as the sequence of feeding and so forth, the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth, and her hymn of praise—each one indeed [is described]. (7.51)
O beloved, tell me in due order the armor-mantra of the young maidens,
by which sequence that knowledge— the young maiden who is the supreme deity— is attained.
In a secluded place, before the practitioner, she herself shall speak the Great Saying:
"For what reason does this beautiful-eyed girl show favor? (7.53)
"O beloved of Ānandabhairava, out of affection, tell me that method.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O Śambhu, I shall proclaim the Kula-mantras of the Kumārīs."
By means of which mere consciousness the Lord of the Earth, the Supreme among Men, may become the form of the Guru for all, including the assembly of young maidens. (7.55)
O Great Lord, [I have told you] the excellent one-year-old [cow] and the supreme mantra for the Sandhyā and other rites; now hear the mantra for the sixteen forms of Śānti. (7.56)
Having brought together the sequence and so forth for all, the rite for the accomplishment of consciousness, a beautiful woman, a maiden, and an excellent mistress; 7.57.
O Lord, one should cause water adorned with jewel ornaments and beautified by conch shells, garments, and so forth to be offered with the Vāgbhava mantra, using the [disciple's] name.
Always meditating upon her with the thought that she is the Goddess, the best of practitioners should worship her;
O Lord, he should likewise offer water for the feet using the *māyā* seed-syllable along with her name.
The wise one should offer the arghya with the Lakṣmī-bīja, the sandalwood paste with the [Śrī-]bīja, and cause the flowers to be given to Kumārī with the Māyā-bīja. (7.60)
Having offered excellent incense and lamps with the Sadāśiva mantra,
the leader of the gods should worship [the deity] with the six-limbed mantra (ṣaḍaṅgamantra).
O Mahādeva, you who assume the form of bliss, listen to that manner [of worship]:
the heart, which consists of great splendor and is radiant white, [is touched] with the right hands. (7.62)
Having meditated thus, the wise one should recite that mantra; listen, O Śaṅkara!
First, having uttered Vāgbhava, then Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Kūrcaka.
Then one should utter the seed-syllable of the Pretas, together with the visarga, the moon, and the bindu;
having pronounced the word "Kula," one should then say "Kumārike. (7.64)
Having uttered "Oṃ, namaḥ to the heart," one should then contemplate [it] upon the head;
having recited the seed-syllable that is white in color and composed of all things, one should install it there.

The syllable *ha* enriched with the *vāgbhava*, the syllable *va* which has the meaning of *vāgbhava*, *māyā*, *lakṣmī*, and *vāgbhava*, followed by the word *śirase* at the end of the *dviṭha*. (7.66)
The practitioner should place the mantra ending with the wife of fire (svāhā) upon his head;
[he should visualize] the black-colored one in the middle of the topknot, possessing the luster of a mass of blue collyrium.
Having meditated thus, the practitioner should perform the ritual renunciation for the sake of attaining success within the Kumārī-kula;
first, having extracted the Praṇava (Om), at its end is Vahnisundarī.
Having extracted [the mantra] for the crest-lock (śikhā), one should then utter the syllable vaṣaṭ;
thereafter, within the armor (kavaca), [one places] the powerful and highly radiant [deity].
Having meditated upon the beautiful body resembling the first flush of dawn,
one should utter the Vāgbhava syllable and then pronounce the word "Kula."

After that, one should utter the word *vāgīśvarī* for the feet; then one should say *kavacāya*, followed by the syllable of the *tārakabrahman* and the entire network of the armor-assignment (*kavaca-nyāsa*).
Then, having meditated upon the three eyes, the great seed-syllable of great radiance,
red in color and adorned with a mandala of ten million times ten million [rays], || 7.72 ||
When the sun, whose splendor is born from ten million merits, has shone forth,
one should then utter the Vāgbhava syllable followed by the word Kuleśvarī.
After the word "śabda," one should utter "vauṣaṭ" for the three eyes; this is the mantra for the eyes.
Then, the practitioner of the mantra should likewise [place it] on the palm of the left hand.
With the middle and index fingers, one should perform two claps;
that mantra possesses a splendor equal to the mass of light from ten million fierce suns. (7.75)
Having diligently extracted the sound arising from the great space, which causes intense and formidable affliction, as well as the seed-syllable of Māyā and the phrase for the weapon (astrāya).
Having extracted the great mantra ending with *pānta* and *ṭhānta*,
one should then meditate upon her retinue within the abode of her heart.
The mantra-practitioner should diligently worship with a stream of medicinal nectar;
he should satisfy and worship Bhairava and Bālabhairava with devotion. (7.78)
Having worshipped the deities and their retinues in due order,
one should then utter the Vāgbhava syllable for the sake of attaining success through speech.
Having first uttered the initial word, "vaktrāya namaḥ" is proclaimed;
then, having uttered the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], one should extract the word "jayāya. (7–80)
Having extracted the northern face ending in the dative case along with the word "namaḥ," one should then diligently utter the seed-syllables Vāgbhava, Māyā, and Śrī.
"O Kubjikā, at the western end, [one should say] 'Salutation to the Face' (vaktrāya namaḥ).
Then, having uttered the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], one should utter the word 'Kālike'. (7-82)
O Lord, O Kuleśvara, after the word *śabda*, the mantra for the right face is proclaimed as "nānā"; having uttered these syllables of this mantra, [one should proceed]. (7–83)
Having worshipped [the preceding deities] in due order, one should worship the Sun;
then one should worship the Moon, the gods who are the guardians of the directions, and the Sandhyās and others.
One should worship Vīrabhadrā, Mahākālī, Kaulinī, Kulagāminī,
and the eighteen-armed Kālī, who bestows the four aims of human life.
Having brought the food offerings and so forth, together with various kinds of eatables and the like—
thickened milk, fresh milk, cooked rice, and ripe, excellent fruits.
Whatever is suitable for the occasion, mixed with sugar and honey—
the five elements (pañcatattva) as the substance of the Kula— increases one's own well-being.
Having thus offered to the young maidens various kinds of food offerings, prepared according to the prescriptions of their respective tantras and adorned with diverse fragrances; (7–88)
The highly wise one, having brought cool water, should give it to them;
then he should impart the beneficial great mantra, which is exceedingly difficult for a maiden to obtain.
Alternatively, by reciting one's own root mantra, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhi).
One should cause those whose vital breaths are capable to hold [the breath], or do so oneself;
while performing prostrations such as the eight-limbed one and reciting hymns of praise, one should bestow [the instruction]. (7.91)
I bow to the beloved of the lineage, who bestows supreme fortune,
who possesses the skill for delighting with Kumāra, and who gladdens all spiritual accomplishments.
I worship the maiden of the world’s speech, who is purified by coral beads, adorned with garments dyed silver, and embellished with ornaments of gold.
Having thus performed the ritual renunciation (saṃnyāsa) with this mantra, one should worship Tāriṇī;
having fully worshipped Śiva and Gaṇeśa, the best of practitioners should prostrate.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Divine State," within the section on "Accomplished Mantras" in the "Arrangement of the Service of the Virgin," in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, the Northern Tantra. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said: "O Mahādeva, I shall now describe the recitation and fire-offering (japa-homa) for the Kumārī."
Having performed one hundred thousand recitations of either Māyā, Vāgbhava, or Ramā.
O Lord, [one may use] either the seed-syllable of Kālī, or Māyā, or the seed-syllable of Kāma, encased by Sadāśiva and adorned with the Bindu and the Moon. (8.2)
Alternatively, O Lord of the Thirty-three, having recited the root mantra encapsulated by the *praṇava* according to the rule of one hundred thousand repetitions; || 8-3 ||
One should perform a great oblation (mahāhoma) consisting of one-tenth of that [number], using bilva leaves smeared with ghee;
or else, with white flowers or kunda flowers, there is a great fruit.
In this manner, one should perform the oblation in sequence with *karavīra* flowers—
either alone or mixed with sandalwood and agallochum— and smeared with clarified butter.
Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the daytime, one should be devoted to worship at night;
one should perform worship with the family substances remaining from one's own previous offerings.
There, assuming the form of supreme bliss, one should recite the mantra an incalculable number of times during the day;
at the conclusion of the recitation, the practitioner of mantra should perform oblations with the substances mentioned by me.
Then, having repeatedly purified the vital air which is the essence of life,
and having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should joyfully prostrate with the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
At the time of prostration, O Lord, the ascetic should recite this hymn;
likewise, the armor-verse (kavaca) should be recited, or else by young maidens.
O Mahādeva, one should then recite the great hymn of praise to one's own goddess, followed by the armor (kavaca),
and the thousand names of the young maidens (kumāris) together with the eight [additional names].
By reciting [this], one attains accomplishment; by reciting it, the supreme practitioner attains success.
Having placed all those [mantras], which are as cool as millions of jewels, before him— || 8-11 ||
Then the wise one, self-controlled and with a concentrated mind— whether devoted to the great divine conduct or characterized by an intense heroic disposition— should recite the hymn of praise.
Thus, one devoted to a state of devotion should recite it in this sequence;
for the Great Vidyā is the Great Service, drunk from by those immersed in devotion and faith.
One shall quickly become a possessor of great wisdom and attain the fulfillment of one's desires.
Ānandabhairava said:
O Indra and other lords of the gods, [worship] the one who dwells in Vārāṇasī, whose rays are like ten million moons;
she is the Vidyā who is the beloved of Vāgbhava, the three-eyed one, blazing with subtle activity.
I worship for the sake of prosperity the excellent Kumārī, who destroys fierce exertion, who is the sustainer of the three worlds, who dwells in the root-lotus, and whose face is like the moon. 8.15.
The young girl was to be meditated upon by hosts of gods, by Śiva, Indra, and ascetics seeking liberation—
she who is the twilight (sandhyā) from which eternal qualities arise, who brings about the supreme rise for the assembly of the twice-born,
who is ruddy, white-hued, the Supreme Goddess, the doer of good, auspicious, and large-faced.
I worship Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Gaṇas, the movement of the day, Kṛṣṇā, and Vṛddhā.
I bow to Caṇḍikā, the youthful one worshipped by children, the sustainer of the hosts, the bestower of liberation upon the learned,
the nurse, the pure Sarasvatī, the ninefold boon-granting goddess, the speaker of speech,
the beloved of Hari residing in the Svādhiṣṭhāna cakra, the doer of what is dear, and the giver of the knowledge of Vedānta.
I worship her, whose form is consciousness, eternally in the body of Yoga for the sake of liberation. 8-17.
I bow to the maiden who is worshipped by the wise in a palace constructed from a multitude of various jewels;
she whose face is the seed of the Siddhānta in the Nandana grove of the Mind-born God.
O Goddess, having abandoned the state of a young girl, grant the true meaning to this man who is devoid of merit.
May Truth protect Kumārikā, who is composed of radiant energy through her threefold form.
O fair-faced one, you who bear the unique seed for the blossoming of the path of the Kula,
who are the formidable one who makes the scent of flesh manifest, and who bestows desires beyond the reach of ordinary longing—
I am but a child, ever taking refuge at the lotus feet of Vaṭukeśvara.
Having abandoned both the young girl and the boy, I worship the Lord who resides upon the white lotus on the crown of the head.

I ever worship the virtuous Bālā-vidyā, who is full of splendor, who dwells upon the sun-petal within the lotus of my heart; she who delights the sun, who removes the heat caused by the great sins of the Kali age, whose limbs are composed of light, who moves upon the sun in this world, and who destroys all fear.
O Kumāri, having directly attained the stainless Rūpeśvarī, who brings about accomplishment.
I constantly worship the beloved of the Śrīkula, the virtuous Kulavatī, Kolā, Umā, and Ambikā; she who dwells in various yogas, the celestial maiden, the eternal one endowed with austerity,
whose garment is the specific meaning of Vedānta, and who abides in the particularities of all languages.
I, Kālapriya, bow to you, the daughter of the king of mountains. 8-21 ||
Kaumārī, the beloved of the Kula, who kindles the mass of fire that agitates the hosts of enemies;
auspicious, with eyes of reddish luster, she bestows the realization of liberation through the supreme path;
the consort of the Lord, the intellect (mati), a lion to the world’s fragrance.
I worship her who is beloved by the five-faced one, who removes fear, and who wards off serpents and other dangers.

O crest-jewel of the lords of kings, those who constantly worship the beautiful Śrī Kubjikā— who delights in the great splendor of her two lotus-feet, who is a river that causes the destruction of delusion and other afflictions, and who possesses excellent hands— will swiftly [attain their goal].
They declare that for one who produces wealth and long life, there is pervasive sovereignty throughout the entire world. || 8-23 ||
The Lord of Yogins, the Sovereign of the World, the beloved one,
who proceeds to the ocean of splendor through the *Śrīkālasandarbha*, the source of Hara’s being, the kindler of the fruit of desires—
for the destruction of the sins of the worlds, [he is praised] by Śivā, the knowledge named *Śrī*.
I meditate upon him as the wish-fulfilling tree for those who bow down to him, whose very life-breath is the Dharma and who is the eternal deity.

Those of meritorious intellect who joyfully worship that Aparājitā Vidyā— the Kātyāyanī Bhairavī, whose face is intoxicated with the fragrance of the state of passion (madana-bhāva), whose sandals reside within the heart-lotus, and who is the essence of the lineage (kula)— [enter] into the midst of the ocean of supreme bliss.
I shall proclaim for the sake of liberation that which is terrifying due to its all-pervading splendor. || 8-25 ||
I bow to Rudrāṇī, whose face is like a lotus, who is composed of the brilliance of ten million suns,
adorned with various ornaments, the bestower of bliss upon the lineage and the arms, endowed with Śrī, Māyā, and Kamalā, residing in the heart, and the source of the rite of the seed of progeny.
I worship her directly in my heart, she who has her sole abode in Ānanda and who remains unattained by me. 8-26.
I bow to Varabhairavī, who is like the primordial fire at the end of time upon the surface of the earth;
she is as delicate and reddish as a lotus stalk, the purifier of the world's defects,
the remover of the world's fear, and she who, as the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśvarī), takes away [all afflictions].
It consists of one thousand great sections and bestows all enjoyments and self-control. || 8-27 ||
The Great-Lakṣaṇā Vidyā grants sovereignty when requested;
Mahālakṣmī herself bestows the eightfold prosperity and destroys the agitation of the lineage.
She is seated upon the beautiful lotus of one’s own ādhāra-cakra, O beloved of the infinite Viṣṇu.
I bow to Kauleśvarī, the Kaulikī, who bestows the status of royalty and brings about auspiciousness.

I bow to Vāruṇī, the sovereign of the seats, the supreme mistress of the seats, the auspicious knowledge, the leader, endowed with all ornaments, who removes the agitation of the three worlds, the mistress of the seat-dwellers,
who overspreads the shadows of the triple universe.
She who brings benefit to all, the victorious one, the sovereign whose very form is bliss.
The field-knower (kṣetrajñā), overwhelmed by intoxication, a woman of noble lineage, fond of spiritual attainments,
the beloved of Śambhu, the illustrious Vaṭukeśvara, who moves within the great bliss— (8.30).
I salute Śākinī, who arises directly from the self and the other, who is conceived in the center of the lotus,
who bears a stream from the great ocean of nectar upon her thousand-petaled head,
and who removes the agitation of one's own mind.
I bow to Mahābhairavī, who manifests external objects and possesses the luster of silver. 8-31 ||
I bow to the Supreme Mother, who bestows the fruit of prostration, who brings all external things under her control, who destroys the defects of the sense-objects,
whose face is radiant with full-blown beauty, and who is conceived as dwelling within the center of a lotus.
Upon her head, she bears a cloud that is a vessel for the streams of the great ocean of nectar, possessing a thousand petals.

Having bowed down before the goddess Sandhyā, who is the lotus-like splendor of the gods, the supreme scholar of the Kula, whose body is visibly filled with the nectar of the three worlds, I worship her within the center of the middle of the hundred petals.
[He saw] that Kauleśvarī, the refuge of all divine beings. || 8-33 ||
O Viśveśvarī, O beautiful girl in the lineage of Svara, I bow daily with devotion to you upon the Siddhāsana;
O servant, grant me devotion, wealth, and the state of victory.
In that [case], one should administer Mahāmadhumatī with a light enema. || 8-34 ||
By the grace of this hymn, one shall become a poet and a master of speech;
divine, a lord of the great siddhis, and devoted to the state of a hero. (8-35)
He attains victory everywhere, for he shall indeed be beloved by the gods;
such a man will quickly become a master of speech and able to assume any form at will.
The Mahāvīra certainly becomes like a divine animal;
all vidyās become propitious, and all the lords of the directions are satisfied. (8-37)
Fire becomes cool and he can cause the solidification of water;
at this time, a man shall become wealthy, possessed of sons, and a king. (8.38)
And others go to Vaikuṇṭha, or to Kailāsa in the presence of Śiva;
O Mahādeva, liberation is indeed attained by one who recites this constantly and at all times.
He indeed beholds with certainty the lotus-feet of the Great Vidyā;
listen, O Lord, as I shall explain the ritual of libation for the Kumārīs and other rites. (8.40)
By the mere act of satisfying them, the accomplishment of the *kula* becomes certain;
[one should worship] the *kulabālā*, who resides in the root-lotus and roams at will. (8.41)
O my beloved, I satisfy you a hundred times with the root mantra—
you who are adorned by the mass of matted locks and the great splendor of the *mūlādhāra*.
I satisfy the goddess Sandhyā with the seed-syllable of desire, O auspicious one;
[I satisfy] Kumārī Śrīsarasvatī, whose limbs are joined with the root-lotus.
I satisfy her with the substances of my lineage for the sake of your satisfaction;
within the wheel of the *mūlādhāra* lotus, I worship the youthful mistress of the three forms (*trimūrti-bālanāyikā*).
I satisfy with supreme nectars the Goddess who bestows all auspiciousness,
who shines within the six petals of the great lotus at the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
I propitiate with the seed-syllable Śrī for the sake of enjoyment and liberation alone—
her who moves toward the secret sign of Viṣṇu and is the manifestation of the Kula within the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
I propitiate Kālikā with the nectar of my own lineage using her seed-syllable—she who dwells in the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna and is Śivā, consisting of great splendor. (8.47)
Now I satisfy the Mistress of the Family (Kuleśvarī), who resides in the solar region at the head,
her beautiful body situated within the ocean of the Maṇipūra.
I satisfy Umādevī, Pārvatī, who is worshipped throughout the three worlds, with the seed-syllable of Māyā in the center of the lotus of Maṇipūra.
I satisfy Mālinī, who resides in the Maṇipūra, the fierce goddess who destroys supreme bliss, for one whose mind is defiled, so that their virtuous intellect may be gratified.
I propitiate the goddess Kubjikā, who travels through the sky;
I propitiate the Great Goddess who is intent upon the great practice (mahāsādhana).
I propitiate the Yoginī Kālasandarbha, whose face is the Kula;
she is Raudrī, the bestower of power and mantras, who is filled with a flickering tongue.
I satisfy Aparājitā, the Great Goddess, the Mistress of the Kula,
who is beloved by the Mahākaula, the perfected one, and the bestower of happiness in the world of Rudra.
I propitiate Rudrāṇī, who possesses fierce rays, who is dear to her bridegroom,
who is perfected by the sixteen vowels, and who destroys the Mahāraurava hell.
I satisfy Bhairavī, whose mind is intent on the great drinking of wine,
the goddess who grants boons to the three worlds and is encircled by the garland of the Śrī-bīja.
I propitiate Mahālakṣmī, the bestower of worldly sovereignty,
the benefactress of the worlds, and she who is beloved by people both virtuous and non-virtuous.
I satisfy Ramābījā, the mistress of the sacred seats (pīṭhanāyikā) beginning with Pīṭha;
Jayantī, the mother of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, and Sūryamātā.
I satisfy with nectars the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) who is veiled by Māyā;
I satisfy the supreme one, whose face is most excellent, the supreme bliss of the lineage.
I satisfy the goddess Ambikā, who dwells in the heart as Māyā-Lakṣmī.

For the sake of happiness, [I worship] the slender form of the two lotus-feet of all [the goddesses], who possesses the knowledge of consciousness, who is joined with the sixteen auspicious vowels, who is crowded with the sixteen Śrīs,
and who sits upon a beautiful throne inlaid with rubies from the ocean of bliss.
I perpetually satiate that entire [deity] seated upon the middle of a white lotus.
Those who constantly recite this beautiful and fruitful hymn of propitiation reach the supreme liberation that is the source of the gift of knowledge;
meanwhile, the hosts of lords of the earth who cause all manner of calamities perish.
They bring kings under their control and, through the entirety of yoga, they become eternal in an instant. || 8-61 ||
If human beings recite this [text] known as liberation consisting of satisfaction, they shall become endowed with the eight sovereign powers and behold her after one year. (8.62)
O Lord, O Master, by practicing for one month, one becomes a great yogi;
he shall swiftly agitate the three worlds and obtain the fruit of his desires. (8.63)
In the center of the earth, the Lord of Kings of kings obtains auspicious boons in the destruction of enemies, as well as in expulsion, imprisonment, and the perils of disease. (8-64)
In a formidable fourfold army, in times of distant dispatch,
or in the great battle of kings, one shall attain success by reciting this.
Whoever recites this with single-minded devotion shall obtain the fruit of complete satisfaction;
through the recitation of this hymn to Kumārī, one attains the full efficacy of worship.
He who does not perform the worship of the Virgin, nor the hymn of constant auspiciousness, shall become like a beast; for him, death awaits at every step. (8.67)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Divine State," within the section on "Accomplished Mantras" in the *Kumāryupacaryāvilāsa*, which is part of the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*. 8.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"Therefore, I shall now fully proclaim the auspicious armor (kavaca) of the Virgin Goddess."
The "Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds" is the destroyer of great sins.
Through recitation and retention, people become great perfected ones and radiant beings;
Śakra, the glorious lord of the gods, and Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, [attained this]. (9.2)
The King of Dharma is a terrifying fire consisting of great splendor;
Varuṇa, indeed worthy of worship by the gods, is himself the lord of the waters.
The great wind that carries everything away, Kubera, the lord of elephants,
the sovereign of the earth, the beloved of Śambhu— all these gods are the lords of the directions.
Meru is not the lord of one; the Lord of All, being stainless, is the master of two.
By the recitation of this armor, all kings become lords of wealth.
May the Praṇava protect my head; may Māyā, being the bestower [of boons], protect [my face];
may Mahāmāyā protect the area above my forehead; and may Śrīsarasvatī protect me.
Kāmākṣā is Vaṭukeśānī, my forehead is Trimūrti; Cāmuṇḍā is the form of the seed-syllable, and Kālikā is my face.
May she who moves in the sun protect me constantly, as well as my two eyes;
may Umā, whose form is the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), protect the pair of my ears, O ascetic lady.
May Vāgdevī Mālinī protect the tip of my tongue;
may Kuñjikā, who dwells in the Ḍāmara and can assume any form at will, protect the tips of my teeth.
May that Goddess Śivā, whose form is the Praṇava, protect my lips and lower lip eternally; she who is of the nature of the Śakti-bīja and whose very essence is Svāhā.
May she who is gripped by Time and whose nature consists of the five vital winds protect my [throat];
may Aparājitā, the most terrible one, protect the region of my throat.
May the seed-syllable *kṣauṃ* protect my throat, and may Rudrāṇī, accompanied by Svāhā, protect [my] heart;
may the sixteen-syllabled Bhairavī Vidyā protect my excellent voice.
May Mahālakṣmī, the foremost goddess, protect both my arms everywhere;
may Pīṭhanāyikā, whose very nature is all mantras, protect my belly.
May Kumārī, whose essence is the Vāgbhava-mantra, protect my two sides;
may Kaiśorī, whose nature is the Māyā-bīja, protect the region of my waist.
May the pair of my shanks be protected by the Yoginī Jayantī, joined with Kullukā;
may the goddess Ambikā, who penetrates the meaning of the mantra, protect my entire body.
May Goddess Kamalā protect the tips of my hair; may Vindhyavāsinī protect the tip of my nose; and may Goddess Caṇḍikā, as Kumārī, always protect my chin.
May the goddess Lalitā protect the heart; may Parvatavāsinī protect the back; and may the goddess Triśakti Ṣoḍaśī always protect the linga and the secret parts.
In the cremation ground is the goddess Ambikā, and in the womb of the Gaṅgā is Vaiṣṇavī;
in the empty house is Pañcamudrā, who reveals the mantras and yantras.
Likewise, may she who holds the vajra protect me at the crossroads—she who sits upon a corpse-seat, is fierce, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads. (9.19)
May she who is the embodiment of the power Vaikharī protect me in Pāṭalī and Kaliṅga;
may Mahābālā protect me in the forest, and Raṇapriyā in the great wilderness.
May Sarasvatī protect me in great waters and in ponds, and in the midst of enemies;
may Śītalā always protect me on the great path of the sky and upon the earth.
May the Goddess of Royal Fortune, the maiden beloved of her family, who is the half-woman form of Śiva, protect the soles of my feet as she stands in the midst of battle. 9.22
The Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) of nine lakhs is the maiden who assumes a form;
she is as radiant as ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons.
"May Vāṇī, the granter of boons and the beloved of Vaṭukeśvara, protect me.
Thus, O Lord, this most wonderful armor has been recounted to you. (9.24)

O you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of the five principles, he who recites this hymn and armor-mantra with the five principles for a maiden who is an heir to the family [attains success]. (9.25)
For him, there will be the accomplishment of traveling through the sky; of this there is no doubt.
One shall quickly become possessed of a vajra-body through the recitation of this armor;
the yogi who recites it becomes a master of all siddhis and a possessor of gnosis. (9-27)
In dispute, in legal proceedings, in battle, in an assembly of his kin, on the great road, and in the cremation ground—he shall become one who has attained perfection in yoga. (9.28)
Having recited it, one attains victory; this is the truth, the truth, O Lord of the Kula!
This auspicious armor for subjugation grants victory everywhere. (9-29)
One who observes meritorious vows should recite this daily; he will certainly become a glorious ascetic, and the maiden Siddhavidyā bestows supreme accomplishment.
Whoever recites or even hears this shall become a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa),
bestowing devotion, liberation, contentment, nourishment, royal splendor, and abundant prosperity.
If the best of practitioners, having memorized it, should recite it,
that wise one shall accomplish even the impossible by reading this auspicious armor (*kavaca*).
And for those who possess wealth, he who is self-controlled shall daily worship the Virgin Goddess at night, bestowing great happiness, virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
By means of a specific ritual application, one may bring the three worlds under control,
using meat, liquor, fish, and the mudrā.
The practitioner [should worship] with various kinds of food and edibles, with fragrant substances,
with garlands, with ornaments of gold and silver, and with fine garments.
Having worshipped, recited the mantra, and offered libations to the fair-faced goddess,
O Maheśvara, through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, and ritual application— (9.36)
Whoever, having offered praise, recites the Kumārī-kavaca with single-minded devotion,
shall quickly attain perfection and become a sovereign lord of kings.
One obtains the fruit of whatever desired object dwells in the mind;
having written this armor (*kavaca*) on birch bark, one should wear it upon the heart. (9.38)
On Saturdays and Tuesdays, on the ninth, eighth,
and fourteenth days, and especially on the full moon day during the dark fortnight.
Having written it down, the wise man should preserve it while facing north;
for even one joined with great sins shall be liberated from all transgressions. (9.40)
Holding a woman by her left arm, one should touch all auspicious objects;
she will be beloved, endowed with many sons, and possessed of all prosperity. (9.41)
Likewise, one who wears the illustrious Puruṣottama on the right arm shall possess a divine body in this world and have a splendor equal to that of a lion. || 9.42 ||
Possessing the speed of the wind and free from disease, he goes to the supreme world of Śiva;
having pierced the solar orb, he shall attain the highest realm.

Victory to you, O auspicious armor arising from the ocean of bliss! You bestow supreme happiness upon the worlds, remove fear, and grant devotion at the feet of Śrī; you are the sole cause for destroying the terrible impurities of the Kali age for the sons of Pṛthā who recite it for the sake of liberation.
Those who indeed recite this incomparable Dharma attain liberation in an instant. || 9-44 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Divine State," within the section on "Accomplished Mantras" in the "Radiance of the Great Tantra," specifically the "Manifestation of the Armor of the Virgin" (Kumārī-kavaca-ullāsa) concerning the ritual service of the Virgin (Kumāry-upacaryā-vinyāsa), in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, the Northern Tantra (*Uttara-tantra*). 9.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"Speak, O beloved, O consort of bliss whose very nature is eternal joy!"
It increases the supreme bliss of the maiden, the chief of goddesses.
If this wondrous and auspicious collection of names known as the Aṣṭottarasahasra exists for me, and if there remains even a trace of pure affection in my heart— 10-2.
Then recite the great hymn that bestows the fruits of the deeds performed by the Virgin Goddess; it shall yield the merit of giving away ten million times ten million maidens in marriage. (10.3)
Ānandabhairavī said:
O Lord, beloved of the Sovereign of All, listen to this most wonderful [hymn] of the Virgin, known as the "One Thousand and Eight," which bestows great merit. (10.4)
By reciting or by retaining it in memory, a person shall be liberated from distress;
it is everywhere difficult to obtain, auspicious, and practiced by the blessed world. 10-5.

It possesses the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* as its limbs, bestows supreme universal bliss, dispels the limbs of illusion through mantra, and grants the perfection of mantra to human beings. (10.6)
There is no need for worship, nor recitation, nor ritual bathing, nor the performance of preparatory rites;
one attains perfection spontaneously through the recitation of the Thousand Names.
O Lord, the practitioner instantly obtains the fruit of all sacrifices by means of the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the essential nature of the *yonimudrā*. (10.8)
Even in a hundred times ten million years, it would be impossible to describe the fruit;
nevertheless, O Lord, I wish to speak for the benefit of the worlds. (10.9)
Of this Thousand-Name Armor (Kavaca) of the Illustrious Virgin (Śrīkumārī):
Vaṭukabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Kumārī is the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the perfection of all mantras. || 10-10 ||
Oṃ! Kumārī, Kauśikī, Kālī, Kurukullā, Kuleśvarī, Kanakābhā, Kāñcanābhā, Kamalā, and Kālakāminī. || 10-11 ||
Kapālinī, Kālarūpā, Kaumārī, Kulapālikā, Kāntā, Kumārakāntā, Kāraṇā, and Karigāminī. || 10-12 ||
The beloved of Kandha, the beloved of Kaula, the bestower of the fruits of performed actions;
she who is fond of what is to be done and what is not to be done, the one beyond the reach of the senses, the slayer of Kaṃsa, and the destroyer of the Kurus. || 10:13 ||
Kṛṣṇakāntā, Kālarātri, Karṇeṣudhāriṇīkarā, Kāmahā, Kapilā, Kālā, Kālikā, and Kurukāminī. || 10-14 ||
She who loves Kurukṣetra, she of the Kaula lineage, the daughter of Kuntī, she who is afflicted by desire, she with beautiful hair,
she who eats forbidden meat (kalañja), the princess of Kekaya, she whose banner bears the tail of a crow, and she who possesses all arts.

She is Kamalā, Kāmalakṣmī, and Kamalānanakāminī; she is the embodiment of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), the destroyer of desire (Kāmahā), and she who is never distressed by desire (Kāmamadīnī). || 10-16 ||
She is the bestower of desires, worshipped by desire, transcendent of desire, and possessed of all arts;
she is Bhairavī, enriched with causes, youthful, and of skillful limbs. || 10.17 ||
With a neck like a conch shell, dark in hue, and possessing a form dear to Kāmarāja;
adorned with bracelets, she is Kaṅkā, the solitary Kākinī Kirā. (10.18)
Kirātinī, Kākabhakṣā, Karālavadanā, Kṛśā, Keśinī, Keśihā, Keśā, Kāsāmbaṣṭhā, and Karipriyā. (10.19)
She whose nature is that of the Lord of Poets (Kavi), she who is pungent speech,
she who dwells in the pungent, she who is the hollow, she who has eyes like a hollow, and she who resides in Karanāṭaka.

She who dwells on the mountain peak, she who rests upon wood, she who is the god of love, she who is fond of the *ketakī* flower, she who delights in play, she who resides upon a woolen blanket, and she who is the destroyer of the demon Kāla. (10.21)
Richly adorned with the beauty of the *ketakī* flower, her tongue filled with camphor,
she is a *kākolī* plant from a mine of camphor, dwelling upon Mount Kailāsa.
Seated upon a grass seat, she is the mother of Kadamba, the mistress of elephants, and the one with a noble face;
she is short of stature, the wielder of the sword, the sword itself, the destroyer of the wicked, and the giver of wisdom to the wicked.
She has the form of a crane and the appearance of an ass; she abides in the midst of alkaline, sour, and bitter [flavors];
she is playful, holds a spittoon in her hand, speaks harsh words, and is fierce with her donkey-like nature. (10.24)
She whose play is as flickering as a firefly, she who is like a firefly, she who rides upon birds;
she who stands upon a shield, she who dwells in the wicked, she who resides in the sky, the sky-farer, beloved of the sky-goers.
She moves through the sky, possesses fierce love, is abundant with goodness, and has a sky-faring face;
she is the sovereign of sky-goers, is harsh and terrible, and speaks words dear to those who move in the sky. || 10-26 ||
Intoxicated by dates-wine, enjoying the fruit of dates, situated in the middle of a pit, she is herself a pit filled with the water of the pit. (10.27)
Her fame brings joy to those whose waters are renowned; she is Khulanā, whose gait is like that of a wagtail;
she is the wise one, yet more clever than the cleverest; she is the measure of grain, and she cuts through the agitation of the harsh.
She who dwells in the sky, she who is fearless, she who resounds with a deep voice;
she who is the Gaṅgā, she who is profound, she who is Gaurī, she who is the beloved of Gaṇanātha, and she who is the ultimate refuge. || 10-29 ||
Devoted to her guru, devoid of a husband, the housewife, she whose speech is the cowherd’s;
she who dwells among the herds of cows, she who belongs to Gaṇapati, the daughter of the mountain, worshipped by the mountain. || 10-30 ||
Girikāntā, Gaṇasthā, Girikanyā, Gaṇeśvarī; Gādhirājasutā, Grīvā, Gurvī, Gurvyambā, Śāṅkarī. (10.31)

She is the beloved of the Gandharvas, she is the Gāyatrī, the giver of qualities, and the qualities themselves; she resides in guggulu resin, she is worthy of worship by the Guru, and she illuminates the bliss of the Gītā. (10.32)
She is the beloved of the demon Gaya, she who dwells within the lattice of the window;
she is the daughter of the Guru, the wife of the Guru, the profound one, and the sister of the great serpents.
Gulphavāyusthitā, Gulphā, Garddabhā, Garddabhapriyā, Guhyā, Guhyagaṇasthā, Garimā, Gaurikā, and Gudā. (10.34)
She resides above the anus, she is the melted one, the courtesan, the sphere, and she who has descended from the throat;
she is the celestial nymph, the city of song, and she who is worshipped by the hosts of Gandharvas. || 10.35 ||
She of the terrible roar, she of the terrible face, the terrible one, the warder-off of heat;
the giver of clouds, cloud-colored, and she whose vehicle is the vehicle of the clouds.
She who is restless with a gurgling sound, the assembly of jars, the shattering of pots,
the one joined through union, the snout, she whose form is dense, and the Mistress of the Dense.
Ghuṇyātītā, Ghargharā, Ghorānanavimohinī, Ghoranetrā, Ghanarucā, and Ghorabhairavakanyakā. (10.38)
She is the slayer and the non-slayer, the slain, the one who smells and the one who is smelled, the wind-like power;
she abides in terrible darkness, she is the devourer, the devouring, and the earth.
Ghoṭakeśvarī, Ghoṭakā, and Ghoṭakeśvaravāhanā;
she who is dark as a sapphire and the beloved of Gharghareśvara.
She is perfected by the peak-syllable *ṅa*, she moves within the wheel of *ṅa*;
she is *ṅakārī*, she is *ṅasaṃśā*, she is led by *ṅī*, and she is *ṅakāriṇī*.
She dwells in the center of the lunar disc, clever and sweetly smiling;
she possesses a beautiful moon-like face and delights in the gait of a moving elephant. || 10.42 ||
She is the flickering, the restless, the fierce, the perceiving, she who abides in the sacrificial oblation;
she is the moving, the faceless, the beautiful, and she who resounds with lovely bees.
She is the destroyer of thieves, whose abode is the moon, the goddess of Indra, and she who dwells in the city of the moon;
she is the Kaula of the wheel, whose form is the wheel, who stands upon the wheel, and who bestows the siddhis of the wheel.
She holds the discus in her hand and possesses a discus; she is beloved by the family of the Lord of the Discus.
She is indivisible by the discus, belongs to the lineage of the discus, and is adorned by the mandala of the discus.
The beloved of the Lord of the Wheel, Celā, who rests upon a deerskin and kusha grass;
she is established in the four Vedas, fierce, yet as cool as ten million moons.
Possessing four qualities, moon-like in complexion, clever, and beloved by the wise;
residing in the eyes, the abode of vision, she is like chickpeas and fond of chickpeas.
She of lovely limbs, whose abode is sandalwood, with eyes like trembling lotuses; the mistress of the Carvvari river, beautiful-faced, with beautiful teeth, she who dwells in motion.
She who dwells in the cup, she who is within the mind, she who is honored by Caitra;
she who is visible to the eye, she who is dark as the moon, and she who possesses the luster of the Candrahāsa jewel.
She who abides in deception, she of subtle form, she who stands under the guise of the shadow of the parasol;
she who knows deception, she who is the mistress of deception, she who is the shadow, she whose auspiciousness is severed, she who is deceptive.
Richly adorned with the splendor of parasols and fly-whisks, she is the bearer of the parasol for those who possess them;
she has severed the past, she is Chinnamastā, she whose hair is severed, and she who arises from deceit.
She who removes deceit, she who bestows victory, she who is like a shadow, she who is concealed, she who is beloved by those who are hidden,
she who cuts through instability, she who possesses guile, and she who dwells in the abode of illusion.
Chadmagandhā, Chadācchannā, Chadmaveśī, Chakārikā, Chagalā, Raktabhakṣā, and Chagalāmodaraktapā. (10.53)
She is the daughter of Chagalaṇḍeśa, the maiden of Chagalaṇḍa;
she holds a knife in her hand, and she dwells among those who wield knives.

She whose nose is severed, whose hands are severed, who is dripping with blood, whose belly is trembling; she who causes trembling and agitation, who wears a garland of severed limbs, and who bestows the boon of severed limbs. || 10-55 ||
She who wears matted hair, who bestows the glory of a full belly, who is born as the beloved of old age, who is victory itself;
she who resides in the body's mechanisms, who takes away life, who is life itself, who grants victory, and who bestows the yoga of living.

She is the victorious one, she who dwells in the *jāmala*, the mistress of the origin of the *jāmala*, the daughter dear to the *jāmala*, the sovereign of the *jāmala*, and she who is fond of the *javā* flower. || 10-57 ||
Resplendent like ten million hibiscus flowers, she is beloved by people who cherish the hibiscus;
she dwells in the waters, pervades the entire world, is beyond old age, and remains established in the water.
Jīvahā, Jīvakanyā, Janārdanakumārikā, Jatukā, Jalapūjyā, and Jagannāthādikāminī. (10.59)
She has aged limbs and is devoid of decay; she is exceedingly beautiful like a cloud;
she is the giver of birth and the destroyer of birth; she is yawning and the wielder of the *jṛmbhaṇa* weapon and other such powers.
She who is born of the lowest [order], yet beloved; she whose intellect increases the joy of the world;
she who destroys the pride of the twin Arjuna trees; she who breaks the twin Arjuna trees. || 10-61 ||
She is the conqueror, the delight of the world, the bestower of the perfection of the Jāmalollāsa;
she is the rosary, the accomplishment of what is to be recited, and the illuminator of the sacrifice of recitation.
Jāmbuvatī, the daughter of Jāmbavān, who is honored by the assembly of women;
she is the destroyer of speed, the intellect of the world, the creator of the world, and the refuge of the world. || 10-63 ||
She is the mother, the giver of life, the wife, the mother of the world, and the sovereign of beings;
she is Jhaṅkalā, residing in the midst of the sound "jhaṅka," and her very nature is the resonance of "jhaṇat."
She whose form is the crackling fire, the mistress of the humming and buzzing;
she of instantaneous vision, the torrent, the tempest, the rattling one, and the daughter of the mountain stream.
Resounding with the sound *jhaṇat*, she is surrounded by a garland of *jhana-jhannā* and *jhakāra* sounds;
she is the maker of the *jhaṅkara* sound, the wielder of the *jharjhara* drum, the *jhallī* dancer, and the dweller in the abode of Jhalveśvara.

She whose form is the letter *ña*, she who is the consort of *ña*, she who is garlanded with the seed-syllable *ña*; she who has *ña* as her end, she who terminates in *ña*, she who is the supreme sovereign of *ña*. (10.67)
She whose form is like a vessel containing the seeds of knowledge; she who is unique and moves toward the One;
she who is the sole delight; she whose nature is consciousness; she who is the necklace; she who is the myrobalan fruit. 10.68
Ṭunṭunī, Ṭaṅkahastā, Ṭāntavargā, and Ṭalāvatī; Ṭapalā, she known as Ṭāpabālā, and she whose form is the sound of the ringing of a ṭaṅka. || 10.69 ||
She who transcends the syllable *ṭa*, she who is beyond the letter *ṭa*, the maiden whose beginning is the sound *ṭi*;
she who wields the axe as her weapon, the *ṭānā* goddess, she who speaks with the sound of the syllable *ṭamoṭa*.
She who makes the sound *ṭaṅkāra*, she who destroys obstacles, the one who utters *ṭākā* and *ṭakāṭaka*, she who deludes the *ṭakāṭakas*,
she whose great name is the bearer of the sound *ṭaṅkāra*, and she who causes the sky-farers to cry out.

She who utters the sound *ṭhaṭhaṃ*, whose form is *ṭhāṭha*, whose causal seed-syllable is *ṭha*; she who is fond of the *ḍamaru* drum, who dwells in the *ḍāmara*, and whose seed-syllable is *ḍa*. (10.72)

She whose syllables belong to the class beginning with *ḍa*, who holds a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), who dwells in the terrible (*ḍara*), who is the fierce *ḍora* and *ḍamara*, who is half of *ḍagara*, who transcends the letter *ḍa*, who is the mistress of the wood of *ḍa* (*ḍadārukeśvarī*), and who is swift (*ḍutā*). (10.73)
She who is the Lord of the Half-Woman (Ardhanārīśvara), the source of the Ḍhāma, the wielder of the ḍhakkā drum, the one who causes the world to dissolve, the one who dissolves away;
she who dwells in the ḍhaka-drum, the daughter of the Lord of the Ḍha, whose nature is the navel of the earth, and who removes all affliction.

The Sovereign Goddess whose end is the letter *ṇa*, who resides in the *ṇa*-group of consonants, who possesses the qualities of *ṇa*, *tu*, and *na*; she who is auspicious with the digit of pride (*māna*) as her mark, and whose seed-syllable is the lute of the eyes of the gods.
She is known as Tulasī, Tantusūkṣmā, Tāralyā, and Tailagandhikā;
she is Tapasyā, the daughter of a Tāpasa, Tāriṇī, Taruṇī, and Talā. (10.76)
Abiding in the Tantra, she is the very nature of the Tāraka-Brahman, situated in the midst of the threads;
she is the devourer of the *tāla* fruit, possessing the three abodes as her forms, the savior (*tārakā*), and the devourer of oil.
Tārogrā, Tālamālā, Takarā, and Tintiḍīpriyā; Tapas, Tālasandarbhā, and Tarjayantī Kumārikā. || 10-78 ||
Tokācārā, Talodvegā, Takṣakā, Takṣakapriyā, Takṣakālaṅkṛtā, Toṣā, Tāvadrūpā, and Talapriyā. || 10-79 ||
She who holds weapons in her hand, she who bestows the fruit of austerities through heat,
she who is delighted by the striking of conch shells, and she who destroys the hosts of enemies.
Tūlā, Taulī, Tolakā, Talasthā, Talapālikā, Taruṇā, Taptabuddhisthā, Taptā, Pradhāriṇī, and Tapā. (10.81)
She who illuminates the Tantras, likewise she who bestows the meaning of the Tantras, she whose body is like the moon, and she of equal radiance—thus she is fourfold. (10.82)
Born from the path of oil, she bestows the fruit of tantric accomplishment;
she has copper-colored leaves and copper-colored hair, and she is most fond of copper vessels.

She who is fond of the quality of *tamas*, the *tolā* [measure], the one who wards off the makers of *takṣaka*, she who is endowed with contentment, the one whose form is darkness, and she who is dear to the Lord of the sixteen *tamas*.
Comparison, equal taste, and equal intellect—such is the threefold wisdom.
The consumption of buttermilk, the accomplishment of the palm tree, and those who abide therein and go therein. (10.85)

Talā is the essence of oil, Tālī is intent on the concealment of the tantra, Tantramantraprakāśā is the illuminator of tantra and mantra, and she is the embodiment of the three arrows (triśareṇu). || 10-86 ||
She who delights in the thirty objects, she who is contented, she who is the beloved of contented people;
she who is the mistress of Thakārakūṭa and Daṇḍīśa, or rather, she who is the beloved of Thadaṇḍīśa. (10.87)
Her limbs are established in the form of the letter *tha*; she is the *kārikā* of the *tha*-ending class of consonants.
She is the Mistress of the *tha*-ending *thamī*, the *thākā*, and she whose garland is the seed-syllable of *tha*. (10.88)

She who is dear to Dakṣa’s bond, she whose faults are like a forest of thicket-like defects, she whose condition is terrible with her ten teeth, the goddess who is dear to her servant, and she who is compassion itself. (10.89)
The slayer of the Daityas, the supreme one, the Daitya, the subduer of the Daityas,
the direction, the tamed, the lover of the tamed, the servant, the giver of bonds, and she with long hair.
Daśanā, Raktavarṇā, Darīgrahanivāsinī, Devamātā, Durlabhā, Dīrghāṅgā, and Dāsakanyakā. || 10-91 ||
Daśanaśrī, Dīrghanetrā, Dīrghanāsā, Doṣahā, Damayantī, Dalasthā, Dveṣyahantrī, and Daśasthitā. (10.92)
She who pervades all directions, she who has gone to the quarters, she who destroys weapons with her teeth;
she who removes poverty, she who dwells among the poor, and she who bestows wealth upon the indigent. (10.93)
She possesses prominent teeth and speaks the local dialect; she is established in the land and is the leader of the teaching.
She has the form of hatred yet is the destroyer of hatred, deluding the host of enemies that is hatred. || 10.94 ||
She is the sound arising from the abode of Dāmodara, the bestower of strength to the petals;
she is the vision of the directions, she who stands in the act of seeing, and she who speaks words dear to those who behold her.
The beloved of Dāmodara, the self-controlled, whose body is Dāmodara;
she who causes motion, the possessor of wealth, the skillful, the daughter of Dakṣa, and she who rends that which is firm.
She possesses the power of a firm seat, she who manifests the duel;
she is fond of curd, she who abides in curd, and she who brings about the auspiciousness of curd.
She is the destroyer of pride, the giver of pride, the haughty one, fond of *darbha* grass and merit,
the curd-like one, established upon *darbha*, the daughter of Drupada, Draupadī, and the beloved of Drupada.
She is the contemplation of Dharma, the presiding deity of wealth, and the bestower of boons upon the lords of wealth;
she is the destroyer of wealth, the giver of wealth, the archer, the one with bow in hand, and the lover of the bow.
She is the earth, the embodiment of fortitude, the abode of wealth, and the one who deludes with riches;
she is the courageous one, dear to the wise, the support, and intent upon upholding the world.
She is the giver of grain, the seed of grain, and the very embodiment of dharma and adharma;
she dwells upon the clouds, she is auspicious, and she resides within the mass of dharma.
She is the beloved daughter of the wealthy, served by blessed people;
she is the embodiment of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, and the bestower of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
She is the upholder of the earth, the bearer of burdens, white, and fair-faced;
she is the earth itself, the embodiment of light, eternal, the essence of permanence, and fond of the Pole Star.
She is the mistress of wealth, known as Dhāraṇā, the destroyer of the revilers of Dharma;
she consists of the splendor of Dharma, is righteous, and deludes even Bharga with her supreme fortitude.
She is the power of retention (dhāraṇā), she whose garments are washed clean, who enjoys the fruit of the dhattūra plant;
she is Nārāyaṇī, who dwells among kings, and whose body is that of Nārāyaṇa.
She is pleased by Nara and Nārāyaṇa, she delights in the praise of Dharma, she is eternal, she is the daughter of a barber, she resides in the eyes, and she is beloved by men. 10-106.
She is named Nāmī, fond of names; she is the women (nārāḥ), the daughter of Nārāyaṇa, and the men (narāḥ);
she is pleased with the new leader, ever-new, and fond of fresh fruit.
Delighting in fresh blossoms, trailing behind the banners of the young,
she is the woman who finds joy in the bliss of those dwelling at the *nimba* tree, and she is the bringer of prosperity.
Greatly delighted by fresh flowers, fragrant with the scent of fresh flowers, dwelling in the Nandana grove, the daughter of Nanda, she is the bestower of joy and liberation. || 10-109 ||
She is Namitā, Nāmabheda, and by name Ārtavanamohinī;
she is Navabuddhipriyā, Anekā, Nākasthā, and Nāmakanyakā.
Free from censure, possessing fresh splendor, she bestows the station of heaven;
residing in the nimba tree, she is Nimbā, who dwells among various trees.
She who destroys the past, who is blue-colored, who is Sarasvatī of blue hue, who dwells in the sky, who is beloved by the Leader, and who desires what is dear to the Leader. || 10-112 ||
She was not of a specific caste, she took no food, she was free from grain, and she delighted in dust; she had a deep navel, a pleasing form, and was honored by the hands of kings.
Abiding in Nala, delighted by Nala, she is the princess of King Nala;
she is the supreme sovereign, the bliss of the transcendent, and the one who distinguishes between the higher and the lower.
She is supreme, she who dwells in the midst of enemy armies, Pārvatī, the beloved of the mountain,
the consort of the Supreme Lord, she who consists of various mountain peaks, and the supreme one who delights in garlands of flowers.
She is the supreme beloved, the giver of joy, joy itself, and the first of lovers;
she is the primordial one, the first, the gratified, and the supreme one who delights in the fragrance of flowers.
Born in the month of Pauṣa, she delights in drinking, is full-bodied, and is beautiful with full breasts;
she is supremely fond of men, holds a noose in her hand, and is dear to those bound by the snares of worldly existence.
She who delights in the essence of straw, whose form is like the smoke of straw, who resembles the *palāśa* flower, and who wears a garland of *palāśa* flowers. || 10.118 ||
She whose essence is love, lotus-faced, beautifully garlanded with rubies, a garland of lotuses, the remover of sins, she who delights in love for her husband. || 10-119 ||
She who captivates the five-faced one, she who reveals the five faces; she who subsists on fruits and roots, the furrowed one, the giver of fruit, and she who is dear to Phālguna.
She is beloved by the Lord of Fruits, the Fruitful One, the Daughter of Phalgu, and she who is intent upon the fruit.
She is the foremost of the Phetkārī Tantras and is worshipped by the host of Phetkāras.

She who causes transformation, the daughter of the jackal, she who arises from the enjoyment of fruit, the fruit itself, she who is fond of fruit, she who is capable of bestowing fruit, and she who grants joy to Phālguna. || 10-122 ||

She who possesses the fruit of enjoyment as her supreme goal, she who dwells in the lotus of the full-blown flower, she who resides in the house of Vasudeva, she who is the daughter of Vasava, and she who is honored by heroes. || 10.123 ||
Viṣabhakṣā is the daughter of Budha; Bluṅkārī bestows boons upon Blū.
Brāhmī is the daughter of Bṛhaspati; she bestows the boons of Vācaspati. || 10-124 ||

She who follows the conduct of the Vedas, who is intent on what is to be known, who resides in the mouth of Vyāsa, who is radiant, who possesses awakening knowledge, who is named Vauṣaṭ, and who is honored by the salutation of the flute. || 10.125 ||
She is the beloved of Vajra, the movement of Vajra, she who increases the lineage of Badarī; she is Bhāratī, the bestower of the glory of existence, the consort of Bhava, and the daughter of Bhava.
Bhavānī, Bhāvinī, Bhīmā, the wife of the physician (Dhanvantari), established on the island, the embodiment of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, deeply afflicted, and crying out like a frog.
She is composed of the elements, she is fond of hemp (bhaṅga), she is the destroyer of the breaking of hemp, she is the remover of worldly attachments;
she is the sustainer, the Blessed One, the fortunate one, and she is saluted by Bhagīratha.
She who possesses a garland of fortune, the sovereign lady of the lords of beings, worshipped by Bhārgava;
she who belongs to the lineage of Bhṛgu, the remover of fear, the earth, and the one who destroys serpents. || 10.129 ||
Her face is like the young moon; she bestows the splendor that transcends worldly existence;
she is seated upon a sea-monster; her gait is intoxicated; she is maddened by passion; and she is fond of intoxication.
Madirā has eighteen arms; she moves with the gait of one intoxicated by wine.
Madirā bestows the attainment of success; she is the slender-waisted one who grants the attainment of entering into the state of intoxication.
She who feeds on fish, whose form is that of a fish, whose movement is fond of seals and beans;
she who holds a pestle, the giver of liberation, who is personified, and who is intent upon rendering others mute. (10.132)
She is afflicted by falsehood, she is a mirage, and she is intent on devouring sheep;
she is the accomplishment of sexual bliss and the bestower of the perfection of the fire of sexual union.
Mahālakṣmī, Bhairavī, the Mistress of Mahendra-pīṭha,
she who dwells in the mind, the foremost of the Mādhavīs, and the one who delights Mahādeva.
Yaśodā, she who is the beloved of Yamarāja, the Yamās, her limbs adorned by a mass of glory, and she who possesses the art of love for the ascetic (Yati). || 10.135 ||
She is Rāmaṇī and the wife of Rāma; she is the destroyer of enemies and dwells within the flow [of creation].
She is Rudrāṇī, the bestower of form, the embodiment of form, and the wearer of beautiful forms. || 10.136 ||
Retasthā, who is pleased with semen, who dwells in the abode of semen;
Rendra, the daughter of the gods; Redā, the beloved of the destroyer of the host of enemies. (10.137)
The mother of the lord of the line of body hair, the mistress of the world of the pores of the skin,
silver-colored, fierce-colored, and adorned with ornaments of silver.
She who possesses color, she who abides in the passion of color, the sovereign of the lineage of the fire of battle;
she is Lakṣmī, holding a plow in her hand, the wielder of the plow, the beloved of the Kula.
She is the form of writing, with licked-up feet, having the nature of a creeper’s fiber;
she anoints, she licks, she is restless, fond of body hair, and the bestower of the success of beloved ones.
She is the worldly one, the worldly accomplishment, the maiden mistress of Laṅkā;
she is Lakṣmaṇā, devoid of fortune (Lakṣmī), the beloved of *la*, and situated between the letters *la* and *ra*.
She is naked, she is the entrance into clothing, she is the girl of the Vivasvat family;
she abides in the wind, she has the form of the wind, and she dwells in the midst of the tides.
Standing in the midst of a cremation ground, she is fond of the practice of the charnel ground;
desiring supreme accomplishment, she is adorned upon the chest of a corpse.
She is the protector of those who have come for refuge, the daughter of Śiva, and the beloved of Śiva;
she pierces the six cakras, and her face is firm with the network of the sixteen-fold nyāsa.
She is Sandhyā, Sarasvatī, Sundarī, Sūryagā, Śāradā, and Satī; she is Haripriyā, the essence of the nectar of Hara’s beauty, Kṣamā, and Kṣudhā.
She is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajñā), the Bestower of Siddhi, Ambikā, and Aparājitā;
she is the Primordial One, the Beloved of Indra, Īśā, Umā, the Married One, and the Lover of Rtu.
Sutuṇḍā, ending with the seed-syllable *svaḥ*, bestows the siddhi of Hariveśa and others;
and Aindrī, established in the Ekādaśī vow, bestows the siddhi of medicinal herbs.
Beneficial, consisting of the constituent parts, and illuminating the seed-syllables of the weapons—this, O Lord of the Kāmukīs, is the great auspiciousness of the virgins. (10.148)
This great hymn, the essence of Dharma, bestows the fruits of the three worlds eternally; it yields a thousand and eight [verses] and grants wealth, grain, and sons. (10.149)
The wise person endowed with devotion who recites this, which radiates the fruit of all knowledge, shall always, by day and by night, be one who has entered the path of liberation. || 10-150 ||
He attains victory everywhere and becomes beloved by heroes;
all the gods come under his control, as do human beings who have been brought into subjection. || 10.151 ||
Those who praise [them] within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) are surely satisfied; there is no doubt in this.
And those who dwell in the world of earth (bhūrloka), possessing prowess equal to that of the gods, [are likewise satisfied]. || 10-152 ||
O Lord of the Family, it is the truth, the absolute truth, that all of them are equal to servants;
yet one attains success suddenly through fire-offerings and sacrificial worship. (10.153)

One may obtain the fruit [of the rite] even without sacrifices, without gifts, and without recitations, by means of the muttering of mantras, the armor-armor (kavaca) and other [protections], and the recitation of the meaning of the great hymns.
Whoever recites this hymn named "The Thousand and Eight," for him peace shall swiftly come; thereafter, one should recite the Hymn to the Virgin.
By reciting it three times, one brings the king under one's control;
by reciting it once, the practitioner partakes in virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (10.156)
If a learned man desires a son, he should recite it for three days,
either in the sequence of three times each day or even once per day.
Having recited this, the practitioner of mantra becomes the lord of wealth and jewels, possessing all knowledge; by reciting it for half a year, he shall delude the three worlds.
Whether one recites it for a year or even with a spirit of devotion,
that person shall become a long-lived yogi who, having attained the state of a sky-walker (khecarī), becomes a master of yoga.
With a steady mind, he beholds the form situated at a great distance;
standing within the circle of women, the wise man, endowed with power, should recite [the mantra]. (10.160)
He shall become the best of practitioners, like a wish-fulfilling tree that yields milk; O Lord, he who always recites this with his body overflowing with devotion. (10.161)
By means of this vision, the practitioner becomes capable of performing immobilization;
he is empowered to arrest water and other elements, and attains the siddhis such as the immobilization of fire. (10.162)
One becomes swift as the wind, a great orator, and certainly a knower of the Vedas;
one becomes a lord of poets, possessed of great knowledge, a binder [of enemies], and a scholar. (10.163)
Having become the sovereign of all lands, he himself shall become the son of a goddess;
the powerful ascetic attains beauty, fortune, fame, and prosperity. (10.164)

O Lord, endowed with the eight siddhis, whoever should recite this for the sake of accomplishing their purpose—in the midst of a dense forest, in the wilderness, on a mountain, or in a fearsome jungle—[shall attain success]. (10.165)
In a forest, on a cremation ground, upon a corpse, or in a great battle;
in a village, in a ruined house, in an empty dwelling, or on a riverbank. (10.166)

In the womb of the Gaṅgā, at the great seat (mahāpīṭha), at the seat of the womb (yonipīṭha), in the house of the Guru, in a field of grain, in a temple, in a maiden’s chamber, or in a family dwelling. || 10-167 ||
In a wilderness, or in the midst of a cow-pen free from fear of kings and other dangers, or in one's own country where there is no fear, or else in a temple of Śiva. || 10.168 ||
In a pit of the earth, or at a solitary linga, in a deserted and undisturbed place, at the root of an Ashvattha or Bilva tree, or near a Kula-tree; || 10-169 ||
In other lands of the Siddhas, practitioners who possess the form of the Kula,
or those established in the divine heroic state (vīrabhāva), having worshipped with a maiden of the Kula and Akula, [attain success].
With various family substances and substances for attaining success,
the practitioner should offer oblations with meat-wine and with liberated mercury.
One should give the remains of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*) as the family substance (*kuladravya*) to them for the sake of perfect accomplishment;
having taken their leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*), one should offer them into a red lotus.
Free from disgust and shame, the practitioner with a steady mind, the mantra-reciter, always joyful and possessed of great strength, should drink the essence of meat. (10.173)
The wise one should recite the mantra consisting of *tāra*, *māyā*, *ramā*, and the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*) over the eight portions of human flesh and the jars filled with wine for them. (10.174)
Having offered [the oblation] according to this rite and having recited the auspicious hymn,
one who partakes of the prasāda himself shall indeed become the sovereign of all vidyās.
The man who recites [this] after offering the meat of a boar and a camel, a fat fish, a seal, and even a jar of great liquor, [attains success]. (10.176)
Surely he shall become all-pervading even without fire-offerings or ritual worship;
he shall eternally take on the form of Rudra and become identical with Mahākāla. (10.177)
O Protector, the practitioner attains in an instant the fruit of all merit;
he becomes the lord of the jewel-treasury of the milk-ocean, pervading the sky, and the king of yogins.
Through devotion, one will certainly attain joy and the state of desirelessness from that ocean of compassion, even when struck by great enemies and terrified by the fear of great enemies. (10.179)
Merely by reciting it once, one shall bring about the slaughter of enemies;
one shall swiftly crush the enemies just as the sun dispels darkness. (10.180)

In cases of expulsion, killing, or in the face of a most terrible enemy, whether one is a mortal, a god, or a rākṣasa and the like, [one is protected] by reciting and retaining [this mantra]. (10.181)
By reciting the names of Kumārī, men on the right arm and likewise women on the left hand immediately attain peace. (10.182)
Having maintained [this], one obtains prosperity such as sons and so forth; there is no doubt in this matter. || 10-183 ||
By my command, the practitioner attains liberation;
