O Lord, whenever a person recites the *Gajāntaka-sahasranāma* with a spirit of devotion—
For then, indeed, one shall obtain the arising of the fruit everywhere. || 10-184 ||

Those who, though agitated by anxious thoughts, constantly recite with joy this supreme hymn— which bestows liberation, yields the enjoyment of excellent fruits, is the very essence, and grants transcendent bliss—
become eternally victorious like Śrī Rāma; they prevail over the lotus of fame.
In beauty and virtue they were equal to ten thousand Kandarpas, yet in anger they were like Rudras.

Thus, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the arrangement of the worship of the Virgin (*Kumāryupacaryāvinyāsa*), in the section on perfected mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the determination of the divine state (*Divyabhāvanirṇaya*),
in the glorious manifestation of the auspicious one thousand and eight names (*Aṣṭottarasahasranāmamaṅgalollāsa*).
The Tenth Chapter. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Therefore, I shall now fully explain the determination of the divine state and so forth."
Relying upon whom Mahārudra bears the name Bhuvaneśvara.
Having known which, the Lord of Kamalā, the sovereign of the deities, Brahmā—the master of the four Vedas and the eternal Brahman himself—[attained his status]. (11.2)
The young ascetic is my son, and Śakra is the presiding deity of heaven;
all the guardians of the quarters, the sky-dwellers, and others are endowed with the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi). || 11-3 ||
O Mahādeva, Ānandanātha Bhairava, you who consist of the bliss of wine, the bliss of the heart, the bliss of knowledge, and compassion! || 11-4 ||
Listen with a single-minded focus, O Lord, if you desire accomplishment;
for you, who are the form of my beloved bliss, abide within my very body. (11.5)
The divine state is threefold: that born from the Vedas, that born from the Āgamas, and that born from discrimination (viveka).
The meaning of the Vedas is declared to be the lowest, while that arising from the Āgamas is the middle.
The entire supreme [practice] is said to arise from the blossoming of discernment;
likewise, there are three types of disposition: the divine, the heroic, and the animal. (11.7)
It is declared to be divine, born of discernment, and the bestower of all perfections;
one should know that supreme state to be an ocean of the essence of bliss.
The middle state is the radiance of the scriptures, characterized by heroic sentiment and accompanied by ritual action;
it originates from the Vedas and is for the sake of attaining results. The lowest state, indeed, is the animalistic state.
The lowest state of being, characteristic of a beast, is pervaded by universal censure;
whereas in the highest state, there is supreme knowledge that bestows the perfection of being upon men. (11.10)
In the middle [of the lineage] is that which arises from the Madhumatī and my own family’s tradition;
it removes untimely death and is exceedingly difficult for beings to attain.
O Lord, without the state of a hero, nothing ever succeeds;
for the lowest [level], the explanation is always base, consisting of words that express censure. (11–12)
If one does not engage in criticism, then one shall obtain the fruit thereof;
even in the state of a beast, success shall be attained if one constantly practices this Veda.
Constant reflection on the meaning of the Vedas, delighting in the sound of Vedic recitation, free from all censure, and entirely devoid of violence and laziness. (11–14)

If the practitioner of mantra remains established in the state of being, even while abiding in the condition of a bound soul (paśu), he shall attain accomplishment, having conquered greed, delusion, lust, anger, pride, and envy.

O Mahādeva, for those on this earth who know the state of the bound soul (paśubhāva) and the state of greatness (mahābhāva), what is impossible to achieve? Through the practice of effort, they attain that [state]. || 11-16 ||
The entire world depends on exertion, and the deities depend on exertion;
the great mantra depends on exertion, and the scorcher of foes depends on exertion. (11.17)
Family conduct dependent on mere physical exertion is a mark of the state of a beast;
merely knowing the meaning of the Vedas while remaining in the state of a beast is dear to the Kula. (11-18)
Having studied the Smṛtis, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and the various meanings of the Vedas,
as well as all the Śāstras, the wise man [attains liberation] through the knowledge of reality.
Like one seeking grain discards husks, the best of practitioners, having become a man of knowledge, should abandon all scriptures and take refuge in the essence of reality. 11-20.
One who honors my spoken word should perform the ritual actions prescribed in the Vedas;
this is declared to be the defining characteristic of those who have exhausted their animal-like toil and suffering. (11.21)
For the sake of the tradition, ritual action should be performed through the activities prescribed by the scripture of my own family,
for the heroes and the exalted ones who follow my body.
This is declared to be the definition of the principles (tattvas) of the Maccheśākula;
it should be understood by those of firm mind through the knowledge of the name "Vivekasūtra. (11.23)
For those who possess equanimity toward all things, mere existence itself is the means of proof;
for everywhere, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings has its origin in my lotus feet.
Whatever action one performs after having asked [for instruction] grants the attainment of unimpeded results; such is the conviction of the discerning whose minds possess unbroken knowledge. (11.25)
Thus has the definition of those who possess stainless bliss and divinity been declared;
he who on this earth understands the threefold state within the divine— || 11-26 ||
O Lord, that supreme practitioner, the great hero, never perishes;
yet without the state of divine being, there is no vision of my lotus feet. (11.27)
O Mahādeva, how can that practitioner who desires [these states] be considered deluded?
He [attains] the state of a Paśu in the first [initiation] and the state of a Vīra in the second. || 11-28 ||
In the third [birth], there is a divine state, and then three divine states in succession;
hear that method, O Śiva, purifier of the three worlds! (11.29)
Then he is one who knows the distinctions of the three states of being, who pierces the six supports,
who understands the reality of the meaning of the five principles, and who delights in divine conduct.
He indeed becomes illustrious, having reached the further shore of the names of the Siddhas and other [attainments];
endowed with the eight sovereign powers, he shall roam about like Śiva.
In all cases, the means for achieving the mass of bliss is through a state of purity;
it consists of maintaining [the practice] from the time of dawn until midday. (11.32)

He who prepares food with the aforementioned substances or by means of the sequence of restraint and so forth, becomes a perfected one (siddha) through the animal stage (paśukrama) in a divine state. || 11-33 ||
I shall speak of the heroic state within the divine state; listen to that further:
the practice with a pure disposition from midday until the evening twilight. (11.34)

Whether performing recitation or even retaining [the mantra], having taken hold of the mind with effort in a solitary and uninhabited place, one certainly becomes a perfected being (siddha). || 11-35 ||
At that time, for the sake of the heroic state (*vīrabhāva*), the mere state of being (*bhāvamātra*) is indeed the means;
through such a state one attains accomplishment, and nowhere else than from the Hero. (11.36)
At night, his mouth filled with betel leaf and complete with perfumes and other offerings,
he was endowed with the bliss of victory regarding the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).
Having concentrated his mind on unity, overwhelmed by an excess of bliss, he who should recite [the mantra] throughout the entire night in a solitary house, free from fear, [attains success]. (11.38)
He would become a servant of Kālikā, the most excellent among the divine ones;
having thus understood these three states, he who then accomplishes the rite [attains success]. (11.39)
Having become endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, one certainly becomes omniscient;
among the three types of existence, this is the determination of the merit of the objective state.
Listen, O Lord, I shall speak; attend with careful attention.
One attains success suddenly by knowing that which is marked by convention. (11.41)
O Mahādeva, for one who knows this, there is accomplishment without a doubt;
I shall now speak of that subtle symbolic meaning in the twelfth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
In the eleventh chapter, there is the determination of the meaning of pure disposition (*bhāva*).
Everything is obtained through disposition; the three worlds are dependent upon disposition. (11.43)
O Mahādeva, without the state of being (bhāva), success never arises anywhere;
nor for those who rely on the state of the fettered (paśubhāva) from the time of dawn. || 11-44 ||
O Lord, for the purpose of answering questions, there is the time based on ten daṇḍas, as well as the wheel of the twelve zodiac signs and the twelve months. (11.45)
A wise person should discern existence and non-existence within a period of ten *daṇḍas*,
by means of the fivefold distinction of vowels through both direct and reverse order.
Childhood, youth, beauty, adolescence, and that which is designated as old age—these eight stages are to be known as the five-syllable ritual (vidhi) itself, occurring in sequence. (11.47)
One's own fifth [element], situated at the tip of the nose, is proclaimed;
O Bhairava, it is the wind that exists within the middle of the nostrils. (11.48)
One should contemplate existence and non-existence within the middle of those nostril-pits:
[the elements] ether, the form of air, fire, and water, O Lord. (11.49)
The earthly [element] is to be known gradually through the sequence beginning with childhood and so forth.
When the left [channel] arises, Vāmā is auspicious; when the right, Puruṣa is auspicious. (11.50)
The movement of the winds should be known to extend as far as the limits of space;
however, the movement of the wind is restricted solely to the central region.
Then one should recognize that as space; the state of childhood is proclaimed [to be there].
The animal state is at the tip of the nose, as well as the arising of the vital breath. (11.52)
One should know that it is merely a wandering, yet it is indeed all-auspicious;
O Lord, one should recognize that as the "Kiśora" state when the breath moves transversely. (11.53)
If the breath moves like a staff solely at the tip of the upward-pointing nose, one should know that it is of the nature of fire; its movement will then become powerful. (11.54)

And when that [state] reaches its full development through excessive exertion, there is delay; yet one attains supreme pleasure during the rising of Varuṇa’s waters [semen], which [otherwise] causes diseases. (11.55)
When it quickly moves downward, even slightly beyond the upper range, and when one exhales, then there is the onset of a violent disease. (11.56)
O Mahādeva, the lofty fortune of the earth, oppressed by the heat of yoga, has set through both direct and reverse order.
The wind moves swiftly, distinguished by its left and right [paths];
it flows through the left nostril as earth and water. (11.58)
Muditā always bestows both fruit and non-fruit within the circle of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍamaṇḍala);
indeed, it is her power as Vāyavī that then obtains the portion of the fruit.
If it is thus, then in the case of a question concerning a woman on the left side,
if a man there asks a question while moving toward the left, [the result is as follows].
Then he incurs disease and will certainly become devoid of merit, provided that the rising of the wind occurs on the left while the person is situated on the right. (11.61)
Then one obtains a fruit as rare as the arrival of wealth;
yet there may also be a sudden loss of wealth that destroys the fruits desired by the mind. (11.62)
There is quarrel with friends and discord when there is a break in the rising; it is auspicious when they rise separately.
For Varuṇa alone, a person in the south is auspicious. (11-63)
Impurity resides in the earth and water; this division is difficult for even the best to attain.
On the other hand, the qualities of air and fire are always rising in the south.
O Lord, one may understand the auspicious or inauspicious results of space if, by the power of destiny alone, the movement of the wind becomes slow. (11.65)
Then, in the middle of the right nostril, there is the auspicious arising of the left;
at that time, one should contemplate the two elements of wind and fire in the left. (11.66)
Having understood its rising, one should know that there is loss for a friend and fear from a deity;
likewise, if the wind [element] moves into the auspicious house or the temple.
At that time, a man who is capable and facing toward the portion of Dakṣa—how such a person obtains the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage at that moment. || 11-68 ||
Then, through the grace of Vāyu, one obtains supreme wealth;
those distressed by the loss of loved ones in foreign lands return, and there is the attainment of sons. (11.69)
One should indicate that the three states beginning with childhood are auspicious when there is a difference in the zodiac signs;
such is the result in this wheel within the twelve-zodiac wheel. (11.70)
One should understand the subtle fruit; O Lord, hear now about that which is called the *cakra*:
the *ājñā-cakra*, the *kāma-cakra*, and the essential *phala-cakra*. (11.71)
The wheel of questions, the wheel of the earth, and beyond that the wheel of heaven;
the wheel of the balance, the wheel of water—this sixfold wheel consists of the three qualities.
O Lord, one should know that the essence-wheel, the meteor-wheel, and the death-wheel follow one another in sequence;
here, one should understand the hexagon according to both direct and reverse order.

If, through one's inner disposition, the knowledge of the vowels arises within every wheel, the movement of the vital breath is perceived everywhere, and the circulation of all inquiries and so forth occurs, [then the goal is attained]. (11.74)
Then, having understood that measure of the ascendant and the rising of the sign, the wise man should conduct an inquiry into the question if he desires success here. (11.75)

Thus ends the eleventh [chapter] in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the section on accomplished mantras (siddhamantra-prakaraṇa), in the *Sārasaṅketa* concerning the investigation of the state of the bound soul (paśubhāva-vicāra), in the determination of the awakening of states (bhāvabodha-nirṇaya), in the illumination of the great tantra (*mahātantroddīpana*), in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the Northern Tantra (*uttaratantra*).
Chapter 11.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Then one should write the eighth sign located at the junction on her left side."
The wise one should write the number seven at the junction located below that.
Above that, in the left corner, one should write the third numeral;
then, above that, in the corner-house, one should likewise write the pair of numerals (the second).
And listen, O Lord, to the single house of the color *aṅka* to its south:
the state of the Vasus, the state of zero, the state of six, and zero. (12-3)

In the middle of this, there is no letter, nor is there a corner-mark (koṇāṅka), even though it possesses color; one should write the *ṭa* and *ta* groups, as well as *śa* and *ṣa*, upon the arrows and directly below the zero.
The *ka*-group and *ca*-group situated in the second square, joined with the letter *e*;
the letter situated in the third square, from *a* to *kṣa*; the *ṭa*-group; and *oṃ*. (12.5)
One should carefully write the two syllables *ta* and *pa*, ending with the letter *ma*,
in its southern house, which is situated in the middle of a single square.
The pair of *u* and *y*, the two *pa* vowels, and the letter *a* at the head of the pairs—this is the Kāmacakra, which yields results at the time of inquiry. (12-7)
One should count the syllables situated in the ten corners by moving counter-clockwise,
according to the names beginning with the five vowels, both in direct and reverse order.
One should count the houses up to that house where the master of the Vedas receives his own name, for the sake of determining the question and for the perfection of the planetary calculation. (12-9)

Having understood the colors and the nine positions of the nine planets, and having understood the states such as childhood and so forth where the planetary position occurs, the one of excellent intelligence [should proceed]. (12.10)
Having brought together that constellation, one should bring it under the authority of the door;
without the yoga of the triangle, the wise man should draw a hexagon.
In the middle of that, having pierced through an eight-cornered [figure], there is an inner abode of the deity;
in the middle of that is a six-cornered [figure], and in the middle of that is a triangle.
One should gradually write the letters in a clockwise direction:
in the upper-left portion, [the vowels] a, ā, i, and the ka-group (kavarga).
To the right of that, the wise one should write the pair *ī ī* and the *ṭa*-group;
on the right side, in the lower portion, the pair *ṛ ṝ* and the *ta*-group.
Below that, the wise one should write the letters ḷ, ḹ, e, and ai, as well as the labial class (pavarga).
And on its left side, one should write o, au, and the semivowels ya, ra, la, and va.
In the remaining houses, one should write the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' in six houses;
in the center and at the beginning of the corners, there is the single-syllabled body of Śarva (the letter 'ha').
The wise one should draw Rudra, Agni, Mūti, and Anila in the southeast corner;
the sacrificer [should draw] Paśupati, Mūti, and the sixth [deity] in the south.
One should draw Mahādeva with the form of Soma as the seventh in the southwest;
the wise one should draw the pair consisting of the form of Jala in the west.
One should draw the fourth [deity], Ugravīra, whose form is wind, in the northwest corner; and the fifth, Bhīmarūpa, whose form is space, in the north. (12-19)
One should draw a six-petaled lotus in the northeast for Īśāna and Sūryamūrti;
then, one should likewise draw a hexagon in the center below the hexagon.
In the upper corner is the summer season, and Śiśira is also in the south;
Varṣā is below that, and Vasantaka is at the very bottom of all.
The autumn season is in the fifth enclosure, and the winter season is in the sixth;
the triangular space in their midst contains the syllable *va*, which has the form of fire.
Having written it down, the mantra-practitioner should calculate [the result] by means of the syllables, deities, numbers, and fires;
this is the wheel of great subtlety, the wheel of results, which is highly proficient. (12.23)
Now, O Lord of the Kula, listen again to the back-wheel;
for without knowledge, this state of being the "back" does not arise. (12-24)
If the supreme practitioner knows the nature of the rear wheel, then, having understood his own result, he will certainly attain accomplishment. || 12-25 ||
Ānandabhairava said:
The practitioner of mantra should cause a hexagon to be made without the ritual means of a triangle;
in its center, a square, and in the center of that, the letters beginning with Śa.

Having written it, the mantra-practitioner should inscribe it there in the center of the six-marked [diagram]; he should cause the six marks to be placed according to the sequence of increasingly long [lines].

In front of that, one should construct a hexagon, and there the wise person should write the syllables of the numerical signs; the learned one should write the *ka*-group in the first house at the top.
In the temple to its south, the wise one should draw the *ca*-group;
the *ṭa*-group below that on the right, and the *ta*-group at the very bottom of all.
O Lord, in the temple to its left is the auspicious letter-group beginning with *pa*;
above that, from *ya* to *va*, arranged in a clockwise direction.
The wise one should inscribe the vowels beginning with 'a' there in the temple;
he should deliberate for as long a time as it takes for the vowels to come to rest. || 12-31 ||
One should write down the presence of the signs beginning with Aries according to the measurement of the *varga* notation, arranging them in both direct and reverse order within the sixth house.
O Lord, whatever the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) may be in the house [of the diagram], beginning with the vowels—
if one brings them together and performs the subtraction, the excellent numerical figure that is obtained— 12.33.
Then, O Lord, one should divide by six;
the quotient obtained there is the zodiacal sign and the moment of that [time]. (12.34)
O Lord of Vidyās, I shall describe that perfected fruit which is the wheel of command (ājñācakra);
by the mere realization of which one certainly becomes omniscient. (12.35)
One suddenly attains power; I bestow that jewel of knowledge, which, when performed on the seven days of the week beginning with Sunday, increases one's welfare.
The seven-day cycle beginning with Śani (Saturn) increases happiness during the Tretā Yuga;
and the seven-day cycle beginning with Guru (Jupiter) is the means for accomplishing dharma during the Dvāpara Yuga.
The seven days of the week, beginning with Venus, bestow the fruits of the Kali age;
therefore, they should be counted starting from Venus onwards by those who are discerning. (12.38)
The wise one, the best among those who know the tantras, should count seven times in the center of the four-petaled lotus, counting the days of the week in order starting from the east.
Whichever leaf contains its own [assigned] day, that is the one upon which the completion and the arising occur;
having brought together the mass of those [leaves], one should bring about the differentiation of the syllables.
The general fruits [are obtained] from the various leaves of the *vadāra* tree and so forth;
the practitioner of mantra, desiring auspiciousness, should contemplate the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*). (12.41)
O scholar of conventions, hear now the greatness of that fruit and its absence.
Ānandabhairava said:
On the eastern petal, the half-moon of the vowel *ā* is clearly manifest;
it bestows the attainment of sovereignty through the sound ending in the letter *ha*.
The attainment of common goals, the union with distinguished objects, engagement in sacrifices and security, as well as the acquisition of sons; || 12-43 ||
A mortal who takes refuge in the ornament of compassion attains victory, a well-conducted marriage,
happiness, O Lord, and the affection of the world along with excellent enjoyments.
Upon the completion of the moments and so forth of the Vibhādhvaka [deities]. || 12-44 ||
On the right petal of the lotus, I am the radiant one who delights in the feet of the Beloved;
by those pure words that bestow various marks and [overcome] suffering, I am shaken.
This is the direct imposition of Yama, which destroys the passion for the union with the nectar of Mahendra.
The mind, which is indeed extremely fickle, is made joyful by the delight in the virtues of the virtuous. || 12-45 ||

Even if the heat of cruel and wicked people advances directly toward one’s gain of a worthy object, they are nevertheless unable to destroy it in the midst of the constituent qualities; rather, it retains its own established nature, such as forbearance and the like.
If the planet occupying the middle portion of the house is indeed the lord of the day and asks about the matter of wealth,
it will certainly be like the beloved of the Moon; it increases the happiness residing in the mind and brings about the joyful destruction of enemies within the family through secret movements.
One should count the crushing of diseases, the communication of those seeking devotion to the state of the Lord,
the joy in the lotus of the heart, the wealth of nectar, the arrival at a sacred ford that destroys sorrow,
the subtle meaning, and then the vision of the Goddess of Speech, who is free from fickleness. (12.48)

In the midst of the Atharva-veda leaf, dwells the tender Kamalā, the giver of musical instruments; she suddenly proclaims news of arrivals and always brings auspiciousness. She eternally and necessarily [bestows] majesty, the welfare of her dear circle, and the state of being a refuge for the sentiment of love.
Constantly longing to drink the pure honey of love from the lotus-face of his beloved.
In Aries, the lion attains satisfaction with arrows; in Aquarius, there is the acquisition of their fruits;
in Scorpio (the slayer of elephants), there is silver; and through theft, whatever has been acquired remains thus until sunrise at one hundred palas of brass.
Situated in the midst of the Śrīkeśara [yantra], it declares the fruit or lack of fruit for the morning time. || 12-50 ||
Observe that when one hundred and one *palas* of the moon's arc occupy the earth, then there is the seizure of wealth; when it is in the water, there is the kingdom and so forth for a friend;
and at the time of its arrival from a distant place and so on, there is great affliction for the enemy.
The rise of one's desires, group, and family is calculated from the conjunction with the Sun. || 12-51 ||
When one hundred and one fruits have accumulated together, Kumbha becomes exceedingly weak;
when shall the talk of poverty find its place in this land adorned by learning and wealth?
[There shall be] gain from traveling to various countries and regions, and the swift arrival of riches and other assets.
Indeed, the speaking for the purpose of seeing the gods is the destruction of delusion. || 12-52 ||

On Friday, during the day of Saturn, and when the sun is in Lavaṭāha, there is always the dawning of knowledge on one's own path; that is the determination of lifespans. Having joyfully attained the eight divisions (vargas), the hero attains greatness.
The world perceives only a mere fraction of the lifespan of the first celestial beings as a defect.
Thus, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*,
in the determination of the meaning of the inquiry into states of being (*bhāva*),
in the *Pāśavakalpa*, in the *Ājñācakrasārasaṅketa*, in the section on accomplished mantras (*siddhamantraprakaraṇa*).
The twelfth chapter in the Dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. || 12 ||
Then the thirteenth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
[I shall explain] the meaning of the inquiry regarding the Command (ājñā), as well as the determination of the arrangement of the phonemes (varṇa).
Now listen, O omniscient one, devoted to the knowledge of reality. || 13-1 ||
If one's own asterism is conjoined with its own day in Aries, it is auspicious;
having understood this from the chart of auspiciousness and other factors, the practitioner [should proceed] by means of the measurement of *pala*.
One should count the essence of the letters by which the determination of that question is reached;
O Lord, hear now the classification of the letters beginning with *ka* on the eastern petal. (13-3)
In the mind, there is an abundance of happiness; thoughts concerning the welfare of one's life and wealth; the acquisition of clothing and travel; suitability for affection, sons, and riches;
and even a firm standing in one’s country and the sight of one’s kinsmen.
And the destruction of all impurities occurs when the letter *ka* is at the beginning of the line. || 13-4 ||
The constant service of one who is overflowing with happiness is like the nostrils of men; devotion to Sadāśiva is the true fruit of one's own home;
and through the glances of Kalādharas, there is the worship by the foremost of people.
The pleasure of the wedding festivities does not obstruct what is beneficial or harmful.

One should then declare that the syllable *ṛ* signifies the destruction of calamities, the awakening of knowledge through fortitude, and the cessation of the afflictions caused by diseases and wicked people. (13.6)
In the letter *u*, there is the state of wind and indeed aimless wandering;
for those two who destroy poverty, there is the attainment of what is difficult to reach through distant journeys.
If a question regarding material substance is asked during the letter *kha*, there is fear when an auspicious task has begun;
one quickly encounters danger and, having fallen into poverty, shall come to ruin. (13-8)
The desire for death alone is true; effort for the arising of pleasures is constant.
Effort against an enemy is for his destruction, while effort against a friend is for his benefit; yet effort toward a heap of grain is like the behavior of a thief toward another's property. (13.9)
For the seeker of liberation, it brings about the attainment of absolute isolation (kaivalya) and removes the wicked tendencies of one's own mind;
for the seeker of enjoyment, it destroys various worldly pleasures yet bestows gold, silver, and sovereignty upon oneself;
it wards off the fear of pestilence and brings about the arising of a mass of bliss from the Lord of Wealth.
One quickly attains the glory of the knowledge of speech, various gains, and a mind preoccupied with the pursuit of dharma and wealth. (13.10)
Worship of Hari, meditation on Hari, and devotion to the lotus feet of Hari—there is no loss of wealth acquired by theft for one whose birth is truly noble. (13.11)
If the form of fire diminishes, there is loss; if it is accompanied by a great sound, there is destruction.
If it moves toward those who have arrived, there will be loss; if it moves with partiality, there is victory.
Those staying in their own homes will suffer from severe afflictions by disease;
there will be a destruction of enthusiasm, and even great scholarship in recitation will be devoid of vigor. (13.13)
And one with the color of the long vowel *l̥* becomes a king with beautiful eyes;
he will possess a mind for which security is lost through shame, and he will be as dear as a friend. (13–14)
In the long prostration of the syllable Oṃ, one who is without support does not live;
indeed, by means of the mere great support, one reduces everything to powder.
If [the Moon] is in Leo during the ascendant of Sagittarius or Aries, one shall obtain constant blessings.
One will appear somewhat valorous and become preeminent among those who possess movement in their actions;
it will somewhat dispel the multitude of faults and increase the enthusiasm of the king.
He becomes prone to anger, ever-exerting his prowess, and possessed of swift desire. || 13-16 ||

Now, O Mahādeva, I shall speak of that which is the most excellent among the excellent for heroes— O you who know the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, O you who are devoted to the knowledge of reality.

The emergence of the meaning through the differentiation of syllables even from the right-hand petal yields a fruit that is the ultimate essence, bestowing the fruit of the words of one's desire. (13–18)
When the seed is favorable, she who dwells in the lotus remains steady in her domestic sphere;
she causes fear from wandering through various lands and is not well-settled anywhere.
When the wicked are destroyed and [the mind] is awakened, she laughs at fierce agitation.
Speech remains under control in the mouths of those who possess the discus, while their losses shall cease.
There shall be beautiful majesty at the feet of one's elders, firm devotion, and grace in one's movements;
furthermore, there will be the encouragement of those who have arrived as favorites of the king, and auspicious results from the peak [of the mountain].
There shall be the state of a fine bee upon the lotus-face of a beloved woman, and the playful charm of a charming lady.
It causes the destruction of the agitation regarding the exhaustion of life-span, and brings about attraction, local happiness, and wealth.
With the letter *ṭa*, there is stability in one's country and happiness at the end of the night; there will be the excellent return of wealth and other possessions from abroad. (13-22)
Without the loss of wealth through falsehood, there is always the destruction of obstacles;

one attains victory over those who desire one's home, just as a lotus-eyed beloved [conquers] her own house. Indeed, this shall become a means for perfect accomplishment through powerful contemplation.
A human being attains victory in this world by seeking to know that which has been asked.
The sages have explained that this fruit is always a time consisting of fruit for one's enemies;
it is the cause of subjugating the worlds, a noble lineage, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and Agamas;
he obtains a beloved son who is the cause of the king’s enthusiasm.
In a matter that involves the affliction of the wicked and the destruction of a multitude of fears, [one should act]. || 13-24 ||
In fame, youth, splendor, and even intellect,
there is an increase in the flourishing of the fruit of one's time through prosperity;
yet even the worship of the gods should not become mere theft.
An extraordinary increase in wealth occurs at the time of buying and selling. (13.25)

In the winter season, there is the acquisition of wealth, the gain of gold, silver, and the like, the birth of a son, and the attainment of happiness; this it declares with certainty even in times of distress. (13-26)
Lakṣmī, delighted to bestow beloved wealth upon the circle of the earth, is born from water; yet her loss occurs through water, not in the divine nor in falsehood. (13.27)
If a person should perform an inquiry into the root vowel of the first syllable of a question and so forth, then there shall be an excellent result. (13.28)
Listen, O Lord, to each of those imperishable sounds contained within this leaf.
In the auspicious Ikārakūla, one who is possessed by thirst for wealth and the like shall obtain paternal wealth characterized by specific virtues. (13-30)

For those of subtle intellect have thus refuted that which is dear to [those seeking] a state of existence, which possesses excellent deities, abundant prosperity, and constant happiness—namely, the womb of the earth. (13.31)
The letter *ī* is dear to others and increases the destruction of opposing doctrines;
it prevents departure to foreign lands, and here, external compassion prevails. (13.32)
When questioned by the accuser, there arises a happiness that is dear to the people of the world, honored even by those with youthful faults, and free from any transformation. (13.33)

And by the second [seed-syllable], one attains contentment with what is bound [to one's lot], the fulfillment of the fruits of one's desires, removal [of obstacles] by means of the wind, and honor from kings. (13.34)

In this single-syllable seed-mantra (*bīja*) "Amaḥ," which serves as the seed of the Lord of the World, one obtains the fruit of giving a maiden in marriage and other such merits, as well as radiant clothing. (13.35)
In the signs of Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn, and Aquarius, there shall be the fortune of beauty;
in the remaining signs, one attains incomparable gains of heaps of gold and the essence of contentment.
In this worldly existence, one's own kin are one’s natural benefactors, and there is the accumulation of jewels and the like.
O Lord, everything that is beneficial is gathered together within the meaning of the question in its initial syllable.
Whatever one may consider regarding the greatness of the third petal,
having brought it into the letters of the syllables of the question and so forth, one should proceed by moving through the sky.
Listen to that method, O beloved of my life, O you who have reached the further shore of love;
by knowing which, the success of this inquiry shall be achieved, yielding fruit for the king even out of season. (13.38)
Having seen and known the mass of existents—superior, inferior, and middling—and likewise knowing the arrangement of worldly states as well as one's own vidyā and so forth; || 13-39 ||
One should contemplate everything as the essence of existence in the form of its objects;
it should be known that the seed-syllable is auspicious, and the fruit bestows ultimate fortune. (13.40)
And likewise, the acquisition of wealth and other such things, as well as results subject to worldly influence.

In the *kūṭa* of the letter *da*, there is hardness for enemies, the dispersal of one who destroys the Dharma, the death of a sovereign, or destruction; yet there is also the attainment of a divine woman and excellent jewels. In the letter *ṭa*, the sight of those dwelling far away certainly occurs.
Marriage and the attainment of sons are obtained within six months. || 13-43 ||
At the end of the syllable *ṭa*, there is no fear of thieves; there shall be the acquisition of wealth.
Through the illumination of the *vidhi-vidyā*, one becomes possessed of devotion to Śiva and Viṣṇu. (13.44)
In the syllable-cluster *dhakāra*, there is the status of a lord of the earth; likewise, there is no fear of disease or of wild beasts.
Merely by entering [this state], even one who has fallen away attains the prosperity of life and so forth, as well as fortune. (13.45)
In the *rabīja* [year], one becomes fully perfected as the best of the bird-lineage (*khagakulavara*) with a steady gait;
there shall be incomparable wealth equal to one's desires, dear to kings and kingdoms,
majesty, sovereignty, and the essence of all the worlds.
All flavors, the entire world, beloved things, great happiness, and various kinds of gain. || 13-46 ||
And by means of the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ), all that is moving and unmoving is conquered;
thus, by proceeding in due order, there is the fruit of good fortune in traveling everywhere.
Indeed, in a region with the letter *ṣa* in its center, news arrives from a foreign land;
one who sends a letter will receive wealth. (13.48)
When one attains a state of friendship and a state of alliance with the letter *kṣa*, and there is great affection arising from that, then there is no fear regarding the question. (13.49)
There shall be happiness in one's own kingdom through the practice of desiring flowers;
likewise, at the end of the letter *ha*, give this "cooker" (*pācaka*) preceded by *ca*. (13.50)
If it were so, O Lord, it would be said that there is no contrary result. (13.51)
O Lord, if there is a combination of planets in the Dīrghīkāra yoga, the intellect will be established in the feet;
if there is an undertaking, he becomes a long-lived king who protects his lineage,
joyfully governing over time and place with his young children.
In the forest of the world, he is the lion-king for the sake of destroying all defilements.

And he moved happily in the eighth house, in the presence of the Great Lord of Wealth. A man would become awakened and would certainly become composed when the great serpent of the breasts possesses wonderful skill, O Lord.
One is made to laugh even in an instant by the sight of the morning sun. || 13-53 ||
One shall attain extreme fortitude and victory through the arising of wondrous speech;
through victory, one obtains the ancient words practiced by the Victorious One in the past, and one attains the service of the people of the world, or perhaps [attains it] oneself. (13-54)
And the lineage-āgama does not yield fruit as excellent or profound as that of the Gayā [pilgrimage];
for one shall always obtain the lotus-feet of the Guru within the ocean of merit. (13.55)
If the *visarjanīya* is well-sounded and endowed with a soft conclusion, it brings the arrival of people, the arrival of wealth, and extensive knowledge. (13.56)
One who harbors such evil thoughts in their mind will abandon their own kinsmen and virtuous people; this act, which portends the ruin of the family, will lead them to obtain a miserable bondage.
The great sages, the most excellent ones, know that what is with family is beloved and what is without family is also beloved;
in the pleasure of laughter there is only the fruit of laughter, for it does not lead to spiritual realization.
At that very moment, by means of the sequence of wrath alone, one should remove everything through the manifestation of the eyes;
if the two hands are joined at the head, it is conjoined with the *kalikāla* [the age of strife].
For in the case of gain, the fruit is indeed the ornament of death.
On the remaining petal of the lotus, she who dispels the sound of the *hāra* (necklace) with her hands granting boons and fearlessness,
surrounded by hosts of young maidens, will surely cause one to arrive from afar;
she brings about the abandonment of terrible calamities and is gladdened by the delight of the qualities of water.
In the peak [of the teaching], there is a surge of the phonetic groups beginning with *kūṭa* and *ghakāra*, along with the essence of the primary and secondary languages (*bhāṣāpabhāṣā*).
In the Javarga: Jatuka, gold, contemplation on the means of livelihood, being overcome by old age and disease, and the taking away of worn-out clothes. (13.61)
If there is a Cakravartin at the peak of the letter *ṭha*,
it is certain that he will fall from the circle of the earth;
for when it occurs at the beginning of a state, it destroys internal happiness.
By the mere syllable *ṭha*, one becomes the supreme enemy. || 13-62 ||
O Lord, the first syllable of the question is the letter *ta*, which is dear to the Youthful One;
it then serves to destroy the mass of darkness consisting of sins. (13.63)
If the eloquent questioner, desiring to know for certain the accumulation of wealth, places the letter *na* at the beginning,

men shall be brought under control merely by conversation, and there shall be entry into the presence of the lord of the royal court. One becomes fearless in one's country and does not suffer in places of danger.
The perfection of ornaments and prosperity are found in the auspicious syllable-cluster *Bha*.
O Lord of the World, by contemplating the first syllable of every word everywhere, even the letter *la* causes one to abandon the suffering of a wife in this world. (13.66)
In the letter *sa*, there is sexual union; for one belonging to a noble family, it increases the lineage.
There shall be an increase of wealth, an increase of the clan, and the grace of Sarasvatī. (13.67)
O Lord, listen as I declare the determination of the greatness of the fruit of the letter *A* on the leaf of the Veda; listen with careful attention. (13.68)
From the letter *ka* to the letter *kṣa*, it exists pervading all in reality;
O Lord, without the letter *a*, where could power (*śakti*) ever arise? (13.69)
Everything—the bodies of all things moving and stationary—is strung upon the letter *a*.
If the letter *a* should appear at the beginning of a question or inquiry, [it signifies this]. (13.70)
Even when the fruit is bad, there is certainly an accumulation of good fruits for those who amass wealth and other resources for the purpose of dwelling among enemies. (13.71)

The ritual procedure for the letter *ya* is said to be employed when people approach [the teacher] during the secret sacrifices (*antaryajana*), as well as in cases of remorse for one's own suffering. (13.72)
O scholar of the meaning of questions, listen to the greatness of the fruit of the letter *u*: it brings about success in matters of theft at dawn and an exaltation of the mind. (13-73)
Dwelling in the highest place, excellent food and the like,
the arising of intense wisdom, and the mind fixed on the state of the goddess Umā.
The letter *ra* is the characteristic of the eye; it may be the speaking of sound.
In the eyes, it is the sight of women; its writing arises from afar. (13-75)
One attains supreme fortune solely for the sake of subjugating the world;
furthermore, there will be a collection of ploughs and the acquisition of land will certainly occur. (13.76)
In the syllable *o*, there shall be the increase of sovereignty as well as the increase of sons;
one always attains contentment, for the *praṇava* bestows all perfections.

When the Sun is in Pisces, Cancer, Scorpio, or Libra, during the rising of the ninth or third house, or when the fourth house is occupied by one who investigates the Vedas, there is auspicious fruit: the gain of fortune, advancement in status,
and the fruits of the ocean of bliss for those who are victorious, including knowledge, Vedic discourse, and so forth.
A mortal joyfully attains the state of one who has perfected their practice, which brings about great delight. || 13-78 ||
The measure of the leaf has been declared as the departure from inferior knowledge.
Listen again to the emergence of Mahākāla and Kali-kāla. (13.79)
O Maheśvara, whatever occurs during the first fortnight of the month, as well as during the first two watches of the day for a child, yields auspicious results. (13.80)
The third [type] consists of only a single staff and yields contrary results;
in that case, if the asterism among the staffs should be inauspicious, [the result will be so]. (13.81)

One should know that the eight lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī are on the first leaf of the east; their stars should be understood as very bright, and there will be happiness even in the presence of evil defects.
From Āśleṣā up to Citrā, [the asterisms] are on the second petal in the south;
their fruit is called "contrary," which destroys the fruit even when it is otherwise fruitful. (13.83)
One should write the asterisms beginning with Svāti and ending with Vasu in the third lower segment;
their respective stars should be known in sequence, for otherwise one would bring about inauspiciousness. (13.84)

In a situation where the result is contrary, that which is contemptible serves for its sake; in the place of an auspicious result, there may be an inauspicious one, and in the place of a bad result, there may be a good one. (13-85)
From the lunar mansion of Uttarāṣāḍhā up to Revatī,
such shall indeed be the fruit for a mortal, provided he is devoted to his duty.

Now, O Great God, O Lord, I shall declare the results of the Aśvinī and other [nakṣatras], knowing which all the deities become the primary protectors in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (13.87)
O God of gods, that manner [of practice] yields great merit and brings about its fruit.
In the three worlds, she is the worship of bliss, renowned throughout the triple universe, perfected through the delight of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*);
she is the vast one who wanders among the *siddhas*, who has shattered [obstacles] by granting boons, who is moist with compassion, and free from fear;
she is the destruction of the qualities of those who are dull-witted and ill-fated, and the consumer of the calamities of the lowly and the wretched.
If she, possessing a body that is the very fruit of the worlds' good fruits, had bestowed it upon Aśvinī; || 13-89 ||
Thus, O Lord of Gods, listen again and again to the fruits and non-fruits of the stars in their proper order, O beloved of life-breath, you who possess a spirit of love. (13.90)

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the section on Accomplished Mantras, in the *Sārasaṅketa* of the *Ājñācakra*, in the *Pāśavakalpa* concerning the determination of the *bhāva*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*. 13.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Therefore, O Śaṅkara, I shall now fully explain [the practice] by way of the path of yoga."
The excellent results for the twenty-seven lunar mansions, beginning with Bharaṇī.
The greatness of its fruit and non-fruit is the fruit of the direct realization of Kali;
for the sake of the fruit, there is the field of Bharaṇī and the determination of dharma, knowledge, and so forth. (14-2)

One attains Bharaṇī, which consists of the letters beginning with 'ma', characterized by the understanding of the contemplation of phenomena and the auspiciousness of non-going, when the moon is in that asterism. (14.3)
Under Kṛttikā, there is the color of a parrot; it brings about the destruction of diseases and misfortunes.
For the sake of health and wealth, one should not undertake the journey toward the sun (east) under that asterism.
That Rohiṇī, which is dearer than life to the wealthy, which brings about neither the loss nor the gain of wealth, which bestows the purity of intelligence upon the wise and the virtuous,
and which pacifies the defects of serpents and other evils within the circle of the earth— [that Rohiṇī is attained].
He attains royal splendor and increases his purity of intellect. || 14-5 ||
Moving with the gait of a lion-king, O lord of men, she bestows treasure in the palace;
she grants freedom from sin in the water, and prosperity in a family devoid of misfortune. With auspicious eyes, she brings well-being to the lineage at the time of marriage.
One should burn away one's own sins by means of the infinite accumulation of wisdom.
Having the form of fresh coral, delighting in the clamor of the arts of love,
she bestows the very offering of her mind, yet at the [wrong] time, she brings about the failure of fruit;
she grants happiness and supreme prosperity, and is as eager to paint with the splendor of slightly blossomed lotuses.
She protects the steadfast man daily; with her glance, she would burn up the limit of peace.
The daughter of Punarvasu, whose well is her youthful form, possesses compassion that removes the defects of the mind devoid of the cultivation of distinguished fruits;
she removes the multitude of abundant sorrows associated with the limit of wealth.
The great planet protects the human being who is most severely afflicted. || 14-8 ||

The auspicious month of Pauṣa suddenly bestows splendor upon the radiant, grants beauty to beloved women, and through the destruction of calamities such as the loss of gold and other wealth, it provides lineage and prosperity. During times of distress, it yields fruit; and for those like the deer, it brings a fortune equal to the joy of the Lord of Beasts.
The goddess Lalitā, whose nature is the knowledge of the fifth letter beginning with *ka*, protects her son here just as a mother does. || 14-9 ||
For on the edge of this previous leaf, the stars appear as bestowers of auspiciousness,
just as they do in the wheel during the auspicious revolution of the planets.
O Lord, one who commits many sins obtains a contrary fruit;
even if the sun is situated in Cancer, he becomes cruel on the day of Puṣya.
O Lord, hear now of the deities of the lunar mansions and the zodiac signs: Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius are the presiding deities of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī. (14–12)
For those whose color remains fixed within its own group and does not fall into the domain of decline, one attains victory everywhere; even when the planet is cruel, it bestows happiness.

In a case where the zodiacal signs are divided, one who is impartial and free from disparaging the teachings should determine the results of one's own birth star and speak gently regarding the matter of the query. (14.14)
If there should be either a good or a bad result for that particular constellation, then, having performed an examination of the colors, one should declare the flower accordingly. (14–15)
By means of the sequence of the rosary beads, through the investigation of those phonemes;
indeed, whatever happiness arises during that investigation of each respective phoneme— || 14–16 ||
But when the web of defects is excessive, there is indeed greater suffering;
yet the supreme practitioner attains abundant happiness and eternal bliss. (14–17)
Now hear the sequence of days for these stars, from Sunday to Sunday, as the auspicious lords of the stars in their respective order. (14–18)
O Rudra, having likewise understood the inauspicious, one should state the meaning of the question;
I shall now declare the determination of its day on the petal in the eastern lotus.
If there is a question concerning children during the period of the Sun, the result will be a kingdom;
likewise, during the twenty-third year and beyond, there will indeed be the attainment of dharma, artha, and profit.
"Union, supreme bliss, and the contemplation of reality through yoga"—such [teachings] are inauspicious for the elderly on Sundays, even if they appear auspicious. (14–21)
One attains a certain jewel, a happiness filled with the fragrance of celestial flowers;
from a young maiden, one obtains the auspicious fruit consisting of the meaning of the mudrās.
There is constant striving for the sake of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) and a longing for love with the wives of kings.
On an auspicious day, there is a pure longing for the abodes of merit and happiness, as well as devotion to Śiva.
The son of the Earth, with a blood-stained face, is exceptionally fierce;
he suddenly burns away the primary task through his rashness within the latent impression.
He generally destroys that which is fruitlessly undertaken, being the very essence of a continuous stream of grief.
On a Monday, during an auspicious time, one always accomplishes meritorious liberation.
O chief of courtesans, when Mercury is present, a mortal attains a great mass of merit; likewise, even one who is weak always overcomes the defects of time and most terrible suffering.
The great pride of prowess of enemies and wealthy men.
Bestow upon the gods various gains of wealth, the distribution [of riches],
majesty, true fame, and the specific fruits of sacrifices ordained by ritual;
grant to people joy, and joy within the hearts of those fallen under the power of battle.
The consecration brings joy to the teacher of latent impressions by leading them toward the True Dharma.
Bearing a body adorned with mandāra garlands, one who is devoted to the gods goes to the celestial realm;
they truly attain devotion to the feet of Hari through this adornment during the auspicious time of Śukravāraka.
On the day of Saturn, there is fear accompanied by worldly defects and delusion;
yet it brings joy to the earth and beloved sons, supreme liberation, and happiness for women.
It bestows distinguished wealth and clouds [of rain], and brings success and prosperity in one's life, O son of the Sun.
If human beings worship Him, the Lord of all desires and so forth, [they obtain their wishes]. || 14-27 ||
Furthermore, the fruit associated with Sunday is a source of extreme suffering;

yet, it is always like the fierce-rayed sun that removes the ailments of the afflicted world. Whatever man performs the meditative contemplation (*paribhāvanā*) upon that very [day], [attains the highest state].
It never perishes, being the source of abundant heat and curses.
Listen to the fruit of Kalādharaphala, O you who rest upon the subtle external of the Praṇava! Indeed, the fruit of those who possess fruit is the fruit of the signs of all the planets;
it is profound speech that brings favor to kings and provides protection.
O Śambhu, when the vessel of the moon performed the auspicious rites for the Kali age, [it was as follows]. || 14-29 ||

I shall now describe the greatness of the second petal, which is surrounded by the circle of lunar mansions (nakṣatras), and the specific results of each star, by means of which the determination of the meaning of a query is made. (14.30)
In Aśleṣā, there is much suffering, falling into calamity, and being shrouded by the splendor of delusion;
there is the resorting of various bees, the loss of wealth for the wealthy,
the abandonment of kings, and being covered and tormented by wicked people.
One will certainly give [one's wealth] to those of the earth-born caste amidst the clamor of hell. || 14-31 ||
O Great Goddess, when [the moon] is in Maghā, it destroys wealth; in the middle [of the asterism], it brings about an increase in great joy and fear for one's enemy.
It brings about an internal state that destroys earthquakes and always causes association with those afflicted by base desires.
One should recite the results for those who have gone afar under the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī:
there will be extreme fortitude against the enemy faction, and losses will certainly come to pass. (14.33)
The fruit is bestowed by Uttaraphalgunī, and the movement belongs to Īśvarī;
O Lord, if one is devoted to the gods, then everything is auspicious everywhere. (14-34)
Modest in her hands and head, she bestows fortune upon the three auspicious worlds;
red-limbed, fickle in her gait, and granting welfare through the joy of her stainless virtues,
she constantly grants a hundred pieces of gold to the devotee who desires sacrifice.
With various kinds of seasoned foods and drinks, one who is exceedingly happy should offer a multitude of perceptions.
In this world, Fortune bestows various riches, yet she is adorned with the agitation of unfulfilled desires;
indeed, one might never encounter her who brings such bodily suffering, but rather one who has attained devotion to the Lord.
May Śukra, the lord of Aśleṣā, never grant us calamity or great suffering;
may he, who removes fear through his play on the right wing, destroy fierce heat.
May the illustrious Jīva, the yellow-hued Brāhmaṇa, bestow various kinds of unfailing wealth and hope.
The lord of Pūrvā-phalgunī is the foremost of those born of lightning; he is blue in color and has his own leaf as an emblem.
The lord of Uttaraphalgunī, with Mars, produces abundant happiness and wealth;
the Moon, lord of Hastā, [produces] prosperity; and the Sun, lord of Citrā, [produces] infinite wealth. (14-38)
O Lord, hear now the constellations of the third leaf below, by which, when distinguished by their respective days, the true results of the inquiry are determined. (14-39)
The Sun protects Svātī with his most fierce splendor;
at the time of destruction, he bestows perverted intellect.
The Moon protects Viśākhā, and Sarasvatī bestows happiness.
Mars [afflicts] Anurādhā, which is the source of calamities. || 14-40 ||
For Mercury indeed protects and accomplishes all purposes;
likewise, Jupiter bestows happiness at the root,
and Venus grants wealth.
Endowed with the *pūrvāṣāḍhā* nakṣatra, he dwells in happiness. (14.41)
The fourth leaf, situated on the left, is the cause of great auspiciousness;
it is the form of the Atharvaveda, filled with the discourse of all inquiries.
In the opposite case, there is great suffering; even when there is excellence of complexion and happiness, there are losses.
However, through the auspicious aspect of the *tāraka* planets, there are great successes. (14.43)

Having observed the consensus regarding the collection of letters used in queries, one should determine the qualities of that Lord of the Stars (the Moon), who bestows both auspicious and inauspicious results. (14.44)
Saturn, presided over by the gods, afflicts Uttarāṣāḍhā, which yields a ripening of loss, characterized by suffering and poverty. (14.45)
The Sun bestows fame along with wealth and other blessings upon Śravaṇā, which is presided over by the principal deities;
likewise, the Moon grants fruit upon Dhaniṣṭhā, while Mars brings misfortune to Śatabhiṣaj, the lord of the Gaṇas. (14.46)
Mercury is the lord of Pūrvabhādrapadā and the increaser of gold;
likewise, O Mahādeva, [Jupiter] is the lord of Uttarabhādrapadā and the ruler of the world.
Bṛhaspati bestows a joyful exuberance, Revatī likewise, and Bhṛgu grants supreme delight, each according to the zodiac signs situated in their respective houses. (14.48)
The illustrious Śani protects Abhijit and Ārdrā; he is the bestower of wealth.
Śani joyfully comes near the royal deer to grant a share of his fruit.
Some say that the Moon’s apogee is situated there, as is the most beloved King Rāhu; the planets are in their respective fields, and Abhijit is encircled by Time. (14.50)
He who at that time knows that subtle form upon the earth should understand it as the time of twilight (saṃdhyākāla), occurring at the end of Saturn and Rāhu. || 14.51 ||
One should know that very moment of conjunction, which brings about the great arising of the qualities of a being, as the *kumbhaka* (retention) born from my body.
For that indeed is a most subtle moment, like the circle of Kuṇḍalinī;
and in its first part, the lord Śani is known as Dhāraṇā.
Brahmā himself shines with joy, his body stainless;
at its end is the pure one named Recana, whose form is that of withdrawal.
Śambhu himself, in the form of Rāhu, was an expert in the ritual application of the five principles;
Mahādeva, in the form of Time (Kāla), had a hideous face and was terrifying.
In the form of the moon, he who produces nectar destroys the fire of all sins;
in the color black, he is Kāla-Yama, the judge of merit and demerit.
Between the two, she is of subtle form, with a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning;
the Goddess who rests upon Mahāsattva, resting upon the grasp of Viṣṇu’s Māyā.
Abhijit is the subtle star, Jayā is the dissolution at the time of the junction;
she has her heart occupied by the breath-retention (kumbhaka) and is preceded by the wheel of the planets.
Situated in the midst of the village of the circle of constellations, she is the sixteenth lunar day;
she is beyond time, a subtle digit, overflowing with youthful bliss.
Residing in her initial portion is the quality of passion (rajas) in the form of Brahmā;
her remainder is the quality of darkness (tamas) in the form of Time (Kāla), who delights in dissolution.
Candra, Brahmā, Śiva, Sūrya, and the supreme body of Mahāmāyā;
Ātreyī is the supreme Śakti who moves within the Suṣumṇā. (14.61)
Remaining impartial toward both Brahmā and Śiva, she grants success to the Vedic scriptures;
by those who know her, she is perceived as the foundation of all things, abiding in the heart of all bliss. (14.62)
By means of those [mantras] endowed with the fruit of bliss, she who brings about the enjoyment of sentient beings—Mahāviṣṇu, the Great Māyā, whose nature is that of Candratārā—is [attained]. (14.63)
The primordial Maheśvarī of Śambhu is the giver of liberation, the giver of enjoyment, and the object of enjoyment;
she is the destroyer of the terrible darkness of ignorance and the ender of time. (14.64)
She who is beloved by the gentle wind and who, as the slayer of Vīra, exists for the sake of his creative conception—she protects the worlds of the universes; this entire world is subject to her.
No one dies at an improper time if they know the power of Vāyu;
"the power of Vāyu is supreme"—this is the definitive meaning of the Tantra. (14.66)
She who, in the form of a subtle arrival, bestows subtle accomplishment upon men for the purpose of worship and for the conquest of the eight sovereign powers. (14.67)
This was previously told by Brahmā to his disciple and his son,
for the purpose of destroying greed, delusion, desire, anger, pride, and envy.
O Lord, that supreme sequence which increases delight on this earth is as follows:
within the center of the wheel of command (ājñācakra), the element of air is established. (14.69)
Having the form of the moon, the sun, and fire, she is free from both merit and demerit;
having the form of mind and the form of intellect, she remains pervading the body. (14.70)
Ājñā is said to be in the middle of the two petals; it consists of fourteen letters, the four Vedas on four petals, with the letters from 'va' to 'sa', possessing great luster.
O Lord, listen now to the majesty of that Veda, which is endowed with the form of fire and accompanied by the Ṛgveda and the others, explained step by step.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the Vedaprakaraṇa concerning the conventions of the Ājñācakra, in the determination of the meaning of inquiries regarding internal states, in the Uttara-tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"The task of the gods is the supreme *praṇava*, which is the sprout of the branches of the Vedas."
I speak of supreme bliss; listen to the joy of Bhairava. 15-1.
On the first leaf, one should know that the letter *a*, the Ṛgveda, the supreme syllable, and Brahmā are the definitive determination of the meaning of the primordial Veda. (15-2)
Everything is obtained through the Veda; this world is dependent upon the Veda.
He who practices the Śakti-vidyā devoid of Vedic mantras [is lost]. (15.3)
"How indeed may he become a yogi devoted to the Kaula path?
Śrī Ānandabhairava said:
"O Goddess, what is the hymn to Brahman (brahmastotra), and of what nature is the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā)? (15.4)
And who might be a knower of Brahman, or who might be a bearer of the body of Brahman? O Kaulinī, who brings joy to the Kula, tell me the manner of that. (15.5)
"Speak quickly, O beautiful one, if you have a look of affection toward me.
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said: "That very hymn of Brahmā is the service of the power of Vāyu (the wind). (15.6)
That which is proclaimed as the Brahma-vidyā, submerged in a subtle form, is always the wind; it is the essence of vital breath, subtle, intoxicated, and clear-minded. (15.7)
Exclusive devotion to the Lord of Śrī is proclaimed as the knowledge of Brahman;
one who has destroyed [obstacles] through the eightfold nyāsa, who removes subtle movement, and is pure—[is thus described]. 15.8
The illustrious knower of Brahman, having established the vital energy (vāyavī śakti) within his heart, should always maintain solitude; he is proclaimed as one who possesses the bliss of Brahman.
The wise one who always worships [the deity] is proclaimed a knower of Brahman, even without the essence of the juice of Vijayā or with external liquor. (15.10)
One who is united with the bliss of Vāyu is proclaimed a knower of Brahman;
he is immersed in the essence of eternal bliss, his body being entirely full. || 15-11 ||
Intoxicated by the flood of tears of bliss, he was recognized as the bearer of the body of Brahman;
the Goddess Kuṇḍalinī, the Mother of the World, is his very own form. (15.12)
By those devoted ones who always attain liberation as the very fruit of their scripture,
they are established upon the first leaf, resting within the array of letters.
The beloved powers of Vāyu reside within the sphere of the cosmic egg;
together with the zodiac signs, lunar mansions, and lunar days, they are the ever-shining mistresses of all. (15.14)
Bhavānī, who abides as the power of Brahman, will certainly grant her refuge in this way;
within a month, the perfection of Khecarī, which dries up the vital breaths, is born.

In two months he shall possess a vajra-body; the man should increase [the practice] gradually. In two months he becomes endowed with the power of a kalpa, through the nature of its connection to him. (15–16)
The Kuṇḍalinī energy is of the nature of consciousness; by the power of its vital force, it resides as the cause for the attainment of consciousness and bestows pure knowledge. || 15–17 ||
Liberation occurs through knowledge alone; one should take refuge in knowledge.
Becoming possessed of great strength and great eloquence, he increases day by day. (15–18)
His lifespan is always increasing, and he is freed from old age and death; O Lord, by the grace of Kuṇḍalinī, nothing whatsoever remains unaccomplished. (15–19)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—beyond them, O Lord, the goddess Vāyavī is conceived. (15–20)
These six Śaṅkaras, who bestow all accomplishments, abide within the mind;
they all remain upon the tips of the petals, drenched by the essence of the stream of nectar. (15–21)
Facing downwards, subtle in form, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
they all abide within the sphere of the six cakras, situated along the path of Brahmā.
By this command, one should indeed thus meditate upon the twelve-spoked wheel,
beloved by Kuṇḍalinī, which is drenched by streams of trickling nectar.
Considering the *kuṇḍalinī* to be of the nature of fire, the six *Śivas*, who delight in the essence of supreme bliss, always perform the internal satiation with the downward stream.
Born from the lunar orb, assuming the form of living beings,
they are fully empowered by the knowledge of the Self and are intent upon the propitiation of Śakti.
O Kuleśvara, the Yajurveda, which constitutes the second petal and brings about success without effort, was concealed by Viṣṇu. (15–26)
It was filled with the terrible roar of the great sound of the tip of the vajra;
[it struck] Hari, Īśvara, Īśāna, Vāsudeva, and Sanātana.
To Kṛṣṇa, the Lord and Master of Yoga, who is the discipline based on sentient beings, who bestows the fruits of the four goals of life, and who gives more than what is desired. (15-28)
He is cherished by Rādhikā, the goddess Rākiṇī, and the power of Vāyu;
he is possessed of great strength, a great hero, and the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
[He is] the Lord Śrīvidyārādhikā, who wears yellow garments, who is the essence of all, who is beautified by the fragrance of youth, and who is embraced by the daughters of the Vedas. 15.30.
When he was the slayer of the Daityas and Dānavas, the bringer of happiness to his own body, the bestower of existence, the abode of devotion, and the moon to the ocean— 15.31.
Seated upon the Garuḍa posture, having the form of Manas and pervading the universe,
he knows the performance of sacrificial rites and is situated above the Ājñā-cakra.
Then, his body intoxicated by drinking the nectar of the supreme [state] below, the practitioner, devoted to yoga, [perceives it] as if it were located in his own *svādhiṣṭhāna*. (15.33)
O Śaṅkara, by quickly meditating upon that form, one attains perfection;
for who on earth is truly a Vaiṣṇava, a Vājika, a Dhāmika, or even a Bhūmika? (15.34)
"Or who indeed becomes a yogin? Tell me that, O Sovereign of the Gods.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Śaṅkara, listen; I shall declare the characteristics for determining the [proper] time."

The status of being a Vaiṣṇava among Vaiṣṇavas, as well as the fruit and non-fruit [of practice], reside in the Ājñācakra; he who knows the Ājñācakra, the Great Wheel (Mahācakra), upon this earth— || 15-36 ||
For him, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that is unattainable;
he is ever pure, established in meditation, and constantly devoted to the recitation of mantras. || 15.37 ||
One who is endowed with mindfulness, discernment, and action, who is dear to the scriptural injunctions, and who maintains equanimity toward all things—he is proclaimed a Vaiṣṇava. (15.38)
One who maintains equanimity toward enemies and friends, is devoted solely to Kṛṣṇa-bhakti, and is constantly intent on the practice of yoga, is proclaimed a Vaiṣṇava. (15.39)
One who is devoted to the study of the Yajurveda, possesses virtuous conduct and discernment, and always maintains association with the righteous is proclaimed as a Vaiṣṇava. (15.40)
Seeking the knowledge of the dharma of discernment and fixing his mind upon Kṛṣṇa, he performs his actions like Śiva; such a one is proclaimed a Vaiṣṇava. (15.41)
The wise Brahmin Yājñika became filled with love and longing;
he dwelt in a forest, a formidable wilderness adorned with the beauty of fresh trees. (15.42)
Alone, one practices the yoga of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman);
the exhaling breath is wind and fire, while the inhaling breath is the sun and likewise the moon.
A blazing crest in the form of the sun, yet not even a *yojana* in size;
furthermore, through the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*), the oblation is offered by means of the moon's radiance. (15.44)

He who, observing silence, constantly performs the fire-oblation (homa) in a blazing fire whose poison is upward-moving and which is flickering with the power of the wind, is called a true sacrificer (yājñika).
He who performs the fire sacrifice within the body by means of the rays of the sun of the individual soul and the fillings from the moon of the Self is proclaimed as a true sacrificer. (15.46)
Wine is Śakti, meat is Śiva, and the one who eats it is Bhairava himself;
the sacrificer is said to offer the meat into the fire of Śakti. (15.47)

The sacrificer who performs the full oblation (pūrṇahoma) according to the rules in the family-pit (kulakuṇḍa) and in the family-fire (kulavahni), which is of the nature of Śiva, is highly praised. || 15-48 ||
On the circle of the earth, in a secluded place, in a hall of Dharma, or in a chamber of desire, he who recites the *Jīvasāra* with firm devotion is indeed a righteous man. (15.49)

Having cultivated equal meditation upon a gem and a clod of earth, upon dharma and adharma, and upon victory and defeat, he who becomes a renunciant is a knower of Brahman; he is a true practitioner. (15.50)
Constant contemplation of the Lord, steadfastness in the command of the guru, being of virtuous character, a friend to the distressed, and righteous—one is thus proclaimed as a *dhārmika*. (15.51)
Knowing the proper time and knowing the ritual procedure, embodying the eightfold yoga, silent on the mountain in a cave, such a devotee is proclaimed as a yogin. (15.52)
One who possesses the knowledge of Brahman, who is an avadhūta, virtuous, meritorious, pure, free from desire, and righteous—that one is proclaimed to be a yogi. (15.53)
One who is a vessel for the compassion of Vāgvādinī, a piercer of the six supports (ṣaḍādhāra), whose semen flows upward, and who is free from women—he is proclaimed a yogin. (15.54)
Preceded by the Yajurveda, bearing the syllables situated upon the leaves of the Yajus,
performing mental recitation with the garland of letters— he is indeed the auspicious king of yogis.
One should worship the lotus of the Command, which is consumed by the twelve months, endowed with the twelve zodiac signs, and joined with the lunar days, weekdays, and constellations.

For the purpose of determining direction, time, and place, and for ascertaining the power of the wind, [the calculation is made] by means of the number of breaths of children, the aged, and others, measured by the duration of a staff-strike. (15.57)
One should worship the supremely purifying essence of the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*), which pervades all;
it bestows happiness everywhere within the wheel, and for the virtuous, O Lord, there is no loss. (15.58)
For the wicked and the slanderous, contrary circumstances arise at every step; here in this world, sufferings manifest as the fruit and consequence of their sinful deeds.
The sinner attains the state of five elements, while the knower goes to the supreme state;
he who knows the time of his breath is declared to be a knower.
That sinner is proclaimed as one who does not know the time of death;
[he disregards] the Yajurveda, which possesses the quality of purity (sattva) and is stainless as the abode of that purity.
By following the sequence of the Guru’s command, one attains Kuṇḍalinī, the Great Power, through the reality of the lower [path] by means of the yoga of the upward and downward sequence.
Through service to the great vessel of the Yajurveda, which is the locus of sentient beings,
and by means of the streams of nectar from the forehead, the Kuṇḍalinī becomes conscious.
Having visualized the double-petaled wheel (dvidala-cakra), the practitioner of mantra should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) day and night;
he should offer oblations with pure clarified butter while meditating on Kuṇḍalī at the base of the mouth [of the fire].
Those whose limbs are beautiful with rays of intense light resort to the excellent four-petaled lotus wheel, which is joined with the purity of restrained senses.
That which possesses a hundred-crore-fold splendor in the Middle Country.
Thus, in the Śrī Rudrayāmala, in the Uttaratantra, in the Mahātantroddīpana,
in the Bhāvanirṇaya, in the Pāśavakalpa, in the Ājñācakrasārasaṅketa, in the Siddhamantraprakaraṇa, in the Vedaprakaraṇollāsa, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
The fifteenth chapter. || 15 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said: Listen, O Lord of Ānandarudra, to the characteristics of the third petal.
The lower wheel is the Sāmaveda, undisturbed by the quality of tamas.
Maheśvara, whose form is Rudra, pervaded by the net of phonemes and other [mantras], is the locus of dissolution, the one who takes any form at will, and the temple of supreme bliss. (16.2)
Having clearly visualized the well-established state of the fire's activity, one becomes a king among yogis;
that state is the dharma of yogis, which bestows the fruit of the Guru’s command. (16.3)
One should meditate again and again, slowly, upon that lotus-foot of the venerable gurus within the two-petaled lotus between the eyebrows, radiant as the abode of the vital breath (samīra).
Having contemplated through mind, speech, action, and the subtle breath, and having caused [the mind] to dissolve, one whose body is filled with joy should always meditate. (16.5)
Just as meditation is performed upon the thousand-petaled lotus, so too is that meditation performed upon the two-petaled lotus,
[visualizing] the Guru, the Self, the Lord, the God of gods, the eternal one.
The bestower of success without effort, who grants the fruit of the eight limbs of yoga. || 16-7 ||
Eternal, consisting of sound, the object of valid cognition, ever-comparable, and venerable;
possessing a subtle radiance like the rising moon, a lotus blooming by the light of a hundred moons;
present in all living beings, yet motionless while abiding in their movement, and the stainless purification through supreme knowledge.
I worship that which is the abode of the quality of established dance, which consists of dissolution, and which is the realization of one's own Self.
If one should worship within oneself the Lord of the worlds, the stainless Sovereign, the Destroyer of Smara, the Guru and the Supreme Lord,
who is filled with the most beautiful moon and the Sāman chants, and upon whom the primordial mass of fire has fallen— || 16-9 ||
O Guru, if you grant equality to those who bow down to you, yet frustrate my efforts,
I shall worship your lotus feet with wondrous devotion, for they lead one across the ocean of worldly existence.

I take refuge in the feet of the Guru, adorned with white lotuses, producing the beautiful sound of golden anklets, possessing lovely moon-like nails that are painted and variegated, and which purify the creator of the world. 16-11.

I worship the soles of the feet, which are tender from protecting all beings who bear auspicious fruit, adorned with the lotuses of pure blood, which guard against the seizure of the earth, and which cause the mountain of the earth to tremble as it is set with jewels.

If you have compassion for me, a base person, then may your lotus-foot protect me from the suffering born of the ocean of worldly existence; I worship that foot which rests upon a seat of gold and jewels, which is the mantra of the supreme swan (paramahaṃsa), which is the form of Hara, and which is the Lord, the Guru who brings all under the control of the senses. 16-13. Paramahaṃsamanuṃ hararūpiṇaṃ sakalamakṣavaśaṅgurumīśvaram.
I take refuge in the lotus-face of Taruguru, which is like the hand of the moon possessing all auspicious marks.
