The wheel of the Guru’s command, which brings about the worlds and consists solely of the syllable *ka*, has the moon of *nāda* as its heart; it is joined with the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*) at the place of dissolution of the vital breath,
where it mingles with the honey-sweet nectar.
Then, in the sacred field of Veda, at that spot devoid of the moon.
In the place adorned with the lower sphere, overcome by the quality of darkness (tamas),
the abode of the two drops, in the station of two petals, is the foot of the illustrious Guru.
The wise one should meditate upon the form of a great flame of fire in the center of that;
by the grace of this yoga, through the seed-syllables, the *vāgbhava*, and the *kūṭaka* syllables.
One shall become long-lived, and even if lowly, one shall attain mastery of speech;
for this is the supreme nectar that has issued from the lotus feet of the venerable Guru.
Having thoroughly satisfied the Mistress of the Kula with streams of that supreme nectar, one should always remember her as awakened, repeatedly contracting [the breath]. 16–19.
The wise one should hold the wind, which has another flavor due to its transformation;
having satisfied the Mistress of the Kula with streams of that supreme nectar.
Then, O beloved, by offering again and again the fruit of all one's merit,
the best of practitioners attains great wealth, jewels, and prosperity.
Everywhere he attains victory—in battle, in anger, and in great fear. Standing in the midst of a great conflict, the man of virtuous conduct proceeds and shall attain liberation. || 16-22 ||
Thus, O Lord, I have explained to you the unsurpassed knowledge of Brahman, pertaining to the petal of the three-sectioned Command Wheel (ājñācakra) from Kāmarūpa. (16–23)
If one contemplates after having investigated, one attains the excellent fruit;
[one should meditate on] the Great Lord Kāmarūpa within the three-sectioned Ājñā-cakra.

Overwhelmed by Chinese customs and surrounded by the lords of the cremation grounds, he is Kāla, the wheel that brings about death, Mahākāla, the treasury of all arts. He is measured by palas, upalas, vipalas, daṇḍas, lunar days (tithis), atipadas, and fortnights (pakṣas). || 16–25 ||
Endowed with months, years, yugas, and great kalpas,
he is the Lord of the Gods, whose eye is like ten million meteors and whose fangs are sharp.

His lotus-face is adorned with a network of millions upon millions of eyes; he is the embodiment of consciousness, whose form is liberation from both being and non-being, and who possesses manifold forms.
Having meditated with extreme ease upon Kālarudra, the Supreme Lord, at the Ājñā-cakra, the great lord, between the eyebrows and above the nose. (16-28)
Having meditated upon the supreme abode, the practitioner of mantra should instantly become one with it; he should then contemplate Hākinī, the destroyer of Raurava and the other hells. (16.29)
She whose radiance is like ten million flashes of lightning, whose form is composed of the bliss of nectar,
who possesses the full splendor of the principle beyond the mother (Amātattva), and who resides in the golden Vārāṇasī.
Her limbs were radiant with various ornaments; she was endowed with fresh youth, possessed full breasts, intoxicated by her strength, and was the very embodiment of the support of all. (16.31)
She was pleasing Trivikrama with the long recitation of the *praṇava*,
the goddess Maunā, who is composed of mind and whose very nature is all knowledge.
Mahākālī, Mahānīlā, the yellow-colored one, she who has the luster of the moon, Tripurā, Sundarī, Vāmā, the wish-fulfilling cow of the left, and Śivā.

Seated upon a single seat, one should meditate on the purifying Śakti of the Supreme Lord, who is situated to his left—the power that is the substratum of all, difficult to restrain, and hard to transcend. (16.34)
A wise person does not settle upon the path of the Kula merely by means of breath;
rather, one is led to the Supreme through the distinction between Kula and Akula.
O Lord, without the practice of breath control, without the practice of the eight limbs,
and without self-restraint and fortitude, the path of the Kula does not succeed.
Likewise, by means of the yoga of inhalation (pūraka) or even exhalation (recaka), one remains; yet, without the presence of retention (kumbhaka), these two do not remain either. (16.37)
Likewise, O Lord, without yoga and without the practice of the eight limbs, the path of the Kula, which possesses the great reality, is never perfected. (16.38)
Who on this earth attains liberation without the Kula path?
[Such a person] does not know the Kula path, which is filled with the words of Yoga and the Agamas. (16.39)
O Lord, how should he worship the Goddess, for what practice has been prescribed for him who performs it without knowing the conduct of the Vīranāthas? (16.40)
For them, the training in yoga will certainly take many days,
including the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), which is a supreme dharma beyond even the scope of the Vedas.
For it is the essence of all merit and the fire for weighing heaps of sin; it is the destroyer of ten million great transgressions and ten million times ten million misdeeds. (16.42)
O Mahādeva, the sins accumulated in previous births, including various evil deeds and transgressions, are surely destroyed through the practice of yoga for six months. (16.43)
He who, being self-controlled, performs sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) again and again every day at both twilight and dawn; 16.44.
Having meditated for a year with self-control, one becomes a sky-walker, a sovereign of yogis;
having become a yogi and resorted to the Kaula path, one becomes immortal.
Having become the lord of great vidyās through discernment, he is the most excellent of practitioners. || 16-46 ||
Thus, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the *Bhāvārthabodhanirṇaya*,
in the *Pāśavakalpa*, in the *Ājñācakrasārasaṅketa*, in the section on *Siddhamantra*, within the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava.
The sixteenth chapter. || 16 ||
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Mahādeva, I shall now describe the characteristics of the Atharvaveda."
For it is the essence of all castes, endowed with power and right conduct.
From the Atharvaveda arose the Sāmaveda, characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas);
from the Sāmaveda arose the Yajurveda, which originates from the great quality of goodness (sattva).
Brahmā consists of the quality of rajas and is established in the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda;
she who resembles a lotus fiber has the form of the Atharvaveda.
In Atharva reside all the Vedas, as well as those beings that move in water, through the air, and on the earth;
there dwell the great sciences, the family traditions, and the great sages.
For the purpose of completing the remainder of the manuscript, [he went] into the presence of Lokamaṇḍala;
he was auspicious, consisting of a divine state, and fully pervaded by the wheel of powers (śakticakra). || 17-5 ||
In that very place is the state of the hero (vīrabhāva), and in that very place is the state of the animal (paśubhāva);
the supreme reality beyond all states is the Atharva, the leaf of the Veda.
The abode situated in the two drops consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
it is the reality endowed with the four Vedas, a body firmly measured out.
There are twenty-four principles within this beautiful body;
Brahmā, overcome by the quality of rajas, protects it through inhalation (pūraka).
Viṣṇu, pervaded by the quality of sattva, [is attained] through kumbhakas with steady contemplation;
Hara, pervaded by the quality of tamas, [is attained] through the recaka breath as well.
The supreme goddess Kuṇḍalinī resides within the wheel of the Atharvaveda;
she is indeed Māyā, whom neither Brahmā, Viṣṇu, nor Śiva can comprehend. (17.10)
Knowing the body to be the abode of the deity and being devoted, she will speak;
for the Goddess consists of all the Vedas and has the nature of all mantras.
The Vidyā consists of all yantras and illuminates the knowledge of the Vedas;
she is consciousness, the knower of all dharmas, and dwells in the abode of her own dharma. || 17-12 ||
She is insentient yet of the nature of knowledge, wearing a garland of golden campaka flowers;
she is stainless, without support, and possesses the speed of the mind of pure knowledge.
She is the destroyer of all calamities and indeed causes the body to fall;
this entire universe is her creation, for she destroys its merits.
And for her, whose mind is always distracted by the effort of producing consciousness, great-souled beings become manifest only if they exercise their conscious intent. (17.15)
By her grace alone, what on this earth is not accomplished?
Through the practice of yoga for six months, Kuṇḍalinī becomes conscious. (17.16)
That goddess is the power of wind, flowing through the supreme ether;
she is the Savior and the Mother of the Vedas, and she goes outward day by day.
Life flows away constantly by the measure of twelve finger-breadths;
and the vital breath, at the rate of twelve finger-breadths, brings about its exhaustion day after day.
To whatever extent the Kuṇḍalinī, the Supreme Deity, moves outward, to that same extent there shall be the shattering of [the ego] and the liberation from sin. (17–19)
Whenever the subtle, wind-like [energy] does not flow, O Mahādeva, the fire-like [energy] flows into the external moon within the lunar orb. (17–20)
When the flame of Caṇḍikā, blazing at the Mūlādhāra in Kāmarūpa, reaches the thousand-petalled lotus in the circle of the head; 17–21.
Then that wise one, the king of yogis, always proceeds as one composed of light toward the Lord Kāmeśvara, the Great God known as Acyuta.
If that goddess flows during the dissolution of the mind in the external moon,
then one should perform the yoga until she reaches the crown of the head.
If she, being the subtle one residing in the subtle body and fond of the subtle abode, comes together at the head and drinks the nectar; || 17-24 ||
That alone is the supreme perfection, the path of devotion; of this there is no doubt.
The essence of the knowledge of the four Vedas is proclaimed to be the Atharva Veda. (17–25)
The Atharvaveda-vidyā is considered to have Vāyu as its presiding deity;
by the mere service of it, a man becomes the very form of Rudra. (17–26)
Abiding solely in the state of *kumbhaka*, she alone reveals Brahman.
Bhairava said:
"O Pārvatī, by what means does the wind-power (*vāyavī śakti*) become compassionate? (17–27)
By what means does one become firm-minded, or how does one become a person of discernment?
By what means is there accomplishment of mantra, and how does there come to be accomplishment of the body? (17-28)
"O Cāmuṇḍā, speak at length, O Ānandabhairaveśvarī!
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Śambhu, O Lord of my life-force and of the Kula."
I shall relate everything in its entirety in a single sentence, in brief,
with supreme faith and devotion, while being intent on the restraint of the mind.
That great ascetic, endowed with fortitude, patience, moderation in food, and tranquility, attains the supreme power of the subtle form of Vāyu. (17.31)
A speaker of truth, a practitioner of celibacy, one whose happiness arises from the dharma of compassion, a knower of the restraint of the mind, with his body naked. (17.32)
Possessing an equanimous mind toward all things and discerning the ultimate truth,
he lay upon the surface of the earth like an arrow, [drinking] the supreme nectar of the wind.
For one who drinks thus quickly, there indeed arises the wind-like compassion toward the steadfast one intent on serving the guru, who possesses the radiance of a body of pure being. (17.34)
Toward a devotee who is devoted to the eightfold path, there arises great compassion for Vāyu;
likewise for one who feeds a guest without having eaten himself. (17.35)
Then, liberated from all evil, there arises a great compassion;
he who performs the concentration on air becomes the inner self, the Great Self. (17.36)
O Maheśvara, for one who possesses truthfulness toward the preceptor of the gods, there arises a wind-like benevolence;
thus, for such a person, even a single moment never passes in vain.
Taking up the mind in the northwest, there arises the compassion of the wind;
they move within the midst of the earth, bound by the training in yoga. (17.38)
Or else, there is the one who desires breath-control (prāṇāyāma), or the one who is well-disposed toward the wind;
those who dwell on every sacred seat (pīṭha) according to the measure of each year.
By chanting the Vāyavī mantra here, one becomes Vāyavī and full of great compassion;
moreover, one eats little, remains free from disease, and is delighted by the bliss of victory. (17-40)
For the yogi who worships the Vāyavī [Śakti], the Vāyavī becomes most gracious, provided he diligently fixes his mind upon the wheel of the seat (pīṭhacakra) during the internal sacrifice. (17.41)

Devoted to the Name, known as Dhāraṇā, and possessing great compassion for the wind-element; yet he is always overcome by the state of a bound soul (paśu), being eternally devoid of semen. || 17-42 ||
Free from sexual intercourse and devoid of semen, he is then possessed of great compassion;
whether at the improper time or the proper time, he is constantly intent upon retention (dhāraṇā).
Even for yogins, he is difficult to associate with; moreover, he is devoid of compassion, lacking kinsmen and relatives, and his mind is overcome by world-weariness. (17.44)

Then, having a state of being equal toward sorrow and joy, possessing great compassion, with a heart always full of bliss, knowing the proper time, he performs the sādhana of the elemental [deity]. (17.45)

He maintained silence and performed recitation; he was compassionate toward the wind [the breath]; thereafter, he delighted in solitary places, remained motionless, and was affectionate toward the distressed. (17.46)
He is free from excessive talk, steady-minded, and renowned; he is devoid of laughter, attachment, violence, and the like, and has mastered the sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 17.47 ||
One who seeks the completion of yoga training is declared to be of stable mind;
he knows the nature of my family's tradition and is a knower of mantras such as Mahāvidyā.
Endowed with pure devotion, peaceful, and steady-minded, he is thus proclaimed;
[he meditates] in the Mūlādhāra, in Kāmarūpa, and likewise in the heart at Jālandhara. (17.49)
In the forehead known as Pūrṇagiri, in Uḍḍīyāna above that, in Vārāṇasī between the eyebrows, and in the blazing [cavity] of the three eyes; || 17-50 ||
O Maheśvara, [the syllables] are in Māyāvatī at the heart, in Sukhavṛtta at the throat, likewise in Aṣṭapura at the navel region,
and in Ayodhyā at the waist and the hips.
Having diligently fixed the mind upon these seats in the world of earth, one should fill the abdomen with air according to the subtle symbolic terminology. (17.52)
On the big toe, the calf, the pair of knees, and the root [perineum], as well as on the four-petalled, six-petalled, and ten-petalled [lotuses]. || 17-53 ||
And on the twelve-petalled [lotus], pure with the established doctrines of accomplishment;
and on the sixteen-petalled [lotus] at the throat, which has two petals and is full of splendor.
In the place called Kailāsa, at the station of the aperture of Brahmā, within the stainless radiance,
in the great thousand-petaled lotus possessing the splendor of tens of millions upon tens of millions of moons.
Having stirred the great wind and having retained it again and again,
having filled [the body] and then expelled it, [the breath] emerges from the pores of the skin.
There are thirty-five million hair-pores on a human being;
indeed, from all these openings of the channels, drops of dharma flow forth. (17.57)
As long as that drop remains steady, for that duration it is known as *laya*;
through the yoga of breath during that time, perspiration arises, which bestows the lower accomplishments (*siddhi*). (17.58)
What on this earth cannot be accomplished by resorting to the subtle vital air?
One should fix the mind upon the hair-pore, the delightful place of dissolution. (17.59)
One should quickly become firm-minded; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Lord, how can there be accomplishment in this world without the service of the vital winds? (17.60)
O Lord, without a steady mind, even the middle path does not arise;
by fixing the mind in various places and through the practice of breath-retention (kumbhaka), [it is attained].
The practitioner, knowing the proper time, should retain the vital air day and night;
staying in a solitary and secluded place, he will certainly become steady-minded. (17.62)
O Śambhu, without a steady mind, how could supreme accomplishment be attained? (17.63)
Having carefully restrained those things known as the five sense-faculties, you, O Lord, possess a future through fortitude;
by means of this proximate practice, he is capable of consuming the poison of worldly existence.
Through the excellent accumulation of three months of practice, one becomes firm in the senses; the lower and other attainments arise.

That attainment of Khecarī is awakened here, but in the fourth month, conceptualization occurs. Then, he who subsists on air becomes an authority on the earth through a mind well-disposed in the bliss of a stable posture.
In this conceptualization, one swiftly attains accomplishment that accords with reality and the state of a preeminent hero.
That youthful power, whose forms are infinite, bestows great bliss within the cavern of those absorbed in greed;
it grants happiness, victory over the fickleness of the senses, and a stable disposition in one who is proficient in the scriptures.
With his body perfected through six months of practice in yogic postures, having attained a form whose essence is the bliss of the exertion of vital breath,
he is capable of casting aside the state of conceptual yoga and composing the Śrutis and Āgamas.
One of steady mind attains great siddhi; there is no doubt in this.
Through practice performed for a year, one shall attain the state of a great *khecara*. (17.69)
As long as the supreme wind-power (vāyavī śakti) does not emerge,
the wise one of steady mind should restrain it at the tip of the nose.
When Caṇḍavegā does not quickly enter the intermediate space, the wise practitioner should remain in that state for as long as he is one who goes everywhere. (17.71)
If the Lord Gaṇeśvara, who is equal to Śiva, is capable of going twelve finger-breadths above the region of the head; || 17-72 ||
"O Śaṅkara, by means of a steady mind, the king of yogins, who is self-controlled and a traveler through the sky, shall become all-pervading; thus, perfection shall be attained within a year. (7.73)
When one who has become a yogi does not maintain steadiness of mind on this earth, he falls like one who, having ascended to a high position with great difficulty, tumbles down into hell.
Therefore, O Mahākāla, remain steady in mind, O Lord;
then you will quickly attain me, who bestow the eight siddhis of the wind.
If one should become accomplished on earth through the compassionate grace of Vāyu and others,
then, having always become firm in desire, one should guard [the practice] like a mother protects her child.
O Mahādeva, whenever one practices yoga, or whenever one performs his duty by bestowing [the teachings] even upon disciples or sons; || 17-77 ||
At that very moment, he attains great perfection; there is no doubt about this.
For one year, he should practice the Dharma, for the path of Yoga is indeed difficult to traverse.
One should never disclose this; having done so, one would meet death.
Through the practice of yoga, liberation arises, and the perfection of mantra remains unbroken. (17.79)
Therefore, this yoga should not be disclosed even for the sake of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation;
one attains eternal bliss and the great dharma after a year has passed.
O Lord of the Kula, one should never reveal the mantra, the yantra, or the scripture that pertains to the bliss of the self and eternal bliss, nor the path of the Kula.
If he practices such dharma, then he shall meet his death;
fallen from yoga, though possessing knowledge and not being dull-witted, he shall attain death. || 17.82 ||
One should not even reveal that which leads one under the power of death;
[for example,] the great yogi Dattātreya, Śuka, and Nārada. (17.83)
By that one Lord of the World, devoted to the path of yoga, was created the net of syllables, the ocean of the Kula, which is the perfected mantra.
Likewise, by means of meditation performed as an auspicious rite, the best of practitioners attains supreme accomplishment within a year through the teaching of Yoga. (17.85)

At the outset, for the sake of attaining all perfections, one should indeed perform the meditation on Brahmā, characterized by the eight limbs of breath-retention (pūraka), and through the worship of Ambikā.
Having meditated upon the Ṛgveda in the mind at the four-petalled mūlādhāra, the wise one should sustain the vital air by means of the wind in the form of the moon. (17.87)
Then everything, including the Ṛgveda and other scriptures, as well as all that is moving and unmoving, emerged from Atharvan;
by means of that full moon, which was his very life-force and nectar.
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with single-minded devotion into the fire situated in the Kuṇḍalinī-sun,
while performing the retention of breath (kumbhaka) preceded by the Yajurveda.
That supreme consciousness of all, presided over by all sentient beings, has the full form of the wind element and designates the yogins. (17.90)
By repeatedly performing the kumbhaka on a being of stainless luster, one becomes a knower of the essence of the great dissolution; of this there is no doubt.

The exhaling breath (recaka) is pervaded by Śambhu; it is the dissolution of the mind into the quality of darkness (tamas), the locus where all lineages of death reside, and it is pervaded by the fruits of dharma, both fruitful and fruitless.
Ending in agitation again and again, it returns by means of exhalation (recaka);
through exhalation it reaches dissolution, and through exhalation it attains the supreme state. || 17-93 ||
The best of practitioners attains success even through exhalation (recaka);
that exhalation is of the nature of fire, blazing with ten million tongues of flame.
Having meditated on that which resides in the center of twelve finger-breadths, one should direct its dissolution outward;
it pervades the entire world as the moon, arising from all merit.
The fire of exhalation (recaka), the mighty friend of wind, burns here;
having drunk that which is the form of the lunar vital force (jīva), it lives by means of the wind.
The fire-goddess burns swiftly; this is considered the supreme oblation.
He who performs this rite shall not fall under the power of death. (17.97)
The time of transition between these two is the *kumbhaka* (retention), which is the means for realizing reality; it is indeed the supreme state for those who cultivate meditative realization.
Remaining steady in the kumbhaka through the practice of the great kumbhaka,
the great immortal should meditate upon the Goddess who moves along the path of the Atharva.

The practitioner of mantra should then meditate upon the Atharvaveda of Śambhu, which possesses infinite contemplation and is beautified by its entire creation, according to the sequence of the wheel of powers (śakticakra).
In the four-petaled lotus abode of the Ājñā-cakra, one should meditate upon the Atharva-yoginī with a mind established in samādhi. (17.101)
Then, within the lotus of his head, he beholds the Lord of the worlds known as Acyuta, the Sovereign of the universe, from whom the eternal, subtle bliss arises.
The purification of all the petals at the *ājñācakra* is proclaimed as the *Atharva*;
in the center of that, within the *jyotiścakra*, is the true cavity by way of the path of yoga. (17.103)
The possessor of great wisdom perceives it as an external lotus;
through time, the practitioner who knows Brahman attains perfection. (17.104)
Then one should follow the Kaula path; through that, one perceives the Vidyā—the Great Vidyā, which is filled with garlands of flames like ten million suns.
O Lord, without this reality, even Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, did not perceive it for a long time despite his excellent practice. (17.106)
The self-controlled one performed the practice of yoga and other disciplines for a hundred thousand years in a secluded place through arduous austerity.
Nevertheless, direct knowledge did not arise upon the surface of the earth;
thereupon, that powerful lord went in anger into the presence of his father.
O Lord, he related all that sequence of his own conduct to the Master:
"O Protector, grant me another mantra; this vidyā does not bestow success. (17.109)
"Otherwise, I shall indeed pronounce a most firm curse in your presence.
Then he restrained him, saying, "O son, do not do this!"
O wise one, worship her again with devotion through the path of yoga;
then, having become a granter of boons, she will appear before you. (17.111)
That goddess is the supreme power (paramā śakti), the savior from all perils;
she possesses the radiance of ten million suns, is blue in color, and is as cool as ten million moons.
Resembling the tip of a steady flash of lightning, she is the beloved of Time;
she protects the worlds of the three realms, and her activity encompasses all that is moving and stationary.
"O son, you who possess steady bliss, why are you prepared to curse me? O son, treasure of compassion, worship [the Lord] with a mind always fixed in solitude. (17.114)
"You will certainly obtain a vision of her in this way.
Having heard these words of the guru, he bowed down again and again. || 17-115 ||
The self-controlled master of Vedānta, pure in conduct, went to the shore of the ocean and performed the supreme recitation perfectly for a thousand years.
No instruction was given; thereafter, the sage Vasiṣṭha, overcome with anger and agitated in spirit, prepared to curse the Great Vidyā.
Having sipped water for purification twice, O Lord, that most terrible and great curse was pronounced by that very sage in the presence of the Muni, O Mistress of the Family.
The Great Vidyā, who bestows fearlessness upon yogins, arrived;
"O Brahmin, you have uttered a most terrible curse without cause. (17.119)
He does not know my service nor the contemplation of the tradition of my lineage;
how, then, can there be a vision of my lotus feet through the power of yoga practice? (17.120)

A human being who desires his lineage, whose mantra is perfected, and who is stainless through my Vedic conduct, attains in the world of the gods a state of contemplation that is free from suffering. (17.121)
"My own meritorious practice is beyond even the scope of the Vedas;
go then to Mahācīna in the land of the Buddhists, where it resides within the Atharvaveda. (17.122)
Having gone there and beheld my glorious lotus feet,
you, O great sage, who know my lineage, shall become a great perfected one (mahāsiddha).
Having spoken these words, she who moves through the air and space quickly became formless, and from that state, she once again moved through the sky with form.
Then, having heard the great vidyā Sarasvatī, the best of sages went to the land of Cīna, where the Buddha resides.
Bowing again and again upon the surface of the earth, Vasiṣṭha said:
"Protect me, protect me, O Mahādeva, O imperishable one who assumes a subtle form! (17.126)
To me, Vasiṣṭha, who was exceedingly dejected and always troubled in mind, the son of Brahmā came for the sake of practicing the sādhana of Mahādevī. || 17.127 ||
O Hara, devoted to the path of the Vedas, I do not know the path to spiritual success;
having observed your conduct, fears arise within my heart. (17.128)
Therefore, O Lord, quickly destroy my evil-mindedness that leads toward division;
may I always cause you to set aside any action that is outside the Vedas.
How is it that liquor, meat, and likewise women are of this nature?
All the Siddhas are naked, O excellent ones, and intent upon drinking blood. (17.130)
Again and again they drink and delight their excellent women;
always filled with meat and liquor, they are intoxicated, their eyes blood-red. (17.131)
Capable of both punishment and favor, with their inner faculties fully aroused, they all transcend the scope of the Vedas and are devoted to the enjoyment of wine and women. (17.132)
Having seen one who was excluded from the Vedas, the great yogi spoke thus, with palms joined in reverence and filled with humility: "O Lord, tell me this: what is his lineage? (17.133)
O Purifier, how does the engagement of their minds come about?
Or how, O Lord, is perfection attained without the performance of Vedic rites? (17.134)
The illustrious Buddha said:
"O Vasiṣṭha, listen; I shall declare the unsurpassed path of the Kula, by the mere knowledge of which one becomes the very form of Rudra in an instant. (17.135)
In brief, for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of the Kula, one should first become pure, steadfast, and have a mind overcome by discernment; such is the scripture. (17.136)
With a mind steady in the state of a beast, yet free from association with beasts, he should remain alone in a secluded place, having abandoned desire, anger, and the like. (17.137)

Devoted to the practice of the yoga of restraint, firm in his vows regarding the training in yoga, always relying on the path of the Vedas, and great in his proficiency in the meaning of the Vedas. (17.138)
Thus, in due order, the righteous one, endowed with the quality of firmness in conduct,
should constantly hold the vital air within the path of the breath, causing the dissolution of the mind.
Thus, through the practice of yoga, the masterful yogi, by gradual and sequential training day by day, should burn [the impurities] until the emergence of sweat; this is the lowest stage.
The abandonment of the earth-element joined with the intermediate [stage] is considered supreme;
through breath control (prāṇāyāma), perfection shall arise, and the man becomes a lord of yoga. || 17-141 ||
Having become a yogi, skilled in breath-retention (kumbhaka), silent, and devoted day and night to Śiva-Kṛṣṇa in the state of Brahman, he is endowed with exclusive devotion. || 17.142 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—these are as fickle as the movement of the wind;
having thus reflected with the mind, one becomes pure through action and speech. (17.143)
First, having concentrated the mind upon the nature of consciousness with a firm resolve,
one then [attains] the state of the Great Hero, the family path of great exaltation.
Having resorted to the wheel of power (śakticakra), the wheel of being (sattvacakra), and the Vaiṣṇava form consisting of nine bodies,
the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should worship the supreme Kulakātyāyanī.
The manifest deity, the bestower of prosperity, who cuts through fierce agitation;
whose form is consciousness, the abode of knowledge, and whose very body is the bliss of pure awareness.
She possesses the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes, embodies the nature of all reality,
has eighteen arms, is fierce, and delights in mountains of the flesh of Śiva.
Relying [on this], a person who takes refuge in the path of the *kula* should recite the mantra;
for who in the three worlds knows a path superior to the path of the *kula*? (17.148)
By the grace of this path, the great Brahmā himself is the creator;
and Viṣṇu, pure and assuming the form of *sattva*, is capable of protecting the world. (17.149)
He is the one to be served by all, the great object of worship, the lord of the Yajurveda, and the Great One;
he is Hara, the agent of dissolution, whose mind is fixed on the supreme Vīreśa. || 17-150 ||
The wrathful one, the king of wrath, possessed of great power, is the end-maker of all;
by the grace of his heroic nature, the guardians of the directions take on the form of Rudra. (17.151)
This entire universe is dependent upon the hero, and the hero is dependent upon the lineage (kula).
Therefore, by relying upon the lineage, even an insentient thing becomes the master of all accomplishments.
Through attraction for one month, success is achieved; in two months, one becomes a master of speech;
through union for three months, one is known as a beloved of happiness. (17.153)
Thus, in the fourth month, he becomes the domain of the Guardians of the Directions;
in the fifth, he becomes the Five-Arrowed One (Kāmadeva); and in the sixth, he certainly becomes Rudra.
For this is indeed the essence of conduct, beyond the reach of all others;
this path is the Kaula path, and there is no path higher than the Kaula path.
For yogis of firm mind who are devoted, the accomplishment of their purpose shall come within one month through the grace of the Kula path of women. (17.156)
A Brahmin becomes a perfected yogi through the practice of yoga for six months;
without Śakti, Śiva is powerless—how much more so others who possess dull intellects? (17.157)
Having spoken thus, he who was in the form of the Buddha caused the ritual practice to be performed:
"O Brahmin, perform the service of the Great Power, the ritual of wine. (17.158)
"You shall obtain the vision of the lotus-feet of Mahāvidyā.
Having heard these words of the guru and having remembered the goddess Sarasvatī, [he proceeded].
He went to the circle of families (kulamaṇḍala) in order to perform the preparation of the intoxicating liquor;
[there he found] wine, meat, flesh, the ritual gesture (mudrā), and sexual union itself.
Having accomplished it again and again, O Lord, he became a master of perfected yoga, [following] the path of yoga, the path of the Kula, and the sequence of the single practice.
Having become a yogin and having meditated upon the *kula*, one becomes the lord of all siddhis;
the time of union (*sandhikāla*) and the path of the *kula* are always rendered insentient through yoga.
Merely by means of this union, one becomes a master of all accomplishments;
one should understand this to be the yoga of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). || 17-163 ||

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the determination of the meaning of questions regarding states of being (*bhāva*), in the section on accomplished mantras (*siddhamantra-prakaraṇa*), in the manifestation of the four Vedas (*caturveda-ullāsa*), within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 17 ||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said: "Listen, O Lord, I shall proclaim the supreme means for accomplishing that which is otherwise unattainable."
The description of the colors of the wheel of desire, and the resolution of the questions. || 18-1 ||
In the central region of the wheel of command (ājñācakra), there is a multitude of millions of channels;
in the midst of that, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate the beautiful wheel of desire (kāmacakra). 18-2.

And having observed the previously mentioned syllables in the wheel of desire (kāmacakra), the practitioner, having encased them within the placement-mantra (nyāsamantre) and recited it, becomes a king among yogis. || 18-3 ||
Standing alone in the center of the temple, one should diligently rely upon the mantra; therein, one should take recourse in that square which corresponds to the syllables of one's own name.
Ānandabhairava said:
O beloved, tell me the secret concerning the fruits and non-fruits of these letters situated within the compartments, arising from the results of the Kāmacakra.
Ānandabhairavī said:
The Wheel of Desire (kāmacakra) is the form of Time; beyond that is the city of Vārāṇasī.
Therein lies the wheel of all sacred seats (pīṭha), the most excellent among all wheels.
By the grace of this wheel, the practitioner attains the vision of your lotus feet;
indeed, the practitioner comes to know everything as truth. (18.7)
For the sake of accomplishing the fruits of one's desires, one should abandon an old or deceased [teacher] and take up an excellent mantra after investigating its meaning and other aspects.
(Ānandabhairavī said:
Listen, O Lord, to the fruit of the letters, which provides the determination for questions that are difficult to resolve.
And listen, O Lord, to the division of the letters according to their zodiacal signs, O Master. (18–9)
The best of practitioners should resort to the classes situated in childhood and the other stages;
he should avoid the state of old age as well as that which has already set. (18.10)

One should consider childhood, youth, and adolescence according to their state as signs (rāśi); furthermore, within the analysis of the divisions of the periods (varga), one should examine childhood through the application of the Vāma method.
O Lord, one should also count the mantras for the rites of inquiry starting from the south;
they should be counted by the wise up to the center corner.
In the practice of divination, one should count by joining the upward and right [fingers];
in the investigation of mantras and the like, one should count by joining the left. (18.13)
Listen to the exceedingly beautiful fruit of those groups of groups;
I, like a bee at the honey of the ocean of the essence of supreme bliss, shall now speak. (18.14)
The guttural class (kavarga) is the abode of Kāmākhyā upon the jeweled throne (maṇipīṭha);
that Dharitrī, the sustainer, dwells eternally there amidst the nine Siddhis.
She is the fire within all fires, the sky, the body of the clouds, and the mother of the space of the sky.
Deep, with the luster of a sword, bestowing fearlessness with her hands, and possessing a terrible face. || 18-15 ||
Through the yoga of practice, she is the purifier of the Kali age;
she is Kālī, the embodiment of the joy of the Kula, the consort of Rama,
whose face and eyes shine with the exuberance of the Great Essence (Mahārasa).
The victor should worship Kāmeśvarī at the Kūrma-pada. || 18-16 ||
The black aloe-wood used by the supreme Siddhas,
the heart-stealing essence of the tree of the sky-farers,
possessing the full brilliance of a meteor, serves as the lamp for existence.
Her body is pure blue, like the peak of a mountain of lapis lazuli. || 18-17 ||
Armed with a sword and holding a skull-bowl,
she is Caṇḍodgamā, a sky-farer (khecarī) situated in the path of the wind;
her movement is the gait of Khañjana, whose eyes are filled with the fear of ignorance.
When the earth is destroyed, she sustains the host of sky-dwellers.
The birds, who dwell in threshing floors and delight in the play of threshing, whose gait is as intoxicated as that of donkeys and mules,
and who always reside in the threshing floor in the form of great birds—
She who stands firm in the power and valor of knowledge causes [them] to fall. || 18-19 ||
Whenever there is the appearance of harsh light from the dense darkness of worldly activity and sleep, and from the contemplation of objects; || 18-20 ||
She is Gāyatrī, the leader of the Gaṇas, the intelligence, the movement, the one whose exhaustion has vanished, and whose intention is unhidden;
she is the Gītā, the beloved of Gokula, the most weighty, the one to be cherished, the one who conquers the arising of the sacrificial fires;
she is the form of the cow, the destroyer of sin, the holy Gaya, the virtuous one, and she who abides on the path of sacred verses.
One should worship her whom they sing as the glorious Guru who protects the three worlds. || 18–21 ||
The wind is the Gharma-karā, the Ānanda-mohinī, the Ghargharā, the Ghanā;
it induces sleep, it is the Ghaṭanā, the Nīlā, and the Ghoṭakavāhinī. (18–22)

Residing in the *bindu*, she is the discourse on poison, food, and fire; she is fond of the exertion of the seed-syllable (*bīja*); enriched by the five [elements], she is nasalized, composed of bliss, the act of knowing, and six-faced. (18–23)
O restless one, grant me the movement of your lotus-feet clad in variegated garments, and bestow upon me the activity of discerning deliberation.
Thus is the description of the *ca*-group of consonants, which destroys great sins;
it is situated in the wheel of desire (*kāmacakra*), just as it appears in the house of mantras within the inquiry.
They repeatedly contemplate the entire series of all syllables with their intellect, which possesses an extremely refined fruit of the *ca*-group and a subtle mode of cultivation. (18–26)
O Śambhu, you know everything; what more can I tell you?
Nevertheless, [I shall speak] of the greatness of the *varga*, which is stainless and situated within the wheel of desire (*kāmacakra*).
He who understands the wheel of desire—that person Yama does not slay;
he is endowed with that mode of being, purified by meditation and contemplation. (18-28)
Having meditated upon all the earthly deities residing in the mūlādhāra and abiding in the form of desire, [one should contemplate] oneself as the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).

Those foolish children do not know this: for the sake of their attainment of yoga and other powers, [there is] the Wheel of Desire (kāmacakra), which can assume any form at will (kāmarūpa) and bestows the accomplishment of the fruits of one's desires.
By the mere reception of that mantra, a person becomes the Lord manifest;
all the Vedas and scriptures are in his hand—of this there is no doubt. (18.31)
One understands everything, beginning with the training in yoga, through the wheel of desire;
by the grace of the wheel of desire, one will certainly become capable of assuming any form at will. (18.32)

The best of practitioners, having reflected upon that which resides within its color, that which is situated inside it, that which is located within the ten-cornered [figure], and likewise that which is situated within the eight-petaled [lotus]. (18–33)
In direct and reverse order, and according to the sequence of the scripture:
childhood, youth, efflorescence, growth, and accomplishment occur during the stage of adolescence. (18.34)
The aged attains old age, and when he sets, his end occurs;
therein are the nine planets, and in the midst of them are indeed the five vital breaths.
One should count [the syllables] in forward and reverse order within the ten-cornered [diagram].
Indeed, all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi) and the eight accomplishments (aṣṭasiddhi) reside therein in that ten-cornered [diagram].
They praise the eight-petaled [lotus] with Ananta in the center below, within the house, and with Brahmā in the upper house; and one should place those very syllables of the mantra there. (18.37)
Relying upon this, the wise should recite the Vidyā in its sequential form;
it bestows the Short Goddess and shortens the intellect of the practitioner. (18.38)
If a vidyā devoted to anger should quickly devour the practitioner,
therefore [one should worship] a goddess who is equal in age and form, and who bestows the eight siddhis.
Having become a god, one should worship the God; then one shall attain liberation.
If he does not know his own caste, even the son of a Kaula shall go to the lower realms.
A ḍākinī devours one who is deficient in the syllables of the initiation mantra;
therefore, I shall explain the consideration of the phonemes in brief. (18.41)
Holding his bow, that lord of men protects even this human being here in the world;
the Moon destroys all obstacles, the Sun destroys abundant fear and sorrows,
and on the fourth lunar day, Māyā bestows even the station of the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu) upon the fickle one here.
The practitioner who exerts himself in yoga with a mind directed toward the goal quickly attains yoga for the sake of the aspirant.
Seated upon a lotus under a parasol, she sustains the glory of the fruits of desire even during the dissolution of existence;
dwelling within the midst of a pavilion of shade, her mass of splendor acts as a parasol by its brilliance.
The three worlds are protected by the Śrīdharas, the lords of sacred fields who follow the Pāśupata path.
The Goddess, who dwells in love for his very life, [protects] that practitioner with her parasol. || 18-43 ||
The unsurpassed renown of her lineage flourishes through this constant practice;

she brings joy by destroying the mountain of suffering for living beings. Moving toward a single goal, she is the diamond-like knowledge situated within life, possessed of motion—the victorious Night.
May she who, being born, wards off birth and intends the destruction of the minds of living beings protect us. 18.44.

With the sound "jhaṃ jhaṃ," free from dispute, the Gaṅgā— whose flow is instantly rushing and whose seed-syllable is the resonance "jhaṅ"— destroys all impurities and, with her face turned toward wealth, bestows the liberation of Kaivalya. Having protected the practitioner, she guards him with the subtle wind and the sound of "jharajhana."
She who destroys desire and anger, whose face is like the moon, and who delights in the sound of the syllable "jhaṅ."
The Yoginī, whose essence is the pure state [born from] the seed-syllable *ña*, strikes down the multitude of arrows;
armed with a sword, intoxicated by the drinking of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), she destroys the suffering of virtuous beings who are overcome by the sleep of cosmic dissolution.
(18.46) Her body is lovely and smooth like moonlight; with her axe-weapon and thunderbolt-weapon, she slays the foremost of his enemies.
By the recitation of the great mantra "ṭiṃ ṭiṃ," she bestows success and destroys both the misfortune and the sins of the base man.

If the wide-eyed Urvaśī, with her beautiful limbs, protects her own seed with the sound "ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ," she destroys the entire host of the army of the ocean of jewels—the multitude of sorrows residing in the mind. (18-48)

Ḍāmarā is the primordial [goddess] of the worlds; she whose essential nature is the syllables ḍaṃ, ḍāṃ, ḍiṃ, and ḍīṃ, bestows bliss within the wheel of desire and thus extends [herself] through her very essence.
The Vidyā whose essence is the seed-syllables *ḍhaṃ* and *ḍhāṃ*, residing in the temple of jewels, is Ḍhakkārī; holding a noose in her hand, that beautiful lady protects the practitioner. (18.50)
The virtuous person, established in the midst of life, mutters *ṇaṃ ṇāṃ ṇiṃ ṇīṃ*;
she who possesses the eight sovereign powers arises in the heart to remove the mass of agitation.
She who destroys all fear in Vārāṇasī bestows prosperity here.
Opening its mouth toward the subtle and ultimate path of fire, it destroys the net of time.

She who is in the form of a star, situated upon a tree, three-eyed, and curved; she who is named Tārakā, the destroyer of the multitude of bodies, who has passed beyond for the sake of protecting the essence of the best of trees;
she whose field is the rhythm (tāla), like lightning, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns.
The pupil protects the eye from excessive light and other such factors. || 18-52 ||
In due course of time, she who bestows liberation, the delightful one with lotus-like eyes and tender limbs,
standing upon the ground of the garland of syllables beginning with the letter *kṣa*, the auspicious goddess brings down the supreme, excellent practitioner. (18.53)

Dālī, the destroyer of the misery of the most wretched and the poor; beloved of the self-controlled; the rending of the Daityas; the burner; she who dwells in the place of giving; the beloved of the Lord of the World; she who bestows compassion; the wife of the melting god. 18-54.
The nurse (Dhātrī), intent on supporting the earth (Dharā), wealthy (Dhanī), bestowing riches (Dhanapradā), the refuge of Dharma (Dharmagati), and the sustainer (Dharitrī);

garlanded with the seeds of wealth (Dhanabījamālinī) and established in meditation (Dhyānasthitā), she bore the steadfast one for the sake of defining the Dharma. Arising as a mass of bliss for the worlds, she was for the protection of Nanda.
May those Yoginīs— who possess the splendor of the radiant flames from their lotus-eyes, who are garlanded with the syllables of the *pramālā*,

and who protect the wise woman who has been brought to the path of the boat— truly protect the practitioner here according to the sequence of time by means of the majesty of their glorious faces. (18.56)
May she protect [us]— she who is yellow-hued, who sports in love, who is the refuge of the knowledge of the supreme path,
who protects, who is worthy of worship, who drinks milk-rice, who is both the transcendent and the immanent state, who is clad in yellow garments, who nourishes, who is mature,
who possesses love, who narrates the Purāṇas, and who was ancient and purifying.
She who has set out toward the illustrious practitioner, a stranger who purifies the Lord of Desire. || 18-57 ||

She who wears a garland of excellent hooded serpents, who is the female jackal and takes the form of a male jackal; she who resides in the ocean of nectar-like words from the lotus-mouths of the serpent-bearers;
she who, in the form of speech, is established as the fruit upon the neck of the boundless Hari.
May she whose crest-jewel is a serpent reaching for its fruit protect [us] upon the blossoming lotus. || 18-58 ||
If one recites the mantra known as Vajrā, the subduer, through the service of the venerable feet,
then the Goddess Śrī Rāmadevī, the daughter of Urvaśī who has transcended childhood,
shall become submissive; seated in the *vīrāsana* posture, she dwells in the hollow of his hand.
The Blessed Goddess Bhūteśvarī resides within all beings, her lotus-face tender and delicate.
My mother is Mandiramālinī, the stainless garland of bliss for the wise;
she who deludes through false sexual union is Melā, the great uniter within my mind. The proud one proclaims that greatness of Maheśvara upon her breast.
Remaining there, she suddenly strikes down death; one should become an observer of silence.
She who is beloved by the wind, she who shines forth as the Yoginī,
she who dwells in the Yāmā [state] like the very seat of the mouth of Yoga—
she resides in the place of the womb (yonisthala) for the ascetic practitioner.
The procession of glory always protects him; it burns away [the faults] beginning with lack of self-restraint. || 18-61 ||
Established in jewels, resplendent with delight, dispelling the fear of the king at the front of battle,
adorned with a golden river, full of aesthetic flavor, removing passion, and destroying disease—
she, the nectar of Rādhā, protects the lord of kings when he is enraged during the night.
She is beautiful in form like Svāhā, a divine maiden, a charming woman, and she whose syllable is the letter Ra.
Lakṣmī, marked by the plough, is a beautiful woman—fickle yet stainless, fearless;
she is like the root of a young tree to the wicked, agitated by salt, and filled with the playful grace of the ocean's splendor;
she is restless, born from the fire-like mouth of the swarm of bees, clinging closely, and agitated by her light burden.
Kaulārka’s Akulalocanā, the bringer of dissolution, protects me, the abode of divine play. || 18-63 ||
The latent impression (vāsanā) residing in the state of the flow of poison,
which brings about subjugation for the sake of bringing a woman under control—
if a master of self-control should resort to her, she protects the hero.
They consume poison and drink the liquor of Varuṇa.
One should honor a woman who is cool, who destroys the specific sorrow of the moon,
who is virtuous, and who becomes a mine of jewels;
she is auspicious, like Śacī, pure and beautiful, and dear to the Lord of the Dead.
She was seated upon a corpse, graced by a cool location.

In the six cakras, she who has six feet, who dwells in the month of Āṣāḍha, who abides in the six limbs, and who has six faces—the sixteen-year-old—joyfully protects the practitioner by bestowing siddhi within the six cakras. (18.66)
She flows subtly, carrying pure water, enriched by the grounds of the seven celestial realms;
she is the essence itself, manifest as the blissful joy of the radiant *samarasa*;
she possesses form, filling the great purpose with her lotus-honeyed speech.
The Vedas are solar, and the multitude of those with divine intellects abide within the Sāmaveda.
By forceful means, the river Sahārā carries away people along with their very life-breath;
yet that river, garlanded with golden food, does not kill those who have cast off their lives.

She is light, characterized by a hundred thousand recitations, possessing the marks of a hundred thousand, equal [to all], free from attachment, and devoid of idle talk; she swiftly protects him who worships her.

The minister of practice, having abandoned the meditation on consumption that removes the disease of wasting, should contemplate something subtler than the subtle, which reaches dissolution upon the earth through very subtle contemplation.
She diminishes the agitation and so forth, as well as the fortnights, lunar digits, and the waning [of life]. || 18-70 ||
O Great Lord, hear the fruit according to the distinction of the sixteen vowels;
it should be explained concisely for those who desire the supreme fruit. (18.71)
O Mahādeva, those who perform the festival of the Kāmacakra according to the method [described] in these three (or two) verses obtain all that fruit and the ultimate means of accomplishment.
He who chants the auspicious mantra of the first eight vowels— *a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ*— from the lotus-like mouth of Śrīnātha,
shall instantly become a perfected one (*siddha*) upon the surface of the earth, having attained the status of the Lord Śrīdhara.
The king, the lord of the royal family, beholding the supreme art (*kalā*) with a garland of blazing lamps on the path of victory, conquers and strikes down the fire of desire.
Ḷ Ḷ E E O AU AṂ AḤ.
The remaining eight vowels are the purifiers; Mandodarī brings joy to her beloved people.
Madānanā destroys the mantra, yet she brings happiness to the most excellent of the virtuous throughout the three worlds.
Having bestowed [her grace], she protects [the devotee] at the time of dissolution; she removes the science of crookedness (kauṭilya-vidyā).
For the sake of devotion, she effects the protection of the earth, while [the practitioner] remains intent on his own recitation and meditation, free from inauspiciousness.
Having thus understood the results of the syllables, he who takes up this supreme mantra shall become a seeker of the yoga of his lineage and a knower of the perfected wisdom upon the earth. (18.75)
O Lord, listen; I shall describe the wonderful result for each group.
He who knows how to explain the questions and so forth is a true practitioner. (18.76)

In the *kavarga*, one attains the fulfillment of desires and a beautiful residence pervaded by prosperity; this is for the purpose of the wheel of desire (*kāmacakra*), as approved by the zodiac signs and lunar mansions. (18–77)
In the *ca*-group, one shall have a long life as well as firm prosperity;
one obtains a livelihood from embodied beings without even seeking it out. (18.78)
One attains the highest conduct in all matters regarding movement;
O Lord, when the *ṭa*-group arises, there is great expulsion (*uccāṭana*) and so forth. (18.79)
There will be an increase even in one's sons; in the *tavarga*, there is the gain of wealth.
O Lord, in the *pavarga* there is death; from *yādi* to *kṣānta*, one is possessed of great virtues.
O Lord, one should apply the fruit of the wheel of desire by means of the *daṇḍa* of the zodiacal sign, having ascertained the sign situated in its own house from the *daṇḍas* of the day. (18.81)
Having calculated the inauspicious [influences] through both direct and reverse order,
the wise one [should know that] everything situated in the pot (ghaṭa) is auspicious when located at the junctions and corners on the side.
Having received the auspicious mantra, the practitioner attains accomplishment.
Thus, in the *Śrīrudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantro*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*,
in the *Bhāvapraśnārthanirṇaya*, in the *Pāśavakalpa*, in the *Kāmacakrasārasaṅketa*, in the *Siddhimantraprakaraṇa*, in the *Caturvedollāsa*, [this is] the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
In the Saṃvāda, the eighteenth chapter. || 18 ||
Chapter Nineteen.
Ānandabhairavī said: Listen now to this which I shall declare, the secret of the meaning of all tantras.
All that occurs in the wheel of questions (praśnacakra) and the piercing of the six supports (ṣaḍādhāra). || 19-1 ||

Therein lies the fruit of Kālacakra, the practice of non-conceptuality and so forth, the wheel of questions, the form of desire, and the consciousness of both the self and the other at all times. (19.2)
He who, having abandoned the sixfold collection [of powers] in the six abodes, the means to liberation and so forth, various enjoyments, and the perfection of yoga, should mutter the mantra; 19-3.
He who betrays the deity will attain success only after ten million eons; however, for one in whose heart great devotion shines forth as a supreme attainment, [success is swift]. 19-4.
For accomplishment would occur in an instant; what need is there for recitations or mantra-practices?
Therefore, one should always cultivate devotion for the sake of attaining the state of being the deity. (19.5)
Bhairava said:
By the grace of this wheel, who might attain what perfection? What is the fruit of its contemplation, and what is the auspicious nature of that contemplation?
"O beautiful one, who indeed is capable of answering questions and the like?
Tell me, according to the prescribed method, for the sake of attaining the fruit. (19.7)
Ānandabhairavī said:
He who performs the *pūrṇahoma* for the sake of a son and for the attainment of yoga, by means of the sequence of Kuṇḍalinī, again and again in due order— || 19-8 ||
O Lord, he who always performs that which is characterized by the exit of the vital breath (vāyu) is indeed the knower of the reality of the meaning of this wheel; of this there is no doubt. (19.9)
Having established [the deity] above according to the rule, the person who performs meditation attains accomplishment; he follows the path of the perfected ones, of this there is no doubt. (19.10)
This is the fruit for the purpose of cultivation, having abandoned desire, anger, and the like;
it is for the sake of accomplishing the fruit of cultivation through the transition of the union with the vital breath.
Having smeared, purified, and consecrated [the object] repeatedly, by means of the opposition of dharma and adharma and through the sequence of the subtle wind. || 19-12 ||
One attains great accomplishment; this is the fruit of that wheel.
And the fruit is said to be twofold, abiding as gross, subtle, and supreme. (19–13)
Whenever the mind, having abandoned the gross, enters the great subtle state,
then indeed there is great accomplishment, and one becomes immortal at that very moment.
Whoever meditates even once upon the colors of the Siddhacakra, for that very person there shall be the attainment of existence; what indeed is not accomplished through such meditation? (19.15)
O Lord, without the Great State (mahadbhāva), who can grasp the fruit of accomplishment?
One who has fallen from yoga may attain accomplishment in a future birth through gross fruits.
One attains success in this very life through the gradual sequence of subtle fruits;
he who knows the subtle fruit certainly becomes a yogi. (19.17)
That practitioner alone is worthy of being addressed in the discourse on the question, who is an enjoyer of subtle fruits and is intent upon the concealment of his ritual actions. (19.18)
Having visualized the wheel of questions situated continuously above the wheel of command, one shall attain the perfection of time, becoming omniscient and a master of the Vedas. (19–19)
The determination of the true meaning is that he who knows the time is omniscient;
the syllable situated in the wheel of questions brings about the subtle results of time. (19–20)
The form of the mind, the distinctions of punishment, the distinctions of months, and the cycle of the seasons—all these are indeed the delusion of the mind; time is one, without a doubt. (19–21)
The king of yogis, who knows the [proper] time, indeed brings death itself under his control;
by time, the entire three worlds, including all that is moving and stationary, are dissolved. (19–22)
This entire universe is dependent on time; therefore, one should bring [all things] under the control of time.
Listen now to the inquiry concerning that time, which is subtle in its abode and difficult to describe. (19–23)
The zodiac sign of Aries (Meṣa) and the supreme sign of Libra (Tulā) are always the causes for the attainment of results in the month of Vaiśākha;
having obtained the guttural consonants (kavarga), he is indeed the vowels themselves.
If one should meditate [thus], he would become a lord of the earth. || 19-24 ||
Having meditated upon all the cakras above the *ājñācakra*, O Great Lord, accomplishment shall be attained in a single moment by means of the supreme nature as the cause. (19–25)
He who on this earth knows the consciousness of the wheel of the Siddheśas attains perfection of speech within a month, through the course of day and night. (19–26)
Having meditated upon the wheel of planets, pervaded by the garland of letters and joined with the zodiac signs and lunar mansions, the practitioner knows everything. (19–27)
And the group [of mantras] situated in Taurus and Pisces is the cause for attaining success in youth;
by practicing them for only two months, one certainly becomes omniscient. (19–28)
Having become the Khecarī Yoginī, she approaches the presence of the virtuous;
by the grace of the wheel of planets, the practitioner becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 19-29 ||
If one performs action with a mind that is entirely pure, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that remains unattainable for them. (19.30)
By the grace of the *praśnacakra*, all indeed become yogis on earth;
if one becomes a yogi on earth, then one shall attain liberation. (19–31)
Without the practice of yoga, who on the surface of the earth has attained perfection?
Without such practice, for which devotee does spiritual accomplishment arise? (19.32)
All the great seers abide in the presence of devotees;
therefore, one should always practice devotion, setting aside all other religious duties. (19–33)
At that time, one attains devotion through the grace of the Wheel of Questions;
for who indeed is capable of describing that great dharma and its specific methods? (19-34)
I shall now describe within the Wheel of Questions that which is the essence of its nature:
through the very contemplation of the *ca*-group, the practitioner attains devotion. (19.35)
O Lord, having concentrated upon the Supreme Deity above the *ājñācakra* and having meditated upon His eternal nature, one indeed attains even a portion (*kalā*) of that [divine] family.

He who experiences tears of joy, horripilation, bodily possession, and the dissolution of the mind, and who performs all actions while having personally renounced them—he is the king of yogis. (19.37)

In the *ṭa*-group, there is the accomplishment of latent impressions (*vāsanāsiddhi*); one becomes free from saṃsāra, powerful, and all-knowing; within three months, one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*). (19–38)
He attains the supreme union with Khecarī from the wheel;
pervading the *ṭa*-group of consonants, they abide as a couple born from jars (*kumbhayoni*).
Having meditated upon his own lunar mansion and his own yoga, he becomes a king among yogins;
within four months, he becomes a perfected yogin even through the practice of the *tavarga* [the dental consonants].
One shall attain the great siddhis such as Vetāla and the siddhi of Indra;
Capricorn, Scorpio, and Cancer remain pervading the *tavarga*. (19–41)
O Lord, he shall become long-lived and as dear as Indra;
he shall endure until the dissolution of the universe, possessing the form of the great dissolution itself.

Having brought time under control, the mantra-practitioner [should place] the Great Abode within the great wind, in the center of the sun within the great wheel, situated in the middle of the fire-mandala. (19.43)
The goddess of speech manifests before him; of this there is no doubt.
Pervading the *pa*-group [of consonants], the energies of consciousness (*citkalā*) abide as the bow and the lion. (19.44)
Having visualized the supreme abode, that great wind does not perish;
in an instant, one perceives with the eye the three worlds, the eightfold group, and the six wheels. (19.45)

Or if, with a stainless eye, one perceives that which has been vomited forth as being of the nature of Brahman, the refuge of all sacred fords, and pervaded by the qualities of great beings; || 19-46 ||
One should observe the path of Brahmā through the zodiac signs of Virgo and Scorpio;
within six months, success shall be attained, and one will certainly become a Mahākaula.
Remaining silent and solely devoted, that best of practitioners attains the vision of the glorious lotus feet and shall obtain the state of union (sāyujya). || 19-48 ||
Then the yogins, who contemplate reality, proceed to the center,
to that square place beginning with 'Śa' and ending with 'Kṣa', which is the locus of all yoga.
Having meditated thus, that wise practitioner, a meditator on the Wheel of Questions, quickly goes to the realm of the illustrious Goddess and becomes Mahākāla. (19.50)
Thus, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*,
in the determination of the meaning of the inquiry into states of being (*bhāva*),
in the *Pāśavakalpa*, in the *Praśnacakra-sārasaṅketa*, in the section on accomplished mantras (*siddhamantra-prakaraṇa*), in the *Caturvedollāsa*.
In the Dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, the nineteenth chapter. 19.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Mahādeva, I shall now declare the investigation of perfected mantras."
Having recited [the mantra] and meditated upon it, a person shall be liberated from distress.
Ānandabhairava said:
In the *phalacakra*, which is the essence of all mantras and dear to the body, perfection arises through the yoga of action by means of serving the power of Vāyu. (20.2)
O Lord, the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ) is situated within a triangle, and outside of that is a hexagon;
having meditated upon the six mantras within the hexagon for six months, one becomes Rudra in form. (20–3)
The wise one, having meditated upon the syllables situated in the eight corners according to the sequence of their numerical values, and likewise outside of them, should proceed.
Having visualized the letters contained within those numbers, one becomes a sky-walker (khecarī);
there, without the application of triangles, one should [visualize] the six-sided [figure] with the letters.
In the central region of the wheel of command (ājñācakra) is the delightful wheel of desire (kāmacakra);
in the central region of the wheel of desire is the arising of the fruit of the great subtle (mahāsūkṣma). || 20-6 ||
The wheel of inquiry consists of six categories and is the means for accomplishing the fruits of the six wheels;
within the wheel of inquiry lies the wheel of results, which bestows the fruits of the eightfold yoga.

In the upper portion of the wheel of fruits (phalacakra), according to the sequence of the garland of syllables, one shall obtain the essence of the fruit through silent recitation (*maunajāpa*) of those syllables. || 20-8 ||
Through the grace of the wheel of the fruit, the intellect intent on the contemplation of reality,
remaining in the hollow of the space between the eyebrows, always meditates upon the Lord.
Even a fool shall quickly become a knower of reality through the power of contemplation.
O Śaṅkara, I shall first describe the subtle fruit according to the distinction of castes.
The fire that incessantly blazes for the destruction of the three worlds is the protector;
the life-force (*jīva*) is the burning of all that is moving and unmoving, the very form of the illustrious Kālikā.
The all-pervading Lord consumes the sprouts of desire within the mind.
Having meditated upon him, one who possesses that same form becomes a knower of Paraśiva at that very moment. || 20-11 ||
The seed-syllable of fire (Ra) is the subtle fruit, the direct and manifest cause;
the seed-syllable of fire situated within the triangle reveals the knowledge of the ritual procedure.
He who worships the bestower of success without effort shall become happy.
O Ānandabhairava, listen now to the mantras consisting of syllables situated within the hexagon. (20.13)
Having known that, all the deities who protect the cardinal and intermediate directions [attain it], which is characterized by delightful objects and marked by the purity of convention. (20.14)
Above the seed-syllable of fire (ra) is the unsurpassed seed-syllable of the moon (sa);
the mantra-practitioner who meditates upon that therein becomes a perfected one—of this there is no doubt. (20.15)
The subtle seed of the moon is the stainless lotus with lovely rays;
it is the eternal abode of the individual soul (jīva) and the place of dissolution, conjoined with the vital breath (vāyu).
From that [arises] the sun on the left, which is the collection that destroys all obstacles and misfortunes.
The virtuous person resorts to the station of the great fire according to the method of meditative cultivation.

And in the house located at the lower corner of that [diagram], one should place the Śrī-bīja with the fifth vowel, the essence of the Bhāvakalpalatā, and the primordial letters beginning with 'A'. (20.17)
Then, having visualized the seed-syllable of Vāyu situated in the fifty-fourth square below that, the lord of men attains the siddhi of Vāyu. (20.18)
Then, O Lord, having visualized the maṇḍala of the seed-syllable of Bhavānī on his right limb, pervaded by a pair of vowels, he becomes a king among yogis. (20.19)
And by visualizing the unsurpassed seed-syllable of Soma in the upper-right corner of that [diagram],
a person shall obtain the vision of the Lord of the worlds.
Above that is the supreme seed-syllable, which bestows the fruit of direct realization;
by meditating upon it for just one month, one shall attain rebirth in the world of the gods.
And in the house at the upper corner of that [diagram] is the wonderful seed-syllable of Rukmiṇī;
through its practice alone, success shall be attained, and one shall become a lord of fortune in this world. (20–22)
The arrangement of vowels is to be understood everywhere according to the sequence of the limbs; by whichever vowel it is encircled, that is the seed-syllable of the fruit.

O Mahādeva, it is indeed the cause for the accomplishment of Vāyu and the other [elements]; O Nātha, on the surface of the eight-cornered [figure], there are indeed six-cornered [figures] and the yonis. (20–24)
Having meditated upon its seed-syllables as bearing excellent fruit, one shall attain the perfection of speech;
above the letter *ra* is the lotus-seed (*kamalabīja*), which is the source of the wish-fulfilling tree of contemplation.
Having visualized everything pervaded by splendor, the Lord of Yoginīs [should place] the seed-syllable of Śītalā below that, according to the sequence of the left side.

Having meditated upon this, the one who possesses great bliss becomes immersed in the essence of supreme bliss; below that is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), which grants the accomplishment of the fruits of all desires.
He who recites this becomes supremely blissful and possesses eternal knowledge through the vital breath (vāyu).
In front of that, in the northwestern corner (vedakoṇa), is the supreme seed-syllable of Varuṇa.
Having meditated upon this and become a practitioner, he lives as one who possesses long life.
Above that, in the fifth corner, is the vajra-seed-syllable *va*.
It directly bestows the eight siddhis upon those who worship it and grants swift accomplishment;
and above that hexagon is the seed-syllable of Surabhi, which yields great fruit.
Success is firmly established for that practitioner who meditates [on this] in his heart.
Now hear the procedure for the garland of letters at the upper region of the eight-cornered [mandala]. (20–31)
By the mere cultivation of which the Omniscient Lord of the World [is attained], he who constantly and incessantly worships *o*, *au*, and the labial class (*pavarga*) in this manner— || 20.32 ||
Its accomplishment occurs in an instant through the meditation on the form of Vāyu;
the seed-syllable of the Moon shines above, radiant with full splendor. (20.33)
The syllable *ḷ*, the letter *e*, the dental class (*tavarga*), and its southern arrangement—the wind-power (*vāyuśakti*) consisting of light bestows all auspiciousness. (20.34)
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the *ṭa*-group conjoined with the vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and *ḷ*;
it constantly bestows the eight sovereign powers and grants the accomplishment of the Lotus Throne.
He who meditates upon that which is below it shall become a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa).
One should visualize the abode beneath the form of the seed-syllable of Bhavānī. (20-36)
By meditating upon the pair *i* and *ī* together with the *ca*-group, one becomes an immortal.
O Lord, when combined with *a*, *ā*, and *i*, it brings victory over the *ka*-group. (20.37)
One who meditates with supreme devotion shall obtain their desired fruit.
Thus, O Lord, has this essential *phalacakra* been described. (20-38)
Through the meditations on this wheel, one becomes a lord of great vidyās, by means of diligent effort at the great seat of Kāmarūpa and the seat of the Liṅga. (20.39)
By meditating upon the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*) as the fourfold wheel, one becomes immortal;
the great yogi Hiraṇyākṣa [attained this] through the power of meditation for a single month. (20.40)
Having become the lord of the seven continents, he finally became Viṣṇu;
that yogi shall possess a steady mind—this is the certain conclusion of the meaning of the Tantra. (20.41)
Having meditated upon these essences of the wheels (cakras) situated within the wheel of command (ājñācakra), one will certainly attain self-perfection through supreme joys. (20.42)
By means of the purification of the subtle breath, one shall become long-lived in this world.
Thus, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*,
in the *Bhāvapraśnārthanirṇaya*, in the *Pāśavakalpa*, in the *Phalacakrasārasaṅketa*, in the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*, in the *Caturvedollāsa*.
In the Dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, the twentieth chapter. || 20 ||
Now the twenty-first chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
"Speak, O beloved, that secret to me by which a man may become a perfected one (siddha)."
That specific manner is especially difficult to obtain even for the gods.
The majesty of the heroic state bestows accomplishment spontaneously, O beautiful one, if there is the compassionate gaze and bliss. (21.2)
Ānandabhairavī said: O Knower of the essence of supreme bliss, protector of the field of yoga,
O Lord who knows Mahākāla and the inner state of being, hear my secret.
Who would resort to the state of a hero (vīrabhāva) according to the path of yoga—that mass of overflowing bliss which is the definitive realization of the meaning of the Śakti-veda? (21.4)
The Great Yoga is dependent on the Vedas, and Kuṇḍalī is dependent on Yoga;
the mind is dependent on Kuṇḍalī, and all that is moving and unmoving is dependent on the mind.
By the mere accomplishment of the mind, the accomplishment of power (śakti) will certainly come to pass;
if power is brought under control, then the three worlds are likewise under control.
O Kuleśvara, he shall indeed become immortal; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Through the application of a thousand verses, there is the definitive determination of the purpose of the Vīrayoga.
In the eleventh chapter, through the yoga of security, there is the Yoga-maṇḍala;
the Vidyā that awakens the six cakras, which is the thousand-petaled lotus. (21.8)
O great hero, I shall describe the subtle path known as Kailāsa for the sake of the yogis' knowledge of Brahman; listen to it step by step. (21.9)
Whatever brings about success directly for heroes, for the most excellent, for those who have fallen, and for those sent forth—that I shall declare all to you. 21.10
He who desires the fruit of perfection according to the very sequence of the Yogaśāstra becomes perfected quickly on the path of Brahman; of this there is no doubt. (21.11)

He who performs recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth by means of the true nature of the knowledge of Brahman for the sake of attaining the fruit, is a knower of Brahman and is pure. (21.12)
He whose mind is intent on the practice and who finds joy in piercing the six cakras will certainly attain accomplishment, whether in the world or in the forest. (21.13)
He who worships the feet of Ambikā even without knowing the meaning of the six cakras finds his sins destroyed and becomes a possessor of siddhis for seven births. (21.14)

"He who, having understood the differentiation of the six cakras, performs the practice incessantly, shall attain perfection within a year; such is the determination of the meaning of the Tantra. (21.15)
By practicing this for three months, one attains perspiration;
after eight months, there is the destruction of [karmic] impressions; and after a year, the power of moving through the sky (khecarī-gati) is attained. (21.16)

The emission of perspiration is declared the lowest; visualization is remembered as the middling; O Lord, the levitation of the body and the state of moving through the sky constitute great bliss. (21.17)
Having established the thirty-two knots and the region extending as far as the *mūlādhāra*, which rests upon the spinal column (*merudaṇḍa*), one becomes identical with Brahman. (21.18)
O Lord, by piercing each successive knot-stage along the Suṣumnā at its external location, one certainly becomes a Khecarī in due order.
Having set his mind upon trivial matters and being devoid of meditative concentration and gnosis, he would surely become insane; yet he becomes a king among yogins of the scriptures. (21.20)
Having meditated upon the root [of the deity] as a young girl, intensely radiant, white as snow, jasmine, and the moon, and bringing joy through the fruit of the Kali age, one shall become a master.
Having meditated upon the root lotus with four beautiful petals as the Great Wisdom, the king of yogis obtains the fruit of giving ten million tawny cows. (21–22)
One should worship the fruit upon the root-lotus, which is joined with ten million digits of the moon, slightly red, and whose lotus-face exudes the fragrance of flowing nectar.
Having visualized on his left side the one who is stainless, possessing the fierce splendor of ten million heroes, and having the form of Brahmā, together with Kuṇḍalinī, one shall become cool.
Then the king of yogis worships the Lord Śrīyāmala-vīra, who has that same form, who arises from him, and who was born from the fire on the forehead of the Goddess.
There, on the eastern petal of the lotus, the king of yogis worships the syllable *Va*, which has a body as red as vermilion and is adorned by ten million flickering flashes of light.
Beside that, on the petal of blood, is the beautiful wheel of command (ājñācakra);
