just as there is meditation on Kuṇḍalinī in the wheel of command, so it is here as well. (21–27)
O Lord Śaṅkara, listen to the sequence of the earth-circles for yogis; by meditating upon which one attains perfection, and the six abodes become bestowers of success. (21–28)

One should meditate upon the house of the Yoginīs, which consists of six houses, the abode of the three times, situated in one place, and possessing great splendor; within the central house, there is the seed-syllable *ra*.
In the southern house, one should visualize the syllable *va*, as well as Hemamālina and Añjana;
one should contemplate the supreme seed-syllable of the Ḍākinīs and the seed-syllable of Brahmā.
And on the left side of the letter *va*, having meditated upon the great seed-syllable of Sadāśiva, which is the means of yoga for practitioners, one becomes a king among yogis. (21–31)

The seed-syllable *vaṃ*, presided over by Varuṇa and as pure as snow, the kunda flower, or the moon—this is the birthplace and abode of Viṣṇu; one should take refuge in that essence, which is fluid. (21.32)
And in the house situated above that, the Lord of Yogins visualizes the seed-syllable *laṃ*, worshipped by Indra, having the color of a flash of lightning and gold. (21.33)

One should properly meditate upon the seed-syllable of Indra on the right side, marked with the dot (bindu) as the seed-syllable of Śrī, having the form of a steady flash of lightning, belonging to Indrāṇī. (21–34)
And having visualized the Praṇava, which is served by Brahmā, on its left side as being like ten million suns,
one certainly becomes a king among yogis.
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable *vaṃ* in the lower chamber of Śrīvidyā as possessing the brilliance of the seed-syllable,
appearing with the radiance of ten million suns, one becomes all-pervading.
On the left side of one's own goddess, below in a golden palace,
one should meditate upon the Lord Vāgbhava, the seed-syllable of the illustrious Guru, as he sports.
Having meditated upon his own goddess on his right side— possessing the splendor of the long *praṇava* and having a form like the radiance of ten million suns— the yogi becomes a *yati*.

There, within the lotus, one should perform meditation upon one's own goddess through the yoga of mind, breath, and speech; as is the meditation, so should be the silence, performing the meditation upon the Lord of the World.
By means of the inhalation of Brahmā, indeed through the sequence of great yoga,
one should perform the recitation upon the earth-wheel, even with the emergence of the subtle breath.
The ground should be square and provided with nine floor-chambers;
having first divided it into eight chambers, the ascetic should perform worship in the chamber that is empty of the eight [directional deities].
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable of the Earth (la), which is the final letter [of the consonant series] and is worshipped by Śakra,
and having realized the principle of Kuṇḍalinī, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers.

There in that celestial realm (nāka), one should worship Indra, the king of the gods, who has four arms, whose vehicle is the white elephant, who is a mass of lightning, and who brings about the destruction of worldly existence.
In the temple of the Ḍākinī, the self-controlled practitioner should worship his beloved Brahmā, who moves upon a swan, who is like the newly risen sun, and who has four arms and four faces. (21.44)
Having visualized Brahmā, joined by a ḍākinī, like the sun drenched in vermilion and intoxicated with supreme fragrance, one becomes a king among yogins. (21.45)
The self-controlled practitioner should meditate upon the illustrious goddess Devaḍākinī, radiant like a flash of lightning, with blood-red eyes, seated upon a swan;
above the swan is the seed-syllable of the lotus, adorned with all ornaments. (21.46)
The great sages worship that which is the very nature of Mahālakṣmī.
To the left of the seed-syllable of Indra and Pṛthivī is the Praṇava, served by Brahmā;
that which bestows the perfection of prāṇāyāma is what the great seers worship.

Having visualized below that, at the abode of the vital breath (prāṇa), the seed-syllable of the Pretas (PRET) with the luster of the moon, one becomes equal to Śiva; Sadāśiva resides in the wheel of the earth (bhūmicakra). || 21-49 ||
Below that, one should meditate upon the Vāgbhava syllable, possessing the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes;
this seed-syllable of the Guru in the Earth-circle (bhūmicakra) becomes the Guru of the Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā).
And having meditated through mental visualization upon the stainless state of Śrīvidyā in the central house on the right, the practitioner becomes a perfected one (siddha). || 21-51 ||
To the south of that, in the remaining house, there should be the supreme mantra ending with the syllable Om (praṇava),
which is the support of all and consists of the words "Brahmā-Viṣṇu-Śiva-Durgā."
All this, for the sake of the Śrībhūmicakra, is the cause of consciousness;
it remains pervading the letter *va* on the eastern petal of the Mūlādhāra.
If one meditates upon that which resides in the letter *va* within the circle of the earth-mandala,
one becomes the lord of the entire cosmic egg, pervading the universe as a single-petaled lotus.
The master of self-control should visualize a single-petaled lotus with blood of stainless luster;
in its center, within the earth-mandala, he should meditate upon the syllable *vaṃ*.
By the grace of this wheel, Varuṇa, the lord of wine, shall have a heart filled with the bliss of nectar and become endowed with all sovereign powers. (21.56)
In the second petal on the right, the lord of yogis, having fixed his mind upon the seed-syllable VĀṂ of great luster, should meditate for the sake of accomplishing the goal of yoga.
There, one should meditate upon the Wheel of Heaven, filled with the splendors of heaven;
having visualized it, one becomes a lord of heaven on earth, equal to the King of the Gods.
Having divided the pentagon, that which shines forth as another pentagon—within its center is a pair of circles; there, one should worship that which resides within the hexagon.
One should visualize this wheel called Svarga situated between two square enclosures (bhūpura), with its petals extending toward the south and north, and having expelled the Lord (Īśvara).
Situated within the hexagon is the letter Vāṃ, possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning;
depending upon that, all the gods abide in the ten corners.
In the eastern corner is Mahendra, seated together with all the gods;
having meditated upon him along with Indrāṇī, one certainly becomes a lord of yogins.
To the south of that, in the red corner, one should visualize the Fire-god accompanied by Svāhā,
flickering like ten million fires of universal destruction, and surrounded by his host of attendants.
To its south shines the Lord Kāmarūpin, endowed with Śakti;
having meditated upon him as accompanied by his retinue, one shall bring death itself under control.
Having visualized the Lord of Yoginīs as Nairṛta, having the form of lightning, the beloved subduer of Kandarpa, endowed with power, and the bliss of the vowels; || 21-65 ||
Having meditated upon Varuṇa below that, who is cherished by his excellent Śakti and is the lord of waters, one becomes a being of constant sattva and the glory of eternal sattva. (21.66)
To its left is the corner of the Maruts, which illuminates the host of Maruts;
the wise one should know that this is the station of Vāyu, the place of dissolution, pervaded by Vāyu. (21.67)
Thereafter, having visualized Gaṇanātha as intoxicated, endowed with Śakti, and bringing joy to his retinue of attendants, one becomes the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśvara).
Thereafter, having meditated upon the Lord, the supreme abode, endowed with Śakti and accompanied by his retinue, the ascetic becomes one who can assume any form at will.
Thereafter, in the corner house, the ascetic should meditate upon Brahmā, who possesses the splendor of the moon, the sun, and fire, who is of a single form, and who is situated above.
Having meditated upon Ananta, who resides in the north-eastern corner of the house and has the form of fire, one becomes like Ananta himself. (21.71)
Within the center of this own wheel, one should visualize a pair of circles of great luster, always pervaded by fire and blazing with flames. (21.72)
And within the circle, there is a hexagon; in each corner of that hexagon, it brings about the destruction of enemies.
It removes the sixfold group beginning with greed and delusion situated within the hexagon. (21.73)
Indrāgnī removes greed, Daṇḍadhṛk removes delusion, Nairṛta and Varuṇa remove desire, and Vāyu removes anger for the yogins. (21.74)
The Lord Brahmā and Ananta indeed remove pride from yogis;
by practicing [this] for three months, they certainly destroy envy.
For the sake of attaining yoga-siddhi, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable VĀṂ, radiant as the moon, adorned with golden ornaments, situated in the center of a hexagon.
The wise one, perceiving that [the body] is always pervaded, protected, and adorned by Kuṇḍalinī—just as a mass of light is sustained by oil—becomes a king among yogis. (21.77)
Having visualized the self-manifested liṅga right there as the lunar disc,
the mantra-master, possessing self-control, should cause it to be immersed along with Kuṇḍalī.
In this manner, through the contraction of Kuṇḍalinī, one shall gradually attain perfection;
then the great yogi, being constantly practiced, should stabilize the vital air.
By means of that which is joined with the appearance of Vāyu and supported by this wheel,
even one who is mute shall become a lord of speech and partake of its fruits day by day.
The greatness of the third petal is supreme, bringing about the arising of the knowledge of yogis;
for one who practices self-contemplation, there shall be the attainment of the state of being. (21.81)
Within it are the scales, the circle, the four corners, and the houses;
there are thirty-two forms of knots for the purpose of piercing those knots.

By means of the channels of the balance-wheel (*tulācakra*), one should effect the piercing of the thirty-two knots; one should practice meditation upon the central Meru as far as the region of the throat. (21.83)
In the center of the house of thirty-two knots, there is an auspicious triple circle;
in its center, within a triangle, the self-controlled one should worship the void of the *mūrdhanya* [cerebral] letter.
The results of the various clusters of phonemes are to be visualized within this house;
by visualizing them through the application of a clockwise rotation, one becomes a master of speech.
He who employs the letter *a* in the first house, the *anusvāra* in the second,
and the *visarga* in the third shall become a master of his senses.
One should contemplate this [mantra] from *ka* to *ha* in other temples, excluding the letters from *va* to *sa*, together with the bindu; thus one becomes a master. (21.87)
Just as the practitioner obtains the fruit according to the name in the *ājñācakra*,
that same fruit indeed resides in the root lotus of the letters within the House of Libra (*tulāgṛha*).
One should resort to the middle of the letter *sa*, situated within a triangle of three circles;
one should take refuge in that which is enriched by thousands of garlands of flames and adorned with gold.
Enveloped by each individual syllable upon the wheel of the scales,
the king of yogis, observing silence, performs silent recitation while pervading the letter *ṣa*.
By the grace of this yoga, Kuṇḍalinī becomes conscious;
he attains mastery over speech, which destroys the threefold suffering.
O Śaṅkara, the accomplishment of the mantra is attained through the mere recitation of its syllables;
having visualized the location within the wheel of the scales, one becomes a possessor of mantra-siddhi.
O Lord, without this wheel, Kuṇḍalinī is not perfected;
and without the knowledge of reality, how can one become a yogi in Bhārata? (21.93)
Now listen to another [account of] the greatness of the *ala*, which I shall explain according to the truth:
it is the essence of the movement of yoga, the means for accomplishing the power of Kuṇḍalinī. (21.94)

The ascetic should meditate upon the seed-syllable of Śakti, joined with the nasal drop (bindu), stainless and situated within an octagon, resembling a mass of lightning and encircled by a garland of gold. (21.95)
Having divided the four-cornered [mandala], which is also beautiful and four-cornered,
one should then meditate upon a four-cornered [space] in its center containing the seed-syllable.

Having meditated upon the Goddess, the mother of the god Kuṇḍalin, who is equal to ten million suns and extends up to the big toe of her foot, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers. || 21-97 ||
If humans perform meditation in the center of the wheel of water, they become immortals established in the yoga of the essence-beings (sattva), enjoying the fruits of the six wheels. || 21-98 ||
Having gathered that quartet, which is pervaded by water and perfectly pure,
the one of great strength should meditate upon it as situated in a counter-clockwise rotation and divided into seven sections.
Above the seven-fold enclosure, one should meditate upon a sixteen-petaled lotus;
at each petal is a great sacred site (mahātīrtha), and one certainly becomes a perfected being (siddha).
O Lord, the sixteen-petaled lotus, encircled by a garland of sacred fords (tīrthas),
shines within that single petal like a flash of lightning.

May he protect [the practitioner] from the east and the south; now hear the fruit of the garland of holy fords (tīrthamālā), by the mere sight of which the practitioner becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 21.102 ||
The Gaṅgā, the goddess Godāvarī, Gayā, Guhyā, and Mahāphalā;
the Yamunā, which bestows ten million-fold fruit, and the Sarasvatī, the giver of intelligence. (21.103)
Maṇidvīpa, Śvetagaṅgā, Mahāpuṇyā, and Mahāphalā; Śvetagaṅgā is of great merit and Bhargagaṅgā yields great fruit.
The Svargagaṅgā is a great sacred field, and Puṣkara is the ultimate among holy fords;
the Kāverī and the Sindhu are meritorious, and the Narmadā always bestows auspiciousness.
In the eight-cornered [mandala], the ascetic should visualize the Eight Siddhis, filled with water and yielding fruit;
in the seven-cornered [mandala], he should visualize the Seven Oceans, starting from the east.
Salt, sugarcane juice, wine, spirituous liquor, curd, milk, water, and the end-maker (fire) remain pervading the letter *sa*; the ascetic should meditate upon the Great Being.
Having visualized the Śakti in the center of the fourfold [mandala], with a body like ten million flashes of lightning,
one becomes a master of ten million vidyās within the water-circle.
The seed-syllable of Śakti is on the left side; she is the primordial Prakṛti, the beautiful one.
That Yoginī, the refuge of the virtuous, shines forth for the destruction of desire. (21.109)
The seed-syllable of Śakti is on the right, while Puṅkalā consists of the nature of Puṃ and Śiva;
he who constantly worships that which shines with the form of Bhāvanā for the sake of attaining mastery over the Lord [shall succeed]. (21.110)
Above the seed-syllable of Śakti is the enchanting full moon;
all practitioners worship it for the sake of attaining dharma, kāma, and artha. (21.111)

Having meditated upon the glorious Sun, born from the fire of time, within the house at the base of the seed-syllable of Śakti—resembling ten million meteors—one shall obtain more than one's desires. (21.112)
By the grace of the water-wheel (vāricakra), a man shall become long-lived;
on the earth, it is in the form of Mahākāla within the four-petaled root-support (mūlādhāra).

Having visualized the water-wheel (*vāricakra*)—consisting of the remaining four petals and ending with the letter *ṣa*—shining with the brilliance of ten million lightning bolts, one becomes a king among yogins. (21.114)

Thus, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra* (Supplementary Tantra), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* (Illumination of the Great Tantra), in the *Bhāvārthanirṇaya* (Ascertainment of the Essential Meaning),

in the *Pāśavakalpa* (Rite for the Bound), in the *Mūlapadmollāsa* (Radiance of the Root Lotus), in the *Sārasaṅketa* (Essential Convention) concerning the *Bhūmicakra* (Earth Circle), *Svargacakra* (Heavenly Circle), *Tulācakra* (Balance Circle), and *Vāricakra* (Water Circle), in the section on *Siddhamantra* (Accomplished Mantras), within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
The twenty-first chapter. || 21 ||
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O Śambhu, I shall proclaim the arising of the fruits of the six chakras."
Knowing which, all yogis remain for a long time upon the surface of the earth. || 22-1 ||
The Mūlādhāra is a great lotus beautifully adorned with four petals;
its letters range from 'va' to 'sa', it is golden in color, and one should proceed to the state of Brahman through Śakti.
The practitioner of mantra should sequentially meditate upon the spheres of earth, water, fire, air, and space within the six lotuses for the sake of accomplishing the root vidyā. (22–3)

And in the region above the root lotus, the ascetic should meditate upon the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), which is of great luster, possesses six petals, and contains Rākiṇī and Viṣṇu within its pericarp. 22-4.
Having meditated upon the six-petaled lotus with the phonemes from *ba* to *la*, the ascetic, the lord of the gods,
should worship at the base of the *liṅga* pervaded by the Kanda-rpa wind.

Above that, at the root of the navel, one should worship the ten-petaled lotus of the yoga-dharma, which possesses a radiance equal to ten million jewels and represents the meaning of the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*.
One should meditate upon Rudra together with Lākinī for the sake of attaining yoga and other perfections;
having beheld the state of supreme liberation, one will certainly become liberated while living. (22.7)
One should worship the Lord Kākinī, who resembles the bandhūka flower, is adorned with twelve petals,
and is accompanied by the letters from Ka to Tha.
Above that, having meditated upon Sadāśiva himself and the Great Goddess Sākinī in the state of the sixteenth unfolding (ullāsa) at the throat, one becomes Śiva. (22.9)
The king of yogis worships that which is called Viśuddha, which possesses great merit and bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; it is the source of smoky smoke and a mass of lightning.
One should worship the white lotus of Ājñā, the abode of snow, jasmine, and the moon;
it is the station of the swan, the place of the *bindu*, having two petals, located between the eyebrows. (22.11)

One should worship that which is enriched by two hundred thousand syllables, joined with the Bindu, wherein the mind dissolves; it is known as the nature of both female and male, and is as radiant as ten million moons. (12)
And at the throat, which has sixteen petals, one should visualize it encircled by the sixteen vowels from *a* to *visarga*, and then lead Kuṇḍalinī there.
Having brought the Kuṇḍalinī from the base of the throat to the Ājñā-cakra, where she meets with ten million moons, one becomes liberated while living in this very world. (22.14)
O Lord, if the yogi does not release the breath into the external moon,
he becomes liberated here by releasing it into the mass of moons between the eyebrows.
One should repeatedly exhale the breath by means of the subtle upward movement of the wind alone;
having brought it from the thousand-petalled lotus to the root, one should likewise lead it back from the root to that very same place.
The moon dissolves into the sun, and the sun into the moon, O Lord;
for one who does not bring sound from the outside [within], there arises a mass of bindus.
As long as the mind goes toward the external moon submerged in the sun,
and when both the moon and the sun have entered within, no evil remains in his body.
For one who brings the mind alone under control while it abides in the subtle breath and is cherished by the power of the wind, there is an increase in yoga and other such attainments.
When the sacred thread has been obtained, that best of Brahmins who is devoted to Śrīdhara and constantly practices yoga shall become beloved by the Yogins.
To whatever extent the *bindu* remains in its state of childhood, to that same extent one will progress on the path of yoga; [but] through the falling of the *bindu*, one will die. (22.21)
Nevertheless, if for a month, or a fortnight, or even ten days,
the supreme drop remains steady through practice, one becomes a victor in person.
When a person is afflicted by the great torment of the fire of desire, who is capable of extinguishing that desire and the rest without yoga? (22–23)
Desire certainly arises from the concealment of close association;
from that desire, anger is born, which destroys the multitude of great enemies. (22–24)
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory, the destruction of the intellect; and from the destruction of the intellect, total ruin. (22–25)

Therefore, having established perfect awareness within the Brahma-maṇḍala at the root and other centers, and having meditated upon the lotus feet of the venerable Lord (Śrīnātha), the practitioner becomes a perfected one (siddha). || 22–26 ||
At the outset, peace shall arise in the heart as the mark of the Lord’s grace;
from peace, knowledge is born, and through knowledge, one attains liberation. (22–27)
Peace, knowledge, establishment, and cessation—these are remembered as such;
therefore, the Supreme Lord is called the God of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha). || 22–28 ||
Agitated by the thought, "This is knowledge, this is the object of knowledge," they study the scriptures day and night, while remaining averse to the supreme reality.
The head bears flowers; the nose perceives fragrance;
they recite my tantras, which are difficult to find and reveal the true nature of reality. (22-30)
At the time of the sacred thread ceremony (yajñopavīta), however, one should take recourse in the state of a bound soul (paśubhāva);
as long as yoga has not been attained, one should not follow the conduct of a hero (vīrācāra).
Conduct, discipline, knowledge, stability, and the practice of yoga—success in these arises only for one whose mind is fixed upon the desired lotus feet of Him. (22-32)
He whose great devotion toward the Lord and the Guru increases constantly will undoubtedly attain perfection within a year; of this there is no doubt.
Having diligently examined the essence of the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas,
one should fix the mind upon the circle of the lotus feet of the beloved Lord.
He who, remaining silent, fixes his mind upon the lotus-field of the heart—the six chakras purified by yoga—shall become a beloved of Yoga. (22.35)
The mind performs actions; the mind is stained by sin.
By becoming the restrainer of the mind, one is not stained by sins or merits.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Speak, O beloved, that secret to me by which a man may become a perfected one (siddha)—
that method specifically which is beyond the reach even of yogis."
Whatever one might conceal, one should gaze upon with joy;
one should worship it, contemplate it, avoid rejecting it, and never feel disgust for it.
Speak the truth in due order, if you have affection for me;
for even without knowing the true nature of beings, a yogi would become subject to delusion. (22.39)
Ānandabhairavī said:
"In the three worlds you are fit for yoga, devoted to the piercing of the six chakras;
you alone, O Supreme Bliss, are stainless through the great empowerment."
O Great Hero, one should crush these greatly fearsome faults known as desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy. (22.41)
The Great Hero should suppress the transformation arising from the senses—sleep, shame, and dejection—as well as the ten fires of time, O Lord. (22.42)
The great hero should conceal the great mantra, the family rites, the meaning of the mudrās, the rosary, and the tantra, as well as the assembly of heroes with women who must be kept secret. (22.43)

One should conceal the transgressive conduct (*atyācāra*), the practice (*sādhana*) of the Bhairavas and Yoginīs, and the measurement of the weaving of the channels (*nāḍīgrathana*), just like one conceals the offspring of one's mother. (22.44)
One should not revile the deity, the guru, the Lord, the liquor, the vidyā, the great field (mahākṣetra), the sacred seat (pīṭha), or one who is authorized for yoga. (22.45)

A yoginī should not revile one who is dull-witted, insane, or one who performs rituals according to their birth, karma, or lineage, nor one who practices dharma through application, as long as that person’s life-force remains established. (22.46)
A great hero should not revile his wife, his brother’s wife, a Buddhist practitioner, a Yoginī, or any action, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
One should never look upon the vulva of a maiden during the day, nor upon a woman engaged in sexual play with an animal, nor one who is naked, nor one who is lustful with her breasts exposed.
One who is vigilant should not look upon a corpse, the stakes used for gambling, a eunuch, excrement and the like, or the ritual implements of one performing malevolent magic (abhicāra). || 22-49 ||
One should worship with supreme devotion the deity, the Guru, the Lord, Śakti, the virtuous one, and the Self in its gross and subtle forms, with diligent effort. (22-50)
One should worship the guest, the mother, the perfected one (siddha), the father, and likewise the yogin with supreme devotion for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of the mantra. (22.51)
One should cultivate with a one-pointed mind the well-spoken means of yoga, as well as the oral instructions of the guru, one's own duty, and the deity of the sacred site. (22.52)
One should meditate upon the family tradition, the hero-mantra, oneself as the Supreme Preceptor (Parameṣṭhin),
the ritual knowledge, and the determination of the goals established by the Tantra.
The best of practitioners should avoid approaching those who are forbidden, as well as association with rogues, deceivers, idle chatter, falsehood, and inauspiciousness. (22.54)
One should avoid sinful conversation, laziness, excessive talk,
wandering about without performing Vedic rites, and the Gosava sacrifice for a Brāhmaṇa.
O Lord, one should never feel disgust toward feces, urine, moisture, blood, a person with missing limbs, flesh, or the carrying of skulls and so forth. (22.56)
One who desires success in this world should not despise liquor, the protection of cattle, one's own sins, or fear of an enemy, nor should one reject the true dharma. (22.57)
This indeed is the conduct of the observance (samayācāra) for yogins who possess heroic realization;
he who performs it by the command of the Guru shall become liberated while living on this earth. (22.58)
Vain is the dharma, vain the conduct, vain the initiation, and vain the austerity;
for men, the transgression of the guru’s command is called vain merit. (22.59)
O Lord, for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others, the practice of yoga and other means comes first; thereafter follows the family rites for the sake of attaining success in yoga and vidyā.
Without the state of being (bhāva) of the Hero (vīra), how can one become a perfected yogin?
First, one should cultivate the state of the bound soul (paśu), and afterwards, the investigation of the Kula.
O Mahādeva, in my tantra, I have set forth the determination of the sole essence for the sake of the sudden attainment of devotion, as well as the family practice (kulācāra) of the yogins. (22-62)
The family tradition of the Brahmins exists solely for the attainment of knowledge;
through knowledge one becomes a yogi, and through yoga one attains an immortal body.
Having become a yogi of noble lineage, one should daily practice yoga and meditate upon the six chakras, the abode of the elements, for the sake of attaining spiritual realization.
In the upper region of the root-lotus, at the base of the *liṅga*, is Mahāśuci;
in the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is the great lotus, which one should worship on its petals with the wind.
Indeed, for one who performs the meditation on the colors of these six petals, O Lord, Viṣṇu himself, together with Rākiṇī, will manifest before him. (22.66)
Having meditated upon an eight-petaled lotus in the central mandala of the six-petaled Svādhiṣṭhāna, that Lord is joined with the Nāgas. (22.67)
One should meditate on the eight serpents appearing like the dawn upon the lotus above the water, situated within the eight petals, as well as the beloved of those serpents.
One should worship Ananta, Vāsuki, Padma, Mahāpadma, Takṣaka, Kulīra, Karkaṭa, and Śaṅkha on the petals beginning with the south.
Upon the eight-petaled lotus, one should meditate on two circles surrounding the pericarp;
above that is a six-petaled lotus, endowed with the consonants from *va* to *la*, each accompanied by the nasal bindu.
By means of the sequence starting from the east and with a clockwise-turning wind,
having repeatedly performed the breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should meditate upon the wind of the six syllables.
One should joyfully meditate upon the pair of filaments in the form of the Kula above;
having visualized them on the eight-petaled and six-petaled lotuses, one becomes a king among yogis.
Above the eight-petaled lotus, one should meditate on a pair of beautiful circles;
above that, again, upon a six-petaled lotus, one should meditate on the letters from *va* to *la*.
One should meditate upon two beautiful circles beneath the eight petals;
beneath the circles, it remains pervading the *vaṃ* seed-syllable, which has the shape of a maṇḍala.

Having meditated upon that seed-syllable, which is circular, firmly established, completely pervasive, and has the appearance of lightning, shining with a brilliance equal to ten million suns— the Lord of Yogins [perceives it].
Below the portions of the seed-syllables of the vowels (ya-anta), one should visualize a hexagonal mandala;
within that hexagon, starting from the south, one should contemplate the letters beginning with ya and ending with la.
In the center of that hexagon is a smoky-colored hexagonal mandala;
in its corners, beginning from the south, one should place the six substances and so forth.
One should contemplate substance, quality, action, generality along with particularity, and inherence, in sequence, within the six corners.

Following the sequence starting from the east, the mantra-practitioner should repeatedly perform the breath-retention (kumbhaka) while visualizing [the wind] moving in a clockwise direction with the southern-turning breeze everywhere.
In the center of the six-cornered [diagram] of the substance, one should meditate upon a six-cornered figure of beautiful luster;
and in each corner, one should contemplate the six groups (ṣaḍvarga), both stable and moving.
And in the center of that, within the triangle, the yogi of vast intellect should meditate upon Hari together with Rākiṇī, abiding amidst the rays of ten million moons.
The lotus situated within the six petals is the means of accomplishment even for yogis;
for one who constantly practices it, yoga becomes perfected. (22.82)
By the grace of this wheel, one becomes free from disease and devoid of ego;
through the contemplation of the feet of Śrīnātha, one quickly becomes omniscient. (22.83)
One should meditate upon Hari within the six cakras as the form of light, the path of yoga, exceedingly subtle and stainless, which accomplishes all desires in the three worlds. (22.84)
He who is Hari, Śeṣa, and Śambhu; he who is Śambhu, the bearer of a subtle form;
and Brahmā, who abides in that subtle form—this entire world is dependent upon Brahmā.
The three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha—are one in essence; united within my body, they create, preserve, and destroy.
These [impurities], arising from the breath, are always obstacles to yoga;
by forcefully suppressing them through breath control (prāṇāyāma), one shall attain perfection.
One should take refuge in the syllable *a*, the color of Brahmā, whose form is sound and possesses great luster,
which is eternally contained within the *praṇava* and serves as the filling of yoga.
One should take refuge in the syllable *ukāra*, the Vaiṣṇava letter, the Lord who differentiates all sounds,
the essence situated within the *praṇava*, which is the *kumbhaka* of yoga.

One should take refuge in the letter *ma*, the form of Śambhu, which has become the seed-syllable, risen from the *vidhu* (the moon), situated at the end of the *praṇava*, the Time that is the locus of dissolution. (22.90)
The *praṇava* is conceived through the division of the three *varṇas*;
from the *praṇava*, the *haṃsa* is born; that *haṃsa* becomes "I am He" (*so'ham*), the Supreme. (22.91)
He who constantly contemplates this knowledge, the great knowledge difficult even for yogis to attain—he alone shall become supreme. (22.92)
I am the male in the form of breath, while she is the moon, which is Prakṛti;
one should know this Haṃsa as the piercer of the solar orb.
When that knowledge arises through the very reverse order,
at that moment one becomes a perfected being (siddha) who has gone to the sun, honored by the gods of his own nature.
Having elided the syllable *ha* and the syllable *sa*, one should thereafter perform the euphonic combination (*sandhi*); that which follows is the Great Mantra, the *praṇava*.
He who worships this great mantra of the Haṃsa, which is the form of the mind, within the abode of the mind at the Svādhiṣṭhāna, shall abide in the center of the sun.
One should know the *haṃsa* to be the sun; "I am he" (*so'ham*) is the moon, without a doubt.
When this becomes reversed, at that very moment one becomes a partaker of liberation.
If one visualizes the form of the swan-manas within the Svādhiṣṭhāna at the station of Hari, it is led to the feet of the venerable Guru; of this there is no doubt. (22.98)
Thus, when that wise one recites the Śaktikūṭa, having encased it within the form of the letter 'A', he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree. || 22-99 ||
Indeed, whoever performs all rites such as recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) by means of the Haṃsa,
at that very moment they become the Moon and the Sun through the grace of the Haṃsa mantra.
O Mahādeva, I perform this recitation within my body:
twenty-one thousand and six hundred repetitions of the *haṃ* mantra.
Having recited the letter *ha* in the form of a male and the letter *sa* in the form of a female,
one provides protection here by means of a hundred moon-drops (*candrabindu*).
The man who constantly recites the great mantra ending with the syllable *praṇava* shall attain mastery over the wind, and the Wind-god will show him great compassion. (22.103)
I shall proclaim the Bṛhadhaṃsa, by which a man becomes perfected; he can assume any form at will in an instant, and the perfection of speech is certain. (22.104)
First, having uttered the Praṇava, one should then write the word "haṃsa";
after that, the Praṇava is to be known, and thereafter one should contemplate the word "para. (22.105)
One should satisfy [the deity] at the end of the word and remember the Praṇava followed by "phaṭ";
for this is indeed the Haṃsa-mantra for the rising of heroes.
By the great grace of Haṃsa, one becomes a piercer of the six cakras;
and all the gods, including those of the moving and unmoving worlds, praise the six cakras. (22-107)
Yogins wander within the body for the sake of obstructing the perfection of yoga;
however, if they recite the *haṃsa* and the *bṛhaddhaṃsa* mantras for the sake of attaining mastery over the vital breath (*vāyu*), [they succeed]. (22.108)
Then everyone flees from him, just as humans flee from Rākṣasas. || 22-109 ||

Thus, in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the determination of the nature of *bhāva*, in the *Pāśavakalpa*, in the *Ṣaṭcakrasārasaṅketa*, in the determination of the rules for the instruction of yoga, and in the section on perfected mantras.
The twenty-second chapter in the Dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. || 22 ||
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
The venerable Bhairavī said: "Therefore, I shall now fully proclaim the unsurpassed path of Brahman."
Having known which [truth], all the gods, known as the Victors (Jayas), sang of the supreme.
O Lord, this description of the measures of food portions is not for the sake of the brilliance of fire, nor for the increase of the dharma of the great, but for the yoga of yogis. (23.2)
He who practices yoga but does not know its consumption here will certainly not become a yogi even in ten million thousand years. (23-3)

Therefore, I shall proclaim in brief the greatness of the consumption [of the sacramental substance], by knowing which one attains perfection through the piercing of one's own centers, beginning with the Svādhiṣṭhāna. (23.4)
O Supreme Lord, he who first becomes a man of discernment on this earth is alone fit to observe the rules regarding food, whether at home or in the forest. (23.5)
Flooded with the supreme bliss of firm bliss arising from the seat of the vital air (vāyvāsana),
one should always practice moderate eating for the sake of the joy of inhalation (pūraka).
Then the perfection of *pūraka* (inhalation) occurs through the determination of eating and so forth;
one should constantly fill the belly by repeatedly performing *kumbhaka* (retention). (23.7)
O Lord, one should fill it completely with [materials] measuring the span of one's own hand;
one should fill and establish that in the skull-bowl of Viśvāmitra.
One should rub it even upon a stone with twelve swallows of breath;
that vessel, being constantly filled, one should consume with a single cooking.
Day after day, he would cause the consumption of rice produced from the *śāli* variety, filling a skull-bowl with a *prastha* measure, through acts such as eating and other activities. (23.10)
By reciting [the mantra] twelve times with the breath of the *haṃsa*, one should bring about its complete dissolution;
upon the stone, one should increase that skull through the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth.
For as long as it remains determined to consume its own [body] until its destruction, for that long one should fill the belly with air, not with the beaks of crows. (23.12)
One should always contract the root [perineum] by holding the food [of breath];
there the yogi should fill [the body] by destroying the movement of the food [of breath]. 23-13.
In due course of time, one who has conquered the senses attains that perfection;
one should fill with ease that very place which is the locus of consumption.
Indeed, by consuming [it] again and again, one attains the perfection of consumption;
for without the yoga of inhalation (pūraka), even consumption does not succeed. (23.15)
Alternatively, there is another way to determine the abandonment of eating,
by which the deities residing in the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) do not fail to attain accomplishment.
Taking thirty-two mouthfuls as they naturally fit within three finger-joints,
one should always practice eating while leaving aside half a mouthful.
The great practitioner, free from fear, should always fill the breath;
having joined it to the place of consumption, he should drink the breath day and night. (23-18)
After sixty-four days have passed and everything has been brought to exhaustion, the wise man,
with a steady mind and conquered senses, should then subsist on milk alone.
I shall describe the measure of milk: three *prasthas* for each of the three hands.
One should gradually restrain the vital breaths like a lordly elephant in rut. (23–20)
Success arises within six months; this is the characteristic of practices such as *pūraka*.
For ascetics who can assume forms at will, the perfection of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-siddhi*) occurs in due course. (23.21)

Having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), the practitioner of mantra, gladdened by the joy of Vijayā, should hold the vital breath (māruta) in the root-support (mūlādhāra) while dissolving the mind therein.
Now, listen to the various types of postures for those who desire my siddhi;
without which, those practicing breath-retention (pūraka) shall not attain perfection on this earth.
I shall now describe the downward-facing Muṇḍāsana, which brings happiness to all living beings.
Placing the feet upon the upward path, the wise practitioner should restrain the vital breath (māruta).
For when one practices with the feet upward, that is indeed the best of all postures;
at that very moment, the element of air bestows great accomplishment.
One should assume this lotus posture (padmāsana) for the mastery of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu); then, having filled [the breath], one should repeatedly meditate upon that auspicious seat. (23–26)
Having placed the left foot at the root of the right thigh, and then placing that right foot upon the left thigh, this is known as the lotus posture (padmāsana). || 23–27 ||
One should arrange the seat by means of the yoga of the left foot;
at the time of that single seat, however, there shall be a second seat. (23–28)
Placing both hands on the back, the wise one should extend the two thumbs;
contracting the body and holding this posture, he should remain in the bound seat (baddhāsana).
Having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and repeatedly restraining the breath,
one should diligently place the chin upon the sun, which is the radiant light of bliss.
Thus, this posture is indeed the cause of success for all living beings; he who practices it for the sake of mastering the vital breath is a yogi—of this there is no doubt. (23–31)
The svastikāsana, which brings about the establishment of one's own nature for all, is formed by placing the sole of the right foot upon the left foot. (23-32)
By means of the yoga of right and left, there are indeed two postures;
having performed this method everywhere, one should extract the essence from the channels.
Listen now to these thirty postures;
by applying them with both the left and right sides, they shall become doubled here. (23–34)
I shall now describe here sixty-four postures for the practice of the vital winds (vāyu).
One should arrange them according to the thirty-two divisions of the drops (bindu) for the increase of the vital winds. (23–35)
Having assumed the bow posture (kārmukāsana), one should comfortably fill the abdomen;
then, in due time, the vital air comes under control through the subtle breath.
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), the practitioner of mantra should encircle and press with his right hand the edge near the left foot.
Twofold, with the right and left [nostrils] respectively, is the posture of the bow;
by means of the union of the two bows, one should draw in the wind like an arrow. (23–38)
I shall describe the cock-posture for the purpose of purifying the channels;
through the yoga of the tradition of my own lineage, one should practice the cultivation of the vital winds.
Having lowered both his hands to the ground, one who has conquered the senses binds his two elbows between his feet. (23.40)
Having bound a cock made by Brahmā with its two wings—the right and left—downward, he who performs the bird-posture (khagāsana) with its head facing down; 23-41.

By the grace of the bird posture (khagāsana), the exhaustion [of the senses] is quickly removed; through repeated practice of this very exhaustion, it brings about the removal of the exhaustion caused by sense objects. (23-42)
One should always practice the lolāsana by striking against the flickering vital air;
through the pacification of the steady breath, one will quickly become steady-minded. (23.43)
Having properly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with the two hands joined in the hollow of the junction between the feet at the middle region, one takes on the form of a cock.
Having placed both pairs of his own hands firmly upon his knees,
having raised his body and remained in the lotus posture (padmāsana), he [controlled] the vital breath (anila).
If the practitioner, having remained on this seat, turns his head downward, it should be known as the *uttamāṅga* posture, which is extremely difficult for yogins to attain. (23.46)
By this mere posture, the body becomes cool;
through repeated grace, the Kuṇḍalinī becomes conscious. (23-47)
Furthermore, by means of the practice of the right and left [nostrils], one who repeatedly fills the subtle breath in the root-lotus should perform the *vikumbhaka* [retention]. (23.48)
Having thus performed the kumbhaka, in which the subtle breath is dissolved according to the rule,
one should establish it in the state of dissolution at the end of the Brahma-randhra, beginning from the mūlādhāra.
Having established this auspicious posture, one should dissolve the mind into the subtle aperture;
just as a thread is drawn through the eye of a needle, one should fill it with the subtle vital air.
This is the characteristic of the *pūraka* [breathing technique] practiced sequentially for six months;
through the cultivation of the eight limbs of yoga, one attains great bliss (*mahāsukha*). (23.51)
Now, O Mahādeva, I shall describe the auspicious mountain-throne, by performing which one becomes established in a stable form through the dissolution of the six cakras and the rest. (23–52)

The Yoni-āsana is like a mountain; one should practice yoga until the vital breath (anila) reaches the fruit of yoga—that is, until it remains in the void (khecara) for as long as the fruit of that specific time persists. (23.53)
One who joins the tip of the *liṅga* to the wheel by means of the foot-position, having placed the other foot upon the thighs, [should perform] the *yonyāsana* there on the ground. (23.54)
In that regard, O Mahādeva, listen to the description of the bound-yoni posture (bandhayonyāsana) in its center;
by performing which, one becomes a sky-walker (khecara) and may move about like a lord.
O Lord, having formed the *yonyāsana* by binding the secret parts with the *liṅga*,
one should likewise [seal] the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears with the little fingers.

One should touch the lower lip with the two little fingers, the two nostrils with the two ring fingers, the pair of eyes with the two middle fingers, and the ears with the other [two] fingers, the index fingers. (23.57)
Having assumed the yoni-āsana, which is extremely difficult for yogins to attain, O Lord, he who fills the breath and, contracting the root, causes it to be restrained; 23-58.
By means of the practice of the left and right [nostrils], the practitioner becomes perfected;
having ascended gradually, he should fill the kumbhaka.
O Sadāśiva, from the time of dawn until the end of the *vasudaṇḍa*,
one should inhale the wind through the left and right nostrils by means of the *savyāpasavya* yoga.
In the second watch of the day, one should perform the delightful worship of Vāyu;
having assumed this posture, the practitioner becomes a Siddha. (23.61)
Now I shall describe another posture, by performing which that practitioner of mine becomes immortal;
being pure and illustrious, he should perform it having gone to a place free from impurity.
Having placed his own chest forward as the seat for the frogs,
he positioned his pair of feet upon his shoulders and his two arms over his feet.
Seated upon an āsana for the sake of bliss, one should meditate on the deluded state of the supreme reality (citpada);
if, having lifted all the limbs, one remains in the sky, that is the khecarī-āsana. (23.64)
The Mahābheka posture is proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments;
he who recites it here obtains the Great Knowledge and the Great Mantra. (23.65)
I shall describe this specific variety: he who performs it is an *āmara*.
Having bound one foot upon the thigh, the other foot is placed as a protector upon the shoulder. (23.66)
This is called Prāṇāsana, which bestows all accomplishments;
having placed the vital air at its root, one should meditate upon it, contract it, and then release it. (23.67)
Having carefully placed only one foot upon his shoulder,
O Lord, he should stand on one leg in the sky like a staff.

This indeed is the seat of the downward breath (apāna), which is the support for all inhalations; having performed it, one should cause [the breath] to ascend through the vital airs into the subtle lotus of the head. (23-69)
Then that mortal becomes perfected through the union of prāṇa and apāna;
having performed this by means of the yoga of the seat of apāna, he becomes a lord of yoga on earth.
I shall describe the equal posture (samānāsana), which is accomplished through the practice of mantras and other means:
having placed one foot upon the thigh, the other [foot] is placed upon the secret organ, the penis, and the face. (23.71)
"O Lord, this is called Vīrāsana, which is synonymous with Samānāsana;
having understood this, one should hold the breath within the four-petaled [lotus] and recite the mantra. (23.72)
One should contemplate the Kuṇḍalinī mantra, having the form of ten million streaks of lightning,
and the Yoginī who is eternally drenched by the nectar-essence of the moon of one's own self.
The heroic posture (vīrāsana) is the mastery of the vital winds through yoga;
he who knows this is a great hero and certainly becomes a yogi. (23.74)
Now I shall explain the practice of the equal seat (samānāsana) of Mahākāla;
by knowing it through its various stages, one becomes a lord among heroes. (23.75)
Having formed the *samānāsana* by grasping the thumb of the elder with one hand, he shall become authorized in the practice of the application of vowels and other techniques.
For he who knows the posture as well as the withdrawal of the vital winds (vāyu), and the determination of time and its other factors, shall never perish. (23.77)
Success is attained through time; he who is the form of time, most brilliantly radiant, should be meditated upon by practitioners and yogis in the posture of the Siddha-vīrāsana.
Now I shall describe the auspicious Nīlakaṇṭha-granthibheda posture;
by practicing the subtle breath after knowing this, one quickly becomes Rudra. (23.79)
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), the mantra-practitioner should place his hands upon his heart,
extending them up to the position of the elbows, while supporting the shoulders.
Having pierced the lotus-seat with five hundred [strokes], the mantra-practitioner performs the striking by which the head is brought low through meditation,
using all the fingers in the hermitage posture.
This is the posture for breaking the knot (granthibhedāsana), which demonstrates the Khecarī and other [mudrās];
having caused the dissolution of the subtle breaths into the Supreme Self, one should meditate upon it. (23.82)
Now I shall describe another posture for the sake of protecting the completion of yoga:
having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), the feet are placed upon the calves and big toes. (23.83)
Having placed one hand upon the shank and the bow (forearm) above the elbow while seated in the lotus posture, one should rotate the thumb.
This is indeed the bow posture (kārmukāsana) through the application of the left and right [nostrils];
having encircled the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should cause the tips of the big toes to move.
O Lord, he who always performs this supreme Kārmukāsana shall bring about the destruction of diseases and enemies, and thus become happy. (23.86)
Now, I shall describe here in brief the supreme posture of all the limbs (sarvāṅgāsana),
by performing which one becomes skilled in yoga, just as a scholar is through his various branches of learning.
Placing the head below and raising the two feet upward, one should assume the lotus posture (padmāsana) right there on the ground with the pair of elbows [resting upon it]. (23.88)
At every stage, the wise man, intent on the pacification of fatigue, should always act;
having abandoned all postures, he should never perform breath-retention (vāyudhāraṇa). (23.89)
Within one month, the movement of the subtle winds is perceived;
in three months, one attains the state of a deity; in three months, one becomes cool. (23.90)
Now, O Mahādeva, I shall describe the supreme Mayūrāsana:
having placed both hands on the ground with the body resting upon the elbows. (23.91)
Placing [the hands] above the elbows with a steady disposition throughout the entire body,
he remains perfectly still, having lowered only his pair of arms to the ground.
By this mere posture, the piercing of the channels occurs;
through inhalation (pūraka), one becomes firm and pervades all parts of the body.
Then, having assumed another posture that wards off all diseases,
the practitioner of yoga will quickly become successful through the grace of the Jñānāsana.
One should place the sole of the left foot at the root of the right thigh,
and join the sole of the right foot to the right side of the body, maintaining this posture.
O Lord, this is the seat of knowledge; through knowledge it illuminates wisdom.
For one who practices this continuously, their knot shall become loosened. (23.96)
Through the practice of the left and right [channels], it is known as the "seated posture of the shaven-headed" (muṇḍāsana);
having performed this, meditated, and become steady, one dissolves into the Supreme Self.
I shall describe the Garuḍa posture, by which meditation becomes firm on the ground;
one becomes liberated from all defects and possesses great strength in this world. (23.98)
Having bound one foot to the earth, standing like a staff on the other foot,
he remains with his consciousness intensely focused on the junction of the calf and the foot.
Having assumed this posture, and having worshipped the Lord of Yoga with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* upon the back [of the seat], one should always [worship] the Lord of All.
Now I shall describe another posture by which a man becomes perfected;
through the posture called Kokila, there occurs a spontaneous movement of the vital air.
Having raised both hands two cubits above him, the wise one should, O Lord, very gradually place the two thumbs at the tips of his feet. (23.102)
Having properly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) with the elbows resting [upon the knees],
I shall now describe, O Vīranātha, the seat that is the temple of bliss (ānandamandirāsana).
Having performed this, the practitioner here indeed becomes wise and immortal;
he should place both hands at the region of the feet and cause both feet to be placed [there].
By nature, the *kaula* posture stands like a staff upon the tips of the buttocks;
I shall now describe the *khañjana* posture, by performing which one becomes perfectly steady. (23.105)
Having bound both feet on the back, one should support the hands on the ground;
O Lord, having placed both hands on the ground, one should drink the wind.
By binding both feet upon the back, one becomes victorious through the Khañjana posture.
Now, I shall describe another posture for the benefit of practitioners. (23.107)
By means of the wind-posture (pavanāsana), the wise yogi becomes a sky-walker (khecarī).
Remaining firm in the bound posture (baddhāsana), he places both hands below the navel.
With the head shaven above, one should drink the wind and restrain it during the turbulence of *yama*.
Now I shall describe the "serpent posture" (*sarpāsana*) solely for the purpose of drinking the wind. (23.109)
The body should remain like a staff, with the feet bound by a rope;
the goddess Kuṇḍalī, who is of the nature of air, is in the form of a coil within the finger [of the nose].
Adorned with ornaments and the like, I shall describe [the deity] seated upon a serpent-throne;
having abandoned sleep, laziness, and fear, one should perform this again and again at night. (23.111)
Having brought all obstacles, such as sleep and the like, under control through the practice of breath-control (vāyusādhana),
I shall now describe the unsurpassed shoulder-seat in the form of a crow (kākarūpaskandhāsana).
One shall be liberated from the sins of the Kali age and bring the wind under control;
the practitioner, having bound his own two feet upon the region of his shoulder. (23.113)
This pair of words is eternal and provides nourishment for both worlds upon the earth.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the section on perfected mantras, in the *Ṣaṭcakrasārasaṅketa*, under the *Pāśavakalpa* concerning the determination of the seat of existence (*bhāvāsana*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, the latter part of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*. Chapter 23.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Mahādeva, I shall now declare the definitive exposition of the meaning of the Yogaśāstra."
By which mere consciousness the knots of the six chakras are pierced. || 24-1 ||

On a day exceeding the lunar joint (parvan), one should perform the practice of the auspicious Yoga, which is the essence of the Kālikā-kula, endowed with its aesthetic phases (kalā) and time (kāla). 24-2.
The seat is knowledge according to the prescribed rule, endowed with millions upon millions of ritual acts;
there are hundreds of lakhs and thousands of seats upon the surface of the earth.

One should always maintain the *sadasana* (the seat of the assembly) in heaven, in the netherworld (*pātāla*), and on earth, as united by the great seers (*maharṣi*) through the very sequence of difference and non-difference.
And having performed those various types [of practices] by which one becomes immortal—they say an immortal is a *siddha*, endowed with the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*). (24.5)
That very meaning appears to one who knows the meaning of the root mantra;
those immortals praise it continuously throughout all worlds. (24.6)
The gods, beloved by Śrī and Kāminī, prevail throughout the three worlds;
and that devotee who is appointed to bring time itself under his control [is likewise empowered]. (24.7)
All of them roam here for hundreds of millions of years;
hear now their respective names of seats and their means of accomplishment (sādhanas).
By means of that very consciousness alone, one becomes directly devoted to the Lord;
then, O Nātha, having assumed the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana), one should fill [the body] with air. (24.9)

One shall quickly become capable of assuming any form at will and destroying the impurities of the Kali age, by placing one's own head upon the tip of the *liṅga* while maintaining a balanced posture. (24.10)
With both hands placed on the buttocks and the body contracted, one should fall to the ground;
I shall now describe the Kumbhīrāsana for the retention of the vital winds (vāyus).
One should remain on the ground in the shape of a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), with both hands placed above the head,
having set one foot upon the other, and both hands above the head.
One should remain on the ground in the shape of a bowl; that indeed is the Kumbhīrāsana.
Now, for Matsyāsana: with the fingers of one hand placed upon the back of the other hand. (24-13)
One should join the two feet at the measure of the big toe of the elder;
I shall describe the makarāsana, and one should perform kumbhaka for the inhalation of air.
Having placed both feet on the back and securing the back with both hands, O Lord, this is the Siṃhāsana; the knees are positioned above the elbows. (24.15)
Having established [the body] and facing upwards, one should practice the breath-holding (vāyupāna).
Now, O Mahādeva, I shall describe the supreme Kuñjarāsana.
One should stand on the ground with one hand and two feet, while the head and the other hand are raised;
now I shall describe the Vyāghrāsana, which destroys the time of anger.

I shall describe the bear posture (*bhallūkāsana*), by performing which one becomes a king among yogis; in it, one stands on one foot with the head positioned in the middle upon the spinal column (*merudaṇḍa*). (24.18)
On the hip, there is the "foot-conversation," and on the hands, the "ring-finger.
Now I shall describe the "seat of desire" (kāmāsana), for the purpose of engaging in amorous play.
Having assumed the Garuḍa posture, one should touch the tip of the little finger to the generative organ;
I shall now describe the circular posture (vartulāsana), by performing which one becomes Bhairava.
One should bind the back with both feet placed in the air;
now I shall describe the liberation posture (mokṣāsana), by performing which one reaches the temple of liberation.
The wise one should place only the right hand and the right foot [down];
this, O Lord, is the *mālāsana*, by performing which one becomes dear to Vāyu.
A man standing with one hand [on the ground] attains the auspicious yoga. Now I shall describe the divine posture (divyāsana): one should bind the back with the hand. (24–23)
O Lord, one should place the middle of the single hand upon the ground, the nose upon the hand,
and fix the entire body in the sky in the posture of half-rising.
Having merely looked at the ground with both hands and the nose,
I shall now describe the moon-seat (candrāsana), [placing] one's body upon the two feet.
One who repeatedly performs the retention [of breath] preceded by the retention of the vital air (vāyudhāraṇa), shall then repeatedly practice the Haṃsāsana with the body. (24–26)
The wise practitioner, firm in the control of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), should strike the ground with his breaths.
Now I shall describe Sūryāsana, which consists of binding the foot against the back.
One should bind the foot, joined with the heel, to the side of his [opponent's] back with one's hand.
Now I shall describe the yogic posture (yogāsana), by performing which one becomes a king among yogis. (24–28)

Having bound both feet together at the soles with the two hands against one's own body, I shall now describe the mace posture (*gadāsana*); one who dwells on the earth in this manner takes on the form of a mace. (24–29)
By means of which the raising of the arms becomes the cause for the purification of the body;
now I shall describe the seat of Lakṣmī: the two soles of the feet [should be placed] in front of the liṅga.
One should bind the two hands with their palms upon the ground at the secret place.
Now I shall describe the Kulyāsana, by performing which one becomes a Kaulika.
I shall describe the Brāhmaṇa-posture, by performing which one becomes a Brāhmaṇa: with one hand placed on the head and the other below the head, while the gaze is unblinking. (24–32)
Placing one foot upon the thigh, one should remain on the ground in the form of a staff;
I shall now describe the Kṣatriya posture, by performing which one becomes wealthy.
Having bound the pair of feet with the hair, one should remain with the face turned downwards.
Now I shall describe the Vaiśya posture, by performing which one becomes truthful. (24–34)

He who stands with both hands upon his own chest, using the thumb of the right hand [to support], that is the posture of the Śūdra; I shall now describe it, by performing which one becomes a servant. (24–35)
Having held the two thumbs joined at the midpoint between the nose-tip and the feet, I shall now describe the *jātyāsana*, by means of which one becomes a rememberer of past births. (24–36)

Then, having performed the movement of hands, feet, and both pairs [of limbs] upon the ground, as well as coming and going, I shall explain the animal-impression (pāśavāsanā); by performing this, one becomes the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati).
Placing both hands on the back with the head resting upon the tips of the elbows—by the practice of these alone, a man shall become long-lived. (24–38)
By practicing for one year, one will certainly become liberated while living;
O Lord, the practice of Śrīvidyā shall be described to you hereafter.
For the sake of attaining success in yoga and as a means to purify the body, O Lord of Gods, now hear the secret concerning the gentle posture (komalāsana). (24.40)
For the investigation of the perfection of yoga, the auspicious leather seat (carmāsana) is a secret;
now I shall describe the human seat (narāsana) in its sixteen and other varieties.
By means of which mere practice the yogi becomes an adept; this method, proclaimed as the sixteenth, arises from the *Matkula* tradition. (24.42)
By means of this very practice, the yogi shall directly [attain] a kalpa in one month on the surface of the earth; in two months, there is the swift accomplishment of a kalpa. (24.43)
In the third month, there is the yoga-stage; in the fourth month, one possesses a firm resolve;
in the fifth month, the subtle stage; and in the sixth month, one attains discernment.
In the seventh month, the practitioner certainly becomes endowed with knowledge;
in the eighth month, he is provided with food and his senses and body are subdued. (24.45)
In the ninth [chapter] there is the meeting with the Siddhas; in the tenth, the piercing of the wheels (cakrabheda);
in the eleventh, the Great Hero; and in the twelfth, one becomes a Khecarī.
Thus, the practitioner who remains established in the yogic posture becomes a yogi;
he who performs the human posture (narāsana) is a perfected one—of this there is no doubt. (24.47)
O Great God, I shall explain that method by which one becomes accomplished in the practice of the human-seat (narāsana) while facing downwards. (24.48)
This must be performed by the foremost of practitioners, who are well-versed in the meaning of the Yoga scriptures:
[an image] with undiminished, unrestrained youth, beautiful, and possessing lovely locks of hair. (24.49)
Having thus gathered all that [remains] of him— the most excellent of men— who had fallen facing the enemy in battle, on an auspicious day at night, [they performed the rites].
Having prepared the seat of the moon and sun, the Kaulika practitioner should accomplish [the rite] therein.
Now I shall further explain another method that brings about all types of siddhis.
He who performs the frog-posture (bhekāsana) is indeed the lord of the yoginīs.
Now I shall explain another [practice], by performing which one becomes a king among yogins. (24.52)
Standing upon the summit of all those [mandalas], one should recite [the mantra] while seated on a lunar throne;
furthermore, there is another method for this, as seen in the Mahāvidyā and other texts. (24–53)
One should perform the recitation there upon a stone seat that is envious and yellow in color;
furthermore, this other method is undoubtedly for the Kaula practitioner of Yoga. (24.54)
If he is thus afflicted by illness, then he should perform recitation upon the auspicious seat;
and at the time of each respective practice, he should do likewise day after day.
On the nineteenth day, there is dancing, instrumental music, singing, passion, and enjoyment;
however, the fourteenth day is not to be observed due to the fear of the terrors of Bhairava.
By the mere application of the mind, a yogi becomes Bhairava; that man who, having assumed his desired seat, mutters the mantra. (24.57)
One who possesses great essence and is free from passion certainly becomes a perfected being (siddha).
Now, listen attentively to me regarding another [aspect of] the greatness of the corpse. (24.58)
Having brought all of that into the house and covered it with a tiger skin,
the mantra-practitioner, having performed a great worship there and entered, should recite the mantra.
Seated in the lotus posture, that very yogi [attains it] instantly; of this there is no doubt. (24.60)
Having quickly performed this kind of tasting,
a person who has conquered the senses and knows the purpose of the fruit of yoga shall indeed become [one with me] by my command.
This group is perfected; he is the sovereign lord of the worlds.
One should worship a tiger that has just died, which is possessed of roots, swords, staffs, clubs, arrows, and so forth, as well as spirits and the king of serpents. (24.62)
O Lord, if death should befall Bhairava, the lord of the gods,
while engaged in a face-to-face battle, one should then bring him [the mantra] and perform the recitation.
There, having assumed the kaula posture or else the lotus posture,
and having recited the great mantra of Mahāvidyā, one shall attain the Liṅga.
One who desires one's own welfare should not accept any of this:
a miserable death from disease, leprosy, subjection to women, being outcast, or dying. (24.65)

One who has died of famine, one who is insane, one whose sectarian marks are indistinct, one with missing limbs, an elder who wanders on the ground, and likewise one intent on flight—[these are not to be cremated]. || 24.66 ||

Those who, having killed the world through their investigation of various other [doctrines], practice recitation—they shall all become food for tigers; they devour [others] while possessing the form of tigers.

A wise man should avoid one who has stayed overnight, one who is just recovered from illness, one with an extra limb, one who is a great sinner, a brahmin, cow-dung, a hero, and one who is hypocritical. (24.68)
Having abandoned women and the practitioner of yoga, one should accomplish the vīrasādhana;
then, by my command, the mantra-practitioner shall become a siddha—of this there is no doubt. (24.69)
Having taken one who is young, beautiful, heroic, skilled in the knowledge of mantras, and radiant, and having performed the recitation, one becomes a perfected being; it is not otherwise.
Within the heart-lotus of a human corpse reside all the Kulākulās of every siddhi; there, indeed, all postures (āsanas) are perfected—of this there is no doubt. (24.71)
Now, there is another method by which one becomes a king among yogis:
the wise man, seated upon a soft seat or similar posture, should restrain the vital breath (māruta).
I shall describe that *komalāsana*; listen to these words of mine:
a child who has died before reaching old age, within six months, is most excellent for the *komala* [practice]. (24.73)
I shall explain its specific varieties: [the mantra] for a great corpse fallen from the womb;
having placed that upon a tiger skin, one should remain there and recite it. (24.74)
From six months up to ten months prior [to birth],
the child dies with a beautiful face, beginning from the eighth month of gestation.
On a pure seat measuring one cubit, two cubits, or four cubits on all sides, one should perform the consecration and then the worship.
When the fifth year is complete, the practitioner himself, free from fear, [should take] one who has died young, whose initiation was deficient or omitted, and who is indeed tender. (24.77)
O Lord, hear [the teaching on] the fruit that falls from the womb; for the attainment of that fruit, the eight siddhis beginning with *aṇiman* shall arise through practice for one year. (24.78)
The practitioner of mantras should recite this auspicious great vidyā while seated upon a corpse;
before long, he shall attain accomplishment—of this there is no need for doubt. (24.79)
Now hear another [account] regarding the greatness of the corpse and the attainment of success through its practice:
the practitioner, having become a king among yogis, shall dwell upon the sole of my foot. (24.80)
When ten years have been completed, if one should die on an auspicious day,
on a Saturday or a Tuesday, one should bring that person and perform the purification.

In that regard, whoever should recite the mantra of Bhadrakālī while assuming the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), or while in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadma), will certainly attain accomplishment. (24.82)

Now I shall explain the results of the [planetary] states, by which the accomplishment of a corpse and so forth occurs through the mere sudden attainment of that which has been prescribed for the corpse. (24.83)
Having brought one who is fifteen years old, handsome, and fallen in battle, one should recite the vidyā at night while seated in the vīrāsana posture.
Success will be swiftly attained; Khecarī, which fills the vital air, shall be mastered.
He who performs this practice here shall attain the perfection of the power of dhāraṇā.
Then, by means of the sādhana of the Lord of the Corpse (Śavendra), who is sixteen years of age and brings about all accomplishments for men, both enjoyment and liberation are held in his hand.
In this manner, having gradually brought a beautiful bridegroom who is fifty years of age, he who accomplishes [the rite] certainly becomes a yogin. (24.87)
Having brought a corpse situated on the battlefield, one who is well-composed should perform the sādhana;
by means of this sādhana of a corpse on the battlefield, O Lord, one becomes equal to Indra. (24.88)
If, in a frontal battle, one hears the blow of a sharp-edged spear,
the lord of heroes, having brought back the corpse and remaining in the hero’s posture, should perform the recitation.
O Mahādeva, having placed that corpse in one's own residence, in a temple, or in a secluded place for the purpose of worship, one should perform the recitation (japa). || 24-90 ||

In that regard, having assumed either the heroic posture (vīrāsana), the yogic posture of the womb (yonimudrāsana), or likewise the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should perform the recitation while holding the vital breath (vāyu). || 24.91 ||
Within one month, the Brahmin becomes a yogi, virtuous and pure;
knowing how to sustain the subtle breath, he should recite [mantras] while standing upon a corpse in its youth.
Whatever rite a person performs at the time of accomplishing power (*śava-sādhana*), by the very accomplishment of that rite, that man becomes a yogi and an immortal. (24.93)

Ānandabhairavī said: Having understood the timing of death and other such matters, as well as the subtle restraint of the vital breaths, the heroic practitioner, who discerns the conduct of heroes, should wander.
O Śiva, whose crest is the moon, hear now the supreme majesty of the ritual for one who has departed from the battlefield, explained through the language of symbols. 24.95
Having established the Lord upon a well-prepared bed within a subterranean chamber measuring half a cubit in depth, O Master, he was overcome by Māyā, O Lord. (24.96)
For one day, though I am the support of the world and remain within that very support, I was deprived of my husband; in my subtle form, I moved through all things, from the lowest to the highest.
"I, Sarasvatī, in the form of the Earth, shall always provide protection for my practitioner’s merit, which leads to virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation. (24.98)
O Śambhu, devoted to yoga, it is solely due to the absence of that [knowledge] that she,
as well as you and I, are submerged in the process of saṃsāra.
In whatever multitude of objects you always abide with joy, there I myself am firmly established and delighted; of this there is no doubt. (24.100)
For what reason do you act in this manner? Your beloved is ever firmly established on your left side, free from desire and anger. (24.101)
Ānandabhairava said:
What indeed is the purpose of practicing such means as the corpse and so forth, if one who has drunk the honey from your venerable lotus feet becomes a true ascetic? (24.102)
O Goddess worshipped by the three worlds, O Terrible One, whose very nature is the Speaker of Speech!
Tell me, by what means can one become a yogi merely through the practice of the corpse-sādhana? (24.103)
The yogi worships the lotus-face, which possesses the essence of bliss and a gentle smile of loveliness;
for what purpose does he practice yoga? Tell me the fruit of that. (24.104)
Ānandabhairavī said:

O Śaṅkara, even if you are my devotee and devoted to the recitation of my mantra, nevertheless, by means of a corpse and with the disposition of a corpse, the practice of the corpse is performed. (24.105)
It should be performed during the conjunction of night; never during the day.
He who remains steadfast toward the corpse is my devotee, without a doubt. (24.106)
A corpse-like substance is the basis of my satisfaction;
a hero, fit for carrying out my commands, should perform the corpse-seat (śavāsana). (24.107)
If I go there, then that very person shall become Śiva;
by the mere act of abandoning everything without remainder, the state of being a corpse—the dissolution of the body—will occur.
O Maheśvara, he who creates a heap of worldly existences within me, the Goddess worshipped by the three worlds, shall resort to a corpse as his own Śiva.
"O Lord of the passionate women, my duty is to protect the devotee from behind; there is no doubt about this on this earth. (24.110)
"When my body is abandoned for the sake of slaughtering animals, then why do all these [others] remain dead while you alone live? (24.111)
He who brings and accomplishes the great substance of that oblation— the Lord of the Dead who has come from the battlefield— is firm in his devotion to me.
He who is always angry is cruel; of this there is no doubt.
How could he, being agitated, accomplish the rite with a corpse during the Vīrarātri? || 24.113 ||
He whose mind is overwhelmed by fear is undoubtedly angry;
there is no sin equal to anger, for because of that sin, one is cast into a corpse.
The devotee who is liberated from sin, perfected in form, independent, discerning, established in meditation, and steadfast, shall accomplish the corpse. (24.115)
As long as one who has conquered the senses does not attain a stable mind, for that long one should not perform even the sādhana of Śavendra. (24.116)
Having brought a corpse to that door and having dug it up by that very [door],
one should accomplish [the rite] by binding and pervading it with that [mantra] from that day until that same day.

Having done this, one who has conquered the senses and eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should joyfully perform the practice of the Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā) and so forth, by means of the eightfold practice (aṣṭāṅgasādhana). || 24-118 ||
This indeed is the fruit of the eight limbs, by performing which one becomes a partaker of accomplishment;
it includes the piercing of the channels and mudrās, and is endowed with the fruits of the Kula conduct.
By the very practice of the eightfold path, one becomes perfected on the surface of the earth;
thereafter, one goes to another heaven, for there is no going elsewhere without first leaving the earth.
First, there shall be the attainment of the earth; he becomes a possessor of the attainment of the world of Bhuvarloka.
He is a lord of the attainments of Janaloka and a possessor of the attainment of Tapoloka. (24.121)
After becoming the lord of perfections in Satyaloka, the practitioner subsequently becomes a perfected one;
in this sequence, O Maheśvara, there shall be the attainment of success regarding the heavenly realms and so forth. (24.122)
For the sake of accomplishing the eightfold path, gods descend to the surface of the earth;
having attained perfection upon the earth, they depart for the abode of Brahmā.
Having thus dissolved those [elements] in due order, one then performs the practice on the surface of the earth;
having placed a corpse upon the ground, the celibate practitioner, pure during the day, [proceeds]. (24.124)
