At night, one should practice with the five principles (pañcatattva), and during the day, perform the eight-limbed discipline (aṣṭāṅga-sādhana). Such a person has conquered his senses, is free from agitation, and possesses wealth; he is no ordinary man. (24.125)
The wise man, free from anxiety and laziness, should accomplish the goal;
for through anxieties greed is born, and from greed desire arises. (24.126)
From desire arises delusion; from delusion comes the accumulation of sloth.
Through the web of the fault of sloth, sleep occurs at that very moment. (24.127)
Death certainly occurs as the ripening of great sleep; anger certainly arises from the interruption of partial sleep. (24.128)
Due to that anger, one's mind becomes deranged; from this derangement comes an increase in breath, and thus one’s life is wasted in vain as the breaths come to an end. (24.129)
One whose intellect is deficient becomes dull-witted and undergoes the decay of strength and wisdom;
through this state of dullness, a person becomes devoid of the recitation of mantras. (24.130)
If the recitation (*japa*) is deficient, the breath perishes; if the breath perishes, the body decays.
Therefore, relying upon the body, one who is pure should be devoted to the practice of recitation. (24.131)
One becomes accomplished solely through the observance of the eight limbs, and not otherwise.
I shall now describe the characteristics of these eight limbs, which directly bring about supreme accomplishment. (24.132)
Through the fruit of thousands of millions of births, a man attains knowledge from Yama; through that knowledge, he becomes a lord of his lineage. (24.133)
He who is the Lord of Yoga is the Lord of the Kula, stainless and abiding in the state of childhood;
through regular practice, worship is accomplished, and by means of worship, one attains Śiva. (24.134)
Where auspiciousness is complete, one is said to be fully pure;
by means of that seat, one becomes long-lived and free from disease and sorrow. (24.135)
By the mere breaking of the knot, the practitioner becomes cool;
he becomes purified through breath control (prāṇāyāma) and by means of mastery over the vital air (prāṇavāyu).
O Lord of Gods, he becomes self-controlled; even while delighting in the Self, his mind—which is fickle and fond of desires—is dissolved through withdrawal (pratyāhāra). (24.137)
One should place [the mind] in the lotus-feet for the destruction of that desire;
through its retention, there is mastery over the vital winds, and beyond that, the eight siddhis.
One attains the perfection of atomization through the subtle wind;
through meditation one obtains liberation, and through liberation one obtains bliss.
Through bliss there shall be an increase of joy; joy is the very form of Brahman.
By means of samādhi, one becomes a possessor of great knowledge, reaching the state of both sun and moon. (24.140)
In the place of dissolution within the Great Void, the ocean of bliss at the feet of Śrī [has arisen];
having fixed the mind upon its waves, which are stainless in their ultimate reality. (24.141)
Having fashioned the form of the venerable feet, one should meditate upon them like ten million suns and moons—
the venerable form which is as swift as ten million lightning-flashes, intensely radiant, and perfectly pure.
The yogi should meditate upon [the city] within the thousand-spoked [lotus], which is the abode of ten million suns and moons.
I bow to that Śrīvidyā, most beautiful, the sovereign lady of the mass of bliss for the three worlds;
she who possesses the splendor of ten million times ten thousand suns, who acts for the pleasure of her beloved, the enemy of Yoga, the daughter of Śaṅkara;
that garland which is both stable and moving, dense as a teacher, mountainous like a serpent, and absolute.
One of steady mind should meditate with subtle concentration; thus, accompanied by the Lord of Śrī, he proceeds. (24.144)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, concerning the means for attaining the power of mantra-siddhi within the section on the Science of Yoga (*yogavidyāprakaraṇa*), titled the *Ṣaṭcakrasārasaṅketa*, in the *Pāśavakalpa* of the *Bhāvanirṇaya*, within the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"O beloved, speak to me of the secret, preceded by a careful attention to its true nature."
Having known each of these, the great yogi enters the fire-lotus.
O Brahmin, if you have regard for me with affection, then speak to this yogi of the essence of yoga, the stainless path of reality, which defines Brahman.
Ānandabhairavī said:
Listen, O Lord of Life, O Master of Yoga, O Guru of Action! I shall speak of the limb of yoga desired by yogis, which is the exposition of the reality of Brahman. (25.3)
I shall describe this method of creation as well as the procedure for its preservation, along with the countless cycles of creation and dissolution; listen to this according to the truth. (25.4)
You alone are the agent of dissolution, O Śaṅkara, beloved of boons; you are the primary principle among these three groups.
You are the state of dissolution that destroys impurity, and you are the primary cause for the protection of the primordial world. (25.5)
In that regard, the creation of Meru, the serpent, and the limbs is indeed the middle mode of manifestation;
and its preservation, as well as its destruction within my own kingdom for the sake of the qualities of *prakṛti*, is likewise my work. (25–6)

O Lord, these three are the causes of fear and so forth; by contemplating that which destroys them—the Praṇava, whose nature consists of the qualities (guṇas)—and that which transcends the three qualities, which is infinite and imperishable, the yogi here becomes a perfected practitioner (sādhaka). || 25-7 ||
For from the unmanifest *praṇava* comes creation, and it is dissolved into that which possesses a manifest form through its contraction;
from the subtle letter *a*, they always appear in the ether, yet they perish from the gross portion which is beyond syllables.
The exceedingly wonderful and diverse conduct of the worlds is ever-changing and cannot be fully described;
those people dwelling in worldly existence, though supported by the *haṃsa*, do not recognize it as residing within their own bodies and thus do not take refuge in it. (25.9)
This Time, presiding over bodies, O God beginning with Praṇava, is asleep, resting upon Māyā;
when Time has reached its long path, it dissolves, and then the people dwelling in the world perish. (25.10)
Time is the devourer of the world, the garment of the Lord; but the boat is worn out, miserable, and without a master.
He alone consumes all that is moving and unmoving ordained by Death—deprived of prosperity and fleeing away. (25.11)
Through the fivefold lunar principle, the creation of Mahendra is established by means of the performance of sacrifice;
he always performs sacrifice in the ocean of existence, providing the excellent sacrificial means at the time of emission.
Perceiving danger therein in that great ocean, people are always overwhelmed by fear;
they enter the circle of the contemptible path, and thus they are devoid of the understanding of those who have transcended the great hells. (25-13)

How could a yogi, following the path of Hari, perish by death which is like the fire of cosmic destruction, when he is absorbed in existence—the fire of the family of dharma—which consists of illusion? And how indeed could such a practitioner [perish]? || 25-14 ||

If that practitioner who possesses the essence of love and true devotion should nonetheless fall back into the cycle of worldly existence, he becomes free from saṃsāra through the grace of the beloved and beautiful Kālī; he becomes a perfected one (siddha), a sovereign emperor of the wish-granting tree. || 25-15 ||
One should not dwell in the abundance of a householder’s life, which withers away the suffering of great calamities;
for if one forms attachments here at this time, then death will surely be most certain. (25.16)

O Lord, if that very lotus-face of yours, which is to be beheld with compassion, were to look upon me alone; for that man who always takes refuge in the company of the virtuous, having meditated upon you who dwell within the secret portion of the intellect— (25.17)
He alone is the virtuous one, dependent on the qualities of nature (prakṛti), skillful, self-controlled, and the expounder of the Vedas and Purāṇas;
he is Sattva and Mahākāla—thus have I declared this definitive truth to you for your prosperity. (25.18)

For those who are superior even to the hosts of lords of devotees by virtue of their qualities, I shall declare the direct fruit—the union known as yoga and recitation—divided into eight limbs, for the sake of victory over the supreme state that transcends all desire. Listen! (25.19)

The yogi who first brings illusion and the like under his control is indeed established among the worlds; listen now to that which is of the nature of the Sun, residing within the latent impressions of *Yama*, and consisting solely of the purpose of the power of Time. (25.20)
Having swiftly conquered desire and the rest in every respect, he is capable of victory; he is the accomplisher of the twin deeds (yamakarma).
[He conquers] desire, as well as anger, excessive greed, delusion, pride, envy, and that which is done by the very wicked. (25.21)
Therefore, having brought under control the twelve sound-slayers which are equal to Mahendra, the yogi acts everywhere for the sake of subduing the wind; otherwise, he would become unsteady. (25.22)
He practices non-violence, truthful and very pleasant speech, and the state of non-stealing like Vasiṣṭha;
he always cultivates excellent celibacy, firm uprightness, and forgiveness and fortitude, with his breath as subtle as the finest air. (25.23)

Likewise, O Lord, that sovereign of practitioners who always maintains moderate diet, possesses a mind free from doubt, avoids the objects of proliferation, and forever shuns the ignorance of festive musical performances—[attains purity]. (25.24)
The self-controlled one, by means of the twelve [limbs], performs the accomplishment of the goal which is the fruit of the eightfold path;
she of the beautiful face [worships] the lotus-feet of Śrī, which are the object of the three eyes [of Śiva] veiled by the ten states of being.

Austerity, contentment, a steady mind, constant faith, likewise the honoring of the twice-born with gifts, the worship of the gods with intense devotion, listening to the pure scriptures, modesty, and discernment; (25–26)
Recitation, oblation, libation, service, meditation, and constant activity—these fourteen rules in this scripture are the auspicious indicators for the practice of devotion. (25–27)
The previously mentioned yonyāsana is indeed the true bhekasana, as well as the bound mahotpalāsana;
one should quickly assume the previously described vīrāsana, bhadrasana, and subhakāsana. (25–28)
O Lord, all the subtle tantras have been composed by me, yet they are not sufficient for the sake of bringing [the breath] under control.
Nevertheless, the fool, having drawn in the inhalation of air, wanders here in the womb as a sinner. (25–29)
Intoxicated by the power of the bliss of the vital breaths, he who walks with the gait of a lordly elephant is remembered as Puruṣottama.
He who is skillful in serving Him alone becomes self-controlled; he is the powerful one who protects the world of the cosmic egg.
O Lord, Master of the gods and other deities, I declare that one should sustain the subtle wind by means of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus becoming a perfected one (siddha), the sovereign of practitioners (sādhaka-cakravartin) beholds the Lord who dwells within all. || 25-31 ||
Ānandabhairava said:

"O beloved, tell me the great knowledge of Brahman, which is auspicious in every respect, by means of which one brings the vital breath under control and becomes a sky-walker (khecarī), a lord of mountains. (25–32)
By the grace of the knowledge of Brahman, the practitioner shall become one whose form is Brahman.
O beautiful lady, tell me: where is there any knowledge superior to the knowledge of Brahman? (25-33)
Ānandabhairavī said:
Listen, O Lord of Yogins, knower of dharma, you who are named Brahman! This is the stainless means for attaining Brahman, which destroys the delusions of the darkness of ignorance. (25–34)
No dharma is ordained that is equal to the knowledge of Brahman;
if one possesses the dharma of the knowledge of Brahman, he is perfected—of this there is no doubt. (25–35)
What fruit is there in giving away ten million maidens or in reciting a mantra ten million times?
No other dharma is ordained that is equal to the knowledge of Brahman.
What is the fruit of a thousand lakes, a mountain of gold weighing a crore, feeding a crore of Brahmins, or visiting a crore of holy fords? (25–37)
If it is obtained by practitioners at the great seat of Kāmarūpa, there is no other dharma prescribed that is equal to the knowledge of Brahman. (25-38)

The imperishable knowledge of Brahman is indeed twofold: that born of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and the path of Brahman consisting of the essence of sound, which is the nature of the words of devotion. || 25-39 ||
Prāṇāyāma is indeed twofold: sagarbha (with seed) and nigarbhaka (without seed).
That which is accompanied by recitation and meditation is sagarbha, while that which is devoid of these is nigarbhaka. || 25-40 ||
The practitioner who has conquered the senses knows, through the knowledge of Brahman, the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) that is beyond the supreme and characterized by the imperishable.
O Lord, those two types are the garland-repetition and the sequence of recitation;
the garland-repetition consists of twelve [units], while the sequence of recitation consists of sixteen.
O Mahādeva, in the nose there are three unsurpassed characteristics:
inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka); these correspond to the triad of deities.
When these [three] also preside together, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Śiva go to the confluence of the Triveṇī, which removes all sins.
Īḍā is considered Bhāratī and Gaṅgā, while Piṅgalā is considered Yamunā; between Īḍā and Piṅgalā lies Suṣumnā, which is Sarasvatī.
Where there is the confluence of the three rivers, that is called the King of Tīrthas;
at the confluence of the Triveṇī, O Hero, one should move them again and again.
Completely liberated from all evil, he becomes a perfected one; it is not otherwise.
Having caused him to circle again and again at the great tīrtha Nirañjana, [he attains this].
One becomes a perfected being (siddha) by [realizing] Mahādeva in the form of wind; it is not otherwise.
[This occurs] within the intensely blazing form of fire, situated between the moon and the sun.
Having meditated on the ten-million-rayed [sun] with coiled rays,
the self-controlled one performs three circumambulations of the wind, which are superior, inferior, and middling.
Wherever the wind goes, there are three and three:
the goddess Iḍā, known as Candra (the Moon), and likewise Piṅgalā, known as Sūrya (the Sun).
Suṣumnā is the primary mother-nāḍī, subtle like the fiber of a lotus stalk;
and in the middle region is the auspicious nāḍī called Vajra.
Therein lies the subtle and variegated Śrīkuṇḍalī;
by means of that channel, one should grasp that most enchanting six-petalled lotus.
The supreme knowledge accessible through meditation consists of six arrows joined with power;
it is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (25.53)
Beyond that is Paraśiva, the Lord; thus the six Śivas are proclaimed.
Likewise, there are Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Lākinī, Kākinī, and Śakti. (25–54)
There, in the six lotuses, are the Sākinīs, the Śaktis accompanied by the six Śivas;
[these are] Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, and the beautiful lotus [Anāhata]. (25–55)
The wheel of command (ājñācakra), known as the Pure (viśuddha), is the great blue lotus of the unstruck (anāhata);
in the center of the wheel of command and the others, there is a moon of cool radiance. (25.56)

Having meditated on that [breath] as it falls into the root-lotus while performing inhalation (pūraka), the duration for which it maintains its quality of stability is known as retention (kumbhaka). || 25-57 ||
The practitioner of self-control should bring under control that exhalation (recaka) as it moves through the Piṅgalā [nāḍī] by closing the right nostril with a single joint of the thumb. (25.58)
Having held [the breath] for sixteen cycles, one should perform the recitation with the *praṇava*.
Having performed this inhalation (*pūraka*), one should perform the wonderful retention (*kumbhaka*).
One should perform the recitation and meditation with the sixty-four *praṇavas*. After the *kumbhaka*, O Lord, the wise one should perform the *recaka* (exhalation). (25–60)
By reciting the root mantra thirty-two times, or with the *praṇava* (OM),
while blocking both nostrils, one performs the *kumbhaka* breath-retention that bestows all accomplishments.
With the little finger and the ring finger, the wise practitioner should again fill the air into the right nostril using the left thumb. (25.62)
Then, one should perform the retention (*kumbhaka*) as before by reciting the *manu* sixteen times;
thereafter, one should perform exhalation (*recaka*) through the left [nostril] thirty-two times with the *praṇava*.
Then, having filled [the left side] again with sixteen *praṇavas*,
one should [hold it] at the tip of the right nostril for a measure of twelve finger-breadths.
O Lord, having retained the breath, one should exhale everywhere as before;
indeed, by means of three such breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one attains the single supreme breath-restraint.
The middling [practice] is said to be twice [daily], and the middling [practice] may also be once [daily];
one should perform it with effort three times a day for the sake of attaining infinite fruit.

He who, being self-restrained and pure, performs the practice with an embryo (sagarbha) through recitation, meditation, and other means at dawn, at midday, and in the evening—indeed, he [attains success]. (25.67)
Having acquired the excellent marks within a month, one who practices the wind-posture for six months shall,
for the sake of attaining yoga-perfection, place the tip of the tongue at the root of the palate.
Through sixteen rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) performed at the three times of day, one attains perfection;
by constant practice, a man becomes self-controlled and brings the vital wind (pavana) under his power.
"Success is attained within six months; such is the determination of the meaning of yoga.
Everything is obtained through yoga; this entire world is dependent upon yoga. (25.70)
Therefore, when the yogi performs supreme yoga, he is then happy;
without yoga, even if Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity, is perfected, [there is no bliss]. (25.71)
Then one should always practice yoga through the vision of the feet of the Goddess;
from the repeated practice of yoga, liberation arises—this is the determination of the meaning of yoga. || 25.72 ||
Whoever desires the accomplishment of mantras should always practice this yoga.
I shall now explain the rhythmic movement [of breath] as well as the "crow-beak" technique.
The consumption of the subtle wind, the movement within the lunar orb, and the threefold repetition—these are the various [practices], among which the triad is supreme. (25.74)

One should visualize the syllable, together with the moon, conjoined with the root mantra or even just the three-syllabled [mantra], situated upon all those seats in the region between the knees and the shanks. (25.75)
One should rotate [the tongue] at the root of the palate with the left hand twelve times;
indeed, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) in the same manner as before, twelve times each.

By reciting the mantra eight thousand times according to the sequence of *mātrā* measures, and performing twelve *prāṇāyāmas* for each [recitation], those eight thousand [recitations] are accomplished. Having done this for one month, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and is freed from sin. (25.77)
The knower of Brahman, free from stain, should practice with effort at the three junctions of the day;
for he who practices constantly becomes a king among yogins—of this there is no doubt. (25.78)
Through the practice of yoga one becomes liberated; through the practice of yoga one becomes a lord of the family (kuleśvara);
and through the practice of yoga one becomes a renunciant, a knower of Brahman, free from all affliction. (25.79)
Through constant practice one becomes a yogi; through constant practice, O scorcher of foes, one becomes a supreme ascetic;
through constant practice, one is freed from sin and becomes a performer of rites and a master of the Vedas.
Forming the hollow of the mouth like a crow’s beak, one should drink air day and night;
by means of this very subtle sequence of breath, one becomes a perfected king of yogis.
Having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and visualized the yogic gesture (yogimudrā),
one should fill the vital air at the base with the "crow-beak" breath-retention technique.
Contracting the root [perineum] during every delightful practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one should awaken Kuṇḍalinī, who is consciousness itself and whose nature is pure awareness.

The upper and lower lips should be pressed like a crow's beak, and the teeth should be firmly set against the teeth; having thus bound [the mouth], the yogi should offer [the breath] and must not extend the tongue at all. (25.84)
O Lord, the wise one, remaining in the vīrāsana posture and forming the hollow of a crow’s beak with the tongue, should not touch the pair of the upper and lower teeth. (25.85)
One should apply another tongue to the region of the palate and the root of the tongue;
one should drink the nectar-essence produced there with the hollow of a crow’s beak. (25.86)
The yogi who effects the entry of subtle air into the hollow of a crow’s beak achieves immobilization; he certainly becomes immortal. (25.87)
By the grace of this yoga, the practitioner becomes liberated while living;
in an instant, he becomes free from the great afflictions of old age and disease. (25.88)
Alternatively, one may perform it with a limited measure, enclosing [the mantra] within the sixteen vowels;
by reciting either his own mantra or the *praṇava*, that man shall become a yogin. (25.89)
Alternatively, having recited the root mantra encased by garlands of syllables according to the sequence of the number of beads in the rosary, one should bring [the target] under the power of time.
One should not utter the syllables with the mouth for the sake of the full attainment of the desired fruit;
the recitation should be performed solely with the tongue for the accomplishment of the fruit of one's desires. (25.91)
The sun, in the form of fire, is at the navel, and likewise the moon is at the forehead;
by the touch of the flame of fire, the lunar orb melts away.
By those streams of supreme nectar, the Sun attains brilliance;
and being satisfied by the *pūraka* breath-retention, he constantly protects the yogins. (25.93)
Then, by means of the yoga of inhalation (pūraka), the wise one should cause nectar to flow;
he should make the blazing fire [blaze] with the excellent fire of exhalation (recaka). || 25-94 ||

Then, having performed silent recitation (maunajapa), the practitioner of yoga, with joy, meditates upon the Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra) while holding the subtle breath; thus he becomes a true contemplator.
As long as the vital breath remains steady, whence can there be fear of death?
As long as one is a perpetual celibate (*ūrdhvaretas*), whence can there be fear of time? (25.96)
As long as the drop (bindu), pure and in the form of the moon, remains in the body, pervaded by the nectar constantly flowing [from it], how can there be any fear of death? (25.97)
Ānandabhairava said: Speak, O beloved, who delights in the essence of Kula, whose form is knowledge;
[tell me] that by which a man becomes perfected through the foremost deity of all splendor.
Mahāmṛtā and Khecarī, who embody the nature of all principles—what is the Śāṅkarī-vidyā like? I wish to hear its ritual procedure.
What is the nature of Bhavitavyatā, the mistress of yoga and inner science?
What is the supreme Goddess like? Tell me the manner of her being.
Ānandabhairavī said:
O Lord, he whose mind is steadfast in the great being that is perfectly pure, and who possesses devotion toward it without any external support, O Master— (25.101)
She whose mind and heart are under her own control, whose senses are subdued,
and whose vision is fixed upon the state of the Sovereign of the World—
she does not look toward the beauty of the moon or the sky.
He whose vital breath is steady even without [the practice of] suppression. || 25-102 ||
Those very mudrās wander as Khecarīs; freed from evil, they drink the vital wind.
Just as for a child, their writhing movements, devoid of sleep, lead them back to sleep. (25.103)

Those who are devoid of knowledge of the right and wrong paths, and whose minds are truly bereft of virtue, wealth, and pleasure—this very Śāṅkarī mudrā moves about without support as the sovereign of the worlds. (25.104)

In order to accomplish the knowledge of the science of the self, one knows the Lord of the Family (kulanāyaka) residing upon the lotus of the wheel of supreme command (adhyājñācakrapadmastha), the very essence of Śiva, through excellent knowledge (suvidyā). || 25-105 ||
A yogi who possesses only internal knowledge is undoubtedly perfected;
indeed, he who pierces the six chakras is called a knower of the inner self. (25.106)

O you who possess the six oceans [of knowledge], he who knows Śiva—who is adorned by himself with the conventions of the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra), whose form is like ten million moons, and who is peace—[attains liberation]. 25-107.
He is the knower, he is the yogi, and he is the god Maheśvara;
he knows me, O beloved, there is no wonder in this, O Śaṅkara. (25.108)
The world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is my form which is identical with all things;
he who knows that it is subject to creation, maintenance, and dissolution is the king of yogis.

Having mastered the inner science (adhyātmavidyā), various treatises have been elucidated; how can those men who are entangled in the net of such treatises be considered knowers of the inner self? (25.110)
One who is devoted to me should always carry the triple staff, be diligent, and be intent on the study of the Vedas;
if he should abandon the scriptures originating from the Vedas and contemplate me alone. (25.111)

Having completed the study of the Vedas and the determination of the meaning of various scriptures, and having perceived the great power that has arisen, the ascetic should devote himself [to it]. (25.112)

The ascetic should worship me, who am the all-pervading power, capable of assuming any form at will, without support, manifest and unmanifest, established in the eternal state, and of the nature of wind. (25.113)
For whom there is incomparable bliss and for whom knowledge is both the fruit and the non-fruit—for yogis, that is the one certain knowledge alone; of this there is no doubt. (25.114)
By the mere power of her, a person intent on contemplating reality [attains it];
she is that supreme goddess Kuṇḍalinī among the kings of serpents.
One should meditate upon that very power of wind, which is subtle in form, stable in disposition, a lover of bliss, Gaurī, who dwells within the breath. (25.116)
Bliss is the form of Brahman, established within the body of reality;
that substance which manifests it is fully drunk by the yogis. (25.117)
One should visualize the Great Goddess residing within that substance—Mānavī, the supreme goddess, possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal and endowed with eighteen arms. (25.118)
[He saw] Kuṇḍalī, the beloved of consciousness, the goddess of pure awareness, the supreme deity, the eternal Ānandabhairavī, who possesses a terrible laugh and is fearsome. || 25.119 ||
To that very supreme goddess, who brings all winds under her control, who is born from the ocean of wine, who is intoxicated, fierce, and bestows boons and fearlessness; 25-120.
The Yoginī, the mother of yoga, equal to the deluder of the wise,
whose form abides in all beings and all sides, and who is most brilliantly radiant.
Having meditated upon the pure and stainless accomplishment that pierces the six cakras and which resides eternally in their intellect, the yogi should worship them in the root-lotus.
But by reciting this chapter, Vibhākara was freed from sin;
like one whose vital energy is drawn upward, he, knowing the Dharma, wandered for the sake of attaining gnosis. (25.123)
By observing this practice, the practitioner becomes a possessor of knowledge;
for liberation arises from knowledge alone, and liberation is accomplished through meditative absorption (samādhi). 25-124.
Having increased that mantra which the wind draws up and which possesses the power of retention (dhāraṇā), one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 25-125 ||
There is nothing superior to breath control for the destruction of heaps of sins;
when all sins have been destroyed, what on this earth cannot be accomplished? (25.126)
Having conquered the extremely fierce vital breath (prāṇavāyu), which is supreme and composed of great splendor,
by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the yogi is like one who has subdued a rutting elephant.
O Lord, without breath control (prāṇāyāma), where could a person become perfected?
Breath control is remembered as the supreme essence of all successful practices. (25.128)
He who repeatedly performs breath control (prāṇāyāma) situated at the triple-confluence (triveṇī) shall attain the perfection of the eight limbs; he is the beloved of yoga among yogis. (25.129)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Radiance of Prāṇāyāma," within the Section on Accomplished Mantras, in the *Ṣaṭcakrasārasaṅketa* of the *Pāśavakalpa*, in the *Bhāvanirṇaya* of the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 25 ||
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O Lord of Life, to the complete exposition of prāṇāyāma."
I shall describe that which consists of breath control (prāṇāyāma), recitation (japa), and meditation (dhyāna) joined with the reality (tattva). || 26-1 ||
I shall describe the manifestation of splendor within the breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), which are beautiful;
Viṣṇu and Īśa are the deities of those [controls], and they are indeed middling-middling.
O Lord, having diligently established the qualities of rajas and tamas within sattva, and having abandoned desire, anger, and the like, one becomes a yogi who knows yoga. (26.3)
The quality of passion (rajas) indeed predominates in kings, while that of darkness (tamas) is excessive;
in animals, it is even greater, whereas in the virtuous (sādhus), there is only the quality of goodness (sattva).

One should take refuge in that which is pure being (*sattva*), Viṣṇu, whose form is the Veda, stainless, free from duality, the object of the realization of the Self, and the root of the three forms. (26.5)
Merely by relying on the qualities of sattva, one becomes free from sin and attains all perfections;
moreover, through the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya), one quickly becomes a master of the senses.
O Lord, since all things, both moving and unmoving, are brought under control by the power of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu),
one should practice recitation and meditation for the sake of that very cause.
I shall describe that method, the two-fold procedure of recitation and meditation;
by the mere performance of this, one becomes a yogi—of this there is no doubt. (26.8)
Japa is said to be of three kinds: manifest, unmanifest, and extremely subtle.
The manifest is vocal, the unmanifest is whispered, and the subtle is mental.
In this regard, I shall explain meditation (dhyāna) in its twenty-one modes;
through meditation, the perfection of recitation (japa-siddhi) is attained, and from recitation, perfection follows—of this there is no doubt. (26.10)
O Śaṅkara, I shall first describe the meditation on the Great Goddess Vidyā;
this goddess is Kuṇḍalinī, whose mind resides in the root-lotus.
The mind always performs all religious and worldly actions;
wherever that illustrious one goes, there the vital breath (vāyu) also goes.
Therefore, having placed the mind in the form of air at the base, one should fix it externally at the tip of the nose at a distance of twelve finger-breadths. || 26-13 ||
Having repeatedly conceptualized a form residing in the mind as a mental phenomenon, the mind goes toward that which resembles it, wherever its course may ever be. (26.14)
But the form consisting of mental modification is indeed one alone, there is no doubt;
for it is only among the ignorant, O Lord of Gods, that there is such a conceptualization of forms of Brahman. (26.15)
Indeed, that unmanifest form of Brahman is established within the body;
the ascetic should worship that which is free from merit and action and accessible only to the mind. (26.16)
At the base, one should worship a beautiful four-petaled lotus, golden in color; in the center of its pericarp, one should revere the Self-born One (Svayambhū). || 26-17 ||
One should worship Kuṇḍalinī, who resembles ten million suns, who travels through the aperture of the Suṣumṇā,
and who is adorned by the stream of nectar flowing upwards.
One should worship the supreme self-manifested liṅga, which is wisdom that increases for a long time, the space subtler than the subtlest, congealed within the kuṇḍalinī. (26.19)
One should visualize there, at the root, the previously mentioned yoga-paṭala;
by the mere meditation on Kuṇḍalinī, one becomes the piercer of the six cakras. (26–20)
One should meditate upon the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, who is dear to the supreme and inferior gurus,
the blissful one situated in the center of the earth, the Yoginī, and the mother of Yoga.
Shining like ten million streaks of lightning, traveling along an extremely subtle path,
moving upward through the upper way, with a body the color of the first blush of dawn.
At the first emergence, she is Kaulī, who illuminates the path of knowledge;
at every departure, she is Pratyakṣā, her form pervaded by nectar.

One should contemplate the Source of Phenomena (Dharmodayā), radiant, containing all that is moving and stationary in the world, abiding within all, free from conceptual construction, and pure with the bliss of consciousness. (26.24)
She who flows through space, eternal, embodying all phonemes and vowels, the Great Kuṇḍalinī who is to be meditated upon by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (26–25)
I bow to the auspicious Kulakuṇḍalinī, who resides within the Praṇava, who is pure and the locus of both pure and impure knowledge, who is the perfection that pierces the lunar orb.
[He meditates on] the primordial one, the source of the universe, beloved of the world, seated upon the root-lotus;
she who dwells in the lotuses beginning with the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the supreme one consisting of all powers.
She is the knowledge of the Self, the bliss of Śiva, seated upon a throne, exceedingly beautiful, having the form of a serpent, red in color, and enchanting with every form. (26–28)
One should worship Kālī, who is Kuṇḍalinī, the beloved woman residing in the form of desire, the Mother who bestows the self, and who consists of the bliss of the path of the Kula.
Having meditated thus, within the stainless root-lotus during the practice of yoga, one should realize the supreme Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is gnosis, within the source of phenomena (dharmodaya).
Merely by the cultivation of Kuṇḍalinī, the practitioner becomes a possessor of the eight siddhis, such as Khecarī;
he attains lordship and becomes a sovereign ruler of the earth.
When the state of realization is attained through the practice of yoga, the wind (vāyu) is remembered as having great success;
one should diligently move that [wind], which is the subduer of the vital breaths (prāṇas). || 26-32 ||
By drawing up the Kuṇḍalinī situated in the root-lotus at every moment, the great wind of the vital breath (prāṇa) will certainly come under control. (26–33)

O Lord, those who are gods within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), in a sacred field (kṣetra), on a seat (pīṭha), at a great holy ford (sutīrthaka), upon a stone, or in an empty place— may they all become perfected beings (siddhas) through the vital breath (prāṇavāyu).
Whatever exists within the universe exists within the body;
all these are bound to the vital breath (prāṇa), while that which transcends the vital breath is the stainless (nirañjana).
As long as the vital breath remains in the body, whence can there be fear of death? When the breath has departed, the deities who abide in consciousness arrive [to depart]. (26-36)
That Kuṇḍalinī, the elemental deity who is the root of all, has the form of wind; consisting of bliss and consciousness, she protects everything. (26-37)
The Kundalinī, the deity of yoga, who is the conscious form of the worlds, when united with the self and the mind, bestows liberation itself. (26-38)

Therefore, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon that Bhavānī, who abides in both worldly enjoyment and liberation, for the sake of attaining the knowledge of reality, if he desires yoga in this world. (26–39)

And at the time of obstructing the vital breaths, the Kuṇḍalinī, consisting of consciousness, should be meditated upon as far as the aperture of Brahmā; this passionate woman protects the yogin. (26.40)

One should always meditate upon the Mistress of the Kula (Kuleśvarī), who is the supreme Goddess in the form of wind, eternal, the sovereign of yoga (Yogeśvarī), victorious, free from conceptual construction, and residing within the triangle. 26-41.
She possesses the infinite radiance of millions of suns and is the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
she is the abode of infinite knowledge, whom those seeking liberation worship. (26.42)
In the terrible darkness of ignorance, that Mistress, seated upon a serpent and fastened to the deluded mind, protects the practitioner while she sleeps at his head.
The sovereign of all beings, who illumines both knowledge and ignorance, who pervades the fruits of merit and demerit, and whose form consists of compassion; || 26-44 ||
The lords of yogis, possessing a golden luster, remain in the Kali age and constantly meditate upon the goddess Kulakuṇḍalinī, who is filled with the bliss of consciousness. (26.45)
Those who perceive me as a garland of letters beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma', enveloped like a flash of lightning, with my limbs adorned with ornaments of gold— they truly know me.
Those who meditate for a year upon the Kuṇḍalinī Vidyā, which illumines the path of the Kula, are liberated; of this there is no doubt. (26-47)
Those who are liberated from the heap of sins and whose minds are well-disposed toward the knowledge of Dharma,
necessarily practice meditation and praise the supreme Kuṇḍalinī.
The meditation on Kulakuṇḍalinī bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
there is no doubt that the great yogi who performs it [attains this] upon the earth. (26-49)
The meditation on Kuṇḍalinī is threefold: the divine, the heroic, and the animal sequence;
through the yoga beginning with the animal state, one becomes a perfected king of yogis.
O Lord, I shall now explain the divine meditation (divyadhyāna) immediately following the general [meditation].
Having first performed the general [rite], one should thereafter perform the divine and other [rites]. (26.51)
Resembling ten million moons, a mass of radiant light, and undisturbed;
enriched with thousands of garlands of flames, it is like hundreds of fires of cosmic destruction.
She was formidable with fangs as terrifying as claws, adorned with a mass of matted locks;
she was of fierce form, exceedingly terrible, and as restless as a thousand billion lightning flashes.
She is as gentle as ten million moons, yet she is terrifying wherever she dwells;
her mind is intoxicated by the infinite processes of creation, destruction, and preservation.
Those seeking liberation meditate upon her, whose form pervades all things, who possesses a body as dark blue as the dawn, and who is the abode of infinite creation. (26.55)
I shall now proclaim the Heroic Meditation (vīradhyāna), by performing which one becomes beloved of heroes;
indeed, he who is beloved of the excellent ones is called liberated while still enjoying worldly pleasures.
Having attained the stainless, divine, and supreme quality of heroism within the conduct of a hero, the great hero becomes a yogi at that very moment. (26.57)
O Lord, without the conduct of the heroes (vīrācāra), the divine conduct (divyācāra) is not attained;
therefore, having performed the dharma of the conduct of the heroes, one should practice the divine conduct. (26.58)
The practice of the hero (vīrācāra) yields ten million-fold fruit through the accomplishment of recitation for a single day;
that devotee destroys the suffering and sins of millions upon millions of births. (26–59)
Having performed the conduct of the *kula*, the right conduct, and the heroic conduct which yields great fruit, there is indeed accomplishment; and my meditation is the *kula*-meditation. (26.60)
Those who meditate upon me, the goddess Kulakuṇḍalinī, and worship me,
become kings among yogis by meditating on me as the Great Hero within the root-lotus.
I bow to Kālī, the mistress of the Kaulas, the sovereign of the Kula; she who is the sun to the fire of time for those whose meditation is born of the clamor of the Kali age;
she who is the radiant flash of the dawn of well-being, the swallower of Time, the one who utters the sound *kilikili* amidst the strife of the Kali age, whose play is the beauty of divine sport;
she known as the Subtle, known as the Destroyer, who consists of subtle splendor within the lotus of the family of destruction.
Those who have bowed down before him resort to her who dwells in intoxication, the beautiful one of lovely complexion. (26.62)
She is endowed with eighteen arms, has eyes like blue lotuses,
was born from the ocean of wine, and embodies the forms of the moon, the sun, and fire.

She stands in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire; she is beautiful, the bestower of boons, the beloved woman, and the dear consort of her husband who has brought an end to the pride of ten million Cupids.
The supreme Ānandabhairavī, who is presided over by Ānandabhairava,
the enjoyer whose limbs are as enchanting as ten million moons.

Indeed, the heroes meditate upon her who has the form of ten million streaks of lightning, who is free from the manifestation of existence and non-existence, and who is devoted to the consciousness of gnosis.
Through the clarity of her meditation, you, Bhairava, are yourself pleased;
I too am pleased, and all in this world are pleased—of this there is no doubt. (26.67)
The practitioner, with a steady mind, performs breath-control (prāṇāyāma);
having meditated upon the Goddess in the root-lotus, the hero shall attain yoga. (26.68)
O Maheśvara, by means of the subtle breath-retention (*sūkṣmavāyudhāraṇa*), the practitioner on earth knows his own death and the perils of birth, as well as the state of a hero (*vīrabhāva*).
Within one month, the accomplishment of attraction is attained, and within two months, the accomplishment of speech;
by practicing for three months, one becomes beloved of the gods through union.
Thus, in the fourth month, one becomes the domain of Dakapāla;
in the fifth, one becomes Pañcabāṇa; and in the sixth, Rudra—of this there is no doubt. (26–71)
Only the best of practitioners, the devotee of the Goddess, that king among yogis, knows the majesty of the heroic state through the fruit of ten million births. (26–72)
The heroic conduct is a great dharma that is the cause of mental stability;
by its mere grace, one becomes established in a divine state. (26.73)
He himself is Rudra, the great yogi, Mahāviṣṇu, and the ocean of compassion;
he alone is the Great Hero, the very Self who enjoys liberation—of this there is no doubt. (26-74)
Now, O Lord, Great Hero, there is the ritual bath of being (*bhāvasnāna*) which relies upon the *kula*;
by performing this, one becomes truly pure—if one is already pure, what could not be accomplished? (26.75)
The family-bath and the great bath are extremely difficult for yogins to obtain;
having performed them, the hero who has conquered his senses should practice the meditation on the family (kuladhyāna).
Bathing is said to be of three kinds: immersion, cleansing the body, and bathing by means of mantras, knowledge, and so forth; the latter is proclaimed as the supreme. (26.77)
Listen to that method, O beloved of Prāṇa, O doer of what is dear:
by merely bathing, one shall be liberated from the mountain of sin and reach the infinite. (26.78)
One should bathe in the pure sacred ford (tīrtha) that is the lotus-heart,
or else one should bathe in the Bindu-tīrtha for the sake of liberation from the sins of all births.
In this body, the two rivers Iḍā and Suṣumnā flow as a sacred ford of Śiva, filled with the water of knowledge;
one who bathes in their waters need not concern themselves even with the Gaṅgā or the Puṣkara lakes. (26.80)
The Yamunā, whose nature is the Sun, flows from the station of Iḍāmalasthāna;
likewise, the Sarasvatī, which goes to the region of Suṣumnāmaladeśa, immerses itself for the purpose of consumption. 26–81.

A person devoted to the mental bath, distinguished by the yoga of mantra-practice and knowing the reality, joyfully bathes in the pure water of the sacred site situated on the earth—the root lotus—and shall become a partaker of liberation. (26.82)

The Gaṅgā, the purifier of all sacred fords, who emerged from the Great Being (Viṣṇu) as a virtuous woman, brings about the destruction of sins and grants liberation directly; she bestows incomparable wealth and merit.

Placing his mind within the beautiful lotus of his own self-abiding (svādhiṣṭhāna), as far as the source of creation and beyond all sacred fords, the lord of yogis bathes just as one would in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
In Maṇipūra, at the divine bathing place, is the lake Pañcakuṇḍa;
this is the Śrīkāmanā-tīrtha, where he who desires liberation bathes.

In the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) is the source of all sacred fords (*sarvatīrtha*), situated in the center of the solar disc; he who desires liberation bathes in all the sacred fords through that manifestation.

Having meditated upon the emergence of the eight sacred fords within the great lotus called Viśuddha— which bestows the liberation of absolute isolation— the hero bathes therein for the sake of final emancipation.
Having always meditated upon Mānasa, Bindutīrtha, and Kālīkuṇḍa— which consists of the Kalās— within the Ājñācakra, one bathes for the sake of attaining the perfection of Nirvāṇa.
In this family, yogins joyfully perform this beloved ritual bath;
therefore, they are heroes endowed with courage, possessed of all accomplishments, and like gods. (26.89)
Having always committed various sins, even including the murder of a Brahmin,
by performing a ritual bath at a great sacred site (mahātīrtha), they shall become perfected beings (siddhas) possessing the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
By merely bathing, one becomes free from sin and capable of restraining the vital breath (vāyu);
for those who behold sacred fords (tīrthas), the yogi will certainly become empowered.

Then, at a great sacred ford, the lord of ascetics, devoted to his lineage, should perform the twilight ritual; through the union of yoga, he [practices] the yoga-science which is the form of the lineage.
At whatever time the union of Śiva and Śakti occurs, that is the twilight (sandhyā) for those established in Kula; it arises when one is situated in samādhi.

Having meditated upon Śiva as the Sun within the heart, where he meets the Moon of the power (Śakti) on the forehead, that *sandhyā* arises for those established in the Kula when they are situated in *samādhi*. (26.94)
Alternatively, having meditated upon the Moon as Śiva, joined with the Power (Śakti) in the Sun of the heart—that Sandhyā, which is the Vidya of Union, arises for one established in samādhi. (26.95)
Thus has been described the Sandhyā, whose nature is knowledge and who pervades the universe;
she is the eternal power of Vāyu, indivisible because she is beyond destruction. (26.96)
O Mahādeva, he who indeed performs the libation at the sacred ford of reality (tattvatīrtha) has thereby satisfied the three worlds; listen, O Lord, to the manner in which that occurs. (26.97)
Having raised up Kuṇḍalinī from the root-lotus— which consists of the forms of the moon, sun, and fire— and having established Kuṇḍalinī in the supreme Bindu.
One should here satisfy the deity of the body with the nectar arising from that;
by [satisfying] Kuleśvarī, the primordial Vidyā, one certainly becomes a perfected being (siddha).
One should satisfy the eternal Kaulinī with a stream of nectar produced from the moon, the sun, and the great fire, and one should visualize her as being anointed with that nectar.

Having performed the propitiation of Kālī, who is the supreme state, and of the female deities, the sciences, and so forth, the yogi shall indeed become [liberated]; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Lord of the Kula. (26.101)
At the base, one should fill the lunar vessel with the nectar from the moon on the forehead;
having filled it by way of the path of knowledge, one should satisfy the Khecarī with that.
In the midst of the ocean of nectar, one should satisfy the maiden of the lineage with streams of wine and ambrosia; thus one becomes a perfected king of yogins.
At that sacred site, one of great wisdom should practice meditation with diligence;
he should constantly practice that which is its womb, for this is indeed the meditation of yogis.
One should indeed feed one's own daughter or even the daughter of another;
for the satisfaction of all, one should cause a young woman to be gratified.
O Lord Śaṅkara, one should satisfy [the deity] with this divine hymn;
having praised the Goddess with the Thousand Names of Kaumārī, one should fully satisfy her.
He who performs the five-limbed *pūrṇayajña* within the practice of recitation (*japa*) should also perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). || 26-107 ||
The vital breath (prāṇavāyu) becomes steady within the body through the practice of receiving worship;
for those who do not bring it within, how can there be any established accomplishment? (26.108)

Therefore, by means of internal worship alone, if the Great Goddess is pleased with a mind satisfied by Kuṇḍalinī, then at that very moment the man becomes a possessor of spiritual perfection (siddhi).
Having consecrated the Mother of the World, the manifest supreme deity,
one should worship her with a stream of drops from the root lotus to the thousand-petaled wheel.
Having sprinkled Pārvatī with a stream shimmering with the nectar of the moon,
the wise one should worship her with supreme devotion while recollecting the root mantra.

Worshipping with the flowers of the sense-objects, one becomes identical with that in an instant; such is the placement (nyāsa), which is the realization of identity with That. One should worship with the sense of "I am He."
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being woven into the power of consciousness (cicchakti),
which resides within the supreme ether (parame vyomni) established in supreme bliss.
O Lord Śaṅkara, that which reveals the true existence of the Self without [the need for] worship, fire-offerings, and so forth, should be known as the internal sacrifice of yogins. (26.114)
He is called the inner self, the great self, and the supreme self;
by the mere remembrance of him, a man becomes a perfected yogi. || 26-115 ||
Free from deceit, free from egoism, likewise free from passion and pride;
free from delusion and hypocrisy, and likewise free from blame and agitation. || 26-116 ||
Absence of envy and absence of greed are the ten flowers of yogins;
non-violence is the supreme flower, and restraint of the senses is a flower. (26.117)
Compassion is a flower, forbearance is a flower, and knowledge is the fifth flower;
with these seventeen flowers, one should worship the Supreme Deity.
Now I shall describe the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
O Lord, I shall tell it to you in the secret symbolic language (saṅketabhāṣā); listen to that.
Having contemplated the self as undivided and remaining in a subtle state, one perceives the nature of the threefold self as the square sacrificial pit of consciousness (citkuṇḍa). || 26-120 ||

The wise one should offer oblation into the fires of knowledge situated at the navel, which is joined with the girdle of bliss, has the form of the half-measure (ardhamātrā), and is adorned by the yoni. || 26-121 ||
With this mantra, one should offer oblations into that fire with the sense of "I am That" (so'ham),
abandoning the ritual for an external woman and [offering] one's own vital energy with the end of the root mantra.
With the ladle of the mind as the oblation, I perpetually offer the activity of the senses into the fire whose nature is consciousness at the navel, which is ever-kindled by knowledge. (26.123)
Thus, with the first oblation, one should perform the ritual at the end of the root mantra;
by offering the second oblation and performing the fire sacrifice, one becomes a subduer.
And with the mind as the sacrificial ladle, I perpetually offer the activity of the senses into the fire of the self, which is kindled by dharma and adharma, via the path of the *suṣumnā*.
Having uttered the mantra ending with "svāhā" and having applied the root-mantra at the beginning,
one should offer oblations with single-minded devotion into the mandala of the root-lotus.
At the fourth full oblation, one should perform it with this mantra;
indeed, this fourth mantra bestows the fruit of complete knowledge. (26–127)
In the fire of consciousness, which blazes forth without end, without interval, and without fuel; which is the adversary of the darkness of illusion;
and which is the ground for the unfolding of certain wondrous rays of light.
I offer the universe, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva.
Having performed the internal sacrifice in this manner, one becomes directly composed of Brahman;
for such a person there are neither merits nor sins, and he certainly becomes liberated while living.
Indeed, for the wise and for yogis alone, the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) bestows accomplishment.
Now, O Śaṅkara, hear about the internal worship of the five *makāras*.
But at the time of the internal sacrifice,
one should meditate with firm conviction upon you and me as being of one essence with the Lord, just as day and night are of one essence.
Wine is Śakti and meat is Śiva; Bhairava himself is the devotee of those two. The bliss arising from their union is the definitive realization of liberation. (26.132)
Bliss is the radiance of Brahman situated within the center of the body;
one should perform the satiation of Brahman and the other [deities] by means of substances that manifest it. (26.133)
One should worship with those substances that manifest that bliss, which is the essence of the worlds, the form of Brahman residing within the body. (26.134)
Having reached the three marks and the seats located at the center of the six lotuses, which pierces the moon, one should proceed to the great forest of lotuses.
One should move the root-lotus and the aperture of Brahmā;
as the consciousness-moon, which is the supreme arising, goes there again and again, it should move the vital breath. (26.136)
The conscious moon is the power Kuṇḍalinī; it is the great arising of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya).
The person who is devoted to drinking the nectar of the vibration from the lotus of the void is truly a man. 26-137.
O Lord, for the virtuous, this drinking of honey exists both externally and internally;
however, the drinking of other liquor destroys the yoga of yogins.
But the Great Hero, free from delusion and wrong livelihood, partakes of the other great drink for the sake of perfecting the eightfold yoga. (26.139)
Having slain the sacrificial animal of merit and demerit with the sword of knowledge, the practitioner who knows yoga unites his mind with Paraśiva.
He alone shall be a meat-eater; others are merely slayers of living beings.
When the great fire resides within the body, one should worship the "burnt fish. (26.141)
Those located in the body, in water, and others that are inauspicious, as well as those arising from the moist and gentle earth, possess great strength through their seals (mudrās). || 26-142 ||
The wise one, having offered all that upon the rays of Brahman, should satisfy [the deities];
therein are the mudrās and offerings which increase bliss. (26.143)

And the others are for the sake of enjoyment; for this indeed is the supreme [state] of yogins, who are filled with the bliss arising from the union of the Supreme Power and the Self as a couple. (26.144)
Those who are liberated may engage in sexual union; others are merely those who serve women. With these five modes, one should worship the supreme consort.
One should always practice this yoga—the worship of the mantra which is the essence of the hidden meaning of the *puraścaraṇa*—while remaining free from sleep and laziness. (26.146)
This vital breath (prāṇavāyu) may bring about [the cessation of] the cause of time by warding it off;
he who performs this practice continuously under the control of the vital breath [attains this]. (26.147)
He shall attain the perfection of yoga and achieve success in time.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the section on the Mantras for Attainment, in the *Ṣaṭcakrasārasaṅketa*, part of the *Pāśavakalpa* concerning the establishment of the accomplishment of subtle yoga, in the determination of the nature [of reality], the illuminator of the great tantras, in the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*. || 26 ||
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"O Bhairavī, you have spoken of various systems of Yoga scriptures."
"O my beloved Priyaṃvadā, it is precisely because she possesses all forms that she is dear to me. (27.1)
The fruits of the eight limbs of yoga and all the waters of reality have been described;
now, however, I wish to hear them according to the sequence of the Śakti-tattva.
The withdrawal of the previously mentioned vital airs is *vāyudhāraṇā*; tell me of *pratyāhāra*, that which is called *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*. (27-2)
Ānandabhairavī said:
Listen, O Lord of the World, I shall declare the fruit and the non-fruit of prāṇāyāma.
One should not hold [the breath] for too long, nor indeed should one perform a very brief retention. (4)
One should practice very gradually and avoid any forceful exertion;
through the accomplishment of the joy of inhalation (pūraka), one should perform hundreds upon hundreds of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).

For the sake of increase, however, the characteristic of the breath is such that on whichever day the movement occurs—whether in the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight—the fruit arises according to the thirty lunar days (tithis). || 27-6 ||
In the bright fortnight, one should indeed proceed through the *iḍā*, but in the dark fortnight, through another;
however, in all cases, one should travel through the multiform *suṣumnā*.
O Great Lord, one should know that the three lunar days of the bright fortnight, beginning with the first day (pratipad), as well as those two [periods], belong to the wind in the right nostril.
The deity pervades and rises through the fourth, fifth, and sixth [fingers];
she is to be meditated upon in the left nostril during the practice of the wind-retention (*vāyudhāraṇa*).
Pervading the seventh, eighth, and ninth [chakras], she resides in the left nostril; she should be meditated upon by practitioners who are learned in the Kula tradition.
When it pervades and remains throughout the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth [finger-breadths], the Lord Vāyu should be meditated upon by yogins at the tip of the right nostril. (27.11)
The wind, pervading the thirteenth, the full moon (fifteenth), and the fourteenth [tithis],
should be meditated upon in the left nostril for the purpose of withdrawal and dissolution.
I shall declare the fruit of the dark fortnight, knowing which one becomes immortal;
one will quickly become a knower of time—of this there is no doubt. (27.13)
Having gathered [the breath] in Piṅgalā during the second watch of this [day] and also the third watch of that [night], one always exhales the vayanas.
The fourth, fifth, and sixth [vowels] abide pervading the left;
then the wind [consonant *ya*] pervades the seventh, eighth, and ninth on the right. (27.15)
The wind always moves pervading the tenth and eleventh [channels],
while the other lunar days and so forth are always present day and night in the left and right [channels].
When that best of men reaches this state of separation, then indeed,
within three fortnights, there shall be death, disease, or the loss of kinsmen.
Having recognized the lunar day of birth as distinct, one should counteract it at that time;
beginning from the destruction of birth, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
When, by means of the state of consciousness, one abandons the body and offers it up,
then, having restrained the breath, one should hold it below in the fire of time (kālāgni).
One should practice for as long as it takes to reach one's own natural state, so long as the body does not waver and the mind does not waver. (27-20)
For a person practicing in due order, the emergence of perspiration in the body is the lowest [stage];
that accompanied by trembling is the middling; but the highest is the leaving of the ground. (27.21)
Within six months, one becomes a seer of beings as well as a hearer of distant sounds;
through a year of practice in yoga, one becomes an illuminator of the science of yoga.
The yogin knows all the tantras and his own successive stages;
if he possesses the vision of the true view, then he is undoubtedly a yogin. (27-23)
I shall describe the fruit of pratyāhāra, by performing which one becomes a sky-walker (khecara);
one attains devotion to the Lord, and the person becomes a knower of dharma. (27.24)

For the sake of attaining the highest qualities, as long as the practice of ethical conduct is required, one should perform *japa* with the subtle breath for the successful accomplishment of sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). (27.25)
The withdrawal of the senses as they roam among their objects, and the forceful drawing back of them from those objects, is prescribed as *pratyāhāra*. (27.26)

O King of Yogis, having brought back the mind that has fallen away from other activities, from worldly duties, or from the duties prescribed by the scriptures, one should establish it in the lotus feet [of the Lord]. (27.27)
The withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is prescribed as the forceful extraction of that world-wandering mind which is firm, difficult to transcend, and unconquered. || 27-28 ||
By the power of this withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), the yogi will certainly become established in his own nature;
the man who is steady in the mass of objective phenomena suddenly attains the state of pure being.
There is nothing higher than mental disposition; this world is dependent upon mental disposition.
Yoga is attained through mental disposition; therefore, one should take refuge in mental disposition. (27–30)
Now I shall explain the dhāraṇā, by practicing which one partakes of the form of steadfastness;
having placed the three worlds within his belly, the king of yogins remains full.
At the thumb, the ankle, the knee, and the thigh; at the perineum and the navel; in the regions of the heart, the neck, and the throat; likewise at the uvula and the nose. (27–32)

The retention of the vital breath (prāṇamarut) at the center of the eyebrows, the forehead, the crown of the head, or at the "twelve-finger limit" (dvādaśānta), according to the prescribed rule, is called *dhāraṇā* (concentration).

The concentration which is performed upon the path of Brahman—in the region of the knots of all the channels, in the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), and in the abode of the deities—is called *dhāraṇā*. (27–34)
Retention (dhāraṇā) consists of holding Kuṇḍalinī at the root region and at the tip of the nose; it is defined as the pacification of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu). || 27-35 ||
There, within the auspicious and beautiful splendor of the lotus feet of Śrī, one should fix the mind with devotion; thus, one shall attain the power of dhāraṇā. (27–36)
Now I shall explain meditation, by performing which one becomes all-pervading;
through the yoga of meditation, liberation occurs, characterized by neither coming nor going from my family. (27–37)
With a concentrated mind and with consciousness turned inward, the meditative absorption (yogadhyāna) upon one's chosen deities within the self is here described. (27–38)

Having fixed the lotus of his mind upon the pair of the Lord’s glorious lotus feet, which are variegated with the filaments of His toenails, he should meditate upon the great assembly of his desired deities.
Now, listen as I speak of the greatness of samādhi according to its true nature;
it is precisely because of this that a person becomes a perfected yogi. (27-40)
O Lord Āndabhairava, by constantly cultivating the equality of the individual self and the supreme self through meditative absorption, one shall become victorious. (27.41)
By the mere accomplishment of union, the great yogi perceives the great person established in samādhi through the characteristics of the eight limbs of samādhi.
Having focused upon this meditative absorption, the yogi becomes endowed with yoga;
then, having fixed the mind upon the moon, he should bring it to manifestation through contemplation. (27.43)
By means of this essence of the eight limbs, a person becomes fit for yoga;
from the practice of yoga, liberation arises, as does unimpeded perfection in mantra.
According to the system of the Yogaśāstra, all indeed are remembered as Bhairavas;
there exists no scripture superior to the Yogaśāstra even within the three worlds. (27-45)
O Śaṅkara, having understood the scriptures that transcend the three worlds and the various limbs of yoga, she who perceives them quickly through manifold meditation; 27-46.
The supreme knowledge for the destruction of defects such as desire has been told;
now listen, for I shall speak the definitive exposition of the meaning of mantra-yoga. (27.47)
O Lord, the entire universe is the body, free from affliction, resting upon the five elements;
through the splendors of the moon, the sun, and fire, it is of one form with the individual soul and Brahman.
It is held that there are thirty-five million channels in the body;
among them, ten are declared to be the principal ones, and among those, three are established as the most essential.

Here, within the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), the Mother of Yoga is established as the primary [power], consisting of the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, and existing in the nature of the three channels (nāḍīs). (27–50)
The channel *iḍā* is situated on the left; it is white and has the form of the moon.
That channel is of the nature of *śakti* and is the very embodiment of nectar. (27.51)
On the right, however, is the one named Piṅgalā, who has a male form and the appearance of the sun;
resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree, she is celebrated as Viṣā. (27–52)
That Suṣumnā, which is situated in the center of Meru and possesses many forms,
truly exists pervading everything from the Visarga up to the Bindu.
In the Mūlādhāra, known as the triangle and consisting of will, knowledge, and action,
is the Svayaṃbhū-liṅga in its center, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Above that is the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), presided over by Kalā, Śānti, and the Moon;
and above that is Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is like a flame and whose nature is Brahman.
Outside of that, one should visualize a lotus with eight petals made of gold, shining with a golden hue, resembling molten gold in appearance. (27–56)
Above that is a six-petaled lotus, resembling fire in brilliance and possessing the luster of a diamond;
it is endowed with the six syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *la*, and consists of six petals. (57)
The stainless center called Svādhiṣṭhāna, which reaches the hearts of yogins, is proclaimed as the Mūlādhāra, the root of the six supports (ādhāras). || 27-58 ||
By its own name, the supreme *liṅga* is the self-abiding (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) which possesses its own characteristic mark;
above that, in the region of the navel, is the Maṇipūra of great radiance.
Then [he sees] that which resembles a cloud, that which resembles lightning, and which consists of great splendor;
then the Maṇipūra, which has a lotus made of various jewels and possesses the luster of the moon.
O Lord, everything has been told; O beloved, hear now of the heart-lotus, which is endowed with ten petals and possessed of the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha*. (61)
The lotus presided over by Śiva causes the illumination of the universe;
above that is the unstruck (anāhata) lotus situated in the heart, filled with rays of light.
Resembling the rising sun, it is endowed with the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*, joined with twelve petals, and accompanied by the [deities] beginning with Īśvara. || 27-63 ||
In the midst of that is the Bāṇaliṅga, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns;
I shall describe it as consisting of the Śabdabrahman, wherein the Unstruck Sound (Anāhata) is perceived.
Therefore, that which is called the unstruck lotus is the means for yogis to achieve yoga;
it is the abode of bliss and is supremely presided over by the Siddha.
Above that, however, is the lotus called Viśuddha, possessing sixteen petals;
it is endowed with sixteen phonemes, smoke-colored, and of great splendor. (27.66)
One should practice the wondrous abode of the yogins, which is described as the perfection;
for by beholding the world of the *haṃsa*, it extends the purity of the individual soul (*jīva*). (67)
The pure lotus is said to be called "space," possessing great radiance;
above that is the wheel of command (ājñācakra), which is supreme and presided over by the syllable *thī*.
The transmission of the command (*ājñāsaṃkramaṇa*) therein is proclaimed as the "Command of the Guru.
Above that is the one called Kailāsa, and above that is Bodhana. (69)
O Lord, such wheels as these have been described to you;
above them is the stainless, supreme thousand-petaled lotus.
The station of the Bindu is to be known as supreme; now hear the doctrine held by the Gaṇas.
The Buddhists speak of the Self, yet for one who knows the Self, there is no Lord.
The Cārvākas assert that everything does not exist and are devoid of various [karmic] actions; all Buddhists are intent on reviling the Vedas and proclaim the doctrine of emptiness. (27.72)
My beloved ones, the inhabitants of the land of Cīna, rely upon my gnosis;
having contemplated the self as undivided, it is meditated upon by me. (27.73)
The auspicious circle of moon-like nails upon the pair of lotus feet, containing the two points (bindu), is proclaimed by the Śaivas, the Śāktas, and the great sages as the abode of Śiva. (27.74)
The Vaiṣṇavas bring joy to the eternal Supreme Person;
other people declare His form to consist of both Hari and Hara.
The foremost sages describe the state of the Goddess as eternally manifest, overflowing with the bliss of her feet, and consisting of both Puruṣa and Prakṛti. (27.76)
"Immersed in the state known as the male principle (puṃprakṛti), they shine upon the surface of the earth.
Thus, O Lord, I have described to you this unsurpassed mantra-yoga. (27.77)
Following the path of yoga, one should meditate with a well-composed mind;
first, by means of the great inhalation, one should join the mind to the root.
Having contracted that power (śakti) between the anus and the genitals, one should awaken it;
by means of the sequence of piercing the lingas, one should cause it to reach the wheel of the bindu.
One should contemplate the supreme Śakti, who is the attainment of Śambhu, as being in a state of oneness;
there, one should contemplate the nectar-essence arising from her, resembling molten lac juice. (27.80)
Having caused the supreme power known as Kṛṣṇā, which bestows the perfection of yoga, to flow [downward],
he pierces the six cakras there and satiates them with a stream of nectar.
Then the wise one should lead [the breath] through that path back to the mūlādhāra;
thus, for one who practices the vital air day after day—
One is liberated from the bondage of existence through [the cessation of] the sufferings of old age, death, and so forth;
all the mantras taught and explained in the Tantra are accomplished, and not otherwise. (27.83)
Indeed, O beloved of Yoga, one shall quickly become self-perfected in yoga;
for whatever qualities belong to the Lord who performs the fivefold cosmic acts, [those are attained]. (27.84)
Those qualities certainly arise in the best of practitioners and not otherwise.
Thus, O Lord, I have explained to you this unsurpassed mantra-yoga. (27.85)
Now listen to that which is called *dhāraṇā*, the supreme ointment:
having fixed the mind upon you, undivided by space, time, and so forth. (27.86)
Or, having meditated upon me, the excellent practitioner shall attain identity with me;
by uniting the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman, he quickly becomes one with that. || 27.87 ||
Having fixed the mind upon the desired foot, which is variegated with the filaments of its nails;
or else, when the mind that reflects does not quickly attain success. (27.88)
Then, through the application of its constituent parts, the yogi should practice yoga;
he should fix his mind upon the lotus-feet, variegated by the filaments of the toenails.
Likewise, her pair of shanks were adorned like the stalks of plantain trees in a grove,
and her two thighs possessed a luster equal to the trunk-staffs of elephants in rut.
Then, in the navel deep as a whirlpool of the Gaṅgā, at the aperture of accomplishment (siddhibila),
and likewise in the belly, the chest, the hands, the Śrīvatsa, and the Kaustubha.
Upon his forehead, which resembles the nectar of the full moon, he wears beautiful earrings;
he is adorned with the staff-like arms bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
The practitioner, purified and with a pure mind, should worship in these locations—the two [spots] of the crown and the earrings, which resemble a thousand suns. (27.93)
"By fixing the mind upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one certainly becomes a Vaiṣṇava.
Thus has been declared the Vaiṣṇava meditation, which is pure sattva and perfectly stainless. (27.94)
Devotees of Viṣṇu, firm in mind, worship their own seat;
until the dissolution of the mind occurs, one should contemplate Kṛṣṇa as the Self. (27.95)
Until the accomplishment of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), such is the determination of the meaning of yoga;
until then, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra and practice recitation and fire-offerings (*japa-homa*). (27.96)
Beyond this, O beautiful one, there is nothing further to be done; once the supreme reality is known, enough with all worldly observances.
Therefore, one should always practice meditation, yoga, and recite mantras;
for in a house enveloped in darkness, a jar is seen by means of a lamp. (27.98)
Thus, that Self which was chosen and made the object of focus by Manu has been described to you, O Lord; this is the unsurpassed mantra-yoga. (27.99)
Having performed [this], one is liberated from the sufferings arising from sin; there is no doubt about this.
It is difficult to attain for those attached to sense objects, yet easily attained even by yogins. (27.100)
If a wise person desires accomplishment in this world, they should not abandon that which is easily attained:
the knowledge of Brahman, yogic meditation, the recitation of mantras, ritual actions, and so forth. (27.101)
He who always acts auspiciously is indeed Vīrabhadra, the king of yogins;
he should always practice devotion toward Śambhu and toward Śrīvidyā, which is higher than the highest.
And at the time of practicing yoga, through meditation and other means alone, one performs reflection, chanting, meditation, remembrance, and service at the feet. (27.103)
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender—by the grace of this devotion, the practitioner indeed becomes liberated while living. (27.104)
Having become beloved by the yogins, the ascetic should remain established in meditative absorption (samādhi).

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the section on accomplished mantras, in the *Ṣaṭcakrasārasaṅketa*, part of the *Pāśavakalpa* for determining the essential meaning, in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*. 27.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"O beloved, worshipped by the three worlds, [this is taught] now for the sake of attaining spiritual perfection."
But the sign of mantra-siddhi is extremely difficult for yogins to attain.
Having drunk the supreme nectar flowing from the blossoming lotus of your face, he composed the Tantras; tell me, what is there that does not exist therein? (28.2)
Ānandabhairavī said:
O Ānandabhairaveśvara, I shall declare to you the definitive characteristics of the attainment of mantra-siddhi in accordance with the path of yoga. (28–3)
When the mind is eternally well-stabilized, there occurs the destruction of defects such as the afflictions on the path;
all excellent signs are manifest, endowed with the accomplishment of supreme mantras;
death is removed, and the vision of the Lord of the World, whose intellect is supreme, is attained.
Yoga increases the absence of affliction; through its application, it possesses the remainder of the applications of origination. (28.4)
It enters forcibly into the bodies of kings and agitates them;
it moves upward through their superior city and downward through their inferior city. One should behold the lower aperture as the union with the woman who traverses the sky.
As the world is blown [with the sound of his fame], he hears the incomparable glories of the worlds. (28.5)
Thus, by means of these auspicious signs such as the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi) and so forth,
he goes to the enchanting city of Vaikuṇṭha when the Lord of Beings perceives his welfare.
One who is an adversary to the world should take refuge in his own side. || 28-6 ||
His fame is his ornament, his devotion is fruitful from the very beginning, and his actions are joined with worldly enjoyment;
his heart is filled with supreme devotion for the gods, he is proficient in all rites,
