and having conquered the three worlds through his skill in the service of his own masters, he lives for a long time.
The practice of the eight limbs brings mastery over the world and leads to supreme consciousness. (28.7)
Free from desire for enjoyments, possessing that which is capable of causing wonder to the people of the world,
the destroyer of diseases, with a heart detached, fond of dispassion and devotion,
[practicing] renunciation and the cessation of wandering, as well as the quelling of the ocean-like net of illusion.
Sovereignty, the essence of poetry, wealth, people, the host of Lakṣmī, and the power of recitation. || 28-8 ||
May there be joy in the lotus of the heart, the acquisition of sons and wealth, honor on the path of the virtuous,

a vessel filled with the jewels of the ocean of desires, delight from a multitude of beloved women, the attainment of Manu’s beloved [the Vedas] and other signs of success, and the realization of the singular nature of Hari, Hara, and Brahmā.
He who bears the singular seal of uninterrupted auspicious bliss, which is the very gravity of the worlds.
Thus has been described by Mahādeva the exposition of the Uttaratantra, including the characteristics of mantra-siddhi as superior, inferior, and middling. (28.10)
In birth after birth, the sages and the chief gods, assuming divine forms within the lineage of Nara, are perpetually and incessantly satisfied. (28.11)
Whether it be for you or even for me, whenever one performs libations, fire-offerings, and meals with a virtuous mind, that mind certainly becomes steadfast. (28.12)
This practice of inhaling the vital breath and fixing it upon the subtle moon should be performed daily as a duty, repeatedly, both by day and by night. (28.13)
Today one should consecrate this ritual, the supreme means for attaining yoga;
by it, even a wicked mantra becomes effective for that illustrious and virtuous person who speaks rightly. (28.14)
Listen, however, as I describe this collection of defects according to the truth:
for those [practices] corrupted by defects such as being "cut" and so forth, success is achieved through the true principle of yoga. (28.15)
The Mistress of the World, who is free from the bonds of the Lord of Gods, bestows perfect accomplishment;
when propitiated, this Great Vidyā is devoid of pride in prowess. (28.16)
The single-syllable [mantra] is devoid of power, but when joined with the *vāgbhava* [syllable], it becomes most radiant;
that goddess is the supreme one, the *haṃsinī* enclosed within the *tāra*. (28.17)
The supreme Vidyā Kāmeśvarī was pierced by the King of Desire;
formerly afflicted by his arrow, she was established as Bhuvaneśī. (28.18)
I am that maiden who is the Great Vidyā, by whom the seven enemies are awakened;
I am Tārā, whose nature is like the moon, and who is solely the power (śakti) of Śiva. (28.19)
O Lord, hear now the web of defects belonging to the Bhairavī Vidyās;
these defects perish for those who follow the path of Yoga. (28.20)
Since the goddess Kuṇḍalinī is brought face-to-face with consciousness through yoga, one should therefore always practice yoga for the sake of accomplishing all mantras. (28.21)
Bhairavī is cursed by Brahmā, burnt, and likewise pinned down;
she is the bringer of destruction, deluded, and yet approved.
With minds intoxicated by great passion, they are fainted, deprived of vigor, paralyzed, slain, severed, pierced, obstructed, and terrified. (28.23)
Seedless, devoid of power, asleep, intoxicated, and emaciated;
turned away, sightless, she is terrified and ill-prepared. (28.24)
Suṣuptā, Bheditā, Prauḍhā, Bālikā, Mālinī, Kṣamā, Bhayadā, Yuvatī, Krūrā, Dāmbhikā, and Śokasaṅkaṭā. (28–25)
One who is devoid of a trident lacks accomplishment; one with a protruding forehead is dull-witted; one with missing ears or a missing nose is excessively wrathful and has crooked limbs. (28.26)

She is quarrelsome, delighting in strife, distressed by the loss of her position and home, fallen from dharma, excessively old or excessively young, and a destroyer of spiritual accomplishments. (28.27)
Kṛtavīryā, Mahābhīmā, Krodhapuñjā, Dhvaṃsinī, Kālavidyā, Sūkṣmadharmā, Vidharmā, and Dharmamohinī. || 28-28 ||
Stationed in a difficult place, with a distracted mind, fierce, and moving with a violent gait;
flickering like a torch, sharp, eating little, and without parts. (28–29)
Devoid of reality, squinting, trembling, embraced, conquered, extremely concealed, afflicted by hunger, cunning, and both steady and unsteady in meditation. (28–30)
These vidyās shall become propitious through the restraint of the time of yoga;
accomplishment shall come through the state of a hero (vīrabhāva) and by means of the rite of preliminary service (puraścaraṇa).
Ānandabhairavī said:
There, the hero should worship a beloved woman, whether she belongs to another or is his own, who is adorned with ornaments, beautiful, and sweetly smiling. (28–32)
Her limbs were heated by the fire of passion, her very form was the bliss of wine;
she was a Yoginī, a Kaulinī, worthy, virtuous in character, and beloved of the Kula.
One should worship a consecrated maiden or young woman who has a restless face, whose lotus-face is enchanting, and who resides in various lands. (28–34)
She was a reciter of mantras, possessing a gentle smile and delighting in a very slow gait;
her body was slender, she was exceedingly beautiful, and her form was adorned with ornaments. (28–35)
Whatever fruit a man obtains by the gift of ten million maidens, that same fruit he obtains immediately from the worship of Kāminī. (28–36)
Then, for the sake of attaining yoga, one should worship the sixteen maidens who are yoginīs with supreme devotion, using garments, ornaments, and decorations. (28–37)
With various kinds of flour-based foods, cooked foods derived from living beings,
as well as curd, milk, ghee, and fresh butter mixed with sugar.
With foods mixed with pieces of stone and endowed with fruits of various flavors, with coconuts such as the *cūḍā* and others, and with yellow oranges; || 28–39 ||
With various fragrant fruits endowed with diverse scents, with musk, sandalwood, and *śrīkhaṇḍa* along with fresh sprouts. || 28–40 ||
One should worship them with diligence using flowers grown in water as well as those grown on land, along with various fragrant blossoms, red sandalwood, and saffron. (28–41)
One should worship the Kula goddess in an empty house or likewise in a secluded forest; having invited her, one should then say, "Welcome."
Having purified [the object] with the *arghya* water, one should perform the rite of *amṛtīkaraṇa* (rendering it nectar).
Having brought the *Śakti* face-to-face, the yogin will certainly become a *vīra*.
And listen, O beloved of my life, to the auspicious sixteen-fold goddess Śakti, who is dear to the Kula-cakra, the great power Śrī Kalāvatī. (28–44)
A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, a Śūdrā, or a beautiful Veśyā; one who is adorned with the ornaments of noble lineage, proud, and not excessively tawny. (28–45)
The washerwoman, the actress, the Kaula woman, the dark-limbed one, the stout-bodied one, she who comes by appointment, the wife, the clever woman, and likewise the dyer. (28.46)
Khaṭakī and Kolakanyā, who follow the path of the Kula, are beautiful in all their limbs, auspicious, with lovely eyes and smiling faces. (28.47)
O Lord, if those who are devoted to initiation are to be given initiation at that time, it has been explained according to the *Sūkṣmatantra*, as previously indicated. (28–48)
Beautiful in all her limbs, pure, born of a family from the world of purity, a young woman devoted to yoga—that goddess is considered a ḍākinī. (28.49)
Having brought her, one should cause her to receive the great mantra for the sake of attaining the desired success.
Thereafter, those [women] should be worshipped; however, one should not perform [the rite] with those who lack initiation.
One should cause [the disciple] to receive the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rāma for the sake of attaining spiritual perfection;
after that, one should first give those [mantras] to them, and thereafter perform the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra.

One should cause [the disciple] to receive the seed-syllable of Ānandabhairavī, the Goddess Śakti, and one's own seed-syllable; or else, one should bestow the perfected mantra (siddhamantra) of Śrīvidyā.
Or else, one should visualize her as consisting of pure illusion alone, with hands red with anger,
blazing within the root-lotus, and originating from the Svayambhū-flower.
Having bestowed this Great Māyā upon him, one shall become victorious. First, in the cavity of the left ear, [recite] the fire-mantra three times; in the other [ear], three times. (28–54)
Therefore, at the conclusion of the initiation into eternal bliss, the wise one should cause the training to be undertaken;
for all recitation has its root in initiation, and the grace of the Guru has its root in initiation.
She who, having taken recourse to initiation, should recite the Māyā-mantra, she is the supreme Khecarī;
by the mere worship of her, I am pleased—of this there is no doubt. (28–56)
The existence of the lords of the worlds in the form of women—I am that woman; there is no doubt, whether beautiful or wretched, or another. (28.57)
For the sake of protecting Sundarī and for her swift destruction, one should contemplate the Saṃhitās as being of a contemptible nature and appearing as delusions to the practitioner. (28.58)
One should fully worship that supreme knowledge which bestows liberation, which is beautiful and moves according to its will; she is Bhāvinī and Bhavānī. || 28-59 ||
O Lord, I am eternally and firmly established within the body of that deity;
and indeed, the yogi who is equal toward all things, being the self of all, shall lead [me] forth.
Otherwise, there would be a loss of accomplishment through the investigation of existence and non-existence;
for without existence, the mass of existents cannot be accomplished. (28.61)
One should perform the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the *kula* for the sake of liberation from both *kula* and *akula*;
for thus the wise yogi becomes imperishable, steadfast, and liberated even while living.
Having established Brāhmaṇī and Sundarī, one should worship them in sequence;
the great arghya is placed in the left hand, while the seat and other offerings are in the right.
One should offer water for the feet and seats, and welcome them by their respective names;
at that time, one should also sprinkle them with the water contained in the arghya vessel.
Having formed the *dhenumudrā* and performed the rite of nectarization (*amṛtīkriyā*) with the mantra "vaṃ," one should bring about the transformation of form at the conclusion of the nectarization.
Having performed the naming with designations, one should offer a seat.
Śrī Bhairavī said:
"Now, O Beloved, I shall explain the practice of piercing the six cakras."
By performing which, the immortals roam in this world of the moving and the unmoving;
it removes untimely death and destroys all diseases. (28.67)
Through yoga, the classes of living beings become possessed of the form of the immortals within the great lotus of the six chakras, which is endowed with the qualities of all sentient beings.
In matters of dharma and adharma, in the kingdom of the mind, in the sacrifice that is the treasury of all sciences,
it is the remover of all sins, foremost among which is the defilement of the Kali age.
Having fixed their minds upon Mahākāla, living beings go everywhere;
having heard this, the great hero, the discerning one who knows the supreme truth— || 28.70 ||
Again, O Śaṅkara, he desired to know through knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Ānandabhairava said:
"O fair-faced one, tell me the story of the piercing of the six cakras."
For the welfare of all living beings, reveal that which is adorned with golden color;
O Giver of Boons, speak of the arising of the yogas.
By whatever yoga the wise desire for the sake of welfare, its accomplishment shall come in due course of time through the destruction of the net of time. (28.73)
And for the purpose of cleansing the time, the completion [of the rite] was performed again.
Ānandabhairavī said: "First, one should effect supreme bliss arising from the ocean of rasa. (28.74)
Listen to that supreme sequence for [overcoming] dullness, which is endowed with mild qualities:
one should perform the praise in the root-lotus as a preliminary rite for Kuṇḍalinī. (28.75)

During the period of *puraścaraṇa*, at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), in daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), in rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*), and likewise in all religious duties and virtuous acts; || 28-76 ||
Having performed devotion toward the guru and others, as well as the eternal [deities], one should recite:
"Oṃ, salutation to the Guru; Oṃ, salutation to the Guru, the supreme deity. (28.77)
To her whose nature is all phenomena, to her whose nature is all-knowledge; Oṃ, to her who is the dissolution of worldly existence, Oṃ, to her who destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice. || 28-78 ||
Oṃ, salutations again and again to Bhadrakālī; oṃ, to Kapālinī; oṃ, to Umā; oṃ, to Māheśvarī;
oṃ, to the savior from all perils; oṃ, to Mahādevī. || 28-79 ||
Oṃ! She who is Māyā, the power that brings about the destruction of the illusory Dānavas, whose instrument is forbearance;
the great Caṇḍā who draws forth the strength of the illustrious Śumbha and the Asura Mahiṣa;
she who is auspicious, compassionate, fond of blood, and the doer of what is dear; she whose body is wrath and whose lotus is red.
Cāmuṇḍā is the night of the blood-seed of battle; she is the moonlight and the blue lotus of her moon-like face. || 28-80 ||

She who is the wife, the bestower of victory, the mistress of men, the remover of fear, the formidable Bhairavī, she who is eternal— may that auspicious Śivā grant protection for the production of Sarasvatī;
may she protect the strength of my senses, which delight in the objects of the physical body.
Adorned with living beings in the form of fierce and blazing flames resting upon his chest.
Having made yourself one who possesses the lineage of yoga in your own abode, always delighting the mind,
ever intent on self-restraint, purified by the practice of devotion to the Supreme,
O Śambhu, always meditate upon the lotus feet of the Lord who has removed the dust of worldly existence.
One who has a pleasing vision of the objects of knowledge becomes a yogi who restrains the three worlds. || 28-82 ||

Free from worldly desire, devoted to the service of his own guru, purifying, overflowing with the joy of love for the stories of the Infallible One, and having no fondness for crookedness, violence, or insult;
free from the web of faults such as wasting time— he is a true devotee of the Śakti, a blessed servant of the Lord.
To the beloved of the illustrious Śakti, who is beyond the reach of beautiful knowledge and who possesses self-respect; || 28-83 ||

To the one whose abode is bound with subtle garlands and extreme subtlety, who possesses auspicious marks, who is the witness, the cause of various causes, who is accompanied by his refuge, and who is the offering of Brahman with form—
to that eternal, great, and awakened one, the knower of yoga and all things.
I bow to that Supreme Person, the highest swan-like sun who is the portion of the three worlds.

O Creator, she appears in the lap of Māyā as the sole seed of delight for those of beautiful conduct; she is agitated by a multitude of waves, incomparable, with a face like the vehicle of the fire of time, her mouth adorned with necklaces and armlets, and her countenance like the bud of the black Kalika of the Kaula tradition, which is the poison of wine.
May she who wears yellow garments, who has a swift seat, and who is affectionate, protect all my limbs. || 28-85 ||
She is the young maiden, the strength, the vehicle, the dense thicket, the honor, the sustenance;
she is Khaṃ Khaṃ Khaṃ, the moving and the unmoving, the one who moves through the lineages, the one who moves in speech, the crooked one;
Caṃ Caṃ Caṃ, the goddess of the yak-tail fan and the lioness, she who has entered the verses, the assembly.
May she whose face is like a lotus, who struck off the heads of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, protect my arms.

Kaṃ kaṃ kaṃ! Kamalākalā, whose fruit is liberation, who possesses a multitude of hissing movements, Paṃ paṃ paṃ! Supreme Ramā, victorious in her gait, free from attachment, moving as a living being; Taṃ taṃ taṃ! She who is ruddy like the dispelling of darkness, compassionate, the Mother, powerful, the Savior.
Bhaṃ bhaṃ bhaṃ! May she who removes fear and acts for my welfare be within me. 28-87.

Jhaṃ jhaṃ jhaṃ! She who stands upon the path of the movement of the wind; she who is delighted by Lakṣmī (Ramā); she who purifies me, who am indeed stained (maṃ maṃ maṃ malinaṃ hi māṃ); she who is mounted upon a horse; she who is the slayer of enemies;
she who removes the fear of her devotees; she who stands as the fire of destruction for the lineage of the enemy at the front of battle.
May she, the mass of splendor, radiant with her two glowing feet, be ever present.
Gaṃ Gaṃ Gaṃ! May she who is the embodiment of the Guru, from whom arises a mass of bliss for Gaṇapati;
whose eyes possess the brilliance of ten million suns and the reddish luster of the essence of Tārā’s lotus;
whose path is dear to Sadāśiva; and who possesses the splendor of ten million rising suns—may she protect my eye forever.
The snout is adorned with a shaven head, while the garland of human heads is dangling and even.

May the Yogeshī, who arises from the intense discourse of the Moon-crested Lord and who is human in form, protect my head; may she, who is infinite and resides upon the peak of Mount Meru in embodied form, always protect my forehead and the pair of ears. May Kaivalī protect my cheeks.
And the earth, the supporter of the world, being pleased, held the surface of the eighth and sixty-fourth [levels].
The two cavities at the tips of the nose are Bhṛgutarā; the three eyes are Tāriṇī; the hair is Kuntalakālikā; she is Su-kapilā, whose seat is the Kailāsa mountain;
she wears a pure garland of skeletons; she is well-clad; and she is the destroyer of Daityas with her rows of teeth.
The external mantra is the boat for crossing the infinite scriptures; it is the paralyzer of names and speech. || 28.91 ||
Haṃ haṃ haṃ! May she who delights in the terrible devouring of men, the wandering one, protect me!
May she who seizes Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa surely effect the crushing of my enemies!
May the terrifying one, blazing with the heat of her majesty, burn them away; may the increasing one bring about my growth.
Intoxicated by the confusion of the fragrance of *mandāra* flowers, they were deluded by their own cleverness. || 28-92 ||
May Śyāmā protect [us]— she who resounds with the cries of ten million suns, who utters *haṃ* and *phaṭ*,

who bestows victory through the essence of all festivals of bliss, and who is the guardian everywhere. *Kṣauṃ kṣauṃ kṣauṃ*— she whose syllables are firm, who causes destruction, and who destroys defects in every limb.
The supreme [goddess] is the one who seizes the hair of the enemy of the body (Śiva), and she is filled with the nectar from the locks of his matted hair.
May the sound "ghaṃ ghaṃ ghaṃ" of the jar-like throat of the Lord of the Family, which shatters obstacles, protect me in every age; may my body everywhere be filled with intense fearlessness,
and may Kālikā, who dispels sleep, protect my lineage as she covers the shores of Laṅkā.
Naṃ naṃ naṃ; she whose face and eyes are like beautiful lotuses is Lākinī, endowed with auspicious marks. || 28-94 ||
May she who consists of mudrās, my wealth, always protect the surface of my back within my womb;

may she who is the dyer of the formidable Kāla, the passionate one who delights in dyeing, protect my liberation; may the Kṛtyā, the barber’s daughter with a moon-like face, the subtle one, protect my life-breath.
She was greatly adorned with a garland of mandāra flowers that had a jeweled knot. || 28-95 ||

May the Goddess Satkriyā, who is worshipped by yogis, who is ever-eager, and who resides at the root, protect my home; may she, the intoxicated and devoted wife, protect my virtue, fame, and ultimate welfare.
May Kālī, the great Yoginī, who appears like a flash of lightning in the midst of the lotus of Dharma, protect me.
The unique digit of the garland on the head of Hara, which destroys the excessive pride of the intoxicated. 28-96.
May she who is my secret victory, even my phallic emblem, protect my root-lotus;
may that maiden, the destroyer of fear for the Snowy Mountain, protect the region of my hips.
May she, the power whose form is the mind, the crest-flame of the fire arising in the hearts of all, protect me.
O Lord, may Lakṣmī, my beloved who is skilled in fulfilling desires, protect my devotion. 28-97.
Gaurī, who bestows dignity upon the earth, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) who destroys great delusion—Vaṃ Vaṃ Vaṃ! May the excellent Varuṇī, the fine wine, protect my waist forever.
That Peak Syllable (Kūṭā), devoid of sun, moon, and fire, consisting of her own will, [protects] my face. (28–98)
Whoever recites this hymn at all times and on every occasion shall become a lord of the yoga of time and a treasury of great knowledge.
In the awakening of the root-lotus, in the accomplishment of the root-primal nature, in the awakening of one's own mantra, and during times of terrible distress; (100)
His calamities perish just as darkness does before the sun;
at all times and in all places, it is the destroyer of great sins. (28.101)
He shall be a son of the Yoginīs in the Kali age; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Kandavāsinī," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Wheels) in the *Pāśavakalpa*, concerning the determination of the seat of the inner state (*bhāvāsana*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* (The Great Tantra Illuminator) of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*. 28.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Now I shall explain here, according to the true principle, the yoga of the six cakras."
Having performed the various practices of Kuṇḍalinī yoga, a man shall become a yogi. || 29-1 ||
The piercing of the six chakras from the root-center (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) is considered [the goal];
indeed, various yoga scriptures reside within these six chakras. (29-2)
He who knows the six wheels here shall become a knower of the meaning of all treatises;
the root-lotus has four petals, arising from the letters beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*.
The yogi should meditate again and again upon that which is golden-hued and stainless, in a solitary, empty forest filled with herds of animals and flocks of birds. (29.4)
In a fearless and beautiful place, free from famine and other such calamities, the practitioner of mantra, having assumed a firm posture, should become devoted to the path of yoga. (29.5)
Then, in accordance with my teaching, the yogi shall quickly become [perfected];
the yogi who always meditates on the syllable *va* on the eastern petal shall be happy. (29-6)

Golden-hued, the benefactor of men, born of the essence of beings, seated upon the eastern petal, auspicious; beloved of the intoxicated, whose abode is the rutting elephant, the fulfiller of the purpose of mantras, bearing a cooling form. (29-7)
I bow to the Guru, the abode of the time of yogic experience, consisting of light, the bestower of the abundance of supernatural powers;
the primordial syllable *vaṃ*, the means for attaining the supreme state, Nārāyaṇa, the fifth object of meditation, the infallible. (29-8)

One should meditate upon the letter Śa, which has the luster of the golden mountain, the ancient instrument of prosperity for the Lord of Gaurī, beloved of Lakṣmī, and eternally adorned with all kinds of gold—the most excellent southern petal, [to be contemplated] with constant joy. (29.9)

I worship that leaf, the golden mountain of attributes, which is adorned with the sixfold qualities of Śamīśvarī, which effects the piercing of the six lotuses, and which dwells in the state that is both supreme and non-supreme. (29.10)
I meditate with joy upon the beloved one, whose essence is the bliss of the letter *Sa* (*sakāra*), who dwells on the peak of the great mountain of gold;
I joyfully meditate upon Jaya, the Lord of the Clouds, the destroyer of the great delusion of *māyā*. 29-11.
For the sake of purifying one's state of being, the practitioner of mantra should always meditate upon [the deity] as having four arms, a pair of arms, eighteen arms, or eight hands. (29.12)
Then, one should meditate upon the beautiful, supreme self-manifested liṅga in the center of the pericarp, which bestows the perfection of yoga upon yogins. (29.13)
In the morning, the Great Goddess Kuṇḍalī, the bestower of yoga, envelops him who is as radiant as the sun and possesses a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
Adorned with three and a half coils and knots, she bestows liberation;
always auspicious while asleep, she destroys even the greatest of sins.
Upon his head, the bearer of the moon shines incessantly;
she is the eternal sustainer of his breath, the sustainer of the life-force of the worlds.
Delusion, like a sleeping serpent, is like hundreds of millions of suns;
when it abandons the *liṅga* and sets out upon the great path, [it perishes]. (29.17)
Then the yogi becomes perfected, pure through the practice of meditation and concentration;
he is eternally composed of bliss when he is the ever-present Caitanya-kuṇḍalinī.
The yogi who, having fixed his mind within the middle of the *suṣumnā* channel in the great subtle aperture, becomes intent upon the path of the breath; || 29-19 ||
Then that supreme Kuṇḍalinī, becoming conscious, quickly flows toward the region of the back,
the great staff, the root of Meru, which is of great luster.
From the base of the spine up to the lower part of the aperture of Brahmā, he eternally assumes the form of a pillar;
and by the name Kanakācala (Golden Mountain), he shines throughout the three worlds.
In the midst of that is the supreme, most subtle Suṣumnā, which possesses many forms; she is the very nature of the mind and sage, and she brings about the consciousness of the mind.
In the midst of that shines the one called Vajrā, who destroys terrible transgressions;
she bestows accomplishment upon those possessing the knowledge of reality and liberation upon those whose form is the Kula.
In the midst of that is the goddess Citriṇī, who increases the satisfaction of the deities;
she is the well-wisher, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), and the destroyer of the net of Time.
She protects all the supreme wheels that bear the form of lotuses,
which pervade the mandala of the three worlds and are the manifest embodiments of nectar.
That goddess Citrā, of beautiful splendor, herself supported [the child] upon her palms, her back, the upper part of her body, her head, her chest, and her navel. (29–26)
In the pit of the throat, within the center of the wheel, the Egg of Brahmā always protects the body for the sake of the Lord—the three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving. (29.27)
The practitioner who visualizes the lotus with its variegated and beautiful arrangement attains yoga through such contemplation; through contemplation, Śiva is realized. (29.28)
Through meditative cultivation one attains power; therefore, one should take recourse in cultivation.
By performing the meditation on the six chakras, a man becomes a great yogi. (29–29)
Having become endowed with all dharmas, he shines upon the circle of the earth;
he becomes one who goes everywhere if his mind is dissolved in the lotus. (29–30)
By the mere meditation on the lotus, one becomes like space;
by fixing the mind upon the Great Lotus, one will certainly become a great devotee. (29–31)
If one is devoted, O Lord, then he is liberated, without a doubt;
if he is liberated, he remains in the midst of the world, solely intent upon the yoga of meditation.
Then, having realized the supreme state of Time, he becomes all-seeing and all-knowing;
there is no doubt that he becomes omniscient and auspicious in every respect. (29–33)
And in the middle region is Citriṇī, the Brahma-nāḍī of great splendor;
she is the eternal Goddess, the possessor of all parts, who bestows all accomplishments. (29–34)
The Blessed Lady is of the nature of space, the embodiment of all consciousness;
she is the Supreme Brahman of a single form, while the three worlds are beyond Brahman. (29–35)
When the three worlds are Brahman, then, O Lord, they are the abode of existence;
by fixing the mind upon the Great Abode (Mahālaya), one shall achieve victory over all time. (29–36)
The conqueror of death, the great hero, the great umbrella, and the great refuge speaks by virtue of his lordship through a form that pervades all. (29–37)
Always born of mantra, large-eyed and of serene intellect, he who remains in one place goes to the constellation; for he, O Śaṅkara, is indeed such. (29–38)
With single-minded vision, free from hunger and thirst, and having conquered speech, one should direct the mind toward the formless; then, O Lord, this person becomes great. (29–39)
But for those who do not know the Lord, there is neither [ordinary] dissolution nor the Great Abode;
rather, for the yogis, it is indeed the Great Dissolution—of this there is no doubt. (29–40)

When one effects the dissolution of the mind day and night for the sake of purifying the yoga of the mind, that very state is liberation; it is the ocean of qualities, the form of the fire of time, and one's own innate deity. (29.41)
Possessing the great yoga of the mind, free from transformation; adorned by the purity of the section on desire and action; beneficial for all states of existence, wise, and unassailable.
The devotee established in Mahālaya is indeed immortal. || 29-42 ||
Proud, with a mind discerning the meaning of reflection, and free from the intensity of cleverness and mental agitation— the yogi becomes a sovereign of practitioners (sādhaka-cakravartin).
One should always perform the relinquishment of the mind within the lotus of the sky.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, named "The Great Dissolution," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, within the *Uttara-tantra*, the illumination of the great tantras, in the revelation of the six chakras, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 29.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Mahākāla, I shall now explain the discernment of the root-lotus."
By performing which, one becomes immortal and may dwell for the four ages of time. || 30-1 ||
Then, for the purpose of piercing the six cakras, one should take recourse to the power that pierces;
one should fully rely upon the Yoginī who cuts through all knots.
I shall proclaim her mantras by which a man becomes accomplished;
first, hear the great mantra, the supreme incantation of Bhedinī.
First, having extracted Kālī, then the Brahma-mantra;
next, having extracted the Praṇava of the Goddess, and immediately after that, the Bhedanī.
Therefore, from that [source], one should take hold of me and cause both to reach [their goal];
at the end of the word *cittacañcī*, protect me and the pair. (30.5)
O destroyer of untimely death, remove the duality within me at the end of sound;
remove your own pair of great sins. Salutations, salutations to the consort of Agni! (30.6)
O Lord, one should recite this mantra there against the ḍākinīs and rākṣasas;
first extracting the Praṇava, and after that, the Brahma-mantra.
Then, having uttered the word "Śāmbhavī," followed by the word "Brāhmaṇī," one establishes the mind upon the two-word phrase "Tāraya. (30.8)
Having extracted the word *chedinī* from my mind,
and having removed the great darkness, [use] the word *chedaya* as a dual form.
Having extracted the mantra ending with "svāhā," the wise one should recite it within the root-lotus;
by the grace of this mantra, a person shall become liberated while living. (30-10)
Likewise, O Śaṅkara, one should mutter the mantra of the Yoginī-strī right there:
"Oṃ, O you of terrible form, O all-pervading one, O Śaṅkara. (30.11)
"O Mahāyoginī, take away my sin, grief, and disease;
cut down my adversaries," having said this, bestow the twofold yoga upon me.
Having extracted the mantra ending with "svāhā," a person who recites it becomes a yogi;
through the practice of yoga, he becomes a king among yogis and attains the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
Having meditated again and again on the Ḍākinī joined with Brahmā at the root, the yogi who knows yoga should constantly recite the mantra with the Brahmā-mantra. (30.14)
I shall proclaim the Brahma-mantra; by its recitation alone, even a dull-witted person becomes a king among yogis through the grace of the Brahma-mantra—of this there is no doubt. (30.15)
Having extracted three *praṇavas*, followed by a pair of long *praṇavas*,
at the end of that [are] three *praṇavas*, and then "Brahma, Brahma" three times each.
At the end of the word *sarvasiddhi*, one should recite the word *pālaya* and then the mantra:
*sattvaṃ guṇo rakṣa rakṣa māyā svāhā*. (30.17)
O Supreme Lord, listen to the king of mantras of the ḍākinīs;
by reciting which, the ḍākinīs who maintain the stability of the three worlds become submissive. (30.18)
Whoever should mutter the mantra of the Ḍākinī, Caitanyā Kuṇḍalī, will instantly attain accomplishment without effort and the manifestation of the Supreme Self. (30.19)
Having extracted the three *māyās*, then the single *praṇava* (oṃ),
then the great sound at the end of *ḍākinī*, and then the word *ḍākinyambā*.
Again, having extracted the *praṇava*, followed by three *māyās*,
and at the end the two-word phrase "sādhaya mama yogasiddhim" (accomplish my yoga-perfection).
O Goddess of the gods, having extracted the *manu*, the yogi becomes dull-witted by merely reciting it;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should recite it and perform worship for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*. (30.22)
Having worshipped everywhere with equanimity of mind, with various substances and so forth, and with the mind as an offering in the root lotus, || 30-23 ||
Then, having recited the *Mānasajāpa* and the *Kālipāvana-stotra*,
one becomes a king among yogis and shall dwell in the abode of the six cakras.
O Maheśvara, for the sake of protecting him who constantly praises the ritual endowed with power, my *yantra* [is established] upon the surface of the earth.
Listen to that hymn for the sake of yoga and attend to it with careful attention;
by the grace of this hymn, one shall come under the power of Mahālaya. (30.26)

I bow to Brahmā, who is like a refuge for hosts of swans, whose mouth is that of a god, who is the sole cause for the bestowal of knowledge, whose eyes are like the fire and moon blooming within a lotus,
the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśa) residing in the path of speech, possessing pure intellect, as radiant as the rising sun, and of beautiful complexion.
One should meditate upon him, the bestower of boons upon gods and men, embraced by the ḍākinī in the root lotus.
One should joyfully meditate upon the eternal Ḍākinī, who is devoted to Brahman and composed of bliss—
red in hue, she who moves along and deludes, who knows the lineage-path (kula-patha), and who possesses the knowledge of the Kula;
she whose radiance resides in the center of the earth-disk, near the middle of the root-lotus.
The science that abides in its cause, which deludes the course [of existence], which has the Vedas as its arms, and which brings joy to worldly existence. || 30-28 ||
The wise one who, meditating upon her as she hangs like a beautiful necklace from the throat at the root-abode of his own lineage, praises with devotion that wielder of the moon—
who emits rays whose essence consists of various forms and transformations— [attains success].
I take refuge in that primary state of being, which abides in the primary person, is established in right-mindedness, and is supported by sentient beings. || 30-29 ||
May that Goddess Navadākinī—the self-delighting, wise, and enchanting one who desires the beloved—protect me; may she, born from the ocean of bliss of the way of existence, illuminate my root;
and may the glorious Śrī indeed increase the wheel of my fame.
She is eternal, the source of the arising of perfected qualities, compassionate toward the gods, and deluded by the name of Śrī.

In the midst of that is the supreme Kalā, who bears the fruit of the Kula, whose hands hold arrows and lotuses, who is full like the moon at its peak, who possesses the beauty of the digits of the moon, who is fickle, stainless, and tender; she is the Mother Navamālinī, my Kula, the root-lotus for all time.
That goddess Lavarākiṇī is the sole seed within which the blossoming of the fruit of the Kali age resides.
The nurse, possessed of fortitude, virtuous, sweet, learned, and eloquent;
auspicious, the daughter of a noble family, bearing the form of a man, indeed having a subtle abode;
established in liberation, honored for her stability, situated in the state of existence—the Mother is auspicious for the yogi.
I bow to the one whose intention is auspicious prosperity, who has gone to Śamana, who is arisen from song, and who bears the name Gopā.

She who is the mistress of the Kalka, the wise lady of the Kula, who severs the knots of the path of the Kula; she who is eternal, skilled in virtues, free from fickleness, and as ruddy as a hundred garlands of suns;
she who is the Vidyā whose fierce qualities arise, the source of all, the imperishable syllable that protects the three worlds.
She dwells in the knowledge of Brahman, arisen from the single seed-syllable of white, auspicious bliss. || 30-33 ||

I worship Kāmākhyā, who is the abode of my birth, whose form is manifest through the supreme means, who is intent on the practice of accomplishment (*siddhi*), who is the ultimate reality, and who is rosy with the radiance of all perfected ones due to her immersion in the experience of the meaning of the *Gītā*. She is the true ritual action that serves as the cause [of liberation]. (30–34)
The knowledge of Brahman is the primary cause, the eye that leads to the treasury of virtues, the vehicle of causal bliss;
it is Brahman, the seed of Brahman, the progenitor of the conquest of passion, and the devotion to the performance of sacrifice. (30–35)

I worship that tree which has transcended sorrow, who is disciplined, whose speech is like the water of men, who knows the methods of all sciences, who is the essence of essences, the destroyer of all darkness, and who moves upon a swan.
This path of connection, possessing ever-fresh petals, is known by those who understand the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
it is the radiance of the root-lotus, its essence having the form of the rising young sun and moon. (30–37)

I worship Him who is called Being, established in existence, the ancient one accessible through meditation, who bestows the method of victory upon victory, who is named the Further Shore, the goal of crossing over, born from the Supreme Person, and whose nature is Brahman. 30–38.
Having performed the meditation on Brahmā together with the ḍākinīs, one should recite the hymn;
through this recitation and retention, the practitioner of mantras will attain union with the yoginīs. (30–39)
By the mere recitation of this, great sins are destroyed;
[one beholds] the Lord of the World, whose form is one, and whose eyes are broad lotuses. (30–40)
Having meditated thus, one should recite the hymn; by having recited it, one becomes a king among yogis. || 30-41 ||

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Ḍākinīs," within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, concerning the accomplishment of the six cakras, in the section on accomplished mantras of the Mahātantroddīpana, the latter part of the Śrī Rudrayāmala.
Then the thirty-first chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said: Now, O Lord, I shall proclaim the supreme practice (*sādhana*) of Bhedinī.
By which mere means of accomplishment, the yogi becomes a destroyer of the Kali age.
O Great Lord, practice Mahāyoga in this Kali age;
if it is not accomplished, that time will be the devourer of the body.
By the very means of piercing, the breaking of the knots occurs;
one should meditate upon Ḍākinī in the heart, whose form is supreme bliss. (31.3)
Eight cubits tall, with large eyes, marked by the features of the moon,
she is the lore that deludes the three worlds, bestowing fear upon the wicked and granting boons to the virtuous.

Having meditated upon her as white-complexioned, three-eyed, and enchanting with a beautiful form within the root-lotus, the yogi should worship her with water for the feet and other offerings. || 31-5 ||
There, having dissolved the mind, the yogi becomes one with the ground;
when the mind reaches dissolution, then he should recite her hymn. (31.6)
By the mere recitation of the hymn, one becomes a refuge for all sentient beings;
by reciting it while maintaining meditative concentration, one becomes composed of all accomplishments.
May she who pierces through all knots, who destroys all bonds,
and who stands as the destroyer of all enemies within the various states of existence,
protect my body at all times, day after day.
The Blessed Lady is the embodiment of time, the performer of auspicious deeds. || 31-8 ||

She who is beloved, composed of compassion, and established as the perfection of bliss for the three worlds; she is eternal, the protector, the artistic essence of the Kula, blue, stainless, and tender;
she is Vāṇī, the bestower of accomplishment, the Śāṅkarī who swiftly arises within the fetters of one whose purpose is fulfilled.
It shatters the distinctions of conceptualization, brings about auspiciousness, and bestows the final conclusion of Vedānta.

Speech is a young maiden, a potter, with feet that ring out; she possesses countless garlands of Yamalas; she is the playful space between the eyebrows; she moves within the lotus-clan; she is restless, the time of the body. (31.10)

May she—whose manifestation is differentiation, who consists of the divisions of the differentiated, whose resonance is the sound of the supreme *nāda*, and who is the light of *nāda* and *bindu*—protect my head, forehead, face, heart, waist, and the principal lotus. 31.11

She is the illuminator of the seat of Kāñcī, whose dissolution is in her own state; she has the eyes and chest of a Yoginī; she is not revealed by excessive yoga; she is composed of hundreds of sacrificial offerings; and she is the agent of the terrible withdrawal.

May she whose nature is the bliss of Brahman, who removes all affliction, who shines with eyes like diamonds, adorned with necklaces and other ornaments, and possessing rays like those of a hundred moons—may she protect me, piercing through my body. 31-13.
May that Bagalāmukhī— who shatters all the fortresses of the enemies that are sins, who bestows both heaven and liberation,
and who is a mass of the power of her own being— protect the desired goal within my body, remaining ever-present within my very form.
This [initiation], which destroys various defects while relying on the objects of desire,
which produces beauty and attire, and which protects the performance of sacrifices;
it is the initiation for the wise and the virtuous, bestowing its own yoga.
She shall always quickly pierce my entire body here. || 31-15 ||
May my beloved, who is the source of the arising of peaceful qualities, who is the eternal hope of my body, who is the wealth of my life,
who protects as the family deity of Śrī, who grants victory, who is the supreme essence of Yoga,
who is directly worshipped by the Lord, who is worthy of honor, and who is sought after by the mind— may she protect me.
In my own family, which is most terrible in its victory, agitated and overwhelmed by Time; || 31-16 ||
May she, who is free from both difference and non-difference, whose lotus-like hand bears the glory of the best of gods,
and who removes the false pride of my very body by her form as Kālapriyā, protect my penis, my root-lotus, and the surface of the seven heavens.
Heḍambāsura-sundara, Pirayavatī, Hemāvatī, and Bhāratī. || 31-17 ||
Whoever recites this hymn and praises me in the root-lotus attains yoga; he shall become beloved by the yogis. (31.18)
The mind quickly becomes steady; one swiftly attains sovereignty. Accomplishment shall come without effort, and the wind shall become subject to his control. (31.19)
Indeed, the vision of the Yoginīs is obtained without effort; having become one who is joined with the ocean of existence, one shall wander like an immortal. (31.20)
The Goddess dwells in the root-lotus, illuminating the root-lotus;
she is Mālatī, Mālavī, Maunā, Mālinī, and Manoharā. (31.21)
Mental, intoxicating, venerable, intent upon the union of mudrās;
abiding on Meru, possessing intoxicating flowers, adorned, and situated within the mandala. || 31-22 ||
O Supreme Lord, those young men by whom the Goddess, the stabilizer of the mind, is meditated upon,
attain perfection suddenly in due time.
Now I shall proclaim the supreme hymn of the Great Goddess Chedinī:
"By my grace, O Lord of Ascetics, you shall be the cutter of all knots. (31.24)
By whose grace indeed the infinite yogi [remains] within the circle of saṃsāra.

She who brings joy to the regions, who bestows all virtues, who is the cutter and the place of cutting; she who abides in the oblation, who is devoted to the manifestation of power, who dwells in the treasure during the night— she,
who resides eternally within the lotus of my lineage, must be kept secret by one who knows the ritual procedure.
May Śrī Vāgeśī, clothed in the sky, bestow all yoga. || 31-26 ||

Delighting in sensual pleasures and devoted to the god of love, she is cultivated within the ocean of existence; she possesses the essence arising from the bliss of desire and is the sustainer of those established in yoga.
She delights in the destruction of bodily affliction... [and so forth].
May she wash away the mass of demerit from my body and grant me a collection of dharma. || 31-27 ||
May Kālikā, who dwells within the lotus bud of time and non-time, who has severed the knots while residing in my stable heart, and who stands within the pathways of the channels of my limbs,
bestow upon people sweet speech from the lotus of her face.
May she who is Pañcānanā protect that vulnerability of mine, whose body is beautiful.

Established in the limbs of yoga, abiding in the splendor of stability and dissolution, dwelling within the lotuses of my pores, may the Mother Gaurī— the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, radiant and blazing with weapons— enter the cavity of my heart, cutting through the root-flood [of ignorance].
May she who dwells on Kailāsa and follows me across the mountains protect me by the grace of Rudra. (31.29)
Not ending within, possessing the qualities of the mind, she has reached the further shore of the established doctrines;
bestowing the bliss of enjoyment, she shines for people within the cavity of the Bhaga;
she is both knowledge and ignorance, the various sky, the cutter, and she whose form is concealed.
That Lākinī, whose nature is love, resides within all internal faculties.

You offer my yoga toward heaven, and a state of love for the Supreme Lord within my mind; you are the mother, the knower, and the compassionate one toward the assembly of householders, the cause of every being’s threefold activities, and the creator of all— O Gaṇeśa, may my mind [be fixed] on You.
She is protection, residing in the syllables of protection; she is both with parts and entirely without parts.
May that Queen of Yogins, Kuṇḍalinī, joyfully protect my anus;
may Jahnukanyā, Kamalanilayā, and Rākiṇī protect it with feelings of love;
and may Vedavaktrā, who is free from the heat of the sun, protect my life-force for the sake of liberation.
May the Siddhā, seated upon the petals of the root-lotus, the purifier, protect the mouth. || 31-32 ||
The command of Heramba is established at the time of dissolution; Kākinī is of the nature of wrath. || 31-33 ||
If one of noble lineage practices the *Krodhavidyā*,
he becomes a supreme yogi through the recitation of the hymn to Chedinī;
there is the destruction of all misfortunes and the attainment of success in rites such as ritual washing.
All people shall be under his control, and he shall possess a perpetual, excellent kingdom. || 31-34 ||
The wise man, intent upon great self-restraint, should recite this hymn;
with his mind fixed on the root, he goes forth as the destroyer of all that is undesirable. (31–35)
All success is in the hand of him who takes refuge in this state;
listen, O Supreme Bliss, you who are born from the ocean of nectar! (31–36)
And by hearing and retaining this *Yoginīstotrasāra*, the ascetic [attains success];
this jewel is not to be disclosed, for it bestows the desired fruits upon men. (31–37)
By the mere knowledge of which, the practitioner becomes Śiva. || 31-38 ||
Kaṅkālī, Kulapaṇḍitā, Kulakalā, Kālānalā, Śyāmalā,
Yogendrendra, Surājyanātha, Yajitā, and the other Yoginī who bestows liberation—
[protect] me alone, who am dull-witted, devoid of happiness, penniless, base, wretched, and wicked.
If you provide such protection, then surely protect her; I take refuge in you. (31.39)
O Mistress of Sacrifice, moon-crested one, you who are yourself the supreme,
the abode of union with Heramba, the giver, devoted to giving, the destroyer of Hari, neither terrible nor divine,
the benefactor of the gods— [save] me, O auspicious one, who am devoid of intellect, paralyzed by the body, and exhausted by worship and recitation.
If you, O Yoginī, protect me—an only son and possessing nothing—then you are truly a compassionate being. || 31-40 ||
She is to be meditated upon by one intent on meditation; she is the *karaṇā* and the *cāraṇā*, the Yoginī.

Residing in the moon, well-situated within the body of her own Lord, adorned with a garland of *mandāra* flowers—O Mistress of Yoga, O Kula-yoginī, O Immortal One, you who veil yourself with a stream of nectar.
She who is established in the Mātṛsiddhi, rendered motionless by the passion of the sacrifice that is the festival of the Lord of Yoga.
Protect me, O Supreme Goddess, the Excellent Tree, the Auspicious Radiance, the Embodiment of Yoga!
The bondage of the noose of Māyā has been severed by the nectar of the conversation of Your words.
I am devoid of various dharmas, living in a family of the Kali age with agitated characteristics.
If even a single glance from me were to become defiled, that would be solely my own fault.
"When that which consists of illusion clings to my heart within the mind,
then what fruit could there be, whether it be the kingdom itself or the means to attain it?"—
with this intention, the Blessed Goddess Śaktidevī [spoke] to me.
O Lord, your offering of your mouth shines within the lotus of the ear in the netherworld.
May that Yoginī— who is enriched by the counsel of all yogas,
who is the Goddess consisting of great qualities, a treasury of compassion,
and whose mind is as intoxicated as an elephant— remove my fear.
May she, who wears her brother's chest as a necklace, be the one who brings about his destruction.
If one who is pleasing to the mind recites this, he becomes the lord of cow's milk;
he brings the host of enemies under his control and destroys the mass of anger.
He shall become a consumer of the wind of the world, a fortunate one, and a skilled singer.
Rāmacandra is equal in qualities to the Lord of Rati (Kāmadeva), just like Īśa.
Whoever recites this hymn becomes a devotee of Pīrāya;
having become firmly established in the root-lotus, he shall attain sovereignty over the six cakras.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Hymn to Bhedinī and Others," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the Section on Siddhi-mantras, in the Illumination of the Great Tantra, the Northern Tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala, concerning the Revelation of the Six Wheels. || 31 ||
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O beloved, I shall now speak; listen to me according to the truth."
The goddess Kuṇḍalinī is power, the piercer of all that is divided. || 32-1 ||
She is the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age and the bestower of liberation upon the worlds;
O Lord, hear now her hymn of praise, as well as her meditation, ritual placement (nyāsa), and mantra. (32–2)
By the mere knowledge of which, the mind dissolves into the root-lotus; through union with Kuṇḍalinī, one becomes devoted to the bliss of consciousness. (32-3)
Kuṇḍalī bestows the siddhi of traveling through the sky;
through the forms of nectar and bliss, you provide protection for human beings. (32-4)

Through the processes of inhalation and exhalation, the body—composed of the three qualities (guṇas) and eternally enveloped by the five elements—is certainly possessed of the five vital airs (anilas). 32-5.

One should meditate upon her who resembles ten million suns, who is without support, who abides everywhere, whose nature is gnosis, and who dwells within the inhalation and exhalation of breath. (32.6)

Born from the flower of the Self-Existent (Svayambhū), illuminating meditative concentration and wisdom, she is the eternal bestower of liberation and power, whose very nature is perpetual knowledge. || 32-7 ||
She is playful, the bearer of grace, the embodiment of all things, and the illuminator of pure knowledge;
she is equal to ten million fires of cosmic destruction and possesses the great splendor of ten million flashes of lightning.
Her rays were pervaded by splendor, shining upward from her base;
she was enriched by the light of the eight worlds, and her eyes were like blooming blue lotuses.
She who possesses all faces, all hands, and stands upon all lotus-feet;
she who illuminates the worlds situated from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 32-10 ||
She possesses three tongues and devours all things; she protects the outgoing breath.
She is Lalitā, Sundarī, Nīlā, Kuṇḍalī, and is shaped like a coil.
She stands outside the circle of the earth, illuminating external knowledge;
she is a female serpent (nāginī), richly adorned with serpent ornaments, and possesses a terrifying body.
Having thus meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity, as pure in form, subtle, and ascending upward within the root-lotus, which is the object of knowledge for yogis; || 32-13 ||
The accomplishment of the state occurs swiftly here through the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī;
thereafter, indeed, come mental recitation (japa), mental fire-oblation (homa), and mental libation (tarpaṇa).
Having joyfully performed the consecration (abhiṣeka) again and again at the time of dawn,
one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and recite the hymn of praise (stotra) and the armor (kavaca).
By the recitation of this hymn, one becomes a knower of the Siddhānta oneself; Kuṇḍalinī will certainly show him great compassion within a month. (32.16)
Having abandoned defects such as sleep and having manifested within my subtle body, I am the giver of excellent yogas;
I am the sovereign in the three worlds.
"I am action, I am dharma, and I am the goddess Kuṇḍalī—he who knows this, O Great Hero, through the practice of the form of Kuṇḍalī. (32.18)
Thus, I have always descended to create that vessel;
for this very reason, [I shall speak] the supreme, auspicious mantra, which is the hymn of Kuṇḍalinī.
One should always recite [this] within the body if Kuṇḍalinī is not brought under control;
one should perform the recitation for as long as perfection has not been attained. (32.20)
The Supreme Goddess resides in the foundation; she is the goddess Kuṇḍalinī who dwells within the abode.
She is the presiding deity of the gods, established as a mass of bliss for the three worlds. (32.21)
She who dwells in the *mūlādhāra*, the thrice-delighting *Jñāninī* and *Mālinī*, established in the mantra of the Mothers, her face is the sole seed of bliss on the path of the *kula*. 32-22.
She who causes stability in all limbs, the sole sign of joy for the hosts of gods, the auspicious one;
she is the ninefold beloved of the lords of heroes, the giver of speech, the bestower of glory, and the giver of knowledge.
She is full of bliss, possessing intense joy, and her hosts are dense; she is the Yoginī who has severed worldly existence.
She is steadfast, endowed with fortitude, one for whom sense objects have come to an end, the auspicious Śrīmaṅgalī, and the one adorned with earrings.
Dwelling in all forms, victorious, supporting the supportless, she is free from attachment;
praised in song, possessing the wealth of the Vedas, consisting of the Guru, she is the treasury of knowledge and the wealth of the cows. 32-25.
She is the moonlight abiding in the domestic fire, the beautiful creeper that removes dullness and bestows passion;
she is the wife who provides wealth in cattle, whose mind is fixed on the deer (the moon), and who shines upon the path of the universe.
The Mother is the object of the mind, she moves with Hari, she is the cause of the lion-throne;
she is the sovereign of the host of Yama’s servants, she is possessed of all virtues, and she dwells in the path of the stars.
Sleeping while the people are agitated, possessing supreme thirst, abiding in the excellence of speech,
destroying the dissolution at the end of existence, and wearing a garland of human heads— she is Kuṇḍalī.

If the daughter of Gaṅgā, Yamunā’s sovereign, the most venerable Godāvarī, and Bhāskarī—each of whom destroys the suffering of her devotees—are endowed with a single-minded devotion toward Śiva equally, [then what need is there for others]? (32.29)
O Kaulika, quickly and with joy fashion that lotus for the aperture of my head;
O Kulavatī, protect me and the deities residing upon its petals, as well as the sacred site of the Mothers.
Above Bhāla is the white digit, the essence of all digits, blazing with the mass of the fire of time;
in the abode that sustains the life of jackals, she is the most weighty, the Guru, the Suguru, the Surā.

May she who is the arising of the supreme delight, who follows the way of the ascetics, who is Māyā that delivers the world, who destroys sleep and sexual passion, and who removes my delusion—may she protect me. 32-32.

Maithilī, whose body was dark blue, who brought about the fulfillment of the aims of the wise, who delighted the foreheads [of her devotees], who was the source of great joy for people, whose face was like a lotus, and who was tender; (32–33)

Clad in garments of various colors upon a beautiful seat, seated in the *siddhāsana*, she is the proclamation; she is the protector in the form of the immobile, the destroyer of strife, the illustrious Kuṇḍalinī—may she protect us.

She who resides between the eyebrows, Bagalāmukhī, Śaśimukhī, Vidyāmukhī, Sammukhī; she who is called Nāgā, who carries mountains, the slayer of Mahiṣa, and she who dwells upon the five-faced one (Śiva). || 32–35 ||
The supreme Śrī Kuṇḍalī, who acts as a bridge and a dam for the fish that cause the movement between this shore and the far shore, protects the Lord residing in Kāśī every day. (32–36)
She who is devoted to drinking the essence arising from the sacrificial vessel (*kuṇḍa*), who removes defects such as delusion (*moha*),
she is the Mother (*Ambikā*) with three eyes, the beautiful-limbed Śrī Kālikā, the Kaulika.
May she protect me—she who stands like a crow, who satisfies with the beak of a crow, who bestows consciousness, the beautiful one, covered by that pure, radiant, and well-shaded *pirayā*. 32-38.
In Śrīkuṇḍa are Raṇacaṇḍikā, Suratikā, Kaṅkālikā, Bālikā, Sākāśā, Parivajītā, Sugatikā, Jñānomīkā, and Utsukā. (32–39)
The purification through the subtle bliss of the *saukā*, the initiation known as the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the state of languor—O Śivā, who dwells in my *kanda*, protect me, protect me! (32–40)

Having recited this hymn—which purifies the three worlds and brings sanctity to worldly people—one shall become a king who is a fire for the consumption of sins, or else a lord of sacrifices here on earth, or one who bestows security upon yogins. (32.41)
He becomes the lord of all and the creator of all within his own abode, a teacher of yoga and its ancillaries;
whether a follower of Śakti or Śiva, he alone is devoted to the Supreme Person, a stainless-souled great soul. (32–42)
He who, being self-controlled and pure, offers praise while encasing [the name] with the *praṇava* (Om), shall become a son of Kuṇḍalin on this earth; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Hymn to Kandavāsinī," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the *Mūlacakrasārasaṅketa* of the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the *Uttaratantra* of the glorious *Rudrayāmala*. 32.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Mahādeva, I shall now declare the auspicious armor (kavaca) of Kuṇḍalī."
It bestows supreme bliss, it is perfected, and it is served by hosts of Siddhas.
Having performed which, all yogins become revealers of dharma and adharma; as wise and honored ones, they move about like immortals. (33.2)
The supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), as well as all the deities, are held in the palm of one's hand;
by the recitation of this armor (kavaca), even the Lord of Devas becomes a sovereign of yogis.
All the sages and yogins, matted-haired and belonging to the Kulabhairava lineage,
[should practice] three times in the morning and twice at midday.
If one recites this armor-mantra (kavaca) for a single period in the evening,
by thus reciting it, the great yogi shall attain the vision of Kuṇḍalinī.

For the Kulakuṇḍalī-kavaca, Brahmā and Indra are the seers (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Kulakuṇḍalī is the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining all desired goals.
Oṃ! May the Sovereign of the worlds, the Sustainer, Lalitā, the Beautiful One, the Supreme, Kuṇḍalinī, who is the form of the Kula, Kulacaṇḍikā, protect me. (33-6)
May Goddess Lalitā protect my head, and she known as Ugrā protect my cheeks;
encased by the Brahma-mantra, may she always protect the space between my eyebrows.
Mahākālī, the devourer of the fire of time, is the three eyes; Viśālākṣī is the crest-lock; and iṣṭānuvāsinī is the row of teeth and the lips.
May the Vidyā, whose essence is the seed-syllable of desire, protect my lower part always; may Māyā, who dwells in the pair of *ḷ* and resides in the six flavors, protect the pair of my cheeks.
May Bhuvaneśī protect my pair of ears, and Krodhakālikā my chin; may Kapilā, who is the embodiment of all seed-syllables, protect my throat.
May Kuṇḍalī, encased within the letters of the Mātṛkā, protect my throat; may Kālapṛthvī and Kaṅkālī protect my heart and my face. (33-11)
May her pair of arms, which destroy the staff-like arms of the fierce goddess Caṇḍī and bestow the fourfold aims of life,
and may her pair of shoulders, which belong to the mother of Skanda and are smeared with hālāhala poison, be mine.
May Śrīvidyā, the joy of her family, protect the tips of the fingers; may Kālikā, the sovereign of the world, always protect the circle of the nails and the region of the back. (33.13)
May the two sides [be protected] by the Great Heroines who hold the heroic posture and grant fearlessness;
may Ambikā, situated upon the *kuladarbha* grass at the navel and abdomen, protect me.
The Great Slayer of the Buffalo is established on the seat at the region of the hips;
Mahāmudrā is at the place of the *liṅga*, and the *mālāmanu* is in the *bhaga*.
The smoke-colored Dhūmrā, the Mistress of the Gaṇas, is worshipped at the four-petaled Mūlādhāra; O Earth, you reside at the tips of its petals.
May Śīrṣā, Rādhā, Raṇākhyā, and Brahmāṇī protect my face;
may Medinī and Kamalā protect it, and may Vāgdevī protect the eastern petal.
May Chedinī protect [the lotus] in the south, and may Caṇḍā Mahātapā protect it;
may Candraghaṇṭā, the Yoginī, always protect the western petal.
May the petal situated in the north protect the earth, guarded by Indra;
may Kāmavidyā protect the four corners, and Brahmavidyā the lotus-corner.
May she who rides upon all vehicles protect the eight-fold spear at all times; may the four-armed Ḍākinī Kulacañcalā protect [me] forever.
May Madanādhārā, residing in the genitals, protect my beautiful lotus; may Svayambhūliṅgā protect my face; and may Koṭarākṣī protect my seat.
May the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Māyā, who dwells in the Kadamba forest, come to protect the Kadamba forest; may she protect my Vaiṣṇava state.
May Rākiṇī protect the six-petaled [lotus]; may Rākiṇī, who dwells in desire, who is the Mistress of Desire and whose form is desire, protect Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is clothed in yellow garments. (33-23)
May Vanamālā protect my forest garland; may the auspicious Śaṅkhinī protect my conch;
may Cakreśvarī protect my discus; and may Kamalākṣī protect my mace.
May Padmā, Padmagandhā, and the enchanting Padmamālā protect me;
may Lākinī, the guardian of the world, protect the syllables from *ra* to *la*.
May she who dwells on Kailāsa protect the deities stationed in the six petals;
may the Supreme Goddess, who is the color of fire, always protect my host.
May Trivikramā, adorned with a garland of jewels, always protect Maṇipūra— the ten-petaled [lotus] of ten colors, consisting of the letters from Ḍa to Pha.
May the blue Mahākālī protect [us], as well as Bhadrā, Bhīmā, Sarasvatī, the Goddess residing in Ayodhyā, and she who dwells in the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha). || 33-28 ||
May the Great Vidyā beginning with Vāgbhava, Kuṇḍalinī, and Kālakuṇḍalinī protect my Rudra, who consists of the essence of Rudra, residing within the ten-petaled lotus. 33-29.
May Rākiṇī, who dwells in the subtle abode, protect [me]—she who is subtler than the subtle;
may she, the mother of the worlds, who resides in the peak-syllable, protect [me]. (33–30)
May the Rajakī, honored by kings, protect the Taijasa-tattva with certainty;
may Vijayā, residing in the Kula-bīja, protect the Ta-group, dispelling all darkness.
May she whose essence is mantra, who pierces the jewel-knot, protect me always;
may the daughter of Bhṛgu, the bestower of the womb, protect me as she dwells in the navel. (33-32)
May Nandinī, who is encircled by a halo and shaken by Time, protect [me] in its entirety;
may she who is called Kālā, smoke-colored and captivating, protect the heart-lotus. (33–33)
May the twelve-syllabled Bhāskarī, who grants the accomplishment of all states of being, protect me; may that supreme Vidyā, who moves at will, protect the *ka*-group of consonants.
May Vyāghrāsyā, wearing beautiful garments and holding a chisel, protect the *ca*-group; may she named Kṛṣṇā protect the letter *ca*; and may Kālikā protect the letter *ka*. (33–35)
May the pure Goddess Ṭakurāṅgī, who possesses the syllable Ṭa, whose nature is life, and who brings great prosperity, protect me; she dwells within the lotus of my heart. (33–36)
May Kaṇīkā, Kālasandarbha, Yoginī, and Yogamātṛ protect [me]; may Indrāṇī and Vāruṇī protect the lineage and the transition between lineages.
May Tāriṇī, Śaktimātā, and Kaṇṭhavākya protect me always;
and Vipracittā, Mahogrā, Ugrā, Prabhā, Dīptā, and Ghanāsanā. (33–38)
She who paralyzes speech, whose body is adamantine, the lady of Videha, she who rides upon a bull;
she whose mind is intoxicated with bliss, the mistress of the moment, she who dwells within the womb. (33–39)
May she who dwells in the body of the Mothers protect my sixteen petals;
may she who knows the Vedas protect the deities, and she who is all languages protect the pericarp.
Seated upon half the throne of Īśvara, may she grant me Sadāśiva; may Śākambharī, Mahāmāyā, and Sākinī protect me at all times.
May Bhavānī, the mother of Bhava, protect the two-petaled lotus between the eyebrows; she is known as Vrata-kāmā and is the bestower of the eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭāṅga-siddhi).
May she who is the source of all bliss, whose form is the mind, who is the love of the world, who is marked by auspicious characteristics, and who is defined by all defining marks, protect our noses.
May the goddess wearing a black antelope skin protect the letter Kṣa at all times;
may the fair-faced one, who dwells within the two petals and contains all the gods, protect [me] always.
May Hākinī, who possesses many forms and universal forms, protect as she stands;
may she protect Aparashiva, the Destroyer, and may the fifth [vowels] protect the mind.
May she who dwells eternally in the six chakras, residing within the family of the six chakras, protect [me]—
she who consists of the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa', endowed with the nasal bindu and the visarga.
May Mātṛkā protect [me] always; may Kuṇḍalī, Jñānakuṇḍalī, Devakālī, Gatipremā, Pūrṇā, and Śivā protect the mountain slope. (33–47)
May the goddess Uḍḍīyāneśvarī protect everything at all times;
may she who dwells on Mount Kailāsa protect Mount Kailāsa.
May the power of the Ḍākinīs—Lākinī, Rākinī, Kalā, Sākinī, and the goddess Hākinī—protect me; may they protect my six cakras and the rest. (33–49)
May she who is born from the body of the five-faced one always protect that which is called Kailāsa— she who is golden-hued, who is the night, and who consumes the moon, the sun, and fire.
May Kulākulā always protect my thousand-petaled lotus;
may Khecarī, residing upon the thousand-petaled lotus, protect the deity.
May Kālī, Tārā, the one known as Ṣoḍaśī, Mātaṅgī, and Padmavāsinī—whose forms drip like ten million moons—protect me from all darkness. (33-52)
In the forest, in a terrible place, in water, on land, in battle, in debate, or in a cremation ground;
wherever I may go, may the Daughter of the Mountain always protect me. 33-53.
May Kuṇḍalinī protect [the practitioner] from various hardships and destruction on the mountain;
may the Sovereign of the Gods protect the entire space from the feet up to the aperture of Brahmā.
May all knowledge and omniscience always protect me; may the Great Knowledge of nine hundred thousand [syllables] protect me in the ten directions. (33-55)
O Goddess, this is the armor of Kuṇḍalinī which bestows success;
those established on the path of Yoga who recite it while engaged in the yoga of meditation [attain their goal]. (33–56)
They attain the path of liberation in this very life; of this there is no doubt.
Having fixed the mind upon the root-lotus while seated in the heart-throne, || 33-57 ||
One should meditate upon the mantra as Kuṇḍalinī, who illumines the root-lotus,
who is the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), who is mounted upon compassion, and who dwells in the station of space.
She who delights in the essence of nectar, who is both deficient and perfectly endowed with all arts, who is cool and unconquered, who is devoid of passion yet possesses a body of blood-red hue.

Having meditated upon her at the base— red-eyed, cast from the family, radiant with the application of the ointment of gnosis, possessing a universal form, and having the nature of the mind— one should worship her.
The yogi who practices in this way becomes a perfected one; of this there is no doubt. The sick shall be freed from disease, and the bound shall be released from bondage.
If one who is deprived of a kingdom recites this, he shall obtain sovereignty and prosperity;
if one is childless, he shall obtain a son; and if one lacks spiritual discipline, he shall become self-controlled.
Whoever wears this armor on the crest-lock, on the right arm,
or holding it in the left hand on the left side, shall obtain all desired objects.
Having placed [the manuscript] in gold, silver, or likewise copper, one should worship it;
by reciting it in any country and at any time, one shall attain perfection.
He shall become the son of Kuṇḍalinī; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Armor of Kandavāsinī," in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Wheels), within the *Siddhividyāprakaraṇa* (Section on the Knowledge of Attainments) of the *Mahātantroddīpana* (Illumination of the Great Tantra) in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, the latter part of the tantra, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 33.
Then the thirty-fourth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Now, O Lord, for the benefit of the worlds, I shall proclaim the various divisions."
He is the stainless self, pure, glorious, the essence of meditation, and the eternally auspicious one.
He is the one who has attained liberation, whose nature is knowledge, and he is the piercer of the meaning of the six cakras;
devoid of the knowledge of the three guṇas, he does not perceive day or night. || 34-2 ||
Due to ignorance day and night, one does not perceive the body;
thus indeed occurs death for men birth after birth. (34-3)
And for the sake of the exhaustion of that birth, one should practice my yoga;
having performed the great yoga of the five sounds, a person shall become immortal. (34–4)
Now listen to that manner, O beloved Piyadarśana; I shall speak out of devotion to you—tell me, O Śaṅkara, where is there any doubt? (34–5)
If the practice of yoga is spoken of in the presence of worldly people, terrible obstacles surely dwell within one's body; how then can there be success in yoga and the like? (34.6)
Through the application of yoga, liberation arises; through its manifestation, [the bonds] are destroyed. Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should not reveal the yoga. (34.7)
Having performed the *pañcāmarā-yoga* every day with devotion, one should recite the thousand names and the eightfold hymn of the goddess Śrī Kuṇḍalī. (34–8)
The Lord shall become a great yogi within six months; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, in the fifth [month], the science of yoga, which illuminates all sciences, [shall arise]. (34.9)
Having accomplished the perfection of the five vowels, one then practices the concentration on the eight limbs and so forth;
first comes the perfection of the five vowels, and thereafter the other yogic concentrations.
I shall declare that method; listen attentively.
In this world, I know only those who are experts in yoga. (34.11)
O Lord, I am indeed the witness for that and for the prosperity of my devotees;
now I shall tell you of my own practice of yoga.
Having acted thus, since yoga is eightfold and possesses an eternal form,
the person will certainly attain perfection in due course of time.
O Śaṅkara, listen now in due order to the five methods of the immortals;
for the Neti-yoga is indeed the destroyer of great phlegm for the perfected ones. (34.14)
I shall now describe the practice of *dantī*, following the piercing of the heart (*hṛdayabheda*);
thereafter, the practice of *dhautī*, which destroys all impurities. (34.15)
The Neulīyoga is another [practice] resulting from the movement of all the limbs and the abdomen;
it is known as the supreme cleansing yoga because it cleanses the channels (nāḍīs). || 34.16 ||
This is the yoga of the five immortals, which is beyond the reach of the senses of those who practice self-restraint;
at the time of the observances of restraint (yama) and discipline (niyama), one should perform the ritual of the five immortals.
By the practice of the Amara-sādhana alone, one will certainly attain immortality;
and at the time of performing this, there is likewise the fivefold seat of the immortals (pañcāmarāsana).
By consuming the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one becomes immortal and attains the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhi*).
O Supreme Lord, I shall describe those substances before you. (34.19)
By that which is deficient, one does not achieve success even in hundreds of millions of eons;
however, one should bring together a single knot of the immortal *dūrvā* grass.
But Vijayā is another goddess, Sarasvatī in the form of spiritual accomplishment (siddhi);
yet another resides upon the bilva leaf, bringing satisfaction to Śiva. (34.21)
But another, Nirguṇḍī, known as Amarā, is considered for the sake of attaining yogic perfection;
yet another is Kālitulasī, which brings supreme satisfaction to Lord Viṣṇu.
These five vowels are to be known for the practice of yoga-sādhana;
from these, the excellent leaf of Vijayā should be taken in double the quantity. (34.23)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are honored everywhere;
having collected these substances, one should consume this excellent powder. (34.24)
At the time of consuming that powder, having recited these five [verses] beginning with the mantra,
a person who has performed the consumption shall be liberated from distress.
Oṃ! O Dūrvā, worthy of worship by the immortals, you who are born from the source of nectar;
O auspicious one, make me forever immortal in the presence of Nṛhari. (34-26)
Oṃ, obeisance to Dūrvā, svāhā—thus [one offers] to Dūrvā. One should purify all the girls with the Punarvīja mantra:
Oṃ, O Saṃvid, born of Brahman, daughter of Brahman, ever sinless!
And for the sake of the satisfaction of the Bhairavas, may you always be pure.
Oṃ, homage to Brāhmaṇī, svāhā!
Oṃ, O Goddess who brings about the root of accomplishment, who awakens inferior understanding, who subjugates princesses, who has a trident at your throat, O wielder of the trident! || 34-28 ||
Oṃ, homage to Kṣatriyā, svāhā!

Oṃ, you who are the blazing fire for the fuel of ignorance, whose form is the flame of the fire of knowledge; having offered the oblation of bliss and the rest, grant me perfect knowledge. || 34-29 ||
Hrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vaiśyā, svāhā! Oṃ! I bow down, I bow down to you, O bestower of the path of yoga; O Mother, victorious over the three worlds, grant me the fruit of samādhi. (34-30)
Śrīṃ, obeisance to the Śūdrā, svāhā!
Oṃ! O Goddess who grants the perfection of poetic art, you who dwell upon the bilva leaf; grant me immortality forever and make me equal to Śiva. 34-31.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śivadā, Svāhā!
O Nirguṇḍī, supreme bliss, presiding deity of yogas, may she protect me; obeisance to her who bestows the attainment of the immortal state. 34-32.
Oṃ, homage to the remover of sorrow, svāhā!
Oṃ, O Viṣṇu’s consort, O Great Illusion, O warder-off of the Great Time (Mahākāla), O Tulasī, protect me always; make me alone immortal. 34-33.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ eṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Amarā, svāhā!
Having performed the ritual once again, one should carry out the purification of all [the goddesses]. || 34-34 ||
Oṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtam ākarṣaya | ākarṣaya siddhiṃ dehi svāhā | One should display the dhenumudrā, the yonimudrā, and the matsyamudrā.
The wise practitioner should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) precisely according to the sequence of the Tattvamudrā.
One should offer [the oblation] seven times without a mantra, dedicating it by the name of the Guru to Śiva;
and seven times by the name of one's own chosen deity, one should cause purification to be bestowed.
Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa), reciting the formula "I offer libations; obeisance, obeisance," preceded by one's own chosen mantra.
Having extracted the Supreme Deity (paradevatā), it is remembered that [the mantra] begins with the Praṇava at the beginning of all [syllables].
Then, one should offer oblations into the mouth, preceded by the name of Kuṇḍalinī.
Oṃ eṃ, speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech! Dwell firmly upon the tip of my tongue!
O Subduer of all beings! O Trident-wielder at the throats of enemies! Svāhā!
