Having recited this, the best of practitioners, though still a student, becomes a master.
The five immortals are knowers of the teaching and experts in the rules of family conduct.
If a yogi whose mind has become steady should attain the five immortals, then listen, O worshipful one of Kailāsa, to the methods of the Neti-yoga. (34–40)
By means of which there shall be a burning of all the phlegm located at the head,
one should insert a very firm, fine thread into the nostril.
Having brought [the breath] into the cavity of the mouth, he should join it through union;
again and again, the yogi should always rub it by means of its coming and going.
O Supreme Lord, one should gradually increase the practice of the thread [neti];
through the yoga of *neti*, the cavity of the nose becomes stainless. (34–43)
O Lord, when the wind moves, there is great bliss;
thereafter, the best of practitioners should perform the yoga of the tusker (dantīyoga).
At the time of cleaning the teeth, one should reveal this yoga;
and the tooth-cleansing stick should be produced from a tree measuring one and a half cubits.
One should carefully select from the tree a branch that is neither too thick nor too thin, fresh, supple, excellent, unripe, and resembling a lotus stalk. (34–46)
Having taken a tooth-stick, the yogi should always chew it;
the tip of the tooth-stick should be the size of the joint of the little finger.
In this manner, one should perform the chewing beautifully with the rows of teeth;
then, having rinsed it with water, one should slowly swallow it. (34–48)
One should gradually perform the purification of body, speech, and mind,
until the tip of the [inner] wood is undivided and remains unbroken at the base of the navel.
One must necessarily practice this increasingly subtle object of perception every day, until the "water-wheel" within the heart ceases to appear as a fragmented form. (34–50)
At that time, every day at dawn, the brushing of the teeth certainly effects the breaking of the vessel of phlegm within the heart. (34–51)
Upon the arrival of the wind, he attains bliss filled with yoga;
may he obtain the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) and that which arises from pungent substances, which is unfading. (34-52)
A yogi who desires yoga in this world must necessarily renounce sweet foods, vegetables with curd-rice, and eating twice a day, as well as eating at night. (34–53)
One part of mung bean and two parts of rice are considered the best; having prepared this as a fine porridge, one should consume it with ghee and milk.
Alternatively, the wise man should cause her to be satiated with milk alone;
he should fully satisfy Kuṇḍalinī, who is the form of the Kula, with milk.
O Śaṅkara, if a yogi knows the satiation of Kuṇḍalinī,
he shall become a yogi without effort and will certainly become a sovereign of the wise.
He who is devoted to the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), established in the practice of Kuṇḍalinī, whether devoid of worldly power or burdened by great responsibilities—
he becomes a supreme yogi, knowable through the meaning of all vidyās.
Lord Gaṇeśa, whose form is liberated, abides in the sky of the multitude of his virtues.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Sadhana of the Five Immortals," in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Wheels) within the *Mahātantroddīpana* (Elucidation of the Great Tantra), the *Uttaratantra* (Supplementary Tantra) of the venerable *Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 34.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
Now I shall declare the secret of Mahākāla, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
By the mere knowledge of which a person may attain the state of Brahman. || 35-1 ||
His kingdom shall be in the sky, and he will certainly become a lord of the sky-dwellers;
he quickly becomes a lord of wealth, and that man becomes a knower of Brahman. (35-2)
King Vīrabhadra is the sovereign lord of yogis, like a poet; may the grace of Viriñci, the Lord of the Gaṇas, be ever-present. (35-3)
He who practices the fivefold yoga shall possess a body like that of the immortals.
I shall now explain the yoga of *dhautī*, by performing which one becomes stainless. (35–4)
This yoga is an absolute secret, the means for humans to achieve meditative absorption;
if one does not practice this yoga, then one shall meet with death.
O Lord, who on this earth attains perfection without the yoga of *dhautī*?
[One should take] a cloth finer than the finest, measuring thirty-two cubits in length. (35–6)
He who performs it very slowly, step by step with a single hand, should carry out the ritual for as long as it takes to reach thirty-two cubits. (35–7)
By the application of this ritual practice, one becomes a yogi at that very moment;
through gradual stages, there shall be the accomplishment of mantra, and one brings [all things] under the power of the net of time.
One should practice these postures as they exist within the body;
for it is the determination of the meaning of the Tantras that the accomplishment of yoga occurs on a firm seat. (35.9)
When the mantra is perfected, there is supreme attainment through the fivefold yoga-posture;
O Lord, the cloth on the side is eight finger-breadths wide and thirty-two [finger-breadths] in length.
Taking this fine garment, which is subtle, the ascetic should wear it;
having conquered his senses and always devoted to knowledge and meditation, he should act thus. (35.11)
One who is of noble birth, learned, honorable, discerning, and of firm resolve should always practice the *dhautī* yoga; only then will he become pure in conduct. (35-12)
Through improper conduct, there shall be a decline of the senses and their strength;
through the fault of association with those guilty of the primary great sins, further degradations occur. (35.13)
O Mahādeva, they arise through the conjunction of time and good karma;
whether one is old, established in youth, a child, or even dull-witted. (35.14)
By performing this, one shall become long-lived, immortal, and beloved by the world;
he attains mantra-perfection and the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi), becoming the sovereign lord of all accomplishments.
One should always act very gradually in order to destroy the defects of time;
by breaking the knot of the heart, there is the growth of all limbs. (35-16)
Then the wise Mahābala, of beautiful complexion and noble intent, [experienced] the desire arising from the practice of *dhautī*, which is the cause of great death. (35.17)
The man who performs its renunciation possesses the prowess of a god;
having abandoned the breath and the suspension [of breath], he should fix his mind upon the great wind (mahānila).
One should certainly practice the counting of the breaths and so forth within the house;
by means of the prescribed method of prāṇāyāma, one shall be happy at all times. || 35-19 ||

One should always practice the breath-control of inhaling air; one should indeed always practice meditation; one should always practice withdrawal of the senses; and one should always practice the fixing of the mind.
One should always practice mental recitation (*mānasajapa*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manolaya*);
indeed, after the yoga of *dhautī*, one should perform the practice of *naulī*. (35.21)
Merely by the application of the blue lotus, one becomes like the blue lotus upon the seat;
through the practice of the blue lotus alone, one becomes long-lived and free from disease. (35-22)
The inner self is eternally silent, the stainless self is eternally happy;
it is always the bliss of equanimity, the embodiment of the bliss of the cause.
One should always practice yoga, such as the cultivation of Kuṇḍalinī;
having done so, the practitioner of mantra attains the state of moving through the sky—of this there is no doubt. (35-24)
I shall explain that method; listen attentively.
Having eaten cooked mung-bean rice, one should wait for one night. (35-25)
Free from fatigue, one should protect the abdomen and repeatedly perform the movement of the central part of the stomach. (35-26)
One should perform the churning of the abdomen like a potter’s wheel;
by the movement of all the limbs, the movement of Kuṇḍalinī occurs. (35-27)
O Lord, through the movement of the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, she becomes conscious;
immediately following this, O Master, the washing (kṣālana) is proclaimed.
By the mere cleansing of the channels (nāḍīs), one becomes a treasury of all knowledge;
one attains victory everywhere and the vision of Kālikā shall occur.
He shall attain mastery over the wind and possess the power of the five elements; his fame shall pervade the three worlds, and he will be equal in strength to the god of love. (35–36)
He shall become all-pervading and shall become the lord of the senses;
indeed, the wise man should always practice the "shaven-seat" (muṇḍāsana) everywhere. (35.31)
Having placed the *muṇḍāsana* (the "shaven-head" posture) above, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) with the hand below;
if one is capable of doing so for three days, that is the *muṇḍikāsana*.
For then, without a doubt, all the channels (nāḍīs) come under control;
through the yoga of cleansing the channels, one becomes a bestower of liberation oneself. (35–36)
Through the yoga of the channels, the accomplishment of all aims shall come from the muṇḍikāsana;
he who performs the muṇḍāsana goes to the perfection of nāḍī.
Engaged in the Neūlī practice, the supreme Neūlī practice, the practitioner then attains accomplishment through the application of cleansing. || 35-35 ||
How can one who does not know the *neūla* (the subtle essence) be considered supreme in his practice?
He alone is wise, he moves within the mind, he is intelligent, and he has conquered his senses. (35–36)
He who is a supreme master of yoga and intends to compose the *Yogasāra* must necessarily perform the cleansing [of the body] through the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth. (35–37)
By means of the Neūlī yoga path, one becomes a master of the purification of the channels (nāḍī-kṣālana),
just like Mahākāla, the Lord of the Kings of Kings.
Devoted to the protection of the earth, your body shall be protected;
through the mere retention of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), purification will occur. || 35-39 ||
Without the application of cleansing, purification of the body does not occur;
the cleansing of the channels and so forth removes phlegm, bile, impurities, and the like. (35–40)
By diligently practicing the seat of the shaven-headed one (muṇḍāsana), the yogi indeed achieves the retention of the vital breath (vāyu) in the regions of Neūlī, Vaśa, and Kālaka. (35–41)
O Lord, one should not practice this alone at other times; rather, one should always practice it.
As long as one does not know the *ūḍī*, so long should one not drink the vital wind (*vāyu*). (35–42)
One should not grasp too much regarding the arrival and other aspects of the breath;
one should simply count the inhalations until the *ūrdhvali* is mastered. (35–43)
The Yoginī who bestows accomplishment is proclaimed as having five vowels;
by the very practice of the five vowels, the five winds will come under control. (35–44)
In his splendor he shall be equal to the sun, the remover of the defects of sorrow;
having attained the utmost stability in all yoga, he becomes a king among yogis. (35–45)

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Practice of the Yoga of the Five Vowels," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, within the *Uttara-tantra*, the illumination of the Great Tantra (*Mahātantroddīpana*), in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 35 ||
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O beloved, I shall now explain the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī and other related matters."
The entirety of the Thousand Names is the beloved bliss of Kuṇḍalinī.
This [mantra] possesses great merit beyond the eightfold [count], bestowing spiritual perfection directly;
out of the power of my love for you, I shall speak it—listen to it. (36-2)
Without the practice of sacrifice and without meditation, one obtains that fruit immediately; may the grace of the Vidyā be upon him. (36-3)
That Vidyā who is the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśānī), worshipped throughout the three worlds—that Goddess Kuṇḍalī, the Mother, protects the three worlds at all times. (36-4)
Her names number one thousand and eight hundred;
by hearing or reciting them, the practitioner of mantra becomes a great devotee in this world. (36.5)
O Lord, he shall become a mighty one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) even in this world.

Of this hymn of one thousand and eight names of the illustrious Mahākuṇḍalī, Brahmā is the seer, the Jagatī is the meter, the blessed goddess Śrīmanmahākuṇḍalī is the deity, and the application is for the sake of attaining the perfection of all yogic accomplishments.
The Mistress of the Kula, the Joy of the Kula, the Noble One, Kulakuṇḍalī, the illustrious Mahākuṇḍalī, the Daughter of the Kula, and the Beloved of the Kula. || 36–7 ||
Established in the field of the Kula, she is the Kaulī who illuminates the meaning of noble lineage;
she is known as Kula, abiding on the path of Kula, and she causes one to attain the goal of the Kula scriptures. || 36-8 ||

She belongs to the Kula, she is fit for the Kula, she is the illuminator of the Kula-flower; she is of noble lineage, the presiding lady of the Kula, and anointed with the sandalwood of the Kula. || 36-9 ||
She has the form of the Kula, she is born from the Kula, she dwells within the Kulakuṇḍalinī;
she is inseparable from the Kula, she is produced from the Kula, and she delights in the conduct of the Kula. || 36-10 ||
Born from the family-tree, she is the garland of the family, the radiance of the family;
she knows the family, abides in the midst of the family, and is adorned with the family-bracelet.
The Kulottarā, the Kaula worship, the discourse on the Kula, the Kula ritual, the divisions of the Kula, the life-breath of the Kula, the Goddess of the Kula, and the praise of the Kula. || 36-12 ||

She is Kaulikā, Kālikā, and Kālyā; she who has transcended the Kali age and is the source of all arts and digits; she is the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age and the eradicator of the defects of the Kali age.
Kaṅkālī, Kevalānandā, Kālajñā, Kāladhāriṇī, Kautukī, Kaumudī, Kekā, Kākā, and Kākalayāntarā. (36.14)
She of tender limbs, she with a formidable mouth, she who is worshipped by Kandarpa and is herself gentle;
she who is in her youth, she who resides upon the tail of a crow, and she who dwells upon a woolen seat. || 36-15 ||
She is honored by Kaikeyī, the daughter of Kola, she whose banner bears the monkey;
she is Kamalā, the lotus-eyed one, and the beloved of Kambala and Aśvatara.
She who abides in the fault of breaking the poetic bud, she who knows the proper time, Kālakuṇḍalī;
she who bestows poetry, the Goddess of Speech, who pierces through the composition of time. (36.17)
The maiden who embodies compassion, the destroyer of the Kuru army;
the beloved who has entered the lineage, the one of desire who destroys desire. || 36-18 ||
Born from desire, she is the maiden of desire, absolute, and the destroyer of time;
she has ascended the peak of Kailāsa and is served by the Lord of Kailāsa.
She who is bowed to by the Lord of Kailāsa, adorned with armlets and necklaces,
the one who is the essence of desire, whose bliss is firm, who dwells in the lineage, and who destroys the deeds of the kīcaka-reed.
Kamalāsyā, Kaṭhorā, Kīṭarūpā, Kaṭisthitā, Kandeśvarī, Kandakarūpā, Kolikā, and Kandavāsinī. || 36-21 ||
She is the immovable one, the devourer of the deceptive, and the destroyer of the Kālakūṭa poison;
she is named Kāmā, the lotus-born Kamalā, the desirable one, and she who was born from the body of Kāmarāja.
She assumes forms at will, she is charming, she is lovely, she is dear to poets; she has a lotus-face, she has hands like lotuses, and her long eyes are like lotus petals. (36.23)
Kākinī, residing in Kāmarūpa, the illuminator of Kāmarūpa;
the destroyer of Kolā, Kaṅkā, who stains the sun with her spot. || 36-24 ||
The great river of noble lineage, she who deludes the ears with her shaft-like words;
she who stands in the arrow, whose compassion is like a shaft, and who dwells in action as the mistress of the household. (36.25)
You possess the luster of a lotus; you are existence, auspiciousness, compassion, and composed of compassion.
You are the Mistress of Compassion, the one who acts with hands, the one whose hand is the agent, and the source of the rise of the arts.
Born from the ocean of compassion, dwelling in the sea of compassion,
she whose hair is the moon, who resides in the moon, and who protects the life-force of the moon.
She is the worshipful treasury of compassion, the performance of ritual action,
the arts, the one who abides for an eon, the dwelling place of the eon, the one who transcends the eon, and the one who is conceptually constructed.
She belongs to the Kula, she possesses Kula-consciousness, she is the grinder, she is the Night of Time;
she bestows absolute liberation, she resides in the heart-lotus, and she delights in the tinkling of her anklets.

She who measures time, whose tongue is Time, she who causes the seat of her servants to be made; she who is the white water-lily, she who is auspiciousness and bliss, she who is the skill of Kausalya, and she who dwells in the ether.
She is the destroyer of the laughter of passions, the source of the qualities of absolute liberation;
she is solitary, of the nature of the sun, the blue water-lily, and resides in the crab. (36-31)
Karkoṭakā has the form of a granary, situated in the hand that carries the fire-altar;
she utters sweet sounds and desires one who possesses auspicious marks. (36-32)
She who delights in the ketakī flower, she who is adorned by the merit of the ketakī, she who is radiant with streams of camphor, and she who is fond of consuming camphor. || 36-33 ||
Holding a skull-bowl in her hand, she bears a skull and the moon;
she is the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), and as Kāmadhenu, she is endowed with creative action.
Kaśyapī, Kāśyapā, Kuntī, Keśāntā, Keśamohinī, Kālakartrī, Kūpakartrī, Kulapā, and Kāmacāriṇī. || 36-35 ||
Shining like saffron, residing in collyrium, she who destroys anger,
abiding in play, engaged in sport, the wrathful one, and dwelling in a rag.
Beyond time, she is the knowledge of time, arising from time, the self, and the person;
she dwells in suffering, she dwells in the affliction of leprosy, she is the destroyer of leprosy, the destroyer of suffering, and the sacred grass (kuśā).
Kālikā, Sphuṭakartrī, Kāmbojā, Kāmalā, Kulā, the one named Kuśalā, Kākakuṣṭhā, Karmasthā, and Kūrmamadhyagā. (36–38)

She who dwells in the wheel shaped like an earring, she who arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, she who is the sky of the fat of the *kapittha* fruit, and she who causes the obstruction of the *kapittha*. || 36-39 ||
Kāhoḍā, Kāhaḍā, Kāḍā, Kaṅkalā Bhāṣakāriṇī; Kanakā, Kanakābhā, and Kanakādrinivāsinī. (36–40)
Wearing a sacrificial thread made of cotton, she accomplishes the aims of those who are false Brahmins;
she is a consumer of *kalañja*, cruel, a mass of anger, and seated upon a monkey. (36–41)
Kapālī, devoted to spiritual practice, dwelling in the space of the little finger; Kuñjareśī, seated upon an elephant, the elephant-like one, whose gait is like that of an elephant. || 36-42 ||
She dwells in the forest groves, she is the beloved of the elephant, and she resides in the temple of the forest grove;
she is both enraged and devoid of anger, transcending both wrath and its absence.
Born from the Kapiñjala tree, she is known as Kapiñjalasthā and Kapiñjā;
she is permeated by the story of her love for Kuntī and is honored in the heart of Kuntī. || 36-44 ||
Kuntalā, Kuntahastā, and Kulakuntalalohinī; she who serves the feet of her beloved, she who is skilled in what is dear to her, and Kośalāvatī. || 36-45 ||
She who destroys hair, she who dwells on the Kakutstha mountain, she who resides in the forest of Kakutstha;
she who rejoices on the peak of Kailāsa, and she who is worshipped by the mountain Kailāsa. || 36–46 ||

She whose form is as pure as ambrosia, she who creates the charm of ambrosia; she who is fierce with her fangs, she who destroys the wicked, she who is the destroyer of obstacles, and she who brings joy through her deceptive forms.

Krauṅkārī, Krauṅkarī, Kāśī, she who abides in the sound "kuhu," Kirātinī; she who warbles, she who causes all speech to be uttered, and she who performs what has been done and what remains to be done. (36–48)
She is the very embodiment of the treasure-house of compassion, dwelling within the ocean of mercy;
she is devoted solely to bliss and is the cause of absolute bliss.
Kṛmilā, the destroyer of the defects of worms; Kṛpā, who has crushed deceit; Kṛśāṅgī, who stands at the breaking of the sequence; Kiṅkarasthā, who resides on the slope. || 36-50 ||
Kāmarūpā, who delights in the forest, bestows the siddhi of Kāmarūpa;
she is the goddess of the Kāmarūpa-pīṭha, born from the lap of Kāmarūpa, and is Kujā.
She whose form is desire, the knowledge of desire, she who exists from the beginning as desire-form and so forth;
she whose art is the form of desire, she who is desirable, the sovereign lady of the family of desire-form. (36–52)
She is the bliss of the people of Kāmarūpa; she possesses the sharpest intellect regarding Kāmarūpa; she is the space that is the hand of Kāmarūpa; she is established upon the tree of Kāmarūpa.
Born of desire, she is the art of desire, sporting in the form of desire;
she abides in the meaning of the science of desire, being the art of the activity of the form of desire.
Kāmarūpa-Mahākālī, who consists of the glory of Kāmarūpa; she who is the supreme bliss of Kāmarūpa, the beloved of Kāmarūpa and the rest. || 36-55 ||
Dwelling at the root of the bank in the center of the lotus of Kāmarūpa, she is fond of the gesture of joined palms; she is Kṛtyā, the goddess Kṛtyā, stationed on the hip.
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, and a bell at her hip that rings melodiously, she has thick hips and is the ultimate goal;
she is Kātyāyanī, the bestower of perfect accomplishment.

Kātyāyanī, she who dwells on Mount Kācala, whose face is like the moon of desire, whose story is told, who delights in the land of Kāśmīra, the lady of Kāśmīra, born of the labor of cultivation. (36-58)
Established in the work of agriculture, she dwells upon the back of the tortoise;
she is Kālaghaṇṭā, devoted to sound, and she who deludes with the tinkling of anklets.
She who measures out the hosts of enemies, incites passion for virtue and vice, desires every object of longing, and illuminates the three worlds. || 36-60 ||
She is Kaulakanyā, Kālakanyā, and Kaulakālakuleśvarī; she resides in the temple of the Kaulas and is the one who mocks the Kula-dharma. || 36-61 ||
She is one who delights in the family dharma, yet she is the destroyer of the family dharma;
she is learned in the family dharma and the bestower of the prosperity of the family dharma. || 36-62 ||

She bestows the liberation and enjoyment of the Kaula, she is the Yoginī of the sovereign enjoyment of the Kaula; she possesses the Kaula rites, she is the ninefold Kula, and she wears a garland of white campaka flowers.
She who is beloved by the garlands of the flowers of the Kula, who is born from the source of the flowers of the Kula,
who causes the tumultuous roar of the Kula, and who is supremely fond of the rites of the Kula.
Kāśīsthitā, Kāśakanyā, Kāśī, Cakṣuḥpriyā, Kuthā, Kāṣṭhāsanapriyā, Kākā, and Kākapakṣakapālikā. || 36-65 ||

She who feeds on the essence of skulls, she who wears a fresh garland of skulls, she who dwells within a skull, she who belongs to the Kāpālikas, and she who bestows the siddhi of the skull. || 36-66 ||
Kapālā is the creator of the Kulas and resides upon the peak of the skull;
she is the giver of fortune to the wretched, known as Kṛpī, and is served by the miserable.
She is the destroyer of karma, situated within karma, and free from both action and inaction;
she delights in the perfection of karma, possesses desire, and dwells in the knowledge of karma.
She is well-disciplined in the duties of action and brings karma and dharma under her control;
she sits upon a great lion-throne fashioned from a golden lotus.
Rich with garlands of golden knots, she is the piercer of golden knots;
she is the maiden born of gold and dwells within the golden lotus.

Established in the peak of the Kālakūṭa poison and other such things, situated within the interval of the sound "kiṭi," with a face resounding with the cry of the Kaṅka bird, she is the digit born from the wish-fulfilling cow.

She has the luster of a golden bracelet; she is the earth; she is the mud; she dwells in the mud; she is covered by water situated in the mud; she is dear to the people dwelling in the mud. || 36-72 ||
She who dwells upon a tortoise, she who dwells upon a bow, she who dwells within the heart, the destroyer of Kaṃsa;
she who is dear to Kaṃsa, the slayer of Kaṃsa, and she who causes terror through her ignorance of Kaṃsa. || 36-73 ||
She who has the luster of gold, the giver of gold, the giver of desires, the giver of steps;
she who is distinct from her beloved, whose thoughts are fixed on her beloved, and who dwells upon the lotus-throne.
Established in the perfection of the lotus-seat, she is the deity of the lotus-seat;
she is Kutsitā, delighting in what is base, yet she is Kutsā, free from the power of curses.

Kuputrarakṣikā (Protector of Bad Sons), Kullā, Kuputramānasāpahā (Remover of the Minds of Bad Sons), Kujarakṣakarī (Protector of Bad Elephants), Kaujī, Kubjākhyā (Named Kubjā), and Kubjavigrahā (Having a Hunchbacked Form). || 36-76 ||
Kunakhī, Kūpadīkṣusthā, Kukarī, Kudhanī, Kudā, Kupriyā, Kokilānandā, Kokilā, and Kāmadāyinī. (36–77)
She who possesses evil desires, who abides in wicked intellect, who carries a crow and deludes [the world],
she who belongs to the Kula, who dwells among the people of the Kula, and who bestows the perfect accomplishment of the Kula-seat.
The goddess Kauśikī is exceedingly fond of the sound of the *kanna* drum; she possesses excellent lips, dwells with good friends, and is the slayer of evil friends and enemies. (36-79)
She is the heap of false knowledge, she who dwells in evil places, she who dwells in the womb, she who bestows suffering;
she whose sound is "ka," she who performs action, and she who deludes those bound by action.
She is the purifier of karma and always bears the weapon of Time (Kālāstra). She is a bad destiny and a good destiny of Time, and she is the destroyer of the intellect of the Kali age. || 36-81 ||
Born from the fruit of the Kali age, she who purifies the Kali age,
Kālī, who removes the sins of the Kali age, bestows the most subtle perfection of the Kali age.

Residing within the words of Kālidāsa, she bestows the perfect accomplishment of Kālidāsa; she is the instruction for the Kali age, the instruction for Time, and is devoted to the instruction of the Kanda.
Delighting in desirable states, bestowing beautiful devotion, having the form of hailstones and people, she is the hand that strikes with the sword and the hand [of grace]. (36-84)

She has the color of a bodice, the color of a crow, the form of a jackal, and is soiled with impurities; she delights in the sound of a jackal, is like a worm, is timid, and is fond of the timid. (36.85)

She who causes distress to the timid, she who is the command of the timid, she who brings joy to the timid; she who has arisen from the kāśamarda tree, she who destroys the kāśamarda tree. || 36-86 ||
She is the destroyer of suffering, the giver of [the power to] inflict suffering, and the bestower of detachment from the world of suffering;
she is the bodily accomplishment attained within the body and the illuminator of physical bliss. || 36-87 ||
She who carries the fragrance of the body, the jar of the body, the firm one;
she who resides in the firm tree, and she who destroys the firm world. || 36-88 ||
Established on a wrong path, she is base and born from the cotton tree;
she resides in the threads of the cotton plant, stays among the wicked, and has hands for her upper garment. (36.89)
Born from the ear of Karṇa, she is Kārṇāṭī, worshipped by Karṇa;
she is the protector of Karṇa’s weapons, Karṇā, the destroyer of Karṇa, and she who wears earrings. || 36-90 ||
Directed by Kuntalā, the potter-woman, accompanied by her family, was drawn away from her ear-ornament and bow by the lotus-hand of Kṛṣṇa. || 36-91 ||
She has a black body, resides within the black body, dwells in an evil land, and is inauspicious; she is established in cruel deeds, is a crow, and is the beloved of the Kirāta clan.
She is fond of the waters of time, fond of desires, fond of poetic speech, and [appears] through anger;
she is like a line of collyrium, like moonlight, like a pale moonbeam, and fond of the art of expression.
Kalanā dwells in the Kapittha forest of all beings; she resides in the pungent Nimba tree, she is called Kā, she is named after the *ka*-group, and she is Kavagīkā. (36.94)

She who cuts through the Kirātas, who is free from the distinction between what should and should not be done, who abides in the ritual manual of Kātyāyana and others, and who brings about the arising of happiness for Kātyāyana. (36.95)
She who dwells in an evil field, she who is free from obstacles for her family, she who enters into the instruments and so forth;
she who is the skeleton woman, the slender one, the dark one, the pierced one, and the beloved of all.
She is fixed by the *kīlita* [mudrā], she is the peak (*kūṭa*), she is smeared with saffron (*kuṅkuma*) paste;
she is the abode of the fragrance of saffron, and she resides in the house of the family (*kuṭumba*). || 36-97 ||
She who possesses compassion for the wretched, who delights in the act of creation, and who is enchanted by the essence of poetry;
she who takes pleasure in the bliss of poetic treatises, who is worshiped by poets, and who is the sovereign of poets. (36.98)
Resounding with the sounds of bracelets and other ornaments, as well as elephants, chariots, horses, and drums;
it is the abode of gamblers, cruel swindlers, and those who dwell amidst the cries of peacocks.
She who is worshipped alone; she who is the enchanting *ketakī* flower;
she who is to be awakened by the quality of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*); she who bestows the wealth of absolute liberation. || 36-100 ||
She is the mother of the lords of wealth (the elephants), she is stained by the hundred eyes of the crow (the sun),
she is the end of the lineage, her radiance is extinguished, and her desire has reached the state of the supreme swans (liberation).

She is the one who cuts, whose mind is beautiful, whose wealth is her beloved, who plows, who feeds upon the plow, whose heart is intent on saffron, and who wears armlets, necklaces, and garlands. || 36-102 ||
She is the sovereign lady, the one with beautiful hair, who holds a water-pot, and is worshipped by the youth;
she delights in the essence of the Kali age and moves with the voice of a cuckoo.
She who removes the body of Kura, she who possesses a jar, she who possesses a family, she who pierces the Kurus;
she who is the dialogue with Kuṇḍalīśvara, she who dwells in the midst of Kuṇḍalīśvara.
She is called Kālasūkṣmā, Kālayajñā, and Kālahārakarī;
she is Kahalasthā, Kalahasthā, Kalahā, and Kalahāṅkurī.
Kuraṅgī, she who dwells in the glorious deer, Koraṅgī, the remover of earrings;
Kukalaṅkī, she whose intellect is dark, Kṛṣṇā, she who resides in meditation. (36.106)
The wooden vine is made of wood; the *kusī* is that which accomplishes its purpose;
the *kasvara* resides in the *kalanaka*; the *kalikā* arises from the breaking of faults.
She whose form is like a flower, who is adorned with garlands of flowers, who possesses filaments, who is the deceptive sun, and from whom lovely water arises. || 36-108 ||
She whose every limb is the syllable-cluster *ka*, who is garlanded with the sky of the syllable *ka*,
who effects the division of time, who is the fire at the end of an aeon, who dwells in the heart-lotus, and who resides in the *kakut* (the crest-lock).

She whose garment is the earth, who wears the matted locks of ascetics, who protects the Kurus, who stands behind the Kurus, who is the most excellent of the Kurus, and who destroys the ignorance of the Kurus. (36.110)
She delights in curiosity, she is beloved, she is pervaded by evil, and her bondage is painful;
she dwells upon the tree of the passions and is born from the essence of those passions.
Which science bestows leprosy, yet releases the leper from sorrow?
Who is she who sits upon a wooden seat, who takes refuge in action, and who is the Kaulika of the refuge? (36.112)
Kālikā, terrified by Time, she who dwells in the meditation of the Kaulikas;
she whose place is fashioned, the mother of all that is fashioned, she who is veiled by what is fashioned, the banner of the Kali age.
She is Keśavā, the delight of Keśava, the destroyer of the Dānavas such as Keśin,
the daughter born from the body of Keśava, and the one who infatuates the son of Keśava.
She is worthy of worship by youths, the deity whose divinity is youth;
she bestows beautiful splendor upon her husband, yet she is deceitful and a slayer of her lover.
Born of base desires, she is Kauñcā, dwelling in Kauñca and residing in Kauñca;
she dwells in the well, resides in the intellect of the well, and is the beautiful garland of wells.

Her splendor rests upon the flowers of the well; her gait is characterized by successive, simultaneous, and non-successive strides; she moves with a deceptive step, abiding in a false progression; she is the deity of the sacrificial pit, residing within the womb of the *kuṇḍalinī*.
Born in Kauṇḍilyanagara, honored by the Kauṇḍilya lineage, she dwells upon the king of monkeys; she is of the monkey clan, possessing the strength and intellect of a monkey. (36.118)

She is devoted to the meditation on the monkey, the foremost, the one who bestows a bad state, the giver of evil witnesses, she who stands in the midst of the wicked, she of evil resolve, and the illuminator of the lineage of the base. (36.119)
Residing within the body of the *kulabhramara*, she is the one who sounds as the *kulabhramara*;
she is attached to the *kula*, the eye of the *kula*, intoxicated by the *kula*, and the wind of the *kula*.
She bears the marks of Kali, the marks of Time, and the marks upon her throat; she is born from the lord of poets (Śukra).
She is the glory of the Lord of Kamalas (Viṣṇu) and the destroyer of the pride of ten million Kandarapas.
She consists of ten million splendors, she wears a garland of ten million lotuses upon her crest,
she is the deluder of ten million [beings], she is the peak, and she is born from ten million times ten million moons.
Her face is equal to ten million suns, resembling ten million fires of cosmic destruction;
she is adorned with the grace of ten million crowns and necklaces, and she bears ten million mountains.

The Goddess who bears a pair of breasts, who manifests the desire for breasts, who is the bliss of the breasts, who is concealed by her breasts, and who brings about the firmness of the breasts. (36.124)

She whose pair of breasts is the enchanting place, she who is distressed by the illusion of the breasts, she who possesses breasts, she who is deluded by the youth of her breasts, and she who bestows the bliss of massaging the breasts. (36.125)
She who dwells in glass, whose body is like glass, and who resides in the filling of glass;
she who stands within glass, who has the color of glass, and who destroys the life-force of the *kīcaka* reed. || 36-126 ||

She whose eyes are like lotuses, who is beloved by the eyes [of the Lord], the tender-eyed one, the beloved of Manu, the lotus-eyed one, the one born from a lotus, the lotus-faced one, and she who is born from Karāla.

She whose feet are like lotuses, who is non-dual, who is desirable, who is called Kara, who wears a garland of hands, who holds a lotus in her hand, who is the root, and who bestows the wisdom of the root. || 36-128 ||
The daughter of the Lotus-born, Kamalā, who desires a son;
she who scatters light, who is covered by rays, and who dwells within the life-force of the rays. || 36-129 ||
Bestower of poetry, whose mind is fixed on poetry, illuminator of the essence of poetry;
Mother Kalā, mother of the Kalpas, seated upon the seat of the divisions of the Kalpas.
She who is the desire for the right time, who resides in the essence of time, who slays and destroys Time;
she who dwells in the lamp of the sequence of rays, who abides in action, and who is the illuminator of the sequence.
She is the Fortune of Time, the fierce Kālacaṇḍā, the beloved of Kulacaṇḍeśvara; she is the Kākinī power residing within the body, the gambler, and the one who brings about destruction.
She is Karañcā, Kañcukā, and Krauñcā; she resides in the hollow of a crow’s beak;
she is named Kākā, abiding in the sound of "kāka"; she has the form of the one who consumes with the fire of time (Kālāgni).
She is the abode of evil vision, the mother of wicked sons, and the protector of the sacrifice;
she has the appearance of a golden reflection and stands in the form of a hand-binding noose.
She whose form is action, whose life-force is action, who wards off anger through action;
she who bestows protection upon the belly, she who is the belly, and she who sustains the cosmic egg within her belly.

She who dwells in the womb, she whose womb is the source of action, she who is intent on action, she who delights in action, she who is the perfection of action, she who finds bliss in action, she whose ritual activity is her work, and she who loves action. || 36-136 ||
Attached to the flow of wholesome merit, she is dear to the life-force of the enemy of Kuśa;
she is the wine from the tree of the enemy of Kuśa, exerting herself under the control of the King of Kāśī.
She resides in the palace of the King of Kāśī and dwells in the home of Karṇa’s brother;
she is richly adorned with ear-ornaments and possesses a necklace as an ornament for her neck. (36.138)
She who resides in the throat, she who is the throat, she who dwells in the lotus of the throat;
she who illumines the throat, she who wears a necklace of rubies around her neck. || 36-139 ||

She who brings about the perfection of the throat-lotus, she who dwells in the space of the throat, she who resides in the *sākinī* of the throat-lotus, and she who possesses sixteen petals in the throat. (36.140)
Vidyā wears a black antelope skin; she is clad in a black antelope skin and fine garments. She stands upon a mountain peak, she stands upon a heap of refuse, her form adorned with earrings. (36.141)
She is the song of Time, the garland of Time, and devoted to the destruction of Time;
she is the moon of Kālī, the digit, the poetry, residing in the breasts, and the bestower of welfare.
She who destroys the wicked thieves, she who dwells in the marsh, she who is born from the lotus;
she whose face is like a lotus petal, she who is the lotus, she whose beak is like a lotus, she who is the life of the lotus.
She resides in the desire realm, among the gods, and in musical instruments; she resounds with the sound of "haṃ-kāra.
She dwells in the sacrificial threads of Kaṇāda and is known as the sacrificial post (kīla) of sacrifice.
She who laughs fiercely, she who stands at the door, she who dwells in the smoke of chaff;
she who is more terrible than the fierce, she who is the crusher, and she who loves the *pāṭala* flower.
Kāmacārābjanetrā, Kāmacodgārasaṃkramā, Kāṣṭhaparvatasaṃdāhā, and Kuṣṭhākuṣṭhanivāriṇī. (36-146)
Kāhalā is established in the perfection of the Kahoḍa-mantra and is fond of the ḍiṇḍima drum;
she resides in the kulamudrā and the ḍiṇḍima instrument, bestowing the siddhi of the Kāmaḍāmara.

She resides in the station of the Kula-amara-vadhū, sounding with the cry of the peacock; she is the one who causes the *kojāgara* festival to swing, abiding in the resonance of the heroic bell-metal cymbal.
She whose instruments are time and the like, who is compassionate like a treasure-house of mercy,
who bestows the glory of sacrifice, who is the glory of fulfilled purpose, who is Kālatārā, and who is the supreme of her lineage.
She whose worship is discourse, who delights in discourse, who is discourse itself, and who is fond of discourse;
she who contemplates the meaning of actions, who possesses the knowledge of the meaning of actions, and who speaks falsely regarding desire.
Resembling the *kadamba* flower, wearing a garland of *kadamba* flowers, she is Kādambarī, satisfied by drinking, free from deceit, and always striving. (36.151)
She who dwells in the midst of the saffron petal, the support of the Kula, the beloved of the Earth;
she whose body is half that of the Kula-deity, the abode of the Kula, the bearer of the Kalās. || 36-152 ||
She is richly adorned with the passion for desire, fond of women who lack virtue, of noble birth, possessing hands like elephant trunks, and riding upon noble elephants. (36.153)
Kāmapūrasthitā, Kopā, Kapālī, Bakulodbhavā, Kārāgārajanāpālyā, and Kārāgāraprapālinī. || 36-154 ||
She is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the succession of time, the lineage of Kṛṣṇa, and the arising of phlegm (*kapha*).
She dwells within the lotus blossoming with desire, and she is both the fruit and the non-fruit of the form of desire.
Kāyaphalā, Kāyapheṇā, Kāntā, Nāḍīphalīśvarā, Kamapherugatā, Gaurī, Kāyavāṇī, and Kuvīragā. (36-156)

She whose hair-knot is bound at the wrist, who is the confluence of the holy ford of the Kāverī, who removes fear from desire, who is beloved, and who is distressed by the delusions of the arrows of Love. (36.157)
She captivates the hearts of poets, Bhāmā who removes the fear of those who desire her;
she is the mother of the gods born from the womb of Kāma, the celestial wish-fulfilling vine of love.
What is the form and what is the support of the female tortoise who eats the flesh dear to the male tortoise, who is beloved by monkeys, and who dwells within the mind of the potter? (36.159)
Established in the sacrifice of desire, she is fierce (Caṇḍā) and wears the sacrificial thread of desire;
she brings about the perfection of the sacrifice of desire and dwells in the night of passionate union.
Kāmākhyā resides at Yamalāśa; she is Kālayāmā, the Kuyoginī, who destroys those unfit for the Kuru-sacrifice and devours the flesh of Kurus.

She who acts for the benefit of the Kurus and those dear to them; she who performs what is pleasing to her servants; the sovereign of the doer; the causal self; the devourer of poets; and she who is beloved by poets.
She is joined with the *praṣṭha* of Kavi and Śatru, resides in the groves of Kailāsa,
has attained the threefold triple-siddhi, and bestows the accomplishment of the three days.
Kālī is free from blemish, the fulfiller of desires even in the Kali age;
she is beautifully adorned with the knots of the thread of the blossoms of noble lineage.
Residing in the lands of Kāmboja and Vaṅga, she is Kulavāsukī and Rakṣikā;
she is the ritual practice of the Kula scriptures, Peace (Śānti), the Peace of the Kula (Kulaśānti), and the Mistress of the Kula (Kuleśvarī). 36-165.
She possesses auspicious eloquence; she is Kāśī, who pierces the six wheels of the family.
She dwells in the center of the six lotuses of the family and illuminates the six lotuses of the family. || 36-166 ||
The *kṛṣṇamārjārakolasthā* consists of black cat and *ṣaṣṭika* rice; the *kṛṣṇamārjāraṣaṣṭikā* consists of black cat and *ṣaṣṭika* rice.
The *kulamārjārakupitā* consists of family cat and *kupita*; the *kulamārjāraṣoḍaśī* consists of family cat and *ṣoḍaśī*.
Born from the mouth of Kālāntaka, she is the slayer of Kapilāntaka;
she is the laughter of strife, the splendor of the end of time, the purpose of conflict, and stainless in her arts.
Kakṣapapakṣarakṣā, Kukṣetrapakṣasaṃkṣayā, Kākśarakṣāsākṣiṇī, and Mahāmokṣapratiṣṭhitā. || 36-169 ||
Possessing the splendor of hundreds of millions of suns, she is acquired through the science of logic (ānvīkṣikī); standing on the banks of the Kāverī, she bears the fire-god’s solar weapon.
May *Iṃ Kiṃ Śrīṃ*, the lotus of desire and protectress of Kailāsa, protect [me];
may *Śrīṃ Īṃ*, Kālī in the form of seed-syllables, protect the region of my head. (36.171)
May Kālikā, who is like a meteor amidst the darkness, protect that entire lotus of the thigh-region;
may Kulamātṛkā, who possesses the brilliance of the sun and is like a camel, protect the region of the anus.

Having made her expectation, possessing action, making the sound "kuṃ," situated in the syllable *li*, with the long vowel *ū* in *kuṃ*, fashioned, and having the syllable *keṃ* as the eye that brings about Kailāsa—[what is she?]. 36-173.
Kaiśorī, Kaiṃkarī, Kaiṃkeṃbījā, Netrayugmaka, Komā, Mataṅgayajitā, Kauśalyā, and others are the Kumārikās. (36.174)
May *Krauṃ Krauṃ Jīvakarālinī* protect the pair of my ears;
may *Kuṇḍalī Aṅkavāsinī* always protect the pair of my cheeks. (36.175)
Resplendent with the brilliance of hundreds of millions of suns, she is garlanded with imperishable syllables;
she is the hand that grants immediate satisfaction, the Kula goddess who is stainless.
May the maiden Kulapuṣpāḍhyā, who is most skillful, protect my back; may she, who fulfills all desires, always protect my sides.
May the goddess Kāmākhyā protect me; may Pratyaṅgirā protect my waist;
and may the deity residing in the waist always protect the base of my lingam. || 36-178 ||
May Kākinī protect my secret place below the penis; may Kulasiṃhikā protect the region of the buttocks; and may Kulanāgeśvarī protect the supreme region of the hips. (36.179)
May the goddess Kaṅkālamālinī protect my beautiful feet;
may Kīrti, who carries away the discus, always protect the pair of my shanks.
May she whose pair of feet is established in the state of ripening (pāka), who protects Indra (Pākaśāsana), and who revolves like a potter’s wheel, protect my toes. (36-181)
May Kālanāśā, who possesses twenty forms—consisting of the ten types of fingernails on her two hands—protect me at all times. (36.182)
She is the form that supports the umbrella of the Kula, hidden within the maṇḍala of the Kula;
she is the Mother Kuṇḍalinī of the Kula, adorned by the scholars of the Kula. || 36-183 ||
Kākānanī, Kākatuṇḍī, Kākāyu, Prakharā, Arkajā, Kākajvarā, Kākajihvā, and Kākājijñā reside in the heart. (36-184)
Kapidhvajā, Kapikrośā, Kapibālā, Hikhasvarā, Kālakāñcī, Viṃśatisthā, and Sadāviṃśanakhāgrahā—[these are the twenty]. 36-185.
May the Goddess, who is the form of Time and the abode of the fruits of the Kali age,
protect [us], whether in the wind, on a mountain, in an empty house, or at a crossroads.
She follows the conduct of the samaya of the lords of families, she is beloved by those who practice the ways of the family,
she resides on the mountain of the family, and she dwells on Kailāsa of the family.

May she protect [us] in the great forest fire, on the evil path, during the seizure by malignant planets, toward those disliked by the king, under the king's power, and for the destruction of great enemies. || 36-188 ||
The great Lakṣmī of the Kali age, the Lakṣmī of ritual action, whose garment is the lineage;
she who is pinned by the Lord of Kali, the pin, residing in the nectar-filled heaven. (36.189)
May Indra and the other ten guardians of the world always protect [me] in the ten directions;
may the nine planets, beginning with the Sun, always protect [me] from the nine interruptions.

May the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī), who dwells within the lotus of the Kula, who is fond of the substances of the Kula, who is the central sixteen-year-old maiden, and who is rich with the meat of the Kula, protect me. (36.191)
In the proclamation of knowledge, in dispute, at a time of intoxication, in great danger, in fear of famine and the like, and when afflicted by the convergence of diseases; || 36-192 ||
May Kālīkullā, Kapālī, Kāmākhyā, and Kāmacāriṇī—who are well-united within the Kaula—protect me always during my association with the Kula. (36.193)
"May she who possesses the form of the Kula protect everywhere and in all places.
Thus, O Lord, has this been told for the sake of the Mother's grace. (36.194)
This one thousand and eight names, dear to Kuṇḍalī, [is for] the complete accomplishment of all mantras of the goddess Kulakuṇḍalinī. (36.195)
For the sake of the consciousness and the perfect accomplishment of all gods and humans,
for the purpose of the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*, and for the benefit of practitioners.
It should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to the wealth of his lineage;
it must not be given to one of low birth or to a non-Brāhmaṇa.
When the wheel of the Kuṇḍalin has been set in motion, all castes become twice-born. || 36-197 ||
When the Bhairavīcakra has ceased, all the castes are distinct;
[the teaching] should be given to one of noble family, and especially to a practitioner (sādhaka).
For success shall come from giving alone, by virtue of the power of my command;
whoever abides in my ritual practice is my son, without a doubt. (36.199)
He comes to my abode as one liberated while living; he is Vāsava himself, [attained] through liquor and meat in the great night within the fire of the lineage.
One should perform the oblation by reciting each name individually for the sake of attaining the perfection of the body;
having become devoted to the fivefold conduct, the ascetic should remain one whose vital energy flows upward.
After one year, he will come to my abode; of this there is no doubt.
In this world, there shall be perfection of the body, and in the hereafter, it bestows all perfections.
Having become self-controlled and established on the three paths, those who dwell in heaven and on earth—
Indra and the other guardians of the world— are his servants and derive their power from him.
He alone is the supreme yogi for whose sake this [teaching] is perfectly stable;
he alone is the true *khecarī*-devotee, equal to Nārada, Śuka, and others. (36.204)
That world which Prajāpati himself thus proclaimed is Śiva and not a mere human;
he is eternally attained through samādhi, established in meditation, and beloved by yogins. (36.205)
The Lord who has manifested in four forms appears instantly; of this there is no doubt—for him who wears [this] with devotion on the neck, the head, or the arm. (36.206)
He shall become Kālikāputra, a self-arisen lord of sciences;
a master of wealth, a father of sons, a yogin, a lord of ascetics, and one who goes everywhere. (36.207)
Holding the Vāmā mudrā with the left hand, one becomes the lord of all siddhis. || 36-208 ||
If a man or a woman recites it with great devotion,
they shall possess all wealth and be masters of their people; they shall have sons, live with their children,
and become the head of their lineage in this world— the sole cause for attaining heaven and liberation.
He becomes the lord of existence, the master beloved by the Yoginīs. || 36-209 ||
The mortal who here constantly recites this with a spirit of devotion effects even the union of the life-force and the vital breath;
the merit of chanting this hymn destroys the sins of ten million births.
I am not even able to speak of it, for I am a consumer of human flesh.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Hymn and Armor of the One Thousand and Eight Names of Mahākulakuṇḍalinī," in the *Bhairavī-Bhairava Saṃvāda* within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantra-prakaraṇa*) of the *Mahātantroddīpana*, the latter part of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"The supreme knowledge that discriminates between dharma and adharma has been heard."
It is the essence of all the Vedāntas, the essence of essences, and higher than the highest.
O Sovereign of the Universe, having heard the hymn to Kuṇḍalinī, I am fulfilled;
now I desire to hear about the illuminating Svādhiṣṭhāna.
If you have the vision of great compassion for this mass of pure bliss,
then tell me of the Śrīkuṇḍalī yoga, which pierces through the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
"Having determined that method by which the differentiation occurs, Ānandabhairavī said:
'O Mahākāla, O Great Hero, O Ocean of the Sea of Bliss! (37-4)
Therefore, you are fit for the paths of yoga; it is for this very reason that [the method] is being proclaimed, by which sequence the piercing of the cakras occurs and one becomes immortal. (37-5)
One who has conquered the enemy of the mind becomes immortal; one who has conquered anger becomes powerful and strong;
and one who possesses knowledge of dharma and adharma becomes a yogi and a virtuous person. || 37-6 ||
The wise one who perceives the time of death, who is devoted to sacrifice and faith, and who is free from egoism—he certainly becomes a yogi. (37.7)
Closely associated with the Great Hero and free from the defects of attachment, the high-souled one becomes a knower of the Supreme Brahman, a king among yogis. (37.8)
Renowned throughout all lands, yet he remains humble toward his own refuge;
a boy who is valorous, an archer, bearing bow and arrow, and imperishable.
He shall become a master of the path of yoga, discerning and free from evil;
rendered motionless regarding the knot of ignorance, he is a *cātaka* bird for the dharma of discernment.
One who has conquered the four through uneven knowledge, who performs sacrifice and is pure—he shall become the son of the Yoginīs and the sovereign of yogas. (37-11)
If the practitioner of mantra, established in yoga and filled with the power of Vāyu, becomes a true yogi within six months—this is my definitive conclusion of the Tantra. (37.12)
He who knows my tantras, which arise from the knowledge of the true meaning—he alone is a yogin of fourfold [attainment] and my devotee; of this there is no doubt. (37-13)
Or if the practitioner, the mantra-master, becomes devoted to the practice of breath-control (vāyupāna). || 37-14 ||
Now, the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], situated in the best of families, located upon six petals, having the form of light, the supreme station of Viṣṇu, the abode of desire,
and the dwelling in the minds of the great lords of yogins, possesses beautiful rays.
It is exceedingly wealthy, filled with the moonlight of the autumn moon, and possesses beautiful objects. || 37-15 ||
When all the wise ones,
following the path of the Vedas, dwell in peace within the field of eternal existence,
then Śrī and the others, devoted to the earth, engage in inquiry.
O King, [he dwells] within the yellow garment of Mahāviṣṇu, whose body is dark-hued—
(the supreme abode of the excellent actor situated behind the curtain of the light)—
residing amidst the shadow of the courtesan, just as [Kṛṣṇa] dwells in the family of Gokula. || 37-16 ||
One who relishes the flavor of boundless great bliss should perform meditation on Hari;
he alone is the manifest Self here, the most excellent youth of sixteen years,
seated upon the great serpent’s enemy (Garuda), established in the act of sustaining, and moving like a serpent.
Who contemplates the face that bears the quality of the sound of the flute? || 37-17 ||
That very Self is eternal, the ascetic here within this soft-petaled lotus,
the essence of the family-abode, the most excellent six-petaled one;
it bestows the glory of divine bliss upon the heavens, making even the gods rejoice.
Who meditates upon Kṛṣṇa, the supreme person, who is as lovely as the moon? || 37-18 ||

I bow to Mukunda, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the perfected master of great vidyās, who is honored by the minds of the heads of lineages; who has entered the petals of the rasa-dance, who is established in his own sacred scriptures,
the enemy of Mura and foe of sin, who has well entered the lotus-heart of young women.
Who can conceive of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Senses, as being composed of the objects of the senses?
Victorious is that lord of yogis, the wise one, who, out of curiosity for the creation,

meditates upon the Lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the antidote to the poison of worldly attachment— who dwells in the mind, is united with Sarasvatī, consists of the essence of his lineage, and is adorned by liberation.
One should worship the excellent preceptor of the gods, who is the limit of pure consciousness; he bestows liberation. || 37-20 ||
The Lord of Ascetics, together with Śrī, proclaims his own ancient domain: the Lord of Yogins, Hari, the abode of all desires,
the great subtle gateway, the beloved of the virtuous wife, and the one with the leftward ray.
The large-eyed Kṛṣṇa, beloved in his own family of aesthetic sentiments, is immortal.
The knowledge that bears witness to compassion, whose body is described as a collection of virtues, which is free from the heat [of passion],
great in conduct, and true— this lotus-hand of the moon-faced one destroys death,
the lord of sins, and the enemy of Śrī.
Even he who worships that very self, Kṛṣṇa, within the lotus of his own lineage. || 37-22 ||

The Lord of the World, who is the origin of the Great Sound (Mahā-śabda), the source of both primordial nature and its transformations, the creator through His causal power, the ocean of compassion, Kṛṣṇa, who is united with the joy of hundreds of noble women— He, the instrument for the sake of the king’s lineage, offers praise.
The Virāṭa is the cosmic egg, the death of Mahāviṣṇu who has entered the instruments [of perception]. || 37-23 ||
Ah, the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Consort of Śrī, has risen in this fierce saṃsāra to proclaim his sport— that abode of eternal being,
born of a lineage that is an ocean of compassion, dark as a great rain-cloud, and possessing the three fruits.
In the priceless wandering [of the mind], the accumulation of the craving for sense objects is poison. (37.24)
That Kṛṣṇa, the illustrious Viṣṇu, constantly slays with his natural mace;
therefore, Kṛṣṇa should be meditated upon by the hosts of gods and men, [visualized] as having five faces,
bearing fruit through meditation within the six-petaled lotus of the heart.
The Kirāti is sweet for the drinking of the lotus-eyes of Rākiṇī. || 37-25 ||

The head of the family who constantly meditates upon Kṛṣṇa— the upholder of the earth, the full one, whose abode is the sky, the personification of time, accessible to the mind, delightful, and the connoisseur of the aesthetic essence of fresh beauty of the eyes— and who is the enemy of the hosts of the Kurus; [he shall attain liberation].
Supportless, dark-complexioned, he dwells among the trees on the banks of the primordial Yamunā.
The noble one, whose side is made happy by the company of the cowherd girls;
the preeminent Knower of the Field, who has conquered the lotus-hands of the lords of the earth;
the luminous Self, the Lord of overflowing compassion—He is to be meditated upon with fervor.
The mind is the dharma-parasol, its handle resting upon the threefold qualities of virtue. || 37-27 ||
O lover of the vital breath, when at dawn you praise that which resides in the three sections, the nectar of the forest arising from the fragments, which is fruitless yet grants beautiful boons,
the great field of liberation joined with the Kula woman, O supreme Kṛṣṇa!
The Lord of qualities, the Lord of Rādhā, who delights in the night, whose abode is the Vedas.
Skilled in action, subtle, awakened by the conjunction of the qualities of the observance (samaya),
situated in the triangle, possessing the essence that has flowed from the waters of the Ganges,
having the form of a star, the bliss of Mahākāla, with the dense color of the sky and full of water.
He possesses a state of being characterized by majesty, endowed with the splendor of a youthful and fresh body, and is utterly pure.
He who, through the digit of the moon on his forehead, assumes the form of great splendor residing within the noble person— his mind fashioned like a lotus blossomed from the forest—
he is a yogi devoted to the yoga of the tongue (*rasanā*) within this worldly existence.
The mind which [directs] the entire black [sacrifice], yielding abundant fruit for the hunter.

When the world here, composed of bliss, daily praises that Brahman— which possesses the enthusiasm of great wisdom, which is beyond the qualities of the [three] states, which is a mass of vital breaths, which delivers the universe, and which is the radiance of infinite great yoga— then [it attains its goal].
The eclipse of all [the planets], including the sun and the moon, is caused by the seizing and obstructing of their movement.

Who meditates upon Him who is the great and terrible devourer, the mass of hundreds upon hundreds of great merits, the joy of His lineage, Viṣṇu, whose rays are like a hundred moons and jars of nectar, who is accessible to the mind, subtle, and yet veiled by the three qualities? 37–32.
Having joyfully meditated upon Kṛṣṇa and performed devotion to Kṛṣṇa, one becomes a renunciant (yati);
for such a person, there is no doubt that devotion resides in the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (37–38)
Kṛṣṇabrahmā, devoted to the threefold meditation,
leads that person and gives him [to Kṛṣṇa], O Śaṅkara.
Without the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, how can there be victory over one's own abode?
O Śaṅkara, through meditation on Kṛṣṇa, one attains the piercing of the great lotus. (37–35)

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Sadhana of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Rākini of the Svādhiṣṭhāna," within the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, the Northern Tantra (*Uttara-tantra*), the Illumination of the Great Tantra (*Mahātantroddīpana*), the Revelation of the Six Wheels (*Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*), in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 37.
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said: "Listen, O Lord, I shall proclaim the supreme sādhana of Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
By which sequence devotion may arise, one should become subject to the net of time. || 38-1 ||
Devotion to my lotus feet arises without a doubt;
if that eminent practitioner, possessed of devotion, should worship Mahāviṣṇu. (38-2)
O Lord, let my devotee on this earth become equal to Śiva.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the universe, whose nature is the bliss and liberation of the three worlds,
who is complete, enveloped by the three qualities yet the sustainer of those qualities, the supreme presiding deity of Sattva,
who stands as the protector of the kingdom beneath the Linga and resides upon the five-faced one.
If a person worships the auspicious Śrī Viṣṇu with devotion, that person shall be happy along with their family.
First, I worship Kāma with the triple-emanation joined by the noble lady, the seed-syllable of desire with the triple-emanation;
Śrī-Kṛṣṇa with a pair of arms, a pair of lovers joined with moonlight and the sky;
the pair of Brahmās, Prakṛti and Puruṣa, and Kākinī who is beyond that.
Again and again, I worship that which resides at the throat and ears, joined with the wife of fire (the letter *ra*). 38-5.
Having recited this mantra ending with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and *namaḥ*, and having joined it thus at the beginning,

and repeatedly ending with *namaḥ* along with the three worlds, one should agitate that [universe] in an instant. Royal fortune shall abide upon his head, and the earth shall remain firmly established in his palace for all time.
Having determined the time for her departure, the fair-faced woman sets out when the time for the "Brahma-staff" has arrived.
Then, O Prāṇa, O Lord of the gods, O increaser of my satisfaction, now hear the mantra of Narasiṃha, O Great Lord. (38-7)
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Kānta, it is traditionally taught as a pair of pairs;
with the Mahānṛsiṃha mantra, I worship: "Obeisance, obeisance! (38-8).
Having established the mind within the great lotus of the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) for the purpose of purifying the mind, the yogi who recites the mantra again and again— || 38-9 ||
By the recitation of this mantra alone, the practitioner becomes accomplished;
by the power of this mantra, one obtains the accomplishment of all states in an instant. (38–10)

If a practitioner established on the [spiritual] stages should accomplish the mantra of Hari, he attains perfection through his vigor in a sequence equal to the number of atoms [in the universe]. (38.11)
Now, O Mahādeva, I shall declare that which is the excellent essence of all phonemes;
one who is not attached to the series of phonemes may attain perfection by reciting it. (38–12)
If a mortal person, being without support, seeks the mantra of accomplishment, he should remain alone in a secluded place, like a lamp burning by itself. (38.13)
One should recite the mantra fearlessly while focused on the lotus of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
Listen now to that sequence by which the entire world is brought under control. (38-14)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should likewise emit the seed-syllable ending in 'na',
joined with the seed-syllable of fire and endowed with the vowel of the lower tooth.
One should utter [the mantra] joined with *nāda* and *bindu* twice more;
at the end of the word "to Narasiṃha," one should utter it three times again. (38–16)
One should utter the mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of the Goddess (devībīja), the seed-syllable of Śakti (śaktibīja), and ending with svāhā;
by the application of this mantra, one shall bring Kuṇḍalinī under control. || 38-17 ||
The foremost of practitioners attains stability in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*;
having become the master of all vital breaths, he becomes powerful upon the earth. (38-18)
Cold and heat, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, victory and defeat—may he always attain knowledge of dharma and adharma as eternal knowledge. || 38-19 ||
Furthermore, the mantras of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are served by all the gods;
having known them, all the deities became the guardians of every quarter of the horizon. (38-20)
O Mahādeva, hear now of its application and the characteristics of its perfection;
for without taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā is never satisfied anywhere. (38.21)
But the goddess Kuṇḍalī is not satisfied without the state of the bound soul (paśubhāva), O Lord;
for in the state of the bound soul there is the attainment of knowledge, while in the state of the hero (vīrabhāva) one possesses liberation.
Established in samādhi within the divine state, he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Having extracted the beautiful seed-syllable, it is joined with the vowel to the left of Indra (the letter *i*). (38-23)
The word for addressing Kṛṣṇa, surmounted by Nāda and Bindu, joined again with the previous mantra, constitutes the great mantra consisting of three syllables. (38-24)
Having performed the recitation of this mantra, the yogi becomes a sovereign among yogis;
this yoga is the cause of supreme bliss and possesses infinite forms. (38.25)
What need is there for much speaking? He who performs [this] shall obtain the fruit:
one should meditate upon the Lord of the Gopīs, the Sovereign of the Rākīṇī-maṇḍala. (38-26)
One should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Gokula and the abode of the beings of the worlds, who resides in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], is dark-complexioned, and possesses four arms. || 38-27 ||
Śrī Govinda, who is exceedingly cool, possesses the great splendor and beauty of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; he is the beloved of all sciences and is sought after by all. (38.28)
The Lord who removes great delusion, adorned with a forest garland,
who surpasses ten million maidens with his lotus-like hands, and who is united with all.
To the crown-wearing great hero, adorned with a crescent moon upon his crest, whose limbs are graced by a garland of *guñjā* berries—Śrīnātha, the Supreme Lord. (38–30)

[One should meditate upon] Hari, the son of Vasudeva, who wears yellow garments, has a gentle smile, resides in the center of the six lotus petals, and is the abode of the life-breath of his beloved. 38–31.
Having meditated thus upon the six-petaled lotus, one should contemplate Śauri, the Lord of the Kings of Kings, who always bears the Kaustubha gem upon his chest and is marked with the Śrīvatsa sign.
A person seeking the perfection of Murāri should meditate on Him as situated in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra].
Having meditated thus in the past, Brahmā attained the manifestation of Nārāyaṇa’s qualities. (38–39)
One should worship the Supreme Lord with substances imagined by the mind;
one should meditate upon Hari and sacrifice within the great six-petaled lotus. (38–39)
Having established Hari as the Guru upon a mentally conceived pedestal, [one should worship him] with the sixteen services originating from the field of the mind.
Having established Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga and the Sovereign of Rādhikā’s heart, within a single-minded heart, one should worship Kṛṣṇa upon the pedestal.
There, having constructed a beautiful lotus with eight petals, a hexagonal pericarp, and the four gates adorned with secondary ornaments; 38–37.
When one meditates again and again upon the eight petals of the six-petaled lotus,
one should worship Śrī Viṣṇu with the ten sets of fivefold offerings.
The fivefold ritual service consists of offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with the food offering:
the seat, welcome, water for the feet, the respectful offering, and water for sipping. (38–39)
The madhuparka offering, sipping water for purification, bathing, garments, ornaments, fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and prostration. || 38–40 ||
One should employ the sixteen modes of service (upacāras) in worship;
this is the rule that applies everywhere for the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Viśveśa, O Lord of the virtuous, let the description of the ten modes of service (daśopacāra) for the one born from you be heard, O Beloved Master. (38–42)
The water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and again the water for sipping;
then the offerings beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya)—these are the ten services in their proper sequence. (38–43)

Having fully worshipped Viṣṇu, the wise man, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with his senses subdued, shall always experience supreme bliss as a servant under the command of Kālikā. (38–44)

The hero, the possessor of all knowledge, the discerning one who perceives everything, being supremely pure, should continuously contemplate [the deity] within his own self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna). 38–45.
Pervaded by the conduct of a child, free from disease, and knowing the true state of being—he who is devoted to the nature of Kṛṣṇa shall become a son of Kālikā. (38–46)
One should contemplate Kṛṣṇa above the root-lotus as the essence of the lineage (kula);
he becomes a son of Kālikā, endowed with the qualities of the eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭāṅga-siddhi).
Having performed the worship mentally, one should carry out the installation of the conch;
for having performed that mental yoga, one need not perform external worship.
In the practice of the deity of the root mantra, one should worship the deity;
and [one should also worship] those situated to the right of the god, who are well-established as objects of prior worship. (38–49)
The knower of mantras should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the appropriate mantra;
thereafter, he should perform meditation upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa until the mind is dissolved [in Him]. (38–50)
In this manner, the king of yogis gradually becomes firm within that lotus, he who cultivates a state of purity toward Hari, the remover of great delusion. (38–51)
Having established [the mind] upon the six lotuses, one shall attain great liberation;
he who knows the primary qualities should rely upon the meaning of my teaching.
In this world and even in the realm of the enemies, the king of yogis dwells;
one should fix the mind upon his lotus feet, which are variegated with the filaments of sacrificial rites.
Her pair of shanks were adorned with lovely, tender plantain stalks;
her two thighs possessed a luster equal to the trunks of elephants in rut. (38–54)
In the navel, deep as the whirlpools of the Gaṅgā, in the pure and stainless cavity, likewise in the belly, the chest, and in Hari, who possesses the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem; (38–55)
With a forehead like ten thousand full moons, adorned with beautiful earrings,
and graced by the staff-like arms bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Resembling a thousand suns, the practitioner, purified and with a pure mind, should worship the two families along with their crowns in these locations. (38–57)
Having fixed the mind upon Kṛṣṇa, one certainly becomes absorbed in Him;
until the mind reaches dissolution in Kṛṣṇa, who is one's own self consisting of consciousness. (38–58)

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Entry of Śrī Kṛṣṇa into His Own Abode," within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*. 38.
Then the thirty-ninth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Now, O Lord, I shall proclaim the supreme means for accomplishing worldly existence."
By means of that very practice alone, the yogi becomes [perfected] at that very moment. || 39-1 ||
If this remains in the mind, accomplishment will be attained without effort;
one may swiftly delude the three worlds and bring the three worlds under one's control. (39-2)
Always accompanied by Rāma, the supreme witness of the worlds, served by the lotus-hand of the son of Jamadagni, and honored by all. (39-3)
It was the abode of infinite beings, agitated by the confluence [of rivers], bestowing great beauty with its eight hand-like peaks, and adorned with various ornaments. (39.4)
Having meditated upon [the deity] residing in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, one becomes cool and self-controlled;
O Lord, hear from me that hymn to him by the recitation of which one attains perfection. (39–5)
Brahmā and the other lords of the gods, as well as the sages who protected the sacrifice, having previously composed this hymn, became liberated while living upon the earth. (39-6)
Therefore, listen to the hymn to Śrī Kālikānātha, which yields great fruit. (39.7)
The Ṛṣi is Brahmā, the metre is Triṣṭup, and the deity is Śrī Viṣṇu, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and Śrī Nārāyaṇa, whose deeds are wonderful;
this is the application for the purpose of attaining the mantra-armor (kavaca) which is the essence of all hymns.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the worlds, the sinless one who grants perfection through meditation;
Govinda, who brings one across the ocean of worldly existence, the cause of deliverance;
Śrī Viṣṇu, the wearer of the forest garland, Nṛsiṃha, and Nārāyaṇa of Gokula.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Yogis, the Sovereign of Men, the Primordial Being, in Vṛndāvana. || 39-8 ||
O Śrīdhara, [I bow to] Śrī Rāma, who is accompanied by the glory of liberation, who has transformed the ocean of Dharma,
who is beautiful, whose nature is pure through Balarāma, who is eternally undisturbed, of noble lineage, dark-complexioned,
and whose protruding belly shines with necklaces of gold and other jewels.
I bow to that Lord Hari, who is the locus of the Māyā possessed of qualities, yet whose own support is himself.
To the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, who is free from all defects, whose nature is liberation through union (sāyujya-mokṣa),

the crest-jewel of the best of kings, adorned with a circle of splendor, the maker of shade for the celestial wish-fulfilling tree, and the object of worship for yogis— my worship, fashioned from various jewels, [is offered].
For the sake of attaining mastery of speech, one should meditate upon [the deity] who is surrounded by the sons of Vidyā and Gopā, and who consists of the qualities (guṇa). || 39-10 ||

The abode of self-consecration, the supreme person, whose wealth is knowledge, the master of illusion, the glorious Lord, the yogi of the Kula, the sole seed of the splendor of the three worlds, the Sovereign,
who delights in attaining the state of the festival of worldly existence— the blissful one who is the primordial source of all.
I bow to the one who bestows firm bliss upon the back of the excellent serpent’s enemy, which is rendered fruitful.

O Śiva, the Lord who is the presiding deity of desire, who is beyond the eight states of existence, who is radiant and removes the dullness born from attachment to worldly life, who is eternal, whose qualities are pure, who is the sole cause of the fragrance of profound intellect, and who bestows fame and security while dispelling great fear.
It is the abode of the singular, beautiful bliss situated in the center of each of those six-petaled lotuses. || 39-12 ||

I bow to the Lord of Śrī, the infallible Narahari, who disciplines the hosts of Daityas, Gandharvas, and others; who delights in the company of beautiful singers, who holds the flute, and who bestows devotion;
the sovereign of jewels, the immovable one who stands as the refuge and who supported Mount Govardhana.
The Taijasa [Tīrtha], frequented by sages such as Viśvāmitra and Tapodhana. || 39-13 ||
I bow to the lotus feet of Govinda, which are unborn and unconquered, shining upon the path of devotion;
which possess sovereignty born of purity, measured by the highest reckoning, and adorned with beautiful anklets and necklaces;
and which take the form of a swan, immersed upon the back of the white Garuḍa of bliss.
The soles of his feet are endowed with a core as red as the bandhūka flower, and the space between [his toes] is always filled. || 39-14 ||
I bow to that primordial one, who is perfected by the love of Rākiṇī, who has attained the bloom of youth, who is the source of passion for song, instrumental music, and the like,

who bestows the fruit of excellent qualities born of divine love, who is the moon bringing joy to Gokula, and who is the beloved of Vāṇī and Lakṣmī, bringing delight to the virtuous throughout the three worlds.
I pay homage to the essence of the Siddhānta, which is free from coming and going, and is the authoritative one signified by the essential [teachings]. 39-15.

Having meditated upon that Supreme Person, the celestial wish-fulfilling tree— who is full of desire, whose head is bowed to the Moon (Śiva), whose seed-syllable ends with the invocation "Kṛṣṇa," who bestows limitless bliss, who is brilliantly radiant, and who is gracious— I worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa.
Having entered the mind within the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, one becomes established in the place of accomplishment.
In the sky, upon a beautiful lotus, [I meditate on] the Lord of Men, who delights in the self, who bestows all pleasures, the primordial slayer of Kaṃsa; he is red in color,
possessing a magnificent trunk, devoid of beginning, middle, or end, moving through the realms of Brahmā and Śiva, and possessing the stainless luster of a sapphire.

For the sake of the perfection of existence, I meditate upon the Supreme Immortal One, who is the enthusiasm for existence and the ultimate cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds.
You always bestow the gift of knowledge upon all within the lotus of the petals of the nectar;
you are the bliss of the Self, the foremost among those who possess the wealth of the nectar of liberation and its qualities.
