Filled with *māyā*, possessing the ever-increasing nectar, you are the region of joy and the sole sovereign.
May the illustrious one named Rāja, who is perfectly full, cast his glance upon me, who am destitute of wealth, at the beginning of your [teaching]. (39.18)
Kālī beheld Śrī Kuṇḍalinī’s supreme abode, which is the form of Brahman for the devotee;

it is the umbrella of liberation, the Lord of the City who sports with his consort in the bliss of his own wealth, leading the assembly-ground as his eye, and presiding over the consecration in this very city. || 39-19 ||
Having meditated, I bow to the Lord of the worlds within the subtle lotus;
I praise Kṛṣṇa, the Vaikuṇṭha, the destroyer of the power of worldly existence for the Kurus,
the ender, who is attainable through knowledge by the peaceful, and who protects the triple path with his own lotus-eyes.
The enemy of Vajra, the enemy of Pūtanā, the hero who destroys the darkness of the two-faced hell. || 39-20 ||
Honored in all the worlds, supreme in mind, absolute and stainless;
the syllable Oṃ, known as the Cause, the mother of those possessed of wisdom and the Sugatas, perfected through the mantra of Mātṛkā;
the first-perfected among the perfected ones, the subduer of the enemies of the gods, the form of Time for his foes.
Having filled Mukunda within the mind—which is situated above the root, at the end of the six petals, and is perfectly pure—[one should meditate].

I constantly honor you for the sake of attaining identity with my own body; I worship you, who are the manifest Lord of all, the bringer of peace, praised by the hands of the Goddess Śrī, the Sovereign of the earth, the one whose nature is dissolution, the possessor of all qualities, the Knower—you alone are the Great One. (39-22)
If you have thus placed my own base and defiled self— destitute of the glorious Dharma—
beneath Your feet, and have surely protected me here as Your own refuge;
[then grant] the stainless lotus-feet of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa and Caitanya, who are intent on liberation.
It is the universal beginning and end, the threefold movement, and the refuge for nirvāṇa and liberation. || 39-23 ||
O Lord, I place upon the leaf of the *rasa* plant the divine one— the destroyer of enemies, consisting of bliss, the abode of absolute liberation (*kaivalya-mokṣa*), praised by the hosts of gods,
the refuge of the world, the lord of ascetics, and established in the liberation of *nirvāṇa*.
Delighting in nirvāṇa and other [liberations], it is not fickle, yet it is filled with the flickering of glory. || 39-24 ||
I bow to the Supreme Lord, the destroyer of the strength and life-force of all the Daityas;
who is mounted upon a swan, who is the protector of the moment, the Lord of Speech, the Sovereign,
the Lord of the wish-fulfilling creeper of desires, the Lord of the lineage, the Lord of Knowledge, and the Lord of the Earth.

I meditate upon you, Bhāskara—the Lord of Śrīvidyā, the Primordial God, the Supreme Person, the beloved of Viśveśvara, and the multitude of the true essence of Kumbhodbhava and Kāla. You who are devoted to the yoga that is the sign of the Siddhas; protect me first of all! (39-26)

O Lord, I joyfully salute Kṛṣṇa, who is beyond all conventions, who is esteemed for his jewels of virtues, who is held by the wise as the ultimate goal for the highest good, who is well-established within the minds of the enlightened, whose great nectar of love has overflowed, and who has conquered the lotus-hand of Śiva. 39-27.
A mass of light, the abode of Rāma, the bestower of non-arrogance, skilled in desire;
the shadow of the great mantra, joined with the night, rendered dull by darkness;
situated in the triangle, poorly situated, the cause of both evil and auspicious destinies.
The configuration of the world has dissolved, along with the dharma of arising for all beings.
Rāmeśa, the Lord of Speech, whose feet are reached through sacred rites, who has attained Śambhu,

the lotus-eye of yogis throughout the three periods of time, devoted to the Word (Śabda), the joy of his lineage, dwelling in the hearts of the cowherd women, and honored by the cowherd women; [I bow to him].
But the ritual ordinance [prescribes] you as Indra, Upendra as more venerable, and Hari as the enemy of the foe.

With joy I salute you, the impetuous one; in that new battle of mine, O you who consist of the faith of the low-born, you who bestow all perfections, you who have transcended impurity, you who have been brought to the state of gods and men, and you who are the abode of the scriptures. (39-30)

I go for refuge to the one who is the delight of women, whose heart is full of aesthetic flavor, who is free from sorrow, the most radiant among sacrifices, beneficial, and possessed of supreme qualities. (39-31)
May the Lord of the Gopīs, who dwells eternally upon the crest of my lineage, protect me constantly; may he daily and incessantly bestow grace upon the region of my forehead.
May the Lord of the Sovereign of the Kings of Kings swiftly protect the region situated below my forehead.
The Lord of the Gods, the protector of the cowherds,
the three-eyed one who is the lord of both preservation and dissolution, whose entire being is bliss, is situated within the umbrella-like throat.

May Śauri, the immortal, protect my back daily; may he who longs for the love of Śambhu protect my hips, which lie outside the linga; may Murāri, who causes the overflow of bliss, eternally protect my secret place, the seat of my lineage, which pervades my entire body.
May Nṛhari, the enemy of the Daityas, protect my two thighs with his shanks and my lotus-feet with his feet.
A wise person who is self-restrained, devoted, and pure should recite this hymn;
within a month he becomes steadfast and, in the six-petaled lotus, partakes in all perfections.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Armor for the Praise of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, the section on accomplished mantras, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, the latter part of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*.
Now, the fortieth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Lord, I shall now speak; listen to me with focused attention."
By which sequence the practice of yoga for the worlds may become firm. || 40-1 ||
O Bhairava, he who is seized by the state of being (bhāva) everywhere becomes a perfected one (siddha);
for he who is the god Bhairava is indeed omnipresent throughout the universe. (40.2)
Skilled in ritual action, a great hero, and a devotee beloved by heroes,
having meditated upon the garland of syllables and having recited it day and night in the center, || 40-3 ||
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) and restraining his vital breaths, he is one who has reached the further shore of Vedānta;
he is a knower of the final conclusions of all the scriptures and is established in their definitive determination.
He was a knower of the Gāthās, possessed of supreme bliss, discerning, and devoted to the inner state;
he was a perceiver of the true nature of existence, a knower of the secret meaning, and a learned scholar versed in the Vedas. (40.5)
Devoted to the knowledge that accomplishes speech, speaking the truth, and firm in posture,
one should meditate upon the syllable as it moves through the six stages and perform meditation individually for each.

Seated upon six lotuses, one who practices the Great Vidyā should indeed meditate upon the six syllables preceded by dhyāna; he should contemplate the letters beginning with va and ending with la. (40.7)
The syllable *baka* (ba), consisting of its own rays of beauty, should be meditated upon as incomparable;
it is situated on the eastern petal, delighting in the nectar of devotion to the splendor of Mukunda,
ending in distinguished knowledge, bowed to by bliss, and possessing ten million rays.
Having meditated upon Śrī Lakṣmī, one swiftly causes the Person of Time (Kālapuruṣa) to depart. || 40-8 ||
The syllable *bha* brings joy to the two-colored Śrīnātha on the petal of taste (*rasa*).
It resides at the side of the triangle, is a fragment of the restless one, the abode of Śambhu, possessing a great red form, youthful, and formidable. It is the *Akula*.
The place of the family abode is joined with the one red with passion for the lady of the family. || 40-9 ||
When the wise one, having cast off sorrow, meditates with boundless joy upon the abode of the three worlds— the refuge of the universe— having attained supreme bliss,
he becomes great at the gateway of supreme liberation, transcending all that is inert.
He was a man of pleasure, the beloved husband of all his ever-new wives. || 40-10 ||
If one worships the Mahākālasthāna with the syllable *sa*, where the mouths of the caves are wide open and emit rays of blood like ten million suns, that Mahākālasthāna...
is a refuge; even before [attaining it], one becomes happy.
The triangle is on the right limb; it has nine eyes and is conquered by yoga and sacrifice. || 40-11 ||

He who meditates upon the letter *ya*, the lord of great speech, who is like a celestial wish-fulfilling tree (*suratara*) on earth and in heaven, bestowing delights and being free from the afflictions of the path to the state of the immortals— he becomes a celestial wish-fulfilling tree himself, rendered motionless by love.
It is the cause of desire, joined with the internal breath within the bliss of Mukunda. || 40-12 ||
Then the world becomes utterly devoid of desire, like a windless place for crows;
it becomes the abode of the great fire, the supreme cloud, and a hundred suns—
when one meditates with bliss upon that giver of supreme wealth through the nectar of sacrifice.

The knowledge of drinking nectar (sudhāpāna) bestows the fruits of one's desires when used for fire-offerings (havana). That which is praised by the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), the lotus-born (Brahmā), and the Lord of the World (Viṣṇu)—the essence (pirayaṃ) situated behind the triangle—is the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. || 40-13 ||
If one meditates alone upon the arrangement of the fires, the pure seed of the Kula, accompanied by compassion,
the fragment of Māyā consisting of blood, and the supreme delight for the flocks of birds,
he suddenly attains manifold prosperity.
Mahendra [is] the Sthānāṅga, which bestows the happiness of the lotus and is the abode of Kṛṣṇa. || 40-14 ||
If one meditates upon Pīraya as a field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra) consisting of bliss—
[the syllable] *la* situated on the moon, possessing the rays of a hundred moons and abiding in the bindu,
[and] Rādhā, the large-eyed one, accompanied by her sweet words and conversation— then [one attains that state].
In the Ramāmoda leaf, there is the method of crossing along with the removal [of obstacles]. || 40-15 ||
Having visualized the Lord of Śrī, who consists of the nine rasas and removes delusion, upon the left side of Rākiṇī, that man skilled in meditation worships Him;
having attained great liberation, he unites with her who possesses the first menses. 40-16.
Then the Great Vidyā, the supreme power Rākiṇī, should be meditated upon constantly, together with Śrī Viṣṇu, by one who is free from the desire for enjoyments through yogic practices. (40.17)
Stainless, the joy of his lineage, veiled by a gentle smile, that great yogi attains the supreme kingdom; of this there is no doubt. (40.18)
O Lord, as long as there is connection with the *mūlādhāra*, so long should one practice *yama* and the other limbs;
at the proper time, one should perform yoga consisting of the five *amṛtas* along with *yama*, *niyama*, and *āsana*. (40.19)
O Mahādeva, one should perform this until that perfection is attained;
if the perfection of the five immortals is achieved, then one becomes a possessor of the perfections such as *māyā*.
At the time of accomplishment, having repeatedly held and held again the five breaths beginning with prāṇa— the five outflows— one should slowly perform the kumbhaka (retention) incessantly.
When the body has become pure, the purity of the vital air (vāyu) arises;
the great wind, which possesses all forms, becomes a pure self within the self. (40.22)
O Lord of Yoga, he bestows success if one relies upon his own task.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Letters of the Six-Petalled [Lotus]," in the dialogue between Ānandabhairavī and Bhairava, within the section on Siddhi-mantras in the Mahātantroddīpana of the Uttara-tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. 40.
Then the forty-first chapter:
Ānandabhairavī said:
[She who is] the enjoyment of the sport and dissolution of Kṛtānta.
O Lord Śaṅkara, whose glorious hands are drenched in nectar,
by your command I shall proclaim this tantra for the sake of spiritual accomplishment, for I have done so under the influence of the bliss arising from the Āgamas. (41.1)
The noble lord of sages, desiring love,
knows the meaning of the Tantra and its infinite means of accomplishment;
he is a devotee of the lotus feet of the Lord at the great dawn.
If one is a vessel for devotion to Govinda and Śambhu. || 41-2 ||
That person who understands the specific means for realizing the distinctions of the six chakras is exceedingly rare;
he alone is the means for the cessation of saṃsāra.
Having always abandoned [worldly things], one should attain unwavering devotion. || 41-3 ||
Ānandabhairava said:
O beloved, if the auspicious practice of the six-petaled lotus has been explained,
[then tell me] the meeting of the Goddess with Rākiṇī and the prowess of Kuṇḍalinī.
Together with the illustrious Viṣṇu, who is the embodiment of Time and possesses manifold forms,
and with the pure, stainless principle (tattva) along with the hosts of his attendants.
Indeed, not all of that has been told—the prowess of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the hymn of praise accompanied by Devarakṣiṇī, and the means for the realization of Kṛṣṇa. (41–6)
This hymn of praise to the manifestation of Kṛṣṇa, joined with the power of Rākiṇī, is the supreme auspiciousness, the means for attaining Brahman, and the increaser of one's lineage. (41.7)
Speak, O Mahākālī, if you have affection for me;
tell the most profound secret, the auspicious Thousand Names.
O Mahāviṣṇu, you have recited the one hundred and eight [verses] together with Rākiṇī;
now, O beautiful woman, O desire-inspiring one, speak the hymn to Rākiṇī.
Ānandabhairavī said:
O Lord of Yogins, O Ocean of Supreme Bliss, O Śrī Candraśekhara, listen to this hymn to Rākiṇī, which increases supreme bliss. (41.10)
This is declared to be a practice that grants happiness everywhere, even for the perfected ones (siddhas). By the recitation of this hymn, a yogi shall attain the state of a lord of yogis. 41-11.
He who practices the fivefold conduct (pañcācāra) in the Vaiṣṇava sādhana attains the most excellent of all spiritual accomplishments and shall not fall from his caste. (41-12)
O Lord of the Vaiṣṇavas, when one who knows reality develops an equanimous attitude toward enemies and friends, and toward actions and non-actions, then indeed such even-mindedness arises. (41.13)
One becomes accomplished only through the sequence of the fivefold conduct, and not otherwise,
[just as it was attained] by Rādhā and the other cowherd girls, together with the hosts of cowherds on all sides.
Having joyfully performed the fivefold conduct and thereby protected all beings, the Lord of Kamalā acted; therefore, one should take recourse in the fivefold conduct.
By means of the sequence of the fivefold conduct alone, Kuṇḍalinī becomes Caitanya;
likewise, O Lord, for the sake of Kṛṣṇacaitanya and Rākiṇī.

O Kulārṇava, listen to the hymn of the navel-ring of Kuṇḍalinī, which serves as the cause for the consciousness of the deities residing in the six petals for the sake of awakening that consciousness. (41.17)
She who is swayed in the ocean of the tongue, yet remains steady like a noble woman;
she who consists of illusion, yet is the hero who destroys all suffering;
she who is seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), established in her state, and easily attained by sages.
May the auspicious Bhavikā, the protectress of the lineage, protect me! || 41-18 ||
She is an ocean of bliss, having drunk the essence of all that is solidified;
she is the young maiden bowed down by the noble clans, residing within the six petals of the *ṣaṭkula*;
she possesses the stainless qualities of the arts of Kālī, and she is the abode of wealth for the wealthy.
O Kṛṣṇeśvarī, O Rākiṇī, bring about my prosperity! || 41-19 ||

She who is Rākiṇī, whose activity is for the arising of the three worlds; who consists of consciousness, possesses a noble lineage, and abides as the beloved of the Lord of the Kula; the Sovereign of the Universe, established in the supreme state of union with the Destroyer of Smara.
May the goddess Kṛṣṇapriyā protect my happiness. || 41-20 ||
She who is served by the lotus-hands of the Lord of the Six Groups (Ṣaḍvarganātha),
the Queen of Rādhā, the bestower of bliss, the beautiful goddess of the gods,
the Mother, the progenitor of Kuleśa, and the one who dwells within the minds of all worlds— [she is the Goddess].
May the supreme knowledge, which removes all enemies, protect my body. || 41-21 ||
May she who is Govindarāma’s beloved, Navamālinī; or she who is the sovereign of the kingdom, Smaraharā, the youthful mistress—
may she eternally protect the deity residing upon my six-petalled lotus.
She is Śrīkuṇḍalī, the utterly pure Kularākiṇī.
Śrīsundarī, supreme among the Kula, worshipped by the assembly of the Kula, she who possesses the power of the twilight ritual and whose sacred ford transcends all;
the bestower of fortune, she who grants the pure state of being to the hosts of the Kula.
May he eternally protect the domain of the six-petaled lotus of the Kula.
Devoted to bestowing consciousness, delightful with the three qualities (guṇas),
dark-complexioned, bearing beautiful jeweled bells upon her hips,
with one hand resting on the Blue Mountain and the other in the gesture of granting boons.
I worship upon the left lotus-hand of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 41-24 ||
To that Rākiṇī, the delighter of the three, the destroyer of all impurities,
who dwells everywhere, the mother of the sky, seated upon a lotus,
resting on a lotus-throne, with ears for arms, born from the Guru, and infinite;
I worship Śāntā upon six lotus petals. || 41-25 ||
I bow to Śānti, who brings peace upon the mask of compassion;
to Nāśamukti, whose feet are worshipped by the supreme Vaiṣṇavas;
to Rādhā, the nectar-like, most excellent one who abides in the qualities of the worlds.
I worship Dharmārṇavā on the sixth petal. || 41-26 ||
I bow to the wielder of the sword, the compassionate and beautiful one of the three emanations; to that Rākiṇī, the exceedingly merciful, whose thoughts are fixed on the stainless goal;
to her who is the delusion, the supreme source of wandering, and the primordial memory worthy of worship.
I worship my wife, who brings exceeding happiness to Hari. || 41-27 ||
She who is the state of boundless affection for the timid, the divine Goddess of Speech who is bowed to by millions of ascetics,
and who is red in color by nature within the copper-hued heart; [to her, I bow].
May she who consists of illusion, the goddess Surakalāvati, protect my limbs. || 41-28 ||

She who is the creeper of intention for the wish-fulfilling trees, appearing in the form of fruit; she who dwells within Śiva and is praised by millions of sages; she who is worshipped with the hand of Hari—may she [bestow] upon me the essence of the Lord of the Kula.
May Rādhā, whose wealth is always forbearance, protect me. 41-29.
She who brings security, she who grants boons, she who is easily attained, she who abides in Hari;
she who is the sow-form, the creator of existence, the Great Goddess Tripurā;
she who dwells in the wind, whose nature is dissolution, and who is attached to the path of stability.
May Rādhā, who is the very essence of all things, protect me at every moment. 41-30.
May Gaṅgā, the bestower of purity, always protect the region of my head;
may Śrī Rādhā, the queen of the family, with her great speech, reside above my forehead;
may the mantra-abiding Jayadā joyfully protect my brow; and may Kumudinī protect the space between my eyebrows.
Vidyā, Vāgbhava, Kuṇḍalī, Phala, Valā, Bālā, and the three eyes. || 41-31 ||
Gaṇḍa is Caṇḍasarasvatī; Śrutikula resides on Mount Kailāsa;
Medhā is Ṭaṃ, residing in the jar (Ghaṭavāsinī); Śaśīmukhī has an extremely subtle disposition;
Jihvāgra is at the chin, Radāvadhivahā flows through the throat and reaches the neck and shoulders.
Skandeśī, whose intellect is stainless with the luster of her teeth, the sovereign lady of the realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
May Bhavānī, the auspicious consort of Śambhu, who delights in various colors, who possesses a gentle essence,
who stands behind him in his rites, who grants him movement, and who is eternally radiant and fierce,
protect my back; may Kulamālinī protect my sides, and may she whose garment is her hips protect my waist and my generative organ.
May she who is Kāmākhyā, the bestower of wealth and full of compassion, protect my two feet. 41.33.

May Gaurī, who wards off the anger of the Mother, who bestows auspiciousness upon me, who creates the beauty of the six-petaled lotus, who dwells in the sacred caru, who protects the tree of the Kula, and who grants supreme bliss— may she,
who resides in the station of consciousness and has gone to the state of the Mother of Govinda, protect me.
May the Earth, the sustainer who dwells in the excellent field, constantly protect consciousness.
Blessed is she with lotus-like eyes and a face like the sun, whose essence is consciousness and action;
may that power, whose nature is forgiveness, surely bring about peace everywhere.
May she, who dwells in my heart, who resides in the wheel of fame, and who is tawny-red as lac, be victorious.
May Jayā, who dwells in the lower wheel, joyfully protect my life. || 41-35 ||
O auspicious one, who possesses the excellent vital breath, one should recite this hymn daily;
it should always be recited by accomplished yogis at the time of piercing the six cakras. (41-36)
At the time of arranging the family lineage and upon entering the wheel of the family,
the wise one must certainly recite the hymn of praise to Rākiṇī and Rādhikā.
If one should perform this at the three junctions of the day, reciting it again and again,
and meditating with intent devotion, one is liberated from the bonds of existence.
One attains unwavering devotion, just as the self-controlled Viśvāmitra did;
by reciting this, O Lord of the Clan, even a commoner goes to the world of Brahmā. (41.39)
By the mere recitation of this, one becomes cool and endowed with virtues.
This hymn, which destroys all that ends in death, must not be disclosed.
Having established equanimity of mind, one becomes self-controlled and liberated while living;
if one then engages in the fivefold conduct and performs the spiritual practice, one shall achieve success.
And at the time of the Kuṇḍalinī-yoga, one should not abandon the Kula practice;
by abandoning the Kula practice, a great loss arises. || 41-42 ||
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, having always maintained an equanimous state of mind, he should adhere to the traditional conduct of his family.
The goddess Kuṇḍalī is the Earth-goddess, and Rākiṇī is the deity of the Svāri [constellation].
The goddess Rādhikā, who desires sovereignty, goes to her abode. (41–44)
And at the time of its practice, one should adhere to the conduct of the pledge (samayācāra).
"In the state of equanimity lies great liberation"—such is the definitive meaning of the Tantra. (41–45)
Having abandoned the discourse on the meaning of equanimity, the yogi becomes perfected.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Hymn to Rākiṇī of the Svādhiṣṭhāna," in the *Bhairavī-Bhairava Saṃvāda* within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Siddha-mantras of the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*. 41.
Now begins the forty-second chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Mahākāla, I shall describe the most wonderful sādhana."
O beloved of the Kula, the Goddess in the form of Kuṇḍalinī belongs to Rākiṇī.
Having brought either mental substances or external substances, one should worship with careful attention, with a mind that is neither distracted nor agitated. (42-2)
With devotion, one should recite the root mantra entirely mentally;
then, having performed worship and recitation, one should perform the fire oblation (homa) with the supreme nectars.
Having regularly offered the arghya with concise cooked offerings, fragrant flowers, and self-arisen blossoms, one should present it.
O Śaṅkara, one should constantly worship Sumukha with honey and meat;
having offered, having offered again, and offering yet again through the union of the vital breath, the wind, and fire. (42–5)
Having caused the mind to wander externally and having established it there again and again,
one should cause it to perform the coming and going repeatedly for the sake of great auspiciousness.
Having caused [the texts] to be recited with beautiful voices and having requested the inclusion of the *savāpika*,
one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with offerings mixed exclusively with *āsava*.
With meats, ritual hand-gestures (mudrās), and the like, with fish, with core ingredients, with flour-cakes, or even with ghee and excellent fruits— whatever comes forth in the Kaula rite.

One attains unwavering devotion, just as the self-controlled Viśvāmitra did; having constantly gratified [the deity] with various offerings, the supreme practitioner should perform the recitation. 42-9.
Having recited this mantra, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa);
at the conclusion of the libation, the practitioner of Tantra should always perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).

At the end of the root mantra, one should add "I consecrate" (abhiṣiñcāmi), followed by the words "namaḥ svāhā. Then, O Lord, one should prostrate with devotion using the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga-nati). || 42-11 ||
The hymn of a thousand names accompanied by the one hundred and eight [names], the hymn of Rākiṇī joined with half the body, and the hymn to Keśava and Rākiṇī. (42–12)
Listen, O Lord, to that whole matter in which you always have faith;
though much has been said for the sake of hearing it, I shall speak it to you out of compassion. (42.13)
Merely by hearing this, there shall be the destruction of all sins;
O Lord, this hymn named *Rākiṇīsaṅgama* is purifying. (42.14)
Whether they recite it with faith or without faith, again and again,
the entire heap of their sins perishes here in an instant.
From time to time, the Great Hero indeed becomes the king of yogins;
endowed with great strength and prowess, he is intent upon delivering beings from the cycle of existence. || 42-16 ||
Oṃ! Śrī Kṛṣṇa is Mahāmāyā; Yādava is Devarākiṇī.
Govinda is Viśvajananī; Mahāviṣṇu is Maheśvarī. (42.17)
Mukunda, Mālatīmālā, Vimalā, Vimalākṛti, Ramānātha, Mahādevī, Mahāyogin, and Prabhāvatī. || 42-18 ||
Vaikuṇṭha, the mother of the gods, the burner, the beloved of the burner;
the enemy of the Daityas, the crusher of the Daityas, the lord of sages, and she who is realized through silence.
Nārāyaṇa is Jayakalā, Karuṇa is Karuṇāmayī;
Hṛṣīkeśa is Kauśikī, and Keśava is Keśighātinī.
She is the youthful maiden, the maidenhood itself; she is Mahākālī, the great art.
She is the great sacrifice and the destroyer of sacrifices; she is the Lord of Dakṣa and the daughter of Dakṣa.
The one of great strength, the one of great power, the boy, the divine girl;
the wielder of the discus, the one with the discus in hand, the one marked by the discus, the one whose splendor is the discus.
The immortal one, the youthful, the formidable, the terrifying, the divine one dwelling in heaven;
the bestower of prosperity, the giver of dwellings, the physician, the possessor of qualities, the yogi, and the one established in the lineage. (42.23)
She knows the commitments, she knows the mind, she is skilled in ritual action and endowed with ritual action;
she is the imperishable one, the forest garland, the form of time, and the syllables of the Kula.
The large-eyed one, the long-eyed one, the giver of victory, the one whose vehicle is victory;
the peaceful one, the bringer of peace, the dark one, and the one with a pure dark form.
Kamaleśa, Mahālakṣmī, Satya, Sādhvī, Śiśu, Prabhā, Vidyutākāravadana, and Vidyutpuñjanabhodayā. (42-26)
Rādheśvara and Rākiṇī are the family deity and the family goddess;
Dakṣiṇa and Dakṣiṇī are the bestowers of fortune and the great abode of ritual action.
She is the knowledge that moves through Vasiṣṭha, the Mistress of Knowledge, and Speech as Sarasvatī;
she is beyond the senses, the Mother of Yoga, the Queen of Battle, and the Expert in War.
The end-maker, the dark child, the desirable one, the one of good desires;
the infinite, the giver of infinite virtues, the lord of speech, the extraordinary one. (42.29)
Gopāla, the cowherd woman, and the daughter of the lineage of cows and cowherds;
the silent one, the delight of the practice of silence, the human being, and the daughter of Manu.
Sarvācchinnā is Mohinī; Māyī is the Illusion born of the body. Akṣuṇṇā resides in the Vajra-body, while Gāruḍī indeed resides upon Garuḍa.
Rukmiṇī is fond of truth; Amṛtāpahā has truth as his life-breath; Satyabhāmā is of truthful deeds; and Trisatyadā is the embodiment of truth.

Śaśīśa (Lord of the Moon), Vidhuvadanā (Moon-faced One), Kṛṣṇavarṇa (Dark-complexioned One), Viśāladhī (Of Vast Intellect), Trivikrama (The Three-strider), Vikramasthā (Abiding in Valor), Sthitimārga (Path of Stability), and Sthitipriyā (She who loves Stability). 42-33.
Śrī Mādhava and Mādhavī; Madhuhā and Madhusūdanī; Vaikuṇṭhanātha and Vikalā; Vivekastha and Vivekinī.
She who stands in dispute, she who causes dispute, the pitcher, the maker of pitchers;
the drinker of nectar, the embodiment of nectar, the one of beautiful attire, and the enchantress of the gods. || 42-35 ||
She who supports the process of manifestation, she whose purpose is auspicious, she whose form is auspicious;
she is the sovereign of the earth, the great infinite one, the infinite one who is dear to Nandana. 42-36.
Priya, Vipriyaharā, Viprapūjyā, Dvijapriyā;
Kānta, Vidhumukhī, Vedya, Vidyā, Vāgīśvarā, and Aruṇā. (42–37)
She is free from desire and devoid of longing; she is passionate and fond of wandering.
She is the white lotus, she dwells in Vikuṇṭha, she is Vaikuṇṭhā, and she is the one who nurtures the child.
Lotus-eyed, garlanded with lotuses, lotus-handed, and lotus-faced;
having a lotus-navel, lotus-eyes, seated upon a lotus, and having a lotus as a vehicle. (42.39)
Vāsudeva, Bṛhadgarbha, Mahāmānin, Mahājana, Kāruṇya, Bālagarbha, Ākāśastha, and Vibhāṇḍaja. (42.40)
A mass of splendor, radiant, concealed by fear yet bestowing fear;
Upendra, situated within the network of colors, established in independence, and traveling in a celestial chariot.
Nagendrastha and Nāginī; Nageśa and Nāganandinī; Sārvabhauma and Mahākālī; Nagendra and Nandinīsutā. (42–42)
The abode of Kāmadeva is Māyā; situated in Mitra is the latent impression (vāsanā) of Mitra; the breaker of pride is Rāvā; the beloved of the enemy of Vāraṇa is Priyā. 42–43.
The slayer of enemies, Rākiṇī, the Mother; Sumitrā, the protector of friends;
the goddess Kālāntakalaha, who is fond of yellow garments. || 42-44 ||
The remover of sin, the destroyer of sin, the sinless one, and the annihilator of sin;
the lover of supreme bliss, the fish, the one in the form of a fish, and the remover of impurity.
Mahendra is dark as a sapphire; Nīlarūpiṇī is blue in form;
Durgā is the beloved of the blue-throated one (Śiva); she is the destroyer of the miserable state of those in distress. || 42–46 ||
She who bestows the glory of the temple of the triangle; she who dwells in the temple of Māyā; she who rejoices in the essence of nectar; she who is fond of the essence of nectar. 42–47.
She is the slayer of terrible enemies and the destroyer of formidable foes;
she is the conduct of the Kali age and the bringer of the fruits of the Kali age.
Kālakṣetra-sthita is Raudrī; Vratastha is Vratadhāriṇī;
Viśālākṣa is Viśālāsyā; Camatkāra is Karodyamā. (42–49)
Lakārasthā, Lākinī, and Lāṅgalī, endowed with playfulness; Nākasthā, Nākapadakā, Nākākṣī, and Nākarakṣakā. (42–50)
Kāmaga is the Name-Connection; Sāmavedaviśodhikā is the Sāmaveda; Sāmaveda is Sāmasandhyā; and Sāmaga is Māṃsabhakṣiṇī. (42–51)
She who devours all, she who devours at night, she who abides in the seed, she who protects the seed;
she who acts at night, the Great Night, the Night of Time, and the Great Midnight.
The remover of various defects, the measure, the slayer of Māra, the destroyer of wine, she whose limbs are sandalwood, the daughter of Nanda, the protector of joy, and the plunderer.
Mudrākārī, Mahāmudrā, Mudrita, Mudritā, Rati, Śākta, Lākṣā, Vedalākṣī, Lopāmudrā, and Narottamā. (42–54)

He is the bearer of great wisdom yet free from ignorance; he is passionless and the destroyer of pride; he abides in true fame and possesses great renown; he is known by his lineage and is the glory of his family. (42–55)
Hope is her dwelling, and that latent impression (vāsanā) is well-guarded by one who knows the Kula;
she resides in the holy fig tree (aśvattha) and dwells within the very essence of the tree.

The eternal tree, the eternal creeper, the fashioned one, the one established in the fashioned state; the wish-fulfilling tree, the wish-fulfilling creeper, the auspicious time, and the devourer of time. (42–57)
Richly adorned with all ornaments, yet adorned by all ornaments;
stainless, abstaining from food, difficult to behold, and free from calamity.
She is the creator of desire, the beloved of desire, whose form is desire, and who possesses great speed;
she is Jayantī, Yājayantī, she who is called Jayā, and the bestower of victory.
Trijīvana, Jīvamātā, the one named Kuśala, Visundarā, Keśadhārī, Keśinī, Kāmaja, and Kāmajāḍyadā. (42-60)
Established in the servant, established in transformation, known as the mind, the wise one;
the destroyer of falsehood, the great falsehood, the false creation, the formless. (42.61)
Wearing a sacred thread of serpents and adorned with a garland of serpents, he is named Nāga, the protector of the serpent lineage; the leader is the consort, the bride. (42–62)

The giver of security to the leader, the woman, the man, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa; she who has the complexion of a Kirāta, the knower of the Rāsa dance, the deliverer, and the one who carries across by means of her virtues. || 42-63 ||
Śaṅkarā is named Ambujākārā; Kṛpaṇa is Kṛpaṇāvatī;
Deśaga is Deśasantoṣā; and Darśa is Darśanivāsinī.
The knower of vision, those established in vision, vision itself, the faculty of vision, the gods, and the asuras;
the guardian of the gods, the protection of the gods, the triple protection, and the deity of protection. (42–65)
The servant of Śrī Rāma, the giver of happiness, the dweller in Vyāsa;
Vṛndā residing in Vṛndāvana, the one who belongs to Vṛndāvana, and the one whose body is the Great Reality. 42-66.
She who has the form of Brahmā is Tritārī; she whose eyes are the stars is indeed Tāriṇī;
she who knows the meaning of the tantras is Tantravidyā; and she who knows the excellent tantras is Sutantrikā.
Tṛpta, Sutṛptā, Tarpaṇasthā, Vilāsinī, Mayūrā, Mandiraratā, Mathurā, and Amalā reside in the temple. (42-68)
Mandira, Mandirādevī, Nirmāyī, Māyāsaṃharā;
Śrīvatsahṛdaya, Vatsā, Vatsala, and Bhaktavatsalā. (42–69)
The beloved of devotion, accessible through devotion, the devotee, devotion, the Lord, the splendor;
the fever, old age, the boon, the sound, the oblation, gold, the patient one, and the earth.
She is the sovereign of the earth, the manifestation of the joy of victory, and she whose form is victory and triumph.
She is the bestower of victory, the wife of the Giver (Dhātṛ), and the protector of the sacrificial offering (Bali).
He in the form of a black cat and she in the form of a black cat;
he mounted on a horse and she mounted on a horse; he riding an elephant and she having an elephant as her vehicle.
Gajeśvarā, Gajādhārā, Gaja, Garjanatatparā, Gayāsura, Gayādevī, Gajadarpa, and Gajāpītā. || 42-73 ||
She is the one who seeks the attainment of the fruits of desire and she who grants the attainment of the fruits of desire;
she is the giver of dharma, the knowledge of dharma, the giver of liberation, and the bestower of liberation.
The refuge of liberation and the agent of liberation is the Sovereign Nandagopālī;
Śrīpati is Śrī Mahākālī, and Kiraṇa is she whose form is the wind.
She whose food is air, who is established in air, whose seed is air, and who is renowned;
she who conquers, the victorious one, who abides in sacrifice, the science of sacrifice, Śiva, and Śivā. (42–76)
Vāsava and Vāsavasthī, Vāsākhya and Dhanavigrahā; Ākhaṇḍala and Vikhaṇḍā, Khaṇḍastha and Khaṇḍakhañjanī.
She holds a sword in her hand, she holds arrows in her hand, she has arrows as her vehicle, and she has arrows as her mount;
she is the knower of the Siddhāntas, the destroyer of darkness, she is established in wealth, and she increases the store of grain.
She is the love of the world, the abode of passion, established in the state of the stabilizing meditation;
though fallen from her station and standing on no footing, her face resembles the autumn moon. (42.79)
The rising moon, moon-colored, beautiful as the moon, abiding in splendor; causing splendor, beloved of splendor, the creator, seated upon creation.
The king of kings, the princess, the world, the refuge of the world;
the omniscient one, the auspicious in every way, the eloquent one, the destroyer of dissolution.
Bearing the form of the *liṅga*, he is the *liṅga*, the Kaliṅga, and the one with black hair;
he is known as the embodiment of absolute bliss, the bestower of liberation and nirvāṇa.
Dense with great clouds, she is the form of great bliss;
a mass of great clouds, she is of most terrible form;
a garland of great clouds, she is the protector of all forms at all times.
She is the dark one, shimmering amidst a stainless garland of great clouds.
Pervading the sky, she pervades all bodies;
she is the great hero of valor and the great heroine of Dharma.
She has the form of Mahākāla and the form of Mahācaṇḍa.
The discerning one, the sole intoxication, the Lord of Kula, and the Mistress of Kula. || 42-84 ||
Sumārgī, Sugītā, Śucisvā, Vinītā; Mahārka, Vitarkā, Sutarkā, Avitarkā;
Kṛtīndrā, Mahendrī, Bhagā, Bhāgyacandrā.
The fourth is Mahārthānaga; Kīrticandrā is [the fifth]. 42-85.
Distinguished, of great resolve, and wise, he is perfectly contented;
abiding in the great six-petalled lotus,
his body is moistened by the nectar-stream from the flowing moon of supreme radiance.
She has a longing for a splendor like ten million suns rising at once. || 42-86 ||
Mahācaṇḍavega, Mahākuṇḍavegī, Mahāruṇḍakhaṇḍa, Mahāmuṇḍakhaṇḍā,
Kulālabhramaccakrasāra, Prakārā.
The potter, the weaver, and the spreader of the loom. || 42-87 ||
The potter’s action is the Great Terrible Fragment;
by the sequence of the potter, the fragment of the knowledge of rotation is established.
The foundation is the foundation, the expectation is the expectation.
Mahākhyo, Mahākhyā, Sukāla, and Atidīkṣā. || 42-88 ||
She who delights in the conduct of the great fifth is Praceṣṭā;

she whose conduct is lovely with great love is Mahāpañcamā; she who possesses the dress of one greatly intoxicated is Mahāmattaveśā; she who possesses the nature of great auspiciousness is Mahāmaṅgaleśī.
Sureśa, Kṣapeśī, Vara, and Dīrghaveśā. || 42-89 ||

She who moves through the beautiful external abodes, she who moves through the beautiful colors; she who is the beginning of the Kula and the beginning of the Akula, she who is the asceticism and the beginning of sacrifice;
she who destroys the worlds of the Kula, she who is the destroyer of great pride.
The yogi Mahāviṣṇu and the yoga of Mahāviṣṇu.
The destroyer of the earth’s agitation, the affliction of the earth’s turmoil,
the highly precious, the most costly, the wealthy one engaged in royal affairs,
the great night, the illumination within dense darkness.
The great night is the entry into dense darkness. || 42-91 ||
She whose sound and resonance are great, terrifying, and profound;
she whose sounds and corrupt words are great, terrifying, and profound;
the lineage that bestows knowledge; Yama, who is the journey of restraint.
The master, whose horses and chariot are subtle, is [known] by name alone.
The slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa, the destroyer of great enemies;
the one who delights in destruction, and she who delights in the destruction of Bāṇa;
the lord of the great Ḍākinīs, the lord of the great Rākiṇīs.
She is Mahāḍākinī; she is Mahārākṣasī. || 42-93 ||
Mukunda, Mahendra, Mahābhadracandrā;
the one who effects the renunciation of the earth, the practitioner of great yoga;
the benefactor, the slayer of Māra, Maheśeśa, and Indra.
The nature of the beauty of movement is a mass of great aesthetic sentiment (mahābhāva).
She is a multitude of moons, possessing the power of ten million moons;
she resides in the *kadamba* tree; she is the foremost among courtesans and yet chaste; she bestows great joy; she is the mother of Mahākāla.
She herself is the mother of all sons; she herself is the daughter of the world.
The destroyer of great sins, the sustainer of the Great State; Hari, Kārtikī, Kārtika, Devasenā;
she who has attained victory, she who is anointed, she who has attained the lineage, she who has attained the Gaṇas.
Possessing great heroism and eloquent speech, the lord of the earth shall advance as an assailant. || 42-96 ||
You are the glory of existence, dear to those with subtle love;
a lord of men, a lord of wealth, compassionate, and the shatterer of pride;
the bestower of great wisdom upon the harsh and arrogant.
Established in action, knowing virtues, and possessing discernment that delights in virtue.
Worshipped by Mahākāla, she who is worshipped by Mahākāla;
named Khaga, named Naga, she who is harsh and holds a sword in her hand;
Atharva, standing swaying upon the Atharva, she of great purpose.
The sky, the beautiful directions, the oblation, the peak, and the wine. 42-98.
She who wears a garland of great lotuses, who belongs to the host of Gaṇeśa, who dwells among the Gaṇas, who is profound, who is the teacher, who is attainable through knowledge,
who bestows life-breath into the jar [of the body], and whose form is like a dense cloud.
He is the creator of fear, purpose, arising, seeds, limbs, water, and the senses. || 42-99 ||
Bhava, Bhāvamātā, Nara, Yāmadhyātā;
Calānta, Acalākhyā, Caya, Añjālikā; Chala-jña, Chalāḍhyā, and Chakāra-chakārā.
Victory! You who abide in life, you who are the lords of the waters, you who are the lords of the waters! 42-100.
The reciter performing recitation, the sovereign life-force of the world,
the lord of the world’s breath, the bringer of joy to the world; the waterfall, the master of the jharjhara drum, the sound of the *jhanat* resonance.
The sounds of *jhana-jhañjana* and the resonance of *jhaṅkāra*. || 42-101 ||
She who brings about non-consciousness, she who is not the woman of isolation (kaivalya);
she who bears the radiance of *hana*, holding a chisel (*ṭaṅka*) in her hand;
she who is the Lord of *ṭhara*, seated upon the peak beginning with the letter *ṭha*.
Ḍara, Ḍākinīśa, Ḍareśa, Ḍamārā. || 42-102 ||
The letter *ḍha* is indeed the drum (*ḍhakkā*), the seed-syllable of the supreme state; the nine letters are the body of the *tamāla* tree, established in their proper places;
the letter *tha* is the measure of the abode, situated in the immeasurable.
The compassionate one, the one moist with compassion, the lord of wealth, and the one rich in wealth. || 42-103 ||
The new one whose bodily movements have descended from the mountain;
the supreme Mistress of the Mountain who protects those on the further shore;
she whose essence is fruit, who is the fruit, who belongs to the month of Phālguna, and who destroys foam.
Abounding in fruits and ornaments, self-controlled, and delightful to dwell in. || 42-104 ||
The Blessed One is the self of Bhavānī, appearing as the great seed;
Mukunda is the garland of great seeds, most subtle. He dwells in the ascetic, he dwells in glory, and he is the creator of the bliss of passion.
Rati is Lākinī; Pracaṇḍā is for the purpose of dissolution.
Wearing coral limbs, adorned with garlands of coral limbs;
whose words are playful with the *halāhala* poison, whose feet are the rhythm of the drum;
the sovereign lord, luminous, dwelling in the most excellent abode.
Śiva, Śrīdharāṅga, Śalākā, and Śilā. || 42-106 ||
Dwelling in the six supports, she is the knowledge of the six supports;
seated upon the six lotuses, she is seated on the six lotuses; always seated upon the seat of the six supports, she is free from passion.
She is established in well-spoken hymns and resides within the refuge of the Palāśa tree. || 42-107 ||
Hara is the one of fierce deeds; Hara-ananda-dhārā is Laghustha;
Lipisthā is Kṣayī and Kṣubdhaka, which is the number;
Ananta is Nirvāṇā, the seed-syllable in the form of Hara.
Though situated in the chest, they are vast; their forms are upward-tending. || 42-108 ||
For you abide in the *ṛc*, you are the essence of the *ṛc*, and you are long-enduring. For you alone are the venerable seed of all things, abiding in the *guṇas*.
You are eternally the color of the syllable *oṃ*, with the seed-syllable *hsauṃ*.
For *asaṅkāra* is *candra*, and *hyusa* is *kāravīrā*. || 42-109 ||
The Lord of Monkeys, the Lord of Monkeys, Hari, whose form is Kṛṣṇa;
Śiva, the language of the Vedas, and Śauri, who is the context;
he who has the form of the Lord of Gaṇas and who consumes supreme bliss.
The Supreme Lord, Gaṇeśa, Rasa, and Vāsapūjyā. || 42-110 ||
She who is the support for the life-force, intellect, and abiding state of the flock of *cakora* birds;
she who is herself the embodiment of the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*), yet appears in diverse forms;
she whose splendor is like the radiance of gold, and whose limbs possess the luster of golden light.
Her body has the hue of the rising sun and the form of the dawn.
She who holds the millions of streams of light, the support of the earth, the treasury;
she who is the Lord of Passion, the peak-syllable of the Pratyādi-mantra, the lower lip, the dhāraṇā, the heroic Āryā;
she who abides in the great sacrifice and is the culmination of the great sacrifice.
Constant attachment to ritual action; always delighting in the stage of worldly entanglement.
The lord of the Kirātīs is Rākiṇī, the daughter of Kāla;
she is Viśālā, whose longing is for the creation of Śilākoṭa;
she abides in a portion of the sun of arts and resides in the small bells of art.
The youth and the maiden, the daughter of Kurukṣetra. || 42-113 ||
The illustrious Mahālāṅgalin is the one who draws forth strength;
he is fearless through the knowledge of potters and the like, and devoid of worldly existence.
He is Mahālākinī, Kākinī, and the Lord of Śākinīs.
The supreme Hākinī is the Great, Perfectly Radiant One.
A resident of Kurukṣetra, the embodiment of love for the Kurus,
an enjoyer of great prosperity, and a great yoginī;
she who acts as the charcoal-maker for the Kula and is the daughter of the Lord of Kulāṅgī.
The third [is] the third; the non-dual [is] the non-dual. || 42-115 ||
Dwelling in Mahākanda, he is the one who brings great bliss to Kāśī;
residing in cities and villages, he is the supreme one established in the sacred seats (mahāpīṭha) and regions.
O Jagannātha, you are stationed upon the chest of the most excellent woman.
She who causes the joy of liberation and she who produces the bliss of aesthetic rasa.
The lamp of the world, the goddess who is the lamp of the world;
she whose form is the great desire, the seat of the great desire;
she who is firm in the seat of the great desire, the purification of the elements.
The purification of the great elements; the accomplishment of the great elements. || 42-117 ||
Radiant, proficient, dwelling with the Guru, and established on the mountain;
wearing the flowing stream of nectar and clad in the garb of great devotion;
his inner self turned away from the fluctuations of momentary pleasure and pain.
Abiding within the six, it goes to the place of dissolution. || 42-118 ||
Desiring the bliss of absorption, she has attained the state of emission;
she is the path for the large-eyed one, the essence of the Kula, and the Kula-essence itself.
Abiding in the mind, she is the glory of the mind, the eternal bestower of fear and bliss.
The giver of the knowledge of elephants, the great Meru-method, [is] the Lāṇa-gītā. || 42-119 ||
Dwelling at the root of the tree, she reveals the knowledge of the tree;
she is the Lord of the Gods, the Mistress of the Equal Ones, the Goddess of the Gods, and the blissful one established in the sword.
She is the protector from fear and the destroyer of the knowledge of fear.
Standing at the sacrifice for the sake of the people, he brought about the destruction of the joy of the sacrifice.
Abiding on the great true path, knowing the great true path;
possessing the great bindu, possessing the great bindu;
seated upon the lord of birds, situated within the visarga.
Having entered the visarga, they become the Great Bindu and Nāda.
He whose devotion is the bliss of nectar, whose liberation is the bliss of Brahmā;
who is well-established in the bliss of Śiva, whose nurse is the bliss of Viṣṇu;
who causes joy to the great vehicle, and whose excellent conveyance is the wind.
She who causes the joy of the gods and brings delight to speech. || 42-122 ||
The one whose splendor is Hayānanda, the deity residing in Mataṅga;
the presiding goddess of Mataṅga, Mahāmatta;
that sole Mahācakrapāṇi, Pracaṇḍā—
She who dwells upon the sacrificial ground, the consort of the Lord of the Unborn.
The creator of the joy of the crest-dress, dwelling in the essence of the crest;
the beautiful Śākambharī, Kroṣṭarī, and she who is fragrant with the altar of the Vedas;
the Yuga, the maiden of Yoga, the forest-fire, the long maiden, the refuge, and the one worthy of refuge.
Accessible through the knowledge of sages, she is most fortunate, she is most fortunate. || 42-124 ||
Śaśī, Vedajanyā, Yamī, Yāmavāmā;
Hyakāma, Hyakāmā, Sadāgrāmakāmā;
Dhṛtīśa, Dhṛtīśā, Sadāhāṭakasthā.
The Lord of the vehicle (yaneśa) is Ayaneśī; the letter *bha* is Bhagīrā.
She stands upon a moving wagtail, she stands amidst the playful sport of the wicked;
she is a Kirāti who blows away obstacles, she whose limbs are whole though her body is desolate;
she dwells in the vast sky, and she is a great sky-walker.
The great nāga king, the garland of great nāgas. || 42-126 ||
The half-syllable *ha* is known as the necklace of garlands (*vṛtohāramālā*);
Pārvatī is the one who strikes Mahākāla and Nemi;
Tamisrā is the destroyer of suffering who is enveloped by darkness.
The maiden Guṇānandā has perished; she is lost. || 42-127 ||
The eternal destroyer of suffering, the remover of great misery; possessing the hue of the morning sun and the splendor of the dawn’s crimson glow;
endowed with a state of love for the great mountain.
Endowed with the state of being the wife of Mahādeva and the Lord. || 42-128 ||
She who bestows great liberation, she who is fond of Nīla, the giver of devotion;
O Ānanda, she who grants devotion, the Mother of the Gods. 42-129.
Thus has this delightful Great Hymn been told, O Lord,
consisting of one thousand names along with its eight auxiliary limbs.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this with devotion—whether pure or impure in mind—attains peace without effort, O King of Yogis. (42.131)
O Lord of the Gods, he who, being pure, performs meditation daily and recites this at the three junctions of the day, becomes a supreme yogi within six months; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
If one recites this even once, it removes untimely death, destroys all diseases, and wards off premature death and other such calamities. (42.133)
Those who do not depart during the time of calamity in the dead of night go,
without effort, across the most terrible ocean of fear.
Whoever recites this constantly at an improper time, for them that very moment shall become an auspicious time;
even in cases such as the seizure of a king's property or the deprivation of one's livelihood.
By reciting it for just one month, he shall certainly obtain royal sovereignty;
great heroes roam in heaven, among mortals, and in the netherworld.
Possessing strength equal to Gaṇeśa and embodying great wrath, by the grace of this hymn, one becomes liberated while living on this earth. (42.137)
The essence of the Mahānāma-stotra, which is the investigation of dharma and adharma;
it bestows success spontaneously, fulfills all desires, and grants supreme accomplishment. 42-138.
In this auspicious practice for the sake of Bhavānī, who possesses the great family *kuṇḍalinī*,
which effects the piercing of the impenetrable and destroys even the greatest of sins.
O Lord, he who indeed performs the paralysis of the six cakras every day shall attain perfection by reciting this even in a most terrible time. (42.140)
That Śiva, who resides within the mind, is in his hand, and not a mere human;
provided that he practices yoga, even if the hymn is not recited. (42.141)
One who transgresses the conduct of the *kula* will quickly fall away from yoga;
[the teaching] should be given to one of noble lineage, and certainly not to a master of a non-*kula* tradition. (42.142)
Having properly performed the family traditions, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others indeed become yogis and eternal immortals through the recitation of this hymn. (42-143)
Ānandabhairava said:
"Speak, O beloved, the secret to me; everything has been forgotten by me after drinking the great poison Kālakūṭa for the sake of protecting the gods and others."
All the deities residing in the throat have been thoroughly gathered and reduced to ashes by the great flame of my poison, as have the deities residing within my own body. (42.145)
All those devoted to liberation pray for it incessantly.
O Lord, having explained the six chakras, grant me satisfaction;
[please explain] the description of the piercing of the six chakras, the hearing of the nectar, and so forth. (42–146)
Having spoken thus, O auspicious beloved, grant me satisfaction, you whose body is sprinkled with nectars in an ocean of the bliss of immortality. (42.147)
"Having done so, tell it to me quickly and increase my lifespan.
Ānandabhairavī said: "O Mahākāla, Lord of Time, Sovereign of the World, [I shall speak] the hidden meaning. (42.148)
O abode of Bhairavānanda, you who partake of the *kālakūṭa* poison!
Now hear from me the meaning of yoga and its very union.
Having heard this ritual to be performed, a person shall become a lord of yogis;
he arises within my stainless sky, which is devoid of all forms.
Having established me within the earth, in the midst of all bodies,
and as that which is unconditioned, a person meditates upon me as being of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Mahākāla, my form is dear to the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
yet by the power of rajas alone, even this body does not remain.

Likewise, it does not abide through pure *tamas* alone, nor does it abide through pure *sattva* alone; how then could the embodied soul remain? Therefore, by means of the union of the three *guṇas*, I sustain this nine-limbed body. (42.153)
The qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas must be conquered gradually;
first having conquered the nature of rajas, one should afterwards conquer that of tamas alone.
When all else is exhausted, a man shall become a master of yoga, possessing the qualities of a being;
he will be virtuous, wise, eloquent, highly prosperous, righteous, and one who has conquered his senses. (42.155)
But by relying on the quality of pure, stainless being, one partakes in liberation;
for it is Time alone that always veils the Person with the quality of being. (42.156)
One never perceives here that supreme person who is free from old age and death, perfectly tranquil, stainless, and devoid of duality.
Time protects everywhere one who has renounced everything—whether in water, on a mountain, in a great forest, or on the field of battle. (42.158)

O Kuleśvara, it is the truth, the absolute truth: even when the earth has sunk into its subterranean abode, when there is fear during the dissolution, and when the conflict with the wicked occurs, the great yogi remains steadfast.
Listen, O beloved of life, abode of glory, to the Mahāyoga—the supreme purpose of yoga for the sake of Brahman, O scorcher of foes. (42.160)
Those men who know Mahāyoga do not perish;
having repeatedly performed the practice of the six-petalled [lotus], they have accomplished the complete sadhana. || 42-161 ||
Then one should perform the movement of Kuṇḍalinī within the root-lotus;
by moving her again and again, a man shall become a lord of yogis.
In a solitary and utterly pure place, free from famine and other such calamities, the yogi, intent on the path of yoga, should remain for one year in a single sitting posture. (42.163)
One should always assume the lotus posture (padmāsana) as well as the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana);
having assumed the great lotus posture (mahāpadmāsana), one likewise performs the application of the seat (āsanamañjana).
Thereafter, one should always perform the posture called Svastika and likewise the Baddhasvastika during the practice of yoga and in rites such as the attainment of mantra-siddhi. (42.165)
In the practice of the yoga-sādhana, the yogin should always assume the wheel-posture (cakrāsana),
which is known as the bound-wheel-posture (baddhacakrāsana) and likewise the great wheel-posture (mahācakrāsana).
Having performed [the previous steps], one should perform them again, having bound the Yogeśvarāsana;
having performed the Yogeśvarāsana, one performs the Mahāyogeśvarāsana.
Then one should perform the vīrāsana and likewise the mahāvīrāsana;
by performing the bound vīrāsana, a man becomes a lord of yoga.
Then, O Mahākāla, one should perform the bound cock posture (*baddhakukkuṭāsana*);
having formed the great cock [posture], it is simply the cock posture (*kukkuṭāsana*). (42.169)
By assuming the posture of the peacock (mayūrāsana), as well as the great peacock (mahāmayūra) and the bound peacock (baddhamayūra), a person shall become a lord of yoga (yogeśvara).

All of this should be explained, having reflected upon it for the delight of the wise, in the section on consecration (*abhiṣeka*), illuminating the methods for the throne and other elements. (42.171)
Now listen specifically to the sixfold sequence that must be explained:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (42–172)
Beyond that is the Lord Paraśiva and the six Śivas who are the six illuminators;
their powers, consisting of the bliss of the six qualities, are the supreme goddesses.
Devoted to piercing the six cakras, these are the presiding deities of the great vidyās;
one should perform their praise together with that of the Supreme Deity.
And whoever, in performing this kind of practice, is daily devoted with reverence,
intent upon the ritual action everywhere, and assumes the form of the grasping of contemplation (bhāvanā)— || 42.175 ||
He beholds Hari, the Lord of the World, seated upon a lotus;
first, he should cause Kuṇḍalin to behold Hari.
Then, through the consciousness of Rudra, O Lord, a person attains the auspicious vision of Lākīnī; indeed, the vision is attained in its entirety and in due order. (42.177)
Gradually, O Mahākāla, there shall be a vision of Kailāsa;
through the practice of the eightfold yoga, all perfections (siddhis) will be attained in due course.

Whatever action one performs during the time of practicing the eightfold path, listen with respect and great effort to all of that; by performing those rites and so forth, one will quickly become a yogi. (42.179)

Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the section on accomplished mantras (*siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the illumination of the six chakras (*ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*), within the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 42.
Now begins the forty-third chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said: Now, for the sake of uprooting the desires of those afflicted by passion, [I shall explain...]
O Mahākāla, I shall tell you that which, when performed, brings women under one's control.
I shall explain that method for the purpose of accomplishing yoga:
having properly assumed the hand-posture, one should perform the upward lotus posture (ūrdhva-padmāsana).
Placing both hands at the base of the head, one should perform the recitation;
one should hold [the breath] very slightly and observe the count of the breaths. (3)
One should then perform the counting of breaths when one is well-established in the kumbhaka;
for how can a self-controlled, excellent yogi [attain mastery] without the counting of breaths? (43-4)
Without the application of counting and without warding off faulty yoga, one should never perform [the practice] apart from the counting and the *kumbhaka* breath-retention. 43–5.
One should perform very gentle breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*) during the practice of *khecarīmudrā*;
it should be performed at all times, and one shall be happy at all times. (43–6)
Having fashioned an image of Ānanda by means of *vijayā*, fermented liquors, and so forth, the practitioner, the king of yogins, should then perform the piercing in due order. (43–7)
For yogins, it is an undivided state that produces the brilliance of lightning,
possessing a luster equal to ten million flashes of lightning, and is filled with torrents of water.
If it is so, those who know the state of being a son fall by way of karmic maturation;
yet they go to the supreme place, and they become rulers of ten million kingdoms.
They are both enjoyers of wealth and practitioners of yoga; they are remembered as the guardians of the world.
Possessing the enjoyment of great virtues, they never fall from their state, nor for what reason could they? || 43-10 ||
They are the most excellent of men; they are like the moon. They are intent on creating division; such people are not gods. || 43-11 ||
They all go everywhere; they are auspicious and they are my servants. They are my devotees, O Mahākāla—this is the arising of my own scripture.
Those who worship your lotus feet with single-minded devotion surely become possessors of knowledge; for them, time shall come under their control.
Those who were devoted to the union with the vital breath and those who protected the life-force,
having avoided self-destruction, went joyfully to the world of Brahmā.
O Lord, those who are devoted to meditation and have abandoned the objects of saṃsāra proceed [to liberation], whether they are men dwelling in the forest or those not dwelling in the forest. (43.15)
In a solitary and uninhabited place, free from all obstacles,
those men who effect the piercing of the six chakras become partakers of the fruit.
He who always desires the fruit of Mahākāla, the goal of the virtuous, is indeed a yogi who, abiding in the center of the earth, becomes all-pervading. (43.17)
Worshipful everywhere and at all times, the Lord of All, stainless and non-dual, whose glory is without beginning or end, he becomes the very soul of Time in an instant. (43-18)
The means for accomplishing these is the swift and well-conceived application of the vidyā-mantra;
having meditated upon this as one's own innate form and having established one's own station, one should effect the differentiation. (43.19)
Having pierced the *mūlādhāra* and the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, the wise one who knows how to discern the divisions should effect the supreme union in the *maṇipūra*. (43.20)
And having beheld the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
the wise one [beholds] the Lord of Devas, who is stainless and endowed with power, beginning from his own abode (svādhiṣṭhāna).
The supreme Rākiṇī-Rādhikā pervades the protection of the three worlds;
she dwells in the supreme ether, consisting of the three qualities and having the form of water.
Beholding that devotee of Śiva and Viṣṇu dwelling at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree of desire, his heart was filled with bliss; he became free from doubt and saw [the truth] everywhere.
Having practiced constantly, the yogi should behold Maṇipūra—the great sign of Maṇipūra, a field of accomplishment consisting of nectar. (43.24)
Whatever fruit a man obtains by the gift of ten million pieces of gold, by the cause of giving ten million cows, and by feeding ten million Brahmins—[that fruit he obtains here]. (43.25)
Having meditated upon the beautiful Maṇipūra, one obtains that fruit;
Maṇipūra is a great station, invisible even to yogins. (43.26)
Subtler than the subtlest, the supreme object of knowledge for the wise,
unmanifest and a great secret, it is attained through the practice of yoga.
Ānandabhairava said:

Where, for the sake of yoga, there is a lotus possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning, joined with ten million fires of cosmic destruction, and resembling ten million moons; (43–28)
By what means is the mind dissolved amidst the rays of ten million suns?
Just as a thread passes through the eye of a needle, that alone is the bliss that yields fruit. (43.29)
O beautiful one, where knowledge has never been seen or heard before, by what means can the fixing of the mind occur there? (43.30)
How can one not know that fruit which belongs to that god, for which there is no going by men? Since it has not been seen, how could there be any going there? (43.31)
Whence comes the prosperity of kings, or whence their vision of their own self-interest?
Whence does success arise, and what fruit would there be in causing division? (43.32)
"You know the reality, O Mistress of the Gods; reveal its manner.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Supreme Lord, all that has been spoken is indeed fruitful."
In that regard, first hear the sequence of the yoga-dharma concerning its own basis;
by the mere recollection of it, you will become liberated while living. (43.34)
O highly fortunate one, the individual soul (jīva) alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for the worlds;
that jīva, possessing great strength and prowess, exists in the form of wind.
He goes daily, constantly, and at all times again and again;
he returns to the earth by his very nature without interruption. (43.36)
He is the abode of manifold existences and the one who defines manifold forms; he is the abode of manifold attributes, the pure one who assumes impure attire, the Great One. (43.37)
The yogi whose abode is in Kāndarpa is that yogi who knows the supreme truth;
he is the man of knowledge, free from ego, yet he is the possessor of ego who sustains the body.
The knower of secrets should meditate upon her as the container of all fragrances, invisible;
he alone is partless, pure, and always devoted to meditation. (43.39)
When one becomes absorbed in You, Śaṅkara, who are Brahman within the self and the universe, and attains dissolution therein, that state is known as the Great State (mahābhāva). || 43-40 ||
That state is supreme knowledge; it is not to be described as anything contrary.
It is the support, ever blissful, eternal, and free from even the slightest interval [of interruption]. (43-41)
Having attained the integration of the ultimate Dharma, a person becomes a yogi;
one should proceed gradually toward that which is well-seen in each respective stage.
Having become a great adept (mahāsiddha) in various places, he possesses sons within saṃsāra;
for yogins, [the state] lasts for a long time, while for those who have died, it lasts for a short time. (43-43)
By practicing breath-retention for a long time, one shall become happy, just like the illustrious Bṛhaspati and like the sun, the maker of day. (43–44)
In that manner, one should cause illumination with millions of hymns and names;
having offered praise, and having become [pure], one should satisfy [the deity] with great materials in due order.
Having been consecrated, he should again meditate and worship according to the ritual rules, using either mental offerings or substances accompanied by the *svadhā* mantra. (43–46)
Having become supremely joyful, one should meditate upon the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Having meditated and then recited [the mantra], one should contemplate dharma and adharma.
Having joined the mind to the deity and established it upon one's own seat,
one should again cause the fully blossomed lotus to be sealed by the retinue.
Having caused the six-petaled lotus to blossom, the wise one should settle upon its tips;
he is eternal bliss, consisting of all things, known by the names of the Vedas and Vedāntas. (43–49)
Having meditated on them all together as a single mass with the *saṃhāramudrā*,
one should place it upon the tip of a downward-facing ten-petaled lotus.
Having joined Mahākāla at the tip of the six-petaled [lotus], one should proceed;
then one should go to the city of the ten-petaled lotus when it is blazing.
Having entered into the center of the pericarp, one becomes identical with that in an instant;
having become identical with that in that very moment, one abides within the wheel of Kuṇḍalinī.

O Lord, when Maṇipūra— the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) located within the maṇipūra, which is stainless and accessible through meditation— is present, everything that was previously unattainable becomes accomplished.
Having fixed his mind [upon this], a person shall be liberated from distress;
he is a yogi of the mind, an enjoyer of the mind, a devotee of the mind, and a youth of the mind.
The mind alone is the cause of both bondage and liberation for human beings;
it is the cause of all states of being. Therefore, the wise man should abandon that [mind]. (43–55)
Even having abandoned all states of being, one should take refuge in the Great Being (Mahābhāva).
Through such being (bhāva) liberation is attained; through such being happiness is attained. || 43-56 ||
One should always maintain this state of being; through such being, one becomes a king among yogis.
Through being, one attains devotion; one should take refuge in being rather than in sense objects. (43–57)
Having abandoned the object of perception, which is subject to transformation and seized by the intellect of the doer, one should take refuge in Maṇipūra, the divine great seat. (43-8)
Having fixed his mind upon the great yantra, the wise one should cause it to be fashioned;
having performed the stringing with jewels, it should be adorned with various gems.
Having drawn either the *supīṭha*, the *kulapīṭha*, or the *liṅgapīṭha*, as well as the *śrīvidyāpīṭha*, one should contemplate them again and again. (43–60)
Then, having placed Mahāviṣṇu upon the tips of the petals of the blossomed six-petaled lotus and having worshipped him with great self-restraint, [one should proceed].
Having recited [the mantra] and become absorbed in that, and having placed it in the *maṇipūra*,
one should protect the firm-formed, upward-pointing six-petaled lotus.
Then, having fixed the mind in a higher station, most lofty and supremely beautiful, one should take refuge in Śakti and Rudra.
The power whose form is consciousness and consciousness itself whose form is Rudra;
therein, the auspicious-natured Raudra and the illuminating Raudrī. (43–64)
With devotion, one whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas) should meditate again and again upon that Lord;
He is the goal reached by those on the upward path and is indeed the object of meditation for yogis.
"I am the goddess Parānandā, residing in Maṇipūra;
likewise, you are Śrī Rudra, the power (śakti) of Śrī Lākinī—of this there is no doubt. (43–66)
Mahādeva has the form of Rudra, and Sarasvatī has the form of Rudra;
she is always upward-moving, for that power (śakti) is upward-moving.
Having likewise meditated upon the Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, who reveals the upward path, as well as Mahārudra, within the perfectly pure Maṇipūra; 43–68.
One should fashion the beautiful Mahāpadma with its face turned upward;
it is the greatly lovely Maṇipūra, as pure as ten million jewels.
One should fashion [the face] with an upward gaze, like the full radiance of ten million times ten million autumn moons; it arises spontaneously by its own nature.
And if the lotus is turned upward and joined with a mechanical mandala,
it appears upon its exceedingly delicate petals as something most wondrous.
Having smeared, joined, and established [the image], and having repeatedly brought forth Mahārudra and Śivā, the mother of the three worlds; || 43-72 ||
Rudrāṇī and Raudraśakti, Lākinī the witness of the world, the retention (kumbhaka) of the vital breath, and the union of the vital breath. (43–73)
Having met together in one place, one should cause meditation to be practiced; through meditation liberation is attained, for meditation itself is one's own refuge. (43-74)
Having fixed the mind there, one situated therein should perform the worship of Rudra, as well as the most wonderful sādhana of the goddess Śrīlākinī. (43–75)
Listen, O Bhairava, supreme bliss, beloved of Pīrā;
without my instruction, no one at all can attain perfection.
Through the power of my command, a human being becomes perfected;
for the root of liberation is the Great State (mahābhāva), and the root of liberation is indeed the means (sādhana).
By the gradual process of liberation over time, the practitioner becomes accomplished through my very method of yoga and by the study of my tantra. (43.78)
O Lord, not everyone indeed becomes a Brahmayogin;
yet all yogins quickly attain power, of this there is no doubt. (43-79)
Having made the petals clearly manifest in form, one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) therein;
one should carry out the placement of the Mahāyoga family and the placement of the Vidyās. (43–80)
One should perform the universal placement (sarvanyāsa), the personal placement (nijanyāsa), and the web of knowledge (jñānajāla);
the body, pervaded by mental activity, is completely saturated with the sweet nectar.
One should perform meditation there upon the Self, which is of the nature of Śiva, belonging to Viṣṇu, possessing the eye of knowledge, and uniform in form, while reciting the root mantra. (43–82)
Having meditated, one should prepare the *arghya* offering according to the sequence of the *kula-cakra*,
and furthermore, one should contemplate oneself as being undivided.

One should meditate upon one’s own consciousness as the deity, the family deity (kuladevatā), and having worshipped it day and night according to the sequence of water for the feet, the respectful offering, and so forth.
Then, having meditated upon the retinue, one should worship them all completely;
thereafter, one should offer incense and lamps according to the procedure for one's own worship. (43–85)
The practitioner should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) at the beginning of the kindling [of the fire] and other rites;
having meditated with devotion and recited the mantra for the deity residing in the Maṇipūra [cakra].
Having offered the recitation according to the prescribed rule, one should again perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
Having prostrated with hymns and protective verses (kavaca), one should then dissolve one's own goddess into the heart.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Method for Piercing the Maṇipūra Cakra," within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, in the section on Siddhi-mantras, in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, the Northern Tantra. 43.
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
Listen; I shall explain in accordance with reality the purpose of piercing the Maṇipūra [cakra].
Knowing which, even deluded people enter the great vessel.
Those practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga attain freedom from delusion and become immortal; they attain the power of moving through the sky.
The destruction of the foremost great sins and the great enemy occurs swiftly;
[this happens] after some time in fire, in defect, in water, on a mountain, or in a forest.
And for those desiring to see [the deity], they bring about subjection to the gods; one who practices breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) should meditate upon Maṇipūra, the great seat (mahāpīṭha). 44-4.
Likewise, having accomplished the five āsavas, one should pierce the full [vessel]:
the true Śivā, the primordial Mother of the three worlds, who possesses the three yogas. (44–5)
Rising from the *mūlādhāra* and proceeding through the six-petaled lotus of taste (*rasa-ṣaḍdala*), she moves forward endowed with radiance, having made that six-petaled lotus luminous. (44–6)
In Maṇipūra, the great cakra, which is the means for the recitation of the three worlds, the abode of accomplishments, desirable, lovely, and the delight of the mind. (44-7)
The great goddess Manaḥpirā, who causes the universal exultation of Sarva, is Khecarī, adorned with supreme bliss, the yoginī of mantra. (44-8)
Therefore, one should indeed contemplate the perfected one who bestows grace;
for from that very source arises the utterly pure self-knowledge, which is a mass of intense bliss.
Having meditated upon Maṇipūra, what on earth cannot be accomplished?
One becomes a possessor of the supreme and most excellent siddhis, such as aṇimā, laghimā, and vyāpti.
Whether he be a Kaula, a Vāramukhya, a man of knowledge, or a supreme practitioner,
whoever practices yoga shall take refuge in Maṇipūra.
The deity residing in Maṇipūra, whom one who is self-restrained and pure praises—by the recitation of this king of hymns, Kuṇḍalinī becomes awakened. (44.12)
That auspicious goddess, the supreme Māyā, resides in Maṇipūra;
when she awakens, the mantra will then become perfected.
When the mantra is perfected, there is the attainment of the Supreme; this is my definitive conclusion regarding the Tantras. If they desire consciousness, it is through the power of Kuṇḍalinī.
And he knows the unsurpassed great awakening within his own body,
O Kuleśvara, for the sake of the consciousness of those deities.
One should perform the Great Praise every day for the sake of attaining accomplishment;
thus one shall achieve the task of accomplishment and the task of Dharma in Maṇipūra. (44.16)
The piercing of the one dwelling in Maṇipūra is the means for attaining knowledge;
it is the stainless Thousand Names, the description of the substance of accomplishment. || 44-17 ||
One should take refuge in Maṇipūra for the attainment of both the constant and the desired goals;
there, with the vital breath and the intellect, one should worship one's own chosen goddess, the supreme Lākinī. (44.18)
One should indeed worship one's own deity in the great abode of Maṇipūra—
the fierce Raudrī, the great power (mahāśakti) of great arising, who resides in Maṇipūra.
One should perform worship, as if worshipping the lotus feet of one's own goddess, toward that supreme state which is all-pervading, worthy, and the secret of the great yogis. (44.20)
Having completed the worship according to the prescribed rite, one should recite the hymn of praise to the Goddess;
for by means of her vital breath and wind, it serves as the cause for the destruction of the supernatural powers (siddhis).
O Jñānaśaṅkara, you perform all this very same manner of praise that was performed by Brahmā, whose soul consists of virtue, using ten million names.
By the grace of this hymn, O Yogin of great luster,
