there arises the knowledge that destroys the jar of egoism and wards off the great disease.
For this great hymn of praise indeed directly increases bliss;
it bestows devotion, is pure, and is beyond the reach even of those who are already purified. (44.24)
The auspicious Śivā, the primordial Śakyā, seated upon the ten petals, the consort of Rudra;
the large-eyed, subtle one, whose crown is a mass of matted hair joined with the moon;
the three-eyed goddess, seated upon a pedestal resplendent with the brilliance of millions of great lightning flashes.
Who meditates upon the ten-petaled [lotus] known as Mahālākinī and its digits? || 44-25 ||
The darkness within the lotus stalks is dispelled by her who is beautiful with the gathering of her manifest banks;
she is the lamp-flame that illumines the field of the lineage and bestows the final state; she whose form is eternal bliss, who removes the movement of the qualities, and whose rays are lovely.
Who meditates upon her who is dark in complexion and luster, and possesses a beautiful face? || 44-26 ||
She whose pair of lotus feet is manifest as an ocean of the bliss of longing;
she who is beautiful, has the color of the sky, and delights in the ritual worship of the best of gods;
she who causes the movement of the gateway of the Great Subtle (Mahāsūkṣma) and effects its piercing.
Who would contemplate that which brings about the auspiciousness of destroying the intense joy of worldly attachments during the day? 44.27
Residing at the sacred seat of Ayodhyā, she is as lovely as the dawn;
she flows with love, yet is intensely fierce and formidable, possessing a multitude of hundreds upon hundreds of tongues.
She is auspicious for the eyes of those afflicted by great suffering, yet she is separated from all worldly emotion.
Who would regard the virtuous Sītā as a mere vessel for the festival of Indra?

She is the nectar from the ocean of ambrosia, a source of delight; she bestows fragrance, is the very form of ritual action, and is worthy of the world. She resides in the essence of the multitude of jewels on earth, arises from the station of the Guru, possesses both fire and tranquility, and is most cooling.
Who worships her who consists of the three principles, who knows the principles, and who is the power of Śiva and Hara? || 44-29 ||
Victory to this most excellent one, whose limbs possess the form of transformation, who bears the splendor of ten million young suns;
she is the support of the lineage, the essence, the stream of the supreme nectar,
and the bestower of auspiciousness within the vessels of the supreme nectar, her desires covered by compassion.
One should worship the Indrās and Rudrās, who possess moon-like faces and hands that bestow a multitude of delights.
She who finds rest in the ocean of aesthetic flavor, who brings peace to angry people, who is endowed with compassion;

who abides in the knowledge of the three worlds, who is the dwelling place of Love, and who is a multitude of yogas; who is the shadow of the Jewel Island, who possesses the digits of the ten petals, and who is the absolute existence.
Who worships Bhavānī, the consort of Rudra, the bestower of boons, in Maṇipūra? || 44-31 ||

In the ocean of compassion, what [is not attained]? She who is bowed to by the crowns of the sons of Anu; she who rests on the lap of Śiva; she who is established at the root; she who is the eternal existence within the full moon of the *maṇipūra*;
she who possesses golden eyes; she who is the artisan; she whose splendor consists of rays that cause destruction.
Who meditates upon Vinodī, who possesses the qualities of the five-faced one? 44-32.

In his heart, which is like an ocean born from the essence of the mass of overflowing, unstable bliss, one should meditate with the heart upon her named Mahāpadmā— she who bestows all virtues, consists of pure happiness, and is as restless as the waves agitated by the granting of all wealth.
The digit that is exceedingly subtle, which burns away darkness, and bestows ten million treasures.
He who constantly recites this ten-fold hymn to Śrīvidyā, the bestower of happiness, should always recite it with a pure soul after meditating upon her beneath the lotus of his heart. (44.34)
The king of yogis beholds the god Rudra situated in Maṇipūra;
having seen Śambhu together with Rudrāṇī, he becomes liberated in an instant. (44-35)
That very self is liberated while living and becomes the beloved of the Yoginīs;
for he is indeed the embodied soul, the supreme soul, and the manifest Lord. (44.36)
Having pierced the ocean filled with jewels, he beheld the stainless, blazing light of Śambhu, the Lord of Yoga, the Master of Action, the Consort of Śrī.
The yogi goes near the goddess’s place; of this there is no doubt. || 44-38 ||

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Power of the Lākinī of the Three Principles," within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, in the section on the Piercing of the Maṇipūra Cakra, in the Illumination of the Great Tantra, in the Practice of Accomplished Mantras, in the Later Tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. || 44 ||
Then the forty-fifth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
Now I shall describe the sequence of time, by which time one becomes a king among yogins.
At that time, [he perceived] the abode of the vital breaths, a subtle accumulation. || 45-1 ||
Through repeated accumulation, he becomes firm and fully self-controlled;
while the yoginīs, the mothers of yoga, indeed move within his practice. (45.2)
O Ocean of the Solar Lineage, at whatever time whatever ought to be performed, at each and every such time the supreme self, free from all affliction, comes under one's control. (45.3)
O Śaṅkara, without the essence of practice and without recitation, who becomes a perfected one or a knower? Or where does one become a yogi? (45.4)
Through the practice of mantra-yoga, a person gradually becomes a yogi;
at dawn, he should perform the purification of knowledge, the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī, and so forth. (45–5)
In the midst of that, one should also perform the yoga consisting of the five nectars and so forth;
thereafter, the rite of the mantra-bath is the sprinkling of water upon the head.
Then one should perform the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana) separately for each;
thereafter, having risen, one should sit upon a pure and soft seat on auspicious ground.
Having sat down, the constant practitioner should maintain a pure body and posture; O Lord, at the time of that activity, one should practice meditation and pure consciousness alone. (45-8)
One should always perform the recitation (japa) within the center of Kuṇḍalinī;
one should prepare a beautiful seat according to the distinction between left and right.
Having assumed the preliminary postures such as āsana, one should perform the susthāsana;
having properly performed the susthāsana, one should perform the ūrdhvapadmāsana. || 45-10 ||
Placing both hands between the hair below the crown of the head, one should recite the mantra eighty-four times multiplied by three; likewise, one should break the seat.
The proximity [of these] increases progressively by double;
furthermore, the number of these seats and so forth must be stated again. (45-12)

O Lord, in the practice of the eight limbs, all the postures (āsanas) must be explained, as well as the sixteen-fold breath control (prāṇāyāma), or that consisting of twelve [recitations] and so forth. (45.13)
Having brought [the breath] beyond the range of one's own ears, the wise one should always drink the air;
then, having completed that task, he should practice mantra-yoga. (45.14)
Having completed the mantra-yoga, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, having arisen and looked toward a river or similar body of water within the inner self, [one should proceed].
Having performed his bath according to the sequence beginning with the mental [bath], the great yogi completes the mental recitation and the recitation itself right there. (45.16)
One should perform a single breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and, having done so, the wise man should go to the bank;
covering his yellow garment, he should contemplate dharma and adharma. (45.17)
Then, having performed the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana), one should carry out the ritual of worship;
having performed retention of breath (kumbhaka) everywhere, one should meditate upon it again and again.
Having meditated upon the Goddess Kuleśvarī at the great seat (pīṭha) of Maṇipūra and having worshipped her according to the prescribed rite, one should again perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then the supreme practitioner should perform the hymn of armor according to the prescribed rite;
by the union with the vital breath everywhere, he certainly becomes a yogi. (45.20)
Alternatively, for the sake of warding off the snares of time, one should perform this rite according to the great sages for the purpose of attaining certainty in yoga. (45.21)
Without the grace of yoga, time cannot be brought under control;
through time one attains yoga, and the meditation of yoga belongs to its own proper time.
The Supreme Brahman is dependent on yoga; the supreme scorcher of foes is dependent on yoga;
all spiritual accomplishment is dependent on yoga; therefore, one should take refuge in yoga.
Through yoga one attains knowledge, and from knowledge one may obtain liberation.
Listen now to that sequence regarding the wheel of the earth (bhūcakra), which is the means for accomplishing all perfections and other goals. (45-24)
By means of the mantra for accomplishing supernatural powers (siddhi), the yogi becomes a lord of the earth;
quickly the yogi becomes a king, and quickly the king becomes an ascetic (yati).
A Brahmin becomes a yogi quickly if he takes refuge in his own duty;
steadfastness in one's own duty is the knowledge of the Supreme Self, which is true knowledge. (45.26)
Through knowledge of that, one attains yoga; the supernatural powers (siddhis) depend upon yoga;
the Supreme Brahman depends upon the supernatural powers; therefore, one should take refuge in yoga.
One should rely upon that knowledge which consists of the realization of steadfastness in one's own duty;
through the application of yoga, liberation arises—this is the determination of the meaning of my Tantra. (45.28)
Brahmā is a yogī, as is Murāri; likewise Maheśvara is a yogī, and Mahākāla is a yogī; there is no doubt that the Kaula is a yogī. || 45-29 ||
A wise person should always make an effort to pierce the Maṇipūra;
for if one becomes a piercer of the deity residing in the Maṇipūra, [the goal is attained]. (45.30)
Having become happy at every moment, he certainly remains for a long time;
[he is] of great splendor, beautiful, and the destroyer of great delusion. (45.31)
Resembling a cloud, resembling lightning, and supremely composed of full splendor;
a lotus strung with jewels, and indeed a multitude of gems.
With sun-stones, moon-stones, fire-stones, and other such gems of great brilliance, everything there was characterized by the arising of the quality of supreme luster. (45.33)
Just as there is the brilliance of ten million lightnings within a dense cloud, so too should that which is the object of the knowledge of the Siddhas be contemplated. (45.34)
Indeed, the eternally abiding place of yogins, situated on an extremely subtle path, is a lotus adorned with jewels; thus it is called Maṇipūra. (45.35)
It was endowed with ten soft petals, captivating to the mind, possessed of the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, and filled with steady flashes of lightning. (45.36)

One who is established in one's own nature should first perform meditation on the lotus presided over by Śiva, which causes the illumination of the universe and consists of the forms of the phonemes. (45.37)
Having fixed the mind upon the Great Lotus, one should cultivate it until it is stainless;
through meditation on the syllables from *ḍa* to *pha*, one becomes firm in gnosis.
Having attained steadiness of mind, one should apply oneself to divine devotion.
O Supreme Lord, listen as I shall explain the meditation on the colors. 45-39.
Having meditated upon that by which a human being becomes immortal and remains for a long time, one should perform the practice of great fortitude and drink air very slowly. (45–40)
Wherever the mind goes, one should instantly become absorbed in that;
beginning from the eastern petal and so forth, one should perform meditation separately for each. (45–41)
Ḍāṃ ḍāṃ ḍāṃ! O Ḍākinī, you who delight in the supreme ḍamaru drum, O Tāriṇī whose form is the syllable *tāra*;
ḍiṃ ḍiṃ ḍiṃ! You who abide in the Ḍāmara, in the house of the ḍamaru and the ḍama-drum, you who are established in the mantra with the sound *ḍaṅka-ḍiṅkiṃ*;
ḍaṃ ḍaṃ ḍaṃ! O Queen of the Ḍāmara, you whose girdle is fashioned from the resonance of the sounds *ḍimi-ḍimi-ḍimi-ga*.
Oṃ oṃ oṃ ḍākaḍaṃ ḍaḥ praḍuma ḍamuḍāṃ; I take refuge in Dāḍimā. || 45-42 ||

Ḍhāṃ ḍhāṃ ḍhāṃ! You who possess a firm drum and a multitude of excellent hands, whose mantras are truly pervasive—ḍhiṃ ḍhiṃ ḍhiṃ! You who have the form of a serpent, worship her, worship her, O manifestation of the mind of stainless bliss! Śrīṃ ḍheṃ ḍhaṃ vajraḍhūṃ khā khavaṭa maṭamaraṃ svāhayā ṭoṃṭa-bījā!
Ḍhoṃ ḍhoṃ ḍhoṃ ḍhakkaḍhakkaḥ! [I praise] that Lākinī, who is the beloved of the compassionate one (Karuṇākāminī). || 45-43 ||
The speech of Bāṇa is not established in the stability of arrows;
it is the cause of the splendor of the sun, rich with the festival of lutes and flutes, compassionate toward the virtues of jewels, and skilled in the art of the brush.
It is agitated by the garlands of mantras for the purification of gems, and it abounds in flowers situated upon the flute.
I meditate upon her whose complexion is red as vermilion, fresh and pure like a newly formed rain-cloud. || 45-44 ||
The Tantrikas [meditate upon] that supreme Tārā, who is as pure as a cluster of stars, who bestows the siddhis of the *tāla* and other gestures,
who possesses earrings of exceeding brilliance, who maintains the mental yoga of the sages,
who is the peerless Tulasī, whose banks are slender, and who is born from logic (*tarka*).
O mind, worship the venerable Mother Tāpasī, who possesses a splendor equal to ten thousand suns.

She who stands amidst the distracted yet well-established, who is the traveler on the path of stability, the peak of the letter *tha*, and the garland of *thas*; she who is the song, the yoga, and the wayward path, who is the syllable *tham* and *tham*, and the *tha* that is the consort of Fire;
she who stands upon the ground of moonlight, who churns the firm station, and who is radiant while seated upon her throne.
I worship the syllable Om, which is the essence of the nine nectars, delightful in its stability, and white as the moon. || 45-46 ||

I meditate upon Kuleśī, who has long fangs with the syllables *drāṃ drīṃ drūṃ*, whose teeth inspire fear, and who laughs with a loud roar; she is the remover of the umbrella of defects, the bestower of the state that grants divine light, established in reverence, radiant with embraced bliss, the source of all wealth, and the illuminator. (45–47)
She who upholds the teachings of Dharma, the goddess Śrī, the training in meditation, the earth-sustaining Dharaṇīdhara, and Dhūmāvatī;
she whose face has the form of a dhūstūra flower, who holds the blue-lotus-bearing earth upon her lotus-hand;
she who possesses the brilliance of lightning, ten million midday suns, and fire, the nectar-like Kokilākṣī, most subtle.
Having meditated upon her who is the singular perfection of bliss and the treasure-trove of the earth's wealth, I worship her, the knowledge of spiritual accomplishment. || 45-48 ||
Eternal, with eternity as her supreme goal, three-eyed, radiant as the bandhūka flower,
as stable as ten million times ten thousand suns, ever-new, with two lotus-hands,
bearing various auspicious marks, and established in the brilliance of millions of rays from the stainless moon.
I meditate upon the Daughter of the Mountain, who is full of bliss, who moves through the three qualities, and whose splendor is "naṃ naṃ. || 45-49 ||

May the fifth [nectar], consisting of flesh and marrow, filled with the light of the Beloved, full of supreme love that transcends even the Supreme, overflowing with perfect qualities, speaking in rapturous whispers,
and characterized by the playful chatter of intimate union— may this drink of nectar serve as my nourishment.
Direct your mind toward the ancient Pārvatī, who wears a beautiful yellow garment. || 45–50 ||

Sphem sphem! Within me is she whose vehicle is the serpent, whose face is a blossoming lotus, whose mouth is wide-open with a most terrible roar from her hissing fangs; she whose face expands at the violent snapping of the snakes, who wears serpents as bracelets, who hisses "Pham pham pham," and who is the fruit of the sole perfection of mantras.
With devotion, I perform meditation constantly for the sake of attaining the fruit of my desire.

Having thus meditated upon all the syllables as being red in color like lightning, arising from the petals of a lotus that is red like lightning, situated in the midst of a flash of lightning; (45–52)
One should always meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī, who moves through the center of the pericarp,
whose hands hold a boon, who has large eyes, and who is marked by the digits of the moon.
Her limbs are smeared with beautiful sandalwood paste, and she is adorned with ornaments of serpent-necklaces;
she has two arms, possesses millions of rays of light, and is beautified by vermilion on her forehead. || 45-54 ||

For the sake of accomplishing the path to spiritual perfection, one should meditate upon Lākinī— who possesses three eyes, who abides in the form of Time (Kāla), and who effects dissolution— by means of the ten syllables in their proper sequence.
[One should meditate on] the goddess Durgā, who has four arms, six arms, eight hands, or ten arms, who is both supreme and non-supreme, and who is well-seated upon her own vehicle. (45–56)
She who wields all weapons, who is adorned with twelve hands, who possesses fourteen arms, who is fierce, and likewise who protects with sixteen [hands]. (45–57)
Having thus meditated upon her who has eighteen arms, is dark-complexioned, and holds twenty hands, and having worshipped her, one should recite the Rudrāṇī-stotra. (45–58)

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Meditation on the Phonemes," within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Siddhi-mantras of the *Mahātantroddīpana* in the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava.
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O Bhairava, I shall proclaim the supreme hymn of praise to Rudrāṇī."
Having heard it, recited it, and retained it within one's own body, O Lord of Gods.
He shall indeed become a great adept (mahāsiddha) and shall come under the power of Mahākāla, for the sake of protecting the three worlds by Brahmā as well as Viṣṇu. (46-2)
Having praised the most fierce [goddess] who is united with Rudra, one shall achieve victory over all;
having heard that, all the sages, who were practitioners of yoga and seers of yoga, [were moved]. (46.3)
All the gods and all the lords of the worlds shall become protectors of one's life through this mere hymn of praise; by this alone, Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā. (46.4)
Viṣṇu attains the state of Viṣṇu, and all the deities attain divinity.
Now listen to that hymn which is the means for accomplishing the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga).
By the recitation of this hymn, the eight-limbed family deities become subject to one's will, as do the deities residing in the seven heavens. (46–6)

Of this hymn of praise to the power of Mahārudra, Mahākālabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the venerable Śrī in the form of Śrī is the deity (devatā), *vāṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *drāṃ* is the power (śakti), *samauṃ spheṃ* is the peg (kīlaka), and the deities beginning with Mahogrā are the presiding divinities; its application (viniyoga) is in recitation (*japa*) for the sake of attaining all desired goals.
May Mahāraudrī— whose multitude of faces is as fierce as Rudra and red with wrath—
remove the sphere of the transformations of phenomena; grant me supreme discernment,
you who are the primordial person of the worlds, even as she is the mother of virtuous sons.
Falling from the village of Vibhākoṭi, her eyes trembled and wavered. || 46-7 ||
You alone, whose origin is auspicious, constantly sustain the three worlds for me;
you are infinite, beyond the reach of the senses, adorned with the arts of the celestial hosts, and clothed in serpents.
O Śivā, your radiance ever arises to bestow prosperity.
O you who are the bliss and joy of Śiva, who have rendered my dull mind languid with delight, bring me joy!
O Hare, O you who resemble a diamond, take away, take away my great greed and sin!
O Mistress of the Senses, destroy the poison of my body that is swollen with the joy of worldly venom!
Grant me the bliss of nectar and bring an end even to the incomparable wrath of Śiva.
O Mother of noble lineage, bestow upon me that divine intoxication, desire, and delusion. || 46-9 ||
If you also grant the true essence of austerity here,
then my mind, ignited and pervaded by the True, shall find its joy in your gift;
O Goddess of Exquisite Glory, conquer me, yet do not abandon your own auspicious devotion.
I praise you alone; perform the protection of all beings forever.

Having reflected upon your own Tantra, you fashion that which is eternally united with bliss; she who resembles a great sword, the handiwork of the three worlds, the beloved of Rudra— O you who joyfully provide protection for the gods amidst the multitude of sacred seats!
In Maṇidvīpa is indeed the radiant [city], and in Maṇipūra is the stainless state.

In the great field, you are the remover of fear through the festival of battle; O Kirātī, the essence of the lineage, protect my entire family during dissolution! O Mother of Yoga, create within my heart the bliss of the knowledge of dissolution!
For the protection of ascetics, the Kula-yuvati-vidyā arises. || 46-12 ||
You are the foundation and the fame; you descend and protect us from darkness.
O young woman, I do not know your true nature, your glory, or your blissful majesty.
Make victory swell like the great ocean, the lord of waters and the source of treasures.
You too, who abide in the joy of gold, are composed of the ocean of compassion.
You protect Viṣṇu, the Ordainer, and the hosts of gods who bow to you, while others are your enemies; you are perfected, bringing about the destruction and dissolution of the worlds of happiness;
joyfully scattering hundreds of millions of rays throughout the three worlds.
O auspicious one, you alone must always protect the beloved of Giriśa.
I truly desire the end of your bliss,
which consists of the syllables *visarga* and *indu*, and is known as *kāmanā*.
O Pure One, protect my mind with the fall of your compassionate glance.
You alone are perfected as the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
You are the savior of the world, you are all-pervading in the world; you are the form of the world’s flame, you are the form of the world’s dharma;
because of your non-duality, you are the form of bliss.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
O Sovereign, you are the ordainer of people;
you are the moonlight that delights my heart and bestows the bliss of liberation;
you reside within the lotus of the command; you are the noble one of the gurus.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Abiding within a circle of light, established in the relinquishment of worldly existence;
you are a garland of land-lotuses worn around your neck;
you are dark-hued like Śiva and possess a great tawny radiance.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 46-18 ||
O Goddess established on the moon, whose fourfold Vedic stations are immovable,
you alone are the great speech of the Vedas in this world;
O Renowned One, be gracious to me who am devoted with the sentiment of great bhakti.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
She who acts as the abode of the world, who is established in the intellect of the world,
who stands in the youth of the world, and who resides in the very being of the world—
may she [protect] me, who am consumed by the great woodworm within the midst of the whirlpool.
You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Abiding in the sequence of time for the great creation and destruction; always delighting in the consumption of human flesh; she who is of the nature of eternal bliss;
O Great Śākyamuni, Queen of Sages, worthy of worship by the lords of gods!
You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Because she delights the sixty-four tantras and because she consists of the great elements, she is the Great Siddhi-Vidyā;
she whose body is severed by guile is known as Annasamjñā.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
O Primordial One, you bestow the state of Śiva, greatness, equanimity, purity, and non-uncertainty; you abide in the ocean of nectar and reside in the Great Delusion.
You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
May the splendor of the lotus-feet [of the Lord], resting upon the back of the great lion and situated within the circle of my glorious crest-jewel,
protect me until the end of this body in the kalpa of the lineage of worldly bliss.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 46-24 ||
She is steadfast, possessing a necklace in the form of great lightning;
she is both intensely flickering and immovable, born of primordial wisdom.
Because she is eternally cultivated, she is eternally established in making known.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
The great Kaula maiden brings joy and delusion to the Kula;
she is the protector of the Kula-field and the maker of the Kula-umbrella.
Due to her great restlessness, she is whirled about by the great wind.
You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
The long-lived one, the radiant lady, the seed of the earth; the destroyer of fear and its absence, like ten million autumn moons;
the manifestation of prosperity, the remover of terror, the most excellent.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
She is the embodiment of existence, resting upon the state of the Great Hero;
she is the Great Śaiva Heroine within both the specific and the non-specific,
because she is radiant with the ocean that is the locus of both emission and liberation.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Because of being possessed of great wisdom, because of being a great sweetmeat,
because of being a great Kaulika, because of being beyond movement,
and because of being unwavering in the practice of devotion to the Kula.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
She is the bestower of the accomplishment of the *vasu* and the creator of the bliss of Śiva,
because she brings about the penetration of the bliss of great sexual union (*mahāmaithuna*). Because she is the reality of easy respiration, asceticism is the protection of the vital breath.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Due to a state of overflowing love and the reality of noble knowledge,
through intense longing and the grace of Śrī, you are the embodiment of the support for existence; for the sake of great sovereignty, you are the daughter of a great king.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 46-31 ||
It is the great science of liberation because of its utter purity;
it is the perfection of the five-crested radiance;
and it is delightful through the practice of the great sound and the bindu.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
She is delightful with a complexion like that of great coral,
because she accomplishes the lineage, joy, the sutras, and so forth;
she possesses the great kingdom, knowledge, and wealth, because she brings about their union.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Because she finds bliss in worshipping the two lotus-feet of yours,
she herself is all knowledge in the form of Mahākālī;
for she is characterized by specific relations such as modification (*vikāra*) and so forth.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
O Daughter of the Great Mountain, [attain] the state of Śiva, the state of auspiciousness,
the state of being worthy of worship, the state of supremacy, and the state of great purity;
realize these through the reality, for there is no other certainty.
You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Having bowed to Mahācetanā, the goddess of sound,
who is the foremost among those whose mental application transcends number,
who destroys opposition, and who slays the life-force of enemies.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
May she who conforms to the twenty-four principles of the wrathful deities,
who shines like the crescent moon in the sky while stationed upon the *kīlaka*,
and whose complexion is like the fierce sun, always protect me.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Her own body, auspicious and in the form of the wish-fulfilling cow,
was always beautiful in color when viewed with faith; its hue was like that of ten million rays of the moon, full and radiant.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Endowed with the great seed-syllable of desire,
she shatters the vast web of faults; slowly bringing [liberation],
she is Śivā, Bhadrakālī, the garland of steadfast bliss.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Always protect Śambhu, the consumer of the great Kālakūṭa poison, whose eyes are piercing, who is excessively moistened by fear,
and who dwells in countless abodes because he protects the world from existence.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 46-40 ||
Carrying away that which is rich in poison, bearing that which is beginning with art (kalā), crying out, dancing, vast, and wandering;
she is the protector and the nourisher of fortunes, being in the state of a young girl.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Whether always with faith for the sake of the bliss of existence,
or at the time of mental union within the center of the lotus feet,
because of the complete washing away of desire beyond the highest reckoning.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
The mantra of the Siddhas and others for the destruction of the earth’s trembling;
she whose face is enriched by the Kula and enriched by all things; she who is subtle and moderate; she who exerts effort in bestowing the bliss of dissolution.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Those who, having summoned great fortitude,
recite your names at the dawn of the Kali age—
at that very time, you grant them accomplishment here.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Abiding for long and shining for long,
you are the knowledge that brings joy to the lineage of the gurus; you are satisfied by the utterance of *svadhā*, and you are the wife of the fire of the arts (*kalā*).
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
She whose signs arise from the fruit at the time of the bliss of wine;
she who bestows great siddhi in the central region of the funeral pyre;
she who is divided into three and yet distinct, the knowledge-mantra of Mahārudra.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
O Mahāpūrvī Kātyāyanī, at the root of wrath,
you first bestow the Dharma beginning with discernment,
for the sake of joyfully protecting the three deities.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 46-47 ||
Because of its pure clarity, because of its great wonder, because of the delusion of meditating on the body, and because of its being established in the infinite;
it is the self that protects the *kula*, the self of the great characteristics (*mahālakṣaṇa*).
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
O Śrī, though you are subtle and exceedingly subtle, you who burn the families and lands of your enemies in an instant— may you always protect my land of bliss.
You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 46-49 ||

O Rudrā, protect the stage of life for those established in the fourth āśrama! O Mahograpratāpā, Mahāraudrī, Bhadrā! Through you, may there be the destruction of great sins and the attainment of immortality.
You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 46–50 ||
In this place delightful with the great wind, accessible through great wisdom,
and renowned for the accomplishment of the recitation of great mantras and other practices— grant me absorption by means of the striking of the external breath.
You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman. || 46-51 ||
I do not know whether it is Amara or Viṣṇu;
even the great Kaulika does not know the worship.
In the recitation beginning with Surendra and ending with Kulādyāsana—
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
O Mahābhadrakālī, you are capable of making my object of temptation manifest;
and with your lotus feet, you are able to destroy the accumulation of great sins.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Carrying a skull, stumbling without purpose,
wearing a great garland of gold, and illuminating the vast sky—
may she, the mistress of Vaiśvānara, grant me auspiciousness and welfare.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Pracaṇḍā becomes gracious for the sake of agitating existence;
Śānti and Pratuṣṭi are for the destruction of disputes and the like. Abiding for some time with a tranquil inner self, she remains serene.
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
You who drink the great wind at the time of the liberation of activity;
you who bestow the knowledge of the Kula and possess a divine form by day;
O Forgiving One, who acts according to desire, exercise your sovereignty!
You alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
If a devotee, having firmly resolved in his heart, "May my name be established as a perfected one beginning with 'Śrīvara'," always prays for this, he quickly attains it.
It may be recited either daily or joyfully on a single occasion. || 46–57 ||
O Mahākāla Śambhu, O great adept of wisdom!
One who recites [this] with a single-pointed mind while always under the control of time shall attain a state of great devotion and know liberation.
Devotion to Mahādeva and yoga at the three times of day.
Visualizing Mahālākinī Kuṇḍalī, the beloved of Mahārudra, in the center of the jewel-throne,
[one should recite] this hymn, the essence of Brahman, which yields great merit.
For the sake of attaining great beauty, for merit, and for spiritual accomplishment. || 46-59 ||
O Mahākālī, Rudrāṇī, Bhadrāṇī, Kṛṣṇe!
May one perform [this] for the manifestation of the form of the bliss of Bhava.
By whomsoever she is worshipped, having assumed the form of bliss—
O Great Goddess Caṇḍī, your perfection lies in meditative absorption.
He swiftly attains the state of great liberation;
he is the great purity, the destroyer of desire, whose form is Time.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Rudra-Śakti-Lākinī," within the *Maṇipūrabhedanakrama* (The Process of Piercing the Maṇipūra Cakra) in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Chakras), in the section on the Siddhi-mantras, within the Great Tantra (*Mahātantra*) that illuminates the *Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter.
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said:
Listen, O Lotus-born Lord of Kailāsa, to the arrangement of the circle of wheels;
pay close attention to the greatness of the piercing of the six wheels. (47–1)
This mantra, which pierces Maṇipūra, is not to be disclosed;
it is for the attainment of the eight sovereign powers and for the bestowal of liberation while living.
I shall tell you, O Mahākāla, that by knowing which yogins become immortal;
indeed, by what yoga is it achieved through the mere performance of ritual action? (47-3)
Through this very practice, one becomes omniscient and possessed of knowledge of all objects;
having meditated upon Rudra together with Rudrāṇī, and having worshipped him, one should perform the recitation of mantras. || 47-4 ||
Now I shall describe the great mantra as well as the section on worship:
the practitioner of mantra, abiding in Maṇipūra, should perform the worship of Rudrāṇī. (47–5)
Now, O Kālakūṭapa, I shall perform the extraction of the mantra:
having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should then speak the word "Namaḥ" (Salutation). (47–6)
Having uttered those syllables and then the word *rudra*, and having pronounced the word *rūpiṇyai*, the mantra of Rudrāṇī is thus declared. (47–7)
Next, I shall declare the mantra of Mahārudra according to its true essence; listen.
At the end of the *praṇava*, one should utter the word "namaḥ" with a great sound. (47–8)
Having extracted the *pada* for Rudra, the *mahārudra-mantra* is remembered;
thereafter, O Lord whose form is Time, listen to another mantra, that of Rudrāṇī.
The mantra is encapsulated at the beginning and end by all the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*;
at the very end of all, the *vahnijāyā* (svāhā) is added—this is the most excellent of great mantras.
By the mere recitation of this, one is victorious in the practice of the six lotuses;
such is the method of Rudra, or else it may be of another kind. (47-11)
One should always meditate upon the various mantras of the Rudras, as determined in the Koṭitantra, within the Maṇipūra [cakra] for the purpose of practicing yoga. (47–12)
In all cases, the mental rite consisting of the procedure for meditation and worship should be performed with mantras known as Pramoda, Akhyāti, Anubhi, Mṛtyuñjaya, and so forth. (47–13)
One should quickly cause consciousness to arise in the two deities residing in the Maṇipūra;
now I shall describe [the procedure] for Maheśa, Rudra, the Supreme Self.
The great mantra known as Prāsāda, which bestows the attainment of the fruits of the three worlds, is joined with the syllable Oṃ at its end and adorned with the Nāda and Bindu. (47.15)
The mantra known as Prāsāda is proclaimed as a wish-fulfilling gem for those who worship it;
if one recites it after first uttering the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā, [it grants all desires]. (47.16)
He performs rites such as paralyzing and so forth; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, [he recites] the great mantra, the great spell, which is the conqueror of death.
One should perform the recitation mentally with that which is to be recited for the protection of the vital breaths:
the *Tāra* (Om), followed by *Sthirā* (Sthi), then *Sakarṇendu* (Ri), and *Bhṛgu* (Bha) conjoined with *Sarga* (Ḥ). (47–18)
The mantra consisting of three syllables is declared to be the essence of Mṛtyuñjaya;
or else, one may recite the essence of Mṛtyuñjaya in another manner.
Having extracted Mṛtyuñjaya, protect the pair that follows;
then, having again extracted Mṛtyuñjaya in reverse order.
This other twelve-syllable mantra is named Mṛtyuñjaya;
O Śaṅkara, listen as I describe its meditation (or worship), as well as its ritual placement (nyāsa). 47-21.
One should employ that which is encapsulated by the Rudra-mantra as the remover of death;
likewise, Śiva [is empowered] when encapsulated by the mantra of Rudrakāntā. (47–22)
Having recited the mantra and performed worship, the self-controlled man shall become a protector;
having performed his morning duties and the like, he should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) with his senses subdued. || 47-23 ||

Being extremely vigilant and devoted to the performance of prescribed rites, one should perform the bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and so forth, and then take recourse to the seat (āsana) and other requirements. || 47-24 ||
Having completed the entire preparation of the seat and covered it with a yellow cloth,
or else having put on two beautiful white garments.
Having gone to a soft seat and washed both feet,
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice according to the rules, and then sit upon a svastika seat for the worship.

Having sat down in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), the lotus posture (padmāsana), or likewise the yoni posture (yonyāsana), one whose self is stainless should become intent upon the path of worship. 47-27.
All substances and foods, whether mentally conceived or actually obtained—or even if they are not obtained at all—are purified by the mind’s conception. (47.28)
One should always perform the ritual even on the outside of one's own [body];
having purified whatever materials are obtainable, one should employ them therein. (47.29)
Then one should especially perform the delightful practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) for sixty-four measures or likewise for sixteen measures.
One should focus on the breath for either twelve measures or for a specific number of repetitions;
then, having completed the prāṇāyāma, one should perform the Rudra-nyāsa.
One should diligently perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the great heroes beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha.
I shall now proclaim the Rudra-placement for the sake of attaining success through the application of mantras and so forth. (47.32)
By means of this practice of nyāsa, a person becomes equal to Rudra;
one should always perform the great nyāsa for the manifestation of all supernatural powers (siddhis). 47-33.
The Great Nyāsa is proclaimed to be both devoid of power and endowed with power;
by performing it endowed with power, one becomes a mighty possessor of great power.
Likewise, the rite is empowered by the destruction of all obstacles;
it is joined with the groups of the Mātṛkā letters within the lotus-wheel of the Mātṛkā.

Having either encapsulated the mantra with the *mātṛkā* or having encapsulated the *mātṛkā* with the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should perform the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*) with careful attention. (47.36)
One who is valorous should be like a lion; seeing him, enemies flee.
Having become silent and having restrained himself, he effects the breaking of the circle of the clan. (47.37)
Becoming firm in Maṇipūra, one becomes filled with great splendor.
I shall proclaim their names, numbering fifty-one.
O Lord, hear likewise the names of the fifty single-shaktis; at the end of all their names, one should utter "Salutation to Īśa. (47-39)
One should join each individual letter of the alphabet to the beginning of the name;
the name should always be conjoined with Śakti and likewise end with Īśa. (47–48)

Endowed with the power to pierce, the great ascetic should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon a seat of kusha grass for the sake of attaining perfection—a seat consisting of cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass, with the kusha on top. (47–48)
Having assumed a single firm posture, the yogi should perform the network of ritual placements (nyāsa),
either on a seat of leopard skin and the like, or even on a soft seat.
The practitioner of yoga, having performed the array of nyāsas, shall become fearless;
those who dwell in the house of Bhadrakālī and practice there continuously [attain this]. (47–43)
O Mahādeva, by means of this great nyāsa, one becomes immortal at that very moment;
one attains long life, health, prosperity, and great glory. (47–48)
By the grace of the yoga of placement (nyāsa), it comes to my station;
through the yoga of maintaining that placement, it shall reside in the maṇipūra at the heart. (47–45)
First, their names should be uttered, followed by the invocation of their powers:
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, and Trimūrti. (47–46)
Amareśvara, Arghīśa, and Bhāvabhūti after that;
then Atithīśa, Sthāṇvīśa, Hara, and Jhiṇṭīśa. (47–47)
Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśvara, Akrūra, Mahāsena, and Nirjarādi— these are the sixteen.
O Mahārudra, these deities are the embodiments of the sixteen vowels:
Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntaka, and Śivottama; || 47–49 ||
Ekarudra, as well as Kūrma, Ekanetreśvara, Caturānana, Ajeśa, Sarva, and Someśa; || 47–50 ||
Lāṅgalīśa, Dārukeśa, and Arddhanārīśvara;
Umākānteśa, Āṣāḍhi, Ḍiṇḍīśa, and Atrīśa;
as well as Mīneśa, Meṣeśa, Lohiteśa, and Śikhīśvara.
Chagalaṇḍe is Dviraṇḍeśa, and after that is Mahākāleśvara;
then Vāṇīśa, Bhujaṅgeśa, and beyond that is Pinākīśa. (47–51)
Khaḍgīśa, Carakeśa, Śyena, Bhṛgvīśa, Nakulīśa, Śiveśa, and Saṃvarttakeśa. (47–52)
These Rudras are fully described as the lords of the Kula at all times;
however, that name in which the word "Īśa" does not appear at the end is not [to be included]. (47–53)
Having performed the rite named Keśānta, one should carry out the deposition (nyāsa) of the Lord of the Crown;
he who performs this continuously for the sake of destroying desire, delusion, and the rest. (47–54)

One should place that which is composed of the letters of the Mātṛkā upon the locus of the Mātṛkā. When the placement (nyāsa) is conjoined with Śakti, at that time there is also the conjunction with Īśa. Alternatively, it is likewise enclosed (sampuṭa) by Rudra-Śakti and by Rudra.
O Lord, by placing [the mantra] within the locus of the Mātṛkās using one's own mantra,
and having performed the threading with Śakti, one may cross over the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) in an instant.
Listen to that method, O Lord of Life, beloved of Śaṅkara:
Pūrṇodarī, Girijā, and after her, Śālmalī. (47–57)
The Lolākṣī, the Vartulākṣī, and after that the Dīrghaghoṇā;
then the Sudīrghamukhī and the Gomukhī, and after that the Dīrghajihvā. (47–58)
Then Kuṇḍodarī, Urdhvamukhī, as well as Vikṛtamukhī, Jvālāmukhī, Vahnimukhī, and Lolajihvā follow thereafter. (47–59)
Likewise, O Lord, Vidyāmukhī and these others are the powers of the vowels;
and I shall now describe, O Lord of Pārvatī, the Vidyās which are the powers of the consonants beginning with *ka*.
Then follow Mahākālī, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī; furthermore, Drāviṇī, Nāgarī, Khecarī, and Mañjarī. (47–61)
Rūpiṇī, Bimbinī, Kākodarī, Pūtanā, Bhadrakālī, Yoginī, Śaṅkhinī, and likewise Gajjinī. || 47–62 ||
Kālarātri, Kuñjikā, and thereafter Kapardinī;
then Vajrā, Jayā, and also Sumukheśvarī, O Lord, O Master. (47–63)
Revatī, Mādhavī, Vāruṇī, and likewise Vāyavī; Vakṣovidāriṇī, Sahajālakṣmī, and [Sahajalakṣmī], O Lord. (47–64)
Vyāpinī and Māyā are the presiding deities of the Rudrāṅka-pīṭha;
they are adorned with all ornaments and possess bodies as red as vermilion.
Holding tridents, skull-bowls, and so forth, as well as arrows, spears, and scimitars;
their hands are eternally in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; they ride upon serpents as their vehicles. || 47–66 ||
The great Rudras, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, hold tridents and skull-bowls;
they carry swords, shields, spears, maces, and pestles.
Constantly bearing various weapons, as beautiful as ten million bandhūka flowers,
their limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste, these supreme beings wear five topknots.
With their lotus-hands adorned by great garlands of red utpala lotuses, one should then perform the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) according to my tantra. (47–69)

Having performed the rite of the deposition of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) either by encasing [the mantra] with the root-mantra on all sides or by encasing it with the syllables, I shall now describe that according to the prescribed rule.
Oṃ, salutation to Ananta; then, "namas" in the heart.
Then, the word "oṃ padmāya namaḥ" in the heart; and after that, [the same] again. (47–71)
Oṃ, to the solar orb at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], whose essence is the [twelve] kalās;
having uttered the word "oṃ namaḥ" at the end, [one should place it] in the heart of the Lord. (47–72)
Oṃ uṃ, salutation to the lunar maṇḍala, whose essence consists of sixteen digits.
In every instance, one should perform the placement of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa) within the heart, wherein the mind is dissolved. 47–73.
Oṃ maṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala, whose self consists of ten kalās.
Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to sattva; oṃ raṃ, obeisance to rajas. || 47-74 ||
Oṃ taṃ, obeisance to Tamas, and [in] the filaments starting from the east;
Oṃ taṃ, obeisance to Ātman, and Oṃ, obeisance to the All-pervading One. || 47-75 ||
Oṃ aṃ, salutation to the inner self (antarātman), and Oṃ, salutation to Manonmanī;
above that, one should then utter "salutation" at the end for the dweller in emptiness (śūnyavāsin).
Oṃ Paṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self (Paramātman) and at the end to Him who has the form of Time (Kālarūpin).
Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Self of Knowledge (Jñānātman) and at the end to the Dweller in Syllables (Varṇavāsin). || 47-77 ||
Then the king of practitioners and yogis should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the power of the seat (pīṭhaśakti);
he should also place it upon the filaments of the heart-lotus, starting from the east.
One should say "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmā" at the end, then "Oṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā," and one should utter the words "Oṃ, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamanī. (47–79)
(One should say: *Oṃ raudrāyai namaḥ* at the end; then one should utter *oṃ kālyai ca namaḥ*.
Then one should utter the word *oṃ kalavikariṇyai namaḥ*. And then one should again utter *oṃ balapramathanyai namaḥ* at the end.)
Having placed these [syllables], O Lord of Gods, one should perform the placement in the center;
having performed the visualization within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, one should carry out the practice. (47–80)
Oṃ, one should then utter "namaśca" for Manonmanī above that;
then at the end, one should recite "oṃ namo bhagavate," followed by the word "sakala. Then the words "guṇāya śaktiyuktāya anantāya" [should be recited]. (47–81)
At the end, one should utter the word "namaḥ" for the essence of the Yoga-pīṭha.
Then, O Mahādeva, one should perform the Nyāsa of the Seers and so forth;
[the Seers] of Rudra-śakti, of Viṣṇu, and likewise of Mṛtyuñjaya.
And Kahoḍa, the son of a sage, is proclaimed as its seer (ṛṣi);
he was one who, through austerity, directly learned the Manu from the mouth of Maheśvara.
He who accomplishes this is called his *ṛṣi*, being of pure soul; and because of his status as a guru, the placement (*nyāsa*) of that name upon the head is prescribed. (47–83)
It is called *chanda* because it covers (*chādana*) all the principles of mantra;
furthermore, because of its syllabic nature and its status as words, it is declared to be *chanda* in the mouth. (47–84)
Because she impels and urges forth all living beings, one should place that deity, who resides within the center of the heart-lotus, there. (47–85)
Due to ignorance of the seer and the meter, a mantra will not yield its fruit;
the efficacy of mantras wanes for those who do not know their ritual application. (47.86)
The wise practitioner should perform the placement of the sages (*ṛṣinyāsa*) on the head, the placement of the meters (*chandonyāsa*) in the lotus of the mouth,
and the placement of the deity (*devatānyāsa*) in the lotus of the heart.

The wise practitioner should diligently perform the placement of the seed-syllables (bījanyāsa) in the mouth and the secret place, the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa) in the two feet, and the placement of the pins (kīlakanyāsa) upon all the limbs.
One should perform the nyāsa consisting of Śiva and Śakti upon the head itself;
on the head, for the protection of the vital breaths, [one says]: "Salutation to Mahāviṣṇu, the Ṛṣi. (47–89)
One should utter the word "namas" for Paṅkti-chandas at the mouth;
one should address Mahārudra, who is joined with Śakti, in the heart. || 47-90 ||

One should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the hands with the mantra "Salutation to the Deity," and thereafter perform the ritual placement upon the limbs; having performed this, one should diligently engage in meditation.
One should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakriyā*) of the mantra using the fire-seed syllable (*vahnibīja*).
I shall now describe the meditation on Rudra; through this meditation, one becomes a sovereign of the earth.
Fierce, of a fierce nature, that primordial Puruṣa, whose name is proclaimed in the profound Gītā;
holding a trident and a sword, bestowing boons and fearlessness, bearing a single lotus, most violent;
possessing a moving web of rays, with the splendor of a hundred moons, having the form of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu).
One should meditate upon one's own power as Raudrī, whose body consists of the dissolution [of the universe] and who shines with the brilliance of ten million suns.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with flowers, one should perform the ritual of the *arghya* offering.
Having performed the *arghya* with the Rudra mantra, one should carry out the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalapadā, and so forth;
Vikaraṇī is declared, as well as Akṣarā, Balā, and the others beginning with Vikaraṇī. (47–95)
Balapramathanī, followed by Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī—these are proclaimed as the Pīṭha-śaktis of Śiva. (47–96)
One should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
the worship should be performed according to the rule, beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ. || 47-97 ||
Having meditated again, one should invoke [the deity] with water for the feet and the guest-offering, and worship thoroughly:
water for the feet, the guest-offering, water for sipping, water for bathing, and again water for sipping.
One should worship the first enclosure with perfumes, flowers, and bilva leaves;
then perform the worship of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) with "vaṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth.
In the center and likewise in the four directions, one should recite the remaining [mantra] twice;
then, having worshipped Indra and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas), one should perform the worship.
O Mahākāla, one should offer vajras and other implements along with incense and lamps;
having prepared an abundance of food offerings, one should also present water for drinking.
Having performed the purification of the body, one should then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma);
purified and with a pure mind, the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] three hundred times. (47.102)
Having performed one thousand and eight repetitions of the Gajāntaka mantra,
or having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should perform the rite of dedication (samarpaṇa).
One should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for the successful accomplishment of one's own mantra;
thereafter, one should perform prostration by means of the power of consciousness (śakti-caitanya). 47-104.
Homage to the god Rudra, whose form is ten million suns and moons;
homage to you, the all-pervading giver of knowledge, the wielder of the trident.
Salutations to you, Kālarudra, to Time itself, whose form is the Veda;
to the one who reveals the path of the Vedas, and who brings about the destruction of enemies. || 47-106 ||
Salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, who is fierce, endowed with power, four-armed, the embodiment of the Vedas, and whose nature is the great ether. || 47-107 ||
Salutation to Brahmā, who holds a choice lotus, a trident, and a sword...
having performed the worship of Rudra’s Śakti together with the Mahārudra [mantra] || 47-108 ||
O Lord of the Kula, it is true, it is truly true that one becomes firm in Maṇipūra.
I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Śakti and the adoration with the root mantra.
The practitioner of mantra should perform this everywhere for the sake of attaining victory over the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭaiśvarya).
First, I shall explain the rite of the deposition of the sages (ṛṣinyāsa); listen to it according to its true nature. (47.110)
Here, one should place the hand on the head with "Rudraśakti," then at the position of Mahāviṣṇu; having uttered "Namaḥ to the Ṛṣi," one should apply the hand to the mouth.
One should place the hand upon the heart with the words "Salutation to Paṅkti-chandas," and likewise utter the words "Mahārudrāṇī" and "Lākinī. (47–112)
At the end of the three powers, [one should say] "Obeisance to the deity Mahāvidyā";
then, having uttered the word *oṃ* at the secret place, [one says] "Obeisance to you, the seed-syllable of one's own nature. (47.113)
Having uttered the word "namaḥ" for the entire body, for the complete Vajra, and for the Kīlaka, one should likewise perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and so forth.
In the rite of the placement (nyāsa) upon the hands and limbs, the entire procedure should be performed like that of Rudra:
first the placement of the ṛṣis and so forth, and after that, the purification of the hands.
The placement [of mantras] pervading the fingers, as well as the placement beginning with the heart (hṛdaya),
and immediately thereafter, the great sixteen-fold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) of Rudra’s power.
Then, having performed the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa), one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa);
thereafter, the triple clapping of the hands (tālatraya), the binding of the directions (digbandha), and the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma).
O Great Lord, one should especially perform meditation through the power of Rudra.
I bow to Rudrāṇī, the beloved of Rudra, who is enraptured by the nine aesthetic sentiments, whose limbs are smeared with saffron,
the sovereign of the world, possessing six arms, unconquered by the three worlds, and radiant as ten million flashes of lightning;
she who stands upon a lotus, holds a lotus in her hand, displays the gestures of granting boons and protection, and wields a sword and a spear.
One should meditate upon Raudrī, who has three eyes, whose pure body is adorned with a garland of skulls and a crescent moon.
O Śaṅkara, worship should be performed like that of Rudra, and likewise for the power (Śakti) of Rudra;
the worship may be conducted with ten services (upacāras) or with five services. || 47-120 ||
Whether with the eighteen services, or with sixteen and so forth;
if these are unavailable, one should perform the rite mentally and offer it as such.
Every mental action performed everywhere shall become multiplied ten million-fold;
having completed the worship according to the rite, one should offer water and engage in recitation and so forth.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and having muttered [the mantra] one hundred and eight times,
or indeed a thousand times, repeating it again and again along with the additional eight.
The wise one should offer the recitation with mantras that are more secret than the most secret;
thereafter, the best of practitioners should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 47-124 ||
One should perform salutation with devotion for the sake of attaining yoga and other perfections:
"O Great Terrible One, homage be to you; salutations, repeated salutations to you, Lākīnī! (47-125)
Salutations always for peace and contentment; salutations again and again to you, O Durgā!
Salutations always to the power of Rudra, O dweller in Maṇipūra! 47-126.
Grant the eight siddhis and the perfection of yoga; salutations, salutations to you, the cutter of all knots, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman. (47.127)
"Protect me, guard me; for you indeed [are the Lord] in Maṇipūra—salutations, salutations!
Having prostrated with this rite, one should perform the conclusion of the worship. (47–128)
Furthermore, one should indeed worship there the Great Lord known as Prāsāda;
likewise, one should worship the god Mṛtyuñjaya in Maṇipūra.
Having performed *prāṇāyāma* and the other preliminary rites, one should perform the *śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa*.
Having performed [the rites] together with *pūrṇodarī* and the others, the wise practitioner should perform the *pīṭha-nyāsa*. (47–130)
Having duly assigned the seat (pīṭha), one should perform the ritual assignment of the seer and the rest (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
Vāsudeva is the seer of this [mantra], and Paṅkti is declared to be its meter. (47-131)
With Sadāśiva as the deity, one should perform the finger assignment (aṅgulinyāsa):
"Hāṃ, salutation to the two thumbs," and after that, "Hrīṃ, salutation to the two index fingers";
at the end, the word "namaḥ" is joined with the six long vowels. (47–132)
Having thus performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), one should carry out the procedure according to the rules;
however, for a Śūdra, the work should extend only up to this point, including the fire oblation (homa) and other such rites.
O Lord of Pārvatī, even the world of women would not act in such a way;
if he were truly wise, O God, he would be a god and not a mere mortal. (47.134)

Or even if he belongs to a low caste such as a Cāṇḍāla, an excellent Brāhmaṇa who possesses knowledge should, when engaged in a debate, perform the ritual deposit (nyāsa) with a staff in hand. (47.135)
One should worship with the realization of "I am He" through the state of being absorbed in that [deity] by means of nyāsa;
he alone is the supreme knower, proficient in the Vedas and the Śāstras. (47.136)
For him, the rites of ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, and so forth, are always necessary; of this there is no doubt.
As long as the notion of "I" persists in the body, one remains subject to death. (47.137)

Likewise, the conqueror of death, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, and so forth, [should do so] with the seed-syllable *ha*, endowed with the six long vowels and the nasal bindu. (138)
The best of practitioners should place the pairs of fingers on both hands in successive order, and then install the five forms beginning with Īśāna.
Then, O Mahādeva, the practitioner of mantras, standing upright facing east, south, and north, should place his fingers against one another at the openings [of the senses]. (47–140)
One should diligently install the respective forms with their respective seed-syllables:
on the remaining portion of the two thumbs, *Hau Ā Īśānāya Oṃ Namaḥ*. (47–141)
With the seed-syllable *ha*, endowed with the six long vowels and the bindu, [one worships] Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, and thereafter Vāmadeva. (47.142)
Then, O Supreme Lord, the best of practitioners should sequentially place the Sadyojāta mantra on two fingers, ending with "namaḥ. (47.143)
The wise one should place [the mantras] on the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet;
he should place them in that sequence using the respective fingers.
O Lord, hear now that method for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the five forms;
one should duly place their respective seed-syllables, beginning with Īśāna, according to the prescribed procedure.
A Śūdra may indeed perform this entire network of ritual deposits (nyāsa) up to this point;
beyond that, [he should do so] facing east, south, west, north, and toward himself.
The five kalās of Īśāna are conjoined with the Brahma-Ṛgveda; they consist of five parts and so forth, O Lord, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ. (47–147)
"Īśānaṃ sarvavidyānām," then "oṃ nalinyai," and thereafter "kalāyai namaḥ"; thus indeed everywhere, in this sequence.
Then "Īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām," followed by "tadaṅgaṃ padakam";
then "dayāyai kalāyai namaḥ," and after that, "brahmādipadam. (47-149)
Oṃ, [to] Brahmā, the bestower of desired objects; and at the end, "Salutation to Kalā.
Then one should utter the phrase "May Śiva be mine," followed by the word "Oṃ" and the word "Sāvitrī. (47–150)
"Oṃ *kalāyai* namaḥ," and likewise "Sadāśiva" at the end; and at the end of the mantra, "Oṃ *aṃśumālinyai*," followed by the word "*kalāyai*" as well. (47–151)
The mantra-practitioner, having mastery, should always place the four digits (kalās) of Tatpuruṣa in the directions beginning with the east, according to their sequential order. (152)
Oṃ, [we] know the state of Tatpuruṣa; immediately after that, at the end of the word "śānti," [one should say] "namaḥ" to Kalā as well. (47–153)
Then the word "dhīmahi" follows after "mahādevāya śabdānte";
then the word "oṃ vidyāyai," and at the end of that word, "kalāyai namaḥ. (47–154)
Then one should write the word "pada" for Rudra; after that, "oṃ," then "pratiṣṭhāyai," then "pada," and then "śrī durgāyai kalāyai namaḥ" followed by "pracodayāt. (47-155)
One should utter the words "Oṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti and to Kalā.
Then, one should install the eight Aghora-kalās within the eight locations.
The wise practitioner should place the eight parts of Aghora upon the heart, the neck, the middle of the body, the navel, the back, and likewise upon the chest. (47.157)
One should indeed utter the word "Umā" ending with "Aghorebhyaḥ," then the word "Umāyai," then "Kalāyai namaḥ," and then one should speak the word "Aghorebhyaḥ. (47.158)
Oṃ, at the end of the word *mohāyai*, one should say *kalāyai namaḥ*;
having uttered the word *aghorāya*, one should pronounce the word *kṣamāyai*. (47–159)
Salutation to Kalā, and also to the most terrible ones;
Oṃ, at the end of the word "nidrā," [one says] "salutation to Kalā. (47–160)
In every direction, one should utter "sarva" ending with "oṃ," followed by the word "vyādhaye. Then one should utter "namaḥ" for the *kalā*, and subsequently the word "sarvebhyaḥ. || 47-161 ||
Oṃ mṛtyave, at the end of the word, [say] "kalāyai namaḥ";
likewise, say "namaste'stu" at the end of the word, and then utter the word "oṃ kṣudhāyai. (47–162)
Oṃ, salutation to Kalā; likewise, Oṃ, salutation to her who is in the form of Rudra.
At the end of the word [Kṛṣṇā], one should also say: Oṃ Kṛṣṇāyai Kalāyai Namaḥ. || 47-163 ||
One should assign the thirteen kalās of the god Vāmadeva to these lotus-locations; O Lord, hear the manner in which this is done.
In the secret place, in the middle of the remainder of the testicles, then on the pair of thighs;
likewise on the two knees, on the pair of shanks, and likewise on the two buttocks. (47–165)
The practitioner should sequentially place [the mantras] on the hips and both sides;
first uttering the *praṇava*, the wise one should then recollect the mantra. (47–166)
"Vāmadevāya," ending with the word "śabda," and "namo jyeṣṭhāya," followed by the word "śabda. (47–167)
"Salutation to Rudra at the end of the word 'salutation'; one should utter the word 'salutation.
Then 'salutation to Kāla' at the end, and likewise 'to Kalavikaraṇa. (47.168)
Homage to Balavikaraṇa and to Balapramathana;
Om, homage to Vāmadeva, and thereafter Om to Vajra. 47-169.
"Oṃ, salutation to Kalā; and likewise, salutation to Jyeṣṭha.
At the end of the word [for the deity], [one should say] 'Oṃ, salutation to Rakṣā' and also 'salutation to Kalā. (47–170)
"Oṃ, salutation to Rudra; salutation to Rati and Kalā.
At the end [of the mantra], one should utter the word "Pālinī" after "Salutation to Kāla. (47–171)
At the end of "namaḥ kalāyai," one should utter the word "pālinyai";
having uttered the word "kāmāyai," one should indeed utter "namaḥ kalāyai. (47–172)
At the end of "Vikaraṇāyai," the wise one should utter the Praṇava (Oṃ);
and at the end of the word "Saṃyaminī," he should also say "Kalāyai namaḥ."
The practitioner should utter "Oṃ Śabda," then pronounce the word "Krodhāya," followed by "Kalāyai Namaḥ" and then "Vikalāyai Namaḥ. || 47-174 ||
Oṃ, to Vṛddhi, at the end of the word; "to Kalā, obeisance"—thus also.
Having uttered the word "Oṃ" for Bala, one should utter the word "Sthirā. (47–175)
Next, "Oṃ, obeisance to Kalā," and then "obeisance to Pramathana";
then, at the end of the word "Raudra," "Oṃ, obeisance to Kalā. (47–176)
One should utter "Oṃ" followed by the word "namaḥ" for the subduing of all beings; at the end of the word "bhrāminyai," one should likewise say "namaḥ" for the syllable "kalāyai. (47-177)
Having uttered the syllable *oṃ*, one should recite the word *namaḥ* and then remember the word *mohinyai*. Then [one should say] *namaḥ kalāyai*, and after that, *unmanāya namaḥ*. (47–178)
Oṃ, at the end of the word *jayāyai*, one should utter "namaḥ" to Kalā;
then, O Mahākāla, follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of those digits (*kalā*) of Sadyojāta. (47–179)
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; Om, one should utter the word for prosperity (vṛddhi).
Then, 'Salutation to Kalā,' and indeed 'Salutation to Sadyojāta. (47-180)
"Oṃ vṛddhyai," at the end of the word *pada*, and likewise "namaḥ kalāyai"; then after the word *bhave pada*, one should utter the word "oṃ sadyaḥ. (47–181)
Oṃ, salutation to Abhavā; thereafter, Oṃ, salutation to Medhā; at the end of the word [Medhā], it is said: "Oṃ, salutation to Kalā. (47-182)
Then, worship me with the word "Om"; one should utter the word "pada" for Prajñā;
then "namaḥ" for Kalā; and then one should pronounce the word "om" for Bhava. (47-183)
Having uttered the word "Prabhāyai," [one says] "Kalāyai namaḥ" as well;
then "Tadbhavāya namaḥ," and after that "Oṃ Sudhāyai namaḥ."
Having uttered "Obeisance to Kalā," one should place the eight digits (kalās) of the Lord known as Īśāna;
thereafter, O Lord, the devotee should place the five Ṛg-verses.
O Lord of Yoga, because it destroys desire, the wise man should first utter the Praṇava and then recollect the mantra upon the five fingers in succession. (47-186)
One should utter "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," and immediately thereafter, "Īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ brahmādhipatiḥ. (47.187)
May Brahmā be my presiding deity in the west, and may Śiva Sadāśiva be mine;
having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then [utter] "Tatpuruṣāya. (47.188)
After the word *vidmahe*, one should say *mahādevāya dhīmahi*;
then, at the end of the word *rudraḥ*, one should again recite *pracodayāt*. (47.189)
Having first extracted the Praṇava, the wise one should then recollect the mantra;
then he should utter the words "aghorebhyaḥ," "ghorebhyaḥ," and the word "ghora. (47–190)
To those who are most terrible, at the end, from all sides, and containing all sounds;
and to all those who are at the end, let there be salutation to you, even to those in the form of Rudras.
And for the cessation of all sins, one should [place them] in these eight locations:
on the two sides, on the two hands, on the nose, and on the head. (47.192)
O Great Hero, you who have pierced Maṇipūra with your two arms—I shall explain that method; listen attentively. (47.193)
At the end of "balapramathanāya," one should utter the word "sarvabhūta"; at the end of "damanāya," however, one should pronounce the word "namaḥ. (47.194)
"Salutation to Unmanā," and thereafter one should again utter the Praṇava:
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation indeed to Sadyojāta. (47-195)
"Bhava-bhavenādibhave bhajasva mām tataḥ param bhavodbhavāya śabdānte" — one should joyfully install this mantra at the end of the word "śabda. || 47-196 ||
O Lord, having gathered [the dust] with both fingers while reciting this five-verse hymn,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in these locations according to this sequence.
Then, with joy, one should place these *ṛc*s upon the head, heart, secret place, and feet;
thereafter, O Mahākāla, one should perform the auspicious further ritual placement (*aṅganyāsa*).
I shall explain that method; listen attentively.
First, having uttered the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], then follow the Kāma-bīja.

The syllable *va* conjoined with the enemy (the letter *k*), joined with the moon (the vowel *i*) of the right-hand letter; then the seed-syllable of the moon (*sa*), with the left eye (the vowel *ī*), and ending with fire (*ra*) shaken by the wind (*ya*). (47–200)

Then, one should take only the lunar seed-syllable (OṂ) together with the visarga (Ḥ), followed by the word "to the Omniscient One" (sarvajñāya), and at the end of that, the phrase "salutation to the Heart" (hṛdayāya namaḥ). || 47-201 ||
Having uttered the word *amṛta*, then the word *kāmabīja*, then the word *tejojvālā*, and finally *māline* and *kḷptāya brahmaṇe*, one may dwell [therein]. (47-202)
Then, for the sake of awakening the beginning of the crest-mantra (śikhā), one should utter "Svāhā" at the end,
followed by the word "jvalitaśikhi," and then "Śikhāyai Vaṣaṭ."
One should utter the word for the one with the vajra in her hand, the independent Vajraṇī; then, one should recite the syllable *tāra* for the armor, and thereafter, another seed-syllable.

The letter *na* joined with the *bindu*, the left eye (*i*) with the *bindu*, the word for "bound soul" (*paśu*), the *tāra* mantra (*oṃ*), and the phrase "to the one of infinite power" (*anantaśaktaye*). (47.205)

Having uttered "Astrāya Phaṭ" and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, the king of yogis should fix his mind upon the Maṇipūra [cakra] and meditate upon the supreme consciousness.

Oṃ! I bow to the Lord who is adorned with five faces—the colors of a pearl, yellow, milk, a pearl, and the *japā* flower—each with three eyes; who wears a crown of the moon and possesses the luster of ten million full moons;
and who holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, fire, a lordly serpent, a bell, and a goad.
I worship him who holds a noose that removes fear, his limbs radiant with immeasurable ornaments.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings,
the worshipper should perform the placement of the *arghya* water and the purification by means of his own mantra.
Then one should perform the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha-pūjā), ending with the mantra of the seat as taught in the Śaiva tradition;
having meditated once more and invoked [the deity] with the mudrās of invocation and so forth.
One should perform the complete worship up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers;
having offered the five handfuls of flowers, one should perform the worship of the face.
One should worship Śiva, Varuṇa, and the gods; hear now that sequence: the wise one should worship in the northeast, saying "Salutation to Īśāna. (47.211)
In the east, one should utter the words "Oṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ"; in the south, one should utter the words "Oṃ aghorāya namaḥ. || 47-212 ||
In the north, one should utter "Oṃ vāmaśabdāya devāya namaḥ";
thereafter, in the west, [one should utter] "Praṇava" (Oṃ) followed by "sadyojātāya" indeed.
Having performed the worship ending with "namas," one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One should worship Nivṛtti and the others in the four directions beginning with Īśāna.
At the end of the *praṇava*, one should worship Nivṛtti with "namaḥ" at the end;
likewise, having diligently worshipped Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, and Śānti. (47.215)
Having joined [the name] with the syllable *praṇava* at the beginning and the word ending in the dative case followed by *namaḥ*,
one should perform the offering during the ritual of great worship.
The wise one should visualize an eight-petalled lotus in the center of the ten-petalled one;
right there he should perform worship for the sake of attaining the eightfold yoga. (47.217)
One should worship the Lord of the Gods with scents, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings, using a word in the dative case preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in *namaḥ*.
One should indeed worship Ananteśa as well as Sūkṣmeśa;
having fully worshipped Śivottameśa and likewise Ekanetreśa. || 47-219 ||
In this manner, one should indeed worship Ekarudreśa; thereafter, one should worship Trimūrtīśa, and there, with devotion, one should worship Śrīkaṇṭheśa and Śikhaṇḍin.

On the outer petals of that [lotus], starting from the north and proceeding in order, the deities beginning with Umā are to be worshipped with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. || 47-221 ||
Having worshipped Umādevī, and likewise Caṇḍeśvara, as well as Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and the Bull; 47-222.
One should worship Bhṛṅgarīṭa and the two sons of Skanda outside of that, in sequence;
and one should worship the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, with perfumes and lamps. (47–223)
The supreme practitioner should worship the vajra and the other [emblems] in their proper sequence;
furthermore, he should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings, as well as a drink and water for rinsing the mouth.
With the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should place the one who has the form of Rudra above;
that ritual action, including the dismissal (*visarjana*) and the subsequent offerings, is concluded. (47.225)
Having completed [the rite] according to this procedure, one should conclude the act of worship;
daily, one should perform mental recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), worship (*arcana*), and libation (*tarpaṇa*).
The best of practitioners, devoted to a state of bhakti, should cause [the mantra] to increase;
its *puraścaraṇa* is prescribed as five hundred thousand recitations. (47–227)
Having meditated thus, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times; or else, he should perform a fire oblation with *karavīra* flowers soaked in honey.
Whenever one fails to obtain the ritual materials, one should constantly perform the mental rite;
one should offer oblations amounting to one-tenth of that [mental rite], and perform libations amounting to one-tenth of that [oblation]. (47.229)
A tenth part of that is the consecration (abhiṣeka), and a tenth part of that is the feeding of Brahmins;
in this manner, the sage Nārāyaṇa formerly performed the recitation and the ritual practice.
Having become cool and composed of the nature of all sentient beings, one becomes a king of yogins;
he who performs the sādhana practices shall before long become immortal. (47.231)
At the conclusion of the worship, during the remnants of the worship, and according to the sequence of the middle of the worship,
the best of practitioners should bow down from Varuṇa to Pāpabhūpati.
Oṃ, salutations! Homage to the Supreme Auspicious One; salutations to you, the Creator of the Universe;
salutations to you, Lord of Pārvatī; O Beloved of Umā, homage be to you. || 47-233 ||

Salutations to you, the soul of the universe, who are to be meditated upon, who possess attributes yet are devoid of attributes, who are righteousness itself, who are liberation through knowledge, and who are the yogi of all.
Salutations to you who are the embodiment of Time, the protector of the three worlds, and the destroyer of Goloka; O Caṇḍeśa, let there be salutation unto you!
Salutations to you, the god Sadyojāta; salutations to the wielder of the trident;
salutations again and again to the end-maker, to the beloved, and to pure consciousness.
Salutation to you, the soul of the Kula, the Kaula, O Moon-crested One!
O Lord of Umā, salutation to you; salutation again and again to the Lord of Yogins.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Self, who is all-pervading, worthy of all worship, established in meditation, whose essence is virtue, and who is the life-giver of Pārvatī. 47-238.
And whoever, having recited this hymn, praises the Supreme Lord,
goes to the abode of the Rudra-family and pierces Maṇipūra.
Śaṅkara becomes pleased by the recitation of this hymn;
the Supreme Lord bestows the eternal state of moving through the sky.
Thereafter, O Mahādeva, I shall describe the ritual procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya, by performing which the practitioner becomes identical with the Supreme Brahman. (47.241)
If a human being indeed recites the mantra of Mṛtyuñjaya,
having remained for a hundred times ten million years, he becomes absorbed in Brahman.
He, Sadāśiva, abides in the form of the all-pervading;
I shall explain that manner—listen attentively. (47.243)
