First, I shall describe the worship according to the ritual procedure composed of the essence; one should also perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha and Sapūrṇodarī upon this [deity]. (47.244)
Then, O Lord of Gods, having projected that [light] into the center of the heart by means of the mudrā of one's own fingers, its manifestation is proclaimed.

Having joined [the name] with the syllable *praṇava* at the beginning, the word ending in the dative case, and the word ending in *namaḥ*, the practitioner, devoted to the state of mantra, should perform the placement (*nyāsa*).
Thus, one should worship the Support Power (Ādhāraśakti), followed by Primordial Nature (Prakṛti);
after that, Kūrma, Ananta, the Earth, and the Ocean of Milk.
After that, one should place Śvetadvīpa and the Maṇimaṇḍapa;
then, O Lord, one should place the jeweled altar beneath the Kalpavṛkṣa.
There, within the mandala of the heart-lotus, is a jeweled lion-throne,
[situated] on the right and left shoulder regions, as well as on the left and right thighs.
In the mouth, on the left side, at the navel, and on the right side, [one should worship] with words ending in the dative case, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in *namaḥ*. (47–250)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) everywhere; hear their names, O Lord.
Everything must be done in the proper sequence, and one should not practice a violation of the order.
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty follow immediately after that; then likewise adharma, ignorance, and lack of dispassion. (47.252)
The most excellent practitioner should place the lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya) in sequence as well;
then, once again, the wise one, with a single-pointed mind, should place it within the heart-lotus.
In this way, there is the infinite lotus; likewise, the solar mandala with the syllable *Aṃ*, together with the sixteen-fold self, and likewise the lunar mandala with *Saṃ*.
Then, one should likewise [place] myself, whose nature consists of sixteen digits (kalās), into the fire-mandala, together with that sattva which consists of ten digits. || 47-255 ||

The practitioner of mantras should place the seed-syllable *raṃ* there for rajas, and likewise *taṃ* for tamas; then he should assign *āṃ* to the Self (*ātman*) with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to the Inner Self (*antarātman*). (47.256)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) ending with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self, whose nature is the knowledge of Māyā," O Lord of Gods, you will attain mastery over the mantra.
He who always performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in Maṇipūra, being devoted to meditation and worship, shall attain the perfection of mantra and all perfections. (47.258)
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, as well as Raudrī, Kālī, and those beginning with Kalapadā, together with the one called Vikaraṇī, and likewise Balavikaraṇī; || 47-259 ||
The best of practitioners should place Balapramathinī;
then he should place Sarvabhūtadamanī, and after that, Manonmanī. (47.260)
Above that, O Lord, one should place the words "Oṃ namo bhagavate," and at the end,
one should utter the word "yuktāya" joined with the power (śakti) of the one whose self is all qualities.

At the end of the word *anantāya*, the wise one should place the word for the *yogapīṭha* (the seat of yoga), ending with *namaḥ*; this is the great mantra (*mahāmantra*) which he should install above all else.
Then, O Lord, the practitioner, free from fear, should himself perform the ritual; he should perform the nyāsa of the sages (ṛṣis) and so forth—listen, O Master, to the method for that. (47-263)
Having uttered the word "pada" on the head, one should say "namaḥ to the sage Kahoḍa";
thereafter, O Lord, one should utter the word "mahāviṣṇu-pada" above that.
Having said "Obeisance to the Seer," one should utter the word "Goddess" for the face;
thereafter, one should pronounce the word "obeisance" for the Gāyatrī metre. (47.265)
In the heart, one should likewise utter the word "namaḥ" to the deity Mṛtyuñjaya;
Kahoḍa is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this goddess, and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas). (47–266)
Mahādeva, the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya), is proclaimed as its presiding deity;
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs together with the six long vowels. (47.267)
O Mahākāla, O Lord, listen to that method regarding the syllable *sa*:
at the end, one should sequentially utter the word *namaḥ* together with the thumb and the *sāman*. (47.268)

O Great Lord, one should thus perform the placement (nyāsa) on the fingers of the hands with the mantra consisting of the letter *sa* together with the bindu, endowed with the six long vowels. (47.269)
One should perform the ritual assignment (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs according to the sequence of the Kula Tantra;
thereafter, being devoted to a pure state of being, one should perform meditation.
I salute Him whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire; whose face is smiling; who resides within the two lotuses;
whose hands shine with the [various] mudrās, the noose, the deer, and the rosary; who possesses the luster of the moon;
whose body is bathed in the nectar flowing from ten million moons; and who is radiant with ornaments such as necklaces.
I meditate upon Paśupati, the conqueror of death, who deludes the entire universe with his splendor.
Having meditated thus, the practitioner should worship with mentally conceived offering materials,
having established the *arghya* water with its respective mantra.
The practitioner, knowing the mantras, should worship the seat with its respective mantra up to the end;
then, having meditated again and invoked [the deity] with the root mantra, the knower of mantras [should proceed].
One should indeed worship with water for the feet and other offerings, beautified by perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
having offered five handfuls of flowers, one should worship the retinue.
One should worship [the deities] upon the filaments in the directions of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna;
in the center, in the cardinal directions, and in their midst—that seed-syllable should be uttered there.
At the end, "namaḥ" for the heart, followed by the seed-syllable *sīṃ*;
then, together with "svāhā" for the head, followed by the seed-syllable *su*.
"Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock," and so forth; immediately after that, one should utter the seed-syllable *Saiṃ*.
At the end of the word "to the armor" (*kavacāya*), one should pronounce the Tāra seed-syllable (*Oṃ*). (47–277)

Having first uttered the seed-syllable *soṃ*, and then the phrase "to the three eyes" (*netratrayāya*), followed by the middle word ending in *vauṣaṭ* and so forth, [one should offer] in the four directions thereafter. (47.278)
At the end of the weapon-mantra, one should worship with "phaṭ" at the end of the word;
having worshipped the six limbs, one should worship them further outside of that.
O Lord, one should cause the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, as well as their weapons, such as the thunderbolt,
to be offered incense, lamps, food offerings, drinks, and so forth.
One should perform the instrumental music according to the prescribed rite for the sake of pleasing Mṛtyuñjaya;
having thus completed the ritual action ending with the dismissal (visarjana) according to this procedure.
With the *saṃhāramudrā*, the wise one should bring [the deity] into his heart;
having become pure-hearted, he should drink the water from the feet.
O Lord of Gods, by this alone one shall attain all perfections;
I drink and worship the nectar flowing from the pair of your lotus feet.
O Conqueror of Death, grant me immortality forever; salutations be unto you.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of Mantras," in the Uttara-tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. || 47 ||
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"O beautiful one, I have heard the meritorious *sādhana* of Mahārudra."
And in Maṇipūra, the illumination and the definitive determination of knowledge have been taught. || 48-1 ||
Speak the praise of the Great Praise that brings about the attainment of success spontaneously;
by the mere hearing or recitation of which, even a yoginī comes under one's control. (48-2)
The illustrious Ānandabhairavī said: O Lord of the gods of supreme bliss, O Master, O Sovereign of yogas!
I shall proclaim the hymn of Rudra, which is the essence of essences and higher than the highest.
Having known which, all yogins become piercers of the six cakras; they all become travelers through the sky, desiring the state of the Siddhas and liberation. 48-4.
All the gods who enjoy the pleasures of heaven are equal to Mahādeva, provided they recite this hymn that grants all protection continuously. (48-5)
Those foremost of perfected ones on the surface of the earth go to the abode of Brahmā.
Oṃ, I worship Śambhu, the cause of happiness and liberation;
Rudra, whose limbs are filled with great power,
who is of a fierce nature, and who has the beautiful moon as his crest-jewel.
[He offered] Kāla, Gaṇeśa, and Śaṅkara to Sumukha. || 48-7 ||
The conqueror of death, the supreme protector of life,
Śiva, the auspicious embodiment of the Supreme Brahman,
possessing a luster like ten million moons.
I worship him who is seated in the midst of the two lotuses. || 48-8 ||
The embodiment of all, the root of the destruction of desire— that one with the moon upon his crest, who dwells in Maṇipūra,
four-armed and enriched by the mudrā of primordial wisdom.
A deer-eyed noose, pervaded by the thread of the qualities. || 48-9 ||
I worship Rudra, who consists of earth, fire, ten million moons, wind, the lord of waters, and the supreme ether; he who has entered the *kulālākinī*.
The union of all limbs, which bestows victory and is the lord of the gods.
The seed (śukra), the ancient and greatly formidable method,
whose essence is the vital breath (prāṇa), the root of destroying disease,
the embodiment of sacrifice, the dispeller of desire, and the Guru.
I worship Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, the Beneficent One.
The supreme and ultimate source of the Vedas and Agamas, from which they arise— the auspicious and beneficial, both transcendent and immanent,
the ender of time, the eternal abode of Brahmā.
I worship Śambhu, who is established in the form of the sky and other elements.
The Śiva-āgama consists of sound, is all-pervading, and is like the sun; it has the form of a blazing, fierce fire,
is a planet situated within the planets, bestows knowledge, and is formidable.
I worship Śambhu, Hara, the Lord of Prakṛti. || 48-13 ||
The maker of shade, the performer of yoga, the lord of happiness;
the intoxicated one, enriched by the festival of the great intoxicated lineage;
the lord of yoga, the treasury of the arts of yoga, the Ordainer.
I worship the one who proclaims the ritual injunctions. || 48-14 ||
I worship the beloved one, adorned with a pure garment embellished by a mountain of gold,
whose very root is the granting of boons and fearlessness,
and who is beautified by a forest garland.
The lineage which wears a pure garland of lotuses reaching down to their roots. || 48-15 ||
I worship Śiva— the ancient one, the Lord of Puruṣas, the Guru— who manifests both false fear and joy;
who is the ocean of devotion and the possessor of the art of love.
And Girīśvara, whose lotus-feet are beautiful. || 48-16 ||
The ocean of meditation, possessing the profound yoga of wisdom;
the abode of fortune, equal to fortune itself, and endowed with auspicious marks;
bearing the trident as a weapon, his limbs adorned with the trident.
I worship the illustrious Śaṅkara, whose action bears the fruit of liberation.
Homage, homage to the hosts of Rudras,
likewise to the conquerors of death, to those who move through the families,
to the lords of power, and to Vijaya and the others for the sake of prosperity.
Salutations, salutations to you, the auspicious and blessed one! || 48-18 ||
The external trident is of an excellent and subtle nature;
it has wide eyes and reaches toward the slender waist;
it is the seed for the destruction of great calamities and suffering.
I worship that which makes wisdom and compassion beautiful. || 48-19 ||
The destroyer of cities, whose body is complete, the Guru, the primordial enemy of Smara, the path of his own reasoning,
the beginningless God who destroys the defects in heaven.
I worship the means for attaining merit through the five syllables. || 48-20 ||

Śiva, whose body is auspicious and whose nature is existence, who is the embodiment of being, who is engaged in the yoga of the activity of abiding, who holds a lotus with its face turned toward the quarters of space in his hand— [I bow to him].
I worship the lion-faced one, who has the color of the sun.
Consisting of illusion, as delicate as a garland of lotuses,
pervading the quarters, the wielder of the staff, the Lord of Hari,
possessing three sides and the nature of the three-syllable seed-mantra.
I worship the root of the three lotuses, which possesses the three qualities. || 48-22 ||
The Vidyādhara, whose function is the performance of the Vedas,
who has attained satisfaction through the sound of the Nīti,
and who is the eternal root of the fruits and other benefits of the four aims of life (caturvarga).
I bow to the Yoga-sūtra, the beginning of the Vedas.
To the one who is to be known through the Vedānta, who is learned in the Kula scriptures, who consists of ritual action, who bestows the yoga of his own dharma,
the Lord of devotion, who is devoted to devotion, the Supreme One;
I worship Bhakta, who bestows great intelligence. || 48-24 ||
The state of having gone and not yet gone, the state of being traversed and not yet traversed;
adorned with the ornament of the ever-shining tip of the digit [of the moon];
consisting of existence and composed of existence; pleasure and pain.
I worship Bharga, whose radiance is like that of the first glow of dawn. || 48-25 ||
The nature of the *bindu* is the proponent of the supreme discourse;
it is like ten thousand midday suns, ever-new,
the bestower of prosperity, and the giver of one's own gift.
I bow down to that God whose nature is generosity.

The destroyer of Kumbha, the slayer of the enemy Nikumbha, the foe of the Daityas, the Lord, the husband of the beloved of his lineage, endowed with affection, the object of meditation, whose nature is inconceivable.
I worship Prabhākarāhlāda. || 48-27 ||
Salutations to the Lord, the source of the three forms, the victorious Śambhu, who assumes a body for the welfare of the world and destroys the obstacles born of fear.
Homage, homage to the one who bears the body of the universe! || 48-28 ||

Salutations to the one who is the fruit of austerity, who assumes a natural form, whose self consists of the qualities, who grants perfection, the perfected yogi; salutations to the renowned one, who is overcome with compassion.
For the purpose of increasing your enthusiasm for the fruit of your desires. || 48-29 ||
I bow to the auspicious, immortal, and great one, who takes refuge in perfect yoga;
who causes the threefold creation to flourish through the lotus-like hands of the mountain-bearer (Śiva);
who destroys untimely death; who is worshipped by Death himself; and who is the Lord of all beings.
I worship and meditate upon Gaṇapati, who is to be served according to the prescribed rite. || 48-30 ||
The wise sage, devoted to yoga, should recite this hymn daily, repeatedly contemplating the Teacher, the Lord of the World. (48.31)
If one who is established in the wind at Maṇipūra should constantly recite this hymn, he becomes liberated while living and, at the end of the body, shall attain supreme Nirvāṇa. (48.32)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Rudra Mṛtyuñjaya," in the *Rudrayāmala*, the Northern Tantra (*Uttaratantra*), which illuminates the Great Tantra (*Mahātantroddīpana*). 48.
Then the forty-ninth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
For the purpose of piercing the six cakras and for the complete attainment of all siddhis, [this is taught].
I shall proclaim the hymn of praise to the goddess Lākinī, which is extremely difficult to obtain.
O Lord, this hymn titled *Lākinīpriya*, which is endowed with the essence of ritual action, brings supreme satisfaction to the ascetic through its recitation. (49-2)

Of this *Śrīlākinī-stotra*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Mahāviṣṇukahoḍa, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Gāyatrī, the deity (*devatā*) is Lākinī Sarasvatī— the Great Siddhi-granting Mṛtyuñjaya-Mahārudra— and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation for the piercing of the Maṇipūra-cakra.
Oṃ! I bow to you—the embodiment of the seed-syllable, the primordial mother, the golden-hued, the noble, the victorious, the bestower of wisdom;

the destroyer of millions of offenses committed by the wretched; the jewel of consciousness for yogis; the first of all, the passionate one, the sole ground and cause of the fragrance of the multitude of virtues.
I joyfully salute Lākinī, the bestower of boons, whose curiosity is fixed upon the end of existence. 49-3 ||
She who has attained the non-dual perfection through the worship of Heramba; she whose radiance is like ten million suns;
she who possesses form and is blazing with rays; she who consists of bliss and whose life-breath is the sound of the Vedas;
she whose characteristics are reddened by anger; she who is most swift in her resolve and intent upon the destruction of doubt.
Having thus acted, may the beautiful Śrīlākinī and Kaṅkinī protect [us]. || 49-4 ||

Adorned with armlets, pure necklaces, and garlands, beautiful, seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), she remains as the consort of the Lord of Rudras; possessing a face like a stainless coral and wearing a garland of blue lotuses,
she is the supreme mother of the practitioners of yoga, the virtuous one who dwells in the highest state, and is enveloped by the essence of honey-wine.
O Śrīdhara, conqueror of death, you who are full of compassion, protect me who have fallen into the power of Yama.
Desiring the number of her family, she brings destruction; she is compassionate toward enemies, power, and the like.
She removes the extreme suffering of her devotees; moon-faced, she has a vulva-like face and is lustful.
She is the abode of desire, yet she swiftly bestows misfortune upon the hundredfold defects of those who lack desire.
Grant me the state of liberation while living, and bring about the destruction of the enemy of creation in battle.

You are worshipped by the five-faced one (Śiva); you are the consumer; you are the path of the knowledge of children; you are truth; among poetic compositions, you are the eloquence of speech; you are the giver of absolute bliss;
you possess a form as red as lac; you are the lowest; you are the destroyer of the linga.
You are the direct bestower of immortality, you are ageless; may you, Lākinī, protect me! (49.7)
Adorned with the sovereignty of various auspicious dharmas, the foundation of refined awakening,

the immovable image residing in the *liṅga*— may that auspicious goddess, as she is being conveyed to her new home, grant me, O Rudranātha, a union upon the *liṅga* that pierces through the wrong path.
"O Goddess, resplendent like ten million moons, quickly have a sword for liberation fashioned! (49.8)
May Lakṣmī— the moonlight resting upon the digit of the moon, the equal splendor of sound,
the illusion that dispels delusion through compassion, the enchanting activity of Kṛṣṇa,
and the jewel whose body is dark blue— protect me always from before.
Śrīvidyā is the bestower of fear; you too are she who arises from the root of my navel.

O Gaurī, you alone are the Mother—the measure (mātrā), the seal (mudrā), the meditation (manana), and the abode; the garlanded one (mālinī), the mantra, and the lore (vidyā); the sovereign of the universe (viśveśānī), devoid of sleep, and situated amidst cold, wind, and heat; both truth and untruth, and dwelling within speech and worldly existence.
Protect your life; take refuge in the Infinite One, the source of the first rays of light. 49-10.
She is both accomplished and unaccomplished, possessing the digits of the moon and sun, and abiding solely within the lotus.
She is the bliss of stability, shining from the center of the lotus of the unmoving eye.
She is eternally the one who provides the path for those with faith, the agent, and the non-seizer of desires.
I do not offer this hymn; worship, worship, I worship You, the infinite one, within Your own essential nature.
Yellow and non-yellow, moving with the speed of the wind, she is the yoga of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *yoga*.
She is both time and non-time, the digit of the multitude of *kalās*, partless, and the embodiment of knowledge.
She is black bliss, the cavern of passion, squinting-eyed, or the consort of Śaṅkara.
I shall describe you as the illustrious Gātrī, the white lotus at the root of the navel. || 49-12 ||
White, with hundreds of white and reddish rays, you are the perfection of meditative realization and knowledge;
you are both pleased and displeased, supremely profound, and the beautiful face of the dawn.
You are that Vidyā, the best among those wise in ritual, attainable through the knowledge of dhāraṇā.
May Nīradā, who is both beautiful and unattractive, and who is intent on dalliance, protect the navel. 49-13.
She who wears a garland of withered creepers, who carries the silent boat;
she who transcends the field and the non-field, who has entered the state beyond others, and who illuminates both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
she whose eyes are directed by the command of Kaula and Akaula, who is the scorcher and is intoxicated by the wind.
Upon the navel of the Lord of Wealth, situated at the center of the earth, [she is] both bewildered and not bewildered.
You are the female swan (*haṃsī*), whose feet rest upon the lion-throne; you are the subtle science of the wheel (*cakravidyā*).
You are Śrīvidyā, the beautiful one moving through the nine [circles], red in color, with an auspicious mind, established in the center of the wheel atop a golden lotus.
All castes, the retinue, the gift, and the lotus are the protection. 49-15.
Her limbs adorned by the great worship of hosts of kings, she whose body is the bliss of Brahman; Śrī Śrīvidyā, possessing all splendor, is to be meditated upon by the great Indras—
seated upon her primary lion-throne in a palace of jewels at the abode of the Siddhas.
And protect me at the root of the navel upon a lotus with eight joined petals. 49-16.

May the sixteen-fold state of Bhairava, which possesses the twofold glory of yogic knowledge and illuminates the science of the Vedas, joyfully abide within my eightfold limbs. O Candrolikā, you are the remover of the fear of worldly existence and the destroyer of grief and suffering.
O Lord, protect him from that sun which rises in the lotus of non-existence.

O you who have been instructed, you who are devoid of passion, O cool one on the Cool Mountain; you who are the manifest embodiment of the words of the multitude of others, full as the full moon at the festival;
protect us, O lioness, with a flood of lightning that consists of equal bliss.
O Goddess, you are she; bestow coolness within the house of auspicious jewels.
O Mother, you who sever all objects of desire for the Chandogas, the mother of the letters, possessing the luster of vermilion rays, worshipped by the cowherds, the daughter of the mountain—
protect my own jewel-like abode; O subtle Bhavānī!
Āṅgirā, who bestows victory upon those dwelling in the forest stage of life, and Annapūrṇā. || 49-19 ||
O Mother Mātaṅgī, you who grant the bliss of your limbs through the radiance of the moon, you who possess long hair and expansive form; O daughter of the world, fierce toward the wicked,
you whose splendor always shines with blood-red speech amidst the web of moonlight.
O Rudra, protect my body, which possesses the form of Hari and Hara, at the base of the navel.
She who is named Vāṇī composes speech while abiding in the description of beauty;
she dwells within the state of existence, possessing a moving form, and is the delight of the union of light.
Pervasive through bodies whose nature is the bliss of awakening, she is intoxicated with wisdom.
O Mother, you are my jeweled pavilion; protect me with the knowledge of all limbs.
O Goddess Śivā, Sovereign of the Universe, you are Knowledge, adorned with a garland of skulls and your body anointed with sandalwood paste; you are the inexhaustible and unfailing form,
the consort of Śambhu, residing within the matted locks of Śiva, bestowing liberation upon those established in the mind.
Make the mind pure, O Cutter, you who cut through the objects of the senses.
O Krodhavidyā, grant me the boon of fearlessness within the palace of my kula which is composed of jewels and shines with the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes;
protect the full enjoyment of all happiness, which is the very form of my life-force.
O Supreme Mistress, [save] me, who am helpless and clinging to the soles of Your feet.

For the sake of the profound mystery of the world, these emanations of the body remain apart from the Creator, the sacrifice, and the Lord of the gods; they constitute the threefold creation beginning with humanity.
Within the lotus of my jewel-clan, there is that which is designated as the eternal form.
Truly, at that time, the essence of the hymns triumphs. || 49-24 ||
O Lākinī, daughter of the gods, let it be so!
Compose a manual of human conduct according to the method of perfected mantras. Carry away, carry away the nature of worldly existence; protect me in the abode of the moon.
O Śaṅkarī, bring about the destruction of this hard-heartedness.
In the midst of the forest near a lotus grove, in a most secret place,
having transformed the destruction of both the object and the subject within the Kaulika system,
and having established the primary cause upon the jeweled pedestal of your own abode—
O Hara, O beloved of Hara, you [must] remove the six defects and dispute.

In this terrible, dense darkness, you are the one who bestows the vision of my own lineage; when you are gracious, you stand as the wish-fulfilling tree for all desires, the bestower of well-being here, and the one whose portion of inheritance is indivisible. You are Kālī, established in Nandinī; you are Māghakā, situated within the vessel of policy and compassion.
The fierce Lākinī, who removes fear with her glance directed toward the feet of Hara, resides in the navel. 49-27.
The wise one, a knower of yoga who is without support, having attained great bliss, being a hero, should recite this hymn for the sake of power and for the sake of immortality. (49.28)
Enjoyment and liberation are in his hand; he becomes a king among yogis in this world, and in the next, the Great Goddess goes to his lotus feet—of this there is no doubt. (49-29)
Bestowing long life in this world and granting all desires, she who resides in Maṇipūra proceeds by the grace of the Kula path. (49.30)

The deity residing in the Maṇipūra, absorbed in that state which is the station on the path of the Kula, the place of dissolution, and the foot of the Sovereign of the Universe, certainly beholds it. (49-31)
At the conclusion of the worship, one devoted to a spirit of devotion should recite the hymn;
indeed, by the grace of the Kula path, one shall quickly become a yogi. (49.32)
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Praise of Lākinī," in the Uttara-tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. 49.
Then the fiftieth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said: "O Lord, O Beloved, I shall proclaim the supreme means for attaining perfection."
By which mere means of accomplishment, a person certainly becomes a yogin. (50.1)
The threefold hero is said to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling.
In that very context, the meeting place is also threefold: the upper world, the netherworld, and the surface of the earth.
O Lord, there are seven realms above, likewise seven on the surface of the earth, and seven indeed in the netherworlds; thus, the number is twenty-one.
In the midst of that, there are three types of dispositions: the divine, the heroic, and the animal.
The gods abide in heaven, and the heroes abide on the surface of the earth.
O Lord, there are animals in Pātāla one after another;
everywhere, the qualities of sattva, rajas, tamas, and so forth, are concealed by the three guṇas. (50.5)
At that time, all those devoted to Viṣṇu possessed the quality of sattva in heaven;
they were all firm in heaven, while on earth the quality of rajas prevailed.
All were devoted to the service of Brahman and were indeed knowers of Brahman;
in Pātāla, they were devoted to the service of Śiva and were truly of the nature of Śiva.
Having attained the state of a bound soul and the vision of darkness through the quality of tamas, and then having abandoned that knowledge, the practitioner becomes a hero (vīra). (50.8)
Having attained the vision of knowledge in the state of a hero and having completed the realization of Brahman,
one quickly becomes a deity within a being of pure disposition.
Becoming firm, Mahādeva indeed becomes so in due course;
the accomplishment of moving through the sky certainly comes about gradually. (50.10)
Indeed, below the mūlādhāra dwell those who reside in the depths of Pātāla;
above that, in the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka), dwell those who inhabit the surface of the earth and other realms. || 50-11 ||
Above that is the abode of beings, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which is indeed the deity;
it is the illumination of the Vidhividya and the prosperity of Varadeva.
Above that, O Mahādeva, is the supreme abode, Maṇipūra, which possesses all forms, is the support of all knowledge, and is enchanting. (50.13)
The wheel consisting of the power of Rudra is the mandala of the Śrīvidyā wheel;
it is Lākinī, the supreme Māyā, served by Mahārudra. (50.14)
And for the illumination of Maṇipūra, the power of Rudra shines forth;
it consists of the bliss of all knowledge and is the source of all types of supernatural attainments. (50.15)
The earring consists of a subtle sound and is the means for attaining knowledge;
by the mere practice of it, the yogi becomes Bhairava. (50.16)
In this very manner, through service, one becomes a lord of the great siddhis;
and all beings, including men upon the surface of the earth, exist like the ground of that [foundation]. (50.17)
For the sake of illuminating their knowledge, the state of a hero (vīrabhāva) has been revealed;
having joyfully attained the state of a hero, one shall gradually become a deity. (50.18)
I shall now declare the determination of the time at which a human being attains the perfection of heroic state and so forth; through the hero, one attains divinity. (50.19)
Within one month, there is success in attracting women; within one month, one becomes a lord of speech; through practice for three months, one becomes beloved by the gods. (50.20)
Thus, in the fourth month, he becomes the domain of the Guardians of the Quarters;
in the fifth, he becomes the Five-Arrowed One (Kāmadeva); and in the sixth, he is Rudra—of this there is no doubt.
Relying upon the state of a hero (vīrabhāva), one should always take recourse to yoga;
O Lord of Gods, the captivating state of a hero is dependent upon the bound soul (paśu). (50.22)
Divine state is dependent upon the Hero; through the divine [rite] of propitiating Rudra, by the mere sight of Rudra, one will certainly become liberated while living. (50.23)

Having attained the state of liberation while living, what on this earth cannot be accomplished? Yet, a man who directs his mind [toward worldly objects] remains dependent upon the nature of a beast. (50.24)
Having first resorted to the state of a hero (vīrabhāva), one should take recourse to yoga;
and always practicing yoga, one should be devoted to the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).

The perfection of yoga, the perfection of knowledge, and thereafter the perfection of liberation—if those bound by ignorance, deluded by the scriptures, desire liberation here [in this world]. (50.26)
Relying on the state of a hero (vīrabhāva) through correct knowledge, one should attain yoga;
and at the very beginning of the practice of yoga, one should purify the body. (50.27)
At the outset, the five immortals (pañcāmara) should be established as independent of all other ritual activities;
by relying solely upon yoga, one should always become the five immortals. (50.28)
O Mahākāla, there are two types known as the five immortals:
Netī, Dantī, Dhautī, Neulī, and Kṣālana. (50-29)
O Supreme Lord, thus has this single method been described: Dantī, Netī, Dhautī, and Neulī, according to the sequence of cleansing. (50.30)
Or, one should always act in this manner for the sake of the perfection and abundance of yoga;
at the time of the practice of the five nectars and so forth, one should perform one's own ritual action.
The fifth [ingredient] to be taken is an herb for the successful accomplishment of the fivefold yoga:
the bilva leaf, the jayā leaf, and the dark tulasī leaf. (50.32)
Likewise, with the leaf of nirguṇḍī and the juice of the dūrvā knot—O Śaṅkara, listen as I shall state the names of these natural substances. (50.33)
The *amarā* is the *bilva* leaf; the *cāmarā* is a petal of the *vijayā*;
the *amaralatā* is the knotted *dūrvā*; and the *nirguṇḍī* is the *cāmareśvarī*. (50.34)
The immortal Śyāma-tulasī and the five types of immortals produced from trees have been described for the sake of attaining success in yoga; hear now their measurements in due order.
One should consume Vijayā leaves measuring five *tolakas*, and for other substances, one *tolaka* each, after first performing the purification (*saṃśodhana*). (50.36)
By merely consuming this, one shall become victorious in the fivefold yoga.
Furthermore, O Mahākāla, I shall explain their mantra according to the true principle. (50.37)
One should consume the entire *cāmara* yoga with this mantra:
having first extracted the two syllables *tāt*, one should then follow them with the pair of *ṛ* sounds. (50.38)
O Amṛtamukhī, that [syllable] is joined with the visarga and the bindu; after that is the pair "maraṇa" and "māraya," and beyond that is "yogasiddhi. (50.39)
At the end of the word "dehi dehi," one should place the supreme mantra ending in "svāhā.
Having uprooted [the plant] with this mantra and consecrated it, one should consume it. (50.40)
One should apply the mantra of this section right there;
O Bhairava, listen as I shall speak the King of Mantras of Nirguṇḍī.
After that, the three seed-syllables of Kāma, and likewise the three seed-syllables of Kālī;
then, after that, the entire yoga and the two means of accomplishment (sādhana).
Then, having offered the power of immortality within me, one should perform the extraction and consumption with the mantra ending in *svāhā*. (50.43)

One should take hold of a bilva leaf; hear that mantra, O Bhairava: first the seed-syllable of modesty (hrīṃ), then the seed-syllable of desire (klīṃ), and after that the seed-syllable of power (śrīṃ). (50.44)
Thereafter, O Gaurasundarī, one should utter the seed-syllable of Brahmā:
"Establish me in the Great Yoga; protect both of us. (50.45)
One should utter the mantra ending with *svāhā*, preceded by the name of Śaṅkara, after having purified and plucked a Tulasī leaf with this mantra. (50.46)
O Mahāmāyā, who brings about the liberation of Viṣṇu and accomplishes the yoga of Śiva; thereafter, effect the severing of illusion and cause the two-fold cycle of worldly existence to perish.
"Grant immortality, grant it, svāhā," beginning with the *praṇava*.
Listen now to the fourfold purification of the leaves of the auspicious *vijayā* plant. (50.48)
Having purified the four castes, both Kulā and Akula, by means of their own respective mantras, I shall explain that sequence; listen attentively.
Having first uttered the *praṇava* (oṃ), then the seed-syllable of the Goddess, and having extracted the mantra ending with *svāhā*, the wise one should purify it and consume it. (50–50)
Having unified them, O Mahādeva, one should consecrate it with this mantra: "Amṛte," followed by the word "amṛta," and then the word "tadbhave. (50–51)
Having sequentially extracted the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Manmatha, and the two seed-syllables of Lajjā, [one should proceed] in order, O Vijayā Jñānasundarī. (50–52)
O bestower of yoga and liberation, O purifier who subsequently cleanses the body; thereafter, grant me the accomplishment of the posterior body, grant it, after that! (50–53)
The showers of nectar resound; thereafter is that nectar.
Afterwards, one should draw forth the pair [of syllables] "dehi" and "analapire," saying: "Grant success! (50–54).
Having purified it with this mantra, one should consume it with careful attention;
one must not make it deficient or excessive, and should practice it gradually. (50–55)
One should eat only as much as is necessary and not exceed that measure; having thus determined one's meal, one should then practice the drinking of milk. (50–56)
Listen, O Lord of Life, O Sovereign Śaṅkara, to that method:
having purified the *marīca* seed, one should perform the purification with milk. (50–57)
I shall describe that twofold method of this kind;
having meditated again and again upon the Guru at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree of desire. (50–58)
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with substances for mental offerings,
one should purify half a *tolaka* of black pepper with this mantra.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and likewise the three seed-syllables of the Earth,
[place them] thereafter, O Marīcakulasundarī, in the most terrible of the terrible.
"O Blue One, become blue within my body and purify this physical form. This mantra, ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā), is thus proclaimed; after that follows the purification of the milk.
Having first eaten black pepper, the drinking of milk bestows great strength;
having chewed black pepper, the drinking of milk bestows great strength. (50–62)
Having extracted the seed-syllable *kṛṣṇa*, then the mantra of Kāmeśvarī,
followed by two *śiva* seed-syllables, and finally *kṛṣṇagovasavāsinī*.
O you who fulfill my desires, having extracted the form of Yoga;
thereafter, O Sovereign of the perfections of Yoga, O Dweller in the sacred field! (50–64)

"Śarīraṃ vasamante ca cālayadvayameva ca | vighnān vāraya-yugmaṃ tu svāhānto 'yaṃ mahāmanuḥ ||" (50–65) This great mantra ends with *svāhā* and consists of: "śarīraṃ vasamante ca," followed by the pair "cālaya," and the pair "vighnān vāraya."
Having recited it twelve times, or else five times,
or joyfully three times, this procedure is prescribed for purification in all cases.
If one should drink the milk of two-footed creatures, one attains the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva);
if it is the milk of only [one-footed] creatures, then fourteen prasthas [are required]. 50–67.
Eating light food, possessing great wisdom, and knowing detachment from the fifth [tattva] and the others,
one should apply the mind to Maṇipūra and become immortal.
The fourfold aims of human life (*caturvarga*) are in the hand of him who takes refuge in the pedestal of this jewel.
Śrī Ānandabhairava said:
[This is] for the purpose of piercing the Maṇipūra [cakra] and for the perfect accomplishment of the yoga of the mind. (50–69)
For the sake of attaining the great yogas such as Khecarī and for the attainment of all perfections,
[this occurs] through the vision of the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya and the Śakti of Rudra.
Likewise, for the sake of stabilizing the seat and for mastery over the net of time,
there are the seed-syllables of the thousand names, numbering one hundred and eight.
O lady of excellent hips, if you have affection for me, please tell me the hymn to Mṛtyuñjaya Lākinī, which consists of the *makārakūṭa* syllables.
O Supreme Goddess, may my body be protected by the power of knowledge. || 50-73 ||

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Classification of Gems," in the section on Accomplished Mantras within the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, the Northern Tantra, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 50.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
Now, for the purpose of [explaining] the piercing [of the centers], I shall speak of the six lotuses.
Of the god Mahārudra and of the illustrious Śrīmṛtyuñjaya. || 51-1 ||
This auspicious *Sahasranāma*, accompanied by Lākinī and Śakti, pervaded by one hundred and eight [names], is secret; may it lead to the attainment of your goals. (51-2)
O supreme bliss, O lord of yogis, O moon-crested one, listen to the auspicious names after having retained them, recited them, or heard them. (51.3)
In order to bring you joy, to attain all perfections,
and for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of the jewel-yoga, listen attentively.

For this auspicious *Aṣṭottarasahasranāma* (The Thousand and Eight Names), Kahoḍa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), and Mahārudra, Mṛtyuñjaya, Lākinī, and Sarasvatī are the deities (*devatā*).
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining the yoga-siddhi of the Śacī-pīṭha that fulfills all desires.
Oṃ, Mṛtyuñjaya, Rudra, and the others; Lākinī, and the others; Sarasvatī!
The conqueror of death, the greatly fierce one, the Sarasvatī of Mahārudra. || 51-5 ||
The Great Fierce One, the Remover of Death, adorned with a great jewel;
the Great God, the Great-Faced One, the Great Illusion, the Great Sovereign Goddess. 51–6.
Mahāvīra, Mahākāla, and Mahācaṇḍeśvarī as his daughter-in-law;
Mahāvāta, Mahābheda, and the greatly distressed Vīrabhadra. (51.7)
Mahācaṇḍeśvara is the Fish (Mīna), the illuminator of Maṇipūra;
he is the Great Drunkard, the Great Night, and she who is seated upon the seat of the Great Hero.
The Illusionist, the Slayer of Māra, Mātaṅgī, Maṅgaleśvarī,
the Remover of Death, the Best of Sages, the Enchanter of the Mind, and the Swift as Thought.
Seated within the mandala, she has a dark-blue body; she is worthy of honor, wearing a crown that deludes;
she possesses the appearance of one intoxicated, great arrows, great strength, and is the great abode.
The destroyer, the remover, the great pestilence, she whose gait is intoxicated by wine;
the refuge of great illusion, the silent one, the great illusion, the beloved of the Maruts.
Mudrāśī is fond of wine, and through mental yoga she brings about great prosperity;
Māṃsāśī eats meat, and Mīnabhakṣī is the deluding one who has the clouds as her vehicle.
She who delights in the breaking of pride, she who is worthy of honor, she who is highly honored, she of great strength;
she who holds the great arrow, she who is preeminent, she who is the great knowledge, she who is most exalted.
The bearer of the great trident, Ananta, the one of great strength, the one of noble lineage;
the dweller on the Malaya mountain, the intellect, and the one fond of the garland-throne. || 51-14 ||
The Lord of Māyā, Mahārudra; she who causes the destruction of the Maruts;
the bearer of garlands; the wearer of a conch-garland; Mañjarī; the eater of flesh. || 51-15 ||
Endowed with the great marks, she whose characteristics are the great marks;
possessed of great wisdom, possessed of great speed; the wielder of the mace, she who is fond of the mace.
Mahokhya, the Lord of Mālinī, the dweller on Mount Mandara, the one residing within the hearts of the silent ones, the breaker of pride, and the high-minded woman.
The Lord of Great Knowledge is the Middle One; the Mountain-Dweller resides in the center.
She whose essence is wine is the Remover of Sloth; she who is neither intoxication nor the seat of passion.
He who dwells in Madana, the field of intoxication; she who resides on the great snowy mountain.
He who is great, the Great-Souled One, the auspicious one; she who bears the great auspiciousness. || 51-19 ||

She possesses a body both great and humble, and she is the enchanting power born from that; she is the mistress of the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), the deluder, and the dweller within the Great Deluder (mahāmoha).
The stainless self of the great-minded dwells amidst impurity;
she stands upon the back of an intoxicated elephant and moves with the gait of an intoxicated elephant.
Makara is the joy of the winds; Mākarī is honored by deer;
she is worshiped with jewels, has the form of the mind, and partakes of fat and flesh. (51.22)

She who possesses great desire, she who is greatly courageous, she who intoxicates the great buffalo-demon; she who dwells within the intellect of the buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura, and she who is the destroyer of the buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura. || 51-23 ||
She who dwells upon the buffalo, she who dwells upon Maheśa, the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
she who is the lord of honey, the bee, and the bestower of success in honey, meat, and other things.
She is the one worshipped by Mahābhairava and she who worships Mahābhairava;
she possesses great luster, is the bliss of her beloved, and is the immortal one established in great luster.
Wearing a garland of ten million [beads], she is garlanded; adorned with a circlet of shaven heads, she is devoted to the knowledge of the mandala and dwells within the circle of jewels. || 51-26 ||
Abiding in the great majesty of wrath, you are the Sarasvatī of false faults;
dwelling on Mount Meru, your abode is Meru, O you who possess the form of Menakā’s younger sister.
Seated upon the great mountain Meru, she who deludes with her splendor, the bearer of clouds;
Mañjughoṣa, Mañjunātha, and she who wields the mallet of delusion. (51.28)
Seated upon the jewel-throne in the generative organ, she is the primordial form, captivating to the mind;
she is the essence of auspiciousness, the great yoginī, born from the flow of the intoxicated elephant.
She who abides in the intellect, whose mind is the ego, whose measure is the mind, she who is the Great Beyond-mind (Mahonmanī);
she who removes dull-wittedness, who is Death, the slayer of Death, and the beloved of the mind.
The great devotee, the greatly empowered one, the great power intoxicated with passion;
the light of Maṇipūra and the piercer of Maṇipūra.
She whose abode is the peak-syllable *makāra*, she who is pride itself yet captivating the mind with pride;
she whose syllable is *māk*, she who is garlanded with the seed-syllables of the *Mātṛkā*.
Possessing great splendor and great radiance, she is wrathful yet fond of honey;
born from honey and meat, she delights in honey and meat.
Delighting in the bliss of sexual union, she is enchanted by talk of sexual union;
she is fully satisfied by love for Murāri and is served by the hand of Murāri.
With her limbs smeared with garlands and sandalwood paste, wearing a wreath, and subsisting on mantras,
she is the mantra-practitioner situated within the net of mantras, bestowing the accomplishment of mantras upon those who recite them.
She who bestows consciousness upon the mantra, she who is fond of the perfection of mantra,
she who is devoted to great sacred fords, she who is like a ram, and she who is seated upon the great lion-throne.
Arisen from the Great Wrath, she bestows great intelligence;
devoid of the knowledge of death, she is the destroyer of great death. || 51-37 ||
The slayer arisen from death, endowed with Mahāmudrā, she who joyfully brings great delight;
she is Māra, the abode of Māra, and the destroyer of Māra.
The destroyer of the great cause, the remover; she who dwells in the great city;
the skull-bearer of the great Kaulika; and the warder-off of the great Daityas.
She possesses the rays of ten million suns; she is the destroyer of death and resides within death.
She is the great mountain, the stainless one, the wielder of *māyā*, and the source of the qualities of Mahākāla.
Mahājaya, Mahārudra, Mahārudrāruṇākarā, Manovarṇa, Mṛjumākhya, Mudrā, and Taruṇarūpiṇī. (51.41)
Wearing a garland of severed heads, she is to be honored; she is the purifier of the flowers of the sacrifice.
Abiding in a state of auspicious love, she is immovable and possesses the radiance of a great lightning flash.

She who bears the mudrās, who is steadfast in the Mata, who manifests the various divisions of the Mata, who is a knower of the Mahāpurāṇa, and who is the immortal one among the great Paurāṇikas. (51.43)
She is the knowledge of silence, the great knowledge, the dweller in great wealth;
she is Maghavatī, situated in the middle of Māgha, possessing a great army, and the great serpent.
She who bears great hoods, whose measure is the Mātṛkā, who dwells within the mantra;
she who is rich in the granting of great sovereignty, and whose vehicle is the one that carries Mount Meru.
She is great joy, the great friend, and she is worshipped by the Great Maitreya;
she is the bestower of perfection upon Mārkaṇḍeya and abides as the longevity of Mārkaṇḍeya.
Mārkaṇḍeya, ever joyful; Mātṛkā, the Sovereign of the Circle of Mothers; she who dwells in the mind; the bestower of honor; and she who is intent upon the concentration of the mind. (51–47)
She whose mind abides in the thought of Māyādānava, she who is adorned with the thought of Māyādānava;
she who is the bliss of one possessing great qualities, she who sports in the great liṅga. || 51-48 ||
Established in Maheśvara, she is the Root, the source of the family of the Root-Vidyā;
she is the one who drinks away Māyā, the deluder, the intoxicant, and the dweller in the Great Guru.
Wearing great white garments, perfumed with Malaya aloe-wood incense,
she is sweetly fragrant, full of honeyed delight, and takes refuge in the essence of honey-wine.
She is the great teacher, the one of great body, possessing great energy and great lotuses;
she is seated upon the central lotus and dwells within the central lotus.
She is the remover of the fear of death, the wrestler, the adversary of the wrestler-graha;
she is the one who causes madness to the circle of great skulls, whose eyes are like bees intoxicated with honey.
Mahāsadyojātakāla, Mahākapilavatīnī, Meghavāha, Mahāvakra, and Manasāmaṇidhāriṇī. || 51–53 ||
The destroyer of the basis of death, abiding amidst the assembly of great gurus;
the mantra established upon the Great Lotus, the sovereign mistress of the treasury of mantras and vidyās.
Seated upon the throne of the sea-monster (makara), she is the great destroyer of death;
she is the Enchanter, the Lord of enchantresses, and she dwells amidst the dance of the intoxicated.
She who shines forth from the family of Mahākāla, she who destroys great desire and the like,
she who dwells in the root-lotus, and she who is the arising of the great root-family.
She is called Māsa, the abode of flesh, the locus of auspiciousness, and possessed of great virtues;
she is more deeply veiled by illusion (māyā), she is the Fish (Mīna), and she is the proponent of the qualities of Mīmāṃsā.
The creator of inquiry, the illusory one, the bestower of the power of the cat;
the security of the beloved of the earth, she who delights in the knowledge of the earth. || 51-58 ||
The Lord of the Mace (Mauṣalīśa) abides in the realm of unreal objects; Keśarī is imagined by the mind;
Śrīdhara is the recitation of the mind; and she is beautifully adorned with a gentle smile. 51–59.
Maināka, the son of Menakā; Māyāchannā of great power;
Mahākriyā; and Lomāṇḍa, who is adorned with the maṇḍala-seat.
She is the upholder of illusion and the destroyer of great hatred;
she has loose hair, is liberated from the body, bestows liberation, and is the one who considers herself liberated.
Wearing a necklace of pearls, she is liberated and illuminates the path to liberation;
she is clothed in the great activity of liberation and delights in the lofty mountain.
She is the destroyer of weapons such as the mace, the mental activity of Mahāgaurī,
the possessor of great wealth, the one of great pride, the one intoxicated by the mind, and the dissolution of the mind.
She is peaceful when entered into the great battle, she who delights with the great lute;
she is the slayer of the great enemy and is garlanded with a multitude of great weapons.
Śivā, Rudrā, Valīśānī, Kitavāmodavadhīnī,
Candracūḍādharā, Vedā, Madonmattā, and Mahojjvalā.
Shining with the luster of ten million moons, possessing the simultaneous arising of ten million suns,
the Hero bears flames and is adorned with thousands of garlands of fire.
Dharma is the one who acts for the beloved of Bharga; she is intent upon the state of great majesty;
she is the banner of Dharma, the performer of Dharma, and she is ever-active in the protection of Dharma.
Residing in a great city of coral, possessing a radiance equal to the luster of coral,
wearing a garland of flowers, she is worthy of honor and the destroyer of the families of her enemies.
Kojāgarā resides in the Visarga, adorned with a garland of seed-syllables;
she is Bījacandrā, Bījapūrā, and Bījābhā, the destroyer of obstacles. || 51-69 ||
Distinguished, established in the ritual of liberation, and perfected in the Vedāṅgas;
she is the glorious mistress of the Kirātins, beloved by both the wise and the ignorant. (51.70)
Standing upon a pedestal, endowed with a pedestal, adorned with a garland of colors,
the hero resides upon a great tree, possessing the radiance of millions of shimmering moons.
The abode of the Great Youth, the Great Desire-Maiden,
the Lord of the activity of the net of desire, the deficient one, and she who has a lotus seat.
The state that destroys fragmentary cognition is difficult to attain;
it is beyond numbering yet possesses a countable form, fulfilling the enumeration of names and so forth. (51.73)
Adorned with a garland of a network of small bells from her treasury,
she possesses ten thousand moon-like lotus-faces and a countenance equal to ten million suns.
The child who steals the intellect of Time; O Blessed One, O Ambika, O you born from the Egg;
he with a skull in hand, the foremost among the four [castes]; she who is free from dispute and unenveloped. (51–75)
Skilled in the five modes of conduct, free from the great stains of the five, devoid of transformation, and invincible—such is the human activity of the two-legged ones. (51.76)
Established in the activity of the Māyā-dānavas, she awakens the functions of the Creator;
mounted upon the operations of the Kali age, she possesses the gurgling sound of the wind.
She is the agent of all movement and the creator of all movement;
she delights in a very slow gait and remains with a very slow gait. || 51-78 ||
Laughing with a loud roar, he is the digit of the moon and the non-terrible torment of Aghora;
he is the destroyer of the great hells and the one who eliminates the ripening of hellish rebirths and the like.
Arising from five rays of light, she is the slayer of Nagas and other powerful beings;
she is to be worshipped while seated upon Garuḍa, and she is the one who increases love for Garuḍa.
Dwelling in the Aśvattha tree, seated at the foot of the Vaṭa tree, she is the ancient-limbed one, the primordial intellect, the union with the essence of phenomenal expansion. 51-81.
She who establishes stability, the shadow of stability, free from intoxication, and the bearer of the parasol;
she whose flowers have the luster of pomegranates, and whose blossoms arise from the pomegranate tree.
Drāḍhya, Dravībharaṇīkā, Ratikālāpavadhinī, Ratnagarbhā, Ratnamālā, and Ratneśvarī have arrived. (51.83)
The well-known Pāvanī, the tail [of the swan], well-established in the tail, the supreme and non-supreme;
Khecarī, established in the sky-goer, the bearer of the great sword, Jayā. (51.84)
Abiding in the playful state of youth, she is the manifestation of Vikhanas and others;
she is the illumination of the Great Sound and the illuminator of the Great Sound. || 51-85 ||
The one with a beautiful smile, the destroyer of adversaries, who stands amidst hosts of enemies and friends;
the wielder of the adamantine staff, the tiger, and the khajjana-bird sporting in the sky.
Gadādhara, Śīladhārī, Śaśikarpūragā, Abalā, Vasanāsanakārī, and Vasanāvasanapriyā. (51–87)
The great Vidyādhara is protected, performing distinguished acts of concealment;
he abides in the singing of the secret Gītā, bestowing the throat of the secret scriptures.
The Purāṇa of Yoga-science and the science of sacrifice are the divisions of the Kalā;
here, there is one time and two times, [and] the lotus of the fruit of time.
She has eighteen arms, she is fierce, she destroys obstacles with her serpents,
she is the protector of knowledge, and she bestows the attainment of knowledge.
Vijayānandagā is Manda; Mahākālamaheśvarī is Mārgī, who delights in bestowing prosperity and illuminates the Great Song. || 51-91 ||
The lineage of Maṅgalā consists of Keśā and others; she is from another family. She has two arms, four arms, and six arms, and she moves according to her will. (51.92)
Wearing a garland of moonstones, she is the one who inspires passion for both the world and that which transcends it;
her body is formed with the three-fold bend, and she delights those who abide in the divisions of existence.
Abiding on the three peaks, existing in the three states, possessing three bodies, born of the three times;
she who has one face, two faces, and is faceless; she who is fond of children.
Established in the network of the Śrīvidyā mantra, she is the wise one, the sovereign of skill;
she resides within the jar and the serpent, the fair-complexioned one, the venerable one, the white-clad one, and the immovable one.
Gandha resides in the knowledge of the Guru; Giridhvajā is the object of enjoyment for Gandha;
Vikaṭā, whose face is like a lotus, stands in the midst of the circle of shadow. (51.96)
Named Kāmā, she is free from ego; she is the daughter of the king of Kāmarūpa;
she is easily attained yet difficult to attain; she is sorrowful, yet her form is subtler than the subtlest. || 51-97 ||
The seed-mantra reciter is fierce; she is the destroyer of the qualities of delusion.
She is the half-moon, the skillful radiance, the all-pervasive form, Sarasvatī. (51.98)
She is the abode of infinite sound, she moves among the flocks of birds,
she stands at the forefront of the Lord of the Imperishable, and she carries a fierce scythe.
Unerring, free from delusion; weary, yet proceeding with firm stability; not in vain, though situated among futile speech; and endowed with doubt regarding what is beyond suspicion. (51.100)
The consort of the Lord of Yamunā, she who carries Mahākāla;
the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa, she whose seat is established upon both the near and far shores.
Holder of the vajra-staff, peaceful, one who has gone beyond the wrong paths and the senses;
resting on the infinite, devoid of deficiency, he is the limit of supreme bliss. (51.102)
The abode of the remaining [breaths] is explained as the dwelling in the nose; she is very dear during the spring season.
Shaken by passion, she is distinct and adorned with pure qualities. (51.103)

The mistress of collyrium, the mistress of the wagtail, she who devours the essence of flesh; she who is bathed in the form and speech of the limbs, and who is intent upon the fruit of the nectar of immortality.
Phalabījadhara, Daurga, Dvārapālanapallava, Pippalāda, Kāraṇa, Vikhyāti, and Ativallabhā. (51–105)
The Brahmin is the form of withdrawal; she who takes any form at will is dejected; the one without speech is without departure; the destroyer of Kaṃsa is the fashioned one.
Therefore, there is neither forceful exertion nor the absence of such exertion; there is no formal disciplinary action.
Everything is covered by universal bliss, wherein the arising of both conquered and unconquered qualities is mastered.
Wearing a radiant crown, resounding with the *rāṅkāra* sound, her inner self is cooled by Varuṇa;
she is enriched by the gift of priceless jewels and is born from the three divisions of day and night.
The great pride of the seed-syllable of Māra is established in the seed-syllables of Hara and the others;
[therein reside] Ananta, Vāsuki, Īśāna, Lākinī, and Kākinī in two ways.
Koṭidhvaja, Bṛhadgarga, Cāmuṇḍā, Raṇacaṇḍikā, Umeśa,
Ratnamāleśī, and he who is worshipped by the Gaṇas of Vikumbha.
Kṛṣṇa is worshipped by Nikumbha; Viṣṇu’s consort is Sudhātmikā;
Alpakālahara is Kunta; and [she] who wields the great Kunta weapon is Mahākuntāstradhāriṇī.
The bearer of the Brahmā-weapon, adorned with a forest garland, is cast forth;
she arises from the one syllable, the two syllables, and the sixteen syllables. (51.112)
Abiding in the exceedingly profound wind, she is the great, profound sound;
she whose nature is threefold, whose nature is the three worlds, and who provides protection in the third [state]. 51-113.
She whose joy wavers for a short time, who has the movement and seat of a bird,
who is the slayer of the arrow of the gods (Kāma), who holds an arrow in her hand, and who is the radiance of the moon.
The one radiant and noble with the dharma of the bindu, the one who causes the sky to blaze, the naked one, the one worshipped by Vyāsa, and the principal deity of the nine regions. (51.115)
With a restless face, left-handed, hairless, and a maker of joy; his body adorned with golden necklaces, he dwells in the beloved of Kaliṅga.

She whose waist is not diminished by anything else, who destroys the splendor of the earth, whose body is the grace of the field of a moment, and who is the sovereign goddess of sages such as Vasiṣṭha. (51.117)
Revātīra-nivāsī and Gaṅgātīra-nivāsinī, Cāṅgeśa and Puṣkareśa, along with the Vyāsabhāṣā-viśeṣikā. (51.118)
The one known as Amalānātha, the well-worshipped Rāmeśvara, the attainment of the Lord Ramānātha, and the one named Kīrtidurgā. (51–119)
Lambodara is the time of love; Lambodarā is the beloved of the family;
Svargadeha is the measure of meditation; Locanāyatadhāriṇī is the one who possesses long eyes. 51-120.
She whose speech is never in vain, who is beloved by Vidyā and Vāgīśvara, whose life-breath is the memory of the measurement of the year, she is the sovereign of the city of Kaliṅga. (51.121)
The knower of the most secret knowledge, she whose nature is the hidden moon, the imperishable one;
she who has gone to the jewel-serpent, the traveler, the mistress of speech, the bestower of strength. (51.122)
She who has attained the seat of the family is Nāśā; Vināśā is most fond of destruction.
She who stands upon the shore is the root of destruction, the sovereign mistress of the family of reabsorption.
The lord of brahmins, possessing the virtues of three sentences, was filled with great wonder;
his circle of followers was overwhelmed with intoxication, shrouded by the quality of being easily pleased.
Virūpākṣī and Lelihanā reveal the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā);
Rudra consists of eighteen syllables and resides within the fine drop of nectar.
The bearer of the parasol and the chowrie is Tripuṇḍrajā, the giver of the parasol;
Vidhātā is Indrātmaka, and Dhanadā is Nādakāriṇī. || 51-126 ||
The supreme bliss of Kuṇḍalinī arises from the honey-flowers;
Rudra resides in the Bilva tree, while she dwells in the lotus of the eye.
Hiraṇyagarbhā, Kaumāro, Virūpākṣī, Ṛtupriyā, Śrīvṛkṣanilayā, Śyāmā, and Mahākulatarūdbhavā. (51.128)

The wise one resides in the family tree; she who is fond of gold and silver is the mistress of the family; she who is the life-force is the giver of life; she who bears the five crests is the bearer of the earth. 51-129.
The mistress of the altar, who discerns between jest and duty;
she is cool and trustworthy, yet devoid of coldness; she brings stability to the mind and is free from decay. (51.130)
Abiding in the womb, existing in the moment of destruction, dwelling upon mountain seats;
half-bodied, serene in nature, and dwelling in the serene forest.
Pratiṣṭheśā, Prāṇadharmā, Jyotīrūpā, Ṛtupriyā, Dharmadhvajapatākeśā, Balākā, and Rasavaddhīnī. (51.132)
The rogue situated on the peak of Meru; the desire of the wicked, intoxicated by rogues;
the infinite one who bestows the perfection of service; and the one who differentiates infinite activities. (51.133)
She is the knower of the unborn nature of all future beings, she who dwells upon the seat of Virāṭ;
she is the one who reveals the scriptures by means of disjunction, severance, and division.
Refined by beautiful craftsmanship, she takes the form of molten gold;
she is a knower of the essence of supreme bliss and a minister to the flow of aesthetic flavor.
Expectant, possessing subtle sound, fond of relevant connection and coherence, free from deceit, born from the ocean, and devoid of the defects of barrenness. (51.136)
She who has conquered all phenomena, she whose parasol blazes, she who is all-pervading, she who carries the fruit;
the yoginī clad in a tiger-skin garment, exceedingly plump, and the bestower of boons. (51.137)
The giver of boons, the giver of essence, the giver of knowledge, the bearer of the excellent;
she who wears beautiful hair, the measurer, the vast one, the giver of virtues, and the celestial garment.
Wearing a garland of earrings and captivating with her earrings, she was born in the Pañcāla country and was beloved for her pure voice. (51.139)
The hunter honored by the Kirātas, she who is intent on the thoughts of Manu,
she who delights in the words of Śiva, Vāmā, and Bhṛgurāmakuleśvarī.
Svayambhū is she who is covered with flowers; Vidhividya is she who illuminates the sciences; Prabhākara is she who is born from the body [of the Sun]; and Viśalyakaraṇī is the Sovereign Lady.
The mistress of the dawn, associated with the Lord, dwelling in the knowledge of yoga;
she is the supreme, the intermediate, and the explained—the woman who is both expressible and inexpressible.
Rich with the seeds of the mango and the uṣāḍha plant, she takes on the form of Mount Mandara;
she is established in the Kṛṣṇa-siddhānta and possesses the power of the means for battle.
The Lord of the beauties of Mathurā, who dwells in the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Mathurā, is devoid of flight and established in both the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya). 51-144.
She is the abode of the vital breath of primordial nature, the destroyer of the knowledge of transformations,
the differentiation of all scriptures, and she whose throne is a maddened lion.
The wise one is a lover of history; Vimalā is of stainless form.
He is seated upon a lion-throne of jewels, and Maṇiparā is the arising of victory.
The bliss of reciting the mantra of Bhadrakālī, she who reveals both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
Śrībhadra and Bhadranātha, and she who destroys and wards off fear. (51.147)
Delighting in the self, with a disciplined mind, she dwells within the beloved of the Trident-bearer;
through the firm practice of transcendent knowledge, she bestows specific wisdom.
She possesses the splendor of the ageless and immortal, she is auspicious and bears millions of beauties;
she is the protector of creatures, seated upon a lotus, the bestower of the Śrīśa-Pāśupata weapon.
She who upholds all scriptures, she who is proud, she who is wise, she who destroys ignorance;
she who is the second lord, she who is half of Īśa, and she who deludes Bādarāyaṇa.
She was a devourer of corpse-flesh, formidable, with terrifying eyes and fearsome;
she was skilled in the sequence of Śiva’s knowledge and devoted to the yoga of ritual action.
Established in giving, perfected in generosity, she who tames the arrogant and is devoted to the Mountain-Dweller (Pārvatī);
she who is the joy of her beloved, the maker of day, and the destroyer of those seated in the night.
Eight cubits tall with tremulous eyes, she is the one who causes the mind to be established;
she has soft hair and a soft parasol, and she is the daughter of Vibhāṅga, who delights in merit.
Situated in the intermediate space, she is the root that reveals the sons of the root;
she is intent on bestowing fearlessness and is enchanting with her garland of moons.

The lord of the four oceans and the Ganges; the daughter of the mountain; one who takes delight in curiosity; the life-breath of the enemy of Śiśupāla; and the protector of the quarters of the foreign land. (51.155)
She is unique, the knower of the ritual, the destroyer of pride, and Trivikramā;
she is the mistress of yoga with a triangular face, possessing a deep navel, and the sovereign of the mountains.

She is endowed with ever-new qualities; she is the immovable mountain for the family of young maidens; she is the Lord of the three worlds; she is free from doubt; she is devoid of fever, yet she is the giver of fever.
And she is the daughter of Atidhāmīka, seated upon a beautiful lion-throne;
she reveals the spiritual accomplishments of virtuous beings belonging to the highest class of consecrators.
Siddhapriya, Viśālākṣa, Dhvaṃsakartrī, Nirañjanā, Śaktīśa, Vikaleśa, and Kratukarmaphalodayā. (51.159)
Viphaleśa moves through the sky; Lalitā has the intellect as her vehicle;
she brings security from the heat of the Malaya mountains and is characterized by the quality of passion (rajas). 51-160.
Dviruṇḍaka is the gatekeeper; Balevīghnavināśinī is the destroyer of obstacles for the army.
Māyāpadmagata is pride; Mārīvidyāvināśinī is the destroyer of the Mārī spell.
The Siddha residing in Hiṅgulāja, the essence of the debates of the learned, Śrīpatīśa, Śrīkareśa, Śrīvidyā, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (51.162)
The first-born of wisdom, the fortunate one, the daughter of the Lord of Mithilā, has attained Rāmacandra’s beloved, the sovereign of the Raghu dynasty. (51.163)
The Tortoise, the Hero situated in the Tortoise, Vasā, the group of letters, Girīśvarī, Rājarājeśvarī, Bālā, and the qualities within the seat of Rati. (51.164)
The splendor of one who assumes forms at will, the clever one who takes various shapes;
Atithīśa, the sustainer of all, adorned with manifold ornaments. (51.165)
Her body is adorned with various ornaments, and she is decorated with garlands of human heads;
she is the Lord of the World, pervading the world, and the bestower of the desired accomplishments upon all beings.
She who desires the world, who pervades the world, the Victorious One, the Bestower of Victory;
she who causes victory, the Sustainer of Life, the Giver of Victory, the Life-Giver, and the Conqueror.
Victory to Gaṇeśa, the bestower of fortune, who dwells in the great seat (mahāpīṭha),
who resides in the uneven Sāmaveda, and who is united with a portion of the Yajurveda.

Profound with qualities pertaining to the three times, possessing twenty-two lotus-hands, abiding in the essence of the thousand-armed one, she who flows through the parts [of the body] and brings about existence.

The path that brings about meditative cultivation, whose lotus-eyes are disciplined, which attracts all things everywhere, and which is the whetstone for the unbroken knowledge of the omniscient one. (51.170)

One whose mental disposition is conquered, who has conquered the learned, who is free from blemish and endowed with virtue; who is without support, without reliance, and who has conquered the objects of the senses through knowledge. (51-171)
One with an exceedingly broad face destroys disputes and wickedness;
one who has no husband for a wife brings about the destruction of enemies, and is honored by the family. (51.172)
She is the swiftness of those with many followers, adorned with beautiful locks of hair;
she possesses supreme intelligence, is subtle, and destroys the darkness of night.
The yoginī who creates a lattice of moonlight, who rests in separation, who moves through the ages, who attains yoga, who bestows victory, Lākinī, the auspicious one. (51.174)
The entity that produces perception and intellect, which deludes the fear of existence;
O Beautiful One, you are Sundarānanda, the beautiful woman who brings about delight. 51-175.
She is the knower of delight, the bliss of delight, and the illuminator of the Lord of Delight;
she is the embodiment of the Buddha, pure awakening, the destroyer of adversaries, and the one who has transcended duality.
She is the bliss that carries away manifold states of being, the bestower of abundant progeny, the performer of the means for sacrifice, O Suyajña, and the liberator in the fifth [state]. 51-177.

The splendor of ten million times ten million moons, a flash of light from ten million times ten million rays, possessing the brilliance of ten million times ten million flickering flames, and as flickering as ten billion times two.
Her body is covered by ten million suns; she possesses the radiance of ten million times ten million suns;
she is like ten million moonstones and is as pure as ten million moonstones.
She possesses the brilliance of a hundred million moon-gems and the splendor of a hundred million moons;
she shines with the luster of a hundred million cosmic fires and is like a hundred million fires of time.
She who has entered the fire of ten million fires, she who is born from the two-fold fire-born woman (svāhā),
she of great splendor, she whose water is fire, and she who wears the garland of the fire of time.
The Lord Kālāgnirudra, she whose form is Kālāgnirudra;
the self of Time, the self of the Kali-age and Time; Kalikā, Kulalākinī. (51.182)
She who conquers death, whose splendor is death, who is dear to the Conqueror of Death;
she who removes great death, who is death itself, and who destroys untimely death.
Victory! The Lord of Victory! The Giver of Victory! The Bestower of Victory! The Destroyer of Victory!
The Bringer of Victory! The Dharma of the World! The Protector of the Life of the World! || 51-184 ||
"O Lord, this which has been described is the designation of the Great Vidyā: 'The All-Conquering,' 'Possessing All Forms,' 'Existing at All Times,' and 'Manifesting as All Beings.'"
Consisting directly of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), having the nature of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa),
it is known by the name "One Thousand and Eight" and is composed of a collection of one hundred [verses].
The field of auspiciousness for the three worlds, which bestows the fruits of perfected knowledge,
it is manifest as both with parts and without parts, endowed with the power of the wish-fulfilling tree.
He who, filled with devotion and avoiding false doctrines, recites this supreme knowledge of the self which brings about the realization of the self for yogins, [attains the goal]. (51.188)
Having become manifest in the Rudrapīṭha, one will certainly become a great yogin;
he attains sudden success through the giver of the lowest garland.
Royal fortune, wealth, sovereignty, great fortitude, horses and the like, a beautiful elephant, a heroic son, a kingdom, happiness, and victory. (51.190)

And he attains the status of a sovereign over the lords of kings, as well as a divine vehicle; thereafter, he obtains the middling accomplishment, which is achieved without hardship within five months.
The total destruction of suffering, preeminence in the circle of the worlds, the enumeration of the gods' devotees, divine nature, and eternal happiness—[these are attained]. (51.192)

In the presence of the gods, during both the waking state and the time of dreams, there appeared the increase of lifespan, the subjugation of the world, full treasuries, wealth in cattle, and royal palaces.
The abandonment of fear regarding long-term perspectives, avoidance of trivial activities, constant love for the Dharma, and knowledge of the Dharma are of great virtue. (51.194)
The practitioner attains bliss, which is the sprout of discernment and is endowed with the grace of the venerable Goddess of Speech;
from that, he achieves the perfection established in the supreme yoga.
Abiding in infinite qualities, free from the objects and manifestations of illusion, dwelling in a solitary place, and application to the treatises on yoga. || 51-196 ||

The state of being empty of all desires, exclusive devotion to the deity, the power of moving through the sky, reaching all destinations, the accomplishment of all states of being, and that which is dear to the gods. || 51-197 ||
It is the yoga of fierce activity at all times, bestowing the eightfold supernatural powers and prosperity;
it is firm knowledge, the capacity to compose all treatises, and an ocean of alchemy.
The state of oneness, devoid of duality, the application to the Great State (mahāpada), the lordship over the knowledge (vidyā) possessing great qualities, and peace itself. || 51-199 ||
The best of practitioners attains [this] who recites it with unwavering devotion;
the wise one should recite it three times a day, once, or twice.
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for this mantra is prescribed as one hundred and eight recitations;
having performed the preliminary rite, one should recite it again and again.
Having become endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, one shall attain the movement of the mind;
for him who, being self-restrained and pure, recites this, auspiciousness pervades everywhere.
Having pierced the jeweled seat of the six chakras, one becomes established in the Unstruck (anāhata);
then, having pierced the Unstruck, one attains union with the Pure (viśuddha). || 51-203 ||
And having split the pure lotus at the crown of the head, it becomes two-petaled;
by the recitation of this hymn, one splits this great lotus consisting of two petals and so forth. (51.204)
Having performed the rites of the fourfold group, one attains the liberation of nirvāṇa at the end;
for the sake of the yogis' accomplishment of yoga, there arises compassion toward all beings.
O Supreme Lord, this has been taught for the sake of attaining nirvāṇa and liberation; what on earth cannot be accomplished by the recitation of this hymn? (51.206)
One should accomplish the practice of yoga through the lineage of one's family;
one should recite the hymn at the end of yoga, in the middle of yoga, and at the beginning of yoga.
During a journey under the conjunction of Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī, likewise in the sign of Gemini;
under Śravaṇā in the group of Aries, when Mars is joined with the Moon. (51–208)
On Saturdays, during the solar transits (saṅkrānti), and repeatedly on Tuesdays,
at the time of twilight, the king of yogis should write this hymn while engaged in meditation and concentration.
Having written it on birch bark, one should wear it around the neck or on the head;
or else, during the conjunction of night, the wise person should write it upon the *kulacakra*.
Reciting everywhere according to the method of the Kula, one shall attain accomplishment;
by offering oblations with this name, one becomes the very form of Kālikā.
Having offered oblations here in this manner ten times that number, the yogi, becoming firmly established in Maṇipūra, shall always obtain the grace of Rudra’s Śakti.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the arrangement of the one hundred and eight thousand names of Lākinī. 51.
Now begins the fifty-second chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairava said:
"O lady of excellent hips, tell me the sequence of Maṇipūra."
Knowing which, all sages attain the eight supernatural powers. || 52-1 ||
Reciting it, one proceeds swiftly, without exertion and unassailed;
it is the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the protection of one's own body. (52.2)
"Having investigated that which resides in the knots of the higher and lower [traditions], you should speak.
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Mahābhairava, O Kālāgni, listen to the knowledge of the Niśā [Tantra]."
Out of affection for you, O Lord, I shall describe the extremely subtle means—the consciousness of mantras within mantras; listen to the subject matter. 52-4.
But in Maṇipūra, by whose grace one becomes steady without effort;
