merely by performing this, one certainly becomes a yogi. (52–5)
The net of mantras consists of ten million times ten million, and their meanings are likewise remembered as being ten million;
from among these, O Kulārṇava, I shall declare the essential portion. (52–6)
Recalling the supreme mantra with an attitude of equanimity toward all things,
one perceives the body as the undivided universe, including all that is moving and unmoving.

From the base (mūlādhāra) up to the maṇipūra, the wise one, taking up the garland of letters which consists of the three qualities and corresponds to the mantra, should mutter it again and again. (52-8)
One should meditate upon one's own deity as consisting of full radiance, having the form of ten million fires of cosmic destruction, always from the base of the spine up to the aperture of Brahmā.
Her form is undivided, dwelling in a hidden place;
she is the bliss of the deep and upward-throbbing throat, residing in the ocean of nectar.
Having known that which, through contemplation at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), becomes equal to Brahman,
one should joyfully meditate upon it at the root-aperture (mūlarandhra) as blazing like ten million fires of cosmic destruction.
One should perform meditation that is blazing, producing the light of upward-pointing flames, charming with the sweetness of the essence of nectar, and radiant like the sacrificial fire. (52.12)
One should contemplate the lovely forehead, crowded with the brilliance of ten million full moons, from which a mass of fluid drips, and whose face is radiant with that fluid. (52.13)
One should meditate on the meaning of the mantra as having a stable wind and a stable form;
or else, as being like pure light, pervaded by the rays of the full Brahman.
Having meditated repeatedly on the root-mantra from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
one should contemplate one's own deity in a subtle form as the Great Guru.
And there is the knowledge of the meaning of the mantra; through that knowledge one shall attain liberation.
Merely by knowing the meaning of the mantra, one shall attain both supernatural accomplishment (siddhi) and nirvāṇa. || 52-16 ||
Neither gross nor too subtle, possessing a body composed of the *guṇas*, the Lord of the Universe, whose own power is his own bliss,
whose mind is delighted by its own joy; who is both immovable and moving, white and red,
having forms such as full and not full, who moves through the path of the three *guṇas* at the mouth of the root-lotus and other centers.
One who has attained the world of the perfected ones (siddhaloka) should meditate upon the Universal Self, known as Kula, which is rendered inert by the qualities of the mind. || 52-17 ||
In the sixty-four fields, she is the triple-generatrix, skilled in meditation;
she whose form is the Great Mantra, whose compassion pervades the world, and who is the primordial Great Vidyā within the sphere of awakening; her body is veiled by the essence of the mantra-nature.
In this world, connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor take refuge here in the path of the lineage, which is like a vast and tranquil ocean. || 52-18 ||
The entire meaning of emptiness consists of silver, the jar, and Nārāyaṇa;
it is the emission (visarga) residing in the bindu, containing the digits of the sun and moon and the rays of fire;
it is the limb for the worldly activity, yet free from becoming and solidified by conceptualization.
The intellect establishes me, the substratum of transformations, within the cavity of the ten-petaled lotus. || 52-19 ||

The sages, kings, ascetics, Indra, the gods, and others worship Him who bestows fearlessness upon the gods and asuras, who creates the splendor of youthful form, whose body is captivating, and who is the manifest consciousness of the entire body.
It resides within the body of primordial nature (prakṛti) in the abode of ten coverings. || 52-20 ||

Placing within the lotus of his heart, or even at the base of his navel, something indescribable, he worships Śiva— who possesses fierce speech, who is the crushing force of a multitude of sounds, who delights in most intense asceticism, and who is easily propitiated.
The great yogi cultivates the contemplation of the qualities of dispassion. 52-21 ||
The bestowing of the perception of a hard heart upon one's own qualities and being;
[worship] of the four-armed body, the ten-fold lord of digits, the blue lotus;
the mind-captivating Hara, the supreme essence, the primordial syllable.
By its very nature, one should superimpose the form of the Praṇava upon the Supreme Lord.
He whose intellect is solitary and stainless, who rests upon a garland of lotus smiles, who is auspicious,
who possesses the splendor of a hundred suns, and who dwells even within the center of every body;
he indeed bears ten thousand arms, supports the earth, and holds the sacred mudrās.
The husbands of women who desire their families resort to the abode of the Lord’s dwelling. || 52-23 ||

May that [devotion] which always contemplates the lotus-feet of the Supreme God of gods— feet characterized by compassion, which possess the marks of auspiciousness, which are the source of all states of being, and which consist of the constant meditation upon His singular virtues— attain the seal of liberation.
The self-controlled one should indeed perform the act of lovemaking with the Mistress of the Three Worlds.
Having acted thus, the person who possesses the meditation on objectless faith suddenly attains the consciousness of the mantra and the definitive realization of its meaning.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Consciousness of Mantric Meaning," in the Uttara-tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. 52.
Now begins the fifty-third chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said: "O most beloved one, who dwells in the midst of the lotus of the ocean of bliss!"
Now, O Bhairava, listen to the warding off of Kālajāla and the others. (53-1)
Having filled and restrained the wind, which is covered by its accumulation and possesses its natural movement, by means of its own nature for a long time, one shall become happy. || 53-2 ||
Having exhaled very slowly, one should always remain absorbed in that;
under the power of the net of time, one proceeds [to liberation] at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. (53.3)
Without the contraction of the vital air (vāyu), no person attains success;
rather, it is achieved merely by the movement of the air and its emergence through the subtle channel. 53–4.
The great yogi indeed attains perfection even while under the sway of the net of time;
yet, due to delusion, he does not bring time under his own control and instead remains excessively attached to pleasure.
Even he who eats at the improper time will go to hell; there is no doubt about this.
Having fixed the mind on Maṇipur, one should always accomplish the deities. (53–6)
Having recited the hymn, meditation, the name, and the qualities again and again,
the wise one should everywhere effect the union of the mind with the vital breath (vāyu).

Having retained [the breath] by means of kumbhaka, having exhaled it by means of recaka, and having brought it under control at all times through repeated practice, one who has conquered the self shall become immortal.
Having abandoned greed and delusion, as well as the sins of lust, anger, and the like,
and having always subsisted on air alone, he remains self-controlled in solitude.
One should constantly practice the breath-control techniques for the purpose of piercing the six cakras; indeed, one should hold the breath very slowly for the sake of attaining long life. (53-10)
If he were not long-lived, or if his nature were Time, serving the vital breath, then even after attaining mastery over the six cakras, the knower would fall under the power of death. (53-11)

Therefore, one should first perform the rite of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for the sake of accomplishing that action, which is the cause for the perfection of the wind [element] through the knowledge of Śiva.
The foremost practitioner should perform the yoga of *neti* by means of purifying his own body, so that he becomes fully self-controlled. (53.13)
Then one should perform the yoga of *dhautī* so that one becomes self-controlled;
one should perform the yoga of *neulī* where the world no longer exists. (53-14)
One should then perform the practice of Dantī when one possesses the primary activity;
then, at that very moment, one who is free from craving shall accomplish it. (53.15)
"The destruction of craving is liberation; this is my definitive conclusion regarding yoga. I shall explain it in detail; listen, O purifier of Kailāsa. (53.16)
Having previously performed this task in heaven, the gods and lords of sages joyfully attained perfection of body, becoming free from shadow and illusion. (53.17)
They shall all travel everywhere, be experts in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, live for a long time, and be endowed with complete prosperity.
I shall proclaim those various distinctions and the practice for protecting the body;
O Mahādeva, he who performs this supreme practice of the body [attains success]. (53.19)
He will come to my abode of bliss; of this there is no doubt—having risen at dawn during the Brāhma hour, when the fruit of the time arises. (53-20)
One should practice meditation upon the lotus feet of the Guru within the thousand-petaled [lotus];
thereafter, the illustrious one should contemplate Sarasvatī in the form of the Guru.
Having bowed his head daily to his own deity— the one who relishes the essence of supreme bliss and possesses the intellect of yoga— he should perform the rite of purification.

Having attained perfection through the very sequence of purificatory rites and being endowed with the quality of purity, he should proceed with diligent effort for the sake of performing acts of purification. (53.23)
Having taken a prastha measure of earth, one should perform purification;
for the evacuation of feces, one should do so repeatedly with seventeen handfuls of earth.
Then, O Śaṅkara, having stirred it with the index finger of the left hand and inserted it into the anal opening, one should indeed perform the cleansing repeatedly.
Until the complete relinquishing of the poison and the total destruction of impurities, the wise person should cleanse and purify the stomach with clay and water. (53.26)
One should perform [the practice] for as long as pleasure has not arisen;
then, having risen according to the rule, one should perform purification with clay.
By which sequence even the odor of excrement is destroyed:
having thoroughly washed both feet, one should resort to internal purification. (53.28)
O Lord, Master of Yoga, listen as I describe the fruit of that rite:
a cord made from fine cloth should be placed through a minute aperture. (53.29)
Firm yet very soft and exceedingly pure, one should gradually bring [the tongue] forward and then place it at the root of the tongue. (53-30)
The wise one, having constantly drawn [the breath] from the root of the tongue for twelve counts, should bring about the piercing by performing very gentle friction. (53.31)
With the three *māyā* seeds, with the three seed-syllables of the Goddesses, and also with the three *ramā* seed-syllables, [one should offer] "Salutation to the Yoginī" as well. (53.32)
With this mantra, the lord of yogis should practice the yoga of "not this" (neti);
having thoroughly drawn up the part located in the head, he should perform the purification of the throat.
Then one should perform the purification of the chest and then the purification of the navel;
one should do this in sequence for the sake of the body. Listen, O Lord, to the method thereof. (53-34)
One should perform the practice of *dhautī* and partake of warm water;
[one should also wear] a white garment of fine thread measuring eight finger-breadths.
The full measurement is declared to be thirty-two cubits;
first, the mantra-practitioner should prepare a cloth measuring four finger-breadths.

One who is long [of stature] should consume [the offering] measuring five cubits, provided with hot water; having placed the remainder on the tip of his tongue, he should comfortably wear his garment. (53.37)
The wise one should consume [the substance] with the mudrās of the index finger, the middle finger, and the thumb;
he should increase it daily in sequence, as well as during long periods and at the time of childbirth.
O Lord of Gods, having purified everything everywhere with this mantra, as well as with the previously mentioned mantra, one should utter the seed-syllable using the initial seed-syllable.
Then follow the three seed-syllables of Śakti, likewise the three seed-syllables of Kāma, and then the three seed-syllables of Lakṣmī; [this is] Mahāghautanivāsinī.
In the Mevāḍī-malam mantra, one should perform two washings;
thereafter, the wife should carry [the substance] and subsequently place it within her womb.
Having gradually brought about the settling [of the breath], until everything is produced;
by the grace of this yoga, the wind becomes well-disposed. (53–42)
Then, for the sake of ensuring the safety of his body, the preeminent practitioner should perform the supreme *neulī* yoga, which provides firm binding to the limbs. (53.43)
O Supreme Lord, one should cause the abdomen to roll about;
one should always perform this movement while maintaining the retention of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu). || 53-44 ||
Having rotated the left [nozzle] upward, one should rotate the right [nozzle] downward;
in this sequence, O Lord of Gods, one should perform the *puṭapāka* (hermetic cooking).
O Lord of Gods, by means of this mantra, one becomes firm upon an auspicious seat.
After that, there are the three seed-syllables of Brahmā, and then the three seed-syllables of Kālī. (53–46)
The mantra consists of the Goddess, the two *praṇavas*, "to her who resides in the limbs" (*gātrasthāyai*), "salutation" (*namaḥ*), and the *dviṭha* (svāhā).
At the end of that is the most wonderful cleansing of the channels (*nāḍikā*) and so forth. (53–47)
O Mahādeva, one should fashion the chest-region by means of the application of ivory;
the tooth-stick, being the measure of an elephant, is considered stainless and beautiful. (53–48)
The foremost of practitioners should indeed wash the tooth-stick with the mantra;
thereafter [he should recite] the three *māyā* seeds and the three seeds of Bhairavī. (53–49)
The pair beginning with *madīnī* and *bīja*, residing in the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), [is uttered as] "Cut the knot of my heart"—this is the pair known as Vahnisundarī. (53–54)
Gradually, by this method, one should cause [the breath] to enter the cavity of the throat until it reaches below the navel and until it becomes filled with bliss. (53–54)
The practice of Dantī-yoga, which accomplishes all tasks, should be performed until dawn;
at the conclusion of this, one should then perform the cleansing of the channels (nāḍī-kṣālana).
O Lord of Heroes, hear that mantra which bestows immortality:
first, having extracted the *praṇava*, [place] a pair of long *praṇavas*. (53–53)
Then follow two seed-syllables of Bhuvaneśī, three seed-syllables of Candra,
three seed-syllables of Kṛṣṇa, and thereafter three seed-syllables of Arka.
Having extracted the three *vāgbhava* syllables, then the three *vahni-bījas*,
followed by the *śrībīja*, *manmatha*, and *lakṣmī*, and then [the syllable] *śītale*.
Those of inferior conduct should daily cleanse their own stomach, the base of the channels, and the pair of excrement-washing organs with the mantra ending in *svāhā*. (53–56)
One should practice for as long as it takes to destroy craving;
the wearing of the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) continues until the power of its emergence [is exhausted].

O Lord, that cleansing which is the means to happiness does not arise until, by the power of fortune alone, the practice of the three staffs and the breath-control of the pot (kumbhaka) occurs. (53–58)
The auspicious cleansing of the channels comes about spontaneously;
as long as there is the subtle flow of breath and the continuous drinking of honey. (53–59)
But that which issues from the lotus-feet increases supreme bliss;
it is unlimited by pleasure and is pure through its consciousness.
Through the nature of consciousness-bliss, there is the shedding of tears of joy;
for then indeed occurs the severing of the knot of the heart and the expansion of the body.
For then there is horripilation, steadiness, and likewise a firm immersion of the body;
then the stainless consciousness and the knowledge of the six-lotus Siddhānta [arise]. (53–62)
Having become composed of consciousness and bliss, free from craving and ignorance,
he is liberated while living, a connoisseur of supreme bliss, and one who delights in love.
He becomes a great yogi of steady mind; of this there is no doubt.
He is a believer, a devotee of the gods, and one who avoids speaking words of censure. (53–64)
That very self indeed becomes a possessor of great knowledge; of this there is no doubt, having fully performed the fivefold yoga, beginning with the daily rites, which is unsurpassed. (53–65)
One should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules at the abode of the King of Tīrthas;
or else, the *iḍā* [nāḍī] is in the waters of the Gaṅgā, and the *piṅgalā* is in the waters of the Yamunā.
In the Suṣumnā, in the Sarasvatī, and in the millions of Vasu-puṣkaras;
nevertheless, regarding external bathing, it must include the entire body except for the head.
One should sprinkle the head seven times with external water,
using either the mantra or the root mantra for the act of cleansing.
Then, having cleansed his limbs, he should perform the twilight worship (sandhyā-vandana);
the external twilight worship with mantras, and internally, the Lord who is the source of nature (prakṛtīśvara).

Having performed the twilight salutation (sandhyāvandana) consisting of the luminous drop (bindu) above and below, encapsulated within the sphere of resonance (nāda), one should consume the great medicinal herb (mahauṣadhi).
O Lord of the Family (Kuleśvara), having consecrated the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the root mantra,
one should then perform the great worship (mahāpūjā) accomplished according to the mantras specific to each [deity].
Then, O Lord, one should meditate upon the meaning of the six cakras according to the prescribed rule;
this is the great worship of Kuṇḍalinī, the auspiciousness of the Thousand Names.
The wise one should recite [the mantra] of the deities at all times for the sake of perfect accomplishment;
having joyfully pierced the *mūlādhāra* with the two subtle winds. (53–73)
Then [he taught] the division, the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), the union of Rākiṇī and Viṣṇu,
their sequential order, O Lord, and the auspicious Thousand Names.

One should joyfully effect the union of the two deities seated upon the jewel-throne by breaking through their separation, revealing the most secret discourse that manifests the various modes of devotion of sentient beings. (53–75)
Meditation, knowledge, constant praise, sacrifice, and the chanting of names—
these are the consciousness of Rudralākinī as well as that of Mṛtyuñjaya.
Having meditated constantly upon the Lord who pervades all and consists of the Guru, one becomes a long-lived great yogi; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Piercing of Maṇipūra," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the Section on Accomplished Mantras of the Mahātantroddīpana, the latter part of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. 53.
Now begins the fifty-fourth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said: O Knower of the distinction between the supreme and the non-supreme, [I shall explain] the means for attaining hidden knowledge.
Now listen, O Omniscient One, to the means of accomplishing the five substances and so forth. || 54-1 ||
That which arises instantaneously through the sequence for the purpose of piercing the lotuses of the six chakras is indeed Amara and Amarā, the bestower of all siddhis. (54-2)

The immortal creeper known as Dūrvā, which is the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman and whose nature is the bliss of Brahman, should likewise be meditated upon as firmly established. (54.3)
Siddhāmarā is Nirguṇḍī, which bestows all perfections;
thereafter, Nīlāmarā is to be taken, accompanied by blue Tulasī.
The *amaru*, the *samayāpatra*, the *cāmara*, and the *vilvapatrikā*—these, beloved of Śiva, should always be worshipped; one should take refuge in the aforementioned dwelling. (54–5)
O Lord of Kailāsa, hear these mantras for consuming [the offerings]:
Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, Śūdrā, Cakramatī, and Jayā. (54–6)
Having purified it with its respective mantra, one should consume it with this mantra; this is declared for the consumption of all [substances], including nectar and the like. (54–7)
The Praṇava, the Long Praṇava, "O Kapilā, accomplisher of knowledge! Accomplish my yoga!"—this pair [of mantras] is encapsulated by the vowel. (54.8)
"In this place filled with clusters of branches and inhabited by great medicinal herbs, grant me alone immortality; thus, having formed a pair, you shall become a *dviṭha* (a twice-born). (54.9)
O Lord of Pārvatī, listen to the mantras for the conquest of immortality, by the mere remembrance of which a man becomes Nārāyaṇa. (54.10)
By eating the *bilva* leaf, one shall roam the world like Śiva;
having extracted the three seed-syllables of Śrī, one should then [place] the triad of Vāgdevīs.
The seed-syllable of Lakṣmī-Kāmeśvarī, the triad of Ramā and Kāma repeated thrice;
O Siddhaviśveśī, O Supreme One, dweller in the most secret tree! (54-12)
"O Yuga-dviṭha, at the end, unite me alone with the reality of knowledge (jñānatattva) by means of this mantra and the mudrā called Vidhitattva; thus [says] the Lord of Heroes. (54-13)
Having purified [the site], O Lord, one should then purify the chowries;
the goddess Dūrvā bestows the essence of immortality throughout the three worlds.
The supreme Ramā, who wards off the piercing and breaking of knots, is preceded by the Praṇava;
from that, one should extract the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu and the seed-syllable of Kiṅkiṇī.

One should write the seed-syllable of the Queen of Queens (Rājarājeśvarī), the seed-syllable of Śrī, and then those three; thereafter, at the end of the phrase "sudhākhaṇḍe māmiha," one should write the word "siddhāmarapada."
Uttering the words "dehi dehi namaḥ svāhā," one should purify [the offering];
by the mere consumption of this, one shall be happy for a long time. (54-17)
By the mere union with all [of these], the practitioner becomes perfected.
Now listen, O illustrious Candraśekhara, to the purification of the perfected immortals. 54-18.
The Siddhāmarā and Nirguṇḍī plants are hidden within the three worlds;
a wise person should employ their primary root or leaves. (54.19)
If the root is unavailable, the leaf should be taken; if the leaf is unavailable, not the root.
The best of practitioners should bring it on an auspicious day. (54.20)
Then success is attained, for there is no restrictive rule for the Kaulas;
all success resides in the Kaula, and the practice of yoga is found in the Kaula. (54.21)
How can there be yoga, enjoyment, and so forth for those who are devoid of family traditions?
Without yoga, how can the accumulation of enjoyments and such come to be? (54.22)
By the mere practice of yoga, one should obtain the means for enjoyment;
that supreme enjoyment is knowledge, which is the partaking of the nectar of time. || 54-23 ||
The enjoyment of the delights of sense objects and so forth increases without effort;
O Lord, this is the primary purpose of the body and dear to embodied beings. (54.24)
Rich in the form of cool nectar, consisting of both manifest and unmanifest modes—this is indeed described as the primary means for the sake of affection. (54.25)
For the sake of protecting the life of one's beloved and for the intense removal of grief,
I shall again declare to you the mantra for the purification of Nirguṇḍī.
Oṃ! O Nirguṇḍī, O Great Illusion, O dweller in Mahāyava, O mother of long life and health, O dweller in the sound of Brahman! || 54-27 ||
Then, purify my entire body with the syllable *yugaṃ*;
it is adorned with the pair of *nāda* and *bindu*, and possesses beautiful luster. (54.28)
Pervaded by the fourteen vowels, the pair [of consonants] adorned with the bindu;
thereafter, one should write the three Lakṣmī-bījas consisting of the Ramā-bīja. || 54-29 ||
"Grant, grant the vajra-body!"—at the end of this sound is Vahnisundarī.
Having purified [the substance] with this mantra, the supreme practitioner should consume it. (54.30)
Then one shall quickly become immortal; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Supreme Lord, listen as I describe the purification of the *tulasī* plant. (54.31)
By performing which one becomes free from disease, powerful, and has conquered the senses—[that is] the Praṇava, the Goddess Vaiṣṇavī, who dwells in the knowledge of pure being (sattva). (54.32)
At the end of the three seeds of desire, however, is the pair "māṃ rakṣa" followed by the letter ṭha (svāhā). He who performs the consumption after having performed this purification— || 54-33 ||
The accomplishment of the body shall belong to that yogin who possesses meditative concentration and dhāraṇī.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Purification of the Five Siddha Substances," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantra-prakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*. 54.
Now begins the fifty-fifth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
Out of affection for you, I shall describe the specific method for bringing the body under control.
Hatha Yoga has been explained; now listen to the sequence [of its practice]. || 55-1 ||
O Śivānanda, O Śivaśaṅkara, O Maṅgala, I shall describe Rudra, who resides in the Maṇipūra [cakra] and who is imperishable like the wind throughout the three worlds. 55-2.
And above the region of the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is the ocean of supreme bliss;
at the root of the navel is a mass of clouds filled with hundreds of flashes of lightning.
This is the most secret of secrets, which reaches the very core of the realization of yogins;
and at the region of the base of the navel is a blue lotus of great luster.
On the tips of its petals, the letters from *ḍa* to *pha* always shine;
outside of that, the form of the triangle of fire is beautifully adorned. (55–5)
Resembling the morning sun, shaped like a crest, and stainless;
there, it has the form of the seed-syllable of fire, yet transcends form and lies beyond the qualities (guṇas).
One should meditate upon the supreme deity, who has the form of the dawn, rides upon the back of a ram, possesses four arms and three eyes, and bears a beautiful body. (55.7)
In her lap shines Rudreśa, whose form is as red as vermilion;
he is the embodiment of Brahmā, three-eyed, and the agent of creation and destruction. (55–8)
The all-pervading Lord, whose limbs are adorned with supernatural powers, bestows desired boons upon the worlds;
on his left side, the supreme goddess Lākinī always shines resplendent. (55.9)
The great goddess has four arms and three eyes; she bestows happiness.
Her body is dark-complexioned, she wears yellow garments, and she is an immortal adorned with various ornaments.
The Mother who bestows all accomplishments, the protectress of all everywhere—may the Goddess, the guardian of the lineage, always protect me with her vidyās. 55-11.
Having meditated thus and performed worship with recitation, sacrifice, hymns, and so forth,
the practitioner of mantra will then become accomplished through the grace of Maṇipūra.
I shall describe the fruit of Maṇipūra in brief; listen to it, for even in a hundred times ten million years, its fruit cannot be fully told. (55.13)
Immediately after Maṇipūra, the Anāhata [cakra] must indeed be described—its hymn, its meditation, its name, and its thousandfold auspicious qualities. (55.14)
The fruit is utterly secret, bestowing the successful attainment of the lotus-like friend;
it grants self-knowledge, the accomplishment of liberation, and the acquisition of love, devotion, and the like. (55.15)
The destroyer of multitudes of people, the protector, the mine of lotuses—
the king of yogis suddenly attains the fortune of an abundance of knowledge.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Piercing of Maṇipūra," in the *Maṇipūraprakāśa* within the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa* of the *Uttaratantroddhāra* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 55.
Now begins the fifty-sixth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairava said:
"Speak, O Kaumārī, O Surānandā, O Kuleśvarī!"
Now you should explain the placement within the heart-lotus.
By the mere knowledge of which a person becomes a lord of yoga—a place for the performance of all accomplishments that is exceedingly difficult for yogins to attain. (56-2)
The very nature of all reality and the illuminator of the path to accomplishment—through the realization of this within the lotus of the heart, one becomes Mārtaṇḍabhairava. (56-3)
Out of affection, and by means of the sequence of vision arising from the yoga of devotion, I wish to hear all of that—the auspicious essence of the six cakras. (56.4)
The piercing, the cultivation, the gnosis, and the very vision of the mind;
the extraction of the mantra and the convention that gives rise to qualities such as omniscience. (56–5)
The sacrifice for the goddess Kākinī, the hymn of praise, the armor, and all the auspicious thousand names of the Lord whose nature is the qualities (guṇātman). || 56-6 ||
Tell me, in brief, the knowledge of the circles of the winds;
O Goddess, you alone are my refuge, so protect me from this peril of suffering. (56–7)
O Mahākāla, free from fear, devoted to the state of devotion; O Īśa, Lord of my Bliss-Bhairava, listen, for I shall speak according to the truth. (56-8)
"O Lord of All, that which was spoken by you here—both heard and unheard, and considered wonderful—has never been told anywhere; it has been revealed out of affection for you."
This jewel, which wards off the web of suffering, must not be disclosed; O Lord of All, perform the practice of yoga with careful heedfulness.
O Mahādeva, having established a connection with me, bring him under the power of time;
he does not establish a connection with me through the practice of spiritual accomplishments, devotion, ritual action, and so forth.
His sudden death is undoubtedly due to Time devouring him;
[I remain] only in the lotus of my heart, where the fruit of fulfillment has arisen.
In every form of the kingdom of the mind, crowded with various wonders, one should always worship and meditate upon me, Kākinī; of this there is no doubt. (56-13)
O Lord, by the grace of the heart-lotus, that yogi is born;
for all the gods, including Indra, reside within the center of the heart-lotus. (56.14)
Those who, devoted to a spirit of devotion, constantly worship me and meditate upon me,
O Great Hero, they behold me along with Indra.
Through the gradual union with the vital breath (prāṇa), they behold me without a doubt—me alone, the meditation on Kākinī, with steady breath and fierce power. (56.16)
Yogins perceive within their own bodies the eightfold sovereign powers of great luster;
through the yoga of devotion alone, they become supreme in the eternal yoga.
Having first performed the lotus-meditation (*padmadhyāna*), a man shall become a perfected one (*siddha*).
Listen, O Lord of Heroes, to that meditation which is difficult to attain here even for yogins. (56.18)
The heart-lotus, protected by the Kula, most beautiful and purified by the swan, is adorned with the brilliance of the tips of Bandhūka flowers; it is meditated upon by practitioners,
joined with an exceedingly sublime mass of rays, and red as if filled with vermilion.
The man who, having meditated, beholds [it] every day as enveloped by the dawn-colored [rays] beginning with the letter Ka; || 56-19 ||
He shall become a lord of ten million riches and an excellent man;
he who constantly performs the meditation on the syllables through the vision of the Eternal Lord (Nityeśvara) will attain success.
I shall now describe that entire meditation in its proper sequence, by which one becomes accomplished.
It is like a lotus situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar, radiant with the color of the sun, beginning with the letter 'Ka'. || 56-20 ||
Then, in the east, one should meditate upon the eternal, infinite Lord who has an exceedingly pure complexion,
whose pair of arms is joined with rays as red as the light of the rising sun,
and who possesses four arms and three eyes, seated within the solar orb.
He stands at the beginning of existence, his body adorned with the jar of his own abode.

On this second leaf, one should joyfully meditate thus upon the supreme wind-god, the divine serpent: his station is the support for the multitude of reddish clouds; he is the station of the venerable Tāriṇī; and he brings delight to both the wind and the sky.
Adorned with golden ornaments, possessing three eyes, and lacking a crown, he is composed of bliss.

On this third leaf, one should always meditate thus upon the Supreme Person, Śrī Gaṇapati, who holds a skull joined with the moon, has three eyes, possesses the luster of vermilion, and is endowed with the beauty of four arms.
Vibrating with a red appearance, adorned with a garland of fresh jewels, it has conquered intoxication.
In a four-petalled [lotus], one should meditate on Yama, tawny-red in hue, making a terrible sound,
skilled in action, possessing a body with three eyes like lotuses and four arms,
and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a shimmering crystal rosary and other attributes.
O Śiva, Śiva! I am the supreme Lord of the face, whose body is adorned with hoods. 56-24.
I bow to the seed-syllable *ṅaṃ*, as red as vermilion, the Lord of all, the three-eyed one;
the abode of great liberation, adorned with ornaments of jewels, gold, and gems;
the four-armed Rudra, the singular Bhava in the world, the all-pervading master of qualities.
I [salute] Him who bears the skull, the Śrīmāla, and the excellent Abhayaka.

I meditate upon that omnipresent Lord, who possesses four arms and the grace of a beautiful smile, who wears a garland of excellent lotuses, whose face is like a hundred moons, who has three eyes, who resembles the rising sun, and who is adorned with ornaments of every kind of jewel and gem.
A mass of great moonlight, whose body arises from drops of the supreme essence.
I meditate upon that one [deity] situated in the eye, who removes the impurity of the world, the ever-new sun, possessing four arms, joined with fair-bodied skulls,
drinking streams of nectar, and whose body is encircled by a golden rosary.
Three-eyed, the lord of yogis, seated upon an eight-petaled lotus, and possessing a beautiful countenance.
One should meditate upon the four-faced Lord, unborn and immortal, with a ruddy body, large eyes, subtle, consisting of the essence of equanimity, possessing the form of Brahman,
the four-armed God who is the foundation of the three worlds and fashioned from the essence.
Holding the great conch, Rudra, the boon-granting, fear-dispelling, and powerful one. || 56-28 ||

On the eighth petal, one should joyfully meditate upon the entire seed-syllable, which is a great body composed of splendor, a sacrificial oblation (caru), and the destroyer of desires, facing forward;
[and] like a mountain of great vermilion, as pure as ten million rays of the sun.
Three-eyed, five-faced, endowed with ten arms, and possessing a universal body.

One should meditate on the Lord of the Sky (Īśvara) as having three eyes and four arms, originating from the seed-syllable *ña* combined with the half-moon and the crest of the syllable *kha*; he is endowed with a beautiful lotus, a mace, and a discus,
pervaded by a great garland, and is the venerable one adorned with the beauty of excellent gold.
On the petal of the sun, [he is] like the morning sun and possesses the form of Viśvācī with matted hair.

On a petal as red as the dawn, one should meditate upon that unique Someśa, who is the Three-eyed Lord concealed by the form of Manu (Ma), possessing the seed-syllable *Ṭa* with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the moon (*indu*), holding a rosary, a water-pot, the gesture of granting boons, the gesture of fearlessness, and a sword, and wearing shimmering jeweled earrings.
With joy, I meditate upon Śambhu in my heart, within the lotus of perfection situated on the petal of auspiciousness.
The three-eyed one known as Kāma, who bestows the fruit of spiritual perfection out of compassion for children;
whose body is radiant with the luster of exquisite jewel ornaments; who is entirely free from sin;
the syllable *ṭha* joined with the *bindu* and the moon, emitting rays like ten million crores of suns.
And on the west, one should meditate upon the Sun-god, who holds an excellent lotus garland and carries a child.
This meditation on the pure abode of the mind is for the sake of attaining perfect consciousness;
if a lord of yogis, like Vasiṣṭha, performs the meditation on the recitation of the phonemes as the maṇḍala of the wish-fulfilling gem, he becomes the master of speech upon the earth.
Indeed, our Lord is not merely human; for he possesses the perfection of speech and dwells eternally throughout all things.
The lotus-circle of the heart is a palace of the wish-fulfilling gem;
in its center is the seat of the wind, circular in shape and radiant.
Pervaded by the flash of intuition (pratibhā), in the midst of that is the syllable of the wind;
resembling smoke shrouded [by mist], it is the supreme, well-known station. (56.35)
In the center of that is the supreme six-cornered mandala, the seat of the deity;
in its center, one should meditate upon the desired [deity], accomplished according to the specific ritual manual (kalpa) for each.
There, one should perform meditation on the wind as having an extremely subtle form—the supreme Brahman, which is formless, yet possesses form in the nature of sound. (56.37)
He is without syllables yet enriched with his own syllables; he is most fierce and possesses a stable form;
he has four arms, pervades the world, and holds a black antelope-skin bow and a barley-corn.

He who grants boons to the three worlds, whose form is the ocean of compassion, whose essence consists of the five elements, who is fierce, known as the vital breath (prāṇa), and who wears a crown. (56.39)
He who bears the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the bell, and the hand-drum;
he who is known by the name Īśa, the Supreme Swan, the Lord of the Kula.

The supreme practitioner should contemplate [the deity] whose limbs are radiant with every ornament, who is the cause for the arising of discernment (viveka), and who is surrounded by a multitude of attendants. (56.41)
There, upon that lotus, one should meditate on the Lord, who possesses color and form—the protector who brings auspiciousness to the three worlds, four-armed and wearing a crown. (56.42)
His limbs are adorned with garlands of jewels, he is white in color and possesses great radiance;
he is the Lord of Yogins, the Master, the Bestower of Boons, the Supreme Sovereign.

Adorned with the splendor of the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the conch, and the lotus; the ancient one, whose limbs are decorated with jewel ornaments, dwelling within the lotus of the heart.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord Paramahaṃsa, who bestows fruits exceeding one's desires and reveals the accomplishment of all states of being, within the circle of the heart-lotus.
Beside that, one should perform meditation upon Kākinī, the Supreme Goddess, the deity worshipped by the three worlds, who shines with a beak like that of a crow. (56.46)
Four-armed, yellow in color, adorned with yellow garments, having the form of nine million flashes of lightning, and possessing lotus-like eyes that flicker. || 56.47 ||
She is occupied with a skull, a moon, a trident weapon, and the gesture of granting boons;
she is adorned with golden ornaments fashioned from various jewels. || 56-48 ||

The Mistress of the Kula, who is the beauty of the three worlds, subtle, with lotus-hands granting boons and fearlessness, intoxicated by her delight in drinking nectar, and possessed of a perfect form.
I meditate upon Bhairavī of supreme bliss, who is adorned with garlands of jewel bracelets,
who dwells in the center of the lotus of the heart, and who moves with the gait of a swan.
In the midst of that collection of seats, one should contemplate a triangle,
[visualizing] the Power of the Seat (Pīṭhaśakti), richly golden and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
One who resembles a *kākinī*, intoxicated, with her inner faculties full and active, richly adorned with all ornaments, and surrounded by a host of attendants. (56–52)
On its southern side, one should meditate upon you as a pure liṅga,
resembling refined gold, stainless, and possessed of beautiful luster.
The bliss beloved by Mahālakṣmī, possessing all forms yet stainless, the dawning of the yoga of knowledge, whose nature is Brahman and who assumes manifold forms. || 56-54 ||
One should meditate upon the Lord Śiva in the form of a lamp-flame;
by grasping the knowledge of these [forms], one becomes the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśa) in an instant. (56–55)
There, O Lord, the practitioner should contemplate the accomplishment of the mantra for its success; there, the foremost of adepts should also contemplate the orb of the sun. (56–57)
One should meditate upon ten thousand Aruṇas within the center of a lotus filament;
by practicing this for just one month, the yogi shall become one whose limbs possess a cooling radiance.
In two months, there shall be the breaking of the knot (granthibheda), and one becomes possessed of infinite qualities;
in three months, one becomes fit for yoga and effects the destruction of poisons such as those of serpents.
For four months, the practitioner, pure in soul and steady-minded, remains thus;
when the fifth month arrives, the Vāyavī [power], endowed with compassion, appears.
The vital breaths became steady, the gaze became fixed, and there was an abundance of supreme happiness;
thereafter, day by day, there was an increase in the power of the vital breaths through his compassion. (56–60)
Within six months, freed from sin, he wanders for a long time like one who is liberated;
indeed, he shall never perish in water, in fire, or in a pit in the earth. (56–61)
He is the self of the Lord, a possessor of great knowledge, free from doubt and free from affliction;
he is a knower of the principles of great discernment, devoid of all sense of duality.
Having become long-lived and partaking in enjoyments day by day,
he was abandoned in the seventh kalpa as Madana, the embodiment of faults.
Day by day, there is the attainment of the qualities of eternal bliss and the relinquishing of the [lower] stages;
on the eighth, one becomes a destroyer of all enemies, liberated through the name of Rāma.

The vision of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the vision of Brahmā and Govinda; in the ninth [chapter], the accomplishment of purification, the abandonment of the earth, and the three-cubit [measure]. 56–65.
In the tenth [chapter], there is the perfection of yoga and the demonstration of the six cakras and so forth;
one who knows the piercing of the aperture of Brahmā becomes the embodiment of great bliss. (56–66)

In the eleventh [day], there is the attainment of all perfections; one wears limbs composed of the five elements, beholds the seven celestial heavens, and has a vision of the six Śivas who are dear to him.
In the twelfth [chapter], there is the honoring of the deity by the gods, the vision of the deity’s feet, the continuous stream of supreme bliss, and the removal of the net of illusion. (56–68)
Possessing divine devotion that brings about all knowledge and all accomplishments, they are the source of auspiciousness;
they are the heroes, they are the lords of yogis, they are the divine ones, and they are the Bhairavas.
All those who dwell for a long time in the great forest or in uninhabited mountains are conquerors of death; they are devotees who partake in liberation.
O Lord of the Family, those who maintain and accomplish this yoga—liberation arises from yoga through yoga; such is my definitive conclusion regarding the truth. (56–71)
Liberation, which is the crossing over from saṃsāra, is expressed by the word "yoga.
For in this world, yoga is difficult to attain; indeed, there is nothing higher than yoga. (56–72)
Yoga is said to be fivefold: one is considered the object [of meditation], the second has two divisions, and the third is *pūjā-yoga*. (56–73)
O Lord of the Kula, bhaktiyoga is the supreme essence of brahmayoga;
through the application of the mind everywhere, one will certainly become bound and then liberated.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Unstruck Lotus," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Wheels), in the section on Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* (Great Tantra Illuminator) of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in its Northern Section (*Uttaratantra*). 56.
Now begins the fifty-seventh chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"Henceforth, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the qualities of discernment."
For worship performed immediately after the meditation on the colors yields great fruit. || 57-1 ||
Through worship one may obtain worship, as well as discernment arising from inner disposition, union with the Lord of Kākinīs, and that state which is most difficult to attain. (57.2)
The sacrifice to the goddess Kākinī and the contemplation of the Lord—
O Śiva, even in the absence of formal worship, great siddhi arises from that very moment.
Through devotion, worship is attained; through worship, one attains solitude.
Through solitude, however, one attains the state of Brahman after ten million births.
Or else, by my grace, it may be obtained by you quickly as well;
listen to that method, O beloved of my life, O Lord of Tripura. (57-5)
He for whom supreme existence arises through mere consciousness should contemplate [the syllables] on the sides of the letters, proceeding in order toward the four directions.
To the Siddheśvaras who are absorbed in yoga and have taken refuge in the Great Being;
to Brahmā, the Supreme Haṃsa; and to Rudra, the Lord of the Universe and the Sovereign. (57–7)
Mṛtyuñjaya, Mahākāla, Nīlakaṇṭha, Sureśvara, Śrī Viṣṇu, Kamalānātha, Pañcacūḍa, and Kumāraka. (57–58)
Candra, Sūrya, Prajānātha, Dakṣa, Munīndra, Pracetas, Marīci, Kaśyapa, and likewise Pulaha. || 57-9 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Gautama, and the sage Kapila; Pulastya, Kratu, Prahlāda, and likewise Kardama. || 57-10 ||
And the seers Atharvan and Aṅgiras, the Bālakhilyas, the Marīcipas,
as well as the Mānasa, the Antarīkṣa, the sciences, and the all-pervading Wind.
Fire and water, earth and touch, as well as sound, form, taste, smell, primordial nature, and its transformations. || 57-12 ||
And for another reason, all beings— whether stationary or moving, and including the entire earth—
all the gods led by Indra constantly wander about its side.
And Agastya of great splendor, the heroic Mārkaṇḍeya, Yamadagni, Bharadvāja, Saṃvarta, and likewise Cyavana. (57-14)
And Durvāsas, O highly fortunate one, as well as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Dhāmīka,
the blessed Sanatkumāra, the teacher of yoga, and a man of great austerity.
Asita Devala, Jaigīṣavya the knower of reality,
Ṛṣabha, Ajitaśakra, and likewise Maṇi of great heroism.
Thus, Āyurveda and its eight branches shine as their own manifestations, like the moon with the constellations and the sun with its rays. (57.17)
The winds, the seasons, as well as Saṅkalpa and Prāṇa—these high-souled beings, possessed of form, are devoted to great vows. || 57-18 ||
These and many others worship the Lord;
these should be meditated upon at the sides by the best of practitioners among the castes. (57–19)
Standing at his side, he appeared radiant, bearing millions of splendors;
[he was] Artha, Dharma, Kāma, Harṣa, Dveṣa, as well as Dama.
There, the chiefs of the Gandharvas together with the Apsarases, as well as twenty-seven others and all the world-protectors (lokapālas), were present. (57.21)
Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Budha, Aṅgāraka, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and likewise all the other planets as well. || 57-22 ||
The mantra, the Rathantara, Haviṣmān, and Vasumān as well—the Ādityas, together with their sovereign kings—are worshipped by various assemblies. (57.23)
The Maruts, Viśvakarman, the Vasus, and the Kapālins, as well as all the hosts of Pitṛs and all the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi). || 57-24 ||
The Rigveda, the Samaveda, and likewise the Yajurveda and its injunctions, as well as the Atharvaveda and indeed all the scriptures. (57.25)
And the instruction of the Itihāsas, all the Vedāṅgas, the planets, the sacrifices, the Soma offerings, and all the deities; 57-26.
Sāvitrī, Tāriṇī, Durgā, and likewise the sevenfold Vāṇī;
as well as Medhā, Dhṛti, Smṛti, Prajñā, Buddhi, Yaśas, and Kṣamā. || 57-27 ||
The Sāman chants, the Vedic scriptures, and likewise various Gāthās, as well as commentaries joined with logic, shine forth as if they possessed bodies. (57.28)
Various dramas (nāṭikās) should be performed, as well as stories, narratives, and verses;
here abide those who are meritorious and those who are meritorious worshippers of their gurus.
O Śaṅkara, the moments, the lava-measures, the muhūrtas, day and night in their entirety, as well as the half-months, the months, and the six seasons [all proceed from you].
The years, the five-fold cycle, the months, and the fourfold night;
that which is the substance of the wheel of time—eternal, imperishable, and undecaying.
Likewise, O Maheśvara, the Wheel of Dharma remains eternally present;
as do Aditi, Diti, Rudra, and Vinatā. (57.32)
Kālikā, the youthful goddess Surasā, and then Gautamī, Prādhā, and Kadru—these indeed are the goddesses who are the mothers of the deities. || 57-33 ||
Rudrāṇī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Bhadrā, and likewise the supreme Ṣaṣṭhī; the goddess known as Pṛthivī, Hrīḥ, Svāhā, Kīrti, and Revā. (57.34)
Surā, Devī, Śacī, as well as Puṣṭi and Arundhatī; Saṃsiddhi, Siddhidā, Vidyā, Mahādevī, and likewise Rati. (57-35)
These and other goddesses, beautifully adorned, attended upon him;
as did the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and the two Aśvins.
O Lord, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Pitṛs, the great Ṛṣis, and the royal sages such as Hariścandra and others shine there. (57.37)
All wore golden earrings and were adorned with every ornament;
they were full of passion, their bodies immersed in the sounds of singing, instrumental music, and the like.
They meditate upon Maheśānī Kākinī, the Supreme Goddess, who is the eternal digit in the form of the phonemes, the devoted wife of Maheśvara. (57.39)
These beings constantly meditate upon and worship the Lord;
they are beautifully adorned, and they bestow the abundance of the eight supernatural powers. (57.40)
These radiant energies (prabhās), who move by the side of Mahākāla’s body and color, are to be worshipped;
one should worship them mentally with the names "Be gracious, O Lord" and "O Master. (57.41)
"Sarasvatī, whose form is the phonemes (varṇa), is to be worshipped with this very mantra: 'I worship Kākinī, the beloved bliss of the Lord of Phonemes (Varṇeśvara). (57–42)
Then, in the Kali age, the Śrīkākinīs become propitious and grant success.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Worship of the Attendants on the Side of Kākinīśvara," within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 57.
Now begins the fifty-eighth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O venerable Candraśekhara, now listen to the majesty of the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi)."
Likewise, the extraction of the mantra, the ritual placement (nyāsa), and the armor for the limbs, which are dear to you. || 58-1 ||
The hymn known as the Thousand Names, together with the beloved eight-and-one-hundred mantra, and the entire visualization with form, bestow the state of Sālokya and other realms. (58-2)
By the mere performance of which a human becomes a god;
just as from the seed of a tree a tree arises, and through faith the fruit comes forth. (58.3)
In that very same way, the arising of mantras occurs through the application of seed-syllables (*bīja*).
The seed-syllable is indeed supreme knowledge; the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is dependent upon the seed-syllable. (58.4)
Depending upon the seed-syllable (bīja), all the great-splendored lords appear, resembling ten million suns, residing in the locus of the vital breath (prāṇa). 58-5.
Some possessed the radiance of ten thousand suns, some the splendor of a hundred suns;
some had the brilliance of twelve suns, and some shone with the light of a single sun.
Who indeed is this radiant sage? Who is this one with a splendor equal to the moon?
Who is this one with rays of glorious beauty, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace? || 58.7 ||
These five deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Ānanda, and Bhairava—are born from seeds and are also seedless; they are the deities of the vital breath. (58–8)
Brahmā enters the path of the breath in the form of Brahma;
the Lord Viṣṇu, as the Vaiṣṇava principle, is within the kumbhaka [retention]. (58–59)
The Lord Śiva, who has reached the great dissolution in his form as the Destroyer, is the glorious Ānandabhairava, the knower of the root-knowledge, higher than the highest. (58–10)

From the root-lotus up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), she enters there in the form of the eternal seed-syllable, which is the very nature of the science of vital breath (prāṇavidyā). || 58-11 ||
That [reality] is to be cultivated by yogis; it is intensely cultivated through the limbs of yoga.
O Lord, without the Yogaśāstra, which great sages could possibly know it? (58.12)
That mind-essence (*manoyavā*), which is to be known by yogis, is extremely difficult to master;
it takes various forms and vast forms, and it manifests as inhalation and exhalation. (58.13)
Residing in the center of the heart-lotus, she dwells in the abode of the Lord;
shining like the beak of Kāla, she is situated in the hearts of all beings. (58.14)
She is the creator of knowledge for all, the producer of all bliss within the heart;
she is that Goddess Kākinī, the Vidyā, the Sovereign, the supreme Kalā. (58-15)
One should meditate upon her who possesses the radiance of ten million suns and a countenance equal to ten million moons;
for her mantra is the great mantra, the mantra of Brahmā for yogins. (58.16)
Listen with joy, O Lord Kulānanda, to the mantra of Bhairavī and the others;
by the power of this mantra, one may bring even the Supreme Self (Parātmā) under one's control.
Having uttered the long *praṇava*, one should extract the left eye;
at the end of *māyā*, one should extract the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbhava*) and the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*).
The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) likewise for sovereignty, followed by "namas" and the Fire-Lady (Svāhā);
by the grace of this mantra, one shall become subject to the power of time in an instant. (58-19)
One attains ultimate happiness and becomes the remover of fear and ignorance;
O Lord, [one should recite] the mantra enveloped by Kāma or by Vāgbhava as well. (58-20)
Having encapsulated it with one's own mantra, success will be attained here without delay.
Now I shall speak of another mantra; listen attentively. (58-21)
Having extracted Bhadrakālī, one should extract the Kiṅkiṇī seed-syllable;
having extracted the Bālā seed-syllable, [the mantra is] "Māheśvaryai namaḥ" ending with Dviṭha (svāhā). || 58-22 ||
One should worship with supreme devotion within the mandala of the heart-lotus, [the deity] encased by the root mantras alone or by the various root mantras. 58-23.
This mantra is not to be disclosed; it is concealed in all tantras.
Through one hundred thousand recitations, success shall be attained, and one shall become firmly established in the lotus of the heart. (58.24)
Suddenly, one perceives the life-force (jīva) in the form of a lamp-flame;
thereafter, through the practice of the mantra of Īśvarī, one becomes a great yogin.
I shall describe the supreme meditation, more secret than the secret of worship;
having meditated [upon the Lord], O Protector, with flowers imagined by the mind, one should offer water for the feet and other honors. (58.26)
One should worship with supreme devotion, being intent upon mantra and meditation. || 58-27 ||
She possesses the splendor of the light of a hundred million moons;
she is the stainless beauty of the qualities of the celestial wish-fulfilling tree, holding the Vedas in her hands;
her forehead is like the rays of the rising sun, and her garland of pearls is shimmering.
In the center of the lotus of my heart, I worship that venerable Sovereign Lady.
Having thus meditated upon her, who possesses all forms, within the lotus of the heart,
one should indeed worship her again and again with flowers born from the three worlds.
One certainly attains success through the power of the yoga of worship;
worship that generates longevity and health yields very great fruit. (58.30)
Then one should recite the great mantra according to the sequence of the garland of syllables;
having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should then perform the placement [of mantras] upon the center of all the limbs.
One should place [the offerings] upon the mass of the *mātṛkā*-knots using the names previously mentioned,
and indeed by those very names which were stated in the preceding chapter.
Having performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) encased within mantras, one should then proceed;
thereafter, one should perform the placement of the eight powers of Kākinī.
Kākajihvā, Dvikāṇḍeśī, Kāmākhyā, Kākinī, Dhvajā, Kākinī, Kākamālā, and Kākacañcuprakāśinī. || 58-34 ||
Having assigned [the letters] on the head by way of the names of the eight powers of the cuckoo (kokilā),
one should subsequently place the sixteen vowels encapsulated within the hollow of the throat.
O Lord, one should place the twelve-fold *kādi* enclosure in the heart;
having placed the mantra according to the rule, one should place the enclosure with the mantra at the navel.

Having placed the letters from *ḍa* to *pha* in one's own *liṅga*, and the letters from *va* to *la* in the *mūlādhāra*, [one should place] the letters from *va* to *sa* encased within the root mantra.

Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) and having bound the limbs [of the mantra], one should then perform a single breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and take refuge in the vital breaths (*prāṇas*). || 58-38 ||
Then the wise one should recite the hymn; listen to all of that, O Śaṅkara.
Having become self-controlled and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), he should accomplish this for the sake of success in this world. (58–39)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Siddhi of Kākinī," in the Uttara-tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala.
Now begins the fifty-ninth chapter.
The auspicious Jñāneśvarī, the bestower of welfare, spoke: "She is to be meditated upon."

I praise that Kākinī, the supreme Śivā, the consort of the Supreme Lord, who dwells within the center of the lotus-throne of my beautiful heart, [and who is worshipped] by the lords of yoga, by Hari and Hara, by the gurus, and by the great Indras. (59–1)
Alone at the time of the destruction of the three worlds,
you, Kākinī, are like the wife of a crow in the ocean of battle;
you stand as the witness to the dissolution of the universe.
Like a female buffalo in a thicket of bushes, we take refuge [in you]. || 59-2 ||
When the time for sustaining the entire body has arrived, you, Kākinī, are sustained alone; when the seat of the vital breath is established and the fluctuations of the mind are swiftly destroyed.
Thus I praise Her, who is moved by the beak of the king of crows. 59.3

O Bhuvaneśvarī, you who delight in the manifestation of being and in the attainment of the beloved; O Supreme Goddess, you who possess the splendor of the joy of yoga and are as beautiful as a garland of Mandāra flowers.
Perform protection first; I take refuge in your wisdom.
At the rising of the moon, you are full of bliss, radiant with millions of rays of light;
when the cowherd girls arrive, those of pure intellect find their own minds purified. O you who are worshipped through the intensity of devotion, may you become the very essence of happiness!
Perform protection; I praise the foot of the first Sun.
I incessantly worship those lotus feet,
which possess a mass of pure being and joyful drops,
and whose limbs are beautifully adorned with garlands of pure guñjā berries and vaṭī beads.
May she alone be the one who grants me the final collection of my existence.
O five-faced one, ten-armed, endowed with all weapons; O Knowledge, O source of fear, O Nṛhari adorned with a necklace of human heads;
seated upon a corpse, three-eyed—you alone are my mother.
O auspicious one, for protection, I take refuge at your lotus-feet. || 59-7 ||
O Śrī Sundarī, protector of those who bow before you, Mother of the Vedas, O Tāreśvarī, may you also protect me at the time of destruction,
if I am a devoted follower and a speaker of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
I praise the lotus feet of Hara, which are eternally beloved.
All of them constantly worship that abode of Śrī, the essence of the world, served by the infinite, the seat of yoga, the refuge for the wise, and the singular union,
for the sake of their own liberation.
I am wretched, O Mother, Sovereign of the World; I worship you with joy. || 59-9 ||
The state worshipped by the three worlds, residing in the lotus of the heart;
experienced as one's own bliss within the lotus that illumines the mind;
resting upon *māyā*, it is the very form of the source of all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
I take refuge in the Supreme One, who is bent by the weight of his anklets and necklaces. || 59-10 ||
O you who are adorned with beautiful garlands of lotuses, necklaces, and crowns;
O bringer of splendor, remain most firmly within the lotus of my heart!
For on this earth, he alone is truly powerful and has accomplished his purpose.
I joyfully take refuge in you, the Sovereign, within my heart with ease. || 59-11 ||
Formerly, for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga, she worshipped the eternal one; she who was known as Śambhugīrīśā went to the side of Īśvara,
and reached the station of the Lord of Union (Sāyujyanātha) at the feet of Īśakāntā.
Alone, she possesses the pair of feet of the Kulavata; what need is there for others? || 59-12 ||
Here, yogins meditate upon the mountain of the multitude of evils for the sake of destroying the constant suffering caused by dissolution,
for the joy of the mind, for spiritual power, and for the victory of the earth.
I am wretched; quickly grant me a place for the sake of your prosperity. || 59-13 ||
O You who possess the colors black, white, pure yellow, and deep red—
protect me, who am utterly wretched, by taking refuge in Your own beautiful lotus feet as my son.
O bestower of desires, make it very firm upon the blue lotus. || 59-14 ||

O Sovereign of All, performer of what is dear, destroyer of worldly existence and its latent tendencies, manifold and wondrous, you who fulfill the desires of those prostrate before you with various sounds— if you grant me the state of bliss, grant me the service of a servant!
And I take refuge in you, whose beautiful complexion has faded. || 59-15 ||
O Ratnākara, compassionate one, with the hue of the rising sun,
whose limbs are adorned with a rosary fashioned from gold and other precious materials—
if you, O Kākinī, cast even a single glance upon me;
Perform everything; rejoice on the path to happiness and liberation.
O you who are pure like fresh coral, adorned with stainless garlands;
O you who are subtle, yet the source of a multitude of most subtle [qualities]; O treasure-house of compassion!
O child, O strength, O restless one, O fickle one, O you of sweet chatter!
O Mistress of Yoga, I take refuge in the lotus feet of the Kula. || 59-17 ||
(kha) You are the sixteenth [digit], most fierce, with a sharp sword in hand;
you are Khaḍgeśvarī, whose face is enriched by harsh words and laughter;
you who are radiant with a necklace of dates, O destroyer of the wicked—to you!
Constant salutations, salutations to you who are served by Upendra and the king of mountains.
I bow eternally to the swift boat that has crossed over the ocean of worldly existence;
to her who is the mistress of the body, the remover of obstacles, and she who is served by the Lord of Ganas;
for they sing the sublime hymn to your lotus feet.
It must not be neglected because of the fierce and turbid nature of the protection [required]. || 59-19 ||
O you of long vowels, of dense excellence, of deep and terrible sound;
O you of the terrible face, of fresh clouds, of the union of the dense;
O abode of the terrible, situated in the jar, the destroyer of the void within the jar!
May you, O Kākinī, protect me from the entire web of faults of the earth. || 59-20 ||
(Ṅa) O Smaraharā, you who possess the science of form;
O you who are the consort, the powerful destroyer of enemies; O Protectress, protect me thoroughly! Have compassion and grant me liberation.
And, O Caṇḍī, whose eyes are fierce, I worship your feet. || 59-21 ||
(Cha) O you who hold the parasol, who remove deceit, who dwell in the heart-lotus; O you who abide in the yoga that is imperishable within the heart-lotus!
(Ja) O bearer of victory, I, the son of the Lord of the Yadus, worship you!
O Victorious One, grant me victory; I worship at your feet. || 59-22 ||
(jha) In the syllable *jhaṅ*, you cause the enemy to tremble here and drink [him];
you are Kauśikī, the purifier of the entire body. (na) You are the eternal one, the state of the nasal sound (*anunāsika*), the bestower of all meanings.
O you who possess a cluster of noble virtues, provide protection against misfortune! (59-23)
(Ṭa) You are the one who utters the sound "ṭaṅkāra," you are the loud laughter, and you are the "ṭalala" of the boisterous laugh.
(Ṭha) You are the one who acts with firm resolve, the destroyer of the deceitful, and you are perfectly established.
You dwell upon the back of the lion, the beloved of the gods, and you possess a state of unwavering yoga.
Always place [her] in the lotus of the heart, O bestower of all goals! || 59-24 ||
The wise one, devoted to meditation and ritual placement (nyāsa), should recite this hymn;
the yogin who praises [the deity] after having meditated upon it shall become a partaker of liberation. 59-25.
He beholds the three worlds situated within the center of the lotus of his heart;
endowed with the eight supernatural powers, that man quickly becomes liberated while living.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Hymn to Kākinī," in the section on Accomplished Mantras within the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, the Great Tantra Illuminator. 59.
Now begins the sixtieth chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"O beloved Parānanda, O Kulasundarī, tell me the secret."
By the mere knowledge of whom, one becomes Hari, the bearer of the Gaṅgā. || 60-1 ||
This supreme hymn to Brahman concerning Īśvara is the means for attaining Nirvāṇa;
it belongs to Yogendra, the Lord of Yoga, who possesses millions of splendors and is the Supreme Lord.
Who does not honor Īśvara, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others?
By the mere remembrance of him, one becomes a great orator and a conqueror of death.
The great seers worship Him as the final conclusion of Vedānta;
gods, humans, and gandharvas worship that Maheśvara. (60.4)
O Śāṅkarī, I desire to hear the divine hymn of praise for him who removes untimely death, who is ever-present and whose face is turned toward all directions. (60.5)
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said: O Kaula, listen to this hymn of praise to the Lord of Him, which is dear to Śaṅkara:
"Salutations with joy to you, O Śrīnātha, Lord of the Kula, Supreme Lord of Life!"

Homage to Sānanda, to Bhava, to the Lord, to the Sovereign of the World; Oṃ, homage! Homage to you, the Lord of Beings, the Master of the Gaṇas, the Ascetic, the Wielder of the Auspicious Trident. || 60-6 ||
Obeisance to the beloved, the primordial sound (*praṇava*), the Lord of Yoga, the Sovereign of Yoga; Oṃ, obeisance!
Constant obeisance to the Great One, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Eternal!
To Hari, the piercer of the *svādhiṣṭhāna* [cakra], who penetrates the root-lotus.
Salutation to the one who pierces the lotus at the navel and causes the ocean of the heart to burst forth.
Constant salutations to the radiant one, who is Time, the primordial *praṇava*, and the master of *māyā*;
salutations to you, the liberation, the lord of the Pramathas, the seer, who holds a skull-topped staff in hand;
salutations to the noble refuge of *māyā*, the treasure-house of devotion and glory, who moves through the sky as the great Indra.
Again, salutations to the one who is consciousness, auspiciousness, subtle in movement, and hidden. || 60-8 ||
Salutations to the Omniscient One, to the Victorious One, to the Lord of Prosperity, to the Sovereign of Beings, O Master!
To the Five-faced One, to Hara, to the Lord of the Gods, to the Lord of Gaurī, to Śrī! To the Enjoyer who dwells within, to Hari-Hara, whose form is blissful consciousness!
Salutations to you, who are auspiciousness and fortune; salutations to you, whose intellect is eternally pure. || 60-9 ||

Salutations again and again to you, O Kāla, the beloved of Govinda, the Creator, the source of the birth of Brahmā and the other gods; to you, the external primordial nature (prakṛti) of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; to you, the Lord of the Universe, the mountain-dweller who manifests through the yoga of cosmic dissolution.
O All-pervading Lord, worshipped by the King of Mountains, you are the knower and the sovereign of all beings, eternally.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Gaurī, who is praised by the Gaṇas, the venerable mind, and the dweller upon the earth;
to you, the primordial principle, whose majesty is the energy of all beings, the Lord of the Earth, the moon-crested one, and the eternally awakened;
to you who are perpetually filled with eternal digits and crowned by serpents.
O Lord of the pacification of splendor, O Lord of the lords of the virtuous, O you who are without clothing, salutations to you! || 60-11 ||

O Lord, salutations again and again to you, who are endowed with millions of splendors, who gladden with the rays of the moon, who are subtle, and who are the festival of the ocean of bliss for those who bow before you;
O Master, beloved of Heramba, Śiva, Skanda, and Janaka!
To the father, the source of all happiness, the lord of all, Śrī Nīlakaṇṭheśvara.

Obeisance to you, O Lord, the Master of the Kula, who brings about the arising of bliss for yogins; who is the threefold Brahman, the yellow one, the source of existence, the divine lover, and the illustrious radiant one;
who is the mountain of silver, the perfected state of beauty, and the lineage of the bliss of Brahman.
Salutation to the Truth, which brings joy to all, which is supreme, and which is abundant. || 60-13 ||
Kāśīśa, Kauśikīśa, the radiance of the celestial tree, known as Kāraṇa and known as Sukha;
Gaurīśa, Gaṅgirīśa, the Guru whose limbs are smeared with the mountain ranges of aguru and vaṅga;
he who is called Ghoṣa, Mañjughoṣa, joined by a multitude of clouds, and possessing a terrible sound of clashing thunder.
O Lord of Cārvīśa, Lord of Rāghaveśa, O Lord who manifests within the heart of the cloud, O Lord of Ghaṭaka! || 60-14 ||

O Śambhu, may you always protect Vaśiṣṭha, the presiding lord of beings, who dwells within your hand—whether stationary or moving—like a vessel of lac; he is ever devoted to his own family circle. Your restless garland of shimmering jewel-rows is not capable of bestowing devotion and knowledge.
Terrified of the world and stained by blemish, he [seeks] your lotus feet, which are the source of glory for the crowns of hundreds of Brahmās.
The rogue Śauri is peaceful, delighting in the pure and sweet fragrance [of your feet], ever vigilant;
he is the goddess of the delusion of illusion, the destroyer of the pride of the gods, and the giver of gifts and honor.
O Lord, how is it that you do not protect your own feet, the stainless lotuses at your base?
Facing east, facing south, with the face of the Lord of Wealth, and facing west—you are the Sage.
O Lord of the Daughter of the Kalagiri Mountain, you are the divider, the one whose rays are the treasure of the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, the cause possessing infinite power,
the manifest wish-fulfilling cow, the lord of the Lord of Wealth, and one who delights in all enjoyments;
for in your lotus feet resides eternally that sovereignty over yogis.
My mind, known as "the flickering," has attained the perfection of yoga through the moon-rayed Lord of Speech. || 60-17 ||
May the victorious conqueror, whose matted locks are adorned with the excellent sword Śrīkhaḍga and who holds a mace in his four arms,
who achieves victory through the art of concealing his true form by shrinking his dense shadow,
and who is most illustrious— may he emulate the victory of Jāyejaya.
In this world, my anger is like a momentary flash in a blazing, violent storm.

Then [there appeared] the Axe, who dwells within the hollow of the wheel of command, his matted locks concealed; he is manifested by the hundreds of millions of points on the edge of his blade to shatter those who violate their vows; he is wrathful, a destroyer of the hard-shelled, and resides upon the back of a tortoise.
Having bowed to the one whose name begins with the letter 'ka' and who possesses ten rays, may he protect me always. (60.19)
O Kulapati, by the recitation of the hymn to the goddess Sudhākhaṇḍā,
one’s own fortune increases, as does the beloved lotus-foot [of the Lord].
If the station of Mṛtyuñjaya prevails upon this preeminent portion of the earth, [all blessings follow].
Trembling with love, he suddenly cooks the abundant amusement.
If one should thus recite this unfixed hymn, joined with the *Kaulāvalī*,
which is the locus of a mind solely intent upon the supreme bliss of the burden of essential secrets,
it bestows the state of a lord of yogis, the fruit of liberation, and the station of sovereignty over all.
One shall obtain that which is the union of the moon and the sun, consisting solely of the bliss of the supreme state. || 60-21 ||

O Śambhu, if that auspicious creeper which is the lotus-foot of yours is always worshipped by the yogin for the sake of attaining the perfection of the qualities of nirvāṇa, [then he succeeds]. (60.22)
What indeed cannot be accomplished between the eyebrows through the grace of devotion to Śiva? || 60-23 ||

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Gods," in the *Anāhata-padmam* of the *Rudrayāmala*, the Northern Tantra (*Uttara-tantra*), which illuminates the Great Tantra (*Mahātantra-uddīpana*). 60.
Now begins the sixty-first chapter.
The illustrious Ānandabhairava said:
"Speak, O auspicious one, O Mistress of Desire, you who are worshipped throughout the three worlds!"
In the infinite abode of the cosmic egg, resplendent upon the peak of Kailāsa; || 61-1 ||
O you who abide in the eternal moment, who dwell in the Night of Time, who are served by Mahākāla,
and whose very nature is the Sound-Brahman— you ought to speak with reverence.
Immediately following is the "One Thousand Names" (Sahasranāma) yoga, consisting of one hundred and eight names;
it is the essence of infinite millions of cosmic eggs and the supreme auspiciousness. (61-3)
It directly brings about the perfection of knowledge, increases ultimate bliss, serves the purpose of liberation through the language of convention, and is united with the Lord Kākinī. (61.4)
O fair-faced one, at the beginning, out of affection and from the joy of being turned toward [the Self], he [perceived] Brahman, which produces supreme bliss and is cherished as the state of Nirvāṇa.

O Mother, O beautiful goddess of the worlds, I desire that you always quickly relate to me the accounts of our connection, which is characterized by an overflowing surge of the essence of affection and bliss.
The illustrious Ānandabhairavī said: O Lord, O Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, adorned with a garland of serpents;
O you enriched by a variegated necklace of the lords of snakes, O Supreme Lord, sovereign of the serpent-kings! (61–7)

This auspicious Thousand Names, rich with the yoga of the Lord of Kākinīs, consists of one hundred and eight verses; it has the form of a circle and possesses the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes.
Listen attentively to me regarding that which generates longevity and health—
the eternal essence of infinite millions of universes, higher than the highest.
This is the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman, the practice of yoga for those engaged in yoga,
the secret refinement for omniscience, and the bestower of the fruits of such refinements and other practices.
It directly accomplishes all desires, destroys great sins, pacifies extreme poverty, and bestows supreme sovereignty. (61.11)
He who, being delighted, recites [the names] in the morning, at midday, and when the sun has set;
having offered salutations, he should recite the name, being devoted to the yoga of meditation. (61-12)
Having first practiced meditation upon the union with Kākinīśvara, which gives rise to the qualities of meditation, one becomes stainless through a pure mind. (61.13)
One should meditate upon the goddess Mahākālī, who is Kākinī, whose form is Time,
who is intoxicated by the essence of supreme bliss, who is dark-hued, the supreme granter of desires.
Four-armed, bearing a sword, a shield, a boon-granting gesture, and a lotus, she is Hara;
she causes the destruction of enemies and is adorned with millions of jewel ornaments. (61.15)
She relishes the essence of youthful bliss, wears yellow garments, and is enchanting; she is graced with armlets and necklaces, and adorned with a pair of earrings.
The Sovereign Goddess, known as Kāmaratnā, with a face like the beak of a crow, beautiful and adorned with a forest garland, seated upon a lovely lion-throne. || 61-17 ||
Having thus meditated on her who possesses the radiance of lightning in the sky within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, one should recite the auspicious names again and again. (61.18)
One should meditate upon the Lord in the circle of the heart, possessing the splendor of ten million suns,
four-armed, heroic in form, and endowed with the beauty arising from his divine nature.
Dark-complexioned, with limbs adorned with golden ornaments, as cool as ten million moons,
the all-pervading Lord holds the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, as well as a lotus and a great sword.
