Wearing a crown, possessing a massive body, radiant with a smiling laugh, situated in the center of the heart-lotus, and adorned with anklets. (61.21)
Having thus mentally visualized the supreme lord, the yogin, as the blazing fire of the end of the aeon (koṭikālānala) situated to the right of Kākinī; 61–22.
Then one should recite that which is called the Thousand-fold; listen to it, O Lord.

Of this *Śrī Kākinīśvara Sahasranāmastotra*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), the goddess Kākinī, sovereign of the world, is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining the yoga of Nirvāṇa and for the attainment of spiritual perfections (*siddhi*) during recitation.
Oṃ. She is the Lord, the Sovereign of Kākinīs, the Ruler, the Mistress of the Lotus.
Īśa, Kākeśvarīśānī, Īśvarīśa, and Kuleśvarī. || 61-24 ||
Īśamokṣa, Kāmadhenu, Kapardīśa, Kapardinī, Kaula, Kulīnāntaragā, Kavi, and Kāvyaprakāśinī. || 61-25 ||
Kalādeśa, Sukavitā, Kāraṇa, Karuṇāmayī, Kañjapatrekṣaṇa, Kālī, Kāma, and Kolāvalīśvarī. (61.26)
The one in the form of a Kirāta, Kaivalya, the ray that destroys desire,
the Lord of Karṇāṭa with Karṇāṭī, Kalika, and she who is the vessel for Kālikā.
The youthful one, whose mass of hair is like a swarm of bees, is the Sovereign of the Family;
she is curved like the filaments of a flower and delights in the King of Desire.
Karakoṭidhara, Kūṭā, Kriyākrūra, Kriyāvatī, Kumbhahā, Kumbhahantrī, Kaṭaka, Chakalāvatī. || 61-29 ||
Kañjavaktra, Kālamukhī, Koṭisūryakarānanā;
Kamra, Kalapa, Samṛddhisthā; Kupa-antastha, Kulācalā. (61.30)
Kuṇapa, Kaulapākāśā, Svakāntā, Kāmavāsinī, Sukṛti, Śāṅkarīvidyā, Kalaka, and Kalanāśrayā. (61.31)
Karkandhustha, Kaulakanyā, Kulīna, Kanyakākulā, Kumāra, Keśarī, Vidyā, Kāmahā, and Kulapaṇḍitā. (61-32)
Kalkīśa has lovely limbs; Kuśalāvatī is skillful.
He is richly adorned with garlands of *ketakī* flowers; she is endowed with *ketakī* blossoms. (61.33)
Rich with garlands that delight in flowers, she is a pure garland of blossoms;
she is the sovereign poet born from poetry, and the one who delights in the anklets of desire.
Seated upon an auspicious throne, she is the sovereign of the family of Kauśalyā;
she is the wish-fulfilling tree, the celestial tree, the wish-granting creeper, free from conceptual construction, and she who proceeds through the eons.
Abiding in the firm, she is like gold, formidable, and dwells in Time;
she is the bliss that takes refuge in the Kālakūṭa poison and flows through the harsh ether.
Having the appearance of smoke from a funeral pyre, seated in a formidable posture, he is a bearer of a body who creates pits; having attained the Karavīra state, he is a ploughman. (61.37)
She whose speech ends with a deep, resonant sound like that of time, whose mind delights in playful discourse;
she who is the Lord of Nature, whose nature is true, who is preeminent, and the sovereign mistress of the senses.
The Blessed One, possessing the complexion of Varuṇī, was of radiant form;
he was of golden hue, shining like gold, great, and honored by Mahendra.
The Great-Souled One, the Great Sovereign Lady, the Great Lord, she of intoxicated gait;
the Great Hero, the Great Velocity, the Lord of Great Lakṣmī, and Intelligence.
Mahādeva, Mahādevī, Mahānanda, Mahākalā;
Mahākāla, Mahākālī, Mahābala, Mahābalā. || 61-41 ||
Mahāmānya, Mahāmānyā; Mahādhanya, Mahādhanī; Mahāmāla, Mahāmālā; Mahākāśa, Mahākāśā. || 61-42 ||
He of great fame, he of great sacrifice, the great king, the great ruler;
he of great knowledge, the great lore, the great leader, the great performer of the *makha* sacrifice. || 61-43 ||
Mahārātra, Mahārātri, Mahādhīra, Mahāśayā;
Mahākṣetra, Mahākṣetrā, Kurukṣetra, Kurupriyā. || 61-44 ||
Mahācaṇḍa and Mahogrā, Mahāmatta and Mahāmati, Mahāveda and Mahāvedā, Mahotsāha and Mahotsavā. || 61-45 ||
Mahākalpa, Mahākalpā, Mahāyoga, Mahāgati; Mahābhadra, Mahābhadra, Mahāsūkṣma, Mahācalā. || 61-46 ||
She is the great utterance, the great speech, the great sacrificer, and the great speed;
she is the great form, the greatly beloved, the great dharma, and the great wealth.
Mahāmahogra, Mahiṣī, Mahābhogya, Mahāprabhā, Mahākṣema, Mahāmāyā, Mahāmāyā, and Mahāramā. || 61-48 ||
The Mother worshipped by Mahendra, Vibhālā, the Sovereign of the Maṇḍala,
Mahāvikālā, Vikalā, and she who moves upon the excellent surface of the earth.
The giver of liberation, the one who delights in liberation, the one who dwells in wonder, the destroyer;
she who is like a young girl, whose husband is a child, who is Balarāma, and from whom the strong-bodied ones are born.
She who is free from stain, the heroine of desire, the mistress of life, and the protector of life;
she who dwells in the fifth conduct, who is beyond the five and the non-five, and the sovereign of the fifth.
She is the manifestation of the five flavors, yet free from conceptual proliferation; she consists of compassion, can assume any form at will, and is devoid of desire and anger.
She whose soul is desire, whose abode is desire, who is named desire, who is as fickle as desire;
she who bears the flower of desire, who is desire itself, who is the Lord of Desire, and who is the one who causes desire to blossom. || 61-53 ||
He who bears the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is the Seal, the True Seal, the Seal of Desire;
he whose forehead shines with the half-moon, his lotus-face possessing a mouth like ten million moons. 61–54.
She who bears the radiance of ten million moons, whose nature is like the light of the moon;
she who has the splendor of the sun, with heroic rays, and who is illumined by ten million suns.
Mihireśa is Mānavakā, Antarggāmī is Nirāśrayā, Prajāpatīśa is Kalyāṇī, and Dakṣeśa is Kularohiṇī. || 61-56 ||
Apracetā, who dwells in the abode of Pracetas; Vyāseśī, who is worshipped by Vyāsa;
Kāśyapeśī, the mistress of Kāśyapa; Bhṛgvīśī, the sovereign of the Bhṛgus. || 61-57 ||
Vasiṣṭha abides in a state of loving-kindness; she who is free from the afflictions of Vasiṣṭha is the goddess honored by Pulastya, dwelling within the mind of Pulastya.
Agastyārghya, Agastyamātā, Prahlādeśa, Valīśvarī, Kardameśa, Kardamādyā, Bālaka, and Bālapūjitā. (51–59)
Abiding in the mind and abiding in the intermediate space, Sarasvatī is the knower of sound;
she transcends form, is void of form, is formless, and deludes all forms. (61–60)
The Lord of Vidyādharas, the Mistress of Vidyās, seated upon the bull, borne by the bull;
the Knower of Tastes, the Bliss of the Connoisseurs, the Tasteless One, and the Conqueror of Passion. 61–62.
Saṇa is the lord of Sanatkumāra; Yogacaryeśvara is his beloved.
Durvāsas is the abode of the vital breaths; [she] is born from Sāṅkhya and Yoga. (61–62)
Asaṅkhyeyā, Māṃsabhakṣā, Sumāṃsāśī, Manoramā, Naramāṃsavibhoktrī, and Naramāṃsavinodinī. (61–63)
Mīnavaktrapriya, Mīna, Mīnabhuṅ, Mīnabhakṣiṇī, Rohitāśī, Matsyagandhā, Matsyanātha, and Rasāpahā. (61–64)
She is a mass of love for Pārvatī, worshipped by Brahmā and the lords of the gods;
she is the bestower of boons upon the Creator, the one to be known, the Veda, and the maiden who embodies the Vedas.
Śyāmeśa is white in color, and [his consort] is dark with a dark form;
she is a great consumer of intoxicating liquor and is fond of great intoxicating liquor. (61–66)

She was one whose outflows were destroyed, free from mental affliction, pure, and devoid of impure intoxicants; she was free from attachment, sober, yet possessed the gait of an elephant in rut. (61–67)
Wearing a garland of jewels, the lord of the Mātṛkās, with a serene intellect; the remover of old age and death, Gaurī, established in song, free from aging and death.
Sucañcalā is exceedingly difficult to subdue; Kaṇṭhasthā is virtuous; Hṛdgatā is free from sorrow; Aśoka resides on Mount Mandara; and Mantriṇī indeed dwells there as well. (61–69)

The bliss of one who wears the garland of mantras; the illuminator of mantras and yantras; the creator of the consciousness of the meaning of mantras; the illuminator of the accomplishment of mantras. || 61–70 ||
She is the knower of mantras, the abode of mantras, the meaning of mantras, and the mantra-practitioner herself.
Abiding everywhere through the meditation on seed-syllables, she is the garland of mantras that bestows supreme accomplishment.
She is the knower of mantras, the perfection of mantra, established in mantra, and the foremost among those who practice mantra.
She is the nature of the seed-syllable, the mistress of the seed-syllables, the garland of seed-syllables, and the possessor of the seed-syllables.
She whose essence is the seed, who dwells in the seed, who is enriched by the seed, who wears a garland of seeds;
she whose meditation is on the seed, whose sacrifice is the seed, who is enriched by the seed, and who wears a garland of seeds.
The bearer of the great seed, the seeds, she who is rich in seeds, the beloved of the seeds;
the garland of clouds, the one with a garland of clouds, the wearer of a forest garland, and the one whose weapon is the plow.
Wearing a black antelope skin, she is fierce, the refuge of fierce hosts, fond of the fierce, the wielder of fierce weapons,
and the radiant bestower of the fierce worlds.
The perishable one, the mistress of all that moves, the mistress of all, the mistress of all prosperity;
the mistress of Nārada, the mistress of Pradhāna, the mistress of Vāraṇa, and the mistress of the forest. (61–76)
Kṛṣṇeśvara has Keśaveśī as his consort; he is dark-complexioned and possesses three eyes.
Kāmeśvara has Rāghaveśī as his consort, or else Bāleśī, who is worshipped by Bāṇa.
Bhavānīśa and Bhavānī; Bhavendra and Bhavavallabhā; Bhavānanda and Atisūkṣmā; Bhavamūrti and Bhaveśvarī. (61–78)
The shadow of existence, the joy of existence, the strength that removes the fear of existence;
the garland of speech, the knowledge of speech, the great life-force, and the transcendence of latent impressions.
Lobhāpamda is the creator of greed, Pralobha is the slayer of greed; Mohātīta is the mother of delusion, and Mahāvatī is the net of delusion. || 61-80 ||
She who wields the mallet of delusion and she who wields the mallet of delusion;
she who is possessed by delusion and she who is enchanted by delusion; the Lord of Desire and the Sovereign Lady of Passion.
The remover of jaundice, she who is desireless yet possesses true desire, the destroyer of longing;
she with the broad face and large eyes, radiant as a lotus, with eyes like water-lilies. || 61-82 ||
Padmamāla and Padmamālā, Śrīdeva and Devarakṣiṇī, Asita and Asitā, and Āhlāda and Devamātṛkā.
Nāgeśvara, Śailamātā, Nāgendra, and indeed Nagātmajā; Nārāyaṇeśvara, Kīrti, Satkīrti, and Kīrtivadhīnī. (61–84)
Kātīkeśa and Kātīkī, Vikartā and Gahanāśrayā, Virakta and Garuḍārūḍhā, for Garuḍastha is indeed Gāruḍī.
Garuḍeśa, Gurumayī, Gurudeva, Gurupradā;
Gaurāṅgeśa, Gaurakanyā, Gaṅgeśa, Prāṅgaṇeśvarī. (61–86)
She has hair upon her hair, she is vast, devoid of light, and lacking sense organs;
she is the very nature of the seed of a preta, adorned with the ornaments of a preta. (61-87)
Premageha and Premahantṛ; Harīndra and Hariṇekṣaṇā; Kāleśa and Kālikeśānī; and Kaulikeśa and Kākinī. (61–88)
The one wearing black anklets, the one who deludes with black anklets;
the one with a formidable face, the dark goddess Kālī, and the narrative that bestows absolute liberation.
Kamalāpālaka, Kuntī, Kaikeyīśa, Suta, Kalā, Kālānala, Kulajñā, Kulagāmī, and Kulāśrayā. (61–90)
Established in the family dharma, she is Kaulā, the path of the Kula, and Kulāturā;
she is Kulajihvā, Kulānandā, Kṛṣṇā, and she who has arisen from Kṛṣṇa. (61–91)
Kṛṣṇeśa, Kṛṣṇamahiṣī, she who dwells in the crow, she who has the beak of a crow, the law of time, she whose form is time, time itself, and she who illumines time. || 61–92 ||
Kālaja, Kālakanyā, Kāleśa, and Kālasundarī;
Khaḍgahasta, Kharparāḍhyā, Kharaga, and Kharakhaḍganī. (61–93)

She who removes the intellect of the wicked, she who sports, the mistress of the Khañjana bird, the ointment of happiness, she who is fond of song, the abode of singers, the protector of the hosts, and she who dwells in the home. 61-94.
Gargapriya, Gayāprāpti, Gargastha, Gabhīriṇa, Gāruḍīśa, Gāndharvī, Gatīśa, and Gārhavahnijā. (61–95)
The leader of the hosts and celestial musicians, the protector of the hosts and celestial musicians, has gone;
he who possesses profound pride is the division, the ocean of profound peaks.

He who abides in the goal, who stands at the head of the Gaṇas, whose body is like a cow, whose door is fragrance, who wears fragrant garlands, who is rich in scent, and from whom fragrance issues forth. (61–97)

Her entire body was enchanted by the fragrance; she was the enchantress who makes one restless for scent, and she was worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and other articles.
Adorned with fragrant aloe-wood, musk, saffron, and other scents, Madhurānandā is the essence of Gokula, abiding within the fragrance of flowers. (61.99)
Adorned with garlands and flower wreaths produced on Mount Gandhamādana, his body is decorated with necklaces and every kind of jewel ornament without exception. || 61-100 ||
Adorned with necklaces and garlands of all kinds of ornaments such as gold, her lotus-like eyes are as red as *karavīra* flowers. (61.101)
Her beautiful lotus-eyes are like hundreds of millions upon millions of hibiscus flowers;
her great nose is like a thick lotus stalk, and her body is as restless as a lotus.
She possesses a gurgling sound from the lotus-face of the ocean of blissful poetry,
and she bears hundreds of millions of marks in the form of garlands of fierce and variegated serpent-kings.
Adorned with a variegated garland, he is a massive, formidable great serpent;
his body is agitated with bliss by the great resonance of millions of bells. || 61.104 ||
She holds a bell, a hand-drum, mantras, and so forth; her lotus-like hands bestow the bliss of meditation;
she is seated upon a hundred thousand times ten million times ten million auspicious thrones.
Her lotus-like hands hold a bell, a conch, a lotus, a wheel, and display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she is the slayer of millions of enemies, such as Śumbha and others, as well as of the virtuous.
Likewise, there were the terrible Daityas who were slayers, as well as those of the Śaṅkhas;
and there was the lotus-face of the one who is skilled in the multitude of Cārvāka doctrines. (61–107)
The Sovereign Lady who speaks words that are the essence of all purposes and the bliss of the restless;
she wears upon her neck a garland as pure as ten million moons.
He is equal to ten million moons;
his head is adorned with a necklace as beautiful as a lotus and radiant like ten thousand moonbeams.
His head is adorned with the luster of thousands of moons,
and his body bears tens of thousands of beautiful moonstone gems and jeweled necklaces.
She wears garlands infused with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron;
she bears ten thousand spotless garlands made from the heads of Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and Mahāmuṇḍa.
Caṇḍamuṇḍa, Ghoramuṇḍa, Nirmāṇa, Kulamālinī, and Caṇḍāṭṭahāsa—[these are] the flickering lotus-faces rich with terrible laughter. (61–112)
Śaṅkara was enchanted by her lotus-eye that trembled like a wagtail;
he, in turn, was enchanted by the flower-arrow of joy from her eyes that were like trembling lotuses. (61.113)
The moonlight of his face was weary from the obstruction of speaking while moving;
he was adorned by the circle of the crest-jewel consisting of the rays from the tip of the crescent moon.
Adorned on his head with a lotus garland of moons,
he is further embellished by a thousand shimmering suns and decorated with necklaces of jewels.
Resplendent with the ascetic power of lotus-faces numbering hundreds of millions of shifting suns,
he is seated in the midst of moonlight upon a beautiful gem-studded lotus-throne.

The lotus of his hand has twelve beautiful petals and so forth, with its pericarp brilliantly illuminated; it possesses the twang of a bowstring and the sound of a sword-blade, and holds five arrows. (61.117)
The fourth Veda, the Gāthās, and so forth, grant the perfect accomplishment of ten million praises;
she whose lotus-eyes are tremulous is endowed with the triad of the Sun, Fire, and Moon.
The rows of lotuses that are her smiles are the illuminators of thousands of moving lotuses and other flowers, appearing like her own wonderful, loud laughter.
Adorned with the great and most terrible *sāṭṭāṭṭahāsa* laughter of wonder,
he is cooled by the breeze of the world-system consisting of thousands of shadows.
Seated upon a lion-throne with the radiance of a full-blown lotus,
she is adorned with a garland of the severed heads of ten million Daitya kings.
She who brings about the consciousness that knows the meaning of mantras whose limits are severed;
he who effects the breaking of the knots in the great darkness of the manifold paths.
She is the bearer of thousands of millions of Brahmāstras, including missiles and counter-missiles;
she flows with the surging tide of the delicious juices of the excellent meat of the unborn and other offerings.
She who manifests upon the left arm with the most formidable weapons such as the scissor-cut (*chedanādi*);
she who is the great *sāman* chant known as *Jayā* and so forth, the illuminator of the meaning of knowledge. (61–124)
O lotus-heart of the assembly of consorts, you who illuminate the wisdom and knowledge [of the Lord];
you who bestow the great wealth and happiness of the state of love for Janārdana.
She dwells like a lotus in the ocean of the lineage of Jagadīśa;
she is the source of the desire for life and other such states for yogins of supreme bliss.
The mother of the Yoga-shastras, compassionate toward her devotees at her lotus feet,
was as kind as a great meteor falling to extinguish a harsh wind.
She plays the jharjharī, madhurī, vīṇā, flute, and conch;
she wields a staff that destroys the flood of the sound *jhanat*.
She is served by the lotus-hands of the mistress of the *jharjharī* drum and others;
she wears the attire of the great vigil that brings about the dissolution of the state of *ṭaṅkāra*.
She carries a ṭaṅka, an axe, the pāśupata weapon, a shield, and a bow;
he is adorned with a silken garment produced by the friction of the fire of his clapping hands.
Resounding with the sounds of *ṭulṭunī* and millions of tinkling bells, it moves with diverse melodies;
the syllables *ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ*, situated at the end of the root mantra, awaken one's own innate light.
Ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ: she who speaks in resonance with the sound of intense joy;
ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ: he who, seated upon the back of a tortoise, shines in the form of Kāmacāka.
*Ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ*, situated within the seed-syllable fire, adorned with the eyebrows of Hātuka;
he is the illuminator of the *vidyā* of accomplishment, which brings joy through the fierce *ḍāmara*. (61.133)
With a voice as sweet as the sound of a drum, her lotus-face is turned toward [the practitioner];
she reveals the rites beginning with *ḍaṃ ḍaṃ ḍaṃ* and ending with the killing of harsh enemies. (61.134)

Taking as its basis the seven musical notes resonant with the sound of the ḍhakkā drum, it is accompanied by the sounds "ḍhauṃ ḍhauṃ ḍhauṃ" and the rhythmic beat of the ḍhakkā, followed by the beloved consort of Fire (Svāhā). 61-135.
"Ḍhaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍhauṃ ḍha ḍhaṃ ḍha"—thus speaks the Vāsinī;
she is established in the Tāraka-Brahma mantra and is devoted to the lotus feet of the Śrīpāda. || 61-136 ||
The great mantra of Tāriṇī and others, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals;
one who is a knower of the essence of the tantras, mantras, great yantras, and the excellent yoga of the Vedas.
[He is] the bestower of the great siddhis such as the *tāla*, *vetāla*, *daitāla*, and *śrītāla*;
[he is] the illuminator of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), the wish-granting creeper (*kalpalatā*), the celestial flower (*puṣpaka*), and the seed of the elephant (*kalabīja*). || 61-138 ||
Born from the family of trees such as the ḍinti, ḍītāla, hintāla, and tulasī;
his form is adorned with the letter ‘a’, the peak-syllable (kūṭa), the bindu, and garlands of crescent moons. || 61-139 ||

He is the one who abides, the one who sets out, the one who spreads, the one who sings verses, the one who is massive, the one who brings about the end of existence, and the one who withdraws all things;
he is adorned with caves, thickets, golden garlands, forest garlands, and so forth.
He is like a hundred fires of the kalpa at the end of time for the fire of the suffering of poverty;
his body is adorned with ten thousand lotus-like faces.
She holds the noose, the gesture of fearlessness, the boon-granting gesture, and the joy of wealth, dharma, and so forth;
she bestows the prosperity of accomplishments and supernatural powers, shining with hundreds of millions of virtues.
She bestows the fruits of the yoga of meditation, the yoga of knowledge, and the yoga of mantras;
she is the deluder of virtues through her infinite fame and hundreds of millions of names. (61.143)
Free from the existence or non-existence of signs, fruits, and being,
[he is] the one whose lotus feet are eager for giving, [bestowing] the state of supreme bliss.
It accomplishes the fruits of meditative absorption, such as *pratiṣṭhā*, *suniḥvṛtta*, and so forth;
it bestows honor from the hosts of jackals and grants the eight great siddhis.
She is the embodiment of the attainment of fruits from the *Phetkārikulatantra* and other scriptures;
she is served by the lotus-hands of tens of millions upon tens of millions of excellent women.
She who bestows boons, the gift of knowledge, and liberation is exceedingly fickle;
she is filled with joy by the one known as Bhairavānandanātha, who possesses a hundred crores [of attendants]. (61.147)
She bestows the accomplishment of existence, the accomplishment of action, and the eightfold accomplishment;
she bears a body of great joy and the delight arising from the five *makāras*.
She bestows the knowledge of nirvāṇa through the five principles beginning with wine;
he grants the fruits of the division of the ritual action and yoga of the sacrificer. || 61-149 ||
His fame abides in thousands of millions, and he is intent upon singing the praises of virtues;
his form possesses a most fierce appearance, like the fire of time (Kālāgni) standing in the midst of battle with a stream of wrath.
The yoga of the powers of Kākinī, Śākinī, and others is the digit (kalā) of Kākinī;
he is endowed with a tilaka on his forehead like ten million moons possessing the marks [of perfection]. (61.151)
She was graced by a beauty with the hue of lac, the bandhūka flower, and vermilion;
while the mountains were made to reel as if their limbs were being shaken by ten thousand winds.
Established in devotion through love for Vivasvat, she is purified by his two feet;
he, whose pure body is the husband of Śrī Sītā, resembles a pervasive sapphire. (61.153)
She bestows coolness, the bliss of the hundred [Nīlās], the ocean of love, and devotion;
she awakens the self-luminous consciousness of the six lotuses, the gods, and others. (61.154)
The lotus of his heart is delighted by the six supports (ṣaḍādhāra) of the great Mīstha;
he is the leader of the entire lineage, whose every limb is bound by the digit of dark-blue love.
She possesses a beautiful neck adorned with a garland of the great seed-syllables *hraḥ* and *sauḥ*, which are the essence of the scriptures concerning saṃsāra and other related teachings.

Enriched by the letter *ha* and the left ear (*vāmakarṇa*), and adorned with the lunar drop (*candrabindu*), she bears the names of dissolution, creation, maintenance, the field (*kṣetra*), and the protector (*pālaka*). (61.157)
He who is the speech that establishes the perfection of the bliss arising from a hundred thousand recitations of the *Lakṣmī* mantra;
he who is the protection of the night that brings about the cessation of hunger; he who is the warder-off of the agitation of hunger.

She who casts her three eyes upon the Kṣatriyas and others at Kurukṣetra and Aruṇa; she who resides in the Itihāsas as Ananta; she who follows the command of the Lord; and she who is the Sovereign (Īśvarī). 61-159.
Umeśa, Uṭakanyeśī, Ṛddhisthahṛdgomukhī, joined with Gakāreśvara, and Trikuṇḍadevatāriṇī. (61–160)
Eṇācī, Īśapriyā, Ānandā, Erāvatakuleśvarī, Oḍhrpuṣpā, Anantadīptā, and Oḍhrpuṣpānakhāgrakā. (61–161)
Established within a hundred million *ehṛti*s, she rests upon the long *praṇava*;
she resides in the limbs, in the deities of the limbs, in the noble ones (*āryas*), and as the sovereign lady of the noble ones (*āryeśvarī*).
She is the abode of the letters of the Mātṛkā, endowed with all the arts of the Mothers;
she resides within the web of Mātṛkā mantras and bestows gracious qualities.
She whose wisdom on the path is exceedingly intense, who abides in the state of the Mother of Virtues, is the Sovereign Goddess of Immovable Bliss, moving within the emission (visarga). 61-164.
She is stainless, free from blemish, without support, and without refuge;
she is without refuge, without support, seedless, yet the Yoginī who possesses the seed.
She is free from fear, the bliss of desirelessness, possessing the luster of a string of jewels from the ocean;
she dwells in the sky, moves through the air, bestows heaven, and is the sovereign goddess Śiveśvarī.
She is to be known through her qualities that are subtle and exceedingly subtle; she removes the suffering of misfortune for her husband.
Born in various lands, she is adorned with various ornaments. (61.167)
She who dwells in the lotus-eye of the ever-new Navīna, whose bliss is the poison of sense-objects, who devours sense-objects, and who removes poison. 61-168.
Abiding in a state beyond sense objects, she destroys the bliss derived from sense objects;
established as the weapon that severs sense objects, she annihilates the cognition of sense objects.
He is the shade that cuts off cyclic existence, the shade that brings an end to becoming,
the one who sets in motion the purpose of cyclic existence, and the one who revolves within cyclic existence.
She is the destroyer of delusion in saṃsāra, the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra;
she is the bestower of the glory that joins one to saṃsāra, and the one who dispels the darkness of delusion in saṃsāra.

She is the very nature of the five principles (*pañcatattva*) and the awakener of the five principles; she is of the earth, the sovereign of the earth, worthy of worship by the vast multitude, and the ancient one.
Varuṇeśā, Vāruṇā, Vārideśā, and Jalodyamā; Marusthā, Jīvanasthā, Jalabhuk, and Jalavāhanā. (61.173)
Tejaḥkāntaḥ, Projjvalasthā, Tejorāśeḥ, Tejasī, Tejasthaḥ, Tejaso mālā, and Tejaḥkītīḥ are [names] residing in their own rays. (61.174)
Pavaneśa is situated in the wind; Paramātman is within the nose.
She is the one who fills the wind and the one who brings about the retention of the wind (vāyukumbhaka).
The wind that creates apertures is Vātā; the seal for the exit of air is Vāyunirgama-mudrā.
It is Kumbhakasthā when situated in retention, Recakasthā when situated in exhalation, and Atipūriṇī when situated in inhalation. || 61-176 ||
She whose form has wind and space as her support, she who causes the movement of the winds,
she who bestows the accomplishment of the winds, she who is the practitioner of the yoga of the winds, and she who moves with the winds.
The Brahmī is of the nature of space, with her gaze fixed within space;
she is the bliss of the space-retention (*ākāśakumbhaka*) and the limit of the joy of the sky. (61.178)
Abiding within the body covered by space, she causes non-differentiation from space;
she is the great siddhi of space and the like, and she pierces the knots of space.
Kalakarmā is Mahākālī, and Kālayogī is Kālikā; Kālachatra is Kālahatyā, for Kālideva is indeed Kālikā. (61.180)
She is the very nature of Kālabrahman, the protectress of the true meaning of the principle of Time (kālatattva);
she is sky-clad, the mistress of the quarters, the self of the directions, and as radiant as the quarters themselves.
She who dwells in the guardians of the directions, she whose faces are the directions, she who is powerful in the directions, the sovereign lady of the hosts of directions;
she who is non-terrible in the directions, she who is clothed in the directions, the heroine of the directions, the supreme mistress of the lords of the directions.

She whose purpose is the Self, who knows the reality of pervasiveness, who possesses self-knowledge, who is identical with the Self, who belongs to the Self, who resides in the seed of the Self, and who deludes the inner Self. (61.183)
She who forms the notion of the self, whose nature is the bliss of the self;
she is the sacrifice of the self, the great soul, and the illuminator of the great self.

Durgā is the destroyer of the transformation of the self, the deity of knowledge, of what belongs to the self, and so forth; she brings about the union with the mind, and as the Mistress, she is the mind made manifest. (61.185)
She is the destroyer of mental existence and the diminisher of mental existence;
she is the yoga of the inner space of the mind and the arising of qualities beyond form.
The yogi who has transcended the forms of the mind, the witness of the lords of mental yoga;
established in the mind, he is free from the doubt of ego through the mind, and his movement is that of the mind alone. || 61.187 ||
She whose hidden meaning is the nine substances, she who wards off kings,
she who possesses the forms of new qualities, actions, and so forth, and she who moves through the sky.
Atyunmattā is the Great Speech; Mahāvāṇī is the Great Wind;
she is the destroyer of all sins and the warder-off of all diseases. || 61-189 ||
The goddess of the gate is Prīti; [the others are] Pralayāgni and Karālinī;
Bhūṣaṇḍa is the father of the Gaṇas; and Bhūṣaṇḍa is the giver of blood. (61-190)
Kākāvalīśa, Sarveśī, Kākapucchadhara, Jayā; Ajiteśa, jitānandā, Vīrabhadra, and Prabhāvatī. || 61-191 ||
With her vital breath (*prāṇa*) moving within the internal channels (*nāḍī*), she manifests special qualities;
seated upon a pedestal inlaid with jewels, she rides upon a lion and travels in a chariot. (61.192)
The teacher of ten million lineages, served by Vāsudeva;
she who knows the knowledge of being devoid of support, whose own nature is the support of all.
Sarvajña, Sarvavijñā, Mārtaṇḍa, Yaśas, Ilvalā, Indreśa, Vindhyaśaileśī, Vāraṇeśa, and Prakāśinī. (61-194)
The sovereign lord of infinite arms, the destroyer of infinite syllables;
may there be blessing, the granting of boons, favor, and the act of grace. (61.195)
Seated upon a corpse-throne, she dwells in the groves of Meru;
situated in the midst of the jeweled palace, she resides upon a jeweled pedestal.
The preta Sarvapraharaṇa, Vidhividyāprakāśinī, Pracaṇḍanayanānanda, and Mañjīrakalarañjinī. || 61-197 ||
She whose lotus feet possess anklets of *kalamañjīra*, who is devoted to the death of Bala;
she whose body is pervaded by a garland of lineages (*kulamālā*), the Lord of the Lineage (*kulendra*), and the Scholar of the Lineage (*kulapaṇḍitā*). 61-198.
Bālikeśa, Rudracaṇḍā, Bālendrā, Prāṇabālikā, Kumārīśa, Kāmamātā, Mandireśa, and Svamandirā. (61.199)
The Lord who gives birth at the improper time, the wise-souled one, the doer of what is dear;
the source of the Vedas, the mother of the Vedas, she who abides in dispassion and bestows detachment.
The lotus-face with a smiling laugh; the enchanting one with a smiling laugh; the jagged-toothed Lord; the jagged-toothed one; the Lord of Elephants; and the radiance of the teeth.
For she has pointed teeth and ten directions for her fangs; she is one whose enjoyment is lost yet is fond of chewing;
she is primarily composed of flesh and is a consumer who eats the finest meats. (61.202)
She who loves fish-meat, the great mudrā, and the consumption of dust and blood;
she who is very fond of wine, meat, the great fish-mudrā, and sexual union. (61.203)
She is the bliss that delights in the substances of the Kula, the bestower of the Kula-perfections such as wine and the rest;
she pierces the heart, throat, eyebrows, and the thousand-spoked wheel, and in the end, she is the ultimate piercer.
She whose heart-lotus is serene, she who possesses a serene heart-lotus;
she who is rich in granting gracious boons, she who bestows gracious boons.
Richly endowed with the illumination of loving devotion, she is the manifestor of the bliss of love.
The arising of the fruit of Prabhākara; the beloved of the supremely subtle city; she who moves with the rays of the morning sun; endowed with the splendor of the first light of dawn;
the subduer of the fierce enemy Manmatha; arisen from the body of the moving moon.
Clad in a mass of Dharma-garments, the color of a dense layer of radiant light.
Worshipped by the hosts of the lords of gods, fully honored by the sovereign of the foremost deities; served by the lineage of the lords of gods, attended by the supreme lords of men;
the lord of the hosts, the leader of the hosts, the lord of the Gaṇas, the son of the gods.
She is the beloved helmsman for those who have entered the ocean of existence.
Born from the lineages of both gods and asuras, she is renowned for her standing among the enemies of the gods;
she is the slayer of the hosts of the god-enemies and the bestower of perfect accomplishment upon the lords of the divine hosts.
She grants the fruits of one's desires and bestows the supernatural powers (siddhis) of the foremost among the gods.
She bestows beloved offspring, fulfills the purpose of the lineage, and grants sons, wealth, and liberation.
Śivasvasvī, Śivakākinī, Hara, Harā, and Bhīmasvanā;
Kṣitīśa, Iṣu, Rakṣakā, Samanadarpa-hantā, Udayā, Guṇeśvarā, Umāpatī, Hṛdayapadmabhedinī, and Gati.
Bearing the moon upon her forehead, she bestows the path to one's own true happiness.
Adorned with a loud, unrestrained laugh upon the banks of the cremation ground;
forcibly cleaving the temple doors upon the surface of the minds of the wicked; increasing the countenance of the God of Love; and a companion to the dear spring season.
Her lotus-face was radiant, and she sat upon a lion-throne adorned with lotuses.
Bhava, born from the splendor of Bhavānīpati, and the poet (Kavi) who is to be contemplated by the Asuras;
Kriyeśvara, Īlāvatī, and Taruṇa who has attained Arāvatī;
the bestower of success upon the lords of sages, and the long life of the gods, the lords of sages, and the Siddhas.
The destruction of the three worlds was brought about by the body of Murāri-Hara.
The pair, the golden kārṣāpaṇa, the golden-topped pillar,
the multitude of lotuses, the stainless garland of the sun of the arts of the lineage, and the one who is well-disposed toward those devoted to the practice of yoga for overcoming darkness.
With a mind fixed on discernment, she was obtained from the hand of Prabhupara.
You alone are the leader of the lineage, the sovereign mistress of the yoga of dissolution;
you are Hara, who removes the pride of the world of gods, mountains, and fierce hosts of attendants;
you dwell within thousands of moving and unmoving beings, abiding in the midst of all forms.
She who fulfills her own name with virtues; she who completely fulfills her own virtues and name.
Thus, O Lord, I have recounted to you this auspicious thousand names, which are most wonderful and bestow the realization of the essence of supreme bliss. (61.215)
Composed of the *mātṛkā* mantras, it is an ocean of all established doctrines;
it is the great manifestation of perfected knowledge and the means for attaining the qualities of bliss. (61.216)
That which is difficult to find in all the worlds has been revealed in the *Yāmala*, O Ānandabhairava, who are enchanted by the fragrant essence of the nectar of affection for you. (61.217)
It has not been stated anywhere else out of fear of the loss of one's own established doctrine;
rather, it is for the sake of establishing the Siddhānta of the primordial Yoga, and for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
That which is difficult to attain has been revealed by the very essence of the joy of love;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes Śrī Bhairaveśvara. (61.219)
No one is capable of describing the auspicious fruit of this name, even in a hundred times ten million years—the fruit which a man obtains [thereby]. (61.220)

That fruit, which is obtained by yogis from the ocean of existence in a single moment, belongs to one who, having risen in the morning, recites this for the sake of warding off difficulties and planetary afflictions. (61-221)
Because it wards off great fear even from the danger of the wicked senses, one should meditate and constantly recite the name, especially at midday. (61.222)
One should accomplish the practice of the Name during the twilight hours and at the junction of night;
likewise during the practice of yoga, the unraveling of knots, and the exposition of yogic meditation.
From recitation, there shall be the perfection of yoga and the daily loosening of the knots;
there shall be the attainment of the knowledge of yoga, and yoga arises from one-pointedness of mind.
For the sake of bringing the gods dwelling within the body under control, for the pacification of great delusion,
and for the immobilization of the enemy's armies, one who is pure should recite this every day.
Through recitation with a spirit of devotion, one becomes capable of all rites;
by merely reciting it once, one may paralyze enemy armies.
By reciting it three times, one shall bring the three worlds under control;
whether he be a fool or even a scholar, whoever recites it three times [attains this]. (61.227)
He attains supreme peace and the lore that fascinates the world;
then, having obtained firm establishment, he shall attain the liberation of nirvāṇa.
By reciting it four times, one shall swiftly destroy enemies;
by reciting it five times, one shall cause an enemy to vanish in an instant.
By reciting it six times, the lord of practitioners shall become a destroyer of enemies;
if he recites it seven times, he shall attract the wealth of others. (61–230)
Having thus meditated upon [the deities] in their sequential order, he who recites [this] with supreme devotion shall become a lord of yoginīs, like a great wish-fulfilling tree.
If one recites it for only a month, one will become capable of breaking the knot [of ignorance], a far-sighted great hero, powerful, and a lord among the wise. (61.232)
One becomes a possessor of great wisdom and a protector of the world; of this there is no doubt.
Within one month, one shall become capable and attain the accomplishment of nirvāṇa and liberation.

For the sake of attaining yogic perfection, the practitioner, who is most dear [to the deity], should recite [the mantra] in an empty house, in a pavilion dug into the earth, or in a desolate place. (61.234)
In the interior of the Gaṅgā, in a great forest, or in a secluded and uninhabited place;
in a land afflicted by famine, or one free from all calamities.
In a cremation ground, in a wilderness, at the foot of an aśvattha tree, on the site of a banyan tree, or in a house made of bricks—wherever people do not frequent. (61.236)
In each of those places, and even at the site of the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha),
one should remain in a firm posture and recite the supreme, auspicious Name.

Pure in limbs through meditation and the practice of *dhāraṇā*, devoted to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship, he who meditates and offers praise at dawn will certainly become a conqueror of death. (61–238)
He attains the eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭāṅgasiddhi) and shall obtain immortality; he will certainly become a devotee of the Guru, the Deity, and the Great Mantra. || 61-239 ||
In his body, sufferings and evil growths do not arise;
seeing that supreme yogin, malevolent planets flee.
The practitioner who constantly recites this mantra will have the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi) in his hand;
and the other deities, residing within the lotus-heart-liṅga, shall likewise attain success for him.
For thousands of millions of aeons, that king of yogins shall possess long life;
pure in conduct and formless, he is indeed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
He is eternal, his purpose is accomplished, and he attains liberation while living. (61–242)

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Hymn of One Thousand and Eight Names of Īśvara, Śakti, and Kākinīs," in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, the latter part of the illustrious *Rudrayāmala*.
Now begins the sixty-second chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Lord, I shall now proclaim [the teaching] concerning Kākinī, the Guru, and the Deity."
The extraction of mantras is your knowledge, by which an ascetic becomes perfected.
By the recitation of this hymn, one immediately attains sovereignty among the thousandfold perfections, or else the state of a yogi in prosperity.
Just as King Janaka was devoted to his teacher within his realm, so does the practitioner become a great adept and one of great wisdom. (62–3)
The Suras, Nāgas, and all the hosts of Rudras are servants seeking the goal of knowledge;
likewise, the Yogins, Jñānins, Siddhas, Khecaras, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas [are there]. (62-4)
The sages, the Krodha-Vetālas, as well as Caṇḍeśvara and the others,
having praised him with this supreme auspicious hymn, attained perfection everywhere.
Pūrṇa, whose lotus-face is like the orb of the full moon, who removes the flood of sins with his sidelong glances,
the creator and ordainer of women, protects those great lords who are fit for yoga;
he is the embodied guardian of infinite, boon-bestowing bliss, united with the life-force of prosperity.
May the Lord of Mṛtyuñjaya, the destroyer of fear, protect my hidden body. 62-6.

May he who destroys desire and anger, who procreates the Bharatas, and who protects the earth— may that yogi, the master of the yoga of contemplation, who bestows the fruit of my lineage, grant me eternal auspiciousness. Within his lap, the wheel of the world appears as subtle as a tiny mustard seed balanced upon a sesame seed.
I meditate upon those two feet of the venerable Lord, which are ageless, within the expanse of my heart.

The discerning one who cuts down the enemy of the hundred deceits and delusions; the impeller residing within; the one who destroys the latent tendencies of greed and hidden sloth; the man born from the earth who abides in great auspiciousness;
he who transcends the world and seeks to cross over it—Victory, victory to you, O Lord of Compassion, the giver, the ascetic!
I praise that Lord of Life who protects the secret meaning of the extraction of mantras here in this world.
He who is the end of all existence, most venerable in the lotus-heart, the subduer of the enemies of the gods;
he who, deluded by the mantra "Obeisance to the Goddess Vāgdevī," became the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati);
and he who, known as the Illuminator of the Meaning of Mantras, is surrounded by tens of millions of friends of victory.
May the performer of a hundred sacrifices (Indra), whose mass of rays brings joy to the rising sun, protect me from the snare of suffering. || 62-9 ||

Having meditated upon Śiva— who is composed of the *praṇava*, who possesses thrilled limbs, whose body is joined with the stainless tips of his matted locks, who is born from the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and who is the stealer of consciousness through mantra— and having offered salutations to Māheśvarī with the recitation of "Namaḥ," one shall become the sovereign lord of Mahendra.
You are that very son of Kālī; he who serves you, the bestower of fearlessness, is liberated.
O Haṃsa, you are the sustainer of the vital breaths; you are the bestower of all boons, the primary cause, and the supreme authority.
You are Śāntīśa, the foundation, the Praṇava, and Śiva—may there be eternal auspiciousness for Maheśvara!
One who recites this mantra here at the end, with the word "namaḥ" at the conclusion and with a loud voice, attains prosperity through the destruction of all defects.
O Lord, you are the master of the ocean of generosity; O Guru, protect me here from my fickle and restless nature.
You are the one who causes an overflow of bliss, yet you are also an ocean of compassion and the bestower of devotion;
you are the giver of Vidyādharīs, yet you are also the enemy of the gods and the life-lord of Pārvatī.

Your single-syllable mantra consists of the syllable *Tā* (tā-re), enriched by the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the lower lip (*adharā*), followed by the perishable (*kṣara*) and then the moon (*vidhu*) filled with nectar.
If there were any king of yogins upon the earth, he would mutter [the mantra] ending with Tārā and ending with the three syllables. || 62-12 ||

The well-perfected one, having daily recited in reverse order the syllable *praṇava*— which resides within the serpent-egg (*sarpāṇḍa*), which possesses the moon and the fire (*haravidhu*) as its lower part, which is the very nature of the lunar dot (*candrabindu*), and which destroys death— and having placed the beloved of fire (*vahnikāntā*,
the letter *ra*) at its end; he who worships this word-form, which has reached the highest state and resounds with the tinkling of golden anklets.
May that which brings joy to the mind through the nectar of contemplation, bestowing bliss upon the noble lineage of victory, enter into your vital breath.

If a wise person, taking refuge at the lotus feet of Śrī, applies those mantras during the rites of eradication (uccāṭana), delusion (mohana), subjugation of enemies (vaśya), pacification (śānti), nourishment (puṣṭi), or internal control (antavaśya), and recites them,
he shall succeed in the essence of the six rites; having approached the Supreme Guru, he becomes a wish-fulfilling tree.
The lord of kings, resembling the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) in all the world, [attained this] through the grace of Śambhunātha. || 62-14 ||

One who recites the mantra of the Lord— beginning with *khānta* (the letter *kha*), followed by the syllable mounted by *Śakra* (*i*), joined with the eye (*na*), the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*, *e*), the three powers (*tri-śakti*, *ai*), *ca* at the beginning and end, *oṃ*, and *śivāya* conjoined with fire (*ra*) and smoke (*u*)— that practitioner, devoted to the path of the Kula, having recited this tradition, becomes most venerable.
What unattainable goal could there be for him? Being happy and facing the path of yoga, he is successful throughout the three worlds.
Transcending all, you dwell as one free from the path of movement; you go everywhere and yet remain at rest.
You are without hands, yet the guide; the bestower of boons beyond limit; possessing all forms, yet formless.
You are the knower of mantras, the excellent counselor, the great illusory commitment, and the destroyer of the core of doubt.
May she who is the thinker of all sovereign goddesses, at the end [of whom is] Parapashupati, protect me as I bow down. 62-16.
You are the yogi, the enjoyer, and the dispassionate one; you are the one of incomparable splendor, the source of existence, and he who wears five crests (Pañcacūḍa).
You are Vāṇī, Śeṣa, and the Lord of Pārvatī; your body is adorned by Mṛḍā entwined with the moon, yet you are truly the bodiless one (Anaṅga).
You are Desire, Māyā, and the Lord of Ramā; you are anointed with the beauty of the first rays of the sun.
He who drank [the nectar] from every limb while seated upon a stainless lotus, and he who cast a glance while in a state of wrath.
Whoever, being self-restrained and pure, recites this hymn to Śrī Śaṅkara, shall attain within a year the perfection that bestows all knowledge. (62.18)
Whether in a pure place or an impure one, that best of practitioners who praises [the deity] with devotion is liberated from all torments; he is a yogi who has pierced the knots.
One attains success spontaneously through this [mantra], which bestows love, bliss, and true devotion;
its preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is traditionally prescribed as one hundred and eight recitations.
Neither bathing, nor recitation, nor the performance of worship and other rites need be undertaken;
by the mere recitation of this hymn, one shall become perfectly steadfast in the unstruck sound (anāhata).
Long-lived, free from passion, and devoid of the mental cultivation of saṃsāra, one who has studied and retained this [teaching] shall not fall away from yoga;
without effort, he attains perfection in yoga and abundant prosperity. (62-22)

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Hymn to Īśvara," in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Wheels), within the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa* (Section on Accomplished Mantras) of the *Mahātantroddīpana* (Great Tantra Illuminator), in the *Uttaratantro* (Later Tantra) of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 62.
Now begins the sixty-third chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Lord of the World, O Consort of Śivā, hear now the armor-vidyā (kavaca) of this very [deity]."
The Supreme Brahman of the Lord bestows the yoga of liberation. || 63-1 ||
This supreme armor, which deludes by name, is difficult to obtain in the world;
merely by meditating upon this armor, one shall partake in the fruit of liberation. 63-2.
What indeed is its greatness? Nevertheless, I shall describe it for the sole purpose of severing the knots [of ignorance], rather than out of attachment to my own body. (63-3)
O Lord of Yogins, for all gods as well as for yogins,
[this is taught] for the sake of attaining accomplishments such as the manifestation of existence, and for the sake of achieving the purity of the body.
O Mahākāla, out of affection for you, I have revealed this:
all mantras become effective when they rely upon the Sammohaka armor. (63.5)
For the Kavaca, Brahmā is declared the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh the meter (chandas);
Īśvara is said to be the deity (devatā), and likewise Kākinī is the power (śakti). (63–6)
The *kīlaka* should be known as *krūṃ* for the sake of accomplishing the practice of meditation;
its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the purpose of piercing the heart-lotus. (63–7)

Of this Śrīsammohana Mahākavaca, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Īśvara is the deity (devatā), Kākinī is the power (śakti), and Krūṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of attaining perfection through meditation and for the sake of piercing the heart-lotus during recitation. May the Praṇava protect my head, and Sadāśiva protect my forehead.
May Prāsāda protect the heart, and Maheśvara the pair of arms.
May Mahādeva protect the back; may the Destroyer of Desire protect the belly;
may Kāmarāja protect the two sides; and may Bāla protect the space between the back and the chest. (63-9)
May the Great Hero, the Lord of Lalitā, the Sovereign, the Conqueror of Death, and the Blue-throated One, ever protect the region of the genitals, the root of the belly. 63-10.
May the ring beneath the *liṅga* protect the pair of feet bestowed by Umā;
may the beloved of Pārvatī’s life-force constantly protect the big toe.
May Tryambaka protect the ankle, and may the Lord of Yuvatis protect the knees;
may the eternal Mañjughoṣa always protect the root of the thighs.
May Bhairava protect the region of the hips; may Krodhabhairava protect [the area] up to the navel.
May the Lord of the World, in the form of the *liṅga*, protect the emergence of the *liṅga*-region. (63.13)
May Maheśa, the Lord of Kākinī, always protect the tip of my heart;
may he who is seated upon the bull protect my neck, and may the sky-clad one protect the region of my throat.
May Gaṇapa protect the uvula; may Bhavanāśaka protect the nose;
may Yogīndra protect the space between the eyebrows; and may Maheśa protect the head. (63.15)
May the Lord of Sages protect the region of the navel, and may Maheśvara, who resides in the twelfth [lotus] and is the beloved of Kākinī’s life-breath, protect the twelve lotuses. 63-16.
May Mahārudra, who pervades the universe, protect the lotus at the root of the navel;
may he whose nature is both Hari and Hara always protect the lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
May Brahmendra, the lord of ḍākinīs, always protect the root lotus;
may the lord of yoginīs, the ḍākinī Kuṇḍalī, protect [it] at all times. || 63-18 ||
May Kuṇḍalī Mātṛkā protect; may Śiva (Hara) as Vaṭukeśa protect;
may Maheśvara Vāmadeva protect the body of Rākiṇī.
May the Five-Faced One always protect Lākinī, whose form is vajra;
and may the Hero protect Sukākinī and his own twelve-spoked abode.
May Vīrendra protect the pericarp; may Viṣāśana protect the twelve-spoked [wheel];
and may Sadāśiva, the heroic Krodha, always protect the sixteen-spoked [wheel]. (63.21)
May Vajranātheśa, the Krodhabhairava, protect me from the fear of enemies;
may Lākinī Śrīsadāśiva always protect the six cakras.
May the protector of Dhūmrākṣa, who dwells within the sixteen lotuses, protect me;
may the Great-bodied Lord of the lords of the quarters, the Supreme Lord, protect me;
and may he whose matted hair is the celestial Gaṅgā protect my supreme pair of eyebrows.
May Gaṅgādhara, the Supreme Lord, always protect Hākinī.
May Hākinī and Paraśiva be my ground; may the Lotus protect [me];
may Daṇḍapāṇīśvara protect the two-petaled [lotus] in the form of the mind.
May Sādhukeśa always protect me, who dwells in Manonmanī and the other [powers];
may Piṅgākṣeśa always protect my body in the midst of fear. (63.25)
May Unmanī, together with Rodhinī, protect my station;
may the jar of nectar always protect my deity, Ānanda.
May Ānandabhairava protect the presiding deity of the secret place;
may Māyāmayopahā protect the portion of the Suṣumnā channel.
May the one who possesses the radiance of ten million suns protect the bearer of the *iḍā* digit;
may the Lord whose crest is the moon protect the sun of the *piṅgalā*.
May the abode of the fire of the end of the eon at the tip [of the central channel] protect me always within the *suṣumnā*;
may the ocean of nectar, the lord of millions of jewels and gems, protect me. (63.29)
May Śivanātha always protect my Kuṇḍalīcakra;
may Mahādeva protect Viṣṇucakra, and Kālarātri protect Kulānvita.
May the Conqueror of Death always protect me;
may Śambhu, who resides upon the thousand-petaled lotus, the Self-born One, protect me at all times.
May Śarva, the Lord of all forms, protect [me] at all times;
may the illustrious Lord Nīlakaṇṭha protect [me] everywhere and at all times.
May he whose nature consists of all seeds always protect my garland of seed-syllables;
may Śiva, the lord of all seeds, protect the letters of the Mātṛkā for me.
May Hara protect my ego-sense and my rosary at all times—
in water, in the forest, in great fear, on a mountain, or in an empty pavilion.
In a great forest defiled by the fear of tigers, bears, buffaloes, beasts, and the like; in a terrible battle; in the sky, on the earth, or in the netherworld (atala).
In the event of an extremely severe wound from a weapon, in fears of enemies, thieves, and the like, in the cruel fear of a great lion, and likewise in the fear of a rutting elephant; (63-36)
In times of great terror from planetary influences and diseases, and always in fear of serpents;
in the presence of fears of piśācas, bhūtas, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, daityas, and the like.
Always amidst revilers and false speakers,
he is the supreme lord Karālakaḷikānātha— fierce, formidable, and transcendent.
The fierce one, with matted hair, with terrifying fangs, whose hands are covered by Time, the seer;
he who is shrouded in wrath, the greatly intoxicated, the Lord of Garuḍa, and the sustainer of Maheśa. (63-39)
The five-faced one, possessing five rays, the purifier, the son of Pavana; he who wears the crest, the measure, and the great mudrā; the lord of the wrathful ones.
May these Great Rudras— Drāvaka, Pūraka, Puṣṭa, Poṣaka, and Pāribhāṣika— protect us from the twenty-two great fears.
All these are endowed with power, adorned with garlands of severed heads;
they are the lords of ego, wrathful yogins who contemplate the ultimate principles.
The great heroes have four arms, holding swords and shields;
they are adorned with garlands of skulls and conchs, and embellished with various jewels. (63–43)
Richly adorned with garlands of networks of tinkling bells, resplendent with golden anklets,
enriched by the beauty of various ornaments, and graced by the moon-crested Lord as their crest-jewel.
May the Blessed One, who bestows prosperity and liberation upon those engaged in the yoga of action, protect us always with eternal bliss;
may the Lords protect us perpetually. 63-45.
May Brahmā protect the root lotus; may Śrī Viṣṇu protect the six-petaled [lotus]; may Rudra protect the ten-petaled [lotus]; and may Īśvara protect the Anāhata [cakra]. (63–64)
May Sadāśiva always protect my sixteen-spoked [lotus]; may Para protect the two-petaled; and may the six Śivas protect me perpetually. || 63-47 ||
May the other Lords of the Family (Kuleśvaras) constantly protect my body;
may the Full Brahman and all the deities always protect every limb.
May he who is the form of Time always protect my mind; may he who is the form of Manu protect my head; may the Lord who is absorbed in the Self and the knower of the Vedas always protect my forehead.
May the Lord of Vārāṇasī protect the seat between my eyebrows;
may the Lord of Yogins always firmly protect the row of my teeth. (63-50)
May Jhilṭīśa, the Lord of the Bhūtas, always protect the upper and lower lips;
may Bhārabhūtīśa, the Lord of Guests, protect the two nostrils. || 63-51 ||
May Sthāṇukeśa, the Lord of Hari, always protect my pair of cheeks;
may Amara, the Lord of Ardhīśvara, always protect the region of my ears.
May Mahāseneśvara protect my snout continuously;
may the great Rudras, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, [protect] the Mātṛkās within the knots of my own limbs.
May Kālarudra protect me, and may he who brings about the destruction of time protect all my limbs; may Akālatāraka protect [me], and Paripūraka protect my belly.
May the supreme sages, Agastya and others, who are lords of yogis, protect me;
may the Lord Īśāna, Śrīnātheśvara, protect my subtle channels. (63–55)
May the Trident-bearer protect in the east; may the Destroyer of Death protect in the south; and may Mahākāla, intoxicated by the wine of Varuṇa, always protect in the west.
In the north, may Bhairava Avadhūteśa protect; in the northeast, may Śāntīśa protect; and in the northwest, may Yogivallabha protect. (63–57)
May Śiva, the slayer of the Daityas, protect me constantly in the north-west corner;
may he whose lotus-face is like the fire of time always protect me in the south-east corner.
May Brahmā always protect above; may Ananta always protect below;
may the Lord of All Devas always protect the bliss residing within the entire body. (63-59)
May the beloved Arha protect me here; may the Lord known as Kāla protect my quality (guṇa);
and may Ravinātha always protect my heart and my mind. (63–60)
May Candreśa, the granter of desires, protect the space between my eyebrows forever;
may Raktāṅgeśa, the bearer of the adamantine staff, protect the three-eyed one.
May Budhaśyāmasundareśa protect the region of my heart;
may Suvarṇavarṇagurvīśa always protect my throat. (63–62)
May the Lord Śukreśvara, who is like the sun covered by clouds of vermilion, protect the throat;
may the Lord Śaniśyāmeśvara always protect the region of the navel.
May Rāhu, with his great mouth, protect my face alone;
may Ketu, with his massive body, always protect my private parts.
May the deities beginning with Indra, accompanied by their hosts of attendants, protect [me];
may the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha protect the form of the circle of my head and the directions.
May the Bhairavas, joined by the Bhairavīs, who have arisen from all bodies, with their terrifying fangs and massive forms, protect me constantly. (63–66)
May Yajñabhuṅ Nīlakaṇṭha protect my heart at all times;
may the Unmattabhairavas protect me, and may the Īśvaras protect me at all times.
May the kings of wrath, joined with Śrī, Māyā, and Madana, protect [you].
This is the armor (kavaca), the saving (tāra) mantra, the auspiciousness of the Tāraka-Brahman. (63–68)
O Lord, that which was spoken with effort has not been revealed anywhere; [I have told it] solely out of affection for you, my heart being filled with grace. (63–69)
Have mercy, O Lord of Compassion; [reveal] this wonderful armor of yours for the welfare of the worlds, for the destruction of delusion, and for the sake of immortality.
It should be recited by the best of practitioners and honored by the lords of yogis;
it is difficult to find in all the worlds, yet easily attained by those who know reality.
By reciting this armor-mantra (kavaca), one shall surely accomplish even that which is impossible to achieve;
by wearing it and by worshipping it, one shall directly obtain the fruit of all sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Forming the hollow of the mouth like a crow’s beak, the wise man should recite the armor-mantra seven or five times, for it is the basis for secret accomplishment.
Having meditated upon the union with Kākinīśvara— the excellent yoga endowed with armor— as the limb of Īśvara, one becomes equal to the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
By reciting this armor-mantra (kavaca), one certainly attains divinity, supreme health, knowledge, enchantment, and mastery over the worlds. (63–75)
If one recites [this] three times, he shall paralyze enemy armies;
he quickly attains peace and becomes capable of performing the six rites.

The practitioner who is free from the desire for the sweetness of aesthetic flavor (rasa) and the longing for sense objects becomes a wish-fulfilling cow; he shall become a possessor of the accomplishments (siddhi) such as the power of will.
Everywhere there shall be the power of movement for women who assume the form of the God of Love;
they shall attain the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), and extension (prāpti). || 63-78 ||
Having become the beloved of the Yoginīs, the foremost of practitioners may wander about;
for he is indeed my son, just like Guha and Gaṇeśa. (63–79)
Glorious, of noble birth, knowing the essence, and liberated from all phenomena, the lord of ascetics proceeds slowly and joyfully toward the sixteen-spoked [wheel]. (63–80)
Wherein the Lord Sadāśiva-guru, the master of the Śākinīs, shines;
through my yoga, one attains the supreme state in due course. (63–81)
O Lord, how can there be devotion to you without my yoga?
[This occurs] through the recitation of this armor known as Sammohana. (63–82)
Speech becomes submissive, fortune becomes stable, and one is endowed with all sovereign powers;

thereafter, the state of renunciation is attained, and like Śiva, one wanders free from attachment. The mind enters into Sadāśiva, and for one whose mantra is perfected, there is the dissolution of the mind.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Armor Named Sammohana of Anāhateśvara," in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*) of the *Mahātantroddīpana* in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*. 63.
Now begins the sixty-fourth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
Now I shall proclaim the various types of restraint of all the sense organs.
And listen with a one-pointed mind, O Śambhu, if you desire the fruit of your wishes.
Furthermore, he attains knowledge that has conquered memory and consciousness,
wherein he performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) as prescribed in my tantra.
Above the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) is the glorious lotus, encircled by sixteen petals;
it is as radiant as ten million suns within the great smoke-like constituent of the pit of the throat.
The field is endowed with five rays; in its center is the splendor of Keśava.
In its center is the location of the pericarp (kaṇīkā), which increases supreme bliss. || 64-4 ||
The wise knower should worship the form of Śiva, Sadāśiva, who is unmanifest and ever to be well-guarded, the beloved of Sākinī and Śakti. (64–5)
Great beings, having blocked the mouth with the seed-syllables of Kāma, Kalā, and the rest,
meditate upon [the deity] who is fierce like a cloud and possesses the brilliance of steady lightning.
Dark-complexioned, with a most beautiful and pure form.
There is no defining, nor the illumination of the states of existence; it is the beholding, the union with the fifth color.
That which is the expounder is the investigation of birth.
I worship Sadāśiva, the refuge of peaceful people. || 64-7 ||
The wheel of time that is not [bound by] time, the wheel of time of the family;
it shines like a celestial tree for those who worship it.
They sacrifice to the wheel, which is as radiant as ten thousand young suns.
Possessing the pure radiance of a mountain of vermilion.
The gods, beginning with Brahmā, pay homage to that state of meditative absorption of the Primordial God.
The goddess Bhalleśī, who is Bhallakullā, sports with her folds upon the forehead of the heroic bear;
she shines with the splendor of the illusion of Śiva, while those distressed by the black serpent of the fleeting moments of fear find no place there.
She is the lineage-holding one (Kaulā), the garland of Kailāsa, the one whose lotus-like waters are crowded with [beings], and she is the playful beauty of the drops.
Blazing in the lotus of the throat, within the honey-house of gold, she is absorbed in meditative concentration upon the fullness of the pedestal.
May that Sākinī, who is to be meditated upon and contemplated, who possesses beautiful radiance and wears yellow garments,
protect him— him who resembles a rain-cloud, who grants boons and supreme bliss, who has the moon as his crest-jewel,
and who is accompanied by his consort; he who, together with Brahmā, Indra, and the foremost of yogis, creates the wondrous arrangement of the petals and their joints.
Resplendent like a mass of lightning and the abode of hosts of sages, let it be resorted to by the foremost of practitioners.
In the luminous path of Brahman known as space, radiant with the sixteen digits (kalās) of the twice-four-petaled lotus,
where the wind moves and which is white as smoke, smokeless fire, and the moon— therein shines the glorious Sun, the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), who illuminates the path of Kula.
The Lord of the Cintāmaṇi, the source of the fragrance of the state of bliss, dwells there with the Sākinīs and Yoginīs. || 64-12 ||
These two alone sustain the entirety of time;
they are Sadāśiva and Madhupūra-vāsin,
who are resplendent with will, action, and knowledge.
May the two principal deities, who are the abode of happiness, protect those who worship them.
In a pure lotus, those two who are the primordial lords,
who pierced Bāṇa, Śiva, and others,
and who are radiant through the mantra of the Guru in the form of the letter *A*.
The meanings of both *kula* and *akula* are to be meditated upon on the path. || 64-14 ||
Mahābhairava said:
O Kulajā, supreme Vidyā, whose nature is eternal bliss!
O beautiful one, out of affection for me, you ought to explain all the divisions [of the Kula]. 64-15.
Completely forgetful due to the intoxication of the most terrifying Kālakūṭa poison, I did not recognize the purposes of yoga—those which lead to eternal life and are dear as a bond. (64.16)
If you are able to protect me, then always protect me, for my body is smeared with poison; how else could there be movement in my throat, or how else could there be this demonic act? (64.17)
How does one become a hater of enemies, or how does the rise of auspiciousness occur?
To what extent is there delight in discipline, and to what extent is it accomplished through time? (64.18)
How does your meditation attain novelty, or what is its nature?
[Tell me] the true essence of your limbs and the revelation of the family seats (kulapīṭha).
Where is the movement of Kuṇḍalinī? Whence is the lineage of practitioners?
Where is the meditation on the letters? And how does the division of the petals occur in the station? (64.20)
For the separation from the knowledge of clarity is indeed the arising of the primordial wisdom of prior cognition.
How is the attainment of the single flavor [achieved], or how is the conceptualization of the body [formed]? (64.21)
How did the churning of Kāmadeva come to be established within the body?
Who is it that is firmly rooted in the lotus of the throat, and who is the person capable of knowing the inner state (bhāva)? 64-22.
"Tell me first, through the grace of your compassionate gaze, regarding the Lord at the beginning.
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Supreme Lord, first hear the movement of Śrīkaṇṭha."
O Lord, ministers must listen to [the counsel], reflect upon it, and act accordingly every day. (64.24)
In the throat is a sixteen-petalled lotus; in its center is the circle of the glorious pericarp.
Outside of that is a square, and within it a hexagon consisting of bliss.
On the outside are four doors, a nine-chambered structure, and then six circles of earth.
One should worship Śrīcandrātapa on the upper part and Madhupurī in its pericarp. || 64-25 ||
In the region hidden within the center of its pericarp,
the land of Madhupūra shines eternally;
in the middle of that, the manifestation of the eight cities appears.
It shall serve for the accomplishment of the Kaula ritual practice.
To those lords of the digits of love, beginning with Pūrva and others,
who shine, glossy and full of the essence of the sweet nectar of passion—
to them, the salutation is performed by the lords of ascetics.
May they always be successful, radiant with the petals of the throat [cakra]. || 64-27 ||
Vāmeśvara goes to the eastern house;
Rāhu [goes] to the house of Jyeṣṭhagaṇeśvarīśa;
likewise, the one whose nature is Raudra [goes] to the house of Mṛtyupati.
Kālīśvara is the golden temple of Nairṛti.

The Lord who is the cause of all transformations—that is the abode of Vāruṇī; the Lord who is the cause of the sacrificial rites—that is the purifying abode; the Lord who is the crusher of the forces of Māra—that is the northern abode.
The supreme deity of all beings entered his own home.
The center is Manonmanīnātha; above that is Sarvālambha, a temple fashioned from gold and silver and inlaid with various jewels.
The powers (śaktis) of these [deities] should be meditated upon, radiant from their respective left feet;
having joined them with their names, either with their own mantras or with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having recited [the mantra] while performing the *sampuṭa* (encasement) practice, even that which is impossible to accomplish is indeed mastered;
it shines in the eastern direction within the upper chamber of the nine-cornered [mandala]. (64.32)
The goddess Vāmā, consisting of great splendor, possesses four arms;
her limbs are beautified by various ornaments, and she always grants the desires of the practitioner. (64.33)
In the fire and in the golden temple, the four-armed Goddess Jyeṣṭhā resides,
adorned with all ornaments and resplendent with a garland of lotuses.
She should always be meditated upon by the foremost of yogis for the attainment of all perfections;
and Raudrī, who bestows supreme accomplishment, resides in the temple of Yama-svarṇa.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with ornaments, she is to be meditated upon;
and in the southwest, in a golden house, is the goddess Kālī, four-armed.
Abounding in the splendor of all ornaments, three-eyed and bestowing boons,
the Goddess holds all weapons and is beautifully adorned with a garland of severed heads.
The supreme goddess Kalavikaraṇī, who bestows knowledge and is meditated upon by the lords of yoga through their vidyās, shines resplendent in the abode of Varuṇa.
The Mother of Yogis, four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with ornaments,
should be meditated upon by the foremost of yogis as the bestower of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*.
In the purifying Golden Abode, she should be meditated upon by the best of practitioners as resembling a Bandhūka flower, adorned with armlets, necklaces, and garlands. (64.40)
The goddess Balavikaraṇī is adorned with all ornaments;
she has four arms and three eyes, and she bestows all primordial siddhis. || 64-41 ||
The Goddess Balapramathinī is the constant bestower of wealth and liberation;
residing in the golden abode of Kubera, she is intent upon bringing joy to all. (64.42)
Śrī Sarvabhūtadamanī, resembling the first flush of dawn and adorned with a garland of karavīra flowers, is to be meditated upon in the temple of Īśāna.
Four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with all ornaments, she is to be meditated upon in the center of the Śrī-kaṇikā by all lords of men. (64.44)
The goddess Sūryaprabhā, the bestower of fortune, who transcends the mind, should always be meditated upon;
she has four arms, great brilliance, and is adorned with ornaments. (64.45)
Three-eyed, bestowing boons, all-pervading, and residing within the inner faculties of all;
endowed with the power whose essence is all virtues, the goddess has four arms. (64.46)
Resembling ten thousand suns, adorned with a garland of severed heads, possessing infinite and boundless majesty, she is to be meditated upon as four-armed and primordial. (64.47)
Having meditated upon these [goddesses] as having three eyes, red garments, and adorned with all ornaments,
one should then worship them according to the prescribed ritual.
Having recited [the mantra] with substances mentally conceived and those directly conceived, and having joined them by their names and offered them according to the rule, the wise one— || 64-49 ||
Having prepared meat and spirits, the yogi should satisfy [the deities] with a stream of honey;
together with the practitioners and yogis, he should perform the consecration with the substances of the family.
The king of yogis should feed the foremost of yogis and brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, with various kinds of family-appropriate substances, as well as foods to be chewed and foods to be eaten.
From that, one attains illumination; or one may offer [the breath] through the union with the mind. O Supreme Lord, such is the manner of the movement within the throat.
By this rite, one may attain [the goal] through a divine state;
thereafter, one obtains perfection as well as the vision of the Sākinīs.
Together with his consort, the supreme practitioner shall attain the perfected mantra. Now, O Mahākāla, I shall describe the supreme ritual of the Rākṣasī.
O Sadāśiva, by that very means of ritual action through which even the state of Śiva is attained— namely,
the conduct of the Cīnas and the noble Rākṣasīs.
The Rākṣasī language and the Vedic language are purified by Vedic mantras; the conduct of the Cīnas and the rites of the Rākṣasīs are accomplished through the very practice of the sādhana. (54–56)
I shall proclaim the practice of Cīna, which yields great fruit for Rākṣasīs;
they declare the practice of Cīna to be of eighteen kinds. (64–57)

In all cases, there is the presence of purity; one who knows the purpose and detachment [attains] that which is designated as "the highest of the high" and indeed "the unsurpassed of the unsurpassed. (64.58)
O Protector, there is that which is known as the absolutely supreme, and that which is the absolutely unsurpassed;
then there is the unsurpassed-superior, and another which is the most excellent.
One should apply the sevenfold supreme [method] in the Chinese practices; likewise, the extremely middling and the exceedingly middling in China. (64–65)
That which is designated as middling-middling is of four kinds; likewise, that which is designated as extremely low is also of four kinds. (64–61)
And likewise the *atyadhamādhama*, as well as the *atyantādhamādhama*;
the *atyadhama*, and furthermore, O Lord, the *adhamādhamam*. (64–62)
Know that the seventh is the lowest [method] for the practice of the Rākṣasī-cīna;
one should perform it in sequence according to the divisions of days, fortnights, months, and years. (64–63)
O Śaṅkara, first listen to the supreme doctrine:
when the earth is in its fertile season for three days, and likewise among the waters. (64–64)
From that gift, for as long as the day lasts, there is indeed the chewing of meat,
and the enjoyment of the five elements through the bliss of Chinese tree liquor.
That which one performs without obstruction is indeed the most excellent;
I shall describe that which is unsurpassed and supreme, which one should employ during the times of worship.
The practice of the five principles (pañcatattva) solely in secret, the non-abandonment of one's own seed, and the churning of the Kula-seat (kulapīṭha). || 64–67 ||
The application of the nectar-essence extracted from the churning of that seat (pīṭha), and the consumption of that liquor among all types of intoxicating drinks. || 64–68 ||
The best of practitioners, always intent on chewing [the offerings] rich with the eight kinds of meat, shall not take any substance except at the time of worship. (64–69)
For that is indeed the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed, existing in all places and at all times;
yet, I shall here describe the practice of the ultimate excellence according to the prescribed ritual.
By means of this, the practitioner of mantra shall achieve the vision of Sadāśiva and others,
persisting daily throughout the year at the hour of midnight.
Having brought together the five principles (pañcatattva) along with the eight female attendants,
the practitioner of mantra, eager to hear their discourse, should worship them in due order.
Having performed churning in due order and having constantly added it to the liquor,
one should take it with a pure disposition and deposit the seed in a Brāhmaṇa woman.
One should sprinkle with that seed-syllable upon the lotuses at the crown and other locations;
having given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth to them, one may also exercise one's own autonomy.
For this is indeed the most excellent, yet it cannot be undertaken without the common people;
know it to be the most unsurpassed, by which a man may become a perfected one (siddha). (64–75)
When Ānanda has departed, one should again take recourse in Ānanda;
always united with Ānanda, one should perform the recitation (japa) during sacrifices and other rites.
There is no distinction between day and night; always well-united with one's consort, seated upon the prescribed seat in a secluded place, one performs the Kula practice. (64–77)
Know this to be the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed, the severer of the net of illusion;
having first abandoned [the distinction between] time and non-time, one's own family or even that which is supreme.
Having summoned him with effort by that name, one should cause him to be given a seat and other offerings;
likewise, O sinless one, having brought a great conch and the family substances.

Having performed worship according to the prescribed rite on the day of his own family star (kulavāra), the practitioner becomes both the giver and the enjoyer of purified consciousness, O Lord of the Kula. (80)
Then, having performed the network of ritual placements (nyāsa) on one's own limbs and subsequently on their limbs,
and having performed the worship of Śiva, one should commence the Kula worship.
Having joined Śambhu with the Pīṭha, the wise one, remaining unperturbed, should perform ten thousand recitations;
he should then offer the recitation into the lotus of her left hand.
