Then follows the dismissal of one's own seed-syllable and the constant satiation [of the deities]. Having joined [the disciple] with the *āsava*, one should drink the honey together with her.
Having established the *kula* on the left side, one should complete the hundred-thousand-fold recitation (*lakṣajāpya*).
There should be a fire-oblation (*homa*) with *kula* substances, and a libation (*tarpaṇa*) consisting of one-tenth of that amount. (64–84)
Then, O Lord, there should be an initiation consisting of a tenth part of that [number], a feeding of Brahmins numbering one-tenth,
and thereafter a feeding of young maidens with honey, meat, and fermented liquors.
Every day for the duration of a year, on the family-day—whether it be Tuesday or Saturday—at the end of that year, he will certainly behold my lotus-feet. (64–86)
This is the most supreme among the unsurpassed methods for the accomplishment of the Rākṣasī Cīna;
I shall now proclaim this most excellent [practice], so listen with full attention. (64–87)
Always having conquered the senses and being devoted to the practice of yoga,
one should satisfy Kālikā, who possesses a terrible roar, with meat, wine, and other offerings.
On the Ekādaśī day, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, on a Kulavāra, and on a Kula-tithi,
having truly brought the Kula before him, he became one with the Supreme Brahman.
One should commence the worship of the Goddess solely through the state of absorption (layabhāva),
intent upon the respective meditations with that awareness and according to the Kula perspective.
In the great wheel of the *mūlādhāra*, adorned by ten million yoginīs, the perfected one—the practitioner—[proceeds] via the subtle path to the abode of ten million Brahmās. (64–91)
The Earth, the mother of Brahmā, whose nature is the bliss of Brahman, was drenched by streams resembling the celestial Gaṅgā flowing through the sky. || 64-92 ||
Likewise, [one should meditate upon] the Goddess Kulakuṇḍalinī, who consists of the Kula, who is eternal, whose nature is eternal bliss, the Mother of the Universe, and the three-eyed one. (64–93)
[She is] the one whose great joy arises from the intense nectar, with hundreds of millions of streams of the Great River falling down as drops of great intoxication and the like.
In the great path of the apertures of light, which is elevated and well-defined,
that which is subtler than the subtle shines here eternally.
The great stream arising from the *bindu*, possessing the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes—O Great Lord, what worship can there be for that form of the Kula-deity? (64–96)
With nothing but streams of drops, I constantly satisfy the sinless Kuladevī, who is the form of the universe and whose nature is both gross and subtle.
"I satisfy the Queen of the Gods from the root-center up to the aperture of Brahmā"—for one who possesses such a [realization] in the mind, what is the use of external worship? (64–98)
Nevertheless, during this great autumn festival, I shall imagine that the mistress of my family is Durgā, the mistress of the lineage. (64.99)
Having drawn forth from the root-lotus the female serpent and the daughter of the Nāgas, as well as the daughters of human hosts who exist in forms produced by illusion; || 64-100 ||
On this delightful Kula-pīṭha, I arrange myself on the left;
now, with this [offering], I worship the Kula-deity in the left quarter.

I satisfy [the deities] with the nectar from jars produced from the great drops (mahābindu), combined with the eight meats, according to the rule, and mixed with fish and ritual gestures (mudrās). 64–102.

Just as that [satisfaction] exists within my inner organ, so may this external gratification be auspicious for me always; and may the Great Night (Mahārātri) be a bestower of happiness upon me. 64.103.
"May my family be happy; may my external worship be auspicious"—for one who thinks thus in their mind, O Lord, how can there be happiness for them? (64.104)
Worship of him at all times is indeed the time that is meaningful;
worship everywhere with the realization of non-duality is the means for attaining the true state of being.
It is declared to be the most supreme for the Kaulas in the practice of yoga;
there, neither birth nor conduct matters, provided one desires the arising of the fruit.
I shall now fully declare the supreme [practice], which brings about the arising of appropriate fruits;
in this tantra, the ritual action is secret, and the Kula is invoked in secrecy.
O Lord, by always keeping the *kularasa* secret and always drinking it in secret, one shall attain complete perfection year after year; of this there is no doubt. (64.108)
Satisfaction [with offerings] month by month, the Kula-rite fortnight by fortnight, and drinking constantly day after day—this is the defining characteristic of the Kaulas. (64–109)
One should achieve success through secret practices; it must never be made public. Only when [the practice] is disclosed would one become a renouncer of everything. (64.110)
Relying upon the supreme state, the practitioner attains accomplishment swiftly;
its characteristics have been eternally described in the *Tantranātha*. (64.111)
All that has been declared by me together with Bhairava regarding the characteristics of Śiva’s speech—by relying upon that entire knowledge, you shall become supreme. (64.112)
I shall now describe the ultimate intermediate [practice] according to the Chinese ritual tradition,
by performing which all sages became possessors of the nature of the Kaula characteristics.
And in the midst of the *pīṭha* and *upapīṭha*, within the great *pīṭha* of the *Kulārṇava*,
which is entwined with the vines of the great *cīna* trees and frequented by practitioners (*sādhakas*).
There, having prepared a single seat on an auspicious day during the three lunar days (tithis), and having brought the prescribed seat there with a resolute mind, [one should proceed].
One should constantly recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while focused on the object of one's desire;
whether during the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight, one should perform the ritual procedures for the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites.
Having fed a young maiden, one should always meditate upon those two [deities] at her throat;
within a month, one attains accomplishment through the grace of the *kuladravya*.
The ultimate-middle *cīna* has been explained to you with care;
now I shall describe the supreme-middle [method], by knowing which one becomes a king among yogis. (64.118)
Then, having abandoned the distinction between proper and improper time, and remaining always within his inner self,
he should meditate upon the Goddess Amṛtā, who is the very embodiment of the Ḍākinīs and others.

Having brought together the five powers, the lord of practitioners should worship them with juices born of the *kula* and with *kula*-flowers; thereafter, he should contemplate [the deity] as one of noble lineage (*kulīna*).
Just as it is externally, so it is within the heart, in the throat, and likewise in the jeweled chamber (maṇigṛha);
again and again in Vaikuṇṭha, in the lotus of Viṣṇu, and in the mūlādhāra.
He who, having meditated again and again, offers libations, shall become a conqueror of desire;
this is exceedingly profound and difficult even for yogis to attain.
I shall now describe the "middling-of-the-middling" [practice], which is an ocean of noble fruits;
it directly brings about the fulfillment of one's desires, and one may wander with joy like Śiva himself. (64.123)
Within the month, one should perform the practice of the five principles five times;
one should constantly complete the sacrifice, the meditation, and the rite of fire-offering.
Skilled in external rites, whether in a cremation ground or even in a forest,
one should meditate upon the beloved Kākinī, Sākinī, and Kalā upon the head.
Having taken either the five powers or the pair, one should perform the libation;
at the conclusion of the libation, being free from affliction, one should recite the Vidyā for the sake of pacifying great calamities.
At the time of the libation with oblations (homatarpaṇa), one should worship the Kula-Śakti;
[offering] a seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering, and water for sipping.
The honey-mixture (madhuparka), as well as fragrant unguents, baths, garments, and ornaments;
perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and cool water. (64.128)
Cooked food, cooked meat, and cooked condiments and the like;
water scented with camphor, and thereafter betel leaf. (64.129)
Having applied a fragrant ointment mixed with cloves and other ingredients,
and having offered perfumes, garlands, and so forth, one should pray for the boon of well-being.
Having given one's own self to her, one should remain firm upon the family seat (kulapīṭha);
through the power of the Śakti-mantra, the mind enters the lotus of the throat.
This indeed is the middling-of-the-middling meal for those of noble family and Brahmins;
one attains accomplishment gradually. Listen now to the middling [rite], O Bhairava. (64.132)
Just as at the proper time, having diligently gathered the materials for the rite, one should procure nine śaktis, one śakti, or three śaktis. 64-133.
Having brought [the deity] to a secluded place, one should worship with secret substances;
one should worship the chosen deity according to the rite of the ten offerings (daśopacāra). || 64-134 ||
Having performed the recitation one thousand times during the four periods— namely at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— one should perform worship.
At midnight, the wise practitioner should place the Śakti alone before him;
he should worship her directly in her naked form with the appropriate mudrā.
O Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī,
Durgā, Śivā, Kṣamā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, Svadhā— salutations be unto you!
Having worshipped her, who is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, with this mantra,
he should thereafter drink the kula-substance given by the Śakti again and again.
Having purified the grace of power according to the ritual rule, one should perform the drinking:
"I purify the Supreme Goddess who has emerged from the lotus of the mouth of Kula. (64.139)
"O Mistress of the Kula, by her grace I drink with supreme joys"—thus and so forth is the middle [practice] proclaimed, which is difficult to find among the Chinese traditions. (64-140)
I shall now specifically describe the practice for those of the most inferior class:
within each month, there should be three days of libations, three times each.
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times for the sole purpose of purifying one's power (*śakti*).
Then, one should perform the ritual assignments (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*), the meters (*chandas*), the hands, and the limbs upon one's own body.
Having gathered [the essence] even from a member of the lineage, one should unite Śambhu upon the seat;
with the mind as the offering-ladle, one should offer the fuel of the digits of dharma and adharma into the fire of the self. (64.143)
"By means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses;
having uttered the mantra ending with *svāhā* and having applied [the breath], one should perform the recitation (*japa*). (64–144)

Having offered the recitation according to the prescribed rite, one should recite the hymn and the armor-mantra (kavaca). At the conclusion of the armor-mantra, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) of his own seed-syllable (bīja).
In the fire of the family, which is radiant with the sky and wind located in the trident of the family,
and upon the surface of the lotus illuminated by the family, [one should act] with this mantra.
Supporting [the vessel] with the hands of light and space,
I offer into the fire with the ladle of *unmanī* that which is filled with the oil of the portions of merit and demerit.
Having uttered the mantra "svāhā," one should then perform the libation with that very same [mantra].
At the conclusion of the libation, there is an ablution with the juices produced from the families of one's own Śaktis.
Feeding the Śaktis in the place of Brāhmaṇas and concluding [the rite] there—these are the characteristics of the most inferior [observance] for three days in a month. (64–149)
O beloved of the family, I shall describe the utterly and extremely base Cīna, which is pervaded by the practice of Rākṣasīs and consists of consuming those who have the form of serpents. (64.150)
One should satisfy the self with the realization that "I alone am the Supreme Brahman";
such a person, though naturally self-sustaining, is eternally intent on the renunciation of power.
And in the interval, there is no renunciation; the means to action is performed with the mind.
Having himself drunk the five principles (pañcatattva), he becomes one whose nature is eternal bliss.
He does not discharge the seed, yet repeatedly places the *liṅga* in the mouth;
in the mouth, which is lined with rows of teeth, he loudly utters the seed-syllable.
Having recited [the mantra] either in a whisper or mentally, one becomes composed of Brahman;
however, there is no external great worship without the Ekādaśī vow.
On the eleventh day, one must certainly worship the goddess Surasundarī;
according to the prescribed ritual, the wise man should satisfy Śakti.
In every land and at every sacred seat (pīṭha), impurity is not found there;
indeed, by conceiving the notion of impurity, one goes to hell.
Whether in excrement thick with its own odor, in the scent of flesh, fat, and so forth, or even in a place of sweet fragrance, one should worship with single-minded devotion. (64.157)
At the conclusion of the worship, one should recite the hymn known as the *Ṣaṭsahasra* and the armor (*kavaca*).
At its end, the hero, having conquered the exhilaration of passion, should dwell [in meditation]. (64.158)
In the interval, joined with Kuṇḍalinī, one becomes the creator of desire oneself;
but not externally, O Lord of the Gods, for there is only the abandonment of one's own seed. (64-159)

Then, one proceeds firmly in yoga through the [categories] beginning with the extremely low and the exceedingly low; I shall describe the lowest of the exceedingly low—O Soul of Time, listen with respect. (64–160)
Once a month, one should perform the family rite (kulācāra) together with the consort (sacīna);
having brought the Kula-garland, one should recite the mantra encircled by the Kula.
Endowed with power, the practitioner of mantra, devoted to the meditation on the mantra, should perform recitation;
the commencement of recitation at night is said to occur when four *daṇḍas* have passed.
One should recite throughout the entire night while remaining firm as a pillar of the Vedas;
indeed, one must not feel any fear, and one should avoid laughter in that situation.
Having offered the worship and recitation according to the ritual procedure of the Kālītantra or the sequence of the Tārātantra, he then joyfully made a formal request to the Śakti.
Having recited the hymn and the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should practice according to the prescribed rule;
by performing this for even a single day within a month, a man becomes a yogi.
By the grace of the Vīra-tantra, he does not fall into the state of a bound beast (paśu).
O Lord, on another day such as this, [offer] rice grains smeared with the five principles (pañcatattva).
Having placed [the mantra] upon the lotus of the face, one should recite it with the mind fixed upon that;
by practicing thus for the duration of a year, a man becomes a yogi. (64–166)
Having rendered even the state of a beast the lowest of the low, O Kuleśa, Supreme Bliss, I shall describe that which is the most base of the base. (64.167)
And there may arise foremost practitioners, heroes in whom the qualities of the bound soul (paśu) have arisen;
having constructed a house on a high place in the very shape of a maṇḍala. (64.168)
In the thirteenth year from birth, one should perform the rite for men even without the *śakti*;
having consecrated the seat there, one should recite the mantra using a conch-shell rosary.
One should worship one’s own self as the Śakti Kuṇḍalinī with supreme devotion, using either substituted substances or directly prepared materials. (64.170)
Alone in a secluded place, intent upon that [deity], he should mutter the mantra;
according to the sequence of the Kula worship, he should fully satisfy his own power (ātmaśakti).

Having recited the hymn and the armor (kavaca), which are auxiliary parts of the Thousand Names, according to the sequence of piercing the six chakras, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) within one's own heart.
By the very sequence of secret recitation, a human being becomes accomplished.
Thus, O Lord, this supreme method which brings about great siddhi has been told. (64.173)
O Śaṅkara, for the practitioner there is no distinction between day and night;
having abandoned the state of a bound soul (paśubhāva), he becomes a Siddha who is far superior even to the lowest of the low. (64.174)
I shall now describe the most inferior [method] according to the Chinese ritual tradition,
by which the practitioner of mantra becomes accomplished and abandons the state of a beast.
Listen, O Lord of Life, O Giver of Boons, O Sovereign of the Lords of Siddhas!
Having constructed a pavilion in the netherworld (pātāla), it was rendered devoid of the exit of fragrance.
There, having properly arranged the seat, one should dwell in its center, O Lord, together with the triple triad of *muṇḍas* and endowed with the *Kula-vidyā*.
A woman of noble birth, learned, adorned with divine ornaments, the abode of all delight, a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, and free from anger. (64.178)
Having thus placed the beautiful Goddess, who delights in the joy of youth and is a yoginī by divine nature— such a divine power (devaśakti)— upon his left side, [he should proceed].
O Lord, one should worship one's chosen deity with supreme devotion;
having performed the worship alone for three days in the family temple.
Then, for seven days, one should perform the ritual of worship and recitation;
one should satisfy the Śakti with devotion, or likewise, a young maiden.
One who desires [liberation], being devoted to the meditation on the *liṅga*, should always satisfy it according to the rules with family assets such as garments, ornaments, and decorations. (64.182)
Likewise, the best of practitioners should always offer incense and lamps,
so that there may be the destruction of the end of reality, and likewise the darkness of that mind.
O Mahākāla, [the obstacle] is indeed destroyed through the grace of the most inferior [initiation].
Now I shall describe the initiation even more inferior than the inferior, for the sake of attaining the aforementioned results. (64.184)
The practitioner, having arrived at the sacred seat (pīṭha), with disheveled hair and naked,
free from disgust and shame, [should practice] even in a solitary forest.

Whether at the source of the Gaṅgā, on a mountain, at the foot of a bilva tree, at a crossroads, at the root of a vaṭa tree, at the root of an aśvattha tree, or even at the base of a cīna tree; || 64.186 ||
Beginning diligently on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should carefully place a single severed head facing downwards, smeared with fragrant sandalwood paste.
O Lord, having approached a Cāṇḍāla of low birth at a distance of half a cubit, the practitioner of mantra should remain there and recite; he should avoid even the slightest fear. (64.188)
O Lord, having brought the power of the Cāṇḍālī and likewise the Kula-substance,
from that burning until that burning, there are one hundred and eight [repetitions].
Having performed the purification according to the prescribed rule and having offered it to the Śakti, one should drink it oneself;
thus immersed in the ocean of bliss, one becomes all-seeing and free from disease. (64.190)
Chewing the seal of meat while becoming filled with constant bliss, one should perform the practice every day for one month within the course of a year. (64.191)
O Lord, one attains accomplishment within a month by following the sequence of the Rākṣasīs;
yet, through this most base of actions, one becomes a beast dependent on the Chinese.
Listen with effort to that which is most difficult for the Kaulas to attain:
by means of the sequence beginning with the lowest, one beholds me within a year.
All ritual actions should be performed like those for the sacrificial animal, and the Kula rites may also be performed at night;
likewise, the rite for the Kula-deity should be performed for three nights at a delightful Kula-pīṭha.
Devoted to the meditation on the Kula, one should worship with supreme joys,
using Kula flowers and Kula substances, together with the limbs and sub-limbs, according to the prescribed rule.
At midnight, the family worship is performed by a Brahmin together with his Brahmin wife,
a Kṣatriya together with his Kṣatriya wife, and a Vaiśya always accompanied by his Vaiśya wife.
A Śūdra, endowed with the qualities of a Śūdra, should, in the absence of his own [mantra], be joined with another;
he should offer oblations into the beautiful lotus-face of Kālasarpīṇī.
One should perform the rite like a *puraścaraṇa* and offer libations day and night;
becoming filled with supreme bliss, one shall become a conqueror of untimely death. (64-198)
Success shall be achieved without effort through the grace of the lowest [mantra];
O God of gods, Lord, listen as I describe the incantation for the enmity of enemies. (64-199)
By the mere grace of whom one becomes free from enemies and superior;
having become firm within the lotus of the throat, [one worships] Sākinī and Śrī Sadāśiva. (64.200)
Having worshipped according to the ritual procedure, if one should meditate with the mind focused upon that, having encapsulated Sadāśiva with the mantra of Mañjughoṣa; 64.201.
Having uttered the two *tāra*s, one should likewise protect oneself and the pair;
thus one cuts down the opposing faction and destroys the enemies of yoga.
Therein, there is a pair and another pair; then three Ramās and three Vahnis;
thereafter, a pair of Māras and likewise two Khādakas.
Having uttered the two syllables "hā ra," one should recite the mantra ending in "svāhā" for the five enemies who are without throats at the tip of the trident in the enemy's throat. (64.204)
He shall become a hater of enemies and himself become a practitioner of yoga.
I shall now proclaim another mantra; listen attentively.
The mantra of the Sākinī, encapsulated by the Aghora mantra, followed at its end by the Kāmarāja mantra [addressed as]: "O enemy who causes obstacles to my yoga! (64.206).
Having uttered the two *dārayat*s, one should speak the two *vidveṣayat*s; then "cut down the enemy faction," followed by the two *harat*s of *kālajāla*. (64.207)
Having recited the mantra ending with "svāhā," one should chant the deity presiding over the throat;
such a person becomes a hater of enemies and a remover of obstacles to yoga and other impediments.
I shall proclaim the arising of auspiciousness by which a man becomes a yogi;
having risen at the end of the night, one should recite [the mantra] until midday.
If one remains constantly steady in the yoga-meditation within the throat-lotus, one attains the arising of auspiciousness and will certainly become long-lived. (64.210)
Having performed that by which the Lord of Yoginīs experiences wonder and joy, and having taken possession of the Kula and the substance, he becomes filled with supreme bliss. (64.211)
Through meditation, one attains dissolution; O Lord, how could there be destruction for him?
Free from buying and selling, he gradually attains the state of the Supreme.
When that [Self] has reached dissolution, whence is the body and whence is death? Its worship alone is always [true]; external worship is useless.
When this dissolution has occurred, how could there be creation or maintenance?
Having become the very essence of creation and maintenance, it certainly undergoes dissolution. (64.214)

I shall explain the means for [attaining] the [right] time, according to which the state of Kuṇḍalinī is reached, when one possesses the bliss of the battle accompanied by a mind full of bliss. (64.215)
One should accomplish that very time which yields fruit at that specific moment; success arises from the practice itself, so one should perform the practice for that particular time.
Listen, O Lord, to that by which the best of men attains novelty [of experience], beginning from the morning time until four *daṇḍas* have passed. (64.217)

Having performed purification such as bathing and so forth, one should take recourse to the practice of sitting; then, O Lord, one should perform the concentration of yoga and thereafter the worship and other rites.
Then, having performed the recitation and other rites, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma),
consisting of six, sixteen, or twelve [cycles], which is the retention of the wind of Kuṇḍalinī.
Then, having recited the ritual placement (nyāsa), the hymn of praise, the armor (kavaca), and the auspicious names,
one should diligently bring the deity back into the heart once again.
Then follows the drinking of the water from the feet, the consumption of the five intoxicants,
and thereafter the drinking of milk, according to the prescribed rule until the time of twilight.
By always practicing meditation at night, one will gradually attain samādhi;
in this manner, O Lord of Gods, one shall attain a state of renewal.
I shall proclaim my meditation; listen attentively.
One should always meditate on that which is without support, through joy, love, and the like. (64.223)
My meditation is proclaimed to be without support and without form;
it transcends form, is free from conceptual construction, is omniscient, and bestows the water of yoga.
A circle of light resembling ten million suns, undisturbed,
enriched with thousands of garlands of flames, and comparable to hundreds of fires of cosmic destruction.
With fangs formidable and difficult to withstand, adorned with a mass of matted locks,
holding a trident in his hand, he was of terrible form and fearsome.
The Lord, whose majesty is infinite and infinite, who goes everywhere,
has hands and feet on all sides, and eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
Constantly performing meditation upon me as abiding, pervading all, situated in the throat and moving with the breath of the throat, one becomes identical with the Supreme Brahman. (64.228)
O Bhairava, listen with diligence to my command regarding the true nature of the Guru:
the deity residing in the throat, who is the form of the divine Guru and possesses great qualities. (64.229)
Afterwards Ānandabhairava, and after that Mahākāla, as well as Jñānānanda, Sadānanda, and Bhairavānanda. (64.230)
Śyāmānanda, Śivānanda, and beyond that Kālānanda;
Sudhānanda, Harānanda, and beyond that Surānanda.
The bliss of the family, the bliss of the beloved, and beyond that the bliss of sacrifice;
then the bliss of meditation, the supreme bliss, and beyond that the bliss of yoga. (64.232)
The bliss of wrath, the bliss of action, and thereafter the bliss of awakening; the bliss of the deity, the bliss of victory, and indeed the bliss of complete victory.
The bliss of Brahman, the bliss of radiance, and the bliss of fullness beyond that, which is the very form of the bliss of the universe, resides within the circle of my command, the Guru. (64.234)
Having established the true presence of my command-guru and having worshipped him, the practitioner, with a steady mind, becomes firm and proceeds to the lotus of the throat. (64.235)
O Lord of the gods of gods, I shall describe the manifestation of the Kula-pīṭhas:
the station of desire, encircled by the digits of desire, which is the station of the Yoginīs.
Kāmarūpa is the great pīṭha, proclaimed as the kula-pīṭha;
by the mere sight of it, one is liberated while living, without a doubt. (64.237)
I shall describe the procedure for that; listen attentively.
Having arrived at the Kula-pīṭha, with one's mind fixed upon it— || 64-238 ||
Having performed worship at that very time, what on earth would not be accomplished?
First, King Kālarūpa shall appear as the bestower of success.
One should worship Kāmeśvarī, the daughter of Time, radiant with the passion of desire, upon one's own seat according to the ritual procedure for the worship of the banks.
Having worshipped her in the form of Kālī, one should then worship her with one's entire being;
[one should offer] the gift of nectar, the gift of water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), meat, and so forth, by means of the mudrā.
Water for sipping, betel with its ingredients, perfumes, embraces and so forth, as well as nail-marks, tooth-marks, and various kinds of flowers. (64.242)
The offering of incense from the collection reveals the family seat (kulapīṭha);
touching it becomes the lamp, for entry indeed occurs into the family lineage (kulāntara).
This food offering is great bliss, hidden in all tantras;
then follows the drinking of the family substance and the consumption of betel.

Know that the ritual sequence of my worship, beginning with the installation and the libation, should be performed according to the method previously stated by me, O Lord, using that root-mantra. (64.245)
I shall describe the journey of Kuṇḍalinī; listen briefly, O beloved.
Having performed the purification of the body, one should practice the postures and other preliminaries.

Having performed the threefold breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement of the elements (bhūtanyāsa). Then, one should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa) according to the sixteen-fold procedure within the ritual placements of the seed-syllables (bījanyāsa).
Having divided the pervasive [element] into five parts, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
having meditated upon the identity with the individual soul (jīva), one should cause it to enter the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Then, having gone to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should take recourse in the opening of the Suṣumṇā.
In its center is the location of the pericarp (kaṇīkā), and in the middle of that is the four-petaled [lotus].
At the edge of the four petals, that goddess shines; one should take refuge in her.
Having diligently contracted her, one who has attained the form of accomplishment shall awaken.
Then, together with the deities, one should go to the six-petaled [lotus] at the site of Kākinī;
together with that Kuṇḍalinī and the deities, one should go to the ten-petaled [lotus]. (64.251)
In this manner, having sequentially split the sixteen-petaled heart-lotus and then the two-petaled one, one should take recourse in the wheel of awakening (bodhinīcakra).
Then, having pierced the cauldron, one should take refuge in the Full Mountain;
thereafter, having indeed pierced the Transmental (unmanī), there is the dissolution of the mind in the support of the jar (ghaṭādhāra).
Above that is the tranquil Wheel of Brahmā (brahmacakra), which has the form of dissolution;
above that is the Staff of Brahmā (brahmadaṇḍa), and above that is pure water alone.
Having taken hold of all the water, which is thousand-spoked and radiant,
above that is the location of the pericarp, and above that is the perfected sword.
Then, O Lord, is the Mātṛkā-maṇḍala consisting of all seeds;
and above the Mātṛkā-maṇḍala is the seed-syllable of the Pretas, which consists of nectar.
One should meditate upon Mahākālakuleśvarī upon a seat of pretas;
right there, one should fix the mind upon the surface of her glorious lotus feet.

One should smear [the site] with the aforementioned deities by means of the yoga of dissolution (layayoga). Remaining right there, O Lord, one should meditate upon the fire-mantra (analamanu) at the root.
Having ignited [the body] with the seed-syllable of air (vāyubīja), the lord of ascetics should burn the body up to the two eyes and as far as the pair of ears, O Lord.
Having burned the eyes within the fold of the eyebrows, one should cause the fire to dissolve into the fire;
by that very mass of flames, the Brahma-bindus drip forth.
Then, one should flood the body with the streams of those drops [emanating] from Varuṇa;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the pure body as the first sprout [arising] from the seed-syllable.
One should meditate upon the coming and going of Kuṇḍalinī by way of the downward path.
Thus, O Lord, has this been told regarding the movement of Kuṇḍalinī and so forth.
I shall explain the object of practice for the practitioner, by which the practitioner indeed becomes accomplished;
through it, there shall be the perfect attainment of the science of vital breath, and one shall obtain long life and health. (64.263)
O Śrīkāruṇa, whose nature is protected without cause,
I contemplate your beloved lotus feet;
thus, having attained constant union of mind.
The very support for the illustrious practitioner is indeed prosperity. || 64-264 ||
Offering oneself with all one's being to the lotus-feet of Sundarī, which are the consciousness of eternal perception—that indeed is the support for the practitioner. (64.265)
Listen with joy, O Śaṅkara, bestower of life, to the meditation on the syllables (varṇadhyāna).
A wise person should meditate upon the letters beginning with 'A' from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (64–266)
Having remembered and strung together [the syllables] with the mantra in reverse order again and again,
the yogi, intent upon the empowerment of sentient beings, should meditate upon them mentally.

Having meditated again and again upon the syllable of the mantra, which is the Supreme Brahman and the radiant sun, possessing the luster of ten million suns due to the piercing of each individual knot.
Having pierced the center of the thousand-spoked wheel, the syllable *kṣa* shines within the moon;
having meditated upon it in both forward and reverse order, one should practice dhyāna.
The meditation on the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* has been described.
Now I shall explain the division of the petals, wherein each syllable is situated. (64.270)
The division of the petals, beginning from the visarga and ending with the bindu, has been proclaimed;
nevertheless, O Lord of Yoga, hear now the definitive determination of the meaning of the conventions.
One should meditate upon the petal by means of the yoga that revolves clockwise toward the deity;
such is the distinction of the lotuses beginning with the root, O Śrīkaṇṭhabhūṣaṇa. (64.272)
Thus, the division of the petals of the thousand-spoked lotus has been proclaimed.
Now I shall explain the *sphūrtī* vidyā, which bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) instantaneously.
One who recites the vidyā continuously, devoted to equanimity,
will suddenly become one whose knowledge has blossomed, a lord of poetic speech, and a master.
The perfection of speech and the very perfection of Kubjikā reside in his hand;
if one meditates on her situated within the lotus of the throat, positioned like the beak of a crow, [these are attained]. (64.275)
These indeed are the Sphūti-vidyās, situated upon all the petals of the lotus;
I shall now fully explain the method of separation by which the mantra-practitioner becomes fearless.
Having abandoned the sins of greed, delusion, and the like toward wife, children, wealth, friends, and so forth, one should resort to discernment, which involves only slight bodily hardship. (64.277)
That indeed should be known as *viyoga*, which is devoted to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of mantras.
Now, O Lord of Triyoga, I shall speak of the arising of the primordial knowledge (*pūrvajñāna*). (64.278)
At the appropriate times, one who desires the accomplishment of his rites should remain by the side of Caṇḍikā;
in the eastern direction during the forenoon, with his lotus-face turned toward the east.
One should contemplate the rising sun through the equal flavor (*samarasa*) of the substance of gnosis;
one will obtain the perfect arising of knowledge regarding one's own previous births and so forth. (64.280)
Having fixed the mind upon space and recollecting the mantra called "Space," one who abides in equanimity gains knowledge of the designations of previous births and so forth. (64.281)
Thus, O Lord, I have explained to you the arising of primordial wisdom from the past;
now I shall fully declare here how the perfected one, pure and partaking of the fruit, [attains it].
O Lord, by whatever sequence the union with the Khecarī may arise,
whatever attainment of the state of equal flavor (samarasa) occurs, that alone bestows the perfection of the fruit.
Listen; I shall speak in brief, for that which is to be said later must indeed be told.
Having assumed the posture and so forth, one should practice the contraction of the body. (64.284)
The *kāmalatā* [mudrā], pierced by very small tips of cloth, should be applied at the root above the base of the palate; thus one becomes a honey-drinker (*madhupa*). (64.285)

At that very moment, having performed the recitation and restrained the breath, one should drink the honey; that shall be the attainment of the state of equal flavor (samarasa), and one becomes firm within the Kāmaliṅga.
Thus has this Vidyā been described; now hear, O Lord, of the different types of creepers—that auspicious creeper which is fashioned from the thread of the white vāṭyāla plant.
Alternatively, the wise practitioner should fashion a creeper out of lotus-fiber,
measuring eighteen finger-breadths, neither too thin nor lacking the proper proportions.
Having conquered it and placed it below, O Kāmasundara, one should then rub it;
then, having been conquered, it goes upward of its own accord through repeated rubbing.

Having conquered [the breath] afterwards, one should perform the practice by placing it at the root of the palate; thus, one certainly attains nectar through the sequential cutting below the tongue. (64.290)
That would be the attainment of the state of equal flavor (samarasa) if one were to resort to the syllables of the mantra;
for those who possess the realization of the individual soul as Brahman abide in the stainless (nirañjana).
One whose body has taken the form of a gourd and who is intent upon the practice of Brahman attains the state of equal flavor (samarasa) at all times without effort. (64.292)
Whether in water, on land, or in a hole in the ground, the body does not perish;
one becomes possessed of a body that is ageless and immortal—this yoga is difficult even for yogis to attain. (64.293)
I shall explain the visualization of the body by which one becomes a lord of the Siddhas; listen with a single-minded focus, O Śambhu, for this is difficult for householders to attain. (64.294)
In a great forest, within a cool lotus grove adorned with fragrance,
having fashioned the body as the [divine] form, one should meditate upon the lotus of the throat.
Possessing a noble mind, he is indeed everywhere intent upon the conduct of a Vaiṣṇava;
and in every lotus, in every petal, he performs the visualization of his own body.
If the lords of yoga gradually perform the visualization of their own body within the lotus of the throat, then there is protection of the body. (64.297)
Otherwise, the man would fall under the power of death and become one who has strayed from yoga.
In this manner, one should perform the visualization of the body everywhere in due order. (64-298)
One is liberated from the distress of delusion and the sufferings of old age, death, and so forth.
Now I shall further explain that very conceptualization of the body. (64.299)

On a various seat that is otherwise unattainable, and having become firm in that which is accessible to the mind—conquering the sense of sight—one should even imagine one's own body [as such]. (64.300)
In the sacred seats (pīṭha) such as Vārāṇasī, at the station of Mahājvālāmukhī, in Kurukṣetra and Prayāga, and in the south at Dvārakā and other such places. || 64-301 ||
At the holy site of Haridvārodaya, at Mārkaṇḍeya and Kāpila,
in Vṛndāvana, at the secret seat (guhyapīṭha), and on the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Having mentally projected the [divine] form at Puṣkara, the Pṛthivītīrtha, Kāyatīrtha, Gayā, and other such places, the person of faith should worship the Supreme.
Having meditated with supreme devotion upon Sadāśiva, the Lord of the Śākinīs, surrounded by the hosts of Śākinīs and Yoginīs, one should fashion the body [of the deity].

Having visualized one's own body there, one should then visualize the form of the deity; whatever form is pleasing to the mind, that is the visualization and the mental construction of the body. (64.305)
By means of this mental construction of the body, the silent sage shall attain perfection of speech.
Now, O Bhairava, hear about the churning of Kāmadeva.
The churning of Kāmadeva bestows supreme happiness and liberation;
as long as the bindu remains stable in the body, whence can there be fear of death? (64.307)
From the falling of the *bindu* (vital essence), destruction occurs; therefore, one must protect the *bindu*.
I shall now describe those various medicinal remedies by which the *bindu* becomes stable. (64.308)
One should perform constant service while gathering the roots of these [plants]:
the root of white aparājitā, and thereafter the root of siddhi.
One root of śataparṇī, the root of kadamba, the root of white kunda flowers, and likewise the root of karavīra, [should be] consumed. (64.310)
O Śambhu, one should bring the root of black dhattūra, the root of sephālī, the root of the funeral pyre (citā), and likewise the root of nirguṇḍī.
O Lord of Yogins, having combined them in equal proportions according to the prescribed method on a Sunday using the roots of the *arka* plant, one should grind each separately into powder.
And on a Friday, in the forenoon, one should perform three mixed offerings;
one should purify the six nights through the mudrās of desire belonging to the Vāmadeva deity.
Raising the middle finger with the right fist and holding it,
the practitioner should first cleanse the roots of the substances.
One should drink two *tolakas* of the powder by means of a preparation with *vijayā*;
[the proportions are] one *tolaka* and a half for *unā*, and three and a half *tolakas* for *vijayā*. (64.315)
Even when mixed according to the prescribed rite on an auspicious day of the respective planet,
one shall bring Madana under control simply by consuming this.
When the mighty Puṣpadhanvan enters the mind, one should worship that Kāmadeva and then restrain him. || 64-317 ||
Thus, hear concerning the churning of desire as it is situated within the body:
[it resides] in the thumbs, the ankles, the knees, the thighs, the navel, the anus, the genitals, and the belly. (64.318)
In the regions of the heart, neck, and throat, as well as in the uvula,
the nose, between the eyebrows, on the forehead, and at the crown of the head— the abode dear to Wind and Space— 64-319.
Having established one's own body in the form of air, one should mutter the mantra;
through the yoga of breath-retention (kumbhaka), there is the stabilization of one's own body.
O Bhairava, hear of that person who remains steadfast upon the lotus of his throat—one who avoids contact with women until the completion of the practice of yoga. (64.321)
He who has no intercourse with women is one whose [seed] remains in the throat;
that righteous-souled one, with a steady mind, constantly practices yoga. (64.322)
He alone certainly becomes firmly established in the lotus of the throat;
I know him to be a wise man who knows the true nature of reality, O Ocean of Compassion. (64.323)
By the mere touch of Kuṇḍalinī, one becomes identical with her in an instant.
Having established the supreme state within all the deities, one should worship them through gnosis.
Having become firm upon every seat (*pīṭha*), the one whose self is knowledge (*jñānātmā*) should perform worship;
through this sequence, the piercing of the throat (*kaṇṭhabheda*) occurs, and the practitioner (*yogī*) quickly becomes [perfected].
Wealth, grain, land, righteousness, fame, longevity, glory, and prosperity; horses, elephants, sons, the worlds, and the rise of all one's possessions. (64.326)
By means of the clarity of this knowledge, the Supreme Lord is attained.
Having realized the wheel of the Lord of Yogins, which illuminates the mass of darkness within the cavities of the three worlds;
who contemplates His play in the root-lotus called *rasa*, pure with ten petals, and in the lotus of the heart;
and who is meditated upon by the lords of the gods in the beautiful two-petaled lotus of the throat.
I worship and meditate upon the Supreme Lord, who is the boundless sky, within a white lotus.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Knowledge for Piercing the Lotus of the Throat," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, within the *Uttaratantra*, the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the Illumination of the Six Chakras (*Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*), in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava.
Now begins the sixty-fifth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Beloved, I shall now proclaim the arising of the fruit of the collective practice."
O Lord, hear now the meditation and the mantra of the letters of the lotus of the throat.
Having constantly worshipped Sadāśiva together with the Śākinīs, even a fool becomes the best among yogins; what then need be said of others who practice the yoga of meditation?
Whoever meditates and worships thus shall obtain their desired fruit;
therefore, O Lord Vīranātha, listen as I describe the meditation. (65-3)
First, one should meditate on Śrī Śākinī, and afterwards on Sadāśiva; by means of the realization of the non-duality of these two, one shall personally become a conqueror of desire. (4)
I bow to the eternal Śākinī, of virtuous character, the bestower of boons upon the three worlds, clad in yellow garments;
the source of the Vedas, the Mother of the Vedas, composed of bliss, graceful, her limbs radiant with the Vedas held in her hands.
I meditate on her smiling, her body moistened by the nectar flowing from a large jar of ambrosia.
The Māyā on the forehead of Śambhu, possessing rays like those of the moon and endowed with glorious eternal bliss. || 65-5 ||
I bow to the Goddess Śrī, who bears the mudrās of the lotus, the trident, and others, as well as the sword and the gesture of granting boons;

she possesses matted locks, is formidable, dark-complexioned, and endowed with full breasts. She has three lotus-like eyes, sits upon a corpse and a linga, is adorned on all her limbs, and bears the splendor of a hundred moons upon her lotus-face.
The bestower of bliss to Śambhu, whose state is the final attribute, and whose nature is both gross and subtle.
Thus, O Śaṅkara, beloved of love, the great yogi should meditate upon her who possesses both gross and subtle forms, and who is the indivisible creator of division. (65–7)

The Vidyā enriched with the Vāgbhava [Bīja], the consort of Hari (Kāma), and Kamalā (Śrī)— when these alone are fruitless— [then] Māyā, Lakṣmī, the Trikūṭa, the Moon-faced one (Candravadanā), below that Śākinī, Kṣetrapāla,
the pair of breasts, and the Trikūṭa: grant me the desired Siddhi, as if it were the nectar of a bride's lip.
This manifestation of Maheśa, ending with the word *svāhā*, is for the sake of bringing joy to all beings in the three worlds. (65-8)
Having first extracted the Praṇava, and immediately after that the Vāgbhava, [one says] "Thou art Śākinī"; at the end of that, [say] "Destroy my faults. (65–9)
The couple and the consort of Fire—these are remembered as the essential meanings of the mantra.
Having extracted Kāmarāja: "O Hiraṇyākṣī, O Eternal One! (65–10).
At the end of Śākinī is Mahāmāyā, joined with the splendor of the fire of illusion;
this is the Vidyā consisting of mantra, which illuminates the lotus of the throat. (65.11)
The great vidyā Śākambharī shines upon his left side;
I shall proclaim her mantra, knowing which the lord who knows yoga becomes powerful. (65.12)
The majesty of this great mantra cannot indeed be fully described; accomplishment may be attained through mere intention, so what need be said of it as a means for liberation? (65.13)

I worship that Goddess Śākambharī, who is Knowledge, the art of desire, clad in variegated garments, seated upon a lotus throne, auspicious, known as Kāmākhyā, and possessing all the vowels; she who is the Great Yoginī of the three worlds with her branches (Śākhā), and who is eternally protected by the Lord.
She is the protector of the lords of yoga, the splendor in the lotus of Śrīkaṇṭha throughout the night and in every direction.
Even today, Śākambharī shines within the cluster of lotuses that is her beloved’s throat;
O smiling-faced one, she is joined with the lotus of knowledge and speech at the edge [of the throat], and she is Śākambharī.
Her two breasts are indeed the fire-seed (Ra), the water-seed (Va), the wind-seed (Ya), and the pair of fire-seeds (Ra-Ra).
Endowed with a portion of the love for Fire, this best of men was himself the direct agitator of the world. || 65-15 ||
One should worship Śākambharī Mahāmāyā as the deity of the door;
thereafter, one should fully worship all the gods, beginning with Śakra.
And having meditated upon the goddess Śākinī to the right of Śākambharī, one should worship her with supreme devotion according to the previously mentioned procedure, O Lord. (65-17)
Śākambharī has three eyes and is joined with the sun, moon, and fire;
she is seated upon a red lotus, is dark-complexioned, and is radiant with the beauty of four arms.
Her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and she is endowed with a sword, a skull-cup, and a lotus;
her limbs are beautified by various ornaments, and she is adorned with loose, flowing tresses of hair. (65.19)
I worship the eternal Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), who is resplendent with a smile upon her serene lotus-face, and who grants the desires of the practitioner. 65-20.
Then, at the conclusion of the meditation, one should perform the mental worship;
having performed meditation once more thereafter, one should carry out the invocation into the mind.
One should worship daily with water for the feet and other offerings, with devotion, for the sake of attaining yoga-siddhi;
thereafter, one should recite [the mantra] either a hundred times or one thousand and eight times.
When the hundred thousand [recitations] are thus completed, one beholds the Goddess in one's throat;
then one should perform the fire offerings and other rites in sequence, followed by the feeding of Brahmins. (65.23)
At the end of that, or even at the beginning, one should perform the worship of the Śākinīs.
Listen to its procedure, O beloved of my life, O Kāmasundarī! (65.24)
First, having purified the water and washed his hands, feet, and body,
the practitioner should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice while reciting the root mantra.
Having performed the binding of the topknot, one should purify the seat;
then, having prepared the pedestal with care, one should perform the placement of the *arghya* water.
Having purified the wheel of seats (pīṭhacakra), one should perform the worship of the seats;
thereafter, one should practice meditation, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsajāla). || 65-27 ||
Again, having performed a pair of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should make the body firm;
then follows meditation (dhyāna), mental worship (mānasārcā), and the display of mudrās.
Then one should provide water for the feet (pādya) and likewise water for the guest-offering (arghya) using a beautiful conch;
thereafter, water for sipping (ācamanīya), then the bath (snāna), and again water for sipping.
One should offer all perfumes, flowers, and bilva leaves, having worshipped the deities of one's own retinue in their proper sequence. (65.30)
Then, having offered incense and lamps, as well as food offerings and a beverage,
and having again given water for sipping (ācamana), one should cause the materials for the bali offering to be presented.
Having offered the bali oblation, one should recite the mantra one thousand times or one hundred and eight times;
whatever recitation one performs during the day, that same recitation should be undertaken at night.
The wise one should offer the recitation with mantras that are more secret than the secret;
then, having performed six sets of three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), he should perform prostrations and circumambulations.
A person who fashions the body as a lotus should daily recite with devotion the hymn, the armor, and the auspicious thousand names within that lotus-throat. (65.34)
Having thus worshipped Sadāśiva according to the prescribed ritual, the rites in this scripture consist of the secret worship of the secret woman (Guptanārī). || 65-35 ||
Alternatively, one should perform all worship, sacrifice, and recitation mentally;
as it is for the Goddess, so it is prescribed for Śambhu regarding recitation and sacrifice. (65.36)
In this manner, the sages situated outside should be worshipped in sequence;
O Lord, the phonemes and kalās should be worshipped, and one should worship that location situated outside them.
For in this way, by means of the monthly rite, one shall more easily attain accomplishment.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Worship of Śākinī and Sadāśiva," in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the section on Accomplished Mantras (Siddhamantra-prakaraṇa) of the Mahātantroddīpana in the Uttara-tantra of the Śrī Rudrayāmala. || 65 ||
Now begins the sixty-sixth chapter.
Ānandabhairavī said:
O five-faced, three-eyed one, who has ascended the peak of Kailāsa!
Now, having worshipped all the bhūtas, listen to the ritual for propitiating the Śākinīs.
Worship is said to be threefold: that consisting of mind, speech, and body.
O Lord, for yogis, mental worship is declared to be the direct temple of worship.
O Lord, O Supreme Sovereign, this worship consisting of speech for kings who are passionate and dominated by tamas has been described as being of three kinds.
That worship bestows accomplishment at the [proper] time, at the three times, and at all times.
For householders, accomplishment comes at the [proper] time; for those practicing celibacy, it comes at the three times. (66-4)
For yogins of wicked mind, [the worship] is fruitless at all times;
for the three states of being in these worships consist of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
O Lord, the worship of the three powers is proclaimed everywhere;
there, one should worship Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, and that Maheśvarī. (66–6)
Having worshipped with the three-fold state and with the power (śakti) through the triad of Brahmās,
one should worship by means of the animal form, the hero form, and the divine form.
For the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) is everywhere the supreme means for liberation alone.
Now listen in due order, O Lord of Yoga, to the worship of all the [deities] beginning with Avidyā. (66–8)
By performing which, the yogi shall soon become one with the Supreme Brahman.

O Heroic Lord, having beheld that place which resembles the abode of Mahendra, marked with the signs of glory, auspicious for the gods in heaven, beautiful, meritorious, pure, and blissful— delightful,
endowed with celestial dwellings, pervaded by excellent waters, and shaded by trees.
In the spring season, or at other times, one should enjoy the breeze from the Mānyasaila mountain amidst fragrant flowers and the like.
In an empty temple, beneath an excellent tree, the ascetic— whose mind is colored by the [thought of] the Lord seated upon a lotus throne on a soft cushion or a tiger skin—
should first purify his two feet as they rest upon the ground, and likewise his two hands.
Having washed [the feet] with water mixed with pure, fragrant sandalwood paste, one should assume the lotus posture.
O Supreme Lord, listen now to the mantra for purifying the water:
first is the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the end of the spreading [of the seat], and after that, the *vajrodaka*.
"I purify; then, svāhā"—this is declared to be the water-mantra.
O Bhairava, O Śaṅkara, one should pour that water into separate water. (66-13)
One should wash the hands and feet with that water according to one's desire;
having performed the ritual purification of the body with the root mantra, two sips of water (ācamana) are prescribed.
O Umattakumāra, listen now to the mantra for binding the topknot;
it is a great mantra, not to be disclosed, which serves as the seat for binding the topknot. (66.15)
O Lord of Tripura, blazing with the crest of the fire of time, purify [this place];
today I purify the seat; O Goddess, be the guardian of the door forever. (66-16)
O Supreme Lord, one should purify with [mantras] beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*;
O Lord of Tripura, blazing with the crest of the fire of time (*kālāgni*), you should purify. (66–17)
"Today I bind the tip of my topknot; O Goddess, be my doorkeeper for all time.
Then the wise one should place the arghya offering upon a beautiful conch-vessel.
Having rinsed it with the root mantra, one should then fill it with water mixed with red sandalwood and sandalwood paste, using the root mantra.
Then the wise one should cause the *dūrvā* grass, the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), and flowers to be placed upon a vessel;
having there recited the root mantra ten times, which consists of nectar.
One should display the dhenumudrā, the matsyamudrā, and the yonimudrā;
there, one should recite the essential mantra while covering it with the matsyamudrā.
First, one should sprinkle oneself; then, one should sprinkle the ritual substances.
Then, having well-prepared a pedestal out of copper with a golden needle... (66.22)
Having drawn a nine-cornered figure and a six-cornered one within it,
and two mandalas on the outside, one should then write the sixteen-syllable mantra.
And outside of that, there is again a pair of earth-mandalas with four gates;
having thus constructed the pedestal (pīṭha), one should then write the syllables upon the petals.
One should draw [the lines] with the mantra: "Oṃ surēkhāyai namaḥ svāhā. And at the end of the word "mahārekhā," one should append "praṇavaṃ ca" and "śōdhayāmi. (66–25)
One should purify the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ) and the other mantras, as well as the circle of seats (pīṭhacakraka).
Then, one should perform the worship of the seats with [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava (OM) and ending with "namaḥ. || 66-26 ||
Having first uttered "Sāṃpadam," and then "Hṛdayāya namaḥ," the wise practitioner should worship from the left with the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels.

Having worshipped [the deities] in the four directions from the east to the northeast, as well as in the center, one should then worship in the middle of that [mandala] preceded by the utterance of the seed-syllables (varṇa).
Having worshipped the power of the seat (pīṭhaśakti), one should worship the lord of the seat;
in every case, one should perform the worship with [mantras] beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ.
Pīṭhaśakti, Śākinī, as well as Śākambharī, Śivā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Caṇḍikā, and Gaṇanāyikā. || 66-30 ||
Bhadrakālī, Viśālākṣī, Śraddhā, Māyā, Dayā, Kalā, Raṇacaṇḍā, Madhumatī, Prasannā, and Ratnamālinī. || 66-31 ||
The golden-hued Kaumārī, the Goddess of Speech, Trijaṭā, the Earth,
the wielder of the trident, the Mother of the Vedas, the foremost of the Siddhas, and the Mistress of Madhu.
One should worship Madhupureśvarī, Kubjā, and likewise Madhumatī;
then Śākā, Śākacakṣu, Varahastā, and Hasanmukhī. (66.33)
She holds a skull-bowl and a sword in her hands; she wears a forest garland and a mādhavī wreath;
her limbs are variegated, her tongue is quivering, she is all-knowing, and she is composed of radiant light.
She who attracts all, she who possesses all forms, the divine wine, the nectar,
she who consists of everything, she who consists of all colors, the garland of severed heads, and she of the three times.
The Sovereign of All, the Mother of the Universe, the Great Eternal Wisdom—these sciences (vidyās) are to be worshipped with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*. (66-36)
Next, I shall explain meditation in brief; listen, O beloved, to [the meditation on] Śākinī, the venerable Vidyā of the Vedas, who possesses both gross and subtle forms.
[One should meditate upon] Gaurī, who is yellow in color, three-eyed, holding the Vedas in her hands, with a smiling face, joined by Sadāśiva, and adorned with all ornaments. (66.38)
She has three eyes and is adorned with the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire;
her lotus-like hands hold a skull and a lotus, and display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
She who is worshipped by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yogins, and siddhas;
she who is seated upon a great sixteen-petaled lotus; she who wears a garland of forest flowers.
She is adorned by the goddess Śākambharī, the Vidyā, Mādhavī, and Śakti;
she is the refuge of the sages, gods, Mahendra, and others, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
"I meditate upon her who resides in the lotus of the throat and bestows the abundance of all spiritual perfections.
Having meditated thus upon her in the lotus of the throat, one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
I shall now describe the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), by which [the breath] becomes stable at the throat;
the siddhi of moving through the sky is obtained—of this there is no doubt. (66.43)
Having joined the individual soul (jīva) within the garment of the lineage (kulavastra) at the root-lotus together with the venerable Kuṇḍalinī,
[the practitioner], with his face turned upward, pierces [the centers] in succession.
The wise one should practice dissolution into the pure lotus. || 66-44 ||
The wise practitioner should establish the *jīva* (life-force) on the side of the *śākinī*,
having brought about its dissolution into the *kuṇḍalinī* by means of the fire-seed syllable (*vahnibīja*), reducing it to ashes.
Then one should fashion the body; one should dry it with the seed-syllable of Vāyu.
Having made it nectar with the syllable of Varuṇa, one becomes free from pain.
With fortitude, one should meditate upon the Lord Sadāśiva, the master of the Śākinīs, the sovereign of the three worlds, who possesses five faces and three eyes. (66.47)
One should perform the previously described meditation and contemplate the syllables of the mantra;
having contemplated the Supreme Self within the power of consciousness (cicchakti) again and again. (66–48)
Having fixed the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) attached to one's self in that state, one should worship it,
meditating upon the great space as having a smoky form and enveloped in radiance.
Having worshipped the form of the deity, which consists of divine play (līlāmaya), with mental offerings,
one should gradually cause it to move through the door of the nostrils by means of the seed-syllable "So 'ham."
Having brought [the deity] and established it upon a seat in front of oneself, one should offer the life-force (jīva).
Remaining steady right there, one should establish its vital breaths (prāṇas) in that very place.
Having uttered the sounds *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ*, followed by *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*, and so forth, one should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); thereafter, one should perform the rite of worship.
Then one should perform the network of nyāsas; listen now to the seat of the principles (tattvāsana) and so forth.
The wise practitioner should place Sadāśiva as the seer (ṛṣi) upon his head.
Salutation to the sage Sadāśiva at the beginning;
having uttered the Praṇava in the mouth, salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre. (66–54)
Having uttered the *praṇava* in the heart, immediately thereafter [one says] "to the Śākinī," and then "salutation to the deity impelled by Sadāśiva. (66–55)

O Lord of the gods, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs using the letters of the Mātṛkā, each encapsulated by a seed-syllable and joined with the six long vowels. 66–56.
Relying upon the locus of the *mātṛkā*, one should practice with the seed-syllable;
one should perform sixteen pervasive repetitions and two cycles of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Again, one should perform meditation as mental worship and display the *yonimudrā*;
then, having formed the *padmamudrā*, one should worship thoroughly with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.
First, having recited the root mantra, one should then contemplate this water for the feet (*pādya*):
"Salutation to the Śākinī employed by Sadāśiva. (66–59)
In this manner, one should successively offer the initial arghya and the water for sipping (ācamanīya);
then one should give the water for bathing (snānīya) in order, followed again by the water for sipping.
One should offer incense and flowers with the root-mantra to Sadāśiva with devotion;
having offered bilva leaves with the root-mantra, one should worship Varuṇa.

One should display the Dhenu-mudrā, the Matsya-mudrā, and the Siṃha-mudrā; one should worship [the deity] in the southeast with the Praṇava, the syllable "Sāṃ," and the mantra "Hṛdayāya Namaḥ. (66-62)
One should worship with the Praṇava and "Sīṃ" and "Svāhā" in the southwest (Nairṛta) for the head;
one should worship in sequence with the Praṇava and "Sūṃ" and "Vaṣaṭ" in the northwest (Vāyu) for the crest-lock (śikhā).

One should worship the Praṇava with "Saiṃ" for the armor (kavaca) and the Kūrca-mantra with "Īśe"; in the center, one should worship with "Sauṃ" for the three eyes (netratraya) and "Vauṣaṭ," placing the Praṇava at the beginning.
Then, having worshipped [the mantra] beginning with *Oṃ* in the four directions and subsequently saying "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should worship the Ṛṣi on the head.
Having first offered the *praṇava* to the root-sage Sadāśiva,
the deities of the retinue and others are to be worshipped starting from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise.
Thereafter, one should worship Ānandabhairava and Mahākāla;
[as well as] Jñānānanda, Sadānanda, Bhairavānanda,
Śyāmānanda, Śivānanda, and thereafter Kālānanda.
One should worship Sudhānanda, Harānanda, and Surānanda.
One should worship Kulānanda, Priyānanda, and thereafter Yajñānanda; then Dhyānānanda, Parānanda, and Yogānanda. (66–68)
One should likewise worship Krodhānanda, Kriyānanda, and Bodhānanda;
as well as Devānanda, Jayānanda, and Vijayānanda.
One should worship Brahmānanda, Prabhānanda, and Pūrṇānanda,
who are the very form of the bliss of the universe and who reside within the circle of my command and my guru.
Having worshipped the power of their bodies (dehaśakti), one should worship these [powers] at their sides:
Kalyāṇī, Kāmakanyā, Tripurā, and likewise Ṣoḍaśī. (66–71)
[One should meditate upon] the Vidyādharī of blue complexion, the youthful Śyāmā seated upon a lion-throne,
Caṇḍikā, Upakanyā, and Sarasvatī with the moon as her crest-jewel.
Kapilā, Meghadūtā, Dhūmravarṇā, Jaṭādhārā, Trilocanā, Khecarī, Gaganā, and Kāmarūpiṇī. || 66–73 ||

[She who has] full breasts, a tiger’s face, who drinks honey, is intoxicated with passion, is beautiful, possesses the essence of affection, is righteous, likewise full of sweetness, and is the destroyer of [worldly] attachment. (66–74)
She who wears a necklace of pearls and a forest garland, the beloved of the Cakora bird and the Kula lineage;
she who is worshipped as the consort of all Gurus and whose essential nature is the totality of all principles (tattvas).
One should worship [the deities] in every direction according to one's capacity, proceeding in order up to Īśāna;
then, having meditated upon Keśava in the center of that, one should worship the vowels on the petals.
The sixteen syllables beginning with *a* and ending with *ḥ*, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and followed by *namaḥ*,
are blue in color, enriched with red, and encircled by saffron and lac.
Resplendent with a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning and as radiant as rubies, they fulfill all desires and increase the joy of the world. (66–78)
Having worshipped those who reveal the Supreme Self through the throat, palate, and other [organs] of Supriya, by means of their names, just as one worships within the orb of the sun.
Thus they shall be honored here, invoked by their respective names:
"Listen, O Lord, O Great-bodied One, O Intoxicated with Pride, O Sky-clad One! (66–80).
Always remaining steady-minded, you must indeed worship the Śākinī;
and there, within the pericarp of the lotus, [worship] Sadāśiva in the form of a corpse.
Having meditated upon that, one should worship the wheel of seats (pīṭhacakra) situated in its center;
at the mūlādhāra is Kāmarūpa, the wheel of desire (kāmacakra) characterized by three aspects.
Having uttered "Namaḥ" for the Pīṭha, one should pronounce the first Tāraka;
[then] the Jālandhara Pīṭha in the heart, the Siddha Pīṭha, and the Tricakra.
On the forehead is the excellent seat named Pūrṇagiri, which is Hiṅgulāda;
above that is Uḍḍiyāna, one's own seat, which is Meghakuñja.
The Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha) is in the middle of the eyebrows, and Vārāṇasī is at the Liṅga;
the Siddha-pīṭha is the blazing [light] in the middle of the three eyes.
Jvālāmukhī and Triveṇī are proclaimed as the three sacred seats (pīṭhas).
At Trilocana, one must certainly worship my triple seat (tripīṭha). || 66-86 ||
One should indeed worship Māyārati Subhadrikā in the lotus-face;
[and one should worship] Kampillanagara, Vaṃśanagara, and Kāmabhañjana.
There, one should worship Hiraṇyanagara, Ekadanta, Arasāya, Kapālapīṭha, and the one called Tālu; and one should worship Phaṇipīṭha in the mouth.
At the throat is the seat of Madhupurī; near that is the seat of Sudhā;
then the seat of Āhlāda, the seat of Śrī, the seat of Śūnya, and the añjali of Priyā.
The city named Purañjana is called Bhadra; in my throat is the city of Ambha.
In my navel is Mahāpīṭharāja, and Ayodhyā is the seat of Bhava.
The Lakṣmī-pīṭha, the Brahma-pīṭha, and the Lāṅgalī-pīṭha, as well as the Māna-pīṭha, the Jñāna-pīṭha, and the Rudra-pīṭha are located near that [place]. (66–91)
Lākinī is the Kula-pīṭha, as well as the Valākā-pīṭha; Raudraprabhā is the Mahā-pīṭha, and Mlecchavāsin is the Supīṭha.
The Makkāsiddhakarī pīṭha, the Nirañjana pīṭha belonging to itself, the Brāhmī pīṭha, the Datta pīṭha, and the Abhayā pīṭha as well. (66–93)
In this manner, one should worship the seat of Raṅgiṇī, as well as the seat of Phetkārī,
the seat of Gargarī-siddha, and the mountain of Candraśekhara.
One should worship the sacred seat (pīṭha) named Haridvāra as the Ocean Seat (samudrapīṭha);
and on the hips, the Saṅketa Seat and the Kāñcī Seat, which has three bells.
Having worshipped the Śūlinī-pīṭha, one should worship the Laṅkā-pīṭha;
having worshipped the Vāruṇī-pīṭha, one should worship the Vajra-pīṭha.
The Siddhakaṭāha-pīṭha and the Mahāsaṃhāra-pīṭha;
the Ṣaṭpīṭha, the Drāviḍa-pīṭha, and the Viṣṇu-pīṭha endowed with mercury (rasa). || 66–97 ||
One should worship the seat of Dalapīṭha, as well as Rādhāpīṭha known as Pañcanala, the seat of the Kuṇḍalī-cakra, and Kāmapīṭha. || 66-98 ||
One should worship the seat of the great wind and space, the seat of the wheel of the three times, the seat of Brahmā, the seat of the earth, and the seat of the enemy. (66–99)
The great pīṭha named Kuñjara and the pīṭha named Kāladharma;
to its left is the Ḍākinī-pīṭha, and near it is the Garbha-pīṭha. (66–100)
Having worshipped the Peacock Throne (mayūrapīṭha), one should worship the Garuda Throne (gāruḍīpīṭha).
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Om), one should [worship] the vowels situated here upon the throne.
I worship with lotus flowers; may they be gracious.
Having worshipped the world of the Pīṭha, one should then honor the world of Śiva.
In this manner, one should worship the world of the Kṣetrapālas, the world of Dhūmra, and the three worlds; likewise, the seven oceans and the fourteen worlds.
Having worshipped those [deities] together with the planets, the hosts of stars, and the world-protectors who have entered [the mandala], one should worship the Śakti-mantras outside of that.
Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Lākinī, Kākinī, as well as Śākinī, Hākinī, and thereafter Prabhā, Nīlā, and Bodhinī. (66–105)
Unmanī, Bhāvinī, Cintā, Priyāṅgī, Mānaseśvarī, Ulkāmukhī, Krodhamukhī, Vipracittā, and Subhadrikā. (66–106)
Nāginī, Nāgamālā, Pṛthivītīrthavāsinī, Akalaṅkā, Jāhnavī, Svargagaṅgā, and Manonmanī. (66–107)
One should worship her who abides in *sattva* as *saṃ*, her who abides in *rajas* as *raṃ*, and her who abides in *tamas* as *taṃ*;
indeed, one should worship every goddess with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
The king of practitioners and yogis should offer incense and lamps with his own root mantra;
having purified the food offering (naivedya), O Lord, he should then offer that which is intended for drink.

Having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should present the special bali offering according to the previously mentioned procedure, by means of the names [of the deities] and the rites of the five elements (pañcatattva) and so forth.
With this mantra, one should offer the three supreme oblations:
"Oṃ, O Kālamāyā, dweller in all sacred seats. (66–111)
At the end of that is the seed-syllable of Kālikā, and immediately after that is one's own seed-syllable;
at the end of "Ākāśavāhinī" follows "gṛhṇa balim" (accept the offering).

Immediately after that, the twice-born [practitioner] should take up the skull joined with the five principles (pañcatattva) and so forth, and thereafter the pair [of hands], and then the seed-syllable of sound (śabdabīja).
With this mantra, one should offer three supreme oblations (*bali*).
Everywhere, the yogi performs worship and offers the *bali* mentally.
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) in three ways, one should recite the mantra according to the rule,
either a thousand times, or a hundred times, or accompanied by eight more than that.
Whatever recitation one performs during the day, one should undertake that same recitation at night;
one should offer the recitation into the left hand of the Goddess with the mantras.
O you who guard the secret more secret than the secret, accept this recitation performed by us;
O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, may success be mine through your grace.
Having performed thirty-six rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), prostration, and circumambulation,
I pay homage to you, O boon-granting Goddess, purifier of the families of the three worlds.
O Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, I bow to you, Śākinī;
you are the illuminator of Vedic knowledge and the delighter in manifold sciences.
O Goddess Bhavānī, bestower of perfection, be forever the granter of boons;
you who are the eternal slayer of demons, destroy my enemies.
O remover of untimely death, O Kulakaumāri, O Śākinī; O eternal one united with Sadāśiva, O you who sport with Sadāśiva! || 66-121 ||
O Goddess who bestows immortality, grant me eternal devotion and bestow liberation upon me;
O Śākinī, O life-giver, O protectress of the lives of the gods!
O Śākambharī, salutations to you; take refuge in my body, O bestower of love who dwells at the root of the wish-fulfilling tree of desires.
O you who transcend all worlds, be firm upon the lotus at the neck of Siddhi.

I bow to the flaming one, the fulfiller of desires, who resides in the perfectly pure lotus-circle of the throat; O Śākinī named Kāmā, grant me the state of Mātaṅgī Śākambharī! For the welfare of the gods and the worlds, I entreat you, O bestower of perfect excellence and glory.
Abide in the sequence beginning with stability, O you who are as flickering as the light of the great void! 66-125.
Thus, by bowing with devotion, one will certainly obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
a person devoted to circumambulation attains the fruit of worship.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Śākinīs," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantra*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Uttaratantra* of the illustrious *Rudrayāmala*. 66.
Now begins the sixty-seventh chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Lord, perform salutation, perform worship, and recite the armor-mantra (kavaca)."
Meditation on the color: O Lord of the World, be steadfast in the lotus of the throat.
The supreme Śākinī-vidyā, the dispeller of great delusion,
shines forever like the sun together with ten million Yoginīs.
Remaining in the city of Vārāṇasī, worship her who resides within the lotus of your throat;
perform devotion to Mahāśivā with this hymn according to the prescribed rite.
Seated upon a flawless sixteen-spoked wheel with pure blue lotus hands,
possessing a golden luster like the flash of lightning, adorned with beautiful golden bracelets, and radiant as ten million moons;
the auspicious maiden, the sovereign of the *śākini*s, who finds delight in worshipping the lotus-hand of the Destroyer of Tripura.
Kāmākhyā, the illusory power of Rudra, endowed with twenty-four eyes and possessing a splendor like that of the beloved of Śakra.
I meditate upon her who dwells on the Sindhu river, radiant with the wives of the Pramatha hosts, endowed with the Vedas;
she who bestows bliss upon the lords of yoga, who wears a lotus bracelet, whose eyes are like dark clouds,
who is the syllable Om, known as the Cause, and who shines within the eight abodes of the collection of honey-houses.
She is eternal bliss and knowledge, possessing two digits of the crescent moon, and she is the beauty of the Vaikuṇṭha at the throat.
When shall I behold her— the bestower of the knowledge of Dharma and Artha, manifested for the sake of delighting the inhabitants of the three worlds;
the maiden of the sacred seat dwelling on the Vindhya mountains, possessing three lotus-eyes and the Vedas as her hand,
gracious, with a smiling face and a countenance like the moon, who is reached through meditation by Hari, Hara, and Vidhi?
I meditate upon her who dwells in the heart of the lotus, who possesses a beautiful form, who removes the fear of worldly existence, and who is the savior. || 67-6 ||

Subtle yet rich with gross radiance, possessing the brilliance of a bandhūka flower on the soles of her feet, the beloved of lovers, the victorious Rati incarnate, the Śākinī who destroys sorrow; she who dwells within the limit of sound, whose abode and dissolution are in the void, and who is adorned with a garland of rubies.
I meditate upon her who illumines the universe with her splendor, who is the source of the seed-syllable of Madanavadhū, and who holds a rosary. 67-7.
I bow to that Kālarājeśvarī, who dwells upon a tiger and wears a tiger-skin garment, whose eyes are like those of a deer, and whose form is absolute bliss;
she is the left-hand Śakti, coral-red in hue, the digit of the waters of the three families,
shining within the ocean of bliss, the destroyer of fear for the hosts of lords, and adorned with the seed-syllables of the Mātṛkās.
I worship her who has a terrible, loud, and boisterous laugh, who laughs joyfully with her teeth bared, and whose eyes are beautiful. || 67-8 ||
