She possesses the radiance of ten thousand rising suns, bestows the final state of liberation, and partakes in the sweetness of wine;
she sits upon the lion-throne of the earth, her hands holding a rosary of jewels and supreme bliss;
she is the essence of the playful arts of the Mother, her body is pure and shimmering, and she rests upon a stainless lotus.
She, whose light is eternal knowledge, dwells within my heart which is ever-blissful and serene. || 67-9 ||
Her limbs intent on drinking the *hālā* wine, she consists of supreme bliss, the progenitor of the Veda,
the creator of the joy of Yoga and other states; terrible in form like a mass of dark clouds, yet formidable (*karālā*),
she shines with limbs pervading the center of the sky-lotus through her unimpeded, eternal life-force.
O Mother, I worship you, who carry Śrī and bestow liberation and devotion throughout the final age of Kali.
That Vidyā, born from the qualities of the wish-fulfilling gem of the Dharma, is ever-yoked for those who are afraid;
she is perceived as the witness of great knowledge, whose sole cause is the abode of the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
You are the Mother, the Mother of the Vedas; remove, remove my impurity, you who deliver the ignorant!
She shatters the delusion of the individual soul regarding the fear of the two-fold destruction and death.
That very mother Śākinī, garlanded with flickering flames,
brings about the destruction of the delusion and confusion caused by the wandering of day and night at the rising of the light of the coming and going [of the breath].
She dwells in the lunar abode on the new moon day, belonging to the lineage of Kārtikeya’s hair.
O Haṃsa, wander here in saṃsāra; move, move! You are fickle within the wheel of sixteen digits.
The seed-soul fashions the meters of speech through prose and verse within the sacrificial pit;
from the earth-trembling Pātāla, where the Kula-yuga is the ear-ornament, the power of the Vedas emerges—
Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and the rest, and Vaikharī, whose nature is speech, moving through the eyes and the voice.
"O Kavitā, you who reside at the throat and at the root of the heart-lotus, I go to you for refuge. (67.13)
O Supreme One, O Mountain-like One, O You who are free from pride and laughter, enter me!

O Dark as a Rain Cloud, O Auspicious One, O You whose forehead is adorned with two lotuses, O You who possess an exquisite crest-lock, O You who are intent on the triple recitation, O You who are not inferior! Carry [the world] while bearing vermilion.
One becomes a subduer of the lotus-face by [meditating on] two Bhavas in the sixteen-petaled [lotus].
O Ramā, Lañjā, Māyā, together with the bride, Madana, and the Kūrca-weapon;
O Mother Śākambharī, who art for our welfare, O Earth, O Bālā, together with Kamalā—at midnight, strike the body of the enemy, kill, kill! Seize the foe in your hand!
The three-syllabled one, the six-peaked one, the daughter of Madana, the daughter of Jahnu—O Hara, destroy my sin! (67-15)
She who bestows the bliss of the Lord of Yoga, whose body is heated by the spreading heat of the sun, who herself causes burning, whose own form is scorched;
she who bewilders the deluded with her enchantment, her appearance veiled by the luster of the moon-gem upon her crown;
she who is named Kāmā, established as the sound of the seed-syllable of Brahma and the seeds of Madana, Kula, and the others.
I meditate upon this Brahmāstra-vidyā, which ends with "svāhā," and is known as the Haṃsa-mantra of the Lord of the Earth-born (the Brahmins).
In the evening, Kāmalakṣmī, joined with the wind and the moon, long-eyed and three-eyed;
at midday, Sāvitrī does not move, yet she moves by faith above the head.
Resplendent like ten million suns, she does not bow, for she is entirely filled with crooked brilliance.
At dawn, she with the white face and reddish limbs delights him who is like a peak of ten million fires from the fire of time.
O Gāyatrī, you whose form and measure are immeasurable, who are honored by the forest-dwellers at Bhālakūpa;
whose body is like the fire of the dissolution of the world, and whose lotus feet are licked by the rays of the sun that dispel darkness;
you are the primordial knowledge beginning with the syllable *vāgbhava*, whose body consists of the *praṇava*, the divine Lakṣmī, and the source of grace.
In the sixteen-spoked and thirty-two-spoked [mandalas], there is a pair shining with half-moons beginning with the sound *nāda*.
O Jāyā, Māyā, Vimāyā, Hayamukhī, Vimalā, Kevalā, Tārahārā;
O you whose limbs are adorned with necklaces and suns, who deliver the pair of Tārās and the pair of moons among the yugas of your own consorts;
you are Svāhā, Medhā, and Svadhā; you are the speaker of words that loosen the knots of the Vedas, praises, and sacred scriptures.
Protect me alone; [the syllables] "rakṣa-yugma," "dharaṇi-dhara-sukhaṃ," and "sañcaya-agni-priyāntā. (67-19)
If a lord of men, having meditated constantly, recites this supreme hymn, he becomes happy;
blessed, he attains merit, and beholding the seats (*pīṭha*) and other sites, he reaches the dissolution of the gods.
He becomes a possessor of the perfections (*siddhi*) even among yogis, and the most beloved knowledge and wealth are obtained.
They suddenly bring the king under their control, and they captivate Rāmā herself with their side-long glances.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Hymn to the Śākinīs," in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, within the *Uttara-tantra*, the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the section on the *Siddhamantra-prakaraṇa*, the *Ṣaṭcakra-prakāśa*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 67.
Now begins the sixty-eighth chapter.
The illustrious Ānandabhairava said:
"O sinless one, for the sake of protecting the three worlds, I worship you."
For the sake of dissolving the cycle of existence, [I take refuge] in your glorious lotus feet.
O Great Goddess, Mother of the World, O Bhavānī, O Bhairavī, bestower of supreme bliss, please tell me clearly the meditation on the phonemes within the vital breath.
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said:
Now, O Kāmeśa, fair-limbed one, revealer of dharma and adharma, listen now, O omniscient one, to the exposition of the Great Knowledge. (68-3)
Out of affection for you, I shall describe my own form through the meditation on colors;
this meditation, which grants success instantaneously, is accomplished by mere knowledge. (68-4)
I meditate upon the syllable *A*, which is to be constantly contemplated by Hari, Hara, the four-faced Brahmā, and the gods; it is white, with arms as beautiful as the moon’s face,
worthy of being practiced, youthful, three-eyed, and adorned with ornaments.
[He] whose rays possess the luster of the moon, honored by skulls, lotuses, weapons, and serpents.
[Visualize her] rich with the seed-syllable *Āṃ*, radiant, possessing golden jars, honey, and joy, [seated upon] a celestial chariot;
bearing a white luster, endowed with ears and arms, and a garland known as the lotus-stalk;
holding a sword, possessing the brilliance of the gems in her crown, [and manifesting] wrath in the expanse of space.
I meditate upon her who is radiant with various ornaments and who rides upon a pale-yellow moon.
I bow to Māyā, who abides in the universe, joined with her bridegroom and endowed with the sixteenfold Śrī;
she who is characterized by the marks of Māyā, who bestows knowledge, fearlessness, and the state of Śrī upon the three worlds;
she who possesses four lotus-hands, has three eyes, and holds a trident, a sword, a garland, and a lotus.
I meditate upon her, adorned with anklets born of various jewels and bowed to by the gods, seated upon a pure lotus.
Shining with the brilliance of ten million suns, adorned with great ornaments of gold, attainable through meditation, her form shaped like the letter *Ī*,
possessing three eyes and a lotus face, her limbs radiant with the laughter of the Vedas,
holding in her excellent hands a conch, a lotus, a sword, and a bell, seated upon the throne of the Goddess;
I worship her who abides in the Vedas, who is established by the Vedas, who is joined with the blood-drinker, and who is the play of childhood. 68-8.
The syllable *ukāra* is Brahmā, accompanied by the three sages, having the nature of gold;
it is a horse mounted upon a swan, joined with the letter *i* as its tongue, sounding like a palace lattice;
it is vast, four-faced, possessing the brilliance of a hundred suns, and three-eyed.
I perpetually bow to the young man who delights in the matted locks and the sacrificial pits.
He who bears the syllable *Uṃ* as his universal form, entwined with a hundred moons, possessing the luster of gold and the threefold creation;

who holds in his two hands a rosary of pure beads made of *mandāra* flowers gathered from the Lake of the Mind, thick with intense nectar; whose nature is bliss through the garlands of the wives of the serpent hosts.
I meditate upon the fulfillment of the desires of the Siddhas, the dense lotus of the Kula, within the sixteen-spoked [wheel].
[One should meditate upon] the syllable *Ṛṃ*, whose body is adorned with a pure rosary accompanied by seven lines,

who abides in *māyā*, who possesses a supreme lotus-face that is serene, whose body has the form of an elephant, who is meritorious, perfected through sacrifices and other rites, who delights in the digit of the moon of passion, and who is endowed with six arms.
I worship that one who possesses a bell, beautiful garments, a sword, a stainless lotus, and a skull as his ornaments. || 68-11 ||
The seed-syllable is *Ṛṃ*, with the Lord of Guests (*Atithīśa*) as its head; it has a white lotus face, is white in color, and possesses three eyes.
It ends with the vowels *Māyā* (I) and *Lakṣmī* (Ī); it has the rays of the rising sun, six arms, and blue garments.
It is most beautiful with various ornaments, its crown-tuft is radiant, and its nature is like the orb of the moon.
I worship Him who holds a sword, a lotus, the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), and honey, and who has a beautiful mace and a noose in His hands.
One should meditate upon the Lord who bears the syllable *laṃ* as his emblem, whose hair stands erect, whose lotus-face shines with the splendor of three eyes,
who is the full Self, the Supreme Ruler, composed of the density of the three qualities (*guṇas*), blue in color, possessing the three states of being,
six-armed, with tawny hair, a pure and unfading circle of matted locks, and adorned with a garland.
I meditate upon Him who is adorned with the Vedas, the sword, the garland of knowledge, the lotus, and the excellent mace. || 68-13 ||
I meditate upon the syllable *ḷṃ*, which is clothed in white garments, possesses white rays,
is submerged in nectar, has deer-like eyes, and is supported by the Vedas as its serpents;
it bestows auspiciousness and possesses the nature of holding a serpent, a lotus, a sword, and granting boons.
The formidable Karāla, who is constantly served by hosts of gods and sages. || 68-14 ||
The seed-syllable *Eṃ* is black in color, attended by a hundred young women, and surrounded by the foremost of gods;
it possesses the luster of the sun, is joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the visarga, has two arms, a lotus on its forehead, and is formidable;
it is adorned with ornaments, wears a crown, has three eyes, is immortal, and shines with anklets like the moon.
I meditate upon Jhiṇṭīśa and Śambarīśa, pervaded by the hosts of Pramatha and Suta.
I meditate upon the essence of the seed-syllable, who has the luster of white lotuses, three-fold folds and three eyes, and pure bandhūka-colored garments;
who is adorned with jewel-ornaments and necklaces, whose word is the three worlds, who possesses six arms,
and who is contemplated within the sixteen-spoked [cakra] as the delighter of the three Madanas amidst five rays of light.
The first of the yoga-mantras, the lord of the elements, which creates the path of the sky and ends with the vowel following the wife of fire (the letter *au*). 68-16.
I worship the face [of the Lord], whose characteristic is the *praṇava*, who possesses cool rays, whose earrings sway,
who is the radiant four-armed one, who holds a lotus, a conch, a trident,
and the gesture of fearlessness, whose body is adorned, and whose garment is pure yellow.
Enveloped by hundreds of white rays, the supreme [deity] is richly adorned with a crown and anklets.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Grace, who is as white as the *praṇava*, whose form is the syllable *oṃ*, and who is most subtle;
who pierces the gateway to Brahman, who is graced by the waters of the Vedas, and who bears a sword, arrows, and a garland of missiles;
who possesses the brilliance of ten million living beings, who wears a crown of a hundred suns, and who is the Great Lord, the King of Wrath.
Resplendent with jewel ornaments, his soles shine with a circle of light, possessing a reddish glow.

He who is the nature of the syllable AṂ and the Bindu, possessing graceful ten arms, clothed in a tiger skin, five-faced, three-eyed, adorned with bracelets upon his own arms, shining with the brilliance of ten million moons,
and bearing a trident, sword, arrow, discus, bow, mace, shield, club, and a garland of lotuses.
And one should meditate upon the non-cruel deity, the autumnal one who possesses the sound of an axe, who is both gross and subtle.
The syllable *Aḥ*, the glorious *Visarga*, seated upon a lotus petal, the sole giver of the wretched;
white in luster like ten million suns, graced with a hundred arms, bearing the weapons of the Vedas, knowledge, and the sword;
with all his limbs dripping red, three-eyed, delighting the Goddess Kamalā, and possessing a gentle smile.
I meditate upon the Cause, whose slender rays arise from the splendor of fifty faces. || 68-20 ||

Having meditated thus, with a steady mind, one should worship Sadāśiva, the Lord of the World, who possesses the form of the phonemes and is endowed with Śakti, within the sixteen-spoked [cakra]. (68.21)

Then the intellect becomes serene, and one is born as an immortal before long; one attains the power of moving through the sky, mastery over speech, and the supernatural powers such as the freezing of water.
One who is free from desire and fear should meditate on them starting from the east and moving counter-clockwise;
the practice of meditation should be performed in a secluded place where those vidyās manifest.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Meditation on the Pure Phonemes," in the *Viśuddhavarṇadhyāna*, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*. 68.
Now begins the sixty-ninth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O five-faced, three-eyed one, you who are mounted upon the peak of Kailāsa!"
O Śrī Sadāśiva, beloved of the vital breath that is both indivisible and the divider! 69-1
To the protector of existence and life, to the remover of the kālakūṭa poison, to the one whose sandals are Pratyāṅgirā—to him, I offer this beloved gift consisting of sound, subdued. (69-2)
Out of a desire to protect my devoted, virtuous yogis,
I shall certainly declare here the characteristics of all that is auspicious.
This [mantra] known as the one consisting of one thousand and eight [syllables], accompanied by Sadāśiva, generates great power and subdues those of wicked mind. (69-4)
It provides all protection in the world for the sake of manifesting the lotus of the throat;
it removes untimely death and wards off all diseases. (69–5)
It directly brings about the perfection of yoga, produces the bliss of immortality,
removes the flames of poison and other afflictions, and is the supreme means for attaining the power of mantras.
Merely by remembering her names, one becomes dear to the yogins;
provided that one worships and meditates upon the Goddess who is united with Sadāśiva. (69–7)
At the end of a month, one attains perfection; there shall be union with the Khecarī.
By reciting this, the power of traveling through the sky is certainly obtained. (69–8)
Through recitation and retention, the yogi shall obtain wealth, jewels, the perfection of action, and the perfection of power; he becomes Mahādeva, the eternally auspicious Sadāśiva. (69–9)
Viṣṇu himself, the wielder of the discus; Brahmā, whose wealth is perpetual austerity;
all the gods who are practitioners of yoga; and the sages, who are likewise practitioners of yoga. (69–10)
Since all the Siddhas wander about having taken up [this text] through its recitation, those who recite it constantly are indeed Siddhas born from Viṣṇu. (69–11)
What more need be said? By merely speaking of it, one may obtain enjoyment and liberation in an instant.

The Ṛṣi of this *Śrībhuvanamaṅgalamahāstotra-aṣṭottarasahasranāman* is Sadāśiva; the metre (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī; the deity (*devatā*) is Sadāśiva-Śākinī; and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining the eight human goals (*puruṣārtha*), the eight supernatural powers (*siddhi*), and the perfection of the timely yoga.
Oṃ. Śākinī is clad in yellow garments; Sadāśiva is the Lord of Umā.
Śākambharī, Mahādevī, Bhavānī, the beloved of the world. || 69-13 ||
The Yoginī is the essence of the yoga-dharma, the self of yoga, the illustrious Sadāśiva;
she is the beginning of the ages, the dharma of the ages, the knowledge of yoga, and the sovereign of excellent yogis. (69.14)
Yoginī, known as Yogajetā, Suyogā, Yogaśaṅkara, Yogapriyā, Yogavidvān, Yogadā, and Yogaṣaḍbhuvi. (69.15)
The soul of the Lord of the World through the three yogas, she who grants success to the reciter;
she who is diligent, who delights in diligence, who is bliss, who knows the ritual rules, and who knows the essence of the Vedas. (69-16)
Supratiṣṭha, Śubhakara, Madirā, Madanapriya, Madhuvidyā, Mādhavīśa, Kṣiti, and Kṣobhavināśana. || 69-17 ||
Vītijña, Manmathaghna, Camarī, Cārulocana, Ekāntarā, Kalpataru, Kṣamābuddha, and Ramāsava. (69–18)
Vasundharā, Vāmadeva, Śrīvidyā, Mandarasthita, Akalaṅkā, Nirātaṅka, Utaṅkā, and Śaṅkarāśraya. || 69-19 ||
Formless and free from conceptual construction, she is the giver of aesthetic delight and the refuge of the connoisseur;
he is Rāma, the lord of Rāmanana, and Lakṣmī, whose eyes are like blue lotuses. (69.20)
Vidyādharī, Dharānanda, Kanakā, Kāñcanāṅgadhṛk;
Śubhā, Śubhakara, Unmatta, Pracaṇḍā, and Caṇḍavikrama. (69–21)
Suśīlā, Devajanaka, Kākinī, Kamalānana;
Kajjalābhā, Kṛṣṇadeha, Śūlinī, and Khaḍgacarmadhṛk. (69.22)
He who is grasped through the states of existence, who is white with radiance, who is the patient earth, who is unshakable, who is auspiciousness itself, who is the source of peace;
he who is speed, the restrainer, the supreme, Hari, Hara, the destroyer of time, and the imperishable among the imperishable.
The eternal one, the eternal, the lord of the dweller in the cremation ground;
the invincible, the imperishable, the one who moves upon the earth, the one of equal arrival, the lord of measure.
He whose lineage is unbroken, whose face is stainless, who is wrinkled yet free from blemish;
he who possesses radiance, who is both transcendent and immanent, who is with essence and without essence, and who is both hand and non-hand.
He is composed of nectar, he is the essence of milk, he is the destroyer of obstacles, and he is the source of compassion;
he is the dispeller of fear, the fearless one, the conqueror of non-victory, the giver of rest, and the lineage of the fruit.
Meeting with the righteous and the unrighteous, pleasure and displeasure, the high and the low; the excellent woman, the mountain-bearer, the light-maker, and the wandering and non-wandering. (69.27)
He is virtuous, happy, endowed with auspicious marks, compassionate, and a treasure-house of mercy;
he is the lord of the earth, beloved by his wife, and the one who transcends the mind.
She is ever-running and immovable; she is trembling and exceedingly fickle.
She is fond of pungent things and is extremely pungent; she is fond of cleverness and is extremely clever. (69.29)
Dhanāvalī, Gaṇāgaṇī, Kharākhara, Phaṇi, Kṣaṇa, Śiromaṇi accompanied by Priyā, Śākinī, and Sadāśiva. || 69-30 ||

Ruddy as the dawn, the destroyer of clouds, the horse, the rider, dissolution, and the state of absorption; possessing beautiful teeth, the arrival of the gift, the remover of the wicked, and the one of great resolve. (69.31)
With quivering breasts, veiled by the speed [of his movement], his throat deep within his chest, he possesses a fierce, gurgling sound as he enters the fire of his beloved’s prowess. 69-32.
Praśānti is established as Unduru, Maheśvarī is Maheśvara;
Mahāśivāvinī is Ghanī, and Raṇeśvarī is Raṇeśvara. || 69-33 ||
The radiant one, the burner, the authoritative one, the knower of authority;
she who dwells in purity, the pure sage, the destroyer of pride, and the most excellent honey.
Tilottamā, the most excellent; eternally free from disease, consisting of compassion;
the tree that carries one across transformations; the god among gods and demons, the preceptor of the immortals. (69.35)
Prakāśikā, Prakāśaka, Pracaṇḍikā, Vibhāṇḍaka, Triśūlinī, Gadādhara, Pravālikā, and Mahābala. || 69-36 ||
Possessing action, he is the lord of old age; clothed in radiance, he is sky-clad;
he has the lineage as his garment and the deer as his garment; he is without interval, yet he is within old age.
Śambhu whose abode is the cremation ground; Bhavānī with her terrifying eyes; the beloved of Kṛtāntahāriṇī; the enraged destroyer of desire.
Four-armed, lotus-eyed, ten-handed, the great preceptor;
ten-faced, ten-necked, with cast-away eyes, he who delights in casting [down] enemies. (69.39)
Vārāṇasī is the resident of the sacred seat (pīṭha); Kāśī is dear to the Universal Teacher;
Kapālinī is Mahākāla; and Kālikā is the purifier of the Kali age.
Vāgmī is situated in the cavity-path; Ratī is the lord who is the preceptor of Rāma;
Sulakṣmī is located in the intermediate space; and Yogikanyā is Kṛtāntaka. || 69-41 ||
The ender of intoxication, the giver of merit, the savior, the lover of the young;
the one who delivers from great fear, Tārā, the deliverer, the lord of the stars. || 69-42 ||
The mother of the Tāraka-Brahman, the greatly proud one born at the peak of existence (Bhavāgra),
she who is accessible through the *liṅga*, whose form is the *liṅga*, Caṇḍikā, and the one whose vehicle is the bull.
Rudrāṇī and Rudradeva; Kāmajā and Kāmamanthana; Vijātīya and Jātitāta; Vidhātrī and Dhātṛpoṣaka. || 69-44 ||
Formless, he is the great space; he is perfect knowledge and the radiant fire;
he is Vāsuki, the protector from falling; he is the triple-stream confluence who reveals the ultimate reality.
Patākā, Padmavāsī, Trivārtā, Kīrtivardhana, Dharaṇī, Dhāraṇāvyāpta, and Vimalānandavardhana. || 69-46 ||
Vipracitta, Kuṇḍakārī, Viraja, Kālakampana, Sūkṣmādhāra, Atijñānin, Mantrasiddhi, and Pramāṇaga. || 69-47 ||
Vācyā, Vāraṇatuṇḍa, Kamalā, Kṛṣṇasevaka;
Dundubhisthā, Vādyabhāṇḍa, Nīlāṅgī, and Vāraṇāśraya. (69–48)
He is the spring and other seasons, the cool-rayed moon, the one to be honored, and the beloved of Śakti;
he is enriched with swords, discuses, and spears, and is fond of the cool season and small wealth.
Durvācya, Mantranilaya, Khaṇḍakālī, Kulāśraya, Vānarī, Hastihāra, Ādya, Praṇaya, and Liṅgapūjaka. (69–50)
Mānuṣī and Manurūpa are blue-colored;
Vidhuprabha holds the moon below; Kāla and Kamalā have long hair. (69.51)
Dīrghakeśī, Viśvakeśī, Trivargā, Khaṇḍanirṇaya, Gṛhiṇī, Grahahartā, Grahapīḍā, and Grahakṣaya. || 69-52 ||
Puṣpagandha, Vāricara, Krodhādevī, Divākara, Añjanā, Krūrahartṛ, Kevala, and Kātarapriya. (69–53)
Padyāmayī, the remover of sins, Vidyādyā, Śailamardaka, Kṛṣṇajihvā, Raktamukha, Bhuvaneśī, and Parātpara. (69–54)
The root of the jujube tree is Kṣetrapāla; Balānala is the contact with that root;
the Preceptor (Ācārya) is situated in the land of the ancestors; and Viṣaya is Bādarāyaṇi. (69.55)
The one who goes before, the leader, the one who goes to heroes, the destroyer of enemies;
the great illusion, the master of illusion, the giver of boons, and the ender of desire. || 69-56 ||
The Fortune of the Animals, the Lord of Animals, the Five Powers, the Destroyer of Night;
the Pervasive One, Concealed by Vijayā, the One Beyond the Species, and the One with the Excellent Face. (69–57)
Kaṭumūti, Śākamūti, Tripura, Padmagarbhaja, Ajābya, Jāraka, Prakṣya, Vātula, and Kṣetrabāndhava. (69–58)
Abiding in infinite and endless forms, established in beauty, free from accumulation; the knower of yoga, the lord of the wheel of knowledge, wandering, yet established in the state beyond wandering.
Śiśupāla, Bhūtanāśa, Bhūtakṛtyā, Kuṭumbapa, Tṛptāśvattha, Varārohā, Vaṭuka, and Proṭikāvaśa. (69–60)

Faith, endowed with faith; nourishment, the nourished; the enraged one, the eighth month of spring (Mādhava); the united, the act of uniting; the earth, the knower of reality, and the lover of the sacrificial pap (caru). (69–71)
The destroyer of fear is unattained; the teeth have reached the mind.
Life is supreme bliss; she is rich in knowledge, born of the deeds of dharma. (69–62)
Apavādaratākāṅkṣī, Vilvānābhadrakambala, Śivivārāhana, Unmatta, Viśālākṣī, and Parantapa. (69–63)
Pārvatī and Parameśvara are the well-guarded and the excellent guardian;
she is the illustrious Mātaṅgī, he is established in the three seats (Tripīṭha), subject to transformation, and purified by meditation. (69–64)
Cāturī is Caturānanda; Putriṇī is Sutavatsala;
Vāmanī is Viṣayānanda; Kiṅkarī is Krodhajīvana. || 69-65 ||
Candrānana, Priyānanda, Kuśala, Ketakīpriya, Pracala, Tārakajñānin, Trikarma, and Narmadāpati. (69–66)
He who dwells in the door-panel, he who dwells in the bundle of grass, the knower of the sciences, he who resides in the *vardhamāna* vessel;
the three-peaked one, the triple bliss, the delighter, and the lover of Nandana. || 69-67 ||
Vicikitsā, Samāptāṅga, Mantrajña, Manuvardhana, Mannikā, Ambikānātha, Vivāśī, and Vaṃśavardhana. || 69-68 ||
Vajrajihvā, Vajradanta, Vikriyā, Kṣetrapālana;
Vikāraṇī, Pārvatīśa, Priyāṅgī, and Pañcacāmara. || 69–69 ||
Āṃśikā, Vāmadeva, and the others, along with Vimāyā, are Parāpara;
Pāyāṅgī possesses supreme sovereignty, and Divākara is the giver and the enjoyer. (69–70)
The Bestower of Desires, Vicitrākṣa, Ripurakṣa, Kṣapāntakṛt, Ghoramukhī, the one named Gharghara, Vilajvā, and Jvālinīpati. (69–71)
Jvālāmukhī, Dharmakartṛ, Śrīkartṛ, and Kāraṇātmaka; Muṇḍālī, Pañcacūḍa, and Triśāvarṇa are established as the elder-born. (69–72)
Virūpākṣī, Bṛhadgarbha, Rākinī, Śrīpitāmaha;
Vaiṣṇavī, Viṣṇubhakta, Ḍākinī, and Ḍiṇḍimapriya. (69–73)
Ratividyā, Rāmanātha, Rādhikā, and Viṣṇulakṣaṇa; Caturbhuja with the Vedas in hand, Lākinī, and Mīnakuntala. (69–74)
Mūrdhaja, Lāṅgalīdeva, Sthavira, Jīrṇavigraha, Lākinīśā, Lākinīśa, Priyākhyā, and Cāruvāhana. (69–75)
He has matted locks, he wears three braids, he possesses four limbs, and he is both moving and unmoving.
He is the triple-streamed one, the lord of Pārvatī, the sovereign of the world, and the lord of men. (69–76)
Pinākinī and Pinākī, Candracūḍā and Vicāravit, Jāḍyahantrī and Jaḍātmā, Jihvāyukta and Jarāmara. (69–77)
O King of kings, she is named Anāhatā, the Kākinī established in sattva;
she has the wind as her form, holds a lotus in her hand, is pure, and has a pure vehicle. (69–78)
Vṛṣalī, she who stands upon the back of the bull; Vibhogā, the increaser of enjoyments;
Yauvanasthā, the witness of the young; Lokādyā, the witness of the worlds. || 69-79 ||
Bagalā, the one named Candracūḍa, Bhairavī, Mattabhairava, Krodhādhipā, Vajradharī, Indrāṇī, and Vahnivallabha. || 69–80 ||
Nivīkāra, Sūtradhārī, Mattapāna, Divāśraya, Śabdagarbha, Śabdamaya, Vāsava, and Vāsavānuja. || 69-81 ||
The guardians of the directions, the lord of the planets, Īśāna, Naravāhana, Yakṣiṇīśa, Bhūtinīśa, Vibhūti, and Bhūtivardhana. || 69-82 ||
Jayāvatī, Kālakārī, Kalkyavidyā, Vidhānavit, Lajjātītā, Lakṣaṇāṅga, Viṣapāyin, and Madāśraya.
She is foreign, yet she resides in the foreign; she is sinless, having abandoned sinful livelihoods.
She is beyond great agitation, transcending the parts (kalās), and free from the arising of the collection of sense organs.
Vācāla, Vacanagranthimandara, Vedamandira, Pañcama, Pañcamīdurga, Durgā, and Durgatināśana. (69–85)
Durgandhā, Gandharāja, Sugandhā, Gandhacālana, Cārvaṅgī, Carvaṇaprīta, Viśaṅkā, and Maralāravit. (69–86)
Atithisthā, Sthāvarādyā, Japasthā, Japamālinī, Vasundharasutā, Tārkṣī, Tākīka, and Prāṇatākīka. (69–87)
He whose nose is covered by palm trees, the husband of the palm-born woman, the wearer of matted hair,
the lord of those with matted hair, the bearer of matted locks, the lord of the seventh, and he who has transcended the seventh.
Kālī, who assumes the form on the eighth lunar day; the Lord of all, the Sovereign of the Sovereigns;
the destroyer of enemies, the eternal counselor; the youthful one, whose refuge is the stars.
Dharmagupti, Sāragupta, Manoyoga, Viṣāpaha, Vajrāvīra, Surāsaurī, Candrikā, and Candraśekhara. || 69–90 ||
Viṭapīndra, Vaṭasthānī, Bhadrapāla, Kuleśvara, Cātakādya, Candradeha, Priyābhārya, and Manoyava. (69–91)
The one whose merit is the sacred ford, the yogi of the ford, the lotus-born, the one who reclines upon the waters;
the one who has become dear to the Lord of Beings, the one garlanded with yonis, the one whose face is the yoni. || 69-92 ||

The Blessed One is the sister; you are the one to be enjoyed; he has terrifying eyes. He is the daughter of Bhṛgu; he is the Lord of the descendants of Bhṛgu; he is the cause of the dissolution and the abode.
Rudrāṇī, Rudragaṇapa, Raudrākṣī, Kṣīṇavāhana;
Kumbhāntakā, Nikumbhāri, Kumbhāntī, Kumbhinī, and Anaga. || 69-94 ||
Kūṣmāṇḍī is rich in wealth and jewels; Mahogrā is a fierce seizer; Śubhā resides in a camp; Śivānanda has made her seat upon a corpse. (69–95)
Praise, equanimity, wisdom, discernment, one with auspicious eyes,
the science of Kuru, the Kuru lineage, a noble maiden, and one who holds a lotus stalk.
Dvidalastha, Parānanda, Nandisevya, Bṛhannalā, Vyāsasevya, Vyāsapūjya, Dharaṇī, and Dhīralocana. (69–97)
The triple forest, the tip of the balance-beam, cotton, the bearer of the body of the skull-bowl;
he who is entered by and worshipped by Vasiṣṭha, the one under control, the one whose life is under control.
She who holds a sword in her hand, the wielder of the sword; she who holds a trident, the radiant one;
the incomparable, the one beyond comparison; the manifold, the determination of meditation. || 69-99 ||
Aprakāśya, Viśodhya, Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍavāhana, Girijā, Gāyanonmatta, Malāmālī, and Calādhama. (69–100)
Piṅgadeha, Piṅgakeśa, Asamartha, Śīlavāhana, Gāruḍī, Garuḍānanda, Viśoka, and Vaṃśavardhana. || 69-101 ||
Veṇīndra, Cātakaprāya, Vidyādyadoṣamardaka, Aṭṭahāsā, Aṭṭahāsa, Madhubhakṣa, and Madhuvrata. (69–102)

She is endowed with sweet bliss, she is Mādhavī, the destroyer of the month of Madhu; she is of the nature of the sea-monster, her love is like that of a sea-monster, she resides in the month of Māgha, and she is borne by Indra. || 69-103 ||
Viśākhā, Susakhā, Sūkṣmā, Jyeṣṭha, and the one dear to the elders;
Āṣāḍhanilaya, Āṣāḍha, Mithilā, and the Lord of Maithilī. || 69-104 ||

He who has attained coolness and coldness, the Lord of the characteristics of pure speech, the progenitor of those who perform what ought not to be done, the auspicious one belonging to the month of Bhādrapada. || 69-105 ||
Pravara was known as Varahaṃsa; Pavaśobhā was a knower of the Purāṇas;
Śrāvaṇī was Harinātha; and Śravaṇā was Śravaṇāṅkura. || 69-106 ||
The good agent, the presiding officer of the means, that which is to be purified, the one whose nature is purity;
the remainder of the one, the moon-bearer, ending with the earth, the supporter of the immobile. (69–107)
The son of Dharma, the embodiment of Dharma, the Victorious One, the bestower of victory;
the protector of servants and so forth, the collection of the ten arts, and the husband of widows. || 69-108 ||
Vidhavādhavala, Dhūrta, Dhūrtāḍhya, Dhūrtapālikā, Śaṅkara, Kāmagāmin, Devala, and Devamāyika. (69–109)
Vināśā, Mandarācchannā, Mandarasthā, Mahādvayā, Atiputrī, Trimuṇḍī, Muṇḍamālā, and Tricaṇḍikā. (69–110)
Karkaṭīśa, Koṭara, Siṃhikā, Siṃhavāhana, Nārasiṃhī, Nṛsiṃha, Narmadā, and Jāhnavīpati. (69–111)
The threefold woman, the weapon of the triple creation, the sky-clad one, and the female sky-clad one; the releaser, the destroyer of the bed, Mālañcā, and the one born before the fickle one.
Kaṭutuṅgī, Vikāśātmā, Ṛddhi, Spṛṣṭākṣara, Antarā, Viriñca, Prabhavānanda, Nandinī, and Mandarādridhṛk. (69–113)

The luster of blackness, the radiance of gold, the intoxication arising from wine and the like, the state of being in Draviḍa, the state of being in the pomegranate, that which transcends the marrow, and the movement of the wind. (69-114)
Patience and wisdom, the wisdom of method, the discernment of the world, zeal, and certainty; non-existence, the defiled form, the prison, and the destruction of discursive thought.
Sound is the breaker of the vessel of the world, a nurse for the infant populace;
she has a face of vast extent and a mind delighted by her own power. (69.116)
Clothed in space, intoxicated, formerly devouring flesh, exceedingly beautiful, tranquil in soul, eternally secret, and moving in the profound. (69.117)
Trigambhīra, Tattvavāsī, Rākṣasī, Pūtanākṣara, Abhogagaṇikā, Hastī, Gaṇeśajananī, and Īśvara. || 69-118 ||

The performer of the Kuṇḍapālaka sacrifice, possessing three forms, bearing a severed head on his forehead, exceedingly powerful, whose soul is free from attachment, whose body is the Goddess herself, and who takes refuge in Nandana. || 69-119 ||

She is to be meditated upon; she removes delusion; she possesses the luster of Kapila; she is captivating; she is the Noble Goddess; she is blue in color; she is the arrow that bestows strength and heroism. (69-120)

He is the giver of happiness, the bestower of liberation, and thus the mother who grants all desires; he may appear in an exceedingly beautiful form or abide in a deformed state, being entirely free from the distinction between the expressible and the inexpressible.
Born from the Great Liṅga, situated at Kākabherī on the riverbank,
she whose body is composed of the digits of the Self-enjoyer is Gaṇeśvarī, the bestower of supernatural powers.
The wish-fulfilling tree, the wish-granting creeper, the family tree, the family tree; the virtuous-minded one, consisting of the glorious guru, the bestower of the guru-mantra. || 69-123 ||
Anantaśayana, Ananta, Jaleśī, Jahnujeśvara, Gaṅgā, Gaṅgādhara, Śrīdā, Bhāskareśa, and Mahābalā. (69–124)
Guptākṣara, Vidhiratā, Vidhānapuruṣeśvara, Siddhakalaṅkā, and Kuṇḍalī—these are the five deities, along with Vāgdeva. (69–125)
Alpātītā, Manohārī, and Tattvalocanā are the threefold [forms];
Amāyāpati, Bhūbhrānti, and Pāñcajanyadhara are the elder-born ones.
Excessively heated, tormented by desire, and utterly devoid of illusion and delusion;
the noble Lord of the Daughter, the Immovable One (Sthāṇu), who stands amidst fire and is immersed in water. (69-127)
Intoxicated by the wine of Vāruṇī, naked with a passion for meat, she has the perfected body within; she is the mistress of the mountain of nectar, the fire of the creative arts. (69.128)
The god who moves through space, the lord of the Kākinīs, the sky-clad one;
he who steals the honey from the beak of the crow, the drinker of the ocean of the sky.
Mudrāhārī, Mahāmudrā, Mīnapa, Mīnabhakṣiṇī, Śākinī, Śivanātheśa, Kākordhveśī, and Sadāśiva. || 69-130 ||
Kamalā, whose lotus-throat is ever-abiding, the heroine of love, who wears a garland of lotus-stalks and is adorned with a wreath of lotus-fibers. || 69-131 ||
Tārā is without beginning or end, the savior from miserable states, and beyond syllables;
she is all syllables, all letters, and the rosary of all mantra-syllables.
Ānandabhairava, Nīlakaṇṭha, adorned by the cosmic egg;
Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, Ananta, transcending all, and stainless. (69–133)
Thus has been told to you, O Lord, this auspicious essence of the three worlds, named Bhuvanamaṅgala, which destroys great sins. (69-134)
Even if one were to spend hundreds of millions of years, it would not be possible to describe all the fruit that a person obtains merely by reciting this. (69-135)
Nevertheless, O ocean of compassion, hear the fruit that comes from your effort:
at the king’s gate, on the riverbank, in battle, in solitude, or amidst fire. (69–136)
Having recited [the mantra] in an empty house, or in a deserted place, or on a night of terrible darkness,
or at a crossroads, or in a cemetery, or upon the sixteenth petal.
Having worshipped with red lotuses while mentally contemplating one's desire,
one should offer oblations daily with ghee-smeared [flowers], pronouncing each name individually.
One should offer clarified butter, consecrated with the root mantra, into the fire;
when the oblation is performed within one's own bliss, it bestows the happiness of all accomplishments.

Reciting the mantra while offering meat mixed with fresh honey into his own lotus-mouth for the sake of great happiness, he should offer it individually, each time encased by the [deity's] name. (69–140)
O Lord, by wearing [this], or reciting it, or praising it according to the prescribed rite, a man shall become liberated while living (jīvanmukta) upon the tongue of the nectar of Kuṇḍalinī. (69–141)
He shall become Mahārudra in person, endowed with my own body;
he shall become a yogi, a man of knowledge, a perfected one (siddha), and a revealer of the essential conventions.
Unconquered in all the world—what other means for attaining the fruit is there?
By wearing it, one attains sovereignty; by placing it upon the neck, one becomes a lord of the earth. (69-143)
By holding it thus in the right hand, one becomes wealthy and virtuous;
it removes untimely death and wards off all diseases. (69–144)
Having offered oblations, the lord of kings, a great orator who is ever fearless, having performed the churning of all, is my Gaṇeśa Kātīka. (69-145)
Having become the sovereign lord of the gods, O Lord, he becomes omniscient;
in whatever manner the great yogin acts, he wanders indeed—of this there is no doubt. (69.146)
Whoever recites this at dawn while holding it over their head will indeed cause the suspension of water as well as the suspension of fluids. (69.147)
The pillar of sovereignty, the pillar of manhood, and likewise the pillar of heroism; the pillar of knowledge, the pillar of happiness, and likewise the pillar of the field. || 69-148 ||

Whoever recites this at midday brings about the immobilization of kings, the immobilization of wealth, and likewise the immobilization of villages; indeed, it even effects the immobilization of fire. (69–149)

It likewise causes the paralysis of time, the paralysis of youth, the paralysis of breath, as well as the paralysis of the vital fluids, the paralysis of the wind, and even the paralysis of the arms. (69–150)
And whoever recites it at evening while wearing it upon their throat or belly, he brings about the paralysis of mantras, the paralysis of stones, and even the paralysis of scriptures. (69–151)
He likewise causes the pillars of gold and silver, as well as pillars of diamond, to become paralyzed; he also brings about the paralysis of untimely phenomena and the paralysis of the wind.
The immobilization of mercury, the mastery of arts and crafts, the immobilization of knowledge, the immobilization of one's seat, the immobilization of disease, and the binding of enemies. (69–153)
Having performed the immobilization of the six lotuses, the yogi certainly becomes [perfected];
even a barren woman shall obtain a son who is handsome and most enchanting. (69.154)

O Indra among kings, even a fallen man [attains merit], let alone other virtuous people, by hearing this on the full-moon day when the moon is in Capricorn, in conjunction with the Citrā asterism. (69–155)

Having inscribed [the name] during the Hiraṇyayoga in the month of Māgha under Vāyu (the northwest), or during the Rājayoga in Vaiśākha, it is especially effective under the asterism named Rohiṇī. (69–156)
The one named Śrīmadbhuvanamangala will certainly become a bestower of fame;
by writing this, those who are dear to kings, as well as immortals and sky-dwellers, are born [in that state]. (69–157)
And the reciters shall attain virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
they obtain fame and the vision of the Self—of this there is no doubt. (69–158)

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Auspicious Thousand-and-Eight Names and the Hymn to Śākinī-Sadāśiva," within the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the *Uttaratantra*, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the section on *Siddhamantra*, in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
Now begins the seventieth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairava said: "The essence of the Śākinīs has been told, which brings about the fruit of Sadāśiva."
I have heard the supremely auspicious [teaching] concerning the emergence of the sequence of the language of differentiation.
Now I desire to hear of the armor, so difficult to obtain even by the essence [of knowledge], by the mere understanding of which one becomes Sadāśiva himself. (70-2)
"Speak, O beloved one, O you who consist of sound, if there is affection toward me.
Having bowed to Ānandabhairava, Ānandabhairavī spoke.
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said:
O embodiment of the bliss of Bhairava, I shall tell you the supremely auspicious armor (kavaca) of Sadāśiva and Śākinī, my Guru. (70.4)
Listen to the wondrous and auspicious armor named Kāmada, which is the essence of the three worlds and the increaser of all knowledge. (70.5)
The destruction of the entire flood of mantras is accomplished by mere gnosis;
it is the bliss dear to all secrets, the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya) that transcends the [lower] kula.
Equal to the fierce Caṇḍikā, the witness of all determinations, the bliss that produces all intelligence, and residing in the minds of the Kula-yogins. (70.7)
This great yoga, which is to be served by Rāma, served by Śiva and Śambhu, the destroyer of poison, is not to be disclosed; it increases wealth and health. (70–8)
It generates all auspiciousness, produces supreme bliss for all, and is difficult to find in any other tantra; it is that which has been taught in the Rudrayāmala. (70–9)

Of this Great Armor (Mahākavaca) named the Desire of Śrī Śākinī Sadāśiva, Sadāśiva is the Seer (Ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the Meter (Chandas), Śākinī is the Deity (Devatā), the syllable *sakalaharīṃ* is the Life-seed (Jīvabīja), Māyā is the Weapon-power (Astra-śakti), *kāmasvāhā* is the Bolt (Kīlaka), and the fierce, gurgling,
most terrible Śākinī is the Vajra-power (Daṃṣṭra-ghora-ghargharā-mahogrā-śākinī-śakti). The application (Viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining the great mantra of Sadāśiva.
Oṃ! May Prabhāvā always protect; may Mahākāśādhiśākinī protect;
and may Triguṇā Caṇḍikā, terrifying with her wrathful fangs, protect. (70.10)
May Gāyatrī, the Sun, whose greatness is infinite and boundless, and who possesses the great weapon of the lotus-like discus, protect me constantly during the forenoon. 70-11.
May the goddess Ākāśavāhinī, the wonderful auspiciousness of the head, always protect my secret organ and my nectar-filled *liṅga* and *cakra*. (70.12)
Abiding in the center of the great maṇḍala, may she protect the circle of my forehead—
the maṇḍala of the host of yoginīs numbering hundreds of millions of moons.
May Mahācakreśvarī protect me; may Mahācakreśvara protect my lotus-face; may Goddess Caṇḍikā protect my lips, and Anantaka protect my teeth. (70.14)
The tip of the tongue is the root of the palate; the root of the palate is the speed of the mind.
The sharp fangs are the middle of the teeth; the chin is the tip of the throat, which is Śiva.
May Śākinī and Śrī Sadāśiva, who possess the sixteen-spoked [wheel], always protect me;
may she who destroys great delusion protect that which is situated in the middle of the throat. (70.16)
May the King of Pretas always protect the great goddess’s own lotus;
the Knowledge Goddess is the Great Power, and Sadāśiva is the station of the Peak-syllable (kūṭa). || 70-17 ||
Mahākāśāvalagnī, Dhūmrā, Bhoja, and Dhūrjaṭī belong to me; Kaumudī and Paṭalāṅgī are known as my sixteen colors.
May the illustrious Goddess protect me with the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa';
may Citriṇī, seated upon a golden, variegated chariot, protect my honey.
May Aparṇā protect my pure sixteenth petal, which consists of sixteen syllables;
may Sahadeva, along with the five Durgās, each protect my [seventeenth] petal.
May Pravarā protect my lamp, month, and plow; may Balā protect me;
and may Vyāpinī and Anavacchinnā protect my circle of petals. 70-21.
May Durgā, who crosses over [the ocean] at the improper time, protect the bright discus forever;
may Mahāmāyā, the mistress of the Śākinīs, protect [us] together with her retinue.
May the Five-Rayed One with the blue throat, who always dwells upon his own lotus-throne, protect even the sounds residing in the lotus of my throat. (70.23)
May Kandarpesha, whose movement is the mind, who is the heaven of the throat, always protect [us];
may Shakini, whose power is the vegetable kingdom, the mistress of vegetables, and that which is born of vegetables [protect us]. (70.24)
May Śākambharīśvarā protect the sixteenth petal;
may Sadāśiva, together with his retinue of attendants, protect forever. (70.25)
May the goddess Śākinī always protect the heart; may Kuleśvarī, together with Kākinī, protect the twelve-spoked [cakra] located at the head.
May Sadāśiva, the Lord of Desire, protect the twelve petals;
may she whose form is non-dual protect for me the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*.
May Vāṇī protect my heart-knot; may Kapileśvara protect the region; may Sūryāsyā protect the cloud; and may Vimāyā protect the pericarp within the hearts. (70.28)
May Mahāvāṇī, holding a palm leaf in her hand, protect the interior of my heart;
may Śoṣiṇī, Mohinī, and Vahni protect my heart-lotus. (70.29)
May the instruction of Pilāpippalā, which is my heart’s desired delight and the tooth of the Yoginī-kula, protect even the vowels of my heart. (70.30)
May Kekareśa, whose secret name is Vajradhārī, who always possesses the single liṅga, protect my heart within the lotus of the heart. (70.31)
May she who is free from both difference and non-difference protect the mandala below that;
may Pāśinī, whose characteristic is the absence of [fixed] time, protect the navel-mandala.
May Kālakūṭasvarūpā descend upon my navel-lotus;
may Candracūḍā, the moon-faced Śākinī, [descend] upon my ten lotuses.
May the Trivṛttākāra-mudrā protect me, and may Rudra protect Lākinī;
may the Arōhaṇa of the Trikhaṇḍā protect the letters from Ḍa to Pha as well.
Kālikā, Kapilā, Kṛṣṇā, Ghanābalā, Kapālinī, Lalitā, Tāriṇī, Sarvā, Mahāmāyā, and Daśacchadā—[these are the ten]. (70.35)
May Lākinī, who protects from the fortress of desire, protect me always;
may Sadāśiva eternally protect Maṇipūra, the seat of the Kula.

May Durgā, who destroys dullness and is adorned with a garland of severed heads, protect me—she whose self consists of the seven obstructions, who dwells in the hair, and who is the Great Abode. 70.37
Abhayā, Caṇḍikā, Kṛṣṇā, Kālikā, Kulapaṇḍitā, Vajravarṇā, Dhāraṇākhyā, Dharā, Dhātrī, Kṣamā, and Ramā. || 70-38 ||
May Vāsukī, Vasudhā, Sarvāṇī, and Sarvamaṅgalā—Pārvatī, who abides in all powers—protect me on the full-moon day. (70.39)
In battle, in the royal court, in gambling, in debate, in honor or dishonor; in the home, in the forest, in the wilderness, in water, or in the midst of fire. (70-40)
May Vijayā, Padmanī, Jāyā, Jānakī, and Kamalāvatī—adorned with the meaning of the Great Tantra—protect all [beings] at all times. (70.41)

May these [deities], who destroy great sins, protect me in the cardinal and intermediate directions; may she who resides in the *liṅga* protect my inner space, and may she protect the lotus at the base of the *liṅga*.
May Śivā, residing on the seat of Kāñcī, constantly protect the pericarp;
may she, endowed with exceeding speed, protect my circle of fire.
May the mistress of the Rākṣasīs, who dwells in Jambudvīpa, always protect [us];
may she be Jāhnavī, Bhāskarā, Maunā, Malayasthā, and Malāṅgajā. (70.44)
May the Radiant One (Vibhākarī), who removes sins when meditated upon, protect me;
may she who is seated upon the Lord of Elephants (Kuñjareśvara) always protect the place of dissolution (layasthāna).
May the Great Vidyā of twenty syllables, who hangs over the seat of the Kula and brings about the destruction of wealth, protect me eternally in the temple. (70.46)

May she who reclines on the infinite [Śeṣa] protect me; may she who dwells at the root of the banyan tree protect me; may Kālī, who dwells upon the leaf of the banyan tree, protect me at the time of universal dissolution.
May she who is known as Kevalā, whose form is that of Mahākūrca, protect me always;
may she, the bestower of long life and health, ever protect my wealth and kingdom. (70.48)
May Mahābalā protect my home, Kāmarūpa, which is a sacred seat (pīṭha);
may Balākā, with her terrible fangs, always protect my belly. (70.49)
May she who removes all diseases and is adorned with a garland of severed heads protect me;
may Ānanda, the Lord of Nandana, ever protect the upper lotus of my heart.
May she who dwells in manifold forms protect the six lotuses at all times—she who is stainless, without support, eternally nourished, and devoid of sense organs. (70.51)
May the great sixteen-petaled lotus above protect [me] at all times;
may the eight powers, beginning with Śākinī, always protect [me] in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (70.52)
May the supreme goddess Pāpanāśakarī protect the most secret place;
may the purifying Prabhā protect my secret organ, known as Kṣālana.
May Vipracittā, Koṭarākṣī, Lipibhūtā, Sarasvatī, and Vibhūti, together with Kāmayā, always protect the four-petaled [lotus]. 70-54.
May these sciences, which destroy the factions of enemies, always protect [me];
may Cāmuṇḍā, the bearer of the trident, always protect the region of the waist.
May she who possesses three eyes and whose nature is the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar protect me at all times;
may she, whose fierce majesty strikes down the lowly, protect the arts beginning with spring.
May she who has six arms protect me always; may she who holds the Vedas in her hand protect me. May Atividya, Sarvavidyā, and Caṇḍavidyā protect me. (70.57)
May Vāruṇī, the intoxicating goddess, protect my entire body;
may Gṛhodarī, the wielder of the thunderbolt, always protect my entire body.
May Ulkāmukhī, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, always protect me;
may Durgā, who crosses over [suffering] even at the improper time, Lalitā, and Dharmadhāriṇī protect me. (70.59)
May the Mahāvidyā of twenty syllables protect me everywhere and at all times;
may the Vidyā *Hasakalaharī*, who is Sadāśiva, protect me always.
May Vāṇī with a thousand faces protect me;
may she who has the form of water and a most radiant body, always protect me from dropsy.
May Pārvatī, the sixteen-year-old who embodies the fullness of all energies, protect everyone;
may she, ever intoxicated with joy and the fulfiller of the desires of her Lord, protect us always.
May Vāmadevī, the deity of the body, always protect all my limbs;
may Durgā, residing in the Kāma-pīṭha and surrounded by her retinue of attendants, protect me. (70–63)
May Sadāśiva, who is the embodiment of the Sāmaveda, always protect [us];
may the Goddess who dwells in the cremation ground, accompanied by Mahākāla, [always protect us]. (70.64)
May the noble Goddess always protect; may the Mother protect; may Mahākalā protect; may Kapilā protect everywhere; may the illustrious Mahābhagavatīśvarī protect.
Thus, O Lord, I have told you this armor (kavaca), which bestows the fruit of great knowledge; it is difficult to find in the world, yet it has been revealed out of affection for you.
This most secret knowledge, the armor that grants all accomplishments,
should be [attained] by one whose mind is stainless and noble, after having worshipped Sadāśiva.
Likewise, the worship of the goddess Śrīśākinī yields very great fruit;
it bestows sovereignty, wealth, the fulfillment of desires, and the accomplishment of dharma. (70–68)
Having attained mastery over speech, the eight siddhis will come into one's hand;
having obtained the vision of the Kākinī, the vision of the Śākinī shall arise.
He shall certainly attain the perfection of mantra, the perfection of tantra, and the perfection of ritual action; the perfection of traveling through the sky shines in his hand. (70–70)
A man, by wearing this king of armor on his right arm, and likewise a woman on her left arm, certainly attains sovereignty. (70–71)
Even after committing ten million great sins (mahāpātaka), one may attain kingship if one stands at the foot of a tree in the forest, specifically at the root of an Aśvattha tree, and recites [this].

Having recited it ten times, a hundred times, or a thousand times at the three junctions of the day, he shall become a lord of the wish-fulfilling tree and a lord of the earth; of this there is no doubt.
That king of yogins shall live for many thousands of millions of years;
he becomes a wise one, a great adept (mahāsiddha), who destroys even the most grievous sins.
Within half a month, a Brahmin endowed with [proper] qualities becomes fit;
a Kṣatriya within one year, and a Vaiśya within four years.
A Śūdra becomes a yogi through twelve years of recitation;
thus, the wise person who constantly recites this armor-mantra (kavaca) attains great fruit. (70–76)
Enjoyment and liberation are in his hand; what is the use of further prolixity? (70–77)

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Declaration of the Fruits of the Armor of Sadāśiva and Śākinī," in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, within the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa* of the *Mahātantroddīpana*, the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 70.
Now begins the seventy-first chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O auspicious God, whose nature is the conquest of the three worlds."
O Lord, the mantra of Sadāśiva is the destroyer of great sins.
This meditation bestows the fruits of long life and health, wards off all enemies, is most secret, and brings happiness even to the ignorant. (71–2)
Having extracted the first seed-syllable, the seed-syllable of Kāma follows it;
thereafter, the seed-syllable of Rudra, the seed-syllable of Ramā, and then always the seed-syllable of Kāla.
Bestow the knowledge that is the bliss dear to Śivanātha; [this is] the pair, the two-stable [syllables], having extracted the seed-syllable of the Serpent, the mantra of Rājarājeśvarī. (71–4)
Having extracted the Vaiṣṇava seed-syllable (Hrīm), the Śiva seed-syllable (Hraum) is placed near it;
then follows "to Sadāśiva," followed by the word "Śabda" (Śabdāya), and finally Hṛllekhā (Hrīm) and Vahnisundarī (Svāhā). 71–5.
Having extracted the primordial seed-syllable, and then [the syllable] situated in the left body, the seed-syllable of sound and the root-seed-syllable—O Sadāśiva, salutations be to you! (71.6)
This supreme mantra, which has two endings, bestows the abundance of all jewels;
the learned man becomes equal to Vāsudeva—of this there is no doubt. (71–7)
Whether he be a Vaiṣṇava, a Mahāśākta, or again a Mahāśaiva, O King of Kings, he should take up this king of mantras, by whose grace one becomes Śiva. (71–8)

There shall be accomplishment of speech that is stainless, and the accomplishment of one's purpose without a doubt; I shall proclaim the Śiva-mantra by which one reaches the further shore of all goals. (71–9)
Even at an improper time, the yogi becomes the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu);
having extracted the Hālāhala [poison] from that, he then [attains] the seed-syllable of Maheśa.
One should extract the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Dharma, the mantra of Kṣetrapāla, and then the mantra of Nīlakaṇṭha, followed by the seed-syllable of Priyā. (71–11)
At the end of that is the seed-syllable of Śiva: "We meditate upon Sadāśiva; may that Śiva inspire us. This mantra consists of two parts, [ending] with the word "dayā" (compassion). (71–12)
After performing the invocation, the offering of water for the feet, the arghya, and the water for sipping,
one should worship with millions of perfumes, flowers, and bilva leaves.
Praising, nourishing, causing growth, splitting, and likewise killing;
sleeping, quarreling, and the worship of those who have been liberated—all these yield very great fruit. (71.14)
Having fully worshipped Śarva and the others, one should then worship Sadyojāta and the rest;
having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite [the mantra] with the mind fixed upon it.
And the god who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, who has five faces and three eyes,
whose mighty arms hold a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a mace, and a club.
To the God of gods, the Great God, the Guru who is the self of all beings,
to Śambhu, the protector of the three worlds, adorned with a necklace of serpents.
Adorned by thousands of attendants such as the Śaktis Aṭṭahāsa and others,
he is Sadāśiva, the Lord of Nīla, blue-throated, seated upon a bull.
Having meditated thus, one who is pure should recite the mantra a thousand times every day;
specifically, one should recite it equally during both day and night. (71–19)
Having meditated upon Tryambaka in that very place, in each of those respective forms,
and having understood and worshipped Him, the practitioner who recites the mantra of Tryambaka— || 71-20 ||
The three worlds would be in his hand like an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm;
both enjoyment and liberation are in his grasp—what need is there for any other means? (71.21)
Whoever recites [the mantra] encapsulated by the Sadāśiva-mantra,
for him there shall be the accomplishment of all aims, whatever resides in his mind.
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, thereafter [utter] "tryambakam"; then, having extracted "yajāmahe," [utter] "sugandhim puṣṭivardhanam. (71–23)
At the end [of the mantra], one should extract the word *padam* as if it were a cucumber from its stalk;
at the end of the words *mṛtyormukṣīya*, [one adds] *māmṛtāt*, which is the beautiful goddess of fire (*vahnisundarī*). (71.24)
The person who recites the mantra encased by Sadāśiva shall become a lord of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru); through worship, he shall obtain immortality.
Having become happy at all times, one certainly attains liberation.
Now listen to another mantra of Tryambaka, which grants all desires. (71.26)
One shall certainly obtain the mantra that bestows sovereignty and wealth, which destroys great sins, which is the very embodiment of the Word-Brahman, and which is manifest omniscience. (71.27)
Having extracted Kālakūṭa, one should extract Mṛtyuñjaya;
then [one should extract] the pair of Haris from my heap of great sins, and then Dviṭha. (71–28)
I shall proclaim another mantra; listen attentively.
O Vidyā, having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should place two pairs of the seed-syllables of Kāma. (71–29)
Make Mṛtyuñjaya, Kṣetrapāla, and Viśuddheśa firm;
[place] the pair ending with the seed-syllable of Kāma, and Vahnisundarī at the end of the Goddess.
I shall proclaim another mantra; listen attentively. First is the pair of Kāmakālī, followed by the two seed-syllables of the Name. (71–31)
Reveal Vaṭuka, the seed-syllable of Kāma, and the sixteen-spoked [wheel];
then the pair, the peak of Śakti, the seed-syllable of Śiva, and thereafter Dviṭha. (71–32)
O Lord, one should perform everything as before, including recitation, worship, and so forth—namely, the worship of Sadāśiva, meditation, fire-offerings, and libations. (71–33)
I shall proclaim another mantra: one should extract the mantra of Mahādeva, then that of Vaṭuka and Kṣetrapāla, and thereafter the mantra of Gaṇeśa.
"O Sadānanda, the lotus of my throat is the pair of *prakāśa* (the letter *ka*) and *dviṭha* (the letter *ṭha*).
Having formed its visualization and recited it one hundred thousand times, one should bring the practice to completion. (71-35)
Holding a skull in his hand, wearing earrings, with a staff in his grasp,
dark blue like the twilight of early night, with a serpent as his sacred thread,
he is the cause for severing obstacles to the worship of the Krama-samaya.
Victorious is Vaṭukanātha, the bestower of siddhi upon the Kaulikas. || 71-36 ||
I salute the Child, who resembles crystal, whose face shines with earrings,
who is radiant in form and clad in pure garments, who is exceedingly gracious, three-eyed, and adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels, such as tinkling bells and anklets.
Holding a trident and a staff incessantly with his two lotus-like hands.
Resembling the rising sun, with three eyes, radiant with red unguents on his limbs, with a smiling face, holding in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
a skull, and a trident; blue-necked, wearing the noble kaustubha gem, and brilliant with the crescent of the cool-rayed moon.
I always meditate upon the God who wears garments as red as the bandhūka flower and who removes all fear. || 71.38 ||
[One should meditate upon] Vaṭuka, the Lord of Gods, the teacher Sadāśiva, the protector of the three worlds; adorned with various ornaments, bearing the moon, radiant as a bandhūka flower,
decorated with white and non-white [ashes], made of jewels, black, and auspiciously blue.
I always meditate upon the Lord, the presiding deity of the gods, who brings about happiness.
Having meditated thus upon Sadāśiva Nīlakaṇṭha, the great yogin,
becoming steady within the lotus of the throat, shall obtain the vision of the Śākinīs.
Having become a great heroic lord, one may attain mental yoga;
I shall proclaim the perfected mantra by which one becomes a master everywhere.

One attains the siddhi of traveling through the sky, as well as the excellent siddhis of paralyzing and other such feats; one achieves mastery over speech and mastery over the body, becoming free from old age and death. (71.42)
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should extract the seed-syllable of Vijayā;
then, at the end of the age of Kāmakālī, one should extract Ramā and Trikūṭa.

Having extracted the three seed-syllables (sphreṃ sphreṃ sphreṃ), [one recites] "to Kāmanātha" by name; at the end of the word, [one says] "to Sadāśiva," followed by "to the Giver of Boons," and then "namas" twice and "ṭhaḥ. (71.44)
By the grace of this mantra, one shall become a yogi; there is no doubt in this matter.
I shall now proclaim another mantra; listen attentively to it as it truly is. (71.45)
Having extracted the seed-syllable *kṣāṃ*, likewise the three seed-syllables *lāṃ*, and having extracted the seed-syllable of Bhavānī, one should then join the pair of *saṅgha*. (71.46)

The pair of seed-syllables of Krodharāja, then "to the Lord of Lakṣmī," then "to the Giver of Boons," at the end of the heart-mantra, then "to the Giver of Desires," and finally the syllable *ṭha*. (71–47)
I shall proclaim another mantra by which a man becomes a yogi:
having extracted the seed-syllable of the sky (ha), one should extract the king of desire (kṣa). (71.48)
The mantra for the God of gods, whose heart is auspiciousness, begins with *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and ends with *devadevāya*; it is flanked by two *hṛt* (the syllable *namaḥ*).
By the grace of this mantra, what on earth cannot be accomplished? (71.49)
One becomes a yogi without effort, how much more so through formal practice?
One becomes a yogi by mere recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter. (71-50)
O Lord of Bhairavas, I shall now declare another [mantra]: the Praṇava, the Kāmarāja, the Śrībīja, the pair of fires (Ra-Ra), and then the pair of "enemy-takers" (Ha-Ha). (71–51)
"Grant me success, svāhā!"—this mantra is difficult even for yogins to obtain.
By performing meditation in this manner as previously described, one indeed attains immortality. (71–52)

I shall proclaim another mantra by which one becomes firm upon the seat (pīṭha): having first uttered the seed-syllable of *am* and so forth, one should then contemplate the Great Abode (*mahāpada*). (71.53)
One should extract [the seed-syllable] for Kāla, then for Vikaraṇa at the end of the Kalās; then for Bala, and for Balavikaraṇa, the sixteen-petaled lotus.

"O Sadāśiva, know that the mantra for installation consists of the pair, the treasure, the station, and at the end, the beautiful Sundarī who is the fire of the lord of Kākinīs; this is the mantra that grants desires. (71.55)
I shall proclaim the single syllable by which the mantra becomes perfected:
one should extract the seed-syllable of *kṣānti* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), and likewise the seed-syllable of the moon. (71.56)
Having joined the lower teeth [to the upper], one should recite [the mantra] with the mind fixed upon it,
while meditating on the god Sadāśiva within each petal.
Success shall be attained without effort, and there shall always be protection of the vital breath.
Furthermore, I shall declare the single syllable by which human beings achieve accomplishment. (71–58)
It should not be given to the wicked, and especially not to those who revile;
this great mantra is proclaimed as Śiva joined with the lunar drop (candrabindu). 71–59.
By the mere accomplishment of this, one shall become beloved by the yogins. || 71-60 ||

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Six Chakras," within the Section on Accomplished Mantras, in the Dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, the Northern Tantra. 71.
Now begins the seventy-second chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said: "O Mahākāla, bliss of Śiva, you who are overflowing with supreme bliss!"
O bestower of success in the three worlds, O beloved of my life, hear this hymn of praise.
That auspicious Goddess, the Mother, shines in the heart as Śākinī;
that Goddess, residing within the heart, is renowned in the world as Kālī. (72-2)
Stainless, formless, and radiant as black collyrium,
she is the primordial goddess known as Kālikā— absolute, partless, and auspicious.
The Śākinī who abides in the heart is infinite and of infinite forms;
she is Tāmasī, the Savior Tārā, most fierce, with a dark-blue body.
She is adorned with skulls and garlands of severed heads, her vehicle being a corpse;
she has a lolling tongue, lotus-like eyes, and a splendor equal to ten million moons. (72.5)
Bhavānī dwells within wind, fire, earth, and water, and she resides in the void;
therefore, this hymn to Kṛṣṇakālī, which brings about the arising of the Kula, must not be disclosed.
And [I shall reveal] the Kulārṇava of the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Nīlā Devī;
it must be guarded with great effort—listen attentively. (72–7)
Mahābhairavī said:
[I worship] the foot of Śrī Kālī, which possesses the qualities of the moving and the unmoving, which paralyzes lightning,
and which is the sole seat of Kṛṣṇa, bringing delight to the face of the sky with its great luster and humming pride.

O glorious Lord, the collyrium for the eyes that consists of union with your lotus-hand shines forth; it is fashioned from the pure *amalakī* fruit gathered in the forest of the hungry ghosts (*preta*) and placed upon the seat of Nanda. (72-8)

Luster, attainment, completion, a dear mind, a happy rebirth, association, coldness, and conduct; falsehood, falsehood, a street, bowing, discontent, virtue, birth, livelihood, the mention of qualities,
one seeking employment, one seeking food, dwelling, the Lord of Rati, light, and the celestial Ganges.
The subtle lotus-feet of Śrī Durgā, Śambhu, and Kālī shine forever. (72.9)
The lords of the gods, the five elements, those crowned by the sun and moon, the wrathful ones, the vetālas, and the kolās—
residing on Kailāsa, these praised ones recite that hymn every day within the heart-lotus of the family-bliss, which is the foot-dust of the lineage of Śrī Dakālī.
Having meditated again and again, O hero, I, whose mind is deeply absorbed in me, am intent on meditation; what more can I praise? || 72-10 ||
Having heard the quality of your praise— the fruit of the desire for your very lotus-feet—
it impels one toward the beloved and brings about liberation according to ultimate reality.
O Mother, we consider this [praise] to be the slender maiden who is the cause of delusion and pride.
May there be happiness at the feet of the worthy one, which are a mass of bliss for the three worlds.

O Mother Śyāmā, be gracious; grant your boon-granting hands and give me the eternal cause. Make my two sons, who are honored by the gods, protectors of the hidden meanings of the Itihāsas and other scriptures.
[Grant] the bliss of Yoga, which culminates in Śiva, bestows the fruit of the celestial tree, and is the commentary on all Vedānta.
Cultivate association with the virtuous and true discernment; cultivate that which illuminates the five elements of poetry.

This hymn of praise to Śrī is the producer of intense joy for those who know the supreme state; it is a brilliant illumination of profound meaning; it is a servant, straightforward with the virtues of a wish-fulfilling gem that considers the welfare of others; it is a song of love that brings fulfillment; it is the essence of all that is essential; it is victorious; it is the abode of the gods; and it leads to the purification of the soul.
The Destroyer of delusion and other afflictions, he is to be meditated upon by the lords of gods and by tens of millions of celestial maidens. || 72-13 ||

By churning the ocean of merit—pure and purifying through the mere utterance of [your] name—you who have reached the further shore of the virtues of the gods dwelling in the stainless mind; you who abide in the smile that is the moon of bliss; O best of men, mountain of yoga, with the long lotus-stalks of your two arms like those of an elephant. (72.14)
By serving the skull of the mutual nature of Hari, Vidhi, and Hara, [one attains] the feet of Sundarī Kālī. || 72-15 ||
Siddhakālī, whose radiant splendor is graced by the qualities of a fierce fire like ten million suns, is the primordial Yoginī;
she has uttered this auspicious composition of the *Yogagītā* verses.
It is a manifestation upon the banks of the Gaṅgā of devotion and sacrifice, within the work titled *Śyāmānandadruma*.
When I am absent, O Giver of Boons, there will be no occurrence of the festival of universal bliss, as if among the gods. || 72-16 ||
O Mother, O Śivā, O Kaulinī, at the beginning of the Kali age, this family— the family of the Guru, filled with the play of beauty,
the family that is the bliss of life, the family of the Kula and Akula, the overflowing family of Kālī—
resides within the innermost core of all.
Constantly employ the illustrious son of Dharma there in worldly existence with the words of the Vedas.
O Mother, source of the lineage beginning with Heramba, you who are fond of the essence of Yoga—
if one thus performs the yoga that is the dust of your lotus feet, which bestows bliss,
he shall himself conquer the god of love and turn the abode of his enemies, pale with distress, into his own.
The glorious one, the destroyer of the god of love, indeed practices the supreme eightfold yoga.
The yogi attains the supreme state— the state of bliss, the locus of desire, and of all prosperity—

if he knows the true nature of the Supreme Lord and, moreover, the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence; thus has your realization and discernment regarding the Daughter of the King of Mountains been understood.
She performs the worship of your glorious lotus feet, which are as radiant as a fresh rain cloud.
At the outset, he speaks of the eightfold yoga, the singular doctrine of devotion to the bliss of existence,
known as the Purifier in the world of mortals, which moves with the speed of the wind, belonging to the daughter of the Lord of Mountains;
and of the eight supernatural powers attained through the mastery of restraints and observances, and through the practice of postures and breath-control.
[One should practice] withdrawal (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna) upon the Lord who is clothed in the ruddy qualities of the upward [breath], and likewise concentration (samādhi). || 72-20 ||
O Mother Śivā, who rests upon the quality of peace, who bestows peace upon yogins,
and who is the consort of the Lord endowed with divine attributes— grant all auspicious rites of pacification!
By whose grace the emergence of sacrifices proceeds swiftly upon the earth.
I shall proclaim all of that for the purpose of paralyzing the fire of desire through the destruction of delusion.

The king of yogis alone lives in supreme happiness; his sons do not live [in such a way]. Seeing that everything born of yoga perishes within this worldly existence while their own life-span proceeds toward its end, having reflected thus, one should take hold of peace regarding all sense-objects.
At the root, on the path of the Kula, radiant with eight petals, meditate upon the venerable Kuṇḍalinī.
She cuts through the delusion of peace, she is the jewel of her own voice, arisen from love, and the giver of devotion;
she is the radiance that is the sole embodiment of joy from the rays of millions of gems in the ocean of beauty;
she is the one whose prowess is of a single form, who is beyond defeat, and who agitates the sequence of anger.
I worship that glorious sweetness which she creates within her root-lotus of stainless purity. || 72-23 ||
O each and every wretched, unfortunate fool, what work do you perform day after day for the sake of Rādhā?
You engage in activities centered on sense objects and do not meditate upon the glorious lotus feet [of the Lord].
This worldly state is false and momentary; joyfully abandon this poison of saṃsāra!
Worship the auspicious Kālī, the wise woman of the lineage, who is virtuous and peaceful.

That peace which is the consort of Śiva, which bestows supreme bliss and generates the true state of being—that discernment has arisen, and you carry it; you shine with it certainly. That discernment, being renounced, produces one as beautiful as the ocean of nectar.
O stainless Yoginī, in the supreme state, intoxication is the supreme knowledge of Brahman.

The supreme knowledge of Brahman is twofold: that consisting of scripture, which is stainless, and that arising from discrimination, which is stainless and unsurpassed. At the root of these two, there is immediately peace, the most beloved, established in the heart.
The light brings about the dissolution of devotion to the pair of Kālī’s lotus feet.

I shall describe and take joy in the state of the Mother Kālī— the first radiance of the sun— which consists of the essence of the supreme nectar of Kulaśrī-kuṇḍalī, which is composed of the nine [tattvas], and which is blissful, auspicious with the letters *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*, and resembles gold.
One should worship Vidhi, Śrī, Ḍākinī, Amarapati, and Dharitrī. || 72-27 ||
The triple station, eternally composed of the sun, moon, and fire,
is a great sacred site (mahātīrtha) situated within the wind and space, which brings about worldly existence.
Having properly severed both [the upper and lower centers] along with the knots of the *kula*, [one attains liberation].
In the great sacred ford of the Suṣumnā, he is absorbed in complete dissolution within the sky.
Having first purified the triad, the great one proceeds to the supreme state;
through well-perceived yogic limbs, he overcomes my pure body.
Therefore, he expands the eight-limbed yoga which is free from the pleasure of impurity.
At the beginning of ritual acts, the best of ascetics should perform the observances of restraint (yama) and regulation (niyama).
Seeking non-violence and truth, he practices excellent yoga for your state;
if he is a yogi possessing wealth, pure in resolve, skilled in compassion and generosity,
endowed with the banner of forbearance, moderate in diet, and adept in the supreme bliss of equanimity.
He is self-perfected, the banner of the virtuous brāhmaṇa clan, and composed of bliss.
Rich in austerity and contentment, devoted to the worship of Hari, possessing faith and great intelligence,
with his heart and life-breath dissolved through hearing the Siddhānta of the ascetics,
immersed in the joy of victory, he performs the fire-sacrifice free from all attachment.
He is a great devotee, possessed of fortune, modesty, and intelligence; though not of noble birth, he has attained your feet.
And at the tip of the lotus-mouth of the Suṣumṇā is a lotus;
if there is a petal with the syllable *ha* at its base,
then the Suṣumṇā is in the middle of the firm backbone.
In the midst [of it], there were lotuses that shone with variegated brilliance like diamonds. || 72-32 ||
From the junction of the Suṣumnā and other channels at the root of the ear,
there extends outward the pair of channels that illuminate the light;
these are Iḍā on the left side and Piṅgalā on the right.
O hero, you shine there eternally like the moon.
You bring forth the Visarga ending in the Bindu, the abode of Your own qualities;
You alone are the auspicious Kālikā, the Mother of Giriśa, through Your creative power (kalā).
If Your beloved ones recite [this mantra] while establishing supreme bliss, [they attain liberation].
Having washed away [defilements] here by means of knowledges, they master the state of the Beloved.
One who slowly inserts a straight tooth-stick eighteen finger-breadths long, fashioned with half of his own fingers' width as a brush,
into the middle of the cavity between the palate, the tongue, and the throat;
One should perform the treatment with *dantī* for the sake of your meditative cultivation.
The king of ascetics, bearing the triple staff and offering his glorious feet to you, performs the cleansing of the channels; through the stabilization of the breath by means of the new staff,
that ascetic daily increases the fruit of *prāṇāyāma* with great effort.
By immersing oneself in the ocean of the bliss of giving, one shall be instantly liberated from the worldly fluids of the family lineages.
I proclaim this auspicious yoga of the lotus feet for supreme glory—
for the welfare of the worlds and for the portioned glory of my beloved host—
by which a person shall always joyfully attain the perfection of all yogas.
At that very moment, O Mother, your servant [offered] a single syllable, O Janani.
Immersed in the ocean of compassion and always possessing stainless splendor, one becomes a lord of yogis by meditating upon your tender lotus feet. (72.38)
By what yoga one becomes stainless and immersed in the ocean of compassion—that yoga is your lotus feet; who is a fool, and who is a great scholar? (72.39)
During the period favorable for restraint and observance (*yamaniyama*), the practice of *neulī* yoga becomes effective;
the triple-threaded cord (*trisūtrī*) destroys phlegm in the aperture of destruction (*nāśarandhra*).
The practice of *dhautikā* yoga destroys phlegm in the heart.
Wearing a garment that slips from her neck and measures sixty cubits in length.
O you of extremely subtle taste, your throat measures sixty cubits— the span of your own arms—
and is five finger-breadths in width due to its continuous expansion;
you are the creator of the pure light of the sacred thread and the remover of all suffering.
I worship Him who is the stainless garland of fearlessness arising from the lotus of His own throat.
