If the Neulī consort is honored by the youth with the vision of yoga,
he becomes a knower of the supreme and cuts through the net of delusion;
yet, O lady of the smiling face, it is only the utterly deluded one who truly lives for you.
O Goddess, you grant the accomplishment of the form of the whirling mudrā to those who have abandoned their wives.
Slowly, the elephant [of breath] extends its union with the pair of lotuses that are its own feet;
in Śiva, the yogi, even within a month, comes to arrest the vital wind.
This practitioner of mantra places the mango-stone and its stalk, well-aligned, within the cavity of the throat.
Having meditated upon the surface of your lotus-like feet, [beginning with] those to be enjoined and so forth... || 72.43 ||
The *vilva* leaf, which purifies the mind of noble and ignoble lineages;
the *jayā*, which bestows the quality of perfect peace; the *nirguṇḍī*, characterized by supreme devotion;
and the *mukunda-tulasī*, the beloved of the virtuous, the bestower of liberation, and the *yoginī*.
You grant the wealth of the immortals to those whose bellies are distended from the separation of their petals.
The great medicinal herb named Pañcāmara, which effects the yoga of the Pañcāmara-sādhana, abides here;
you alone are the bearer of the form of the Lord of All, and he by whom you are worshipped attains both worldly and supreme success.
If you recite this hymn to Bhavānī, the goddess whose body is that of a Śākinī,
who is crimson-hued and radiant with the splendor of the sun,
you shall attain the supreme kingdom, honored by the gods and firmly established.
Possessing the excellent conduct of a human being, he playfully assumed the form of Śambhu.
By reciting it three times seven hundred times at dawn, at midday, and in the evening, there shall be liberation, and one obtains the fruit of the preliminary ritual (puraścaryā). || 72-47 ||

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Hymn to Kālī Composed by the Śākinīs," within the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, in the *Ṣaṭcakra-prakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*siddhamantra*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*.
Now begins the seventy-third chapter:
Listen to that most wonderful great song which the practitioner indeed hears from her whose face shines as she rests upon a tender lotus.
Sound contains within it light; light contains within it the mind.
That mind dissolves into sounds that reach the pinnacle of knowledge.
Yogis hear that cognition which is the consciousness of sound. || 73-3 ||

In his body, which is profoundly deep with supreme virtues and possesses steady waters, and which is exceedingly beautiful through its repeated births; in that ocean of knowledge adorned with pure and sweet speech, his mind is perfectly tranquil.
The Goddess of Speech established [him] as the jewel of all words.
Oṃ! With a mouth fierce and steady speech, she deludes the color of living beings;
her conduct is free from fear and distress, and she is deluded by the lethargy of knowledge.
Adorned with ornaments, with very harsh hands, she carries a garland of words.
Beholding her with pure compassion, one should worship her at the root-cakra. || 73-5 ||
In this world, O Lord of Pārvatī, may there be infinite [merit] for kings or yogins whose bodies are marked by the signs of youth, women, and great compassion;
who possess the life-force of knowledge of the Siddhānta; whose qualities are equal to the final [state];
and who are pervaded by the sweet resonance of the masters of the Vedas.
He he! O you who dwell upon the peak of the beloved body of Kālaprakāla, may you become a mass of garments. || 73-6 ||

I worship those two lotus feet, which are supremely stable in their movement, which are Hari and Hara, the possessors of knowledge, and the upholders of the earth; which possess form yet are the source of compassion, and in which one’s own dissolution occurs;
and which, consisting of eternal wisdom, are victorious and dwell within the shade of the celestial wish-fulfilling tree.
O Mother Kālī, O holder of the digits, O Śākambharī, O Śākinī, [residing] in the cavity of the throat! 73-7 ||
In the abode of the Hero Śrīkaṇṭha, who possesses the splendor of bliss from the mass of rays of ten million suns,

there is a circle of light within the lotus-feet of the venerable Guru in the form of the Goddess, which is fashioned from the essence in the center of the heart-lotus and bestows the birth of Sarasvatī.
The jeweled palace of Padmanābha, situated below [the earth], causes the rising of the lord of mountains.
The Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, who dwells upon the wish-fulfilling tree of desires and bestows the fruits of sustenance and dissolution;
she is the praise of subtle bliss, as sweet as the song of a young cuckoo;
she is affectionate, with limbs that touch with tenderness; she is crowned by the new moon, beautiful in complexion, and vast.
May that Durgā, the destroyer of suffering, be the bestower of the fulfillment of desires in the abode of Śiva. || 73-9 ||
O Kālī, through devotion I have taken refuge in your state which is without support;
O you of pure being, for my prosperity, may the host of cows abide in all states of being.
With a beautiful glance, joyfully bestow upon me the wealth that is dear to you and happiness.
At that very moment, [he was] in the middle of the sky-lotus, which forms the portion of the throat.

In that eternal mass of fruitless forms and manifestations which protects the three worlds and serves as a dwelling for the darkness of dharma, he reckons the application of knowledge as something distinct; such is the earthly king,
whose dear retinue is born from his lotus feet and who is supported by his very life-breath.
O Mother, daughter of the king of mountains, [this is] for the sake of attaining merit and purity.
The source of light, the creator of the burden, the dissolution of the roar of worldly existence, the support for the weight of prosperity;
the manifestation of both being and non-being, the sovereign power that prevails in the world, whose radiance is the devotion to Bhīma;
the state of bliss arising from the non-existence of the fear of birth and the terror produced by the elements of the earth—[to him I bow].
Through the ever-increasing joy of serving the stainless soles of your lotus feet, O Mother. || 73-12 ||

May Gaṇeśvarī, the mother of Gaṇapati, protect me eternally; I take refuge in the Mother. May she who grants the accomplishment of previous goals protect my vital breath while I am seated in the Siddhāsana;
may she who bestows the singular bliss of immersion in the ocean of bliss and resides upon the forehead protect me.
The pericarp of the lotus of his throat is the supreme, melodious song of the hosts of gods.
O ocean of compassion, O stainless being with a fair form,

I did not know that my desire for you— composed of the wish-fulfilling gem of longing during our physical separation— was the lowliest man, whom I mistook for the Son of the Earth (Naraka) while he lay upon the primary breast of the Earth.
The best of gods does not lead you, who are weary from the road of affection, to the further shore.
Victory, victory, victory to the conqueror who is the support of light!
He is worshipped by hosts of gods and men in the midst of the circle of planets;
he possesses majesty that humbles the lotus-like hands of worldly existence.
He causes [him] to go by the power of service to your lotus feet. || 73-15 ||
Having praised her with these principal verses and with various other melodies of song,
and having meditated upon her who consists of the Supreme Brahman, he himself attained the body of Brahman.
Suddenly, the attainment of enjoyments, the auspicious paths to liberation, and the eighteen branches of knowledge arise spontaneously, bringing forth all virtues. (73.17)
The Lord Sadāśiva, who resembles a dark blue cloud, who has the moon as his crest-jewel,
and who is situated on the left side with the Great Śakti Śākinī.
Having again sung the Bhāvagīta to the four-armed God of gods, the infinite and imperishable Hara, one shall become equal to the Supreme Brahman. (73.19)
The yogi of steady resolve, having reached the center of the sixteen-fold throat, becomes a master of the eight siddhis and will certainly attain the perfection of being. (73.20)
One shall attain the perfection of beholding [the deity] with you in a state of mutual joy. || 73.21 ||

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Song of Vāṇī," in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*. 73.
Now, the seventy-fourth chapter.
Śrī Ānandabhairava said:
O Daughter of the Mountain, O Goddess of the Lords of Gods, O You who are worshipped by all the Āmnāyas!
O Goddess, everything has been told to me, yet the armor (kavaca) has not been revealed.
Reveal to me the armor (kavaca) of the mantra known as Prāsāda,
which is meditated upon by Sadāśiva Mahādeva and bestows spiritual accomplishments.
O Goddess, if you have affection for me, [then hear] this great mantra, which is not to be disclosed, arising from Bhairava and Bhairavī, and which provides protection against all things. (74.3)
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O Lord, O Bhagavān Mahākāla, O Ocean of Kula! [I shall speak] the armor-mantra of the Prāsāda, which is the source of the lineage of Sadāśiva."
For the mantra of the deity Prāsāda, Vāmadeva is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi);
Paṅkti is the meter (chandas), and Sadāśiva, the Lord of Gods, is the deity (devatā) here. (74–5)
The application for the accomplishment of the practitioner's desired goal has been proclaimed:
"May Sadāśiva, known as Prāsāda, protect my head at all times. (74–6)
May Maheśvara, whose nature is the six-syllabled mantra, protect my mouth;
may he who is restrained by the power of the eight-syllabled mantra always protect my two eyes. (74–7)
May the Blessed One, whose self consists of five syllables, protect my two arms;
may Mṛtyuñjaya, whose self consists of three seed-syllables, always protect my life.
Seated at the foot of the banyan tree, the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who assumes the form of the thirty-six phonemes, may he always protect me from all sides. (74–9)
May Rudra, consisting of twenty-two syllables, protect my belly; may Nīlakaṇṭha, enriched by three syllables, always protect my throat. (74–10)
May Hara, the wish-fulfilling gem in the form of a seed-syllable, who is Ardhanārīśvara and the bestower of all prosperity, ever protect my secret organ. (74.11)
May Maheśvara, whose nature is the single syllable, who pervades the peak [of existence], the Sun, and Bhairava, eternally protect my feet. (74.12)
May he known as Tumburu, whose nature is the great seed-syllable, the destroyer of Tripura, and the lord of the thirty gods, always protect me on the ground of slaying. (74.13)
May Īśāna, whose face is turned upward, protect me always from above;
may Tatpuruṣa, the leader of the mountains, protect my southern face.
May Mahādeva, known as Aghora, protect my eastern face;
may Vāmadeva always protect my western face. (74–15)
May he who bears the form of Sadyojāta always protect my northern face;
may Mṛtyujetā always protect me in water, in the forest, and in great danger.
May the remover of poison always protect [me] on mountains and in difficult places;
may Kālarudra, the deity of Time, always protect my entire body.
May Kālāgnirudra protect me from the fears of great diseases and the like;
may Sadāśiva, the bearer of the sword who grants liberation at the untimely hour, protect me. (74.18)
May Kavacī and Vāmadeva always protect [me] in great danger;
may Rudra as Kālabhakṣa, Ruruka, and Kṣetrapālaka protect [me]. || 74-19 ||
May the one who bears the full moon upon his crest protect the maṇḍala of the Mātṛkās;
may the long-lived husband of the Śākinīs always protect my life-force.
May he with the shoulders of a lion protect me; may the beloved of Rudrāṇī protect me.
May the one who draws the line of the thunderbolt upon his forehead, whose form is all-pervading, protect my forehead.
May the Discerner, beloved of the Sky-wanderers and the Lord of the Sky, protect me always;
may the wearer of the jewel-garland protect me, and may the Lord of the Red-faced One guard me.
May the five-faced one protect my face, eyes, and ears;
may the sound of the Vedas always protect the two nostrils of my face.
May the bearer of the skull-fragment, the bringer of the end of the age, protect my two cheeks;
may the lord of the blood-red tongue protect me, residing in my upper and lower lips. (74.24)
May Śiva, the Lord of Bhṛgu and Rāmeśvara, protect the two rows of teeth;
may the Eater of the Universe, who is the nectar of taste, always protect the root of the palate.
May Vākpatīśa protect the tip of my tongue, and may Śiva, the lord of Bhavānī, protect my mouth;
may Mahāsena, the lord of poets, always protect the circumference of my face.
May Krodhanātha always protect from the base of the right hand up to the right elbow;
may Kukkureśvara protect its tip.
May the long-lived one always protect the region at the base of the fingers;
may the Lord Brahmā, the bearer of the Brahman-linga, always protect the tips of the fingers. (74.28)
May Vidyāpati, the Lord of Pārvatī, protect the base of my left hand;
may the Lord Vāmakeśvara protect my left elbow.
May Kuṇḍavāsī always protect the tip of the elbow; may the Lord of the Kulācala mountains protect it;
may the Lord of the Mother of the Vedas protect it; and may the Lord who is the Master of Kāmadhenu protect it. (74-30)
May the Five-faced One protect the base of my finger;
may he who is worshipped by the mountain protect the tip of my left finger. (74.31)
May the Lord Kūrmacakradhara, the beloved of Śākinī, protect the middle part of my right foot, which has a slender root and tip. (74.32)
May Gargarīnātha protect the tip of the ankle; may Mūladevatā protect the tip of the foot;
and may Abhayāvallabha protect the tips of the toes of the right hand.
May the Yogin who destroys Smara protect the region at the root of the left thigh;
may the Lord of the Middle Region protect the middle part of the left foot.
May the Blessed Lord Śambhu protect the region above my ankles;
may he protect the root-region of my left foot and the base of my big toe.
May the causal self, Nīlakaṇṭha, the bearer of radiance, the ender of Yama,
and the lord of the Suṣumnā channel, always protect the tip of the thumb.
May Mahārudreśvara protect my navel; may Gaganādhāra, the destroyer of desire, protect the heart-lotus. (74.37)
May Śiva, whose nature is all-bliss, protect my pair of shoulders;
may the Destroyer of Sorrow protect [me] from the heart to the tips of the right hand.
May the Supreme Lord protect from the heart to the tips of my left hand;
may Śiva protect me from the heart to the nails of my right foot. (74.39)
May Sadānanda always protect the heart and the other limbs; may Unmada protect the region from the heart down to the anus.
May Vāsukīvallabha protect the area from the heart down to the anus. (74–40)
May Anantanātha protect the heart and the regions from the head downwards;
may Sadāśiva, the Lord of Umā, who is all-pervasive, protect [me] at all times. (74.41)
May Tārātmaka, Kāyasiddha, Śaktīśa, Śukradevatā, and Pañcacūḍa—who embodies the form of the five principles—protect me always. (74.42)
May Kāmadhenu always protect [me], from the head down to the feet, in water, in the forest, in the terrible jungle, in danger, and on the great road. (74.43)
May Kāmarāja, the protector with hidden eyes in the wilderness, protect us;
may Ardhanārīśvara, the supreme lord of the Mātṛkās, protect us. 74-44.
Enveloped by the *mātṛkā* mantra, may he always protect his respective station;
may the righteous one protect my connection to Dharma, and may Piṅgalā Caṇḍikā protect me. (74.45)
May Bholānātha, who is ever agitated [with compassion], protect me;
may he always protect me in every land, in every sacred seat (pīṭha), and especially in Kāmarūpa.
May the Supreme Self, the Lord of Yoginīs, protect [us] forever;
and may the fifty deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), beginning with the seat known as Kāmarūpa, [protect us]. (74.47)
The fifty seats are indeed Māyā; Kāmarūpa is Sadāśiva;
Bhava, Rudra, Maheśa, Śaṅkara, and Manmathāntaka. (74–48)
The Lord of the Guhyakas, the remover of sin, the bearer of the skull, the wielder of the trident, the five-faced one with ten arms, adorned with serpents—Hara. (74.49)
Mahākāla, Mahārudra, and Mahāvīra reside in the heart;
he is Mahādeva, the Great Secret, Mahāmāyā, and possessed of great qualities.
Paśupati, Vīrūpākṣa, Harīśa, Dhavaleśvara, Vaṭukeśa, Kramācārya, Pañcaśūlī, and Hṛdudbhava. (74–51)
Unmanīśa, Sāhasika, Parākhya, Parvateśvara, Sarvātmā, Mahātmā, Śivātmā, and Śmaśānaga. (74–52)
Krodhavīra, Kālakārī, Sūkṣmadharmā, Dhurandhara, Śyāmaka, Krūrahartā, Gaṇeśa, and Kālamāghava. (74–53)
The Self of Knowledge, the Self of Kapila, the Self of the Siddhas, and the Lord of Yoginīs;
these fifty-one Lords are as radiant as ten million suns. (74–54)
May those who reside in the Mātṛkā seats—whose natures consist of maintenance, creation, and dissolution—protect [us] always.
The primordial seat is Kāmarūpa, and the Kāñcī seat is near it. (74–55)
Ayodhyā is the city of the pīṭha; above that is Jālandhara;
and above that, near it, is the Siddhapīṭha.
Above that is the Kālī-pīṭha, while at the tip is the Caṇḍikā-pīṭha;
the great pīṭha of the eight cities is in the region of the throat, which is Sadāśiva.
May the Great Hero, the Lord of Time, who is higher than the highest, protect forever the great seat of Madhupurī, situated within the eight cities. (74-58)
The great pīṭha of Māyāvatī is proclaimed above that;
the great pīṭha of Vārāṇasī, the pīṭha of Dharma, is near it. (74–59)
The great pīṭha Jvālāmukhī is proclaimed as being situated within that;
above that is the great pīṭha, namely the pīṭha Jvalantī.
Above that is the place called Pūrṇagiri, and Kurukṣetra is near it;
above that is Uḍḍayāna, and likewise Kamalāpīṭha.
Haridvāra is a great pīṭha, as is Badarīpīṭha;
there is also Vyāsapīṭha and the one called Nārada, and above that is Vāḍavānala.
Above that is Hiṅgulāda, and above that is the Laṅkā-pīṭha;
above that is the Śāradā-pīṭha, and above that is the Ratipīṭha.
The Liṅgapīṭha, Kalāpīṭha, and Dvārakāpīṭha, as well as Kapālapīṭha, are in the one called Harya; Varadāpīṭha is in the north.
Above that is the Kālī-pīṭha, and above that is the Tārā-pīṭha;
[then] the great pīṭha of Ugratārā and the Mahogrā-pīṭha.
Nīlasarasvatīpīṭha and Jarāpīṭha are above that;
above those are Gaganāpīṭha and Khecarīpīṭha.
Above that is the Tāriṇī-pīṭha in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus;
above that is the Kartrī-pīṭha, and above that is the Devī-pīṭha.
The seat of Rājarājeśvarī, as well as the seat of Ṣoḍaśī,
and the thousandfold seat within the center of the thousand-petaled lotus.
In the center is the seat of Ekajaṭā upon the edge of a curved knife;
the digit of Tāriṇī is surrounded by the sixteen-faced Vidyās. (74–69)
Kālī, Nīlā, Mahāvidyā, Tvaritā, Chinnamastakā, Vāgvādinī, Annapūrṇā, and again the goddess Pratyaṅgirā. (74–75)
Kāmākhyā, Vāsalī, Bālā, Mātaṅgī, Śailavāsinī, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśānī, Bhairavī, and Bagalāmukhī. (74–75)
Dhūmāvatī, Vedamātā, Harasiddhā, and Dakṣiṇā—these are the Vidyās, the Great Vidyās, adorned by their service to Śiva. (74–72)
May the twenty-two Great Vidyās, the twenty-two doors, and the twenty-two sites—the Kalās—protect me always within the thousand-spoked Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha). 74–73.
May Sadāśiva, joined with Śakti, protect; may Hara, as Caṇḍeśvara, protect;
may he who bears the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) protect; may the Lord of the Goddesses protect forever.
May the Lord of Pārvatī’s life protect my entire body at all times—
he who is Aghoranātha, Īśāna, the bestower of boons, and the destroyer of Madana.
The destroyer of the sacrifice, Dakṣakhaṇḍa, Vīrabhadra, who is sky-clad, eighteen-armed, fierce, and has eyes like blue lotuses. (74–76)
The three-eyed one, the lover of Kālī, Mahārudra, the lord of the Gaṇas, the beloved of Kākinī, the wielder of the trident, the performer of yoga, and Maheśvara. (74–77)
Lord of Speech, Destroyer of Smara, Great Mantra, Halāyudha;
Śrīnātha, the Child, Lord of the New Moon, whose vehicle is Bala. (74–78)
Balarāma, Kṛṣṇarāma, Govinda, Mādhavīśvara, Jitāmitreśvara, Cūḍāmaṇīśa, Mānada, and Sukhī. (74–79)
May the Face, situated upon the six-petaled lotus, protect Vṛndāvana;
may the Beloved of Vaiṣṇavī, the Kulakuṇḍalin, protect Brahmā.
May Viṣṇunātha, whose banner bears Garuḍa, always protect Brahmāgni;
may he who wears a garland of flames protect, and may he who holds the fire of time (Kālānala) grant protection.
May the beloved of Kākinī protect us; may the Lord, the Sovereign of Bhairava, the Great Rudra, the Blue-throated One, protect Maṇipūra and Sulākinī. (74–82)
May Mahārudra, the blue-throated one, who is the beloved of Rudrāṇī and the favorite of Maṇigṛha, always protect Mahāviṣṇu. (74–83)
May Rākiṇī and Viṣṇulakṣmī protect my Vaiṣṇava portion;
may Sadāśiva, the blue-throated one, protect the region of my heart.
May Īśvara, the Supreme Self, protect me from the Śākinī;
may Sadāśiva always protect me, as does the other Hara residing within the two petals.
May Śiva protect the thousand-petaled lotus from the power of Hākinī;
may the ritual of Tārānātha protect her who dwells in the thousand-petaled lotus.
May Mahākāśa always protect [the realm] above; below that, may the Vāyumaṇḍala protect;
and below that, may the Lord of Śākinīs protect the Vahnimaṇḍala.
May the Kaula deity, whose essence is that [nectar], always protect the sacrificial liquor (kīlāla);
may Sadāśiva, the lord of the earth, always protect the earth as the one and only reality.
Thus, O Lord, he who recites this protective armor (*kavaca*), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, at the time of dawn, shall attain his desired fruit. (74–89)
The best of practitioners who recites this armor-mantra at the time of worship will certainly be increased in fame, prosperity, beauty, intelligence, and longevity. (74–90)
This armor of the Great Hero, which bestows all perfections, must not be disclosed;
by mere knowledge of it, the king of yogis becomes a conqueror of Time in the world of mortals.
By the mere wearing of this, one becomes the ender of the Kālasūtra hell;
by the wearing and recitation of this, one certainly becomes omniscient. (74–92)
All the great perfected ones (mahāsiddhas) and yogis, such as Vyāsa and Vasiṣṭha,
having studied and retained this, became the foremost among those who contemplate reality (tattva).
Whoever wears this armor, which is your very form,
born from the lotus of my mouth, shall be granted the perfection of knowledge and speech.
The practitioner who wears this armor on his right arm attains victory in battle, in gambling, and in debate. (74–95)
Gods, humans, and gandharvas will undoubtedly be under his control—he who, with a disciplined mind, wears this armor upon his head. (74–96)
O Goddess of gods, the eight siddhis, beginning with aṇimā, reside in his hand.
This vidyā, wrapped in a white cloth, [should be written] upon a birch leaf.
Having placed it within a silver vessel, the wise man should wear it;
having attained great fortune, he shall bear your body at the end.
It must never be given to just anyone, nor should it ever be disclosed.
One should reveal it only to a disciple who is endowed with devotion and to a practitioner (sādhaka).
It should always be given to a yogi who is endowed with knowledge and whose nature is dharma;
otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Out of affection for you, O Mahādeva, this auspicious armor has been told.
This perfected armor must not be given to anyone who desires his own welfare.

Even if this armor is obtained through the fruit of one's fortune—whether one is a rogue, a hypocrite, a wicked person, or situated under an unfavorable planetary influence—[it shall protect]. (74–102)
One must certainly cause the abandonment of the fruits of one's own actions;
then one attains perfection and becomes a bearer of the stream of Dharma. || 74-103 ||
The wise one attains the fruit of the worship of success day after day, having abandoned deceit, wickedness, falsehood, and hypocrisy. (74–104)
Having become a sovereign lord of kings, he is undoubtedly liberated while living,
he who worships with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings this armor (kavaca) spoken from my own mouth.
By him, O Mahādeva, all the gods were undoubtedly acquired;
[as well as] that which is passionate, mental, and dark, O scorcher of foes.

Meditating on the mental form within the heart is considered *rājasa* worship; that performed amidst the world is considered *tāmasa*. Thus, the worship of the armor (*kavaca*) is regarded as being of three kinds. (74–107)
O Parameśvara, this Siddhakavaca has been declared solely for the attainment of knowledge, for the liberation of the worlds, and as dear to Śambhu. (74–108)
In this tantra, one should proclaim within the interior of the mind the essential compendium, as well as the worship, the ritual installation, and all other rites. (74–109)
And one should recite the hymn and the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) within the kingdom for the attainment of knowledge.
Thus, O Lord, this auspicious [teaching] regarding the Supreme Self has been told to you. (74–110)
O Lord, what more need be said? Merely by propitiating him, one attains the state of Śiva. (74.111)

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Recitation of the Armor of Sadāśiva," in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, within the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa* of the *Mahātantroddīpana* in the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 74.
Now begins the seventy-fifth chapter.
Ānandabhairava said:
"The autumnal abode, which yields fruit when it is not disclosed, has been told."
Now speak, O beloved of my life; be a bestower of boons.
What kind of assembly is that in the lotus of the throat, which is supremely enchanting, where the Yoginīs sing, performing [the dance] and increasing supreme bliss? (75.2)
O expounder of Brahman, conduct the assembly of perfected beings, which is most excellent;
then my knowledge shall be fruitful, and my determination of the essential truth shall be fruitful.
"O Goddess, if that assembly is described as being established in all things," Śrī Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O Lord of the God of Gods, O Filler of All Bliss! (75.4)
The assembly hall consists of knowledge, is eternal, and illuminates sixteen spokes;
it is seventy yojanas wide and possesses a brilliant white luster.
Her splendor was fashioned by asceticism and adorned with the auspiciousness of knowledge;
she possessed the radiance of a celestial body, moved through the air, and resembled the peak of Mount Kailāsa. (75–6)
Carried by the Guhyakas, it filled the air with sweet sounds and was adorned with lofty,
divine trees made of gold.
It was radiant with rays of light, shining, and delightful with divine fragrances;
it had the form of a peak of white clouds and was adorned with golden archways.
Adorned with divine, golden peaks as if variegated by flashes of lightning, her manifestation shines forth,
victorious over the entire universe, within the pericarp of the sixteen-spoked wheel.
In that [city], the illustrious Lord Sadāśiva resides, adorned with various ornaments and weapons,
surrounded by thousands of women, and wearing blazing earrings.
Seated upon a supreme throne, which was as beautiful as the sun, provided with divine coverings, and furnished with divine footstools and pillows.
The pure wind, carrying the fragrances of the magnificent and sweet-smelling groves of Mandāra trees and Saugandhika flowers, blew forth.
A breeze, gladdening the mind and heart, attended upon him from the lotus pond called Cāṇakā and from the grove of sandalwood trees. (75.13)
There, O Supreme Lord, the gods together with the gandharvas, surrounded by hosts of apsarases, sing songs to a divine rhythm.
Miśrakeśī, Rambhā, Citrasenā, Śucismitā, Cārunetrā, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, and Muñjikastanī. (75.15)
Viśvācī, Sahajanyā, Pramlocā, Urvaśī, Irā, Vargā, Saurabheyī, Samīcī, Buddhidā, and Latā. (75.16)
Ratnāvatī, Mahāmāyā, Kamalā, Gandhakeśikā, Bāṇamātā, Mahābhargā, Jyotis, Prajñā, Bhavā, and Abhavā. (75.17)
Prabhavā, Sambhavā, Guñjā, Sārāṅgī, Sāravikramā, Trilocanī, Trivedisthā, Ambikā, and Saptaśāyakā. (75.18)
Viralā, Varadā, Māyā, Siddhā, and likewise Kātyāyanī;
Yoginī, Khecarī, Siddhā, Jīvāṅgī, and Dīrghalocanī. (75.19)
And there was Ramaṇī, Hiraṇyākṣī, Padmavaktrā, and Hiraṇmayī;
these and thousands of others were experts in dance and song.
The hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases wait upon Īśāna;
that assembly is never without divine musical instruments, dances, and songs. (75.21)
It shines, beautiful and not empty, with hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases;
likewise there are Kinnaras, Uragas, Gandharvas, and others called Naras. (75.22)
Then Mānabhadra, Dhanada, Śvetabhadra, Guhyaka, Kāśabala, Gaṇḍakaṇḍū, Patyodra, and Mahābala. (75.23)
Kustumburu, Piśāca, Viśānaka, Gajakarṇa, Varāhakarṇa, Tāmrauṣṭha, Phalabhakṣa, and Phalodaka; || 75-24 ||
Aṅgacūḍa, Śikhāvarta, Hemanetra, Vibhīṣaṇa, Puṣpānana, Piṅgalaka, Śoṇitoda, and Pravālaka. || 75-25 ||
Vṛkavān, Aniketa, Cīravāsas by nature, Bharadvāja, Vāridhara, Mahāmāya, and Dhanañjaya. (75.26)
Kapila, the preceptor Kapila, the great yogi Kṣamādhara—
these and many other yakṣas by the hundreds of thousands.
The goddess Lakṣmī was always there, as was Nalakūbara;
all their attendants were makers of the liquor vāruṇī.
Therefore, it is named Madhupurī, and Madhusthala is filled with eight [sweets];
outside of that, the assembly hall shines with a splendor equal to ten million moons.
I dwell here, as do others like me;
there are Brahman-sages here, as well as other divine sages.
Carnivorous beings, other Rākṣasas, and mighty Gandharvas attend upon that high-souled Lord Śiva in that city. (75.31)
The Blessed One, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of hosts of spirits—the Lord of Umā, the Lord of Creatures, the wielder of the trident, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes—[approached]. (75.32)
Tryambaka, that tiger among kings, and the goddess, free from fatigue, were accompanied by Vāmanas, Vikaṭas, and Kubjas, as well as by their beloved Yakṣas of great strength.
The mighty Ugradhanvan, with fierce liquors of honey and meat,
and with various terrible weapons like swift-moving hammers, [attacked].
There Śrī Sadāśiva always resides surrounded by his attendants; may the excellent retinue of Śambhu also protect us constantly. (75.35)
And the lords of the Gandharvas are Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, Huhū, Tumburu, Parvata, and another, Śailūra. || 75-36 ||
Citrasena, who is skilled in song, as well as Citraratha—
these and other Gandharvas constantly worship Sadāśiva.
And Cakravarman, the lord of the Vidyādharas, who follows the Himālaya,
likewise waited upon the Lord Dhanada, the master, there.
Himavat, Pāribhadra, Vindhya, Kailāsa, and Mandara were there, along with hundreds of Kinnaras, [all honoring] the Lord, the Master of the wise. (75.39)
And there, hundreds of hosts led by Bhagadatta,
as well as Druma and Kimpuruṣa, wait upon the Lord of the Giver of Boons.
And Mahendra Gandhamādana, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
together with sacrifices, with the Gandharvas, and with all the Nīśācaras.
And Vibhīṣaṇa, most devoted to dharma, worships Śrī Sadāśiva;
as do Malaya, Mandara, Mahendra, and Gandhamādana.
Indrakīla, Sanābha, and likewise the two divine mountains—these and many others, all headed by Meru. (75.43)
The venerable Nandīśvara and likewise Mahākāla worship the Great-Souled One, Sadāśiva, the Supreme Lord. (75.44)

All those headed by Karṇa, as well as all the attendants of the Goddess, were capable; so too was Vijayā, who was superior in asceticism and whose mouth revealed her teeth with a frown like a wooden beam.
And a white bull, bellowing, stands there, possessed of great strength;
other Rākṣasas and Piśācas sit around the Giver of Boons.
[He saw] Maheśvara, surrounded by his attendants and Umā—the Lord of the gods, Śiva, the creator of the three worlds—ever present there. (75.47)
Having bowed his head to Umāpati, who appeared in the form of a kinsman,
Paulastya then received permission from Mahādeva, the Lord of the family.
Once the Blessed Lord Bhava, the friend of the Lord of Wealth, was seated there, along with Śaṅkha and Padma, the two foremost among the chief treasures and lords of wealth. (75.49)
Then, having taken hold of all the treasures, she indeed worshipped Sadāśiva; such a beautiful equanimity was maintained by me while remaining hidden within the intermediate space.
Above that, the assembly hall of the Grandfather shines forth, resplendent before the assembly halls of the world-protectors, with a brilliance like steady lightning. (75.51)
I shall proclaim Mahādeva, who bestows the perfection of meditation upon the assembly of sages who are silent by nature, within the lotus-like throats of the virtuous. (75.52)
The description of Brahmā’s assembly destroys millions of great sins; I am not capable of describing that assembly even in hundreds of years. (75.53)
Nevertheless, O Lord, for the sake of your accomplishment, the assembly of the Grandfather (Brahmā) is described by me in brief, O Protector, for the sake of purification. (75.54)
That radiant [power] cannot be pointed out as being of such-and-such a form;
it is eternally and firmly established therein, just as it is firmly established in Nārāyaṇa.
Having perceived him as equal to herself, the venerable Grandfather, together with Śākinī, who was filled with fear, worshipped that high-souled Supreme Lord. (75.56)
The divine assembly hall, immeasurable, both celestial and human, eternally manifest, invisible by virtue of its power, and enchanting to all beings. || 75.57 ||
Or likewise, that supreme assembly hall of the goddess Manmathā, which is never-ending and prepared with medicinal herbs, is neither cold nor heat-giving. (75.58)
There was neither hunger nor thirst, nor exhaustion, neither of the past nor of the future;
it was as if fashioned from various forms of jewels together with weapons.
It was not supported by pillars, yet it was eternal; it was not composed of syllables, yet it was filled with various divine manifestations of radiant and intense splendor.
That radiance itself shines forth, surpassing both the moon and the sun;
blazing as it stands upon the vault of heaven, it seems to illuminate even the sun. (75.61)
In that [city], the Blessed One, the Lord and Grandfather of all the worlds, dwells alone and eternally, bestowing [boons] upon gods and men. (75.62)
And the lords of creatures also wait upon that Lord:
Dakṣa, Pracetas, Pulaha, Marīci, Kaśyapa, and Yati.
Bhṛgu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and likewise Aṅgiras;
Pulastya, Kratu, Prahlāda, and Kardama as well. || 75–64 ||
The Atharvans and Aṅgirasas, the Bālakhilyas, the Marīcipas;
mind, the intermediate space, the sciences, wind, fire, water, and earth.
Sound, touch, as well as form, taste, and smell, the ego (dhāmīka), primordial nature (prakṛti), the I-principle (ahaṅkāra), and whatever else is the cause of the earth. || 75-66 ||
And Agastya of great splendor, Mārkaṇḍeya the lord of sages, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Saṃvarta, and likewise Cyavana. || 75.67 ||
Durvāsas, the conqueror of enemies; Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, whose wealth is asceticism;
and the blessed Sanatkumāra, the teacher of yoga and one of great austerity.
Asita Devala, Jaigīṣavya the knower of reality, Ṛṣabha who conquered Śakra, and Mahāvīrya, the sage of austerity; || 75-69 ||
Āyurveda, likewise the eight-limbed [Yoga], the embodied one, the bearer of virility, the one with upward-flowing vital seed, the great yogin, Devadatta, and Bhagīratha. (75–76)
Kapilācārya, Īśāpta, Dhanada, Sārasaṅgata, Mahāvāgmīśvara, Kāla, Priyakarmā, and Suvrata. || 75–71 ||
Varuṇa, Sārvabhauma, Devācārya, Dhanañjaya, Kāmaputra, Vasiṣṭha, Mandāra, and Aśvattha. (75–72)
Ravimukhya, Vidhātṛ, Nairṛta, Yama, Agni, Śakra, Vibhāṇḍa, Mahāvīra, and Gaṇeśvara. (75–73)
Kārtikeya, Jīvanātha, Grahacakra, Śubhaṅkara, Vedajñātā, Dharmavettā, Vārendra, Nandana, and Prabhu. (75–74)
Bṛhaspati, the god Śukra, the wise one who wields radiant weapons, and many others who are chaste and devoted to the Lord. || 75-75 ||
Within her, O Mahākāla, shine those whose forms consist of absolute bliss:
the moon together with the constellations, and the suns with their rays. (75–76)
The winds, the sacrificial rites, volition, and vital breath itself—
these high-souled beings possess form and are devoted to great vows.
These and many others always worship Sadāśiva:
Artha (wealth), Dharma (righteousness), Kāma (desire), Harṣa (joy), Adveṣa (freedom from hatred), Tapas (austerity), and Dama (self-restraint). || 75-78 ||
To that [assembly] come the Gandharvas together with the Apsarases, as well as twenty-seven others and all the world-protectors (lokapālas). (75–79)
The nine planets are present there, experts in various modes of worship; the Rathantara mantra is there, as well as Hariman and Vasuman. (75–80)
The Ādityas, with Adhirāja at their head, arrived in various groups;
as did the Maruts, Viśvakarman, the Vasus, and the lords of the directions.
Likewise, all the hosts of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas), as well as all the sacrificial offerings (havīṃṣi),
the Ṛgveda, the Sāmaveda, the Yajurveda, and Sadāśiva.
The Atharvaveda is its conclusion, as are all the scriptures,
the historical narratives and instructions, and all the auxiliary limbs of the Vedas (vedāṅgas) in their entirety.
The planets, the yakṣas, the moons, and all the deities; Sāvitrī, Durgataraṇī, and likewise the sevenfold Vāṇī. || 75-84 ||
Memory, intelligence, fortitude, discernment, wisdom, forbearance, and fame; as well as hymns, sacred scriptures, Sāman chants, and various types of verses. (75–85)
Commentaries with mouths of logic shine forth in embodied form;
there are various dramas, poems, tales, narratives, and extensive verses. (75–86)
There abide those who are meritorious and others who worship their gurus;
there dwell the moments (kṣaṇas), the instants (lavas), the muhūrtas, and the day and night as they dawn.
O Bhairava, there are half-months, months, and the six seasons;
five years constitute a *yuga*, and the fourfold divisions of the month are its nights. (75–88)
The substance that is the Kālacakra is eternal, imperishable, and undecaying; likewise, the Dharmacakra is also eternal, for its forms persist even at the end. (75–89)
Aditi, Dakṣa, Surasā, Vinatā, Irā, the goddess Kālakā, Surabhī, Saramā, and then Gautamī.
Pradhā and Kadrū were indeed goddesses, the mothers of the deities;
as were Rudrāṇī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Bhadrā, and another, Ṣaṣṭhī. (75–91)
The goddess Pṛthivī, Gāṅgā, Hrīḥ, Svāhā, and Kīrti; as well as the goddess Surā, Śacī, Puṣṭi, and Undhatī. (75–92)
Saṃvṛddhi, Āśā, Niyati, the goddess Iḍā, as well as Rati, Kāminī, Paramānandā, and the goddess Śrītripureśvarī. (75–93)
Kāmamātā, Mahābalā, Varadā, Ādyā, Sarasvatī, Mandākinī, Viyadgaṅgā, Svargagaṅgā, and Manojavā. (75–94)
The river Trisrotā, the Candrabhāgā, and the Mahāvegavatī; the oceans arising from the sea, which possess five sacred bathing places, digits, and lotuses. || 75–95 ||
The Kālindī, Vaiṣṇavī, Siddhā, Taralā, Puṣkarodayā, Bhānumatī, Mahāvegā, Caṇḍaśukrā, and the Mahānadī. || 75-96 ||
Vetravatī, Kāverī, Mahābhargā, Vasundharā, Vibhāvatī, Padmalakṣmī, Prabhā, Bhadrā, and Kirātinī. || 75-97 ||
Ambālikā, Ahalyā, Trituṇḍā, Maṇḍaleśvarī, Mandodarī, Mandavegā, Madirā, and the river Śāradā. (75–98)
Nirmalā, Mandaragranthi, Prajñā, Jvālāvatī, Rati, Avantī, Raṭantī, Yugādyā, and Māghasaptamī. (75–99)
Pañcatuṇḍā, Ghoranādā, Santoṣī, Tuṣṭavaṃśinī, Bharadvājeśvarī, Dharmā, Śatadhārā, and Dharāvatī. || 75–100 ||
Mallikā, Mālinī, Mandā, Hindolā, Liṅgavāhinī, Vartulā, Siddhalaṅkā, and the river situated at Kurukṣetra. (75–101)
Ākāśagaṅgā, Siddhāṅgī, Gautamī, Bālikā, Gayā, Daityajihvā, Kālajihvā, and the stainless Catuṣkoṭikalā. || 75-102 ||
The channels (nāḍikā), numbering three and a half, are situated in their respective locations;
within them shine the embodied Sindhu goddesses and others as well. 75–103.
In the assembly hall, there is a river named Kṛṣṇā, which possesses noble lineage and power;
among them, the Trinadī is preeminent, flowing from the left, right, and middle.
Iḍāvatī, the one called Piṅgalā, and Sarasvatī, beginning with Suṣumnā—the goddess Suṣumnā, who possesses many forms, is worshipped in the midst of these three. (75–105)
The rivers are also said to be equal in number to that, totaling three and a half crores:
the Nanda, the Śoṇa, the Mahāśoṇa, the Vaṭuka, the Balavān, and the Hara. (75–106)
Tarūṇa, Tāraka, Bhadra, Vibhadra, Narmadāpati, Prabhānātha, Vīramukhya, Viśāla, and Baladevaka. || 75–107 ||
Padmarāga, Māraketu, Trivṛtta, Nandana, Ghana, Akālajihma, Hiṃsāḍhya, Vidhṛta, and Avadhūtaka. || 75-108 ||
Brahmaputra, Vibhākara, Kapila, and Añjana; Sāmba, Eka, Mahāsaṃkhya, Maṇḍalākhya, and Bṛhannala. (75–109)
Rudra, who bears a hundred stalks, who goes everywhere, the winner of wealth (Dhanañjaya), the thousand-faced, the eloquent, the gurgling, and likewise Damanaka. (75–110)
The pit named Sitā, the pit named Kula, the lord of the uneven [pits], Bhavakuṇḍa, the one named Visarga, Jyotiṣṭoma, and Phalākara. || 75-111 ||
Dhavala, the one called Badara, Vīrabhadra, Makha, Marmahantṛ, Śūlagarta, Mānabhaṅga, and Divāgama. (75–112)
Śūra, Kālakūṭa, Madhugāmin, Jalāntaka, Dadhidhāra, the one called Ghṛta, Sudhādhāra, and Mahānada. || 75-113 ||
The one named Hiṅgula is Mālaketu; Payasvān is the lord of milk;
the one named Lavaṇa is the son of Dharma; and Jīvaputra is the mine of wealth.
Māyāpati, Kalānātha, Vindhyala, Lavaṇāśraya, Ikṣudhārādharo, Māna, Vidhuvarṇa, and Dharājala. (75–115)
Puṣkara, Duṣkara, Śaṅkara, and Sadaiśava—these and many others likewise worship Puṣkara. (75–116)
Among the three, Puṣkara is the most excellent, residing in the Suṣumṇā channel;
that which is named Puṣkara is in the Iḍā, and Śaṅkara is in the Piṅgalā. (75–117)
Furthermore, many rivers possessing form shine forth;
both the rivers and those possessing form have always taken refuge in Sadāśiva.
They worship [him] in the center of the assembly hall of the Lord Brahmā;
the assembly of Brahmā is radiant in the midst of the assembly of Sadāśiva. (75.119)
In that [city], the assembly hall of Śakra shines, captivating even the mind;
it should be meditated upon according to the sequence starting from the east, like a celestial being moving through the sky.
In the southeast corner is the supreme assembly hall of Fire, consisting of great splendor;
and to the south of the pericarp is the great assembly hall of Dharmarāja.
In the southwest is the assembly hall of the lord of the Rākṣasas, which completely deludes all;
in the west shines the assembly hall of Varuṇa known as Dīptā, another celestial assembly.
In the northwest is the assembly hall of Vāyu, and in the north is the hall of Kubera;
below shines the hall of Nanda, and above, O Lord, is the hall of Brahmā.
And in its center shines the assembly hall of Sadāśiva, O Lord, possessing the splendor of ten million suns, arisen from the cosmic egg within the mandala.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and even the two Aśvins always shine within the subtle path as the embodied form of the Lord.
The Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Pitṛs, and the great ṛṣis—O royal sage, it is the One alone who shines as the preeminent principle therein. (75–126)
Likewise, royal sages endowed with thirteen virtues shine forth:
Pṛthu, Dharmarāja, Hariścandra, and Yudhiṣṭhira.
Rāmacandra, Ramānātha, Bhagīratha, Ilāpati, Prahlāda, Kardama, Vibhīṣaṇa, and Dhāmīka. || 75-128 ||
And Nala, wearing a golden garland, along with ascetics arrogant in their prowess, were indeed blazing on the ground at the lower part of the left side. (75.129)
And there are other sages who, having surrounded Sadāśiva, being great devotees, behold the supreme state of Sadāśiva. (75.130)
It removes untimely death and destroys all diseases through the remembrance, recitation, and meditation upon the Lord Sadāśiva, the Master. (75–131)
Whosoever on this earth are devoted—whether they be old, children, or even men in the prime of youth—they all attain success without effort. (75.132)
Having attained the fruit without effort, they behold Sadāśiva; having formed a mental image of these [deities], they worship Sadāśiva. (75.133)
Having performed the worship of the goddesses, those who meditate upon Sadāśiva go swiftly, O Lord, to the supreme state of Sadāśiva. (75–134)
Suddenly beholding the three worlds, they always perceive Sadāśiva,
whether at the proper time, in a secluded place, or even within the hollow of a cow’s udder.
Having remained there with a one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon the supreme state of Sadāśiva;
through such meditation, one who has attained Brahman quickly reaches the state of Śiva. (75.136)
That brahmin swiftly attains the supreme state of Sadāśiva, as he meditates here upon the lotus feet of Sadāśiva in such a manner. (75.137)
Rich with the sound of jeweled anklets, adorned with moving ornaments,
and graced by fingers of ruby, it is like a red lotus.
It was frequented by assemblies of *siddhas* and served as a refuge for the *siddhas*;
it was inhabited by gods, *dānavas*, *gandharvas*, *siddhas*, and *cāraṇas*.
He is worshipped by the hosts of the lords of sages, the eternal embodiment of the ocean of Dharma,
the bestower of fruits such as those desired, beautiful, and possessing a luster equal to a hundred suns.
One should meditate upon that which consists of all vidyās within the stainless path of Haṃsa.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Assembly for Removing Untimely Death," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on Accomplished Mantras (*siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*.
Now begins the sixty-seventh chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said: "O Mahākāla! I shall describe an extremely wonderful method of practice."
The armor-mantra of the goddess Kākinī consists of one hundred and eight syllables.
Having worn it on one's house, hand, head, neck, the center of the heart, the middle of the arms, or the waist, [one stands] upon the earth. || 76-2 ||
Does not the practitioner, the lord of the Yoginīs, surely achieve accomplishment?
There is the accomplishment of yoga, the accomplishment of ritual action, and likewise the supreme accomplishment of Śivā.
Mahāsiddhi, Khecarī, and Suṣumṇāsiddhi;
Phalasiddhi, Kālasiddhi, Kriyāsiddhi, and Śivāmbikā. (76-4)

The power of the shanks, the supreme power, the power of the sword, the ability to move with extreme subtlety, and the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) shall become firmly established in his hand. (76–5)
This armor of the goddess Kākinī bestows all accomplishments;
by reciting it, whether at an improper time or a favorable time, there is an accumulation of merit.
Victorious through the accumulation of dharma, victory lies where Śiva is;
where Śivā is, there is Śiva. The two, whose essence is armor, are dear to one another.
Pārvatī and Parameśvara are those two who are always the saviors;
both are the creators of cause and effect, and they are higher than the highest.
And in the form consisting of armor, they abide as the two whose nature is power;
I shall declare its name-syllable—listen, O Lord Bhairava. (76–9)
Bhairavī is of terrifying form, deformed, and devoid of form;
she is of a subtler-than-the-subtlest form, self-luminous, and Śākinī. (76–10)
Japalā, Jañcalā, Bhīmā, Candradevī, Parāparā, Kamalākṣī, Devamātā, the bearer of the sword and skull-cup. (76.11)
Gurvī, Gaurī, Ghanacchāyā, Oṃkārādyā, Carupriyā; Chāyā, Jayā, Jāñjanā, Oṅkārātmā, and Kalāvatī. (76–12)
Aṅkāriṇī, Ḍākinī, Ṭakkādevī, Ruṇapriyā, Tāriṇī, Sthūlapuṣṭā, Dayādharmapriyā, and Nuti. (76–13)
She is supreme intellectual power, the bestower of fruits, the digit of Phālgunī,
the shower of wealth, Vāsukī, Bhadrakālī, and the source of both existence and non-existence.
She is the mother who deludes the mind, Yaśodā, the illustrious performer of sacrifices;
she is the mistress of beauty, whose life is in battle, Lakṣmī, adorned with auspicious marks.
Vasupriyā, Vasuratā, Bālarakṣā, Śaśiprabhā, Ṣaḍakṣarī, Śāradā, Haridrā, and Hāramālinī. (76–16)
Lāvaṇyaniratā, Laṅkā, Kṣayarogavināśinī, Kṣetrapālā, Kṣetrī, Kṣatriyā, Kṣemadā, and Kṣamā. (76.17)
She who brings an end to hunger, she who is agitated, she known as Kṣālanā, she who is both perishable and imperishable;
she called Anantā, Umā, Durgā, Ṛṣabhā, and the beloved of Īśvara. (76–18)
Established in the seed-syllable *ḷ*, possessing a long life through the syllable *ḷ*,
Cāmuṇḍā of the Eraṇḍa forest is the consort of Indra, situated within the beloved of *ḍa* and *ṭ*.
The herb Tunutuṇḍā is superior, inferior, and middling;
she is the impeller, residing in herbs, and united with the self of Aṭṭahāsa.
Arthadā has eight arms and moves amidst rays like ten million suns;
she is to be worshipped as Ardhanārīśvarā, equal [to her consort], and bearing the Arbuda weapon.
The eightfold sovereign powers are the offerings; Ambhasthā and Arundhatī are also there;
she is named Arpaṇā, Arkamuni, Arpaṇā, and Askhalasthitā. (76-22)
Rich in worship, abiding in worship, the enemy of foes, with reddish lips—
having recited the nectar known as the "Eighty-one," one should recite the armor (kavaca).
Then there shall be an abundance of fruits, which is the means for attaining long life and health.
Sadāśiva is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of this Śākinī-kavaca. || 76-24 ||
The Gāyatrī metre itself is Śākinī, the deity of the body. Om Śrīṃ Klīṃ, may she protect my head; Blūṃ Hlūṃ, may she protect my forehead. (76–25)
May Khecarī protect my two eyes; may Śivaśākinī protect my ears;
and may the goddess Śākambharī, who is Ramā, always protect the pair of my cheeks.
Svāhā protects the bridge of the nose; may she protect the upper and lower lips and the head.
Drīṃ Hīṃ Śrīṃ—may the deity of the body protect my rows of teeth and the tip of my tongue. (76-27)
May the goddess Kamalā protect my chin; may Vāgdātrī protect my forehead; may Kālikā, whose essence is the seed-syllable of sound, protect my face and throat.
May Kaṇṭhadevī and Śākinī protect my throat-lotus;
may Surādevī, who can assume any form at will, always protect the heart-lotus.
May Kalāvatī, Kāmakāmā, and Kāmamālā protect my pure path of Sadāśiva; may Lakṣmī protect the lotus of my navel. (76-30)
May Ulkāmukhī, the mother of the gods, always protect the six-syllable mantra;
may she always protect the lotus of Viṣṇu, and may Rākiṇī protect its petal.
May Bhedadā, the bestower of knowledge and liberation, always protect the region of the hips;
may Kākinī, the supreme sovereign goddess, always protect the mūlādhāra.
May she who is always of one form, yet possesses manifold forms, protect the support of the *liṅga*;
may the Goddess Mārkaṇḍa-pūjitā, Mṛkuṇḍā, who dwells in the root, protect us. (76.33)
O Goddess of the gods, may Abhayā always protect my beautiful region;
may the Great Goddess named Darśanā protect the space between the feet that supports the Liṅga.
May the goddess Hiraṇyākṣī, who is all the deities, protect my entire body—she who exists in a subtle form as the Ordainer, yet possesses a gross body and a slender waist. (76.35)
May the goddess Śākambharī protect me everywhere and at all times;
may Kālikā, who resides in the heart, always protect my entire body in every place.
Thus, O Lord, this armor (kavaca), difficult even for the gods to obtain, has been told to you;
by reciting it, a man attains perfection and gains sovereignty.
Suddenly one becomes equal to the sun and becomes a conqueror of desire by oneself;
through its retention, there shall be growth of the body, as well as the attainment of longevity and health. (76.38)
It directly effects the mastery over the vital winds and is the embodiment of the bliss of nectar;
it indeed brings about the immobilization of fire, the immobilization of water, and the immobilization of wind. (76.39)
The Khecarī becomes a conqueror through yoga and brings about the destruction of all desires;
thereafter, one should recite the Kāma-mantra and perform meditation at its conclusion.
Oṃ! Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives; day and night are your two sides;
the stars are your form; the Aśvins are your open mouth.
Bestowing [blessings], bestow them upon me; bestow them upon all the world. 76-41.
Having recited the Kāma-mantra, one shall indeed obtain the fruit of all desires;
then, having meditated upon it, he who meditates on the Śākini-Śiva [should do so] while wearing the armor (kavaca).
He attains mastery over the Vedas through the yoga of meditation on the Śākinīs. || 76-43 ||

I meditate upon Śākinī, who resides without limit in the white lotus known as Prāṇa; she is clad in yellow garments, subtle, her body trembling with the intense manifestation of ornaments, flickering and longing for spiritual perfection;
she shines with four lotus-like hands and beautiful lotus-eyes, and is enriched by Śiva.
I worship Śākamātā, who is accompanied by Padmā, Abhīti, Pracaṇḍā, and Asiknī. || 76-44 ||
Having meditated in a cremation ground, at the base of an excellent mountain, in the midst of the region of the ḍākinīs,
in an empty pit, a forest, on the floor of a house in the sky, or in a well-inhabited empty house—
the one whose nature is gnosis, who is self-controlled, constantly recites this yoga of the body of the śākinīs.
In the Gaṅgā, within her own womb, the armor that grants fearlessness and bestows everything attains perfection.
Having worshipped the Goddess with the armor-mantra according to the prescribed rites and through the proper causes,
one shall suddenly attain perfection of the body, endowed with the eight sovereign powers.
One attains liberation through devotion, and finds happiness at every step; may young children be born to her, and may she never be one whose sons are like crows. (76.47)
Having retained this vidyā, one is not defiled by these faults;
whoever wears this, which holds arrows in battle, around their neck, [is likewise protected].
One who is merely a living being attains imperishability as Sadāśiva by means of gorocanā, saffron, kālāguru, and turmeric. (76.49)
Having written it with lac juice and having worn it, one shall obtain immortality.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Armor of Śakinī," in the *Śakinī-kavaca* section of the *Ṣaṭcakra-prakāśa*, within the *Siddhamantra-prakaraṇa* of the *Mahātantroddīpana*, the *Uttara-tantra* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 76.
Now begins the seventy-seventh chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairava said:
"O beautiful Kaumārī, beloved of my life, speak now!"
In the eightieth chapter, speak on the accumulation of the purpose of yoga.
The illustrious Ānandabhairavī said: Listen, O King of Bhairavas, to [the teaching on] Sadāśiva and the Śākinīs;
for the yoga of the delight of these two indeed results in the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (77–2)
The vision of the atoms of space by those with the distinguished, stainless eye is suddenly attained by the wise one, as if struck by lightning. (77.3)
Above the station of the family of Sadāśiva is the station of Śrīśākinī;
he who indeed knows the distinction between these two attains the siddhi of the sky-farer of knowledge.
I shall describe that station of the family as it truly is; listen attentively.
It is located on all sides at the tips and at the bases of the sixteen petals. (77–5)
One should contemplate the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja), the abode of the family of Sadāśiva;
having contemplated it a hundred times, what is there that the yogi cannot accomplish on this earth? (77–6)
Having become the lord of all beings, he stands firm upon the earth before the Blessed One,
the Great-bodied One, the Supreme God, Sadāśiva.
The great yogi perceives the Kālacakra situated within the wheel, situated outside the wheel, external, internal, and supreme; beyond that, there is nothing further. (77–8)
Having effortlessly pierced the knot of space and dissolved into the beyond, one becomes capable of moving everywhere through the grace of the King of Wheels. || 77-9 ||
Having pierced the thirty-two knots of the *kaṭhina*, one rises like a bird into the sky;
beyond that is the wheel of the bliss of Paraśiva, which consists of the nature of Śakti.
Beyond that is the locus of the multitude of sounds; beyond that is the supreme locus;
then follows the locus of both the manifest and the unmanifest, the maṇḍala of awakening.
Above that, having pierced the seat of Unmanī, and immediately after that,
having pierced the city of Bhṛgu, and beyond that, the city of Nāda.
Then, having pierced through to the End of Sound (nādānta), which has the form of the jars of Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
one reaches the place of sacrifice (yajñasthāna)— the abode of the crest-lock (śikhāpada)— which effects action and is the dissolution of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Then, having pierced Pūrṇagiri and Uḍḍiyāna, he reaches his own abode;
thereafter, having pierced the place of difficulty as well as the place of manifestation.
Above that is the location of Piṅgalā; above that is that state (tat-pada);
then, having pierced the sphere of Suṣumnā, one reaches the great abode (mahālaya) at the corner of Dhaumira.
Above that is the Great Bindu (mahābindu), and above that is a hexagon;
above that is the Vāsanāpūra, and above that is the Bījapūra.
Above that, however, stands the discus of Viṣṇu, situated like the wheel of a spider;
having pierced that, one reaches the city of Kāma, which bestows the fruits of all desires. (77–17)
Above that is the wheel of Indra, above that the wheel of the earth;
above that is the wheel of the treasury, and above that the wheel of wind.
Above that is the fire-wheel (vahnicakra), and above that is the nectar-wheel (amṛtacakra). Above that is the water-wheel (jalacakra), and above that is the day-wheel (divācakra).
Above that is the wheel of night; above that is the wheel of stars;
above that is the wheel of Dharma; and above that is the wheel of time (Kālacakra).
Pervading at all times and forever the world of the moving and the stationary,
it always stands above that, [extending over] the circle of the seven oceans.
Above that, the illustrious circle of the end of the waters shines eternally;
above that, moreover, is the great wheel, which has the appearance of a forest of great lotuses.
One should visualize a beautiful thousand-petaled lotus above the palate;
having pierced that, one beholds the lotus of gnosis within the pericarp.
One should visualize the form of Mahādeva in the shape of a corpse, appearing as a hungry ghost (preta) and devoid of activity;
upon his chest is the seed-syllable of the preta, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns. (77-24)
And at the base of his thighs is the seed-syllable of Wrath, red as a hundred suns;
upon that, he certainly beholds Mahākālī.

I bow to Ambā, who stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, whose eyes are like lotuses, whose face is smiling, who possesses four arms, and whose lotus-hands hold a sword, a severed head, and display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The mother of the three worlds, whose form is Brahman, radiant with a crown,
bearing a garland of severed heads, possessing all weapons, and the cause of all things.
She whose form pervades the Brahmās of infinite millions of cosmic eggs;
she who has a gracious countenance, yet is formidable, with ears like corpses and a terrifying appearance.
The eternal Bhavānī, the mother of the lords of yogis, who liberates one from worldly existence,
who is stainless, whose bliss is pure, and whose very nature is the bliss of knowledge.
She who abides in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; she with loose hair, naked, graceful, beautiful, dark-complexioned, and served by Mahākāla.
She is most formidable, her hips adorned with a jeweled girdle rich with moon-shaped bells;
she possesses a form of fierce splendor like a thousand infinite suns, and she is beloved by the Kula.
To Durgā, who dwells in the cremation ground, whose abode is the cemetery,
the one of terrible roar, the most fierce, Kālikā, the supreme Dakṣiṇā.
She who was terrifying with a pair of severed heads used as ear-ornaments, possessing fierce fangs and a gaping mouth, and endowed with full, elevated breasts. || 77-33 ||
She had fashioned a girdle from the hands of corpses, was sweet-spoken,
and her face was made radiant by streams of blood trickling down both corners of her mouth.
Adorned with three lotus-eyes like the orb of the rising sun,
she is formidable, with the beauty of her breasts graced by hanging pearls that extend across her right side.
She is seated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a Śava,
surrounded on all four sides by Śivās of terrible roar.
Pervaded by Mahākāla, she is distressed by perverse passion;
her face is serene with bliss, and her lotus-like eyes are smiling and reddish. (77.37)
Abounding in the chewing of honey and meat, the bestower of boons, afflicted by passion, she is born from noble qualities through the knowledge of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. || 77-38 ||
She who destroys the pride of the Daityas and Dānavas, and whose body is adorned with a garland of skulls.
One should meditate upon Kālī of the Kaula tradition, seated at the foot of the Kula tree,
the glorious Kalpalatikā, whose earrings are adorned with ten million flashes of lightning.
She is enriched by a serpent used as a sacred thread, has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel,
is adorned with all ornaments, and possesses eyes like fire, the sun, and the moon.
She has a lolling tongue, can assume any form at will, and dwells in the sacred seat of Kāma; her face is exceedingly beautiful, and its radiance flashes like a torrential stream.
Bestowing desires, she was being praised by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, gods, and Cāraṇas with their dances, as well as by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śakra, and the great ṛṣis.
I bow to Tārā, who is worshipped at all times, whose bodily radiance resembles ten million clouds, who enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, and whose nature is the Brahman that delivers.
She who flashes with the brilliance of a row of moonstones and sapphires;
she who is naked with the love for her beloved, which is the sweet bliss that is the abode of Śrī. || 77.45 ||
She who has transcended shame, transcended family, and transcended knowledge, who is stainless,
whose hips shine with a tiger skin produced from a mass of wrath.
One should always meditate upon her, worshipped by Nīlā, Ghanā, Balā, Māyā, Mātrā, Mudrā, Kalā, and the others, within the supreme lotus of the thousand petals.

Having thus meditated upon Mahākālī— dark-hued, the fulfiller of desires, auspicious, and moving through the sky— the self-controlled practitioner will certainly attain the siddhi of traveling through space.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Collection of the Meaning of Yoga," in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the *Siddhamantra* in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*, concerning the description of the sequence of the *Sadāśivakulacakra*. 77.
Now begins the seventy-eighth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O Bhairava, I shall explain the definitive determination of the meaning of the secret signs."
The sequence of the Kula-cakra is established, as is that of Śakti and Sadāśiva.
By the mere consciousness of this, one becomes established in the throat-lotus;
and at the tip of that lotus is the essential wheel, which is exceedingly dear to yogins. (78–2)
O mighty-armed one, through meditation alone [one attains] that which reveals all wheels;
[he becomes] one whose vital energy flows upward, a conqueror of desire, a man of knowledge, a silent sage, and one clad in the directions as his garment. (78.3)
The glorious Khecaro, the bearer [of the lineage], the Kaulika, shall become a practitioner (sādhaka).
Thus, the meditation on that wheel has two doors facing forward.
At the end of that, there is also a double door, half a sesame-seed [in measure], with a broken line;
between the two lines there is a single door, and thus again there are two doors.
The wise practitioner should meditate twice from the beginning to the northern limit,
and between those two, the mandala of the lines of the four Vedas.
In the space between those, a hexagon; within that, a double hexagon;
in the center of that, an eight-petalled lotus; and in the center of that, a lunar maṇḍala.
In the midst of that is the form of emptiness, formless and stainless;
it is my abode, whose nature is the bliss and wisdom resting upon the knowledge of reality.
My own self is composed of the gross and the subtle, pure, consisting of the relationship between the signified and the signifier, non-dual, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
He who has the form of the radiance of ten million lightning bolts, who is as cool as ten million moons,
who is all-pervading, the Lord, and the cause of non-dual knowledge.
The creator, the supreme Brahman, the omniscient, the all-seeing, the expounder of all scriptures, the knower and the knowable, and that which is moving and unmoving. (78-11)
Eight-armed, large-eyed, bearing a trident, wearing a garland of skulls, beyond old age, free from conceptual construction, youthful, the savior, Hara. (78-12)
Hari, Brahmā, and Īśāna, the luminous lord of the three worlds,
the accomplished one who cannot be pierced yet pierces all, the divine one who bestows the Siddhāsana.
The city of the Gandharvas, the region, the distinction, that which faces in all directions, the untimely star, together with Svāhā, Svadhā, and Śakti. || 78-14 ||
He is Bhava, who has the form of the apocalyptic fire at the end of an aeon, who is fierce and whose very nature is Rudra;
he is the light shining within the circle of the girdle of Kanyā, Śrī, and Sundarī.
The radiant orb of splendor, which destroys all diseases,
is perfected by Hṛṣīkeśa and Ānanda, and brings about the fruit of Trivikrama.
The abode of the wrath of Nṛsiṃha, the destroyer of all Daityas,
and the cause for the recovery of the meaning of the Vedas through the Fish Incarnation.
The Supreme Lord, whose wheel has the tortoise’s back as its foundation, who is adorned with the tusk of the Boar, and who protects his devotees in the form of Narasiṃha. || 78-18 ||
Vāmana, the protector of Mahendra and the destroyer of the pride of the Daityas;
and Paraśurāma, the lord of the twice-born and the destroyer of the pride of the Kṣatriya Daityas.
To Śrī Rāma, the lord of the lineage of Bhṛgu, the supreme incarnation of truth and knowledge, the purifier, the slayer of demons, the ascetic, and the preceptor.

The supreme wielder of the plow, the support of the three worlds, whose nature is bliss, the infinite and primordial one among yogis, endowed with a thousand hoods marked by the sign of the sun. (78.21)
The Buddha is the formless reality that increases the meaning of all scriptures;
he is eternally exalted by the joy arising from sacred revelation and is entirely free from both merit and demerit. (78.22)
The self-existent, self-luminous, supreme Self, the auspicious one, uniform in nature, the knower of the wheel of Dharma, whose resolve is pure. (78.23)
To the subduer of the wicked, the great hero Dhanañjaya, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who is worshipped with all services, who is identical with that [Dhanañjaya], and who is auspicious—[I bow]. (78-24)
Free from intoxication, a protector, illuminating meditative concentration, primordial wisdom, and liberation;
the Lord of the Kings of Kings, the one to be dwelt in, who is served by all the worlds. (78.25)

The Dharma residing within all bodies, whose very nature is Dharma, the dispeller [of suffering], all-pervasive, the support of the pervasive, free from conceptual construction, and consisting of nectar.
To the distinguished one who dwells upon the great seat of the five stones (Pañcapāṣāṇamahāpīṭha),
whose majesty is infinite and infinite, and who bears the skull and the trident.
The locus of the maṇḍala of three lines, the source of the sequence of the four Vedas;
having one face and two feet, and also two faces and four feet. (78–28)
The Lord has three faces and six arms; he is the supreme four-faced Brahmā, with eight lotus-like arms and five faces and three eyes. (78.29)
Śiva, who possesses ten arms, is auspiciousness, bliss, and beautiful; the illustrious Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) is eternal, twelve-armed, and perpetually bearing all weapons. (78.30)
Seven-faced and large-bodied, beloved with fourteen arms;
eight-faced, the delight of Śiva, adorned with sixteen arms. (78.31)
The Lord Unmattabhairava, who has a face like a fresh lotus, possesses eighteen arms, and is the beloved of ten million Mahāvidyās and other deities. (78.32)
Amareśa, of massive body, the lord of eighteen arms, a heap of Time, black in color, and wearing a garland of variegated serpents. || 78.33 ||
He has a hundred faces and ten million hands, with a thousand lotus-like mouths;
he possesses hundreds of millions of mouths and is the abode of the continuous flow of eternal bliss.
His lotus feet are infinite, served by infinite people;
his lotus hands are infinite, radiant with infinite ornaments. (78.35)
The mass of internal illumination, the source of infinite qualities,
the creator of infinite emanations, and the cause of infinite maintenance.
He who is other than the infinite lotuses, who is fond of infinite dissolution,
who is a multitude of infinite seeds, and who is the certainty of infinite scriptures.
Satisfied by the quelling of infinite heat, situated in the midst of infinite waters, the infinite supreme support, and the bearer of infinite fire. || 78-38 ||
He who possesses a mass of infinite space, who is the lord of infinite earths, who is enriched by infinite garlands of flames, and who is the cause of infinite wisdom. || 78-39 ||
Rich with worship at infinite locations, it bestows the accomplishment of infinite names;
it is the knowledge of infinite states and the bliss that grants infinite sovereignty.
It radiates the meaning of infinite treatises on dharma, is honored by poetry, is the abode of infinite deities, and bestows the accomplishment of infinite deeds. (78.41)
He who recites the mantra of the infinite garland of pills bestows eternal accomplishment;
his mental activity is infinite, and his prowess is infinitely infinite. (78.42)
He whose consciousness of living beings is infinite, who delights in infinite meditation, whose stainless bliss is infinite, and who is dear to infinite living beings. (78.43)
To the author of the Anantagāthā, who dwells within the infinite ocean, whose hands and feet extend everywhere, and whose eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides; (78.44)
Having meditated upon the unconquered Lord, who stands pervading all, as the blissful God, and the practitioner in the center of the seat— 78.45.
To the one who is devoted to the bliss of love for the goddess Śākinī and the power of the gods,
the God of gods, who consists of the universe, who takes the form of a Śākya, and who is eternal.
When the yogin, free from support and naked, meditates upon my form that delights the senses and praises it by name within the city of the wheel (cakrapura), [he attains success]. 78-47.
Having meditated upon the essence of the wheel established in the sky under its family name, the lord of yogins becomes a fearless master who moves through the air. (78.48)
Success shall be achieved without effort, and one shall become a knower possessed of wisdom.
The lotus of the throat is turned upward, and at its tip is the circle of the wheel. (78.49)
The lotus of the eye is downward-facing, having two petals and being exceedingly beautiful;
at its tip is a great wheel, shaped like it and possessing great radiance. (78–50)
O Lord of Gods, when the conjunction of two wheels is seen through the yoga of night, then there arises that which is enchanting and possesses four gates.
O Śiva, O Mahādeva, he who knows the stainless wheel, which consists of mantra and is both knowledge and the object of knowledge, shall become a wish-fulfilling tree. (78.52)
Thus, the greatness of the throat has been briefly described by me;
the yogi knows it through meditation with a mind endowed with knowledge. (78.53)
One beholds the Great-Souled One, who consists of gnosis and the object of gnosis, and is composed of nectar;
even in a hundred times ten million years, he cannot be fully described.
O Mahādeva, through devotion to you and because of your protection of my life and my field,
I have now described this auspicious movement within the lotus of the throat.
It is not to be revealed, a great secret, the very nature of the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), [to be practiced] in a solitary place free from defects and devoid of the affliction of disease. (78.56)
Remaining there in a place free from scarcity and reproach, firm in his vows, he should meditate with supreme devotion while contemplating your form. (78.57)
Before long, one shall become perfected in yoga and attain mastery in the knowledge of diagnosis;
[she is] the illustrious Great Goddess Mātṛkā, the auspicious and virtuous Līlāvatī. (78-58)
May my mother, the venerable Guruśakti, protect me who am exceedingly distressed;
having bowed again and again to that Mother, the lotus-eyed one. (78-59)
Now, O Lord, tell me the definitive teaching on the knowledge of the lotus of the eyebrows.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Piercing of the Lotus of the Throat," within the *Kaṇṭhāmbhojabhedaprakāśa* (Illumination of the Piercing of the Lotus of the Throat) in the *Bhairavībhairavasaṃvāda* (Dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava), in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Wheels), in the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa* (Section on Accomplished Mantras), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* (Illumination of the Great Tantra), in the *Uttaratantro* (Supplementary Tantra) of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*. 78.
Now, the seventy-ninth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairava said:
"O lady of excellent hips, tell me of the auspicious accomplishment of desires."
If you have affection for me, this great knowledge should not be disclosed [to others]. (79-1)

That which is hidden in the beginningless scriptures and concealed in all tantras—the most auspicious of all principles—is [revealed] through the compassionate gaze of affection for [the disciple’s] happiness. (79-2)
Accessible through wisdom, this web of sounds reveals the tender inner light;
it generates long life and health, and bestows virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (79.3)
The two petals of the lotus of her eyebrows were filled with the circles of perfected sages,
and there occurred a gathering of the knowledge of the essential tenets of the self for those possessed of wisdom.
O fair-faced one, explain with effort and in detail the Yāmala, which is served by Mahārudra, since it is the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). (79.5)
O you who are composed of compassion, by your grace it is obtained at that very moment;
through the power of Kālakūṭa, my own forgetfulness has departed. (79.6)
Having completely eradicated that forgetfulness, bestow upon me the knowledge of mindfulness—
the first sprout of the nirvāṇa that carries forth supreme bliss.
The illustrious Ānandabhairavī said:
I shall describe the two-petaled lotus of Vibhāṇḍaka, agitated by the fire of time (kālānala),
which enchants and delights with its beauty, and is radiant with a garland of skulls and flickering eyes.

May that Supreme Śiva—who has entered the beautiful cavity of the row of flames, who is the beloved of the illustrious Śākinī, who resides as the cause of the life-breath of all living beings, and who moves through all things—protect us. 79-8.

He is a mass of lovely splendors blazing with the power of withdrawal; he blazes from the well of dissolution; he is the great crest of light whose nature is energy and who is the state of bliss; he delights in the oil of nectar;
he is the embodiment of the brilliance of the Moon and the Sun; and he exerts himself to overcome the transgressions of Māyā.
I worship the two friends who are like leaves, honored by the essence of the state of being the beloved of knowledge. 79-9.
In the expanse of space, at the pinnacle of light, possessing a fierce gait and the essence that sustains the earth,
the Lord of Śrī, the Sovereign of the Earth, whose neck is adorned with a crest of rows of many moon-like jewels—
Śrīkaṇṭha, the Blue-throated One— is manifest as the creator of the world’s bliss and the accomplisher of all aims.
Vidyā is Śrī Hākinīśa in a house of crystal gems, and Haṃsa is with the red Śakti. || 79-10 ||
Within the circle of the pericarp of the lotus,
the preeminent power Hākinī shines forth as the savior from misfortune;
yet, she is fully realized here by men who sing the songs of the excellent mantras and tantras.
At that time, he would attain supremacy; otherwise, he would remain far away and unstable. || 79.11 ||
In the center of the two-petaled lotus is Hākinī, the mother of the gods;
she is the youthful maiden of the ninefold manifestation, a yoginī perfected in yoga.
If she moves, smeared with [sandalwood paste], she is seated upon the upward path.
Through her compassion for the three worlds, she is gracious toward the practitioner. 79-12.
A person who is devoted to recitation and the supreme mantra,
performing the breath-recitation (*prāṇajāpa*) of the goddess Hākinī, becomes one of pure mind;
having constantly contemplated the mantra within his heart, he is firmly established.
He travels to the families of other cities, possessing the merit of meditative concentration and higher knowledge. || 79-13 ||
Victorious over the enemy by conquering the thirst for the sweetness of sense objects,
he is the nature of supreme light within the lotus of his lineage. Having conquered the defects of his family caused by fate, he shines forth, free from blemish.
The practitioner, whose beauty is equal to that of the Lord of Rati, has reached the ultimate end. || 79-14 ||
For the sake of human wealth, he performs recitation; for the sake of the festival of the burnt offering,
this most excellent among the human race, having set aside other [rites] by means of Kālī,
[utters] hundreds of ten-thousand mantras consisting of a mass of syllables that destroy [evil].
The practitioner, the slayer of enemies and lord of the Hākinīs, brings forth [the result]. || 79-15 ||
Entering within through the inclination toward the ninefold state of Paraśiva,
she who rivals the splendor of a two-petaled lotus with her millions of manifestations is meditated upon by those contemplating her through the traditional lineages of their own families.
And the first Hākinī becomes exceedingly gracious and agile. || 79-16 ||
The lotus named Ājñā is reddish with the radiance that delights like a hundred moons;
it is elevated by flashes of lightning and bestows the blissful consciousness of the white pedestal.
It is brilliantly illuminated by two hands shining with the luster of gold.
