One should meditate on the supreme bliss, which is unmoved by the fear of the Hākinī-kalā.
Victorious is he who expands the abode of meditative concentration, gnosis, and the like, dispelling the spread of his enemies;

having attained the Lord, Hākinī— by means of her two golden-hued hands, adorned with the young sun and moon— having fashioned from the subtle, the subtler, and the most subtle, produces the nectar of immortality.
On the seat of clouds, she who possesses the splendor of ten million moons, whose essence is the wealth of forceful joy, brings delight.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, supreme and enriched with excellence, the mother of the three worlds, six-faced, with the Vedas in her hands;
blazing, holding the gestures of knowledge (vidyāmudrā), a skull-bowl, a rosary, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru);
bestowing peace upon the mind, possessing a moon-jewel mirror, both terrifying and equanimous.
In the six-cornered [mandala], at the base of the bindu, within a lotus of two petals, endowed with two pairs of gates. || 79-19 ||
In the center of this wheel, radiant with the form of lightning and surrounded by all the hosts of gods,
there eternally shines a garland of lotuses, adorned by all wise beings, which completely destroys every defect within the state of the great mandala extending to its sides.
Known as Prāṇā, she is the flame of fire, consisting of bliss, stainless, the Yoginī, and the foremost of yogas. || 79-20 ||
The sign of mental union is well-known as extremely subtle;
it is the mind in the form of a flame within the auspicious lotus,
in the pericarp of the great source-wheel, O Beloved.
The self-controlled one beheld the formidable and pure abode of Śiva.

The lord of practitioners, with a steady vital breath and intellect, should contemplate that which has the form of a great flash of lightning, shining as the supreme awakening of the Brahma-thread and the delight of the Great Kaula path, in due order. (79–22)
One should quickly meditate upon the beloved of the Lord, Pañcacūḍa, who illuminates the seeds of the Mahāveda-sūtra and other scriptures, and who possesses the radiance of a hundred moons of bliss.
He is one who goes toward great liberation, having conquered anger and desire. || 79-23 ||
The supreme practitioner who is endowed with this, joined with the meditation on the All-pervading One, dear to himself and great-souled,
moves swiftly through the city of others among men.
The Lord of Sages, the Sovereign of the Earth, the great expounder of the Vedas.
Emptied of both conceptual cognition and sensory consciousness, he becomes the supreme one,
the all-seeing king of omniscience;
forever established in perfect accomplishment, he is the slayer of the enemy.
The performer of the great creation, destruction, protection, and so forth. || 79-25 ||
Having manifested himself at the beginning of a moment, the Lord becomes long-lived, wise,
a knower of the meaning of all scriptures, possessed of excellent counsel,
endowed with great knowledge, and single-minded.
Bali is equal to Bāṇa and is praised by the Creator. || 79-26 ||
Within the interior of one's own wheel-mandala, upon a triangular ground-image,
and further within that, sixteen petals shine forth on the left;
they are well-formed, beautiful, and have the appearance of the flame of a lamp.
Extremely brilliant and with radiating luster, it is outside the four chambers. || 79-27 ||
The King of Wheels (cakrarāja), adorned with the arrangements of the *praṇava*, shines above that;
above that is the splendor of the beautiful crescent moon (*candrakhaṇḍa*);
and above that is the letter *ma*, radiant with a dripping drop (*bindu*).
Above that, the cool-sounding moon shines as a mass of nectar. || 79-28 ||
The wise one who meditates here in this sacred field (*kṣetraka*) upon the beloved series of feet,
having bound within his mind the multitude of emotional intensities (*bhāvapuñja*) proclaimed by the venerable Lord,

and being devotedly intent on the supreme state free from support according to the yoga teachings declared by the lords of yogins— *Note: The text provided is incomplete, but the translation reflects the portion available.*
Through constant practice, the self-controlled person certainly perceives the fierce power of the Supreme Being.
In the midst of that, I take refuge in the primordial self-luminosity, which is pure light and possesses an extremely stainless fraction;
established in the first sense-organ, it is attained through its own station and possesses the glory of supreme bliss.
It is the lotus-circle of radiance at the feet of Hākinī, endowed with great beauty, charm, and fortitude.
Fortune shines sweetly upon one devoted to meditation; I shall apply myself to that meditation. (79-30)
Bearing a mass of oil in the form of millions of blazing lamps, crying out with the splendor of the new sun,
and possessing a shimmering light situated between the sky, the earth, and the moon;
Indeed, upon seeing this, the yogi would quickly become like Mahendra himself.
Here, outside of Ānanda, the Supreme Lord is indeed manifest, the imperishable power of Mahāpūrṇabhūti;
he is the excellent orb of the great fire, moon, and sun, or Śrī Hari upon the discus of Mahāviṣṇu. (79–32)

Then, having beheld the power of the *Nārāyaṇīya-tantra*— which is served by the great Viṣṇu-yogi and the lords of great yogis— the great Indra entered into the state of dissolution (*pañcatva*) at that time.
One should quickly behold the abode of *laya*, which is like space and wind, belonging to *añjana* who is exceedingly fond of heat;
above that is the form of great reverence, the half of Śiva, vast-eyed in form and having the measure of the form of Śivā. (79–34)

In this world, he beheld the one who is perfectly peaceful, great, whose end is the beloved earth, whose lotus-hand is raised to grant boons, who bestows fearlessness, who possesses the pure awakening of a Buddha, and who practices compassion and generosity. (79.35)
The person who is absorbed in the joy of the lotus feet of the gurus beholds the Supreme Lord as the Master of Life;
that yogi, free from disease, beholds Him as the Sun, the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of Wealth, the Lord of Men, and one of most pure appearance. (79.36)
He attains perfect mastery and purity of speech,
as well as the excellence of sovereignty over the fortune of desire and greatness;
may there never again be for him the state of rebirth within the three worlds.
Śrīpati or Nārada always sings it. || 79-37 ||

The illustrious Ānandabhairava said: "O auspicious Goddess, you have not heard the *hākinī*-syllable mantra, nor the procedure for worship, the meditation, the recitation, or the exhalation of the vital breath. (79-38)
O beautiful one, by the grace of Śrī Varanātha, tell me the yoga beginning with these [mantras], as well as the hymns, the Thousand Names, and the auspicious rites. (79–39)

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Śākinī Mantras," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the Section on Accomplished Mantras of the Great Tantra-illuminator, the Northern Tantra of the glorious Rudrayāmala. 79.
Now begins the eightieth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, O beloved one who makes drinking the cause of supreme bliss."
And even for another, the mantra of Hākinī is most wonderful.
O Lord, in the eighty-third [chapter], within this ocean of joy from recitation,
[is found] the secret mantra that increases supreme bliss and grants all desires.
O Sadāśiva, he who is the creator of this [state] is a yogi and not a mere human;
he possesses supreme knowledge, immense wealth, and great sovereignty.
"By the mere propitiation of this [deity], one shall attain [the goal] by oneself.
For this reason, I shall explain the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra) in its proper sequence. (80.4)
This most wonderful,
auspicious, and great mantra, which is the refuge of mental recitation, bestows the state that is the source of primordial wisdom and grants a vast treasury of discernment.
O Lord of Bhairavas, hear this merit-bestowing and purifying [teaching]. (80.5)

The Tāra-Brahman mantra, together with the cremation ground, Śambhu, Vibhu, Hāntaka, Bhānta, Rānta, Jala, that which consists of fire (Hutāśana), Vāyu, and Vāmākṣi; joined with the syllable of Vāyu, and endowed with Tripurā and the Śrī-Kāmakūṭa.
And at the end [is] "Hākini Devī Vahniyuvatī"; this mantra bestows bliss. || 80-6 ||
The Goddess, the beloved of Śiva, is joined with the syllables *bhāṣā*, *māra*, *kalā*, *rāmā*, and *vadhū*.
O Vidyā Hākinī, [the mantra] is encased within the *tāra* mantra and endowed with *māyā* and *agnijāyā*.
It is saluted by the lords of yoga, recited by Mahendra, and animated by inhalation and exhalation.
Those who meditate upon their beloved wife on the surface of the earth, who is devoted to her husband with love; 80-7.

ĀKĀŚAṂ VAHNIKŪṬAṂ VADHUŚIVADAYITĀŚAKTİKĀMATRIKŪṬAṂ | HĀKINYAI PARANĀTHABHĀSURAGUROḤ ŚAKTYAI NAMO’GNIPRIYĀ || If a wise man recites this mantra of love for Hākinī, he becomes a sovereign lord of kings.
May he, submerged in the ocean of bliss, cause the radiance that illuminates the mass of all existents to increase. (80-8)

With two hundred thousand recitations, the accomplishment of the mantra occurs within one's own lineage; possessing the nature of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetravijña)—the lord of men—subjugates the world through the essence of its dispositions.
At the end of that is the seed-syllable of Vidyā, enriched by Ramā and joined with the celestial river (Suradhunī), which is the peak of desire (Kāmakūṭa).
O young woman, O Mistress of the World, the reality of Brahman known as Sound is the venerable Hākinī after death. (80.9)
The king of mantras ends with *svāhā*; it is honored by all the gods and is to be worshipped with devotion.
I shall proclaim this great mantra, by which a person becomes accomplished. (80–10)
This is the auspicious mantra of Hākinīśa, the Supreme Lord and Sovereign;
by the mere propitiation of which one becomes a conqueror of death, without a doubt. (80-11)
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the preta, then the seed-syllable of poison,
then the seed-syllable of fire, and immediately after that the seed-syllable of kālakūṭa.
Completely destroy the net of my suffering; tear asunder the pair, namely the peak of desire and the seed of universal dissolution. (80.13)
At the end of that, one should utter the seed-syllable of Śiva, "Haṃsaḥ So'ham," followed by "Svāhā"; O Maheśvara, this mantra, when recited one hundred thousand times, is indeed effective. (80–14)
Having performed retention and exhalation, one should hold the auspicious breath;
having done this, O Mahādeva, one realizes the bliss of Śiva and primordial nature. (80-15)
He remains eternally steadfast even at the time of the great dissolution;
indeed, the supernatural powers (siddhis) always abide in his lotus-like hand.
O Supreme Lord, by reciting two hundred thousand [mantras] with diligence, one attains perfection of speech and the ability to travel to the world of the gods in one's own body. (80.17)
By the mere sight of him, people would become free from disease;
by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eighty thousand times, one becomes a shatterer of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The mind enters that very thousand-spoked [wheel]; of this there is no doubt.
Then it becomes the locus for the destruction, preservation, and creation of saṃsāra. (80.19)

Through the recitation of these two mantras, the entire cycle of existence and even all ten million world-systems shall become as accomplished for the wise one as if they were already achieved. (80.20)
He has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures, the meaning of the Vedas, the meaning of Sāṅkhya, and so forth;
before him, those [deities] certainly shine in personified form. (80.21)
Sometimes, once in a while, he comes to her lotus-like face;
yet the fourfold liberation and the perfections of desire always abide in her heart.
For they shine resplendently; what else can I say?
At the end of the *vala* period, he who is the son of Rāma shall be that very Kṛṣṇa, endowed with glory. (80.23)
At the end of the word *kṛṣṇa*, the name of Rāma should be placed; he shall become the protector of kings and will be very dear to Śrī Rudra, the supreme God of gods. (80.24)

If he stands in the city of Kāma, having reached the further shore of the fourfold Yāmala and knowing the sixty-four Tantras, [he is the master] of the nine islands and the multitudes of continents. (80.25)

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Division," in the *Bhedopakrama*, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Wheels) in the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa* (Section on Accomplished Mantras) of the *Mahātantroddīpana* (Great Tantra Illuminator), in the *Uttaratantra* (Supplemental Tantra) of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. 80.
Now begins the eighty-first chapter.
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Lord of the World, I shall now describe the extraction of mantras at the time of the end."
Listen to the sādhana and worship of Hākinī, the Supreme Lord. (81-1)
At the end of the eighty-third [year], in my eighty-fourth year,
there shall be a great and wonderful worship of Hākinī by the Supreme Lord.
O Maheśvara, hear the sequence of the piercing of the lotus-brows and other [centers], which is not to be disclosed, most secret, the essence of essences, and higher than the highest. (81-3)
For he who knows the sequence for piercing the lotus of the eyebrows between the brows comes before me, liberated while still alive from the ocean of worldly existence. (81.4)
Knowledge of that sequence and its commencement destroys great sins;
it constantly bestows spontaneous perfection and grants the state of eternal bliss. (81.5)
One's wife becomes a mistress of desire, and one will certainly become the lord of Lakṣmī.
Ānandabhairava said:
Now, by what means does one attain the essence of the practice of sovereignty on this earth?
By what means does sovereignty over the circles of disciples arise, or by what does their differentiation occur?
[It is through] the direct knowledge of the sequence of accomplishment and the sequence for piercing the lotus of the brow. (81.7)
"If you have faith and compassion for me, please tell me quickly.
Ānandabhairavī said:
"I shall explain here at length the auspicious *sārasaṅketa* (the essential convention)."
Having heard that which is revealed by the mantra from the lotus-face of the venerable Guru, the yogi certainly becomes fit for yoga; of this there is no doubt. (81-9)
The great radiant light of the ravishing sound shines downward; by means of the fierce binding and surrounding [energies],
at the time of the yoga of gradual piercing.
For by applying effort, one indeed becomes a yogi. || 81-10 ||

Having assumed the bound single-posture (baddha-mekāsana) and having diligently fixed the mind upon the cluster of lotuses at the brow, which is filled with the bliss of the circle of splendor; 81-11.
Having pierced the knot of the vital essence (*sattva*), one whose mind is steadfast shall certainly become firm;
how could there be untimely death for such a person?
He is adorned by the splendor of the abode of the light-making knowledge.
He travels through the sky, presides over the worlds, possesses a steadfast resolve, and moves within the expanse of the arts of love. || 81-12 ||
In the seven openings of the knots, the deities [reside] with joy in seven ways.
Lākinī shines forth for the protection of yogis and for mastery over yogic illusion;
she is the steady illusion, the yogic illusion, and the illusion of time. (81.14)
Devamāyā, Dharmamāyā, and Vimāyā—these seven deities, jewel-colored and bestowers of stainless bliss, reside within the center of the knot. (81-15)
O Mahādeva, the knot of the *sattva* indeed shines at the pinnacle of space;
its division as well occurs initially through the application of a single sequential order. (81–16)
He whose mind, having pierced through the circle of yogis by means of the sequence of subtle winds, proceeds swiftly, is a hero and not a mere mortal. (81.17)
I shall state the names of the knots; listen attentively and take them to heart: Khaginī, Drāviṇī, Dhūmrā, Kaṭhinā, and likewise Karkaṭī. (81–18)
Śyāmalā and Kapilā are established in the form of the seven knots;
having uttered the Khaginī mantra, one should do so by means of the sequence of subtle breaths.
Having also left behind the upper path, one should [employ] the Praṇava, Bhuvaneśānī, and the seed-syllable of Khaginī, along with one hundred and eight [repetitions].
At the end of existence, however, there are both distinctions and non-distinctions, as well as the seed-syllable of space;
having recited the mantra ending with the weapon-syllable, one should become firm in the act of piercing.
O Bhairava, having uttered the Drāviṇī mantra,
one should always recite it one hundred and eight times through the subtle path.
First is the Praṇava, the supreme seed-syllable, the seed of Brahman;
outside of that is the Vāgbhava, the seed of Drāviṇī, which causes the two knots to melt away.

Having meditated again and again upon the great mantra ending with *svāhā* and *tryanta*, and having recited it while gazing at the space between the eyebrows with a subtle vision through the petals of the brows; 81–24.
O Lord, why does one suddenly undergo dissolution due to the affliction of bondage?
I shall proclaim the *dhūmra* mantra by which a man becomes perfected (*siddha*). (81-25)
The Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kamalā, and thereafter the seed-syllable of the Goddess;
at the end of that, the seed-syllable of Dhūmra, followed by the word "O Destroyer of Death" (Mṛtyunāśini).
At the end of the pair of joints, however, the rule is "Astrāya Phaṭ";
thus one should recite this mantra a thousand times, or a hundred, or one hundred and eight times.
Having assumed either the wheel posture (cakrāsana) or the frog posture (bhekāsana),
one should focus on the two-petaled lotus within the space between the eyebrows, which is a beautiful orb.
In the interval there, within the pericarp, the wise one should contemplate the great seat (mahāpīṭha),
having drawn a six-pointed figure with a central dot, situated inside a triangle.
Outside of that, one should contemplate a beautiful, divine lotus with seven layers of petals and a hundred filaments,
possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
In each and every vessel is the station of Mahāmudrā, which is extremely difficult to attain;
having meditated again and again upon the divine station and the station of the retinue. (81.31)
Then, one should meditate upon Hākinīparameśvara in the pericarp;
I shall now declare the mantra of Kaṭhinā, by which one becomes a cutter of knots.
By this very sequence of yoga, one should bring the entire web of scriptures under control:
first the *praṇava*, then *vāgbhava*, *māyā*, *ramā*, and after that, *kāma*. (81.33)
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause the hard knot to be severed with the pair [of mantras];
this is declared to be the great mantra ending in *māyāstrāya phaṭ*. (81-34)
A wise person should daily recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, or a thousand times;
having placed a cushion with a shaven head underneath, he should sit there in the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Having placed the mind upon the lotus of the eyebrows in the delightful Great Seat (mahāpīṭha),
one should [visualize] the seat as a triangle in the center, along with a drop (bindu) and a hexagon.
Outside of that, one should contemplate the form of seven earths; there, in the north of that, one should visualize a red lotus with a hundred petals and four gates.
In each petal, one should meditate upon three filaments in sequence,
which are the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others.
I shall declare the mantra of Karkaṭī, which directly effects the piercing of the earth:
the seed-syllable of Brahmā, the word Māyā, and the word Māyākarkaṭī. (81.39)
"Break the false knot," then "the two" (dvaya), then "Kāmakalā," and finally "Astrāya Phaṭ"—this is known as the most excellent of great mantras. || 81-40 ||
Having meditated one hundred and eight times upon the mantra within the maṇḍala of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), O Great Lord Bhairaveśa, I shall now declare the mantra of Śyāmalā. (81-41)
Listen and propitiate the knowledge that bestows the accomplishment of omniscience;
the wise one should utter the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, three times. (81-42)
At the end of that is a pair of *māyā* syllables, and immediately after that is the *śrī* seed-syllable;
at the end of that is the *śyāmalā* seed-syllable, which pierces firm knots.
At the end of the sound, utter "vīlaṃ nirmalaṃ" and likewise "mā kuru dvayam eva ca," followed by "kāmāstrāya phaṭ"; this is the essence of the mantra that bestows its application.
Seated upon his seat, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times every day;
gradually endowed with accomplishment, he becomes a wise man, silent, and possessed of great virtues.
He shall become a preeminent practitioner and shall take refuge in my body.
O Lord of Bhairava, listen as I proclaim the mantra of Kapilā. (81.46)
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable of Bālā, the most excellent seed-syllable of Kapilā;
[one should command her] to pierce that knot and to cut through the pair.
Afterwards, place the pair "cittaṃ me bhūgṛhe" [in the heart];
then one should utter the seed-syllable of Kapila and the seed-syllable of Māyā. (81.48)
This supreme among the most excellent great mantras ends with "phaṭ" for the weapon of Ramā;
if one should recite it one hundred and eight times, or even a thousand times—
In two months, one shall become a breaker of the seven knots like Bhairava himself.
Thus has been declared the knowledge of the sequence for breaking the knots. (81–50)

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Piercing of the Seven Knots of the Brow-Lotus," in the *Bhrūpadmasaptagranthibheda*, within the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa* (Illumination of the Six Wheels), in the section on Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* (Illumination of the Great Tantra), the *Uttaratantra* (Supplementary Tantra) of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. || 81 ||
Then, the eighty-second chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said: "Now, O beloved, I shall speak; you should always practice this at night."
If you desire the eightfold accomplishment, let the knowledge of the Siddhānta reside in your heart. || 82-1 ||
Guard this with great effort and impart it to a worthy disciple;
do not reveal it to the wicked, to deceivers, or even to your own sons. (82–2)
Having risen early in the morning in a secluded place and performing the morning rites,
the best of practitioners first performs the external bath for the body.
One should have even a single seat made to be well-concealed;
one should employ seats that bear the previously mentioned signs of yoga. (82-4)
In the beginning, there are the glorious Fish, Tortoise, Lotus, Vikaṭa, Kaṭa, Svastika, and Indrāsana [mudrās],
which bestow knowledge of the various Atharva-mantras, liberation, the faces, the uneven and even [meters], the moon, and sovereignty; as well as the Kokā,
Vāk, Tāmracūḍā, Śava, Bhaga, Mṛga, Bhīmā, Ādyā, and Vīrotkaṭā [mudrās].
[The mantras] Krodha, Akṣatraṅga, Siddhāhi, Garuḍa, Mukuṭā, Yoni, and Bheka-thrones. || 82-5 ||
In this context, the seat consists of thirty-four morsels (*kavala*);
it is awakened, free from the fear of bodily decay or death,
and enriched by the word "Great" (*mahaḥ*) if the three aforementioned sacrificial sessions (*satra*) have been declared.
At dawn, at midday, and at night, he whose heart is yoga performs transformations.
Who indeed is capable of [attaining] through sacrifices that lotus-foot of Gaurī— which is heavy with dignity, which burns the great fire of the senses,
which bestows yoga, and whose qualities follow the infinite states of existence— whose tender lotus-foot the wise Savitṛ holds?
Having visualized the Hākinī as having the body of the deity Paranātha, she is worshipped. || 82-7 ||
Having made these the foundations of his seat, the wise man, becoming more steadfast, should perform worship in a solitary place if he desires well-being. (82-8)
The yogi, with a divine conch in his lotus-hand, should resort to yoga;
having assumed the great lotus posture (mahāpadmāsana) at the end of his seat, he should worship with joy. (82–9)
Thus [ends the section on] the time for the practice of yoga; now listen to the worship.
Having first completed the external worship, one should perform the internal worship within the heart. (82.10)
O Lord, O Master, hear in brief the knowledge of the method for practicing yoga, the determination of the meaning of the scriptures, and the definitive explanation of worship. 82-11.
At the conclusion of that, however, the mantra for the procedure of worship should be recited;
through constant practice and yoga, one shall attain the state of liberation while living. || 82-12 ||
O Lord, first is the sipping of water (ācamana), then at its conclusion is the purification of the water;
then follows the purification of the seat and so forth, as well as the meditation on the wheel-maṇḍala.
The tying of the topknot-knot, the construction of the pedestal, the purification of the flower and the bell, and likewise the purification of the conch. || 82-14 ||

The worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhapūjā), meditation in the heart, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) thereafter, the network of ritual placements (nyāsajāla), and then the contemplation of the perfected beings (siddhapuruṣas). || 82-15 ||
Furthermore, there is the meditation of the Ṛṣis, the meditation of Hākinī and the Supreme Goddess;
indeed, this is the consecration of the vital breath (jīva), and after that follows the bestowal of life.
The visualization of Mahāmudrā is performed with the mudrās of invocation and so forth;
having prepared the water for the feet and the arghya offering, one should likewise perform the pair [of offerings]. (82–17)

One should perform the auspicious worship with water for the feet and other offerings, along with the ritual services (upacāras)—either the ten-fold or the five-fold service—using the root mantra. || 82-18 ||
The practitioner should present the eighteen-fold service with great devotion,
or otherwise worship with the sixteen-fold service.
Then, having performed a pair of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), the best of practitioners should recite [the mantra] one thousand times, or one hundred times, accompanied by eight more.
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times or one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind;
having performed the dedication of the recitation, one should practice three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Therefore, one should always recite the salutation, the hymn of praise, and the armor-mantra,
as well as the lineage of the thousand names accompanied by one hundred and eight repetitions.
Having recited this and discerned its divisions, a person shall become a lord of yogis;
through hearing, seeing, knowing, and the chanting of my glories, one attains me. (82.23)
Whatever kind of faith arises, one should resort to that proximity; having performed three hundred thousand recitations, one should offer oblations with a tenth part of that amount. (82.24)
One-tenth of that is the libation (tarpaṇa), one-tenth of that is the consecration (abhiṣeka),
one-tenth of that is the feeding of Brahmins, and likewise the feeding of young girls.
There, one should recite the Kumārī-tantra;
a man should certainly recite the Thousand Names of Kumārī. (82.26)
Then the yogi should perform the family rite (kulakriyā), and he shall become a lord of yoga;
the power of the primordial Śakti shall reside within the circle of his heart-lotus.
Just as my worship is performed in the Mūlādhāra, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and the Maṇipūra, so too is the worship performed in the heart-lotus and the throat-lotus. (82.28)
One should perform that worship with my mantra at the great lotus of the eyebrows;
then, there shall always be satisfaction toward the [first] three and an increase in my affection.
By my mere satisfaction, one shall become a breaker of the knot oneself;
O Śaṅkara, one should perform the triple sipping of water (ācamana) with the root mantra. (82–30)
Likewise, having performed the sipping of water (ācamana) once, the great wise one should then purify the water by reciting the water-seed syllable at the end of the root mantra.
O Śodhānandabhairava and Prāṇabhairavī, [this] is united with a stainless fragment of the moon and fragrant sandalwood. 82-32.
Having purified it with this mantra, one should thoroughly purify the seat;
O Goddess, when the seat is established, you who dwell within the Kūrma-cakra [are present].
"O Parahākini, bestower of success, you must purify my seat. Having thus purified it with the mantra, one should contemplate the wheel-maṇḍala.
Having always meditated upon the exceedingly lofty and great mandala of Yogin Mahāviṣṇu, which pervades the three worlds, one should place one's own seat above it.
Having meditated upon her, one should worship the Goddess within the mandala-circle of the brow-pīṭha.
Now listen, O Bhairava, King of the Earth, to the mantra for binding the topknot. (82–36)
Even those who cause great obstacles flee from him because of this;
he binds the two—the *praṇava* and the crest-lock (*śikhābandha*). (82-37)
*Tāram māyāstrāya phaṭ*—this mantra is difficult even for the wise to obtain.
At the end of the *praṇava*, [one says] "I bind the dwelling-knot; *namaḥ* twice and *ṭhaḥ*. (82-38)
I shall describe the construction of the pedestal; listen attentively.
Within the triangle, the wise one should draw a dot and a hexagon. (82–39)
At its end, having drawn the orb of the earth, then a hundred-petaled lotus,
and four gates, one should perform the consecration with mantras.
One should write upon a broad copper plate with a golden stylus,
or else with a silver pen, or even with thorns from a bilva tree.
Having fashioned the yantra, one should perform the consecration with the Śrītattvamudrā;
the king of yantras consists of the Praṇava and is filled with beautiful lines.
One should purify the family seat (kulapīṭha), which has a form most dear to women;
having recited the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should contemplate it as being red in color.
Having drawn [the maṇḍala] with the essence of white sandalwood, or with red sandalwood,
or even with saffron, one should perform the consecration with this [mantra].
I shall describe the purification of the flower: [the seed-syllable] Praṇava, [and] Bhuvaneśvarī.
"I purify this excellent flower, fragrant and red-pale pink. (82.45)
"White, yellow, blue, and black—the flower, the ocean of fragrance;
I purify the pair, svāhā!"—with this mantra one should perform the purification. (82–46)
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable of sound, nourished by the seed-syllable of space;
Ghaṃ, I purify the bell today—O Hākinī, grant me your boon!
The foremost of practitioners, with single-minded devotion and no other thought, should worship [the goddess] upon the seat;
he should worship the Mistress of the Seat, who is red in color, upon the six-petaled lotus. (82–48)
Kamalā, Sundarī, Ramyā, Mohinī, and Haramekhalā;
Tejorūpā, Śikhāvahni-jvālā, and Kālānaleśvarī. (82.49)
Samayā, Ramaṇī, Bhīmā, Rati, Kāmasarasvatī, Vīṇāvatī, Madhumatī, and likewise Vāmanākaṣiṇī. || 82-50 ||
Īrā, Śuddhātmikā, Bhadrā, Śāntinī, Nirmālyavāsinī, Arundhatī, Sāvitrī, and likewise Kiraṇācchādinī. || 82-51 ||
Svāhā, Svadhā, Viśālākṣī, Madanā, Madanāturā, Bhrānti, Prabhāvatī, Jñānadātrī, and Vijñānadāyinī. || 82-52 ||
Kokilākṣī, Kuraṅgākṣī, Bodhinī, Saptamaṇḍalī, Hiraṇyā, Mandirā, Cetaḥśuddhidā, and likewise Siddhidā. (82–53)
Mandākinī, Bṛhadgaṅgā, Siddhā, Bhogavatī, as well as Taraśminī, Mohā, Triveṇī, and Mūrtadhāriṇī. || 82-54 ||
Gurvī, Taraṅgapūjyā, Vimalā, Tripurā, Parā, Tritārī, Tāriṇī, Bhadrakālikā, and Granthibhedinī. (82–55)
Ratnamālā, Pāpaharā, Pārvatī, Mānasīśvarā, Bhagamālinī, Umā Devī, Devamātā, and Kalāvatī. || 82-56 ||
Pañcānanā, Kālajitvā, Dṛptā, Pañcaśikhā, as well as Madīnī, Raṇamātaṅgī, Khaḍgahastā, and Hasanmukhī. (82.57)
Padmamālā, Kiṅkiṇī, Dharitrī, Vasundharā, and Phālgunī—these five reside upon the seats; they are radiant, resounding, and full of vigor.
Pavitrā, Dhūminī, Dīrghajaṅghā, Vyāghramukhī, as well as Kātarā, Taruṇī, Hakṣā, Hākinī, Indrāvatī, and Jayā. || 82-59 ||
When worshipped in the abode of the hundred-petaled lotus, these [energies] bestow victory.
Having worshipped Parāśakti, one should worship Mantraśakti. (82.60)
Taralā, Cañcalā, Dhātrī, Cāruṇā, Sūryagā, Dayā, Smṛti, Dīkṣā, Dhāraṇākṣā, Daṃśinī, and Bhadrakālikā. || 82-61 ||
Crossing over the six periods of time, encircled by Rudra, and possessing the form of the phonemes—these Yoginīs, the powers of mantra, O Mahādeva, are to be worshipped. (82–62)
I shall now explain meditation upon the heart, for the practitioner is one whose very self is meditation.
Visualize the great seed-syllable, red in color... || 82-63 ||
Having visualized with the mind a most beautiful form, radiant like ten million suns, the yogi should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having meditated again and again on the body being consumed by fire,
one should dry the body with wind and then drench it repeatedly with water.
Having meditated upon the entire body as being born from the ocean of nectar and consisting of divine essence by means of the root mantra, one should thereafter perform the mental worship.
I shall proclaim the network of ritual placements (nyāsajāla) for the benefit of practitioners;
by the power of this network of placements, the practitioner becomes a sovereign among yogis. (82.67)
One shall possess a body that cannot be cut or pierced and will personally become a conqueror of death.
Following that, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sages (*ṛṣi*), the mothers (*mātṛkā*), and the limbs (*aṅga*).
One should perform [the rite] with devotion as before, using both the root mantra and the first syllable.
Sadāśiva is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is indeed the meter (chandas). || 82-69 ||
The deity is the goddess Hākinī, who brings delight to the Supreme Lord;
the deity is the essence of the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, which is both the *kīlaka* and the root mantra. (82–70)
One should always perform the Ṛṣinyāsa on the head, the face, the heart, the knot, the mūlādhāra, and the body; this increases the pleasure of the Ḍākinīs. (72.71)
Oṃ, at the end of the feet and on the head, [one should say] "to Sadāśiva" by means of the word;
having uttered "Salutation to the Seer," one should then speak the word in the mouth. (82.72)
One should say "namas" after "gāyatrīcchandase," and then say "to the goddess Śrīhākinī, the supreme power (paraśakti) in the heart."
One should say "Salutation to the Deity" at the back [of the head], then at the mūlādhāra;
thereafter one should say "Salutation to the seed-syllable *klīṃ*," and then at all the limbs. || 82-74 ||
One should first utter the word "Namo" to the root noble deity;
then, O Mahādeva, one should perform [the rite] for the sake of accomplishing all limbs—listen! (82.75)
Placing his hand upon his heart with the Śrītattvamudrā, the wise one should first install [the seed-syllable] joined with the Bindu, and then he should install it on the right arm.
O Lord, the best of practitioners should place the four castes beginning with *eka* (E), conjoined with the root mantra and endowed with the nasal drop (*bindu*), upon the right hand. (82–77)

Likewise, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) on the left arm with the mantra enclosed; one should perform the placement using the syllables beginning with *ṭha* and ending with *ḍha*, joined with the seed-syllable *biṃ*. 82–78.

The wise one should place [the seed-syllables] on the right foot with the syllables beginning with *na*, *dha*, *bha*, and *nta*, joined with the nasal bindu and encapsulated by his own mantra; thereafter, he should place them on the left foot.
Having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa using the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa' joined with the nasal bindu and encapsulated by the mantra, one should perform the Kara-nyāsa.

O Kuleśvara, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and with the vowels accompanied by the six long vowels; likewise, the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) should be performed according to the prescribed rule.
One should also complete the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa) by means of what was previously described;
thereafter, one should perform the sixfold [placement] for both Dhākinī and the Supreme Deity.
The first locus for ritual placement (nyāsa) is called the Root, located in the position of the Mothers and possessing excellent characteristics;
the second placement consists of the Rudras, while the third is joined with the Planets.
The third [mandala] should consist of the World-Guardians (lokapālas); the fourth by Śiva’s Power (śivaśakti);
the fifth by the Powers and so forth; and the sixth is said to be by the Seats (pīṭhas).
One should place Rudra, encased by the mantra, in the position of the Mothers:
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣmeśa, Trimūrtīśa, and Amareśaka. (82–85)
Arghīśa, Bhārabhūtīśa, and then indeed Atithīśa;
Sthāṇukeśa, Hareśa, Jhiṇṭīśa, and Bhautikeśvara. (82–86)
Sadyojāteśvara is in the west, followed by Anugrāheśvara; then Akrūreśa, Mahāsena, and Sūrāṇāmadhipeśvara. || 82-87 ||
Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntakeśa, Atrīśa as spoken by Śiva, and then Ekarudreśvara. (82–88)
Kūrmeśa, Ekanetreśa, Caturānana, Ajeśa, Sarveśa, and after that Someśa. (82–89)
Lāṅgalīśa, Dārūkeśa, and Ardhanārīśvara;
then Umākānteśvara, and after that Āṣāḍhīśa. (82–90)
Daṇḍīśa, Drīśa, Mīneśa, Megheśa immediately after that,
Lohiteśa, Śikhīśa, and Chāgalaṇḍeśa.
Dviraṇḍeśa, Mahākāleśvara, and Vāṇīśa;
then Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākīśa, and Khaḍgīśa. (82–92)
Bakeśvara and Śveteśa, followed by Bhṛgvīśa;
then Nakulīśa, Śiveśa, and Saṃvartakeśa. (82–93)
There are fifty-one Rudras and others, beginning with Krodha and Bhairava.
First is the root, and then the single syllable of the Mother (Mātṛ) in sequence.
In the midst of the locus of the Mātṛkās, [one should place] the lords beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha;
then the word "namaḥ" ending in the dative case, and then the root mantra again and again.
Thus, O Kulabhairava, the placement of the venerable Kaṇṭha has been told.
Now, listen; I shall explain the placement of the planets according to their true nature.
Then in the heart, in the middle of the eyebrows, and in the three eyes;
then in the heart, in the hollow of the throat, and thereafter in the region of the neck.
One should place the planets at the root of the navel, in the lotus-face, and in the secret place:
the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, and likewise Jupiter.
One should place Venus, Saturn, Rāhu behind him, and Ketu further beyond,
each with their respective mudrās, in the maṇḍala at the locations prescribed by me.
One should worship Sūrya with the vowels; Soma with the letters from *ka* to *śa*;
Kuja with the five letters beginning with *ca*; Budha with the letter *na*; and Guru with the letters from *ṭa* to *śa*. (82–100)
Likewise, one should worship Venus with the letters from ḍa to ha; Saturn with the letters from pa to ma; Rāhu with the letters from śa to ha; and Ketu with the letters from la to kṣa. (82–101)
O Kulabhairava, I shall first describe the placement (nyāsa) of the world-protectors (lokapāla) within the circle of the head, following a clockwise sequence. (82–102)
Always encircled at its base by a lower-limit garland:
Oṃ, salutation to Indra, who holds a spear in his hand and is accompanied by his vehicle. || 82-103 ||
The wise practitioner should also place [the seed-syllable] at the end of the root-mantra using the short fifth vowel;
likewise: "Salutation to Vahni (Fire) joined with the eleventh vowel. (82–104)
Salutations to Yama, who is accompanied by his vehicle, who wields all weapons, who is of such a nature, who is mounted upon his mount, and who bears the trident weapon. || 82-105 ||

With the essences of the five syllables beginning with *ka*, even when encapsulated by the root mantra, [one should place it] on the right ear at the upper part of the head with the hand in the *tattva-mudrā*. (82–106)
Having first performed the Yamanyāsa according to the ritual procedure, one should quickly perform the Nyāsa in the Nairṛtya direction;
at the beginning is the seed-syllable (bīja), and at the end of the five initial seed-syllables is "nairṛtāya."
"Obeisance to Vāsava, the lord, who rides upon all weapons and the like as his vehicle"—this is the visualization for every instance, with the root mantra at the end. (82–108)
Then, for Varuṇa, the root mantra consists of five syllables beginning with *ṭa*, followed by:
"Salutation to him who possesses a vehicle and wields all weapons. (82-109)
At the end of that, one should perform the root mantra for Varuṇa;
at the end of the root mantra, [one offers] the five syllables beginning with *tā* for Vāyu, together with his vehicle.
After that, [one should say] "Salutation to the bearer of all weapons," and thereafter the root mantra;
then one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Kubera, which is most difficult to attain.
First, having uttered the root mantra consisting of five syllables beginning with *pā*, the practitioner [should worship] Kubera, the bearer of all weapons, who is carried by men. (82.112)
One should place the root mantra at the end of the word "namas" upon the left ear;
first the root [mantra], then from 'pa' to 'va', and thereafter for Īśāna.
One should utter "Salutation to the one with his vehicle and the wielder of all weapons";
at the end of that, the placement of the seed-syllables is declared to be the Nyāsa of Īśāna. (82–114)
First, placing the hand above Indra (the letter *i*) while extending it from the root (*śa*) to the end (*ha*),
one then [places it] below for the god Ananta, the wielder of all weapons.
One should recite the heart-mantra together with its vehicle, and the root-mantra within that interval;
first the root-mantra, then one hundred thousand times for Brahmā, who bears the weapons and other attributes.
Having placed the word "heart" along with its vehicle and the root mantra immediately thereafter into the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), one shall attain the knowledge of Brahman. || 82-117 ||
Thus, O Kālabhairava, the placement of the guardians of the directions has been described;
now hear the most wonderful array for the placement of Śiva and Śakti.
By the mere performance of which one becomes a piercer of the six chakras;
first, I shall describe the location where the ritual placement (nyāsa) is to be performed with its own mudrā. (82.119)
Then, in the center of the *mūlādhāra* lotus, in the *svādhiṣṭhāna* lotus, in the great lotus of the *maṇipūra*, and in the circle of the heart-lotus. (82.120)
One should install Śiva, joined with Śakti, in these six lotuses: in the throat, in the lotus of purification (viśuddha), and likewise in the circle of the brow-lotus. 82–121.
First, having uttered the root mantra from *vā* to *sā*, together with "to the Ḍākinīs," and then "Obeisance to Brahmā" (*brahmaṇe namaḥ*), [one should recite] the root mantra thereafter. (82–122)
First, having uttered the root mantra from *ba* to *la*, followed by "to him who is accompanied by Rākiṇī," and then pronouncing "namaḥ to Viṣṇu," one should thereafter recite the root vidyā.
First, having uttered the root mantra followed by the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, together with *lākinī*, and then "to Rudra, obeisance," one should thereafter install the root mantra. (82–124)
First, the foremost of practitioners should perform the placement of the root mantra, from *ka* to *ṭha*, together with Kākinī, saying "Obeisance to Īśvara," as the root. (82–125)

First the root mantra, then the vowels, followed by "to the one accompanied by the Śākinīs" and "to Sadāśiva"; having uttered the word *hṛt* (heart) and the root mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*).

First the root mantra, then *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*, followed by "and to him together with Hākinī," and finally "salutation to Paraśiva"; one should thus properly install the root mantra at the end. (82–127)
Thus has the ritual placement of Śiva and Śakti been explained to you with care;
now I shall describe the ritual placement of Śakti—listen to that.

In the aperture of Brahmā, on the forehead, between the eyebrows, in the cavity of the throat, in the heart, at the base of the navel, at the base of the linga, and at the base of one's own [perineum]. (82–129)
The wise one should likewise place [the syllables] at the base of the thighs, on the pair of shanks,
on the two feet, in the secret place, and on the soles of the pair of feet.
The wise one should arrange them in sequence, encapsulated by the root mantra.
O beloved of life, protector of life, hear now the name of Śakti. (82–131)
Śakti, Māyā, Ramādevī, Bhavānī who is compassionate toward the distressed, Sumanā, Kākinī, Haṃsī, and likewise Saṃsāratāriṇī. || 82-132 ||
Yoginī, Gopikā, Mālā, the one named Vajrā, Citriṇī, as well as Naṭinī, Bhāravī, Durgā, Rati, and Mahiṣamardinī. (82–133)
These eighteen principal Śaktis are for the rite of renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
At the beginning, one should place the root [syllable] and a single vowel, according to the sequence starting from sixteen.

At the end of that, having uttered the Śakti-mantra accompanied by a word in the dative case, the wise one should then utter the word "namaḥ" at its end, and thereafter recite the root mantra. (82–135)
Having placed the seed-syllable at the beginning of the letters from *ka* to *na*,
one should place the root mantra "Ratye namaḥ" upon the pair of thumbs.

First the root mantra ending with the feet and the *kṣānta* [syllable], and immediately after that the *śakti*; [these] in the dative case followed by the root mantra and *namaḥ*—this is declared to be the *śaktinyāsa*. (82–137)
I shall now proclaim the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa); listen attentively.
One should place Kāmarūpa at the mūlādhāra and Kāmākhya at the base of the liṅga.
Kāmarāja is in the triangle, and likewise Jvālandhara is in the heart;
the station of Madhukara is above the heart, and above that is the one called Gaganaka.
On the forehead is the seat named Pūrṇagiri; above that is Uḍḍiyāna;
above that is the Śāṅkarī-pīṭha; and above that is the Rudra-pīṭha.
Above that is the seat of Compassion (karuṇā-pīṭha) and the seat of Beyond-mind (unmanī-pīṭha);
likewise, there is the seat of Obstruction (rodhanī-pīṭha), and above that is the seat of the Bindu (bindu-pīṭha).
Above that is the Jewel Seat (ratnapīṭha), above that the Semen Seat (śukrapīṭhaka), above that the Impression Seat (vāsanāpīṭha), and indeed the Emission Seat (visargapīṭha). || 82-142 ||
Above that is the Brahmapīṭha, and above that is the Kālīpīṭha;
above that is the Tāriṇīpīṭha, and above that is the Ekapīṭha.
Above that, one should place the Jaṭāpīṭha and the Piṅgalāpīṭha,
as well as the great Vārāṇasīpīṭha, in the middle of the eyebrows.
In the midst of the three eyes is the sacred seat of Avanti;
Māyāvatī is on the circumference of the face, and the finest honey is on the tip of the tongue.
In the middle of that is the Rasana-pīṭha; near it is the Daṃṣṭra-pīṭha;
at its front is the Vidyā-pīṭha, and likewise the Yoginī-pīṭha.
In the throat is the seat of the eight cities (aṣṭapurīpīṭha), as well as the triad of Madhupurī;
on the two arms is the seat of enjoyment (bhogapīṭha), and on the pair of sides is the Śrīpīṭha.
In the belly is the Rahnalāpīṭha; in the nivītaka region is the Dharmapīṭha;
on the slope of the hips is the Kāñcīpīṭha; and above that is the Devapīṭha.
Below that, one should place the Śyāmalā-pīṭha; near that, the Gopī-pīṭha; and the Ayodhyā-pīṭha-cakra at the base of the navel. (82–149)
One should duly install the Śmaśāna-pīṭha in the secret place (guhya), the Śiva-pīṭha on the soles of the feet, and the pair of Śītala-pīṭhas upon the two thighs. (82–150)
The city of Raṅkiṇīpīṭha is said to be in the two shanks;
one should place Kṣīrapīṭha on the two breasts and the two Aṅguṣṭhas.
The foremost of practitioners should install the seat of Time (Kālapīṭha) and the seat of Wrath (Krodhapīṭha);
the fifty-one seats [should be installed], and the seat of Sovereignty (Rājyapīṭha) at the tips of the hair.
First the root mantra, then the phoneme, then the name of the location;
after that, the name of the sacred seat (pīṭha) ending in the dative case, followed by the root "namaḥ. (82-153)
Thus, the root of the pīṭha-nyāsa has been explained to you with care;
by the mere performance of this, the yogin shall attain perfection. (82–154)
The long-lived Lord himself is powerful like the sun;
O Maheśānī, those whose bodies are formed by the sixteen-fold [mantra] bow down to him. (82-155)
"He would immediately become short-lived; the deity trembles with fear.
Thus, O Lord, I have explained to you the highly auspicious Ṣoḍhānyāsa.
Thereafter, O Śaṅkara, hear the meditation upon the perfected beings (siddhapuruṣas):
the illustrious Guru Mīnanātha, Āgastya, and Devarājaka. || 82-157 ||
Kālānana, Somarāja, Vīranātha, Dhanañjaya, Kṛṣṇa, Kāntamati, Buddhi, and Dharmāvatāra. || 82-158 ||
Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Śuka, and Prahlāda; Janaka, the lord of the Bhārgavas, and likewise the Lord of Kurukṣetra. || 82-159 ||
Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, Maināka, and Meru; Ananta, Yoganātha, Mahendra, and Madireśvara. || 82-160 ||
Brahmānanda, Śivānanda, and Sanakānanda; Sarveśvara, Kāmadeva, Śukrācārya, and Kuleśvara. || 82-161 ||
Having thus performed the meditation on the perfected beings (siddhapuruṣas), one should visualize the Great Being, a person of red color, adorned with all ornaments. (82.162)
Having meditated [upon this], one should perform the visualization of Hākinī and the Supreme Deity;
first, O Maheśvara, hear the visualization of the illustrious Supreme Deity.
I bow to the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Śiva, who is white in luster, subtler than the subtlest,
the Guru whose body is adorned with every ornament, the essence of the three worlds,
the supreme and stainless, non-dual, possessing ten lotus-palms, the bestower of prosperity, the three-eyed Śiva.
It is worshipped by the lords of the gods, consisting of bliss, and bestowing supreme joy upon the true consciousness.
One should meditate upon the five-faced one, the bestower of great weapons, who is always worshipped by his devotees.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Lord and having worshipped him with intense mental offerings, one should pay homage and then practice the meditation on Hākinī.

She who is worshipped by the festivals of the three worlds, whose arising fulfills the joy of the three realms, adorned with various ornaments, possessing the singular splendor of the seed-syllable shining from her beautiful crown,
dark-complexioned, holding a book and a lotus in her hands as bestowers of liberation, and an ocean of compassion.
On the path, I worship the Sovereign Śrī Hākinī, adorned with a circle of splendor. 82-167 ||
The meditation on her seven families must indeed be explained later;
but now, O Bhairava, listen to the teaching on the Mahāmudrā.
The *yonimudrā* and the *mahāmudrā* are concealed in all tantras; by means of them, the practitioner, with an unwavering mind, should perform the invocation. (82.169)
Having placed two *arghya* offerings according to the sequence of the previous wheel,
Sadāśiva, having meditated again, should offer them at their lotus feet.
Then the wise one should worship with the sixteen materials of ritual service (upacāra).
I shall now describe the meditation on the Ṛṣi, whom one should place upon the head.
The embodied Lord Sadāśiva, adorned with various ornaments, two-armed, clad in yellow garments, and the revealer of dharma and adharma. || 82-172 ||

O Lord, having visualized [the deity] as peaceful, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, situated upon the head of Hākinī, one should worship him there with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

I shall describe the consecration of the living being (*jīva-saṃskāra*) by which the stability of the living being is achieved; [this is done] in one's own heart and on the right hand according to the sequence of mudrās. (82–174)
Having repeatedly recited the mantra of Hākinī, the Supreme Deity, I establish my own mind together with Hākinī and all prosperity. (82-175)
"Be firm, O Great Life-force; fulfill my command! Having recited this mantra ending with *svāhā*, one should then consecrate the life-force (*jīva*). || 82-176 ||
Therefore, I shall describe the bestowal of life for Hākinī and the Supreme Goddess;
first, O Lord, hear the bestowal of life for the venerable goddess Hākinī.

Having uttered the seed-syllables *āṃ hrīṃ krā* [and so forth], one should perform the placement of the life-force (*jīva*) as before, and recite [the mantra] twenty-one times into the heart of Hākinī. (82–178)
The consecration of the vital breath (jīvasaṃskāra) is declared to be performed even with a mantra ending in "svāhā.
Thus has the bestowing of life-breath upon the illustrious Supreme Deity been described. (82–179)
I shall speak again of meditation; listen, O Bhairava, beloved one!
By meditating upon which Hari himself became the destroyer of all knots. (82.180)
O Lord of auspicious belly, listen to the pair concerning the presentation of the *arghya* offering.
I bow to Hākinī, whose splendor is as radiant as the Vedāṅgas, who shines with a mind solely devoted to the bliss of the Three-eyed Lord,
who possesses beauty, sweet speech, and a multitude of enchanting powers, who is the auspicious and noble-faced one,
and who holds a great sword as bright as a stainless lotus upon the forehead of a Caṇḍāla.
I worship her who incessantly invokes the excellent Chāyāputras, the dispellers of fear.
Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Śrīṃ! [I bow to] the Lord of Bhairava, the personification of bliss, who shines with the brilliance of ten million lamps;
who is adorned with ten million ornaments, who grants boons to the three worlds, and is clothed in a tiger-skin garment;
and who is eternally worshipped by the lords of yogis, the foremost of practitioners, and the most excellent of youthful gods.
The five-faced one, whose moon-like arms radiate light, the supreme crest-jewel of yogis.
I meditate upon Śaṅkara, the most beloved refuge, who rests in Māyā;
whose body has the luster of a silver mountain, whose face is that of a corpse, and whose lotus-face is like the void-moon;
who possesses the rays of six hundred suns and moons in his six locations, and who is the supreme being with three radiant eyes.
I worship the Lord of the Kula and the Kalās, who bestows the state known as Nirvāṇa, upon the petal of the eyebrows.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess Hākinī, the glorious Supreme Lord,
who is eternal, self-arisen, and resounds with the bells and hand-drums of the lords of serpents.
He whose lotus-like hands are worshipped by those of great body, who wears five topknots, whose face possesses extreme beauty, and who is adorned with necklaces of lordly serpents. 82-186.
Consisting of great splendor, with a radiance flashing like the luster of ten million moons,
his lotus feet have the form of swans and anklets that produce a gurgling sound.
[He beheld] the Lord of Yogins, the Supreme Lord Hākinī, seated upon a bull-throne, illuminating with the lightning-like splendor of the beauty of his consort, the beautiful Hākinī. || 82-188 ||

To her who is the wave of supreme beauty, whose very nature is the power of yoga (yogamāyā), who is known as the embodiment of the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu), and who deludes the entire universe with her own radiance. || 82-189 ||
With a form resembling a mountain of silver, possessing variegated coral creepers, with disheveled hair like a mass of clouds, how much of the silver mountain remains to be covered? 82-190.
She has three eyes consisting of the sun, moon, and fire, with millions of moving bees [as her eyebrows];
she has six faces, holds the Vedas in her hands, and possesses a luster equal to that of rubies.
She wears a garland lovely as rubies, is exceedingly dear to her cause, and—though terrifying with skull and sword—is for the benefit of practitioners. (82.192)
She who bestows all auspicious fortune, who is eternal, who holds a hand-drum and a rosary,
and who is the Great Vidyā, the witness to the arising of bliss.
Within the pericarp of the lotus of the eyebrows, in the lotus whose petals have vanished,
she dwells, destroying all forms of beauty and being beloved by Kākinī and Sākinī.
I worship her who is to be meditated upon by Lākinī and Rākiṇī, who is honored by Ḍākinīs, and who is the mother of the Kuṇḍalinī, upon the surface of the earth.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the pair [of rites] in sequence using the essence of the *arghya*;
having first drawn two triangular mandalas with a finger's breadth in front.
Then, one should fill [the vessel] with perfumes such as *tīrtha*, *vāhana*, and *kāla*; likewise, at the beginning of that, one should fill the sword-receptacle and the conch with *phaṭ* syllables.
One should wash with this mantra; listen, O Kulabhairava: "Oṃ! You, the conch, reside within the conch; you are meritorious and the most auspicious of all auspicious things. (82-198)
"Supported eternally by Viṣṇu, be the bestower of peace upon me.
Om, I purify the base of the conch with its radiant tortoise-form. (82.199)
I place the Visarga within the Bindu and the Aham within the Triangle;
one should recite the mantra ten times while performing the Dhenu-mudrā and the Matsya-mudrā.
First, one should sprinkle oneself, and then sprinkle the ritual materials and so forth;
O Lord of Gods, God of Gods, Great Lord, this is the sequence.
Placing two *arghya* offerings before him, the illustrious Kaulika practitioner should perform worship with special care, especially during the remainder of the night. (82–202)
One should practice the vision of Mahāmudrā even now; for the practitioner who is endowed with the proper cause will certainly attain accomplishment. (82.203)
The Mahāmudrā is described in all tantras as the Yonimudrā;
O Great God, he who knows this is a yogin—of this there is no doubt. (82.204)
One should perform the great worship as proclaimed by me, O God of gods;
for one who is united with meditation, that worship alone is fruitful on this earth.
With a concentrated mind, one should always perform worship just like the worship of Kālī;
and that [worship] should be performed having gone to a sacred place or even to a city of the Gandharvas.
On a mountain, or in a desolate place, or in an empty house, or in a cremation ground,
one should worship Hākinī, the Great Vidyā who is the Cow of Plenty.

I shall proclaim the mantra for the water for the feet: O Great Goddess, it consists of the Praṇava, Ratisundarī, and the seed-syllable of Ramā; at the end of that is the excellent water for the feet.
"Seize, seize the scent-arisen for Hākinī! HŪṂ DVIṬHAḤ, O Lord!
In this manner it should be done everywhere; one should perform it according to the distinction of names. || 82-209 ||
O Bhairava, one should cause all the ritual substances to be offered under various names:
the seat, welcome, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
The honey-mixture, water for sipping, bathing materials, garments, and ornaments;
likewise, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and salutation. || 82-211 ||
The offering of water for drinking, followed by the offering of the bali-oblation,
and the eighteen modes of service (upacāra) are secrets concealed in all the Tantras.
The practitioner, pure and fearless, should perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) and especially perform the recitation (japa) according to the sequence of the Great Rosary (mahāmālā).
O Lord Bhairava, Master of men, hear another [mantra]:
the Praṇava, then the King of the Pretas, and the seed-syllable of Fire following that. (82.214)
We meditate upon Hālāhala Mahākāla, the Supreme Lord; [the mantra consists of] the seed-syllable of Kāma and Hākinī, formed with words ending in the dative case. (82-215)
Therefore, the wise man should mutter the great mantra "So 'haṃ haṃsaḥ svāhā.
Through one hundred thousand recitations, success shall be attained; the ignorant shall become possessed of knowledge.
One who was unaccomplished shall become accomplished in form; his fame and renown increase.
He becomes a great orator, a knower of all scriptures, and a possessor of the siddhi of omniscience. (82.217)

The perfection of speech, the eightfold accomplishment, and its manifestations shine in the hand of one who becomes immortal through the performance of the preliminary ritual (*puraścaryā*) according to the method of the pairs of ages. 82–218.
The yogi shall become one who abides in dissolution, whose self is meditation, who possesses knowledge, and is pure;
having become one whose qualities are unmanifest, he shall become the Lord of the Kings of Kings.
You are the guardian of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign, may success be mine through your grace.
Having thus offered it into his hand while visualizing it as gold, he should then recite the mantra three times, accompanied by breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 82-221 ||
I shall now describe the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial oblation (balidāna); listen, O venerable Kulapaṇḍita!
First, there is the root-oblation (mūlabali), the Siddhabali, accompanied by nectar and meat. (82.222)
It is stamped with the fish-seal (mīnamudrā), or else it consists of a sweet and excellent offering;
likewise, there is a pair of "take" (gṛhṇa) mantras, and then a pair of "cause to take" (gṛhṇāpaya) mantras, followed by the word *dviṭha*.
The best of practitioners should cause [the offering] to be given with devotion for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of desires;
thereafter, the wise one should recite the hymn of praise, distinguished by prose, verse, and so forth.
And one should recite the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) esteemed by Brahmā for the protection of the body,
or one should recite the lineage of the thousand names with the *hara-mudrā*.
O Lord, one should establish the Supreme Lord in his own place by means of Hākinī.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Worship of Hākinī and Paraśiva," in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, within the *Siddhamantraprakaraṇa* of the *Mahātantroddīpana*, in the *Uttaratantra* of the *Śrīrudrayāmala*. 82.
Now begins the eighty-third chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairava said:
"O lady of excellent hips, tell me the supreme hymn of praise to Hākinī."
By the recitation of which one becomes eloquent; O Compassionate One, full of mercy! (83-1)
Śrī Ānandabhairavī said:
O Lord, hear this most wonderful and excellent hymn, the primordial secret meditated upon by all the lords;
it is recited by those very perfected masters (*siddhas*), the lords of the circle of practitioners, who are highly learned in the Dharma. (83–2)

I praise the perfected one known as Hākinī, the consort of Śambhu, who is called Brahmā, the science of desire, the mother of Narasiṃha, whose nature is the peak-syllable of desire, the triple-wedded wife who pacifies Madana, and the deliverer;
she who is the science that delights Heramba, the subduer of the three-fold Sama, the long-haired one with three eyes.
In the midst of a grove of Mandāra trees, she shines with the laughter of her blossoming lotus-face. || 83-3 ||

He constantly praises her who is adorned with golden ornaments, who has three eyes, who wears silken garments, who is exceedingly lustrous, pure, the best among noble women, moon-faced, the giver of fortune, compassionate toward the world, and ever-youthful in spirit.
With a body like the white luster of the confluence of three rivers, she has two eyebrows like a pair of lotus petals.
O Hākinī, you who dwell joyfully in that place made delightful by the abundance of the great lotus forest, and who have arrived from the Dharmakuru region—I praise you with delight. (83-5)

I bow to the most beautiful Śrī Hākinī, the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra; she whose mind is uplifted by the longing for love for Narahari; she who is the sole abode for the relinquishing of the undertaking of worldly existence; she who is Māyā; she who dwells upon a lion-seat of many millions of radiant jewels; and she who bestows the power of attraction.
I praise her who is intent upon the inspection of sacred fields, and who is cherished by the illustrious Goddess of Speech.
She suddenly spreads the glory of refined activity before the beloved of Śrī Pārvatī;
she is the wealth that is the cause of the great knowledge arising from the sight of various collections of jewels.
She is the manifest sovereign of all, radiant with the singular drop of the bliss of Supreme Śiva.
May she who acts for my welfare protect me first; I praise her within the sacred seat. 83.7
Abiding in the Linga of the Sky of Consciousness, united with the path of persistence, she shines as the one with blood-red plumage.
May that Kālī protect me, O Mother— she who arises from the path of the Kula, who brings about both wrath and its cessation,
and whose garland of bees is the devotion of the three worlds to her glorious lotus feet.
I praise that Vidyā, which is joined with the two petals of infinite purity and is worthy of worship by all Indras. 83-8.
Having honored Your beloved pair of feet, complete with all their limbs— the two soles which possess the excellence of two lotus petals, adorned with anklets and wondrous necklaces—
I offer my praise; for by meditating upon them, the Lord Hari, the possessor of all virtues and conqueror of the great demon Mura, [attains victory] in an instant.
He is the sole abode for the relinquishing of fetters and bonds, and the protector of the three worlds.

O you who are the very essence of movement, who dwell in vows, whose face is like the moon, and who delight in the flesh of goats and other animals—protect me alone! I praise you, the all-pervading Śivā of singular form, who are beloved by Indra’s prostrations, and who bestow the sole cause of bliss accompanied by liberation through speech. (83–10)

I bow to the Supreme Excellence, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the Sovereign of the Beyond, who humbles the pride of the King of Mountains with his form; who is the deep cavern containing the seed of the cremation ground;
who is adorned with gold and jewels, and possesses the splendor of a hundred moons.
Again, he beheld his own body as auspicious, a maker of light through the radiance of another.
To the one worthy of praise, the most excellent, the bringer of great desire and fortune;
the Great God of gods, born from the beginning of the three times;
whose limbs are anointed with the fierce ashes of the cremation ground.
I always praise the impregnation, which is the essence of saṃsāra. || 83-12 ||
Every day at night, I suddenly bow my mind to Paraśiva, the primordial one, who is accompanied by her whose face is like the moon and who possesses the splendor of a hundred moons.
It is the means for accomplishing worship and the bestower of the fruit of the true result. || 83-13 ||
The lotus feet of Paraśiva, served by the power Hākinī,
which bestow happiness upon the three worlds, manifest through meditation alone,
and bear the splendor of exceedingly beautiful lotus-hands.
On this earth, I praise the essence of my own lineage, which is accessible only to the lords of yogis.
He indeed brings about the cessation of the desire for life and body, which is the play of the series of sorrows;
he is the Lord of the Hākinī, the bringer of peace from worldly existence, and the wearer of a diamond garland.
He is that very one who fashions the eternal bud of the lamp of the mind within the essence of the lotus of the eyebrows.
I praise his glorious lotus-feet, which are honored by the multitude of their virtues, upon my forehead.
The sole dwelling place whose abode is the peak of Mount Meru, served by Goloka,
frequented by those who delight in sacrifice, the supreme essence that is the ground of the minds of the lords of yogis;
undisturbed by the drinking of wine, it is the chewing of the fragrance of the sacrificial offering equal to that of a beast.
I bow to the cause of the universe, who is worshipped by the most excellent among the great Bhairavas, such as Nandi and others.
You are the Lord of Kapila through the illusory power of the path of Māyā;
You are the sole wheel, the Lord of the Earth who assumes the form of the Lord of the Waters; and You are the manifestation of the sky within all things, taking the nature of fire.
I take refuge in the shelter that dwells in the wind and faces the new moon. || 83-17 ||
Seated upon a golden lion-throne at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree of desire,
devoted to the sport of love with the illustrious Hākinī, manifesting the play of passion,
he who brings about the destruction of illusion and delusion and possesses supreme bliss, dwells upon the peak of the Vindhya mountain.
I salute the Lord, the supreme Śiva who is Hara, the illuminator of the network of forms.
Whoever recites this for the sake of the hymn becomes happy and proficient in yoga;
there is the destruction of hunger and thirst, and the attainment of learning, retention, fame, and the essence of the nectar of residence [in the divine].
That lord of yogis, within a month, brings about the state of supreme bliss.
Enveloped [by that], he produces within the one called Prāṇa a nectarine essence as sweet as the ocean of nectar.
The wise man should recite this hymn, accompanied by meditation and ritual placement (nyāsa),
while visualizing [the deity] as white, red, yellow, blue, and black.
By reciting this constantly throughout the four periods of the day, one shall attain perfection.
O Lord, even if there be tens of millions of obstacles in the sky, on the earth, or in the netherworld; || 83-21 ||
For yogis, [these obstacles] perish here at that very moment simply by reciting this;
he shall become one who goes everywhere, as a result of the arising of supreme fortune. (83.22)
This hymn, which removes great sins, originates from the heart of Hākinī;
it is dear to Sadāśiva, bestows the perfection of yoga, and is served by the gods. (83-23)
By reciting it one thousand times, one obtains the fruit of *puraścaryā*.
Having recited this king of hymns in a cremation ground or in a secluded forest, [one attains the goal]. (83-24)
Or else, O Lord, he shall become a great immortal yogi in the intermediate space;
by reciting this, one becomes eloquent, possessed of knowledge, and a conqueror of the senses. (83.25)
One whose nature is meditation shall quickly come into being together with a host of attendants—at dawn, at night, at midday, or at any other time. (83.26)
The best of practitioners, whose very self is devotion, should recite this essence of hymns;
he will certainly become steady in the lotus of the eyebrows without effort. (83-27)
He who, having meditated upon the lotus feet of the glorious Guru as the determination of meditation within his heart, recites this hymn, shall become a wish-fulfilling tree.
Now, O Lord, I shall speak of the armor (kavaca) within this chapter.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Hymn to Paranātha Hākinī," in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, within the Section on Accomplished Mantras, in the *Mahātantroddīpana*, the latter part of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*. 83.
Now begins the eighty-fourth chapter.
Śrī Ānandabhairava said:
"O Ānandabhairavī, O beloved of my life-breath, I shall now first speak."
This is the armor of the goddess Hākinī, which increases supreme bliss.
O Ānanda, abiding in the ocean of compassion, quickly compose for me, out of faith and with reason, this essential and auspicious armor.
The illustrious Ānandabhairavī said:
First listen, O great hero, O ocean of supreme bliss, to the armor (*kavaca*) of the goddess Hākinī, which delivers one from the ocean of worldly existence. (84-3)
By the mere remembrance of whom the yogi becomes firm in yoga—[those who dwell] in the intermediate space, on the earth, and in the netherworld, whether moving or stationary. || 84-4 ||

Through the mere sound of the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), even *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas* become paralyzed and trembling upon hearing the recitation of the *Vidyā*, the command (*ājñā*), and so forth. (84–85)
Afflicted by fear, they indeed flee due to the power of Kālarudra, just as a living being certainly cannot remain steady in the midst of a fire. (84.6)

Oṃ. Of this great armor (*mahākavaca*) of the auspiciousness of the essential joy of the Goddess Śrī Hākinī: Sadāśiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), the supreme deity Śrī Hākinī is the divinity (*devatā*), *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and Siddhalakṣmī is the root-pin (*mūlakīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation for the sake of attaining the great desire residing within the body.
Oṃ, may [it] protect my head-wheel; klīṃ, may it protect the orb of my forehead;
may my own root-mantra protect my three eyes eternally. || 84-6 ||
May the beautiful Vāgbhavādyā always protect the pair of cheeks;
may Śrīṃ Hrīṃ protect the pair of ears, O Hākinī, the supreme deity. || 84-7 ||
May the Great Vidyā always protect the cavity of my lips;
may the supreme sovereign Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Svāhā protect the two rows of my teeth. || 84-9 ||
Klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hākinīdevī svāhā—may she protect the one who delights in nectar. May the power Madhu, the bestower of desired boons, constantly protect the corners of the mouth. || 84-10 ||
Svāhā, the power of the crest, may she protect [me]; may she always protect the space between the eyebrows.
Hākinī, the supreme sovereign of the lords of others, may she protect the mandala. || 84-11 ||
May Sundarī always protect [me]; may Kāmasundarī protect my two eyelids; and may she known as Amṛtā always protect the region where my eyebrows shine. || 84-12 ||
May the flame of fire always protect the cremation ground between my eyebrows;
may Surabhi protect the illusory weapon (māyāstra), and Svāhā protect the eyelid situated upon my brow. || 84-13 ||
May Kāmākhyā protect the triangle; may the supreme goddess Hākinī protect it; and may Tripurasundarī always protect my hexagon. || 84-14 ||
May Hiṅgulādeśvarī protect the circle of the six-cornered bindu;
may she who illuminates the interior of the earth protect the reflection of the seven worlds unto the end of the earth.

May she who possesses a hundred great petals protect me; may she who is dear to the Lord of a Hundred Peaks protect me; may my speech, consisting of the weighty Vidyā, protect me as it moves with intoxicated grace. || 84-16 ||
May the Supreme Goddess protect my entire circle of four gates;
may she, the destroyer of my extreme suffering, ever protect the circle of my mind.

May Durgā, who consists of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), who delivers one across the ocean of time, and who effects creation, preservation, and destruction, protect my very orb of the moon. || 84-18 ||
May Hākinī, whose form is that of a Great Being and who consists of the colors of my mandala, protect me; may Tārā, the Queen of the Gods, who bears the crescent moon, protect me.
May she who dwells in the fire-pit protect Unmanīnagara;
may Madirā, the destroyer of poison, constantly protect my forehead.
May Dharmadā, the giver of knowledge, protect my state of dharma and wisdom;
may Tālapatnīśvarī, who brings the bliss of immortality, protect me. || 84-21 ||
May Mahābalā, the collection of dispassion, protect the station of the Bindu;
may the Triple Star, the Peak Power (Kūṭaśakti), always protect my Viśuddha [cakra]. || 84-22 ||
May the Lord of Śākinīs protect me always; may Kulabhairavī protect me;
may Saptadvīpeśvarī protect my sixteenth lotus. || 84-23 ||
May Śākinī, Bhairavī, Caṇḍadurgā, Sarasvatī, Kumārī, Kulajā, and Lakṣmī always protect me for the sake of my spiritual success. || 84-24 ||
May the Supreme Goddess Śākinī protect my heart forever;
may the Goddess, who is the form of the seed-syllable and the slayer of the great Mahiṣa, always protect me.
May Umā, the Great Goddess, together with ten million Yoginīs, constantly protect my belly; may Pracaṇḍā protect my back. || 84-26 ||
May Cāmuṇḍā, Bhairavī, and Bālā always protect the pair of sides;
may Paramā and Īśvarī, the Mother of the Gods, protect the two breasts.
May the goddess Saubhāgyahākinī protect the beloved of the Yakṣa;
may the primordial goddess, in the form of the crest, always protect the pair of arms.
May the auspicious Kāmavidyā, who removes all my transgressions, who consists of ten syllables, and whose abode is Maṇipūra, protect me always. (84.29)
May Lākinī, who dwells in the lotus, always protect the navel-cakra;
may Pārvatī, the guardian of the Vedas, protect the eternal region of the petals. || 84-30 ||
May Mahārudreśvarī protect my jewel in the form of the sacred seat;
may Rudrāṇī, the wielder of the trident, protect the circle of splendor.
May Abhayā always protect [me]; may Yogavidyā protect my hips;
may Śaila protect the foundational wheel (ādhāracakra) of my hips; and may Nitambinī protect [it]. || 84.32 ||
May Hākinīśā, the youthful Vaiṣṇavī residing within the network of mantras at the Liṅgamaṇḍala, always protect my Mahāviṣṇusthala. || 84-33 ||
May Vaiṣṇavī, Lalitā, Māyā, and Goddess Ramā protect my hips; may Sarasvatī, in her secret form, always protect my Svādhiṣṭhāna.
May Bhavānī, the consort of the Blessed One; Śmaśānakālikā, the anus;
Raṇamātaṅgī; and Rākinī, the circle of the Kula—protect me. (84.35)
May Jñānakuṇḍalī, whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, always protect my mūlādhāra; may she protect my four-petaled [cakra], which possesses four colors. || 84-36 ||
May Tapasvinī always protect; may Pāvanī guard the root.
May Ratikā, Ghaṭikā, Veśyā, Dhariṇī, and Kāmasundarī [protect me]. || 84.37 ||
May Vahnikāntā always protect my pair of thighs;
may Ulkāmukhī, the Siddhā of the field, always protect my pair of shanks.
May Śrī Kulabhairavī, the bestower of prosperity, protect Bālāmukhī;
may Parahākinī protect both her lotus feet and all her limbs.
Madanā, Medinī, Dhanyā, Cāmuṇḍā, Muṇḍamālinī, Ramā, Kāmakalā, Jyeṣṭhā, as well as Ājñā and Ratisundarī. || 84-40 ||
May Manoyogā always protect [me], as well as Nirmalā, Vimalā, Amalā, Kāñcanī, Bagalā, Rātri, Pañcamī, and Ratisundarī. || 84.41 ||

May she who is tender with love for Yoga protect [us] everywhere and at all times—on the mountain, in the forest, in the desolate place, in the most terrible battle, and in worldly existence. || 84-42 ||
May she who dwells in the cremation ground protect [us], she who is borne by all vehicles;
may the fifth goddess, who loves the fifth, protect us, she who wields all weapons. || 84-43 ||
May Hākinī, the deity of the body, who has four arms, whose face is like ten thousand times ten million moons, and who is the Supreme Sovereign, protect me always.
May she, together with the yoginīs, always protect [me] in every land at all times;
