Ākaṣīṇī, Stambhinī, Trijaṭā, Rukmamālinī, Saptikā, Sukalā, Gīryā, Gabhīrā, and Muṣalāvatī. (88.21)
Bṛhannitambā, Mohākṣī, Mandirā, Candrikā, Siddhā, Vidyādharā, Hārā, Rati, and Kaiśoradharmiṇī. || 88-22 ||
Taptā, Śānti, Bhadradā, Vikārī, Mañcavāsinī, Mahāvidyā, Bhavānī, and Tāra, who is the very nature of Brahman. || 88-23 ||
Mātaṅgī, Bagalā, Kṛṣṇā, Śivā, Haimavatīśvarā, the auspicious Kālī who removes all calamities, and Kandarpavanitā. (88-24)

The sovereign lady of Vārāṇasī, the youthful maiden, the lotus-like one with a beautiful smile, the unborn, the daughter of the snow-mountain, the consort of Śarva, and she who moves through the lineage. || 88-25 ||
The ascetic princess Umā-Pārvatī is stainless;
she is the foundational support, Sāvitrī, that which is expressible and inexpressible, and the totality of the moving and the unmoving. (88.26)
Kalkyeśī, Śaśivadanā, Nivikalpasupakṣaṇī, Bhuvaneśī, Sundarī, Satī, Siddhipradā, and Kalā. (88.27)
Kṛpaṇā, Padmavadanā, Śabdeśī, Bhagamālinī, Ārādhitā, Śokaharā, Harā, and Hīrakamālinī. || 88-28 ||
She who destroys the poison Hālāhala, the necklace, the delight, the extinguisher of the fire of time (Kālānala), Bhairavī, the mother of heroes, the highly fortunate Umā. 88-29.
Sulabhā, Durgamātā, Sugandhā, Gandhamālinī, Amāvāsyā, Sitā, Bhadrā, Cāruṇī, and Sūryaputriṇī. || 88-30 ||
Bestower of gifts, giver of wealth, bestower of success, bestower of enjoyments;
Ilāvatī, Ratnamālā, she who dwells in the union with the mind. || 88-31 ||
The wise one is the Root Mother, whose nature is that of the Root Mantra;
having visualized these [deities] in the four directions in due order. (88-32)
Having meditated upon her entire radiant form, which destroys the garland of light and possesses a wave of extreme beauty within the grove of *pārijāta* trees, (88-33).
In the center of the great maṇḍala, which is adorned with a continuous stream of jewels, one should visualize Mahākāla as the planet, possessing four gates. (88.34)
Adorned with four archways fashioned from ten million jewels,
and above the pavilion, a great white moonlight.
Beautiful and radiant as a hundred suns, adorned with strings of pearls, and likewise charming with a canopy-marked ceiling in the center of the pavilion. (88-36)
Beneath that is a radiant parasol fashioned of gold and adorned with jewels;
beneath that, O lion-eyed one, is the supreme lion-throne.
Above that, the seed-syllable of the preta is known to resemble the form of a preta;
having meditated upon a golden mandala above the preta-form, [one should proceed]. (88-38)
The great seat is triangular, possessing great luster within the pericarp;
it is a white lotus of great beauty, adorned with sixteen petals. || 88-39 ||
One should contemplate the form of lightning, joined with the sixteen vowels and colored streaks upon the hair, arranged in a clockwise direction. (88-40)
Thereafter, one should contemplate the three four-cornered [enclosures] with four beautiful gates; therein, one should visualize the Goddess Vāruṇī, whose form is intoxicated.
One should always meditate upon Tārā, who has the form of Parāmbā and resembles the rising sun, as well as the mandala of the gods at the four gates. (88-42)
One should contemplate Indra at the eastern gate as a lovely deity with a luster like sapphire, accompanied by his vehicle and his retinue. (88.43)
Likewise, having meditated upon the fire-maṇḍala facing all directions in the south-eastern corner,
accompanied by its retinue, one should likewise visualize the world of Yama in the south.
Then one should meditate upon Yama, who is dark-complexioned, exceedingly handsome, accompanied by his retinue, together with his vehicle, and situated in the city of the Rākṣasas in the southwest.
To the north of that, one should always meditate upon Varuṇa, who has a ram as his vehicle;
one should contemplate him there as white, radiant, and accompanied by his retinue.
To the north of that, one should meditate upon Marulloka, who has a black antelope as his vehicle and is accompanied by his retinue; thereafter, one should contemplate him to the east of that.
At the northern gate is Kubera, accompanied by his retinue, together with his vehicle, Kutsita, and adorned with all kinds of jewels. || 88-48 ||
In the northeast, one should worship the Supreme Lord, the Ruler of the World, together with his retinue of attendants, along with his vehicle, and honored by all the worlds. (88.49)
Having meditated upon him accompanied by his retinue and provided with various musical instruments, as well as thousands of millions of kettledrums, trumpets, and *dhudhurīs*, [88-50]
One should contemplate the eastern world filled with the joy of singing and the fragrance of the Dundubhi flower, abounding in various beautiful musical instruments. (88–51)
The realm of Yama, situated in the southwest, resounds with the music of thousands of millions of flutes, lutes, and drums, and is endowed with tens of millions of mantras.
The great world of Jaleśvara was filled with tens of millions of sounds from cymbals, bronze gongs, and drums, and was enchanted by the resonance of kettledrums.

There, one should contemplate the delightful sound resounding from the bodies of those whose limbs are struck by the *jharjharī* and *parpaṭī*, which has enchanted [the world] with a succession of sounds from ten million mechanical instruments. 88.54.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the world of the gods and the abode of Kubera,
which is enchanted by the sounds of musical instruments such as the dundubhi, śreṇī, and ḍhakkā drums.
One should then contemplate the form, mantra, passion, rhythm, dance, and song, as well as the lovely city of the Gandharvas, which bears a series of radiant lights. (88.56)
The wise man should contemplate everywhere in the city that connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, who is surrounded by Apsarases, who delights in song, and who is the source of all auspiciousness. (88.57)
May the splendor residing in all worlds, the splendor that utterly deludes all, come together from everywhere for the god, the sage, and the singer of the yantra. 88-58.
One who plays a musical instrument should likewise contemplate the supreme enclosure;
within it is the maṇḍala of Brahmā’s consort, accompanied by all the singers. (88–59)
Having thus meditated upon the self-singing jewel of the words of all-knowing divine sages according to this procedure, one should contemplate one's own seat.
Having quickly contemplated the power of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) and the lord of the seat as well, one should become immersed in bliss; before long, one shall attain perfection.
One should meditate on the seat of Vārāṇasī below; hear now its sequence.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Rootless Abode of the Supreme Power," in the Dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, within the Illumination of the Great Tantra, the Section on Accomplished Mantras, in the Revelation of the Six Chakras, in the Śrī Rudrayāmala, the Northern Tantra. 88.
Then, the eighty-ninth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"O Mahādeva, you who are the form of Time, O lover of the wine of Kālakūṭa!"
Now listen, O Lord of Gods, to the beloved place of Vārāṇasī. || 89-1 ||
A yogi who desires his own welfare should always meditate upon that mandala of a hundred million yoginīs, which is frequented by yogis. (89-2)

One should contemplate that which shines constantly between the eyebrows, beautified by the form of a circle, having the nature of the *mātṛkā* machine, and containing the essence of all things. (89-3)
A place enriched with ten million self-manifested liṅgas, where the fruit of ten million merits arises, a region that bestows supreme siddhi, and a station dear to the Lord of the Doctrine. (89–4)
Endowed with tens of millions upon tens of millions of pure lotuses,
it is full above the trident, shaped like an umbrella and resembling a fruit.
The Lord Śiva, the Master of Yoga, is preeminent among the ten million liṅgas;
he possesses a body of one hundred and eight blisses and is the destroyer of Manmatha. (89–6)

He is perfected, displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a hand-drum and an umbrella, and adorned with weapons such as the trident and mallet, as well as a shield and other implements. (89–7)
Having meditated upon Śambhu as having five faces, ten arms, and holding a rosary and a skull-cup, one should then contemplate him sequentially in the ten directions.
In each respective place, one should contemplate ten mudrā-marks;
they are red in luster and like lightning, serving as the cause for protecting the city. (89–9)

One should meditate upon the two couples—He who is dear to the Cause mounted on an elephant and He mounted on a bull—and by means of this visualization, one should bring the Pīṭha-Vidyā under control. (89–90)
Pervading the ten directions, they abide in the form of a mandala according to the sequence of the subtle channels;
there are ten thousand Śiva-liṅgas in the ten directions and ten in the [central] place. (89–11)
One should contemplate the Lord of ten forms in the eastern direction, white in color, radiant and adorned with golden ornaments, surrounded by at least ten thousand attendants. (89–12)
I shall proclaim ten names; listen, O King Bhairava:
Jaṭila, Kāla, Unmatta, Krodharāja, and Sadāśiva. (89–13)
Paro, Dadhīcinātha, Suvāśī, Pramatheśvara, Yajñanātheśvara, and Ayuteśvaravallabha; || 89-14 ||
In the southeast corner, ten Śivās always shine in embodied form:
Vajradhara, Mahākāla, and Kapileśvara; || 89-15 ||
Pañcānana, Yoginātha, Gharghareśa, Pinākadhṛk, Paśupāla, Kṣemada, and Brahmanātha—these ten are remembered. (89–16)
And these lords of the ten thousand liṅgas shine forth in embodied form;
having visualized their meditation-forms, one should worship them with a stream of clarified butter. (89–17)
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the ten forms of Śiva in the south:
Vīra, Śūleśvara, Siddheśvara, and Śrīpārvatīśvara. (89–18)
Gaṇanātheśvara, Śambhu, Pracaṇḍa, Dakṣayajñahā, Kāśīpati, Paśupati, and Śiva—these are remembered as the ten [forms]. (89–19)
Ten thousand lords of the liṅgas, bearing skull-bowls and tridents,
possessing embodied forms, shine here within the center of the Śiva-maṇḍala.
One should contemplate these with devotion in the southern sacred field (kṣetra) and the seat (pīṭha);
thereafter, one should contemplate Kāmākhya, which is a Śiva-liṅga, in the southwest.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Īśāna, Vāmaneśa, Manohara, Vāmadeva, Bāṇanātha, and thereafter Raghuvīreśvara. || 89-22 ||
Kāmarājeśvara, Kāmakaleśa, and the ten Īśvaras—these manifest here, O Lord, as embodied lords of ten thousand liṅgas. (89-23)
Having reflected with supreme devotion, one should worship with bilva leaves;
everywhere there is mental worship, as well as the previously mentioned visualization of the forms.
Then, within Varuṇa, one should meditate upon the ten [deities] situated in the maṇḍala in sequence:
Aruṇeśvara, Yogendra, Kāśīrāja, and Surāntaka; || 89-25 ||
Triśūlī, Varuṇeśa, the one named Kāla who grants desires, and Kālāgnirudra Bhadreśa—these are proclaimed as the ten Rudras. (89–26)
The ten thousand Śivaliṅgas and Īśas, endowed with all powers—these Rudras who protect the ten thousand liṅgas—are situated in the northwestern corner. (89-27)
Mahārudra is the Lord of Wind, the very soul of Rudra, possessing a fierce form;
indeed, Hanumān is the Lord of Form, the Lord of the Sun, and the Sovereign of the Earth. || 89-28 ||
Vāsukīvallabha, Satyapati—these are the great lords (maheśvaras), excellent and accompanied by their retinues, who are beloved by Mahārudra and the others. || 89-29 ||
These are to be worshipped and meditated upon for the sake of attaining the fruits of one's desires;
and further to the north, facing north, is the Lord Kubereśvara.
Pañcādhāra, Pārameśa, Parahaṃsaprabhākara, Ananteśa, Kāyarakṣa, Ratneśvara, and Umāpati. (89–31)
These eleven Rudras are eternal lords of ten thousand hosts;
they are to be worshipped and meditated upon according to the previously described visualization of their forms.
Then, O Supreme Lord, one should meditate upon the lords in the northeast:
Īśa, Vaiśvānareśa, and likewise Viśvāmitreśvara. (89-33)
Īśāna, Māyeśa, Baṭukeśa, Rameśvara, Kālāntakeśa, Kāmākhya, and Mahākāmapurīśvara. || 89-34 ||
The Lord of the gods dwelling in the cremation ground, the illuminator of all forms—these eleven Rudras reside in the sacred seat of Kāma. (89-35)
The lords of the Liṅgas of Ayutānanda, when contemplated and worshipped, [reside] there;
and in the central seat (pīṭha) of Vārāṇasī, there are thirteen Śiveśvaras. (89-36)
Having meditated upon [him] in the center of the lower mandala, one should worship him:
Mṛtyuñjaya, Mokṣada, Śiveśa, and Bhairaveśvara. (89-37)
Lord of beings, creator of beings, protector of the field, the supreme and the non-supreme;
Lord of Mañjughoṣa, tamer of time, Lord of Kauśala. || 89-38 ||
The Lord of Sages, Varṇamālin, and the Rudras in the form of Bhairavas—
these thirteen lords of the gods are of the nature of Śiva-bliss.
The lords of the Liṅgas at Ayutānanda, being worshipped by gods and demons, bestow boons and fearlessness, and reveal the five principles (pañcatattva). || 89-40 ||
And at Vārāṇasī and Ūrdhvapīṭha, one who seeks supreme bliss should worship the thirteen Śivas with a steady mind after having meditated upon them. (89–41)
Brahmeśa, Brahmakuleśa, Brahmaliṅga, Vidhīśvara, Brahmāṇḍabhedaka, Ātmārāma, and likewise Vakreśvara. || 89-42 ||
Balīśa, Bhārgaveśa, Sadānandeśvara, Hara, Kṛṣṇeśvara, and Rāmanātha are remembered as the thirteen Rudras. (89-43)
The lords of the Liṅgas, the Ayutānandas, are proclaimed as the Bhairavendra-s;
these Mahākālas, the Rudras who are the lords of the three worlds, are to be worshipped. (89-44)
Kapālīśa and the others, whose minds are stainless, consist of knowledge and the objects of knowledge;
they are enriched by the splendor of all ornaments and adorned with jeweled earrings. (89.45)
These are the performers of creation and destruction, appointed for the work of the gods;
having formed their visualization, one should worship them with the flowers of the mind. (89-46)
Then one attains perfection; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvara!
These are the untimely stars (Akālatārakas), which bestow the abundance of all perfections.
These Kulapaṇḍitas, who bring delight to Ānandabhairava, are Rudras who worship the Mahāvidyās endowed with auspicious marks. 89-48.
I shall proclaim their names; listen in order, O Bhairava.
Drāṃ and Drīṃ are the ten Mahāvidyās that illuminate the five principles.
O Lord, they bestow all accomplishments and worship [you] upon the surface of the earth;
in the Satya, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages, they grant the full fruit [of their practice]. (89–50)
I shall declare their names, for each of them has been worshipped by Rudra:
the goddess Tripurasundarī, as well as Tripurabhairavī.
Bhuvaneśī, Annapūrṇā, Mātaṅgī, Vindhyavāsinī, Chinnamastā, Bagalā, and likewise Trikūṭā as the fifth. (89–52)
The wise one must certainly perform the external worship and other rites as prescribed in the Tantras for the goddess Kālikā Tāriṇī, who is worshipped by the Lord of Kāśī. 89-53.
By means of the sequence of the Kula worship, the practitioner attains accomplishment;
he attains the perfection of yoga within a mere month—of this there is no doubt.
At the time of piercing the lotus of the eyebrows, one must certainly perform worship. || 89-55 ||

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Inner Worship of the Lord of the Vārāṇasī Pīṭha," within the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava, in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*Siddhamantraprakaraṇa*), in the *Mahātantroddīpana* of the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*. 89.
Now begins the ninetieth chapter.
The venerable Ānandabhairavī said:
"Listen, my beloved, I shall explain the fivefold maṇḍala of Hākinī."
In the central seat of Vārāṇasī, one should contemplate a five-cornered [mandala]. || 90-1 ||
There, one should contemplate the five seats of the goddess Śrī Hākinī;
within those five seats are the five deities, adorned with a garland of jewels. (90–2)
One should visualize a five-cornered [mandala], enriched by all the worlds and surrounded by millions of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, yakṣas, and dānavas. (90–3)
In the five corners is the fivefold seat, which grants desires and bestows the siddhi of the serpent;
it grants the siddhi of nirvāṇa, O God—what else shall I tell you? (90-4)
In the five corners are the five principles (pañcatattva) and their respective five seed-syllables;
in the eastern corner is the seed-syllable of Indra, and that of Earth is in a triangle.
To its south is the seed-syllable of Vāyu and the maṇḍala of the power of Vāyu;
it possesses the fierce speed of wind and is known as the shatterer of the earth. (90.6)
Below that, upon the pedestal of the house, which is radiant with a triangular mandala,
is the seed-syllable of water known as Vāruṇa, situated on a seat of all kinds of jewels.
It is cool and multiform, the destroyer of the winds of the three worlds;
it is the fiery form at the very bottom, the seed-syllable of fire, possessed of great splendor.
Always possessing that form, surrounded by garlands of splendor, most fierce, devouring all, and the destroyer of the defects of water. || 90-9 ||
Space is called the remainder of all things; it is the meeting place of the great dissolution.
It is the wheel that is the support of the *kumbhaka* breath, having the form of the seed-syllable of space. (90–10)
The stainless abode of dissolution for all bestows the accomplishment of reality;
it is the five seats of Hākinī, and within that are the five vital breaths. (90–91)
The vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—manifest here in embodied form through the destruction of death for the worlds. (90-12)
In these wind-pits (vāyukuṇḍa), one should worship the five winds:
Prāṇeśī resides in the breath, Apānā in the anus, and Samāneśī within the body. (90–13)
The mistress of udāna, the mother of vyāna, and those belonging to vāyu—these five are honored.
O Lord of the Kula, he who practices the yoga of the five vital breaths [attains success]. (90.14)
The practitioner of excellent yoga should daily offer the five elements to Vāyu:
pure liquor, pure meat, pure fish, and likewise the other two.
One should likewise offer a pure mudrā and pure sandalwood from one's own lineage;
he who bestows the five principles (pañcatattva) does so for the sake of binding himself to the accomplishment of the lineage.
Hākinī, the supreme, should come; one should satisfy her with the highest [offerings].
Now listen to the Vidyā of the wheel of the central seat (pīṭha) within Vārāṇasī. || 90-17 ||
The maṇḍala of Vārāṇasī is triangular and has sixteen petals;
there are two filaments, each established upon every petal. (90.18)
Above that are three quadrangles and four gates;
this is the Cakra of Vārāṇasī, which bestows the perfect accomplishment of all desires.

Within the triangle in the center of the Vārāṇasī-cakra, the wise man should [meditate upon] the five-pointed [star], which removes the miseries arising from the qualities of phenomenal existence. (90.20)
What on earth cannot be accomplished by meditating upon the interior of the triangle?
He who meditates incessantly upon this revealed wheel [attains all]. (90–21)
He attains the state of accomplishment in mental yoga; of this there is no doubt.
At the time of accomplishing mental yoga, he should always reflect with certainty. (90.22)
In the five corners are the five principles (pañcatattva), and at the seat of Kāśī are the wearers of the linga; assuming millions of forms, they shine here eternally.
In the center of the Hākinī-maṇḍala, within the triangular yantra of Kāśī,
resides Hākinī, who is known as the five principles (pañcatattva) and who illumines the five elements (pañcabhūta).
One should meditate upon the forms of earth, water, fire, wind, and space in succession, following the path of a clockwise rotation.
Having visualized the fifth goddess, Hākinī, one should worship her within the maṇḍala;
for by performing the internal sacrifice everywhere, one shall attain accomplishment.
Thus, situated in the center of the Vārāṇasī-cakra is the five-cornered mandala of Hākinī, adorned by the host of goddesses who are its leaders. (90.27)
Abounding in the splendor of all ornaments and resplendent with a golden garland, this wheel, whose essence is Śiva and Śakti, bestows the supreme siddhi. || 90-28 ||
That which is not to be revealed in any tantra has been disclosed here in the Rudrayāmala.
I shall now describe the hexagonal mandala of Hākinī, which pertains to Śiva and Śakti. || 90-29 ||
One should contemplate the pure sovereign wheel consisting of Śiva and Śakti, which shines continuously at the forefront of the Vārāṇasī maṇḍala. (90.30)
Above that is the region of Unmanī, and above that is the city of Bodhanī;
listen with diligence to the mandala by which one attains internal worship.
A hexagon in the center of the pericarp, and outside of that, a group of eight mandalas;
above that, a sixteen-petaled lotus joined with two filaments.
Above that, it always remains pervading the four gates;
in the center of the hexagon, however, is the Supreme Lord accompanied by Parā.
In the hexagon, the powers residing in the six cakras always shine;
together with their lords, O Goddess of Gods, is Dākinī, who is dear to Kuṇḍalinī. (90.34)
The goddesses Rākiṇī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī,
and likewise Hākinī are to be meditated upon on the right side, situated near Śiva.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
beyond them, Paraśiva, who resides within the sphere of one's own liberation, is to be meditated upon.

Having meditated, one should worship within the wheel the supreme [deity] consisting of Śiva and Śakti, who is pervaded by the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) and has the form of a self-manifested liṅga (svayambhūliṅga). || 90-37 ||
The abode of all philosophical systems, the singer of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, beyond illusion, free from conceptual construction, self-luminous, and stainless. || 90-38 ||
Having meditated upon [the deity] situated within the hexagon, endowed with the Supreme Power (Parāśakti),
one should then pervade the eight mandalas above that by the thousands of millions.
The Yoginīs are eternally present, bestowing the accomplishment of supreme bliss;
above that, in the sixteen-spoked [wheel], they shine forth endowed with their own essential sounds.
Then, one should draw the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) in the form of light at the four gates;
by means of the sequence of the eight groups [of consonants], one should contemplate the attainment of all siddhis.
One attains the worship of accomplishment through the meditation on the form of the maṇḍala;
if one meditates upon the maṇḍala above the eyebrows of Mahākāla, O beloved. (90.42)
O Lord of the Kula, this is the truth, the absolute truth: the great siddhi is attained;
O Lord of Yogins, one shall obtain the siddhi of the Yoginīs without effort. (90.43)
Having quickly visualized this wheel, one shall attain the accomplishment of existence (*bhāvasiddhi*).
The wheel established in the accomplishment of existence bestows the perfect accomplishment of mental yoga.
One should contemplate another wheel, the Unmanī-jñāna-cakra, which bestows the accomplishment of omniscience, situated below the Śrī-bodhinī-cakra. 90-45.
One should contemplate the seed-syllable of the preta, which is nine-cornered and joined with the bindu;
it pervades that nine-cornered [mandala] as well as the three mandalas themselves. (90.46)
Outside of that is a sixteen-spoked [wheel], and outside of that are four gates;
one should meditate upon the deities on each petal and then write down the eight groups.
Having visualized the eight-cornered mandala with four gates,
one should contemplate the city of Unmanī in its center, and within that, the one whose form is the Supreme (pararūpin).
Having quickly visualized it as endowed with power, it bestows the desired accomplishment.
One should visualize the nine objects there, conjoined with their seed-syllables. (90.49)
I shall explain the meanings of those terms; listen, O Lord Bhairava:
[the elements] of earth, the line of water, that which is of the nature of fire, and that of air. (90.50)

Having written the goddess who moves through space, whose form is Time, and who is naked, as one's own power and the power of the mind, enriched with her respective seed-syllables according to the clockwise rotation, one should meditate upon her by way of the Kula path.

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Five Seats of Vārāṇasī," within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī in the *Ṣaṭcakraprakāśa*, in the section on the Accomplished Mantras (*siddhamantra-prakaraṇa*) of the *Mahātantroddīpana* in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Uttaratantra*.
